## 77

## P001: Anterior cervical hybrid constructs reduce upper adjacent segment
hypermobility compared to anterior cervical discectomy and fusion

Fenil Bhatt

1

, Lindsay Orosz

2

, Tarek Yamout

1

, Christopher Good

1

, Anthony Bucci

2

, Brandon Allen

2

, Thomas Schuler

1

, Ehsan Jazini

1

, and Colin Haines

1

1

The Virginia Spine Institute, Reston, United States

2

National Spine Health Foundation, Reston, United States

Introduction: The traditional surgical treatment for symptomatic
cervical degenerative disc disease is anterior cervical discectomy and
fusion (ACDF). Despite its effectiveness, one long-term consequence of
fusion may be an increased risk of adjacent segment degeneration resulting
in the need for additional surgery. Cervical disc arthroplasty has been
shown to preserve physiologic range of motion (ROM) and decrease the need
for adjacent segment surgery. For patients with multilevel pathology
requiring at least one level of fusion, there is growing interest in
combining anterior cervical fusion with arthroplasty to maintain as much
motion as possible with a partial motion-preserving procedure. This study
primarily aims to compare postoperative adjacent segment motion between
anterior cervical hybrid surgery (ACH) and ACDF. Secondarily, total global
(C2-7) motion, construct motion, and alignment parameters will be compared
between groups. Material and Methods: In this retrospective
cohort study at a multi-surgeon spine practice, 2- and 3-level ACH and ACDF
cases were identified between 2013 and 2021. Patients with incomplete
records, imaging, or less than 6 months of follow-up were excluded.
Demographic and radiographic data were obtained from medical and imaging
records. Motion detection in degrees was analyzed on flexion/extension views
using Cobb angles to measure lordosis at C2-C7 (global), the construct, and
upper and lower adjacent segments. Pre- and post-operative neutral lateral
x-rays were analyzed for alignment parameters: C2-C7 global lordosis,
cervical sagittal vertical axis (cSVA), and T1 slope (T1S). Differences
between ACH and ACDF cohorts were determined using independent t-tests for
continuous variables and Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables.
Results: There were 50 patients in each cohort (2-level
cases: 18 ACH, 20 ACDF) (3-level cases: 32 ACH, 30 ACDF). Hybrid patients
were overall younger in age, (51 ACH, 59 ACDF, p < 0.001) with lower CCI
scores (0.8 ACH, 1.7 ACDF, p < 0.001). Postoperatively, total ROM across
the construct was significantly greater in the ACH cohort (16.3° ACH, 4.7°
ACDF, p < 0.001) as was total global ROM (38.0° ACH, 28.0°, p <
0.001). The degrees of motion that decreased at the level of the construct
(postoperative minus preoperative construct motion) were significantly less
in the ACH cohort (-10.0° ACH, -18.1° ACDF, p < 0.001). Postoperatively,
the degrees of motion at the upper adjacent segment were significantly
increased compared to preoperatively in the ACDF cohort (-1.3° ACH, 1.6°
ACDF, p < 0.005). Conclusion: In this study, 2- and 3-level
ACH constructs partially preserved motion across the operative levels
compared to ACDF constructs. As a result, postoperative total global ROM was
better in the ACH cohort and postoperative upper adjacent segment
hypermobility was seen only in the ACDF cohort. This supports the
consideration of combining fusion with arthroplasty in patients with
multilevel cervical pathology that require at least 1 level of fusion.

## 423

## P002: To accomplish laminoplasty cross tightening and C3 laminectomy for
laminoplasty

Takahiro Iizuka

1

, Tokuji Kashiro

1

, Tetsuro Takai

1

, and Hiroshige Debata

1

1

Kouseikai Takai Hospital, Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Nara,
Japan

Introduction: Neck pain following cervical laminoplasty and loss
of kinematic ROM are still the major concerns as well as neurological
recovery. We reported Cross Tightening for laminoplasty at Global Spine
Congress 2023 in Las Vegas. This procedure dramatically reduces
postoperative neck pain. Considering ROM of cervical motion, kinematic ROM
is limited by laminoplasty because enlarged lamina may interrupt the
cervical extension. From a kinematic point of view, the upper cervical spine
C0-1-2 is more flexible in extension and flexion of the cervical spine. We
arranged the procedure for the next step to make it a cutting-edge method
for cervical laminoplasty. We combined Cross Tightening and C3 laminectomy
for postoperative axial neck pain and also postoperative neck motion
preservation. We report the preliminary results of cervical laminoplasty
with Cross Tightening and C3 laminectomy regarding axial pain and
kinematical ROM after surgery. Aim: We aimed to report the
results of Cross Tightening and C3 laminectomy (combined laminoplasty)
regarding postoperative neck pain (axial pain) and kinematic ROM of the
cervical spine. Materials and Methods: We introduce the
preliminary results of 5 patients who had Cross Tightening and C3
laminectomy compared with 21 patients who had C3-7 laminoplasty with Cross
Tightening. Techniques of Cross Tightening Muscle and C3 laminectomy. 1.
Patients positioned in the prone position with Mayfield. 2. Skin incision
was made in the midline over C2-Th1. 3. Multifidus Muscles attached to C2
were ligated with 5 Ethbond before detaching. 4. Multifidus Muscles attached
to C7 were also ligated with 5 Ethbond before detaching. 5. Laminoplasty
C4-7 and C3 laminectomy was performed with the left side open using spacers
Camber from NuVasive. 6. Muscles were reconstructed in anatomical direction
tightening to the opposite fascia. We evaluated the cervical vertebral
alignment (C1-Th1) for each patient and neck pain (VAS) and ROM on lateral
X-rays at 12 weeks after surgery. Results: Laminoplasty with C3
laminectomy improved ROM of the cervical spine compared with C3-7
laminoplasty. Neck Pain was also significantly reduced at 12 weeks after
surgery in all of them. Conclusion: CSM often requires C3 to C7
laminoplasty, but post-operative neck pain is the major concern though many
reports suggest us the preservation of C7 muscle structures. In preparing
laminoplasty we require the removal of muscle attachment from the laminae.
We often observe Multifidus Muscles attached to spinous processes are
shortened as if they were gum bands. Besides C2 and C7 have a larger spinous
process which seems to have a major role in cervical motion. Enlargement of
the laminae would interrupt the extension motion. We focused on muscle
function restoration to reduce postoperative neck pain and ROM. We report
the preliminary restoration methods for cervical motor function with Cross
Tightening Multifidus Muscles. This procedure which is combined with Cross
Tightening and C3 laminectomy may restore the muscular function in cervical
motion in the normal anatomical direction and may be superior to the
conventional procedure in terms of postoperative neck pain and ROM.

## 566

## P003: Comparison of relative value units per operative time between
anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) vs cervical disc replacement
(CDR)

Amanda Faust

1

, Don Moore

1

, and Mathew Resnick

1

1

Missouri Orthopedic Institute, Orthopedic Surgery, Columbia, United
States

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) has
been the gold standard for surgical treatment of cervical radiculopathy for
many years. Recently however, cervical disc replacement (CDR) has become an
alternative to treat cervical radiculopathy and myelopathy. Data supports
favorable outcomes for both myelopathy and non-myelopathy use of disc
arthroplasty (Samuel). It is important to assess and contrast all aspects of
the two procedures to compare their strengths and weaknesses and assist
surgeons in procedure selection. Material and Methods:
Retrospective study including patients treated at the University of Missouri
Hospital and the Missouri Orthopaedic Institute from 2019-2022. Patients
will be identified via CPT codes used for 1-level ACDF and CDR and data will
be extracted via chart review. Results: The total patient
cohort consisted of 361 patients. 124 patients met inclusion criteria, but
of these patients only 33 underwent a CDR. Due to the relatively smaller CDR
patient population, data analysis was collected on the most recent 33 ACDF
operations to keep the two groups of comparable size. The mean RVU per hour
for ACDF was 24.21 (p < 0.001) while the mean RVU per hour for CDR was
14.83 (p < 0.001). Patients who had a pre-op diagnosis of myelopathy
and/or stenosis were more likely to receive an ACDF than a CDR. Older age,
hypertension, and an ASA score of greater than 3 were more common in the
ACDF group. Pre-operatively ACDF patients had higher PROMIS Pain Intensity
scores (67.59 vs. 62.55 p < 0.03) as well as higher Neck Disability Index
(NDI) scores (47.43 for ACDF vs. 34.33 for CDR p < 0.01). Post-op length
of stay was significantly longer for patients who underwent an ACDF than
those in the CDR group (0.89 vs. 0.49 days p < 0.05). Post-operatively
ACDF patients had higher NDI scores within the 6-12 week follow up window
than patients who underwent CDR (27.75 vs 16.15 p < 0.03). There were not
significant differences in NDI scores between the two groups within the 6-12
month follow up period. Conclusion: ACDF was associated with
significantly higher RVUs per minute compared to CDR. The difference in
pre-operative pain and disability scores shows that patients with more
severe symptoms are more likely to undergo an ACDF than a CDR. Despite the
difference in patient population, patients in both groups had similar
6-12-month NDI and PROMIS scores post-operatively. These findings highlight
the importance of considering physician reimbursement and patient reported
outcomes in selecting surgical treatment options for patients with cervical
spinal problems.

## 1101

## P004: Wear-related osteolysis after implantation of the M6-C artificial
cervical disc: first longterm follow-up results

Sonja Häckel

1,2,3

, Jessica Gaff

2

, Andrew Miles

2,4

, Paul Taylor

2,4

, Michael Kern

2,4

, and Gregory Cunningham

1,2,4

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Fiona Stanley Hospital, Murdoch,
Australia

2

NeuroSpine Institute, Murdoch, Australia

3

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Inselspital,
Bern University Hospital, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland

4

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, St John of God Hospital, Murdoch,
Australia

Introduction: The M6-C™ artificial cervical disc (Orthofix,
Lewisville, Texas) is a routinely used cervical total disc replacement
(CTDR) implant. In June 2020 Australian Therapeutic and Goods Administration
published an implant hazard report because the Instructions for Use
contained insufficient information regarding the potential consequences of
peri-prosthetic osteolysis associated with the use of the M6-CTM. In a
recent study, it was reported that after mid-term follow-up, 34% of patients
implanted with the M6-C™ required revision surgery for wear-related
osteolysis with an average of 5.5 years postop. However, their study did not
report on the incidence and grade of osteolysis, as well as indication for
revision surgery. Methods: We retrospectively analysed the
radiographic and clinical outcomes (EuroQuol-5D, Neck Disability Index,
Visual analogue scale for neck and arm pain) of data collected during
long-term follow-up of patients who underwent CTDR with the
M6-CTM implant at a multi-centre between 2011 and 2015. All
patients were followed up with radiographic imaging (conventional X-ray, CT
scan) of the cervical spine to detect osteolysis. Clinical outcome was
determined by collecting patient-related questionnaires (EuroQuol-5D, Neck
Disability Index, Visual analogue scale for neck and arm pain). Ethical
approval was obtained from the local Institutional Review Board.
Results: A total of 86 patients underwent CTDR with the
M6-C™. Follow-up was completed in 40 patients with a mean age of 44 years
(53% women). The mean follow-up time was 8.6 years (7.5-11 years). Prior to
our follow-up, only 4 patients (10 %) had revision surgery, but not due to
osteolysis. Radiographs showed abnormal findings in 33/40 patients (83 %):
17/40 patients (40 %) had osteolysis. Three patients had mild, 8 patients
had moderate, and 5 patients had severe osteolysis. In addition, 16/40
patients (40 %) had various degrees of heterotopic ossification which led to
a fused and immobile disc in 13 of these patients. There was no significant
correlation between osteolysis and clinical outcome.
Conclusion: In our cohort, we see a lower reoperation rate
of the M6-C™ implant compared to the literature. However, osteolysis can be
asymptomatic. Additional revision surgeries might have to be done after
imaging and clinical follow-up will be completed. Our study has some
limitations. The study design is retrospective, and we do not have a control
group. Furthermore, 20% of patients refused to follow up which is a
potential bias. The long-term radiographic follow-up results of the M6-C™ in
this cohort are not favourable. Patients with this implant should undergo
interval monitoring for major osteolysis or implant failure.

## 1257

## P005: The position of the cervical prosthesis in hybrid surgery for
two-level cervical degenerative disc disease and its effect on cervical
range of motion

Matjaz Vorsic

1

, Rok Koncnik

1

, and Valentin Rokavec

1

1

Neurosurgery, University Hospital Maribor, Maribor,
Slovenia

Background: There are no clear indications at which level the
cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) should be performed in the Hybrid surgery
(HS), involving the combination of ACDF and CDA. Retrospective analysis
comparing the clinical and radiographic results in the treatment of
two-level cervical degenerative disease was performed comparing the patients
who underwent the HS and had the artificial disc implanted at different
levels. Materials and Methods: After applying the inclusion
criteria, 34 patients with two-level cervical degenerative disc disease
where conservative treatment failed were included in the study. All the
patients had been operated with the hybrid procedure. The CDAs in 18
patients were implanted above and in 16 patients bellow the ACDF level.
Clinical outcomes were assessed before and at regular intervals until one
year after the procedure using neurological examination, the Neck Disability
Index (NDI) and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for neck and arm pain, with 15%
improvement in NDI and 20% in VAS defined as a clinically significant. The
cervical range of motion was evaluated using flexion-extension parameters.
Results: The groups were similar at baseline both
clinically and statistically. Both groups had a statistically significant
improvement in NDI and VAS for neck and arm pain (p > .05) and there was
no statistically significant difference between groups at any point of
investigation. There was no statistically significant difference in the
C2-C7 ROM between the two groups at 12 and 24 months postoperatively (p >
.05). The location of the arthroplasty at the level C5/6 or C4/5 provided
better ROM compared to the level C6/7. Conclusions: Both groups
resulted in significant pain reduction and functional outcome for the
patients in short and long term period. The combination of fusion and
arthroplasty can be adjusted to each level allowing segmental motion
preservation at the affected levels and minimizing hypermobility at adjacent
levels. The ROM was more affected by the level of the artificial disc
implantation than relationship of the CDA towards ACDF.

## 1288

## P006: Static finite element method analysis of 3D printed compressible
non-articulating cervical disc prosthesis

Samuel Brehm

1

, Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Hau-Ju Ting

2

, Aspen Chadderdon

2

, Aneesh Syal,

2

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Abby Carey-Ewend

1

, Matthew De la Paz

1

, Ahmed Hanafy

1

, Julio Jauregui

3

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, and Camilo Molina

1

1

Neurosurgery

2

Biomedical Engineering

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis,
United States

Introduction: Non-articulating disc prothesis were created to
mimic the compressive and flexural stiffness of natural discs. These discs
are designed with two metallic endplates with a homogeneous elastic core or
a mobile central core with peripheral fibers. However, these
non-articulating discs have a variety of issues including an unstable center
of rotation, friction of fibers on endplates, endplate to elastomeric core
binding failure, and anteroposterior shift of one endplate relative to the
other. In order to solve some of these problems, we designed a unibody, all
metal, compressible, non-articulating cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA). We
quantified the theoretical elastic stiffness of the design in compression,
flexion-extension bending, lateral bending, and axial rotation and compared
the numbers to that of natural cervical discs. A prototype was also produced
to check manufacturability. Material and Methods: We ran finite
element analysis (FEA) using Fusion 360 for the novel disc prosthesis in
compression, lateral bending, and axial rotation. In all simulations the
material choice was Ti-6Al-4V the inferior endplate was rigidly fixed, and
the superior endplate had the external force/moment distributed evenly over
its superior surface. For compression, lateral bending, and axial rotation
the applied force/moment was 1 N, 1 Nm, and 1 Nm respectively. Stiffness was
calculated by dividing the resultant displacements by the applied
force/moment. The prototype of the novel disc prothesis was 3D printed out
of Ti-6Al-4V alloy by a direct metal laser sintering service.
Manufacturability was assessed by gross examination of the geometry of the
delivered prototype. Results: The artificial disc and natural
cervical discs have a compressive stiffness of 513 N/mm and 492 N/mm
respectively (4.4% error). Due to symmetry, the artificial disc had equal
flexion-extension and lateral bending stiffnesses. The artificial disc and
natural cervical discs have a lateral bending stiffness of 0.12 Nm/deg and
0.9 Nm/deg respectively (87% error). The artificial disc and natural
cervical discs have a axial rotation stiffness of 5 Nm/deg and 0.8 Nm/deg
respectively (525% error). The gross examination of the printed prototype
revealed correct geometrical features with no missing or additional
features. Additionally, the prototype length, width, and height were all
within 0.5 mm error. Conclusion: The novel device produced
overall similar mechanics to natural discs in terms of elastic stiffness.
The disc was the worst at matching axial stiffness rotation, which would
mean loss of axial rotation range of motion when implanted. The gross
examination of the prototype showed that the device was manufacturable and
had no feature size errors or overhang errors common to 3D prints. The 3D
printable nature of the device means it has the potential to be easily
individualized to each patient. This is good because optimizing disc height
would minimize over or under distraction and optimizing endplate convexity
and size would minimize bone preparation and lower heterotopic ossification.
The next steps would be static and dynamic mechanical testing of the
prototype as a further proof of concept.

## 2020

## P007: How does the type of multilevel anterior cervical constructs
influence cervical sagittal parameters and adjacent disk measurements? A
retrospective analysis

Diogo Morgado

1

, João Paulo Andrade

1

, and Mário Vale Campos

1

1

Neurosurgery, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisbon,
Portugal

Introduction: Cervical sagittal parameters are related with
clinical outcomes after multilevel anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
However, there is no comparison of these parameters after fusion (cage or
cage plus plate), total disc replacement (TDR) or hybrid constructs. The aim
of this work was to assess the impact of the type of multilevel anterior
cervical constructs in the cervical sagittal parameters and adjacent levels.
Material and Methods: The authors performed a retrospective
analysis of all the multilevel (more than one) anterior cervical spine
surgeries performed between 2015 and 2021 due to degenerative disease.
Cervical sagittal parameters included: superior and inferior level disk
height and angle, cervical lordosis using the Jackson physiological stress
line method, C2-C7 Sagittal Vertical Axis (SVA), Thoracic Inlet Angle (TIA),
neck tilt, T1 Slope and cervical tilt. Then a delta of the pre- and
postoperative of the superior and inferior disk height and angle, and
cervical lordosis was performed. Clinical data was evaluated by
IBM® SPSS Statistics (version 27.0). Quantitative data was
first tested for its normality and homogeneity of variance and according to
different situations, they were tested by Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U
test. Qualitative data was tested by Chi-square test. p value < 0.05 was
considered statistically significant. Results: There were 140
patients analysed with a mean age of 57.7 (± 11.6). From these 54.3% were
female and 36.5% were smokers. Myelopathy was present in 52.7% and
radiculopathy in 63%. Longer constructs were associated with myelopathy (p
< 0.05). In 83.6% a 2-level construct was performed, in 15.7% a 3-level
and in 0.7% a 4-level. In 81.4% fusion was performed, in 5.7% a TDR and in
12.9% a hybrid construct. Operative complications were described in three
cases (all fusion) and four patients underwent second surgery (three after
fusion procedures and one after TDR). The following values are organized
respectively according to the sequence - cage, cage plus plate, TDR and
hybrid construct. The mean superior level disc height delta was 0.64, 0.18,
0.74, and 0.08, the mean superior level disc angle was 0.34°, 1.00°, -1.90°
and -1.13°. The mean preoperative cervical lordosis was 9.52°, 13.48°, 7.42°
and 7.74°. The mean cervical lordosis delta was 4.84°, 4.06°, 7.02° and
6.98°. The mean TIA was 79.21°, 81.98°, 81.68° and 73.86°. The correlation
between the mean preoperative cervical lordosis and the mean TIA was
statistically significant (p < 0.01). Conclusion: There was
no significant difference in the type of construct and the rate of
reoperation or complications, rendering them all equally safe. There was a
significant association between the TIA and pre-operative cervical lordosis,
providing support that there’s a compensating increase in cervical lordosis
with higher TIA. While the TIA was lower in hybrid constructs, both these
and TDR were associated with a greater increase in cervical lordosis.
Further studies, namely prospective randomized studies are needed to
evaluate the impact of TDR and hybrid constructs in cervical sagittal
parameters and adjacent segment disease.

## P008: Efficacy and safety of the ultrasound bone scalpel in lumbar
laminectomies

Anthony Steinle

1

, Jeffrey Chen

1

, Alexander O'Brien

1

, Wilson Vaughan

1

, Andrew Croft

1

, William Waddell

1

, Justin Vickery

1

, Robert Elrod

1

, Hani Chanbour

2

, Julian Lugo-Pico

1

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,2

, Amir Abtahi

1,2,3

, and Byron Stephens

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Department of Neurological Surgery

3

Center for Musculoskeletal Research, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Lumbar laminectomy is commonly performed to
address complaints of neurogenic claudication or radicular leg pain. Despite
recent advances in applied instruments and surgical techniques, the
incidence of inadvertent dural injuries caused by traditional laminectomy
techniques is still considerable. The ultrasonic bone scalpel (UBS) uses
high-frequency oscillation to create localized tissue disruption and
preferentially cut through hard surfaces such as bone. It has been shown to
improve speed and reduce intraoperative complications in laminectomies for
cervical and thoracic spondylotic myelopathy when compared to traditional
methods using a high-speed burr, punch forceps, rongeurs, etc. We sought to
evaluate whether the use of the UBS in lumbar laminectomies would result in
equivalent safety, efficacy, and PROs compared to traditional methods. We
hypothesize that using the UBS will demonstrate equivalent safety, efficacy
and PROs while decreasing rates of durotomies compared to traditional
methods. Material and Methods: Data from a prospectively
collected, single-institution registry was queried between 01/01/2019 -
09/01/2021 for patients with a primary diagnosis of lumbar stenosis who
underwent an isolated laminectomy, laminectomy and fusion, or laminectomy
and fusion with an interbody. Two patient groups included: laminectomies
using traditional methods vs UBS method. Outcomes included 3-month values
for all PROMIS subdomains, NRS pain scores, ODI percentage, and PHQ-9
scores, as well as complications, reoperations, or readmissions within 3
months. Patients who received a lumbar laminectomy by traditional methods
were propensity matched against patients who received a lumbar laminectomy
by the UBS in 2:1 fashion. Covariates selected for matching included age,
operation type, and number of levels. A variety of statistical tests were
used to compare groups. Results: 231 patients who received a
laminectomy with traditional methods were propensity matched against 32
patients treated with the ultrasound bone scalpel, resulting in 64
“traditional group” patients and 32 “UBS group” patients. Analysis found no
differences between groups for demographic and baseline measures except for
race and ethnicity. There were no differences between groups at 3 months for
all PROMIS subdomain scores, NRS back/leg pain scores, %ODI or PHQ-9.
Additionally, there were no significant differences for any PROs at 12
months. There was a significant difference in rates of durotomies between
the traditional and UBS groups (12.5% vs 0.0%, p = 0.049). Among those
experiencing intraoperative durotomy, 16.67% required re-operation. There
were no significant differences between groups in any other complication
rate as well as reoperation and readmission rates. Conclusion:
Laminectomies are commonly performed on the lumbar spine to remedy a variety
of spine pathologies, with the most common complication being an iatrogenic
durotomy. We sought to compare outcomes between patients who received a
lumbar laminectomy through traditional methods versus the UBS. Our results
suggest the UBS helps decrease the rate of injury to the dura, thus reducing
the incidence of durotomies. We believe this data provides valuable
information to surgeons and patients about the safety and efficacy of the
UBS in lumbar laminectomies. Further studies should investigate if the UBS
decreases operative time for lumbar laminectomies compared to traditional
methods.

## 656

## P009: Patterns of opioid use prior to single-level lumbar fusion are
associated with postoperative opioid use and adverse events

Jayme Koltsov

1

, Tanmaya Sambare

2

, John Kleimeyer

1

, Eugene Carragee

1

, Kirkham Wood

1

, Todd Alamin

1

, and Serena Hu

1

1
Orthopaedic Surgery, Stanford University
School of Medicine, Palo Alto, United States

2
Orthopaedic Surgery, Harbor-UCLA Medical
Center, West Carson, United States
Introduction: Opioid pain medication use is common among lumbar
spine surgery patients and has been related to increased rates of chronic
dependence, poorer surgical outcomes, and increased surgical costs. We
hypothesize that it is possible to identify phenotypes of patients based on
their patterns of pain medication use preoperatively, and that these
phenotypes will relate to postoperative opioid use, complications, discharge
disposition, length of stay, costs and healthcare resource utilization.
Materials and Methods: Adult patients undergoing primary
single level lumbar fusion with a diagnosis of stenosis were identified from
the IBM® Marketscan® databases (2007-2015). Patients
were required to have at least 1 year of continuous health plan enrollment
pre and postoperatively in a plan providing outpatient pharmacy data. Group
based trajectory modeling was used to identify distinct patient phenotypes
based on their preoperative patterns of opioid usage. Multivariable logistic
regression was used to assess relationships between these phenotypes and
postoperative outcomes after adjusting for patient and surgical factors.
Results: The final analysis comprised 9,464 patients (age
58 ± 12 years, 58.6% female). 60% of patients used opioids within the 3
months preceding their fusion procedure. 5 distinct phenotypes of
preoperative opioid use were identified: A 
high
 dose phenotype (17.1% of patients), using on average 60 morphine
milligram equivalents (MME) per day 1 year prior to surgery and increasing
linearly to > 80 MME per day preoperatively; a 
medium
 dose phenotype (16.4%), using 10 MME per day 1 year prior to
surgery and increasing linearly to 25 MME per day preoperatively, a
phenotype with no use 1 year prior to surgery who began using increasing
amounts of opioids ∼6 months preoperatively, increasing to > 30 MME per
day (
steep 6m rise
 phenotype, 11.6%); a phenotype with very low opioid use 1 year
preoperatively (likely those taking intermittently only as needed) who began
increasing 3 months prior to surgery, reaching 15 MME per day (
intermittent to 3m
 phenotype, 19.8%); and a group using no opioids until 3 months
prior to surgery, who began increasing 3 months prior to surgery, reaching
15 MME per day (
naïve to 3m
 phenotype, 35.0%). These phenotypes were related in a
dose-response manner (based on duration and maximum preoperative dosage) to
postoperative opioid use at 3m, 6m, 1yr, and 2 years, and complications and
all-cause readmissions within 90-days (p < 0.001 for all). For example,
patients in the intermittent to 3m phenotype had 8.3 (4.7,
14.6) times the odds for opioid use 3m postoperatively, those in the
medium phenotype had 16.7 (7.4, 38.1) times the odds
for use 3m postoperatively, and those in the high phenotype
had 90.7 (12.6, 653.1) times the odds for opioid use 3 months
postoperatively relative to patients not taking opioids prior to surgery (p
< 0.001 for each). Interestingly, patients in the naïve to
3m phenotype did not have increased odds for opioid use at 3m
postoperatively relative to those who did not use opioids preoperatively.
Conclusion: Distinct phenotypes of preoperative opioid use
can be identified and are associated with postoperative opioid use,
complications, and readmissions. Analysis of LOS, discharge disposition,
costs and HCRU are ongoing.

## 1379

## P010: Spondylolysis with vertebral listhesis: choice of the surgical
technique according to the injury degree

Carlos Mariano Nirino

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology, Hospital Santamarina, Monte Grande,
Argentina

Introduction: The aim of this paper is to describe the correct
choice of the surgical technique depending on the injury degree in diagnosis
of spondylolysis with listhesis grade 1, 2 and 3 according to Meyerding
classification and the results obtained. 31 patients were evaluated between
2010 and 2021; all operated by the Orthopedics and Traumatology department
of the Santamarina Hospital of Monte Grande in Buenos Aires, Argentina. As
service criteria for listhesis grade 1 and 2 we use the “smile” technique
due to the great postoperative reduction achieved; this consists of fixing
the lysis with total or partial reduction of the listhesis with
transpedicular screws and a subspinous bar. For grade 3, we performed a two
level arthrodesis with screws and bars because of the great risk of injury
with a great reduction and the complexity of the previous technique in this
grade. Surgical treatment was indicated in all cases for low back and/or
sciatic pain. Postoperative follow-up is 10 months to 3 years.
Materials and methods: 31 patients were evaluated. 18 men
and 13 women. All studied by Rx and CT and treated by the same surgeon. All
lysis and listhesis were at L4-L5 (11 cases) and L5-S1 (20 cases) level,
only patients with grades 1, 2 and 3 were included. Higher grades and
patients older than 45 years old were excluded from this study. Surgical
technique: Smile technique (grade 1-2): Remove the periostium of the lamina;
locate of the lysis, clean it until leaving two facing bone surfaces.
Placement of two transpedicular screws in the lytic vertebra and a “U” bar
under its spinous process. Reduction of the listhesis using an approximator
which grasps the bar under the spinous and above the tulip transpedicular
screw, upon placing in the lysis a bone graft taken from the spiny overlying
vertebra. Arthrodesis (grade 3): Posterior fixation of two levels with 4
screws and 2 bars. Arthrodesis was made by performing a decortication of the
lamina, imbrication of the spinous and using blood from the posterior
superior iliac crest pulled out through an abbocath and chipped local bone.
Results: The results were uniformly good with total or
partial remission of the symptoms, consolidation of the lysis and total or
partial reduction of listhesis in grades 1 and 2 with recovery of the
ability of flexion extension of the lumbar spine in all grades. Only in one
case we had a postoperative complication with the smile technique (listhesis
grade 2) with partial deficit of the peroneal muscles which was fully
recovered after 3 months; we attribute this to a root compression during the
reduction of the listhesis with this technique. The rest of the patients did
not present postoperative complications. Conclusions: We
consider that the correct choice of surgical technique is imperative to
obtain good results and to avoid possible injuries and secuelas. We have
used this selection of surgical techniques for years with great results; the
patients do not present postoperative complications with a good remission of
their symptoms.

## P011: Pin fracture in magnetically controlled growing rods: influence of
the year of manufacture

Martina Tognini

1

, Harry Hothi

1

, Elisabetta Dal Gal

1

, Johann Henckel

1

, Masood Shafafy

2

, Stewart Tucker

3

, Edel Broomfield

3

, John Skinner

1

, and Alister Hart

1

1

University College London, The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital
and Institute of Orthopaedics and Musculoskeletal Science, Stanmore,
United Kingdom

2

Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics, Nottingham University
Hospitals NHS Trust, Nottingham, United Kingdom

3

Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust,
London, United Kingdom

Introduction: In 2019 the manufacturer released a field safety
notice, indicating that rods manufactured prior to 26th March
2015 had a 5% risk of post-implantation pin fracture occurring. Rods made
after this date have locking pins that are thicker in diameter and of a
tougher stainless-steel alloy; the FSN indicated that these rods did not
exhibit the same fracture issue based on post-market surveillance data
available at the time. A previous retrieval study reported evidence of
locking pin fractures in 62 out of 105 (59%) and 6 out of 29 (21%) of rods
collected at their centre that had been manufactured before and after this
date, respectively. The aim of this retrieval study was to better understand
the impact of the design changes on the performance of MCGRs collected at
our retrieval centre. To achieve this, we compared the prevalence of locking
pin fractures between MAGEC rods manufactured before and after
26th March of 2015. Material and Methods: This
was a retrieval study investigating 86 MCGRs that were consecutively
received at our centre after having been removed from fifty-two patients.
The implants were explanted by 11 different surgeons across 8 different
hospitals. The implants were divided into two groups: those manufactured
before 26th March 2015 (n = 54) and those that were manufactured
on or after this date (n = 32). Clinical and implant data was collected for
all MCGRs. Retrieval analysis comprised plain radiographs evaluations, force
and elongation testing, disassembly and scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
of 5 pin surfaces. Results: The two patient groups were
statistically comparable. We found that 15 out of 31 patients belonging
implanted with rods manufactured before 26th March 2015 had a
fracture of their locking pins. 3 of the 18 (7%) patients with rods
manufactured after this date were also found to have a fractured pin. Rods
with a pin fracture had been implanted for a significantly longer period of
time than those with an intact pin (39 months versus 30.5 months). Analysis
of the fracture sites of the pins showed that all examined had failed due to
brittle fractures. Conclusion: We found that 21 out of 54
retrieved rods at our centre that had been manufactured before
26th March 2015 had a fracture of their locking pins. 3 of
the 32 rods manufactured after this date were also found to have a fractured
pin. Rods with a fractured pin had been implanted for significantly more
time than those with an intact pin (median 39 versus 32 months). Whilst the
mechanisms and risk factors for failure are multifactorial, our retrieval
evidence and clinical experience to date suggests that the use of thicker,
tougher locking pins in newer designs have had a beneficial impact on their
performance.

## P012: Blood titanium levels in patients with large and sliding titanium
implants

Martina Tognini

1

, Harry Hithi

1

, Stewart Tucker

2

, Edel Broomfield

2

, Masood Shafafy

3

, Panos Gikas

1

, Anna Di Laura

1

, Johann Henckel

1

, and Alister Hart

1

1

University College London, The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital
and Institute of Orthopaedics and Musculoskeletal Science, Stanmore,
United Kingdom

2

Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust,
London, United Kingdom

3

Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics, Nottingham University
Hospitals NHS Trust, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: Titanium, which is known to be a highly
biologically inert, is one of the most commonly used metals in orthopaedic
implants. While cobalt and chromium blood metal ion testing is routinely
used in the clinical monitoring of patients with metal-on-metal hip
implants, much less is known about the levels of titanium in patients with
other implant types. A better understanding is required about the levels of
titanium in these patients, and the potential for using blood titanium tests
as a biomarker for function, in particular those that are susceptible to
generating greater titanium particles or ions. In the current study, we
investigated these levels in three such titanium-based implant groups: (1)
MCGRs, (2) massive acetabular implants, and (3) long bone tumour implants.
The aim of this study was to better understand the normal ranges of blood
titanium levels in patients implanted with large and sliding titanium
constructs by comparison with reference levels from conventional titanium
hips. Material and Methods: This study examined data collected
from 136 patients. Over a period of 24 months, whole blood samples were
collected from 41 patients implanted with large titanium implants:
Magnetically Controlled Growing Rods (MCGRs, n = 18), long bone tumour
implants (n=13) and 3D-printed customised massive acetabular defect implants
(n = 10). Blood samples were collected during routine outpatient visit
(tumour and massive acetabular implants) or before surgery (MCGRs). Whole
blood samples were quantified for titanium content on an Element 2 high
resolution ICP-MS instrument. This data was compared with previously
established reference levels in well-functioning, conventional titanium hip
implants (n=95). Clinical, imaging and blood titanium levels data were
collected for all patients and compared statistically between the different
groups. Results: The median (range) follow-up time of the
standard hips, MCGRs, tumour implants and massive acetabular implants were
102 months (64-143), 30 months (12-57), 60 months (28-221) and 36.5 (14-200)
respectively. The median (range) of blood titanium levels of the standard
hip, MCGRs, tumour implants and massive acetabular implants were 1.2 ppb
(0.6-4.9), 9.7 ppb (4.0-25.4), 2.6 ppb (0.4-104.4) and 5.7 ppb (1.6-31.5)
respectively. Age at first implantation was significantly different between
each of the large/sliding implants groups and the titanium hips reference
group. Follow-up time differed significantly between the MCGRs vs. both the
standard hips and the long bone tumour implants, also between the massive
acetabular implants vs. the standard hips group. Both MCGRs and the massive
acetabular implants groups blood titanium levels were significantly higher
than the standard hip implants group (p < 0.001). No correlation between
follow-up time and blood titanium levels was found. Conclusion:
This study showed that larger constructs and/or the presence of sliding
mechanisms leads to increased blood titanium levels, compared to
well-functioning standard titanium unilateral hip constructs. Reassuringly,
these increased levels did not appear to induce adverse metal reactions. The
relationship between implant failure and titanium release remains unclear
and threshold levels for the different construct types should be determined,
in order to understand the role of blood titanium testing as a biomarker for
function.

## P013: Rod fracture in magnetically controlled growing rods

Martina Tognini

1

, Harry Hithi

1

, Sean Bergiers

1

, Johann Henckel

1

, Edel Broomfield

2

, Stewart Tucker

2

, and Alister Hart

1

1

University College London, The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital
and Institute of Orthopaedics and Musculoskeletal Science, Stanmore,
United Kingdom

2

Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust,
London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Magnetically Controlled Growing Rods (MCGRs) have
been shown to experience implant failure in several ways, including an
inability to distract due to corrosion or internal pin fracture issues. A
fracture of the MCGR itself is estimated occur in 10.6% of the total number
of complications however the risk factors for this are poorly understood.
The mechanisms of fracture in Magnetically Controlled Growing Rods (MCGRs)
and the risk factors associated with this are poorly understood. The aim of
this study was to identify the mechanisms of fracture of explanted fracture
MCGRs and assess the risk factors for this by 1) assessing the implant’s
state at retrieval (by means of retrieval analysis) 2) analysing the
fracture surface (fractographic analysis) and 3) using imaging analysis to
evaluate eventual patient or surgical risk factors for rod fracture, through
comparison with a control group of intact rods. Material and
Methods: From our cohort of over 120 retrieved MCGRs, we
identified seven rods that had fractured; all were single rod constructs,
retrieved from six patients. These were examined and compared with fifteen
intact single rod constructs. Clinical data (age at implantation surgery,
gender, time to removal, aetiology, and eventual prior surgeries) and
implant data (rod configuration, rod size, rod generation) were recorded for
all implants. Retrieval and fractographic analysis were used to determine
the failure mode at the fracture site and the implants functionality. Cobb
angle, degree of rod contouring and the distance between anchoring points
were computed on antero- posterior (AP) and lateral radiographs.
Results: Age at insertion surgery was higher in the
fractured rod group (5 vs 9 years old in the control and fractured groups,
respectively) without reaching statistical significance (p = 0.0954). Time
to removal was significantly lower in the fractured rods group (p = 0.0143).
Five of the fractured rods had been inserted following removal of a
previously inserted rod (Figure 4), while in the control group 3 constructs
were revisions. 5/7 vs 3/15 rods had been inserted following removal of a
previously inserted rod, in the fractured vs control groups. All fractured
rods failed due to bending fatigue. Fractured rods had greater rod
contouring angles in the frontal plane (p = 0.0407) and lateral plane (p =
0.0306), and greater distances between anchoring points in both AP and
lateral planes (p = 0.0061 and p = 0.0074 respectively).
Conclusion: This is the first study to investigate the
mechanisms of failure of explanted, fractured MCGRs and to assess eventual
risk factors. We found fatigue failure as the failure mode for all fractured
implants, with the crack initiation point in correspondence with mechanical
indentation marks on the rod, probably induced during implantation surgery.
We also found that fractured constructs, usually revisions of previous
implants, had a significantly greater distance between anchoring points and
more pronounced contouring compared to the control group. These results
suggest the use of double rod constructs when proceeding with rod exchange
if the patient’s characteristics allow it.

## P014: The performance of the latest generation of magnetically controlled
growing spine rods: a comparative retrieval study
Martina Tognini
1
, Harry Hothi
1
, Sean Bergiers
1
, Masood Shafafy
2
, Edel Broomfield
3
, Stewart Tucker
3
, Johann Henckel
1
, and Alister Hart
1

1

University College London, The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital
and Institute of Orthopaedics and Musculoskeletal Science, Stanmore,
United Kingdom

2

Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics, Nottingham University
Hospitals NHS Trust, Nottingham, United Kingdom

3

Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust,
London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Magnetically Controlled Growing Rods (MCGRs) are
distraction-based systems that use an external magnetic distraction system
aimed at avoiding repeated surgery for rod lengthening used for the
treatment of severe early-onset scoliosis. Recently, concerns regarding the
risks associated with the use of MCGRs have been raised. The latest design
iteration (MAGEC X) was recalled in 2020 following an Urgent Field Safety
Notice (FSN) describing a .5% probability of post-implantation separation of
an actuator end cap component. On 1st April 2020, a second FSN was issued by
the manufacturer, voluntarily suspending the supply of all MAGEC rods to the
UK. The Medicines & Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA, UK) on
the same day released an Medical Device Alert (MDA) advising surgeons not to
implant MAGEC rods until further notice in the UK and Republic of Ireland.
Currently, the supply of all MCGRs was temporarily suspended in the UK.
Objective of this study is to compare the performance of MAGEC X to the
earlier design iteration MAGEC 1.3, by means of retrieval analysis.
Material and Methods: Fifteen of both latest and earlier
rods were consecutively collected from five different hospitals following
removal surgery and matched by time to removal. Clinical data (age at
implantation surgery, gender, time to removal, reason for revision) and
implant data (rod generation, length size, diameter size, configuration)
were recorded for all MCGRs. Analysis comprised visual assessments of
external damage, plain radiograph evaluations, force and elongation testing,
MAGEC X end-cap torque testing and disassembly. Mann-Whitney U tests were
used to statistically compare groups. Results: Rod distraction
reached in vivo was significantly higher in the MAGEC 1.3 group (p = 0.002).
There was no statistically significant difference in the total external
damage score (p = 0.870), maximum force produced (p = 0.695) or distraction
reached during force test (p = 0.880). No pin fracture was detected.
Elongation of stroke was mildly higher (p = 0.051) for the MAGEC X group.
One MAGEC X implant had evident end cap component loosening, yet it did not
show any evident sign of internal wear or corrosion. Internal damage scores
were mildly lower in the MAGEC X group. Conclusion: This is one
of the first studies to present comparative retrieval findings of the latest
generation of MCGRs (MAGEC X). We found no evidence of pin fracture in MAGEC
X rods nor in the control group, MAGEC 1.3. There was comparatively less
evidence of internal damage in the MAGEC X designs, de- spite a variability
in the measured loosening torque of the end- cap component. One MAGEC X was
revised due to evident end-cap component loosening, however the implant was
found to be functional at mechanical testing and there was no greater sign
of internal damage at disassembly.

## P015: A novel "Yadav-Kunal" reflex for UMN lesion spasticity

Sandeep Yadav

1

and Kishor Kunal

1

1

Orthopaedics, AIIMS, Jodhpur, India

Introduction: Various reflexes have been described as
modification to Babinski sign in UMN lesion, though rarely has been a reflex
described other than these, which is independent to extensor plantar
response in some sort. Mostly these reflexes form a polysynaptic arc with a
nociceptive stimulus as afferent. Here we present a novel reflex which is
different from above in many ways- it’s response in independent of extensor
plantar response and thus cannot be classified as a modification of
Babinski’s sign and its afferent is forced motor afferent in a spastic
muscle. Material and Methods: The reflex was demonstrated
incidentally in patients suffering from UMN lesion spasticity and followed
up until loss of spasticity after surgery and was validated in patients
admitted in the centre with spastic and flaccid paraplegia.
Results: It was found that this reflex was present in
patients having spastic paraparesis and resolved once spasticity resolved.
Also, it was absent in patients suffering from flaccid paraplegia
Yadav-Kunal reflex. The reflex can be stated as, “a forced plantarflexion of
toes in spastic parparesis shall lead to sudden jerky knee flexion in the
same limb”. Conclusion: Spasticity is a stretch reflex
disorder, manifested clinically as an increase in muscle tone that becomes
more apparent with more rapid stretching movement, commonly caused by upper
motor neuron lesion. The muscle spindle of toe dorsiflexors (predominantly
by L5) gets activated when they are forcefully stretched. In this case, due
to UMN lesion above L5, these inhibitions have been dropped off and the
response is flexion of knee joint due to action of hamstrings (supplied by
L5-S2 predominantly).

## P016: Characteristics of baseline frequency data in spinal RCTs do not
suggest widespread fraud

Manon Levayer

1

, Gem Chew

2

, Kyle Sheldrick

2

, and Ashish Diwan

3,4

1

School of Biomedical Engineering, The University of Sydney,
Darlington, Australia

2

Faculty of Medicine

3

Spine Labs, University of New South Wales, Kensington,
Australia

4

Spine Service, St George Private Hospital, Koagarah,
Australia

Introduction: Fraud in clinical research is a reality. A recent
scandal identified apparent non-genuine data in a set of randomised clinical
trials investigating cognitive therapy in back pain. This has highlighted
the risk of fraud impacting the assessment of treatment effects. In this
case, fraudulent data appears to have exaggerated treatment efficacy in
recent meta-analyses. Clinical treatment of spinal conditions is guided by
such influential RCT evidence, so it is urgent to understand whether the
conclusions of other RCTs published in spine journals are genuine or
infected with fraud. We sought to investigate whether evidence of non-random
baseline data in purportedly randomized studies in spine was a widespread
problem or if the previously identified case was an anomaly. Material
and Methods: We performed a PubMed search to identify all papers
published in 4 major spine journals (Spine, The Spine Journal, the Journal
of Neurosurgery Spine, and the European Spine Journal) classified by the
journal as RCTs between 2016 and 2020. We extracted all baseline covariates
which were reported as frequencies and calculated p values using a Pearson
Chi Square test of independence. Individual variable p-values were combined
into a study wise p-value using the Stouffer method. We calculated the
proportion of studies with a study wise p-value of < 0.01, < 0.05,
> 0.95 and > 0.99. All studies with p values > 0.99 or < 0.01
were examined for possible explanations. Results: Our
literature search returned 228 studies, of which 169 were included. In
total, we extracted 938 variables. After calculating all study wise p-values
and calculating the proportions that presented a study wise p-value of <
0.01, < 0.05, > 0.95 or > 0.99. The distribution of variable wise
p-values follows the expected distribution for genuine trial data without
any signs of fraud. We observed the expected number of trials with p-values
< 0.01, < 0.05 and > 0.95. There were three more trials with a
p-value of > 0.99 than expected, however, these had either obvious
innocent explanations or had already been identified as fraudulent.
Conclusion: We conclude that the overall distribution of
frequency baseline similarities between study arms in RCTs published in
major spine journals is not suspicious. No evidence of systemic presentation
of false data was found. While research fraud is a threat requiring
vigilance, we did not find any evidence that it is common in spinal RCTs.
However, these results were derived from major spine journals and may not be
applicable to research published in non-spine journals or predatory
journals. We will examine continuous variables in future work.

## P017: Functional recovery in relation to the posttraumatic restitution of
the blood-spinal-cord-barrier after experimental spinal cord injury in the
mouse

Lea Meyer

1

, Lilly Waldmann

1

, Laurens Roolfs

1

, Nima Taheri

1

, Katharina Kersting

1

, Melina Nieminen-Kelhä

1

, Irina Kremenetskaia

1

, Adnan Ghori

1

, Andre Rex

2

, Michael Fehlings

3

, Peter Vajkoczy

1

, and Vanessa Hubertus

1

1

Neurosurgery

2

Experimental Neurology, Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin and
Berlin Institute of Health, Berlin, Germany

3

Division of Spine Surgery, Toronto Western Hospital, University
Health Network, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) is a devastating
condition that presents a major socioeconomic burden for healthcare systems.
The posttraumatic disruption of the Blood-Spinal-Cord-Barrier (BSCB) is a
leading pathophysiology in SCI and its restitution plays a crucial role in
structural spinal cord regeneration. A deeper understanding of the
pathophysiology and its timeframe will enhance the search for restorative
therapies facilitating functional regeneration. With this study we
characterize the posttraumatic BSCB disruption and restitution in relation
to functional recovery in a mouse model up to 28 days post SCI.
Material and Methods: Adult C57BL/6J mice (m/f, n = 55)
underwent mid-thoracic (Th6/7) clip-compression SCI using a modified
aneurysm clip (5g, 60s) or sham injury (two-level-laminectomy).
Perioperative antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin and postoperative pain
medication with buprenorphine was applied. Longitudinal
neurobehavioral analysis was performed (n = 23) using Catwalk® automated
gait analysis and Basso Mouse Scale with Tally sub-score at days 1, 3, 7, 14
and 28 post SCI. Additionally, in vivo imaging with 7T MRI
was performed for tissue morphology analysis. Individual specimens were
sacrificed at each time point for qualitative histological analysis
(Luxol-Fast-Blue + H&E, CD31+Evans-Blue, n = 5). BSCB disruption was
quantified by measuring Evans-Blue (EVB)–extravasation via fluorescence
microplate reader (Tecan, n = 50). Results: As the
posttraumatic disruption of the BSCB is most severe up to day 7 post SCI,
histological analysis up to this point showed vast structural damage and
edema to the spinal cord with considerable EVB-leakage, supported by MRI
findings, with an increasing restitution in the chronic phase (14d, 28d).
Quantitative assessment of EVB-extravasation displayed a significant
disruption of the BSCB up to 14 days post SCI (14d: p = 0.001), with
restitution after 28 days (p = 0.096). Neurological recovery started between
days 7 and 14 post SCI, with most specimens having regained hindlimb
function by day 28 (p = 0.552). Conclusion: Functional recovery
following SCI is associated with the restitution of the BSCB, which remains
significantly disrupted up to 14d post SCI, revealing a potential time frame
for therapy application. Further detailed examinations of the regenerative
capacities and the molecular players involved in BSCB regeneration are
necessary for the development of restorative therapies targeting the
neurovascular unit.

## P018: Posttraumatic disruption of the blood-spinal-cord-barrier is
aggravated in the acute and subacute phase by the endothelial cell-specific
knock-out of Ephrin-B2 signaling after experimental spinal cord
injury

Katharina Kersting

1

, Laurens Roolfs

1

, Lilly Waldmann

1

, Lea Meyer

1

, Melina Nieminen-Kelhä

1

, Irina Kremenetskaia

, Adnan Ghori

, and Vanessa Hubertus

Neurosurgery

2

Introduction: The disruption of the Blood-Spinal-Cord-Barrier
(BSCB) is a leading pathophysiology in traumatic Spinal Cord Injury (SCI),
and its restitution plays a crucial role in spinal cord regeneration. The
guidance molecule Ephrin-B2 promotes cell-cell-contacts in the neurovascular
unit. However, its specific role in endothelial cells following SCI is

aggravated secondary injury. Whilst no significant recovery of hindlimb
function is achieved post SCI up to 7d, analyses of longer recovery periods
are necessary to evaluate the impact on functional recovery.

vivo white light and fluorescence microscopy was possible up to
28 days postoperatively after both SCI and sham injury. Only mild
inflammation was observed in individual specimens at early timepoints (up to
7d). Specimens with an implanted spinal window chamber did not show any
differences in automated gait analysis (Catwalk®), Basso Mouse
Scale, postoperative body weight development or histologically assessed
spinal cord integrity compared with specimens which received the same
surgery without spinal window chamber implantation. Conclusion:
The implantation of a spinal window chamber after clip compression SCI in
the mouse is feasible and allows for longitudinal in vivo
imaging up to the chronic injury phase without modifying neurological
function or spinal cord integrity compared to specimens without chamber
implantation. To achieve more detailed in vivo imaging at a
greater depth, longitudinal two-photon microscopy can be integrated in the
setup.

## P020: Nanomechanical properties of native human ligamentum flavum

Jakub Jezek

1

, Jiri Skala-Rosenbaum

1

, Josef Sepitka

2

, and Vaclav Tolar

1

1

Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Third Medical Faculty of
Charles University and University Hospital Kralovske Vinohrady, Prague,
Czech Republic

2

Division of Biomechanics, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Czech
Technical University in Prague, Czech Republic

Introduction: Degenerative changes of ligamentum flavum (LF)
significantly contribute to the development of lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS),
which is a serious and relatively common disease in the aging population.
LSS often leads to disability. There is no prophylaxis of this disease in
current knowledge yet. Although it is natural to consider that the
mechanical properties of ligamentum flavum can be altered due to ligamentous
hypertrophy, only few studies have mentioned on this point. Only one study
shows significantly inferior stiffness of LF in cases with LSS. However, to
date, there are no reports describing local nanomechanical properties of
ligamentum flavum depending on anatomical localization. The aim of this
study was (1) to quantify and compare nanomechanical properties of the
insertion part with central part of LF and (2) to compare nanomechanical
properties of each ligamentum flavum regardless of spinal segment levels
(L3-4, L4-5 and L5-S1). Design of study: measurement of micromechanical
properties of degenerated and healthy human ligamentum flavum.
Materials and Methods: The study involved patients who
underwent surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis. The tissues used for analysis
of nanomechanical properties from 12 patients were sectioned into 1-2 mm
thick sections using microtome blade and glued using Epiglu on the Petri
dishes. All testing was performed submerged in 1x Phosphate buffered saline
(PBS) containing 1% (v/v) Protease Inhibitors. Quasistatic nanoindentation
of samples was performed to obtain loading curves from the cuts on the
cranial, medial, and caudal part of each ligamentum flavum.
Results: Average elastic moduli were in the range from 3
kPa up to 178 kPa. We described the local nanomechanical properties of
ligamentum flavum depending on anatomical localization. We found the
gradients of the mechanical properties across the cranial, medial, and
caudal cuts of native ligamentum flavum. Conclusion: This study
showed that: (1) medial part of ligamentum is significantly stiffer than
cranial and caudal, (2) central region of cranial, medial, and caudal cut is
significantly stiffer than outer region.
Acknowledgment: This work has been supported by the Czech Health
Research Council [Project number NU21-06-00356].

## P021: Comparison of bone density between traditional pedicle screw,
cortical bone screw and modified cortical bone screw tract of lumbar
spine

Dipak Shrestha

1

, Bikash Parajuli

1

, Sabik Kayastha

1

, and Suman Lamichhane

1

1

Orthopedics, Dhulikhel Hospital, Kathmandu University Hospital,
KUSMS, Dhulikhel, Nepal

Introduction: Cortical bone trajectory (CBT) has better pullout
strength, insertional torque, and toggle test performance. However,
divergent oblique caudo-cranial trajectory and shorter screws are limiting
factors. The Dhulikhel Hospital modification in CBT (CBT-DH) has been
proposed with straight caudo-cranial trajectory without divergence which
allows longer screw placement with technical ease. The aim of this study is
to compare bone density of CBT, CBT-DH, and traditional pedicle screw (TPS)
tract of lumbar vertebrae by using CT Hounsfield Unit (HU) as surrogate
marker of bone density. Material and Methods: Abdomen CT scan
with non-spinal pathologies of 200 patients (1000 lumbar vertebrae) were
selected (Male :112 and Female: 88). Axial slices of each lumbar vertebra
(L1 to L5) were cut into three planes representing TPS (parallel to the
pedicle in sagittal section), CBT (caudo-cranial plane parallel to inferior
pedicle boarder targeting midpoint of superior endplate) and CBT-DH
(caudo-cranial plane along the inferior pedicle boarder targeting
anterio-superior margin of vertebral body) representing tract for the
pedicle screw in each technique. For each trajectory, CT HU at four points,
namely near cortex, mid pedicle, mid-body, and far cortex was measured.
Inter and Intra observer variation was analyzed in 40 vertebrae separately.
Results: The mean age of the patients was 40.4 ± 13 years.
The difference of mean value of CT HU of TPT, CBT-DH and CBT were 354.2 ±
70, 457.3 ± 90, and 529.9 ± 75 respectively were statistically significant
(p < 0.05). The difference was highly significant for near cortex. The CT
HU value of the near cortex in CBT-DH was 65.6% higher compared to TPS but
14.9% lesser compared to CBT. The difference in density between CBT-DH (305
HU) and CBT (302 HU) in mid pedicle was not significantly different. The
average specific value SV1 (mean value CT HU of CBT-DH/ mean CT HU of TPS)
and SV2 (mean value CT HU of CBT/ mean CT HU of TPS) was 1.31 ± 0.25 and
1.53 ± 0.29 respectively with significant positive correlation with age
(Pearson coefficient: 0.2, p < 0.01 for SV1 and age, Pearson coefficient:
0.3, p < 0.01 for SV2 and age). Conclusion: CBT-DH has
significantly higher bone density compared to traditional pedicle screw
(TPS) tract but lesser than CBT for lumbar vertebrae.

## P022: Is facet tropism associated with recurrent herniated disc after

Kanthika Wasinpongwanich

, Verapan Kuansongtham

Spine, Spine, Bangkok, Thailand

2

Spine, Orthopedics, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand

3

Research, Bangkok, Thailand

Background: Lumbar herniated disc recurrence is not uncommon and
might be related to the facet tropism. This study aims to explore if
recurrent herniated disc patients have different facet angle or tropism.
Methods: This case-control study was nested in the
Bumrungrad Spine Cohort containing data of 545 patients underwent full
endoscopic discectomy during 2011-2015. A patient was considered a case if
he/she experience a recurrent herniated disc. An age and gender matched
controls were randomly selected from the non-case group. Facet angle were

## P023: A large animal in vitro model to study nerve ingrowth in the
intervertebral disc

Junxuan Ma

1

, Janick Eglauf

1,2

, Riccardo Tognato

1

, Sibylle Grad

1,2

, Mauro Alini

1

, and Tiziano Serra

1

1

AO Research Institute Davos, Davos, Switzerland

2

ETH Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland

Introduction: Low back pain (LBP) is one leading cause of
disability worldwide. In many cases LBP is discogenic in origin. The painful
intervertebral disc (IVD) is associated with a deep ingrowth of axons, or
nerve fibers, which express neuropeptides such as substance P and calcitonin
gene-related peptide (CGRP). For basic investigation of this pathology,
clinically relevant models are needed. Commonly used LBP models are based on
rodents which cannot always predict human condition. In addition, the
experimental manipulation and optical observation in vivo
are challenging. Animal models investigating pain conditions also raise
ethical concerns. To address these problems, an in vitro
IVD-nerve co-culture model was created using large animal tissues. We
furthermore hypothesized that IVD inflammation would trigger axon growth.
Material and Methods: Bovine dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and
caudal IVD tissues were obtained from a local abattoir. Explants of the
outer annulus fibrosus (AF) (1.5x1.5x1.5 mm3) were treated with
IL-1β and TNF-α (each 10 ng/mL) for 24h to induce an inflammatory condition.
AF explants without cytokine treatment served as control. After a wash-out,
each AF tissue was placed in the center of a tissue culture frame. DRG were
enzymatically disintegrated into micro-tissue units and then re-assembled at
predetermined distances to the AF explant using "Sound Induced
Morphogenesis" (SIM). SIM also formed a dense cell-packing multicellular
system to recapitulate the native DRG tissue architecture. The viability and
the morphology of the multicellular system were evaluated by live-dead
staining and immunofluorescence, respectively. The multicellular system was
functionally evaluated using calcium imaging (Fluo4). In the AF-DRG
co-culture system, axons were labelled by CGRP and neurofilament
immunofluorescence. The axons in the immunofluorescent images were segmented
and statistically evaluated. Results: The SIM assembling did
not influence DRG cell viability (92.8%). Neurons in the DRG multicellular
system could be potassium depolarized, confirming their functionality. The
multicellular system supported spontaneous calcium signal transmitting from
one cell to its close counterparts at day 4. Satellite cells self-organized
to an oriented structure at day 8. The cytokine-treated AF tissue increased
the axon length of CGRP(+) neurons by 52% compared to non-cytokine control
at day 2. The axons had a turning angle pointing towards AF in 86.7% and
50.0% of CGRP(+) neurons in cytokine-treated AF and non-cytokine control,
respectively. There was no obvious turning angle for non-cytokine control
(-0.4°), while the turning angle was averaged to be 4.3° towards the
cytokine-treated AF. These axons were influenced only when neurons were
positioned within 1.3 mm from AF explants (n = 27 neurons and 355 axons).
Conclusion: Large animal AF and DRG can be cultured in a
physiologically relevant multicellular system recapitulating native tissue
architecture and supporting tissue-level functions. The AF-DRG communication
depends on their distance which can be controlled by SIM. The axon of
CGRP(+) neurons is elongated and attracted by the cytokine-treated AF
tissue. This pioneering study demonstrates the AF's influence on guided axon
sprouting can be reproduced in vitro. This model will be
instrumental to test new treatments targeting nerve ingrowth mechanisms,
replacing animal models in line with 3Rs principles.

The present work is a study on the prevalence of low back pain in nurses at

questionnaire containing social issues such as weight, age, height, work
sector, workload, physical activity, presence and frequency of low back
pain, in addition to the Oswestry questionnaire, which is a tool used to
quantify the degree of disability of low back pain in daily activities. This
research has the general objective of determining the prevalence of low back
pain in nurses at Santa Marcelina Hospital and establishing a relationship
with social aspects. According to the bibliographic study developed, it is
possible to show the high prevalence of low back pain in nurses and how much

low back pain. The method used in the research was an epidemiological
cross-sectional cohort. From the results of this work, it is concluded that
there is a high prevalence of low back pain in nurses at Santa Marcelina
Hospital. It was not possible to determine a direct risk factor for low back
pain. Therefore, it is assumed that several factors such as sex, age, BMI,
sedentary lifestyle, working time, work sector, posture and work activities
addressed in the research such as psychological factors, musculoskeletal
changes and socioeconomic conditions not addressed in the research can be in
set predisposing to low back pain.

## P025: Matching sub-groups of neck pain patients and best fit specific

Julia Szita

1

, Istvan Klemencsics

, Zoltan Hoffer

1

, and Aron Lazary

1,2

1

National Center for Spinal Disorders, Hungary

2

Department of Spine Surgery, Semmelweis University, Hungary

Neck pain is one of the leading causes of days lived with disability by
generating an immense burden of an individual’s quality of life. To
objectively measure the impact of musculoskeletal diseases patient reported
outcome measures (PROMs) have been developed which now are considered as
gold standard tools in research and everyday practice in spinal care.
The primary aim of our study was the cross-cultural language adaptation into
Hungarian language and the evaluation of the psychometric properties for the
NDI, NPAD and COMI-neck. Secondly, we focused on forming a recommendation of
appliance by investigating how well the PROMs perform in specific subgroups
of neck pain related symptoms.
At the outpatient clinic of the National Center for Spinal Disorders, 110
neck pain (with or without irradiating pain to the upper extremity) patients
were prospectively recruited. Internal consistency, construct validity,
reliability and responsiveness were explored for each questionnaire.
Subgroups were generated based on pain localization, radicular pain, type of
therapy and neurological deficit.
The COMI- neck, NDI and NPAD showed excellent reliability (ICC > 0.7),
construct validity and adequate responsiveness (AUC > 0.7) in relation of
global treatment outcome at 6 months follow up. All investigated PROMs had a
comparable factor structure as the original version and Cronbach α proved to
be < 0.70 thus adequate internal consistency was found. Based on our
results, the COMI neck proved to be superior compared to the NDI and NPAD in
most of the subgroups. Considering the available evidence which shows that
musculoskeletal neck pain should be considered as a multifactorial disease
where several non-biomedical factors play an immense role thus in our
opinion the multidimensional COMI-neck should be advocated in clinical
research as it is a short questionnaire and covers a wide aspect of the
disease.

## P028.1: Epigenetic and genetic factors related to curve progression in
adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a systematic scoping review of the current
literature

Marco Manzetti

1

, Francesca Barile

1

, Giovanni Viroli

1

, matteo traversari

1

, Marco Ialuna

1

, fabio vita

1

, azzurra paolucci

1

, Simona Neri

2

, Francesco Ursini

2

, Alberto Ruffilli

1

, and Cesare Faldini

1

1

Clinica Ortopedica e TraumatologicaI

2

Medicine and Rheumatology Unit, IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli,
Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a progressive
three-dimensional deformity of the spine, with different grade of involvement of
the frontal, sagittal and axial planes. Scoliotic curves progress until skeletal
maturity, causing important aesthetic problems, such as humps, with
psychological issues and loss of self-esteem, coronal and\or sagittal imbalance
and muscle fatigue. In rare cases, the curve may progress to develop a severe
deformity. While the Cobb angle is a straightforward tool in initial curve
magnitude measurement, assessing the risk of curve progression at the time of
diagnosis may be more challenging. Epidemiological and genetic studies indicated
AIS as a polygenic disease and several studies investigated genetic and
epigenetic factors associated with an increased risk of onset of the scoliotic
curve. Less information is available regarding candidate genetic and epigenetic
factors related to scoliotic curve progression and its prediction. Thus,
epigenetic and genetic markers could represent potential prognostic tools to
predict curve progression. The aim of this study is to review the available
literature regarding the epigenetic and genetic factors associated with the risk
of AIS curve progression. Material and Methods: Pubmed-MEDLINE, The
Cochrane Central Registry of Controlled Trials, Google Scholar and Embase
Biomedical Database were searched over the years 1990-2022 to identify eligible
studies in the English literature describing the epigenetic and genetic factors
associated to AIS curve progression. Inclusion criteria considered papers
describing genetic and epigenetic factors associated with AIS curve progression
published in English peer-reviewed journals. Isolated case reports\series with
less than 5 patients, literature reviews and meta-analyses were excluded. The
study selection was carried out in accordance with Preferential Reporting Items
for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and has been
accepted for registration in PROSPERO database for systematic reviews. The
search was carried out in January 2022. Results: Forty studies were
included; 15 genes were reported as having SNPs with significant association
with progressive AIS, but none showed sufficient power to sustain clinical
application. Therefore, available data on genetic factors correlated to AIS
evolution did not allow the prediction of disease progression only based on
genetic information. In contrast, 9 studies reporting epigenetic modifications
showed promising results in terms of reliable markers. Epigenetic marks
principally included DNA methylation, histone post-translational modifications
and regulation by non-coding RNAs, such as microRNA. Conclusion: In
conclusion, prognostic testing for AIS has the potential to significantly modify
disease management. This will be achieved only after the identification of
reliable markers and an understanding of the underlying biologic pathways.
Genetic studies identified a series of loci associated with disease progression,
whose power appears, however, insufficient to guide clinical choices. More
recent evidence suggests epigenetics as a more promising field for the
identification of factors associated with AIS progression, offering a rationale
for further investigation in this field. More data are needed, and studies on
tissues involved in the pathology, rather than peripheral blood, are
necessary.
