## 134

## P029: Are augmented lumbar soft tissue properties indicative of
physiological stress shielding as a potential biomarker for female low back
pain patients? An in vivo study

Emily Newell

1

, Jean Ouellet

2

, and Mark Driscoll

1

1

Department of Mechanical Engineering

2

Department of Paediatic Surgery & Surgery, McGill University
Health Centre, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Despite 85% of low back pain (LBP) cases being
considered idiopathic, few biomarkers are available to diagnose LBP.
Previous clinical studies have correlated LBP with changes to
spine-stabilizing lumbar soft tissues, including atrophy in the multifidus
(MF) and erector spinae (ES), and increased thoracolumbar fascia (TLF)
thickness. Tissue morphology augmentation of the quadratus lumborum (QL) and
psoas major (PM) within LBP patients has been inconsistent. Collectively,
these tissue property modifications suggest a load allocation bias within
the lumbar soft tissues with the potential for physiological stress
shielding. Thus, this study seeks to analyze changes within tissue
properties of LBP and healthy subjects to investigate the potential for
physiological stress shielding as a contributor to LBP. Materials and
Methods: MRI data of 100 female subjects was obtained from the
Mayo Clinic following ethical approval. Exclusion criteria included subjects
with spinal pathology, prior musculoskeletal surgical intervention, and
pregnancy. Healthy control subjects had no known LBP at the time of the MRI
scan. A total of 36 subjects (16 control, 20 LBP) were included in this
study. Using T2-weighted axial images the total and functional
cross-sectional areas (tCSA, fCSA) and fatty infiltration of the MF, ES, QL,
and PM were measured from the midline of the L1/L2 to L5/S1 intervertebral
discs (IVDs). The TLF tCSA was measured at the L3/L4 and L4/L5 IVD levels.
ANCOVA was conducted to compare the tCSA, fCSA, and fatty infiltration of
the soft tissues at each IVD level between control and LBP subjects. Results
obtained were adjusted for age and BMI during statistical analysis. P-values
< 0.05 were deemed statistically significant. Results: The
tCSA and fCSA demonstrated no significant differences between control and
LBP subjects regardless of IVD level. However, LBP subjects demonstrated
significantly larger average fatty infiltration within the L1/L2 MF (p =
0.034), L2/L3 MF (p = 0.040) and ES (p = 0.016), and L4/L5 QL (p = 0.013).
Increased fatty infiltration within the L3/L4 PM of LBP subjects approached
significance (p = 0.080). Conclusion: Results suggest
degenerative tissue property modification of the LBP MF, ES, and PM at the
L3/L4 IVD level due to increased fatty infiltration coupled with minimal
change in the tissues’ tCSA and fCSA. Additionally, the LBP TLF tCSA at
L3/L4 increased by 7.86% (p = 0.183) and may be clinically significant. This
increase in TLF tCSA may suggest tissue hypertrophy consequential of
elevated loading, while increased muscle fatty infiltration may suggest
muscle disuse. As such, LBP may result in physiological stress shielding
wherein the TLF withstands the majority of stress due to physiological
motion, preventing the ES, MF, and PM from receiving regular loading. In
turn, the muscles may undergo elevated fatty infiltration and eventual
muscle atrophy. These muscles may become unable to withstand normal stress,
resulting in LBP subjects subconsciously recruiting other muscles to
accommodate the desired motion, further distorting stress distributions and
leading to degenerative stress shielding. Therefore, this study suggests
that the progression of LBP may be due to stress shielding caused by
mechanical property changes to the lumbar soft tissues.

## 299

## P030: A biomechanical analysis of sex-specific differences between load
distribution and intersegmental motion in the thoracolumbar spine: a finite
element study

Brittany Stott

1,2

 and Mark Driscoll

1,2

1

McGill University, Montreal, Canada

2

Montreal General Hospital, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Musculoskeletal disorders and low back pain (LBP)
are a leading cause of global disability, but despite this, many LBP cases
are idiopathic. Further, female patients tend to experience a higher
occurrence of LBP and musculoskeletal disorders compared to males. Finite
element models (FEM) provide a means to objectively study the biomechanics
of the spine. While there is a growing interest in the influence of
biological sex on pain, current biomechanical modelling approaches seldom
consider the differences between male and female spines. Hence, utilizing
FEM to study important differences between biological sexes with respect to
physiological motion and load distribution may better guide targeted
treatments in clinical settings. Thus, this study aimed to compare the load
distribution between male and female spines through FEM. Material and
Methods: A male thoracolumbar spine model was developed,
consisting of the vertebrae and adjacent intervertebral discs (IVDs)
(T1-S1), tendons, thoracolumbar fascia, and surrounding muscles. From this
model, the cross-sectional area of the geometry and the material properties
of the tendons and IVDs were adapted to represent female anatomy, resulting
in two FEMs (one male and one female). The lumbar portion of the models
(L1-S1) were subjected to a 1175N follower load with 7.5Nm moment, as well
as pure moments from -10 to 10Nm applied at L1. The full thoracolumbar spine
models were subjected to pure moments from -7.5 to 7.5Nm applied at T1. The
models underwent extensive validation against in silico,
ex vivo, and in vivo comparators from
previously published literature. Following validation, intersegmental
rotation, IVD stress, and vertebral body stress were assessed.
Results: Model validation was successfully completed
through comparison of published literature for IVD stress and intersegmental
rotation. Under the follower load scenario, the lumbar FEMs demonstrated
negligible change in intersegmental rotation, however, the female model was
subjected to a 23% increase in IVD stress. When subjected to pure moments
inducing flexion and extension, the female lumbar and thoracolumbar spine
models exhibited a larger range of motion relative to the male model. Under
pure moments inducing flexion, the female lumbar model demonstrated an 18%
and 51% increase IVD stress and vertebral body stress, respectively,
meanwhile the female thoracolumbar spine model experienced a 36% and 55%
increase in IVD and vertebral body stress, respectively, when compared to
the male model. Conclusion: Sex-specific lumbar and
thoracolumbar spine FEMs were successfully developed and validated,
demonstrating substantial differences in load sharing and stress
distribution between biological sexes. The female model was subjected to
augmented stresses; these differences maybe be attributed to the reduced
bone volume and cross-sectional area in females, as well as the changes in
tissue material properties. The observed higher stresses may contribute to
the greater occurrences of LBP and musculoskeletal disorders observed in
female patients as the female body may be subjected to augmented loading on
a daily basis. This study highlights the importance of utilizing
biologically accurate models for each sex, as the resultant stress
distribution, and consequently the patient outcomes and suggested treatment
approaches, may differ significantly.

## 312

## P031: Comparison of dynamic spinal cord stress for single and multi-level
anterior cervical discectomy and fusion using a 3D patient-specific finite
element spinal cord model

Aditya Vedantam

1

, Yuvaraj Purushothaman

1

, Balaji Harinathan

1

, Matthew Budde

1

, and Narayan Yoganandan

1

1

Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, United States

Introduction: Dynamic spinal cord stress is a known contributor
to the pathophysiology of degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM). Although
the goal of surgery is to eliminate static spinal cord compression in DCM,
its impact on dynamic spinal cord stress is unclear. The effect of surgery
on dynamic spinal cord stress is expected to change with the number of
surgical levels as well as patient-specific anatomy. The aim of this study
was to use patient-specific 3D finite element model (FEM) of the cervical
spinal cord to model single- and multi-level anterior cervical diskectomy
and fusion (ACDF) to determine differences in post-surgical spinal cord
stress patterns. Material and Methods: A 3D patient-specific
FEM of the cervical spine and spinal cord was created using MRI-derived
geometries from a single patient with mild DCM (modified Japanese
Orthopedics score = 16). Using a MRI-derived patient-specific finite element
model, we simulated one-, two- and three-level anterior cervical diskectomy
and fusion surgery for DCM. The model uses material properties from human
spinal cord tissue that have been reported previously. The single-level ACDF
procedure was simulated by inserting a bone graft centrally at C5-C6 and a
titanium plate with variable angle screws. A similar procedure was performed
for 2-level ACDF at C5-C6 and C6-C7, and 3-level ACDF at C4-C5, C5-C6 and
C6-C7. The model was constrained at the inferior surface of the T1 vertebra
in all degrees-of-freedom, and the sagittal moment loads were applied at the
superior vertebra. The pure moment load level was 2 Nm each in flexion and
extension modes. An additional follower force of 75N to simulate the head
mass and muscle force was applied. Von Mises stress of the spinal cord was
calculated at each segment during flexion and extension, and compared to
segmental range of motion and intradiscal pressures. Results:
Decrease in spinal cord stress at the level of surgical decompression was
equivalent in all simulations (-62% [1-level] vs 61.5% [2-level] vs 59%
[3-level]). There was an increase in spinal cord stress rostral to the
surgical level, and the change in spinal cord stress at the superior
adjacent segment during neck flexion was greater in multi-level surgery
compared to single-level surgery (160% [3-level] vs 56% [2-level] vs 20%
[1-level]). Increased segmental spinal cord stress after surgery correlated
with a corresponding increase in segmental range of motion (r = 0.69, p =
0.002) and disk pressure (r = 0.57, p = 0.05). Conclusion: This
is the first study to use a patient-specific cervical spinal cord model to
simulate surgical intervention and measure post-surgical spinal cord stress
specific to the patient. Our results indicate that ACDF for DCM does not
completely eliminate dynamic spinal cord stress, and adverse stress patterns
are seen adjacent to the fusion construct. Further research is needed to
determine if the altered spinal cord stress is associated with the
pathogenesis of clinical adjacent segment disease in DCM.

## 366

## P032: Rotational stiffness in a fully 3D printed biomechanical analogue
of the lumbar spine

Siril Teja Dukkipati

1,2

 and Mark Driscoll

1,2

1

Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Lab, Department of Mechanical
Engineering, McGill University, Montréal, Canada

2

Orthopaedic Research Laboratory, Research Institute MUHC, Montreal
General Hospital, Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Conventional spine biomechanical studies deal with
cadavers and finite element models, both of which have their respective
limitation in cost and time. Cadaveric studies introduce high variability in
measurements across patients due to their dependency in patient medical
history. Finite element models are constrained by the quality of patient
data available and are computationally demanding. Validated analogue spine
models can aid and compliment these conventional methods with low cost and
increased fidelity. Materials and Methods: A 3D printed L1-S1
analogue model of the spine was developed which consisted of vertebral
bodies, intervertebral discs along with intertransverse, interspinous
ligaments. Stereolithography 3D printing was used to manufacture these
models and assembled post printing. The soft tissues and the vertebrae were
3D printed using Flexible 80A and Durable resins on Form 3L printer
(Formlabs, MA, USA). The model was then subjected to load-controlled pure
bending loading up to a cyclic amplitude of 7.5Nm at 1/60Hz in
flexion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation along with a custom
bending jig (Instron Electroplus E10000, MA, USA). The resulting rotation of
motion (ROM) was recorded and plotted against applied load to calculate
model rotational stiffness. The performance of the model was compared to
that of existing in vitro and in silico models in literature.
Results: Due to the viscoelastic nature of the materials
used in the model, a hysteretic response was exhibited while loading and
unloading much like the human lumbar spine. At +7.5Nm flexion, the model ROM
was 12.92 ± 0.11° (in vitro: 16.58°[1] and in silico: 14.92°[1]; 12.96°[2]).
In lateral bending and axial rotation, the model exhibited left-right
symmetry owing to its superior manufacturing process. The model ROM in
lateral bending was found to be 13.55 ± 0.11° at +7.5Nm (in vitro: 13.32°[1]
and in silico: 16.1°[1]; 15.26°[2]) and -13.79 ± 0.19° at -7.5Nm (in vitro:
-17.1°[1] and in silico: -16.45°[1]; -15.73°[2]). In axial rotation, the
model ROM was recorded as 19.82 ± 0.19° at +7.5Nm (in vitro: 14.44°[1] and
in silico: 16.21°[1]; 15.63°[2]) and -15.57 ± 0.12° at -7.5Nm (in vitro:
-13.81°[1] and in silico: -16°[1]; -16.2°[2]). In extension, the model
exhibited approximately twice the stiffness compared to its human
counterpart. But in all the other five bending modes, the model stiffness
response is strongly comparable to that of in vitro and in silico
literature. Conclusion: This custom 3D printed analogue model
of the lumbar spine has rotational stiffness comparable to existing
cadaveric, finite element models in flexion, lateral bending, and axial
rotation motions and offers high degree of reproducibility. More material
choices and testing is needed to statistically quantify the model. Within
the context of use, such analogue experimental models can be effective tools
in upcoming spinal biomechanics research.

## References
1. Rao M. Explicit Finite Element Modeling of the Human Lumbar Spine.
University of Denver, Denver, CO, 2012.
2. Campbell JQ, Coombs DJ, Rao M, Rullkoetter P J, Petrella AJ. Automated
finite element meshing of the lumbar spine: Verification and validation with
18 specimen-specific models. J Biomech 2016; 49: 2669-76, doi:
10.1016/J.JBIOMECH.2016.05.025.

## 526

## P033: Changes of the biomechanical environment during intervertebral
fusion process after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a finite
element study

Yi-Wei Shen

1

, Yi Yang

1

, and Hao Liu

1

1

Department of Orthopedics, Orthopedic Research Institute, West China
Hospital, Sichuan University, Department of Orthopedics, Chengdu,
China

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is
a widely-accepted surgical procedure in the treatment of cervical
radiculopathy and myelopathy. A solid interbody fusion is of critical
significance in achieving satisfactory outcomes after ACDF. However, the
current radiographic techniques to determine the degree of fusion are
inaccurate and radiative. Several animal experiments suggested that the
mechanical load on the spinal instrumentation could reflect the fusion
process and evaluate the stability of the implant. This study aims to
investigate the changes in the biomechanical environment during the fusion
process and explore the feasibility of reflecting the fusion status after
ACDF through the load changes borne by the interbody fusion cage.
Material and Methods: The computed tomography (CT) scans
preoperatively, immediately after surgery, at 3 months, and 6 months
follow-up of a patient who underwent ACDF at C5/6 were used to construct the
C2-C7 finite element (FE) models representing the different course of fusion
stages. A 75-N follower load with 1.0 N·m moments was applied to the top of
the C2 vertebra in the models to simulate flexion, extension, lateral
bending, and axial rotation with the C7 vertebra fixed. The Von Mises stress
at the surfaces of instrumentation and the adjacent intervertebral disc and
force at the facet joints were analyzed. Results: The facet
contact force at C5/6 suggested a significantly stepwise reduction as the
fusion proceeded while the intradiscal pressure and facet contact force of
adjacent levels changed slightly. The stress on the surfaces of the titanium
plate and screws significantly decreased at 3 months and 6 months follow-up.
A markedly changed stress distribution in extension among the three models
was noted in different fusion stages. After solid fusion is achieved, the
stress was more uniformly distributed interbody fusion in all loading
conditions. Conclusion: Through a follow-up study of 6 months,
the stress on the surfaces of cervical instrumentation remarkably decreased
in all loading conditions. After solid intervertebral fusion formed, the
stress distributions on the surfaces of the interbody cage and screws were
more uniform. The stress distribution in extension altered significantly in
different fusion statuses. Future studies are needed to develop the
interbody fusion device with wireless sensors to achieve longitudinal
real-time monitoring of the stress distribution during the course of
fusion.

## 598

## P034: Titanium mesh cage placement after corpectomy. Does the anatomical
location have an effect on stability? A biomechanical comparison of three
different cage localizations. A finite element analysis

Tuna Pehlivanoglu

1

, Bahadir Gokcen

2

, Tugrul Ergun

3

, O. Nuri Eroglu

1

, Ufuk Aydinli

2

, and Cagatay Ozturk

1

1

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Liv Hospital Ulus,
Liv Spine Center certified by AOSpine, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Liv Hospital Vadi,
Liv Spine Center certified by AOSpine, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Istinye University
Liv Hospital, Liv Spine Center certified by AOSpine, Istanbul,
Turkey

Introduction: Anterior column restoration following corpectomy
is paramount to restore the vertebral body height and to reconstruct the
corpectomy defect, in order to have a stable spinal segment yielding a
balanced spine in coronal and sagittal planes. The aim of this study based
on a finite element analysis was to compare the biomechanical properties of
three different titanium mesh cage localizations (anterior/middle/posterior)
in the vertebral body simulated to reconstruct the corpectomy defect to
question the ideal localization providing the highest stability.
Materials and Methods: A three-dimensional, non-linear
finite element model (FEM) of L4-L6 segment combined with corpectomy at the
level of L5 was constructed. It was modified to test the titanium mesh cage
(1 cm in diameter) placed on L6’s vertebral body’s upper endplate centrally
to reconstruct the L5-corpectomy defect under three conditions: (Group 1)
the cage is placed centrally on anterior 1/3rd of vertebral body,
(Group 2) the cage is placed centrally in the middle of the vertebral body,
(Group 3) the cage is placed centrally on posterior 1/3rd of
vertebral body. Finite element analyses were performed to investigate the
effect of axial compressive loadings, while average tensions recorded from
the surface of cages were recorded and assessed for distal force
transmission and segmental stability. Results: Average surface
tension (AST) in Group 1 was 320 MPa. AST in Group 2 was 124 MPa. AST in
Group 3 was 45 MPa. Intergroup comparison yielded the superiority of cages
in Group 3 (p < 0.001 for all), indicating the lowest axial compressive
load transmission to cages placed centrally on posterior 1/3rd of
the vertebral body providing least amount of force transmission to distal
segments accompanied with highest segmental stability.
Conclusion: The present study based on finite element
analysis concluded, that following corpectomy, titanium mesh cages placed
centrally on the posterior 1/3rd of the lower vertebral endplate
to reconstruct the corpectomy defect in order to restore the vertebral
height and restore the spinal balance together with spinal stability, was
subjected to least axial compressive loading resulting in the least amount
of force transmitted to distal segments and was therefore detected to yield
highest stability against axial loading.

## 761

## P035: Influence of the iliolumbar ligament on the lumbar segmental range
of motion in the sagittal plane: a finite element approach

Adi Mithani

1

, Ahmed Aoude

2

, and Mark Driscoll

3

1

Biological and Biomedical Engineering

2

Department of Surgery, McGill University Health Centre,
Canada

3

Mechanical Engineering, McGill University, Canada

Introduction: The iliolumbar ligament (ILL) is a major
lumbopelvic ligament that has been implicated in the stability of the
sacroiliac and lumbosacral joints, particularly in cases with increasing
disc degeneration or L5 spondylolysis. While the ILL plays a role in lower
lumbar dysfunction, no biomechanical modelling has been conducted to
evaluate the relationship between changes in the material properties of the
ILL and the lumbar range of motion (ROM). The primary objective of this
research was to develop a validated and representative finite element (FE)
spine model to evaluate the influence of the ILL on the lumbar segmental ROM
in the sagittal plane under flexion-extension conditions. Material and
Methods: In this study, a FE spine model was developed and
validated against in-vivo published findings of intervertebral rotations
(IVR) at lumbar spine levels L2-S1. The model included the thoracolumbar
vertebrae, rib cage, intervertebral disc, facet cartilage, joint capsule,
pelvis, and spinal ligaments (ILL, supraspinous, intertransverse, and
interspinous ligaments). The ILL was modelled as a tension-only spring
element, originating at the transverse process of the 5th vertebra and
inserted onto the ilia of the pelvis, anteriorly and posteriorly. A follower
load of 1000N was applied perpendicularly to the surface of the T1
vertebra’s superior endplate to S1 using pre-loaded springs, increasing by
2.4% at each vertebral level. The perpendicular orientation of loading
ensured the resultant forces remained tangential to the spinal profile. A
60˚ and -55˚ remote rotation was applied to the body of the T1 vertebra to
simulate forward flexion and maximum extension, respectively, with the
pelvis as the fixed support. Case scenarios were executed and IVRs were
calculated based on the intersection between lines running parallel to the
superior and inferior endplate at an intervertebral level.
Results: The application of flexion and extension generated
IVRs that fell within a 20% margin of the mean values acquired from in-vivo
studies by Breen et al. (2021) and Lin et al. (1994), respectively,
remaining within the standard deviation associated with each intervertebral
segment. Flexion-extension rotation following bilateral ILL removal
increased IVR at L5-S1 and decreased it at L4-L5, by 23.37% and 12.33%,
respectively. Sensitivity analysis relating ILL stiffness to lumbar
segmental IVRs in the sagittal plane found that as stiffness increased from
50 N/mm to 3000 N/mm, IVR decreased at L5-S1 and increased at L4-L5 by
21.94% and 15.53%, respectively. Lumbar ROM varied by a maximum of 2.5%
across all stiffness values tested. Conclusion: Removal of the
ILL or changes to its material properties alters the IVRs at L5-S1,
producing a compensatory rotation at L4-L5 in the sagittal plane. Decreasing
the magnitude of support at L5-S1 increases the amount of flexion-extension
rotation imparted at this level, which reduces rotation at adjacent levels
until the maximum allowable rotation is achieved. This permits the lumbar
spine to retain its normal ROM. Clinically, in patients with iliolumbar
syndrome, the inflammation of the ILL may not directly contribute to lumbar
dysfunction as adjacent vertebral levels could alter their segmental
rotation to preserve some degree of lumbar ROM.

## 853

## P036: There is significant variability in segmental lumbar motion

Emily Mills

1

, Jennifer Wang

1

, Brian Chung

1

, Lucas Mayer

1

, Mary Richardson

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, and Nathanael Heckmann

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

Introduction: The variability in change of lordosis throughout
common positions has not been well-studied. Additionally, the relationship
between lumbar and hip motion has not been established. Here, we sought to
establish 1) normative values for lumbar segmental motion and 2) the
relationship between hip and lumbar flexion. Material and
Methods: Fifty subjects, 25 male and 25 female, without prior hip
or spine disease were prospectively recruited to participate in this study.
Three lateral radiographs were obtained: standing, relaxed seated, and
flexed-forward seated. Radiographic variables measured included lumbar
lordosis (LL), motion at each lumbar level (L1-L2, L2-L3, L3-L4, L4-L5,
L5-S1), and pelvic-femoral angle (PFA), an established measure of hip motion
used in the arthroplasty literature. The motion through each lumbar segment
was calculated as the change in angle between a standing position and the
target motion (i.e. seated or flexed-forward seated). Each segment’s
contribution to overall lumbar motion was calculated as the ratio of the
individual segment to the overall lumbar lordosis. The correlation between
hip flexion and lumbar flexion between the standing and seated positions was
evaluated. Results: Subjects had an average age of 25.70 ± 2.34
years and body mass index (BMI) of 24.10 ± 3.02 kg/m2. From
standing to relaxed seated, the most mobile segment was L4-L5 (10.92 ±
3.95°) and from standing to a seated flexed-forward position was L4-L5
(16.42 ± 4.22°). The largest percentage contribution to lordosis was L4-L5
while standing (26.81 ± 5.78%) and was L1-L2 while seated (28.12 ± 25.42%).
During the standing to relaxed seated position, maximal motion occurred at
L4-L5 (25/50, 50.0%) followed by L5-S1 (13/50, 26.0%), L3-L4 (10/50, 20.0%),
and L2-L3 (2/50, 4.0%). During the standing to flexed-forward seated
position, maximal motion occurred at L4-L5 in 26/50, (52.0%), L3-L4 in 11/50
(22.0%), L5-S1 in 10/50 (20.0%), and L2-L3 in 3/50 (6.0%). Hip flexion
(ΔPFA) was strongly negatively correlated with lumbar flexion (ΔLL). For
every degree increase of hip flexion, the lumbar flexion decreased 0.86° (R
= -0.75, p < 0.001). Conclusion: The greatest contribution
to segmental motion and lumbar lordosis was L4-L5; however, there was
significant variability, with some subjects having the greatest contribution
from upper lumbar segments. Additionally, hip flexion was found to be
strongly negatively correlated with lumbar flexion.

## 867

## P037: Biomechanical evaluation of different fixation strategies for S1
pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO); A finite element analysis

Niloufar Shekouhi

1

, Sudharshan Tripathi

1

, Vijay Goel

1

, and Alekos Theologis

2

1

Departments of Bioengineering, Engineering Center for Orthopaedic
Research Excellence (E-CORE), University of Toledo, Toledo, United
States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, UCSF, San Francisco, United States

Introduction: While pedicle subtraction osteotomies (PSO) are
most commonly performed in the middle/low lumbar spine, sacral PSOs are
ideal for correcting sacral deformities. As sacral PSOs raise unique
challenges for stabilization given relatively limited fixation caudal to the
PSO, this study’s purpose is to compare biomechanics of different
instrumentation configurations used to stabilize a S1-PSO. Material
and Methods: A validated spinopelvic finite element model was
used to create a 300 PSO in S1. Fixation cranial to the PSO was T11-L5
pedicle screws and distal to the PSO was dual iliac screws. The PSO was
stabilized with a combination of the following rods to create different
multi-rod (4-,5-,6-) constructs: (1) main midline rods (10R) engaging the
T11-L5 pedicle screws; (2) a horizontal rod (HR) connecting the two distal
iliac screws; (3) lateral accessory rods (LR) connected to the cranial iliac
screws and 10R proximally; (4) medial accessory rods (MR) connected to the
HR and 10R proximally. Five different instrumentation strategies were
evaluated: (A) 4-Rod(LR): 10R + bilateral LR; (B) 4-Rod(MR+HR): 10R combined
with a MR connected to a HR; (C) 4-Rod(LR+HR): 10R connected to a HR
combined with bilateral LR; (D) 5-Rod(LR+HR+1MR): 10R connected to a HR
combined with bilateral LR and one MR; 6-Rod(LR+HR+2MR): 10R connected to a
HR combined with bilateral LR and two MR. After loadings of 300N, 400N, and
400N were applied to the thoracic, lumbar, and sacrum, respectively, pure
moments (7.5Nm) were applied to the top endplate (T10) in all anatomic
directions. The L5-S1 ranges of motion (PSO-ROM) were recorded. PSO-force
and maximum von Mises stresses on 10R, LR, and HR were recorded.
Results: Maximum PSO-ROM was noted for 4-Rod(MR+HR) in
flexion, extension, and lateral-bendin. Compared to 4-Rod(MR+HR), 4-Rod(LR),
4-Rod(LR+HR), 5-Rod, and 6-Rod showed up to 49%, 41%, 35%, and 36% lower
PSO-ROMs, respectively. Von Mises stresses were lowest on 10Rs in 5- and
6-Rod constructs. Of the 4-Rod techniques, 4-Rod(LR+HR) had the lowest von
Mises stresses. 4-Rod(MR+HR) showed lowest von Mises stresses on accessory
rods and horizontal rods in all directions. 5-Rod and 6-Rod configurations
demonstrated greatest von Mises stresses on HR. Maximum PSO-force was
observed in 4-Rod(MR+HR) in all motions except extension.
Conclusion: In this finite element analysis of various
multi-rod (4-,5-,6-) constructs stabilizing a S1 PSO, the construct
consisting of primary midline rods connected to cranial iliac bolts
supplemented with medial accessory rods connected vertically to a horizontal
rod connecting distal iliac screws [4-Rod(MR+HR)] demonstrated highest
PSO-ROMs and greatest PSO forces.
Acknowledgement: Work supported by NSF Industry/University Cooperative
Research Center, UCSF, UT, and Ohio State University.

## 940

## P038: Influence of the rib cage on the lumbar segmental range of motion
in the sagittal plane: a finite element approach

Adi Mithani

1

, Ahmed Aoude

2

, and Mark Driscoll

3

1

Biological and Biomedical Engineering

2

Department of Surgery

3

Mechanical Engineering, McGill University, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Local and distant tissues influence the degree of
lumbar range of motion (ROM), eluding to multiple causes of spinal
dysfunction. A recent systematic review further supports that rib cage
removal leads to reduced thoracic stiffness and increased ROM at the
thoracic spine level. However, no biomechanical studies have evaluated the
impact of the rib cage on the lumbar ROM. The primary objective of this
research was to develop a validated and representative finite element (FE)
spine model to evaluate the contribution of the rib cage to the lumbar
segmental ROM in the sagittal plane under flexion-extension conditions.
Material and Methods: In this study, a FE spine model was
developed and validated against in-vivo published findings of intervertebral
rotations (IVR) at the lumbar spine levels L2-S1. The model included the
thoracolumbar vertebrae, rib cage, intervertebral disc, facet cartilage,
joint capsule, pelvis, and spinal ligaments (iliolumbar, supraspinous,
intertransverse, and interspinous ligaments). Rib-vertebrae contact was
modelled as a fixed joint with zero degrees of freedom. A follower load of
1000N was applied perpendicularly to the surface of the T1 vertebra’s
superior endplate to S1 using pre-loaded springs, increasing by 2.4% at each
vertebral level. The perpendicular orientation of loading ensured the
resultant forces remained tangential to the spinal profile. A 60˚ and -55˚
remote rotation was applied to the body of the T1 vertebra to simulate
forward flexion and maximum extension, respectively, with the pelvis as the
fixed support. Different components of the rib cage were removed and IVRs
were calculated based on the intersection between lines running parallel to
the superior and inferior endplate at a given intervertebral level.
Results: The application of flexion and extension generated
IVRs that fell within a 20% margin of the mean values acquired from in-vivo
studies by Breen et al. (2021) and Lin et al. (1994), respectively,
remaining within the standard deviation associated with each intervertebral
segment. Flexion-extension rotation during removal of the rib cage decreased
IVR at L4-L5 and L5-S1 by -20.81% and -15.48%, respectively, with lumbar ROM
dropping by 10.12% compared to the validated model. Removal of the true ribs
bilaterally decreased IVR at L4-L5 and L5-S1 by -18.29% and -19.26%,
respectively. However, no significant change in ROM was observed after the
removal of the sternum and the false and floating ribs. Flexion-extension
rotation following the sternal release with non-in-tact ribs reduced IVR at
L4-L5 and L5-S1 by 14.63% and 15.48%, respectively, and was associated with
a 7.46% reduction in lumbar ROM. Conclusion: The findings
reveal the importance of the rib cage, specifically the true ribs, in
contributing to the lumbar ROM in the sagittal plane during
flexion-extension conditions. The sternal release, a potential treatment for
spinal sagittal plane deformity, increased segmental ROM in the lower lumbar
levels but only in the case when the ribs were removed. Therefore, unless
another method is implemented to account for the rib cage’s stiffness
contribution, the inclusion of ribs may be necessary to produce a
representative FE spinal model that reflects the lumbar spine’s ROM.

## 984

## P039: Effect of ligaments on spinal stiffness by systematic construction
of an L1-S1 analogue spine model

Siril Teja Dukkipati

1,2

 and Mark Driscoll

1,2

1

Department of Mechanical Engineering, Musculoskeletal Biomechanics
Research Lab, McGill University, Montréal, Canada

2

Orthopaedic Research Laboratory, Research Institute MUHC, Montreal
General Hospital, Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Conventional spine biomechanical studies deal with
cadavers and finite element models, both of which have their respective
limitation in cost and time. These can be overcome by incorporating
validated analogue models of the spine for biomechanical testing. To develop
such models, it is important to quantify the effects of all the underlying
soft tissues on the model biomechanical response. This study considered the
effect of intertransverse and interspinous ligaments on the overall
rotational stiffness of the lumbar spine by sequential construction of an
analogue lumbar spine. Materials and Methods: A 3D printed
L1-S1 analogue model of the spine was developed which consisted of vertebral
bodies, intervertebral discs (IVDs) along with intertransverse, interspinous
ligaments. Stereolithography 3D printing was used to manufacture the
individual tissues. The soft tissues and the vertebrae were 3D printed using
Flexible 80A and Durable resins on Form 3L printer (Formlabs, MA, USA). The
model construction had three phases (P1, P2, P3) and after each phase, the
corresponding model rotational stiffness was estimated by subjecting it to
load-controlled pure bending load up to a cyclic amplitude of 5Nm at 1/60Hz
in flexion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation along with a
custom bending jig (Instron Electroplus E10000, MA, USA). Five cycles of
loading is applied and the resulting rotation of motion (ROM) was recorded
and plotted against applied load to calculate rotational stiffness. P1
consisted of the assembly of vertebral bodies and the corresponding IVDs. P2
consisted of adding the interspinous ligament to the P1 model. P3 completed
the model construction by adding the intertransverse ligaments on both sides
of the P2 model. Results: The analogue spine model exhibited
hysteretic behavior during load-unload cycles very much like the human spine
due to the viscoelastic elastomers used in its construction. In
flexion-extension motion, addition of ligaments considerably increased model
rotational stiffness (flexion – P1 = 9.87 ± 0.05°; P2 = 9.41 ± 0.1°; P3 =
8.33 ± 0.11° and extension – P1 = 8.99 ± 0.09°; P2 = 6.7 ± 0.05°; P3 = 7.12
± 0.04°). In lateral bending motion, there was no noticeable change in
rotational stiffness from P1 to P2 but an increase from P2 to P3 on both
directions (left – P1 = 9.01 ± 0.07°; P2 = 8.93 ± 0.1°; P3 = 8.66 ± 0.09°
and right – P1 = 9.11 ± 0.09°; P2 = 9.18 ± 0.06°; P3 = 8.5 6± 0.05°). In
axial rotation, there was no noticeable trends in the stiffness as
construction progressed on either direction (left – P1 = 12.8 ± 0.11°; P2 =
14.3 ± 0.2°; P3 = 12.56 ± 0.14° and right - P1 = 12.08 ± 0.24°; P2 = 10.75 ±
0.04°; P3 = 11.41 ± 0.15°). The model exhibited noticeable left-right
symmetry in lateral bending and axial rotation motions.
Conclusion: The presence of interspinous and
intertransverse ligaments increases the flexion and lateral bending
stiffnesses respectively in the model. This observation agrees with the
consensus of the current understanding of lumbar spine biomechanics. In
extension and axial rotation motions, the model stiffness does not follow
any trends with the addition of ligaments. Further testing with more
material choices is needed to statistically quantify the results. The
developed L1-S1 analogue spine model can be an effective research and
educational tool in studying dependency of ligaments and any of their damage
modes on the lumbar spine structure.

## 986

## P040: On the effect of thoracolumbar fascia on lumbar spine stiffness
under loading in an analogue spine setup

Siril Teja Dukkipati

1,2

 and Mark Driscoll

1,2

1

Department of Mechanical Engineering, Musculoskeletal Biomechanics
Research Lab, McGill University, Montréal, Canada

2

Orthopaedic Research Laboratory, Research Institute MUHC, Montreal
General Hospital, Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Analogue biomechanical models serve as fast and
reliable alternatives to conventional spine biomechanical studies which
involve cadaveric and finite element studies. Both these methods have their
respective limitations in cost and time as opposed to analogue models. To
develop and validate such models, it is important to characterize the
dependency of all the underlying soft tissues on model performance. An
analogue model of the thoracolumbar fascia (TLF) was developed and
integrated with a previously validated L1-S1 analogue lumbar spine model and
its effect on spinal stiffness was characterized. Materials and
Methods: A 3D model of the TLF based on patient MRI data was
constructed from L1 to S1 level. Stereolithography 3D printing was used to
manufacture the model with Flexible 80A resin and printed on Form 3L
(Formlabs, MA, USA). A custom jig was developed to anchor the model along
the iliac arch. Prior to integrating with the analogue lumbar spine, the TLF
model was tested in tension and its mechanical hysteresis and stress
relaxation were determined. Then the model was attached to the analogue
lumbar spine and the combined model was subjected to pure bending loading in
all three axes (Instron Electroplus E10000, MA, USA). Five cycles of
load-controlled moments up to 7.5Nm at 1/60Hz were applied in
flexion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation. The rotational
stiffness of the TLF integrated analogue lumbar spine was determined by
plotting the resultant rotation of motion against applied moment.
Results: The analogue TLF model exhibited viscoelastic
properties much like its human counterpart. The TLF model hysteresis was
estimated to be 34.3 ± 0.68% as compared to 28.3 ± 7.4% in a porcine TLF
model (Nelson-Wong et al., 2018). Force-time curve at a constant deformation
of 10mm revealed that there was a 40.1 ± 3.0% drop in resisting force after
500 sec. This is comparable to 42.3% drop in human TLF samples according to
(Yahia et al., 1993). When the TLF model was attached to the L1-S1 analogue
lumbar spine, its rotational stiffness significantly increased in
flexion-extension and axial rotation motions under pure bending loading. The
combined model recorded 9.95 ± 0.05° and 7.1 ± 0.08° in flexion and
extension as opposed to 12.92 ± 0.11° and 10.15 ± 0.1° respectively in the
original L1-S1 analogue spine model. Similarly in axial rotation, the
combined model recorded 16.3 ± 0.18° and 12.25 ± 0.12° in left and right
directions as opposed to 19.82 ± 0.19° and 15.5 ± 0.12° respectively in the
original model. In lateral bending, no significant impact of TLF on spinal
stiffness was noticed. The combined model recorded 12.6 ± 0.1° and 13.37 ±
0.17° in left and right as compared to 13.55 ± 0.11° and 13.79 ± 0.19°
respectively in the original model. Conclusion: The developed
TLF model mechanical response is comparable to that of the human tissue. The
combined model stiffness response suggests that the presence of TLF aids in
restricting the lumbar spine in flexion-extension and axial rotation
motions. Further testing with more material choices is warranted to increase
model accuracy. The developed TLF model along with the L1-S1 analogue spine
model can act as cost effective spinal biomechanics educational and research
tools in future research.

## P041: Biomechanics of the spine while wearing different types of
orthopedic braces

Justyna Fercho

1

, Michal Krakowiak

1

, Rami Yuser

1

, Tomasz Szmuda

1

, Grzegorz Mi´kisiak

2

, and Piotr Zieliński

1

1

Neurosurgery Department, Medical University of Gdansk, Gdańsk,
Poland

2

Department of Neurosurgery, Institute of Medicine, Opole,
Poland

Aim: Despite the frequent use of orthopedic braces or spine
stabilizers in diseases such as kyphosis, lordosis, and scoliosis, as well
as in the case of injuries and rehabilitation and after surgeries, there is
no clear evidence of their proper stabilization of the spine while
performing day-to-day activities. This study sought to assess the spine's
mobility while wearing three different types of orthopedic braces while
performing certain basic activities. Methods: Ten healthy
subjects were enrolled. Three inertial measuring units were attached
superficially along the spine at the T2, T12, and sacrum. The angle between
sensors was monitored to provide data on the sagittal profile. In addition,
the displacement along the longitudinal axis of the spine was measured
(rotation). Three types of orthopedic braces: the semi-rigid LSO orthosis,
Jewett brace, and TLSO orthosis. Three tasks were monitored: when standing,
sitting, walking, and picking up an item from the floor with one hand.
Results: When performing a dynamic task of lifting an item
all braces provide a similar level of stability in both the sagittal plane
and rotational axis. On the other hand during walking and sitting the TLSO
was the only orthosis providing a statistically significant rigidity in the
sagittal plane. The findings from this study currently provide the most
precise understanding of the biomechanics behind the spine parameters while
wearing orthopedic braces. Conclusion: Despite various levels
of perceived rigidity the three orthoses performed similarly during
deliberate dynamic testing (pick up an item). This is likely caused by the
increased kinesthetic effect of all devices. On the other hand, when
performing rather involuntary postures when walking and standing the
superiority of the most rigid TLSO brace was apparent.
Keywords: spine, motion analysis, wearable sensors, biomechanics, braces

## 1539

## P042: Differences across various ideal lumbar lordosis measurement
formulas for patient-specific sagittal alignment goals

David Polly

1

, Paul Soriano

1

, Jason Haselhuhn

1

, Gurmit Singh

1

, Kenneth Holton

1

, Kristen Jones

1

, and Jonathan N. Sembrano

1

1

University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

Introduction: Multiple studies in the past have developed
differing equations to determine the ideal lumbar lordosis (ILL) in the
sagittal plane. These equations differ slightly, but all look to accomplish
the same goal of providing the surgeon with specific alignment targets
during surgery. However, to the authors’ knowledge, no study has compared
the different equations of ILL against each other. This study aims to
compare five different target alignment formulas in high, normal, and low
pelvic incidence (PI) patients. Methods: We conducted a
retrospective chart review from January 2015 through April 2022 and reviewed
available full-standing spine radiographs. We classified patients by PI:
high (65-95°), normal (50-60°), and low (30-45°), and included five patients
for each classification. A single faculty member performed all PI
measurements. We calculated ILL based on the measured PI using five
different formulas: Hamamatsu University (2016), ESSG-GAP score (2017),
Abelin-Genevois et al. (2018), Hyun et al. (2019), and Dial et al. (2022).
We employed Tukey’s HSD post hoc pair-wise comparison of homogenous groups
of means (α=0.05) to determine if there were significant differences. We
considered any measurement ±3° as equivalent to account for measurement
variability. Results: Fifteen patients were included in the
data analysis, five in each PI cohort. The GAP score, Hyun, and Dial
equations differ statistically from Hamamatsu University and Abelin-Genevois
(p<0.001). At high and normal PI classification, GAP score, Hyun, and
Dial significantly differ from Hamamatsu University and Abelin-Genevois
(p<0.05). At low PI classification, only the GAP score and Dial
significantly differ from Hamamatsu University and Abelin-Genevois
(p<0.05); Hyun does not differ significantly from all the other formulas.
Conclusion: Variation exists among the five different ILL
equations, with three formulas being statistically different from the other
two. The equations for high and low PI patients predict differing ideal
lumbar lordosis. One must take note of these differences when considering
patient-specific sagittal alignment goals. Further study is needed to refine
the understanding of ideal lumbar alignment.

## P043: Biomechanical analysis of cortical bone trajectory screwcombined
with pedicle screw fixation in lumbar spine: in-vitro experiments and finite
element validation

Zihao Ding

1

, Hongtao Ding

1

, Yuzeng Liu

1

, and Yong Hai

1

1

Spine Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital Medical
University, Beijing, China

Introduction: To compare the mechanical characteristics of
pedicle screw fixation (PS), cortical bone trajectory screw (CBTS) fixation
and the combination use of PS and CBTS (PS-CBTS) in L4/5 fixation.
Material and Methods: A three-dimensional finite element
(FE) analysis model (T12-Sacral) based on a patient with osteoporosis was
developed to analyze the range of motion (RoM) and internal fixation stress
of three different groups, which were PS fixation (group A), CBTS fixation
(group B), and hybrid fixation (L4-CBTS and L5-PS) (group C). And six human
cadaveric lumbar spine specimens (L1-Sacral) were used for the biomechanical
experiment to further compare the different fixations’ strengths and
weaknesses. Results: In the cadaveric specimen study, group C
had the highest stiffness, followed by groups B and A. The range of motion
(RoM) of the cranial adjacent segment was significantly higher in group C
than in groups A and B. In the FE model, group C had the highest screws and
connecting rod fixation stress in the six-dimensional motion of the lumbar
spine, followed by Groups B and A. The stresses of interbody cage in the
three groups were 318.8 Mpa (group A), 319.6 Mpa (group B), and 311.4 Mpa
(group C), respectively. Group B had the smallest RoM in flexion and
extension, and the largest RoM in lateral flexion and rotation.
Conclusion: The combined application of CBTS and PS can
increase the stress of internal fixation, improve lumbar stiffness, and
decrease stress on the interbody cage. However, the impact on the adjacent
segments requires further research.

## P044: Elasticity change of the paravertebral fascia and muscle in
adolescent idiopathic scoliosis after posterior selective fusion
surgery

Aixing Pan

1

 and Yong Hai

1

1

Orthopedic, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital Medical University,
Beijing, China

Introduction: We sought to assess the elasticity change of the
paravertebral fascia and muscle in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients
with Lenke Type 1, 2, or 3 curves after posterior selective fusion surgery.
Material and Methods: The shear wave elasticity imaging
system was used to assess the elasticity of the thoracic paravertebral
muscles and fascia both on the concave and convex sides. Three regions of
interest, including the apex, upper end, and lower end of the main curve,
were tested. Results: Ten female patients, with an average age
of 16.6 ± 2.7 years old, were included. The average post-operation follow-up
period was 9.0 ± 2.4 months. The Cobb angle was significantly corrected from
63.6 ± 12.0° to 10.7 ± 5.4° (p < 0.05). The length of the trunk increased
from 40.4 ± 2.5 cm to 46.0 ± 2.8 cm (p < 0.05). The elasticity of deep
fascia didn't show a significant change post-operation (p > 0.05). The
elasticity of the paravertebral muscle on the concave side had a significant
increase at the final follow-up (p < 0.05). The elasticity of the
paravertebral muscle on the convex side also increased at the upper end (p
< 0.05). The elasticity asymmetry of the deep fascia decreased, but the
elasticity asymmetry of the paravertebral muscle increased at the upper end
of the curve (p < 0.05). Conclusion: The paravertebral
muscle on the concave side is stiffer after surgery. Elastic asymmetry of
paravertebral muscle increased and elastic asymmetry of the deep fascia
decreased at the upper end of the curvature. Further study is needed to
elucidate the mechanism by which the paravertebral soft tissue responds
after surgery.

## P046: Ideal surgical strategy for dropped head syndrome (DHS)

Takahiro Iizuka

1

, Tetsuro Takai

1

, Tokuji Kashiro

1

, and Hiroshige Debata

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Takai Hospital, Nara, Japan

Background of Data: Dropped Head Syndrome (DHS) is little known
in Spine Community. Patients complain of difficulties in forwarding gaze.
Some reports on these clinical symptoms are reported in the literatures as a
case report. Most DHS surgeries report posterior cervical reconstruction
with posterior cervical long fusions. We report four patients with DHS who
underwent anterior segmental correction of cervical vertebrae as possible as
short. And the patients are enabled to gaze forward after surgery.
Patients and Methods: Four patients are enrolled in this
report (Average age: 74.5, female 3, male1). They complained of difficulties
in forwarding gaze and posterior neck stiffness preoperatively. All patients
had no other pathologies ie Parkinson’s syndrome. They were evaluated by
MRI, myelography, and CT myelography for making surgical strategies.
Cervical alignment (C3-C7 cervical kyphosis angle) and Cervico-Thoracic
Inlet Angle (between C2-Th1 line and clavicle line) were recorded by lateral
X-ray at upright position preoperatively and postoperatively. Clinical
complaints were also documented on gazing forward and neck pain/stiffness.
All patients performed anterior segmental reconstruction for correction of
cervical kyphosis. Results: All patients are enabled to gaze
forward. No apparent neurological deficit and complications associated with
surgery were not reported in those patients. Cervical kyphosis C3-7 angle
was improved. Conclusion: Dropped Head Syndrome is little-known
pathology in the Spine community. In this report, patients complained of
difficulties in forwarding gaze and swallowing foods and neck stiffness
preoperatively. Anterior segmental reconstruction spinal fusion (ASR-SF) is
less invasive than posterior cervical correction with instruments because of
less damage to PVM, mechanical reduction with instruments, and possible
short segmental fusions. We conclude that ASR-SF is the most suitable
surgical strategy for DHS as less invasive surgery.

## P047: Endoscopic endonasal odontoidectomy: a long-term follow-up for a

Federica Penner

Introduction: Endoscopic endonasal odontoidectomy (EEO) has been

endonasal route potentially represents a valid option to treat lesions above

## P048: Concomitant atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital rotatory dislocation
in children: radiological features, diagnostic pitfalls, and long-term
outcome

Paul Koljonen

1

 and Kenneth Man Chee Cheung

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, The University of Hong
Kong, Hong Kong

Introduction: While the pathological manifestation of
atlantoaxial rotatory dislocation has been well described in the medical
literature, the combined dislocation of the atlantoaxial and
atlanto-occipital joints, or OAARD - short for occipital-atlantoaxial
rotatory dislocation - is a condition which has been poorly elucidated and
probably underdiagnosed. We believe that the pathogenesis of combined
atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital dislocation is most likely a result of
untreated atlantoaxial rotatory dislocation leading to chronic secondary
compensation measures occurring at the occiput-C1 joints. Unique clinical
and radiological features lead to difficulty in diagnosis, and conventional
treatment algorithms may not apply. This paper describes a combination of
clinical and radiological features which can help clinicians correctly
diagnose and treat OAARD. Material and Methods: A case series
of paediatric occipital atlantoaxial rotatory dislocation is presented in
this abstract. 3D-reconstructed computer tomography images and 3D printed
models of the cervical spine are used to illustrate the deformity as well as
dysplastic changes occurring in the dislocated occipital condyles, C1 and C2
facet surfaces. Xray and Dynamic CT scans for rotational deformity are
discussed in detail, including the introduction of 2 novel radiological
signs termed the “trapezoidal anterior C1 shadow” and “isolated C1 spin-out”
sign, which are pathognomonic of dislocation of the C1 ring. Diagnostic
pitfalls, surgical technique, and long-term outcome are presented.
Conclusion: Concomitant occiput-atlantoaxial dislocation is
a unique condition that is probably underdiagnosed in common daily practice.
We emphasize the need for clinicians to exercise a high index of suspicion
in children presenting with neck pain and torticollis. Early diagnosis and
aggressive treatment of isolated atlantoaxial dislocation may help prevent
chronic secondary dislocation at the occiput-C1 level. This paper describes
a combination of clinical and radiological features which can help
clinicians correctly diagnose and treat OAARD. More research is required on
the long-term outcome following upper cervical spinal fusion in
children.

## P051: Comparison of the efficacy of anterior combined with posterior

Xiaoyu Cai

1

 and Tao Xu

1

1

Department of Spine Surgery, First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang

Introduction: To compare the clinical efficacy of anterior
combined with posterior (A-P) approach and posterior-only (P-O) approach

irreducible AAD. Material and Methods: The clinical records of
49 patients diagnosed with BI with irreducible AAD from July 2000 to June

ML, ADI, CMA, and CCA were 2.04 ± 3.61 mm, -3.12 ±1.81 mm, -1.72 ± 2.79 mm,
1.15 ± 1.20 mm, 146.69 °± 11.2 °, 137.49° ± 10.3°, which were statistically

group. A total of 8 patients presented postoperative complications,
including 6 patients in the A-P group (25.0%) and 2 patients in the P-O
group (8.0%). The incidence of postoperative complications in the P-O was
significantly lower than that in the A-P group. Conclusion: The
clinical efficacy of the P-O approach release, reduction, and internal
fixation in the treatment of BI with irreducible AAD is basically the same

## P052: Hybrid surgery for the treatment of cervical myelopathy and
adjacent level radiculopathy

David Felzensztein

1

, Eilat Sapirstein

1

, and Eyal Itshayek

1

1

Neurosurgery, Rabin Medical Center, Holon, Israel

Introduction: Patients with multilevel degenerative disc disease
suffering from cervical myelopathy and adjacent foraminal stenosis, tend to
be managed with multilevel anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) or
cervical laminectomy and fusion. Fusion sparing techniques have been used in
an attempt to decrease the number of fused levels. The combination of ACDF
and Transvertebral Foraminotomy could reduce the need for adjacent segment
fusion, reduce costs and decrease the number of fused levels in such cases.
We present our experience and preliminary results with patients undergoing
ACDF and skip level transvertebral foraminotomy. Material and Methods:
We retrospectively evaluated prospectively collected clinical and
radiological data from January 2017. Currently a total of 15 patients have

transvertebral foraminotomy at an adjacent disc space. The Modified Japanese
Orthopedic Association (mJOA) score and Odom’s criteria were analyzed.
Radiological assessment included the C2-7 Cobb angle and disc height of
segments adjacent to the ACDF. Adjacent segment degeneration, which includes
disc degeneration, was evaluated. All surgeries were performed at two
adjacent segments. Results: The JOA scores significantly
improved. There were no significant differences in the C2-7 Cobb angle and
DH of the adjacent segment to ACDF. Conclusion: Combination of
ACDF and transvertebral foraminotomy provides a safe and effective method in
reducing the number of levels fused with good clinical outcome.

## P053: Unilateral spacer distraction (USD) of the subaxial cervical facet
joint for the treatment of fixed coronal malalignment of the craniovertebral
junction

Juan P. Cabrera

1

, Igor Ebert Cechin

, Alderico Girão Campos de Barros

, and Luis Eduardo Carelli Texeira da Silva

University of Concepción, Concepcion, Chile

Instituto Nacional de Traumatologia e Ortopedia Jammil Haddad

Introduction: The standard treatment for a fixed coronal
malalignment of the craniovertebral junction is an anterior and/or posterior
column osteotomy plus instrumentation. However, the procedure is very

## P054: Cross-sectional area of the longus colli and cervical degenerative
spondylolisthesis: a retrospective review evaluating this anatomic
consideration

Aditya Mazmudar

1

, Khoa Tran

1

, Taylor Paziuk

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Eric Tecce

1

, Olivia Blaber

1

, Daniel Habbal

1

, Kamil Okroj

1

, Brian Karamian

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Jeffrey Rihn

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas Jefferson University,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Limited literature is available to define the
impact of the longus colli muscle, a deep flexor of the spine, on cervical
spine stability despite its close proximity to the vertebrae. No studies
have investigated longus colli cross-sectional area (CSA) in patients with
cervical spondylolisthesis. The purpose of this study was to determine if
longus colli CSA is associated with the severity preoperative cervical
degenerative spondylolisthesis. Material and Methods: A
retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients who underwent one- to
five-level ACDF between 2010 and 2021 at a single, academic center for
clinical symptoms of radiculopathy, myelopathy, or mixed radiculomyelopathy
in the setting of cervical spondylolisthesis. Patient data was obtained
using a Structured Query Language search and manual chart review. Patients
who lacked a preoperative cervical spine MRI or radiograph or had surgical
intervention to address infection, trauma, tumor, or revision of a prior
instrumented cervical fusion surgery were excluded from analysis. Longus
colli cross-sectional areas (CSA) were measured from preoperative MRI images
at the C5 level. Preoperative spondylolisthesis measurements were recorded
with cervical radiographs. For each patient, the highest degree of
spondylolisthesis measured among levels fused was determined as the “maximum
spondylolisthesis measured.” Patients were grouped by quartiles respectively
according to longus colli CSAs. Statistical tests compared patient
demographics, surgical characteristics, and surgical outcomes between
groups. Multiple linear regression analysis was utilized to assess if longus
colli CSA predicted cervical spondylolisthesis. Results: A
total of 157 patients met inclusion criteria. Group 1 (first quartile) was
the oldest (60.4 ± 12.0 years, p = 0.024) and was predominantly female
(59.0%, p = 0.001). Group 1 also had the highest maximum spondylolisthesis
(0.19 mm, p = 0.031) and highest proportion of grade 2 spondylolisthesis
(23.1%, p = 0.003). On regression analysis, lowest quartile of longus colli
CSA was an independent predictor of larger measured maximum
spondylolisthesis (β: 0.04, p = 0.012). There were no differences for levels
fused, revisions, readmissions, or surgical complications between groups (p
> 0.05). Conclusion: Smaller longus colli CSA is
independently associated with a higher grade and degree of preoperative
cervical spondylolisthesis, but this finding does not result in adverse
postsurgical outcomes. Further research targeted at improving our
understanding of how longus colli strengthening affects cervical
spondylolisthesis is indicated given our findings.

## P055: Lower hounsfield units at the planned lowest instrumented vertebra
is an independent risk factor for distal junctional kyphosis following adult

Peter Passias

, Tyler Williamson

, Rachel Joujon-Roche

1

, Peter Tretiakov

, Bailey Imbo

, Pooja Dave

, Heiko Koller

, Renaud Lafage

6

, Virginie Lafage

, and Themistocles Protopsaltis

NYU Langone Medical Center, New York, United States

SUNY Downstate Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: The association of Hounsfield units (HU) and
junctional pathologies has emerged as a topic of interest in thoracolumbar
surgery. The relationships between HUs and complications like distal
junctional kyphosis (DJK) in cervical deformity (CD) surgery have not been
elucidated. The objective of this study is to assess whether bone mineral
density of the LIV, as assessed by HUs, is prognostic for the risk of DJK
after CD surgery. Methods: CD patients with 2-year (2Y) data
included. HUs were measured at the LIV, LIV+1, C3 and C7 on all preoperative
CT scans, averaging the widest region of interest (ROI) ellipse within
sub-cortical bone across three axial slices for each vertebra. The primary

5.0, [1.2-17.7]; p = .023). Conclusion: Low bone mineral
density at the lowest instrumented vertebra, as assessed by a threshold
lower than 245 Hounsfield units, may be a crucial risk factor for the
development of distal junctional kyphosis after cervical deformity surgery.

mitigate this modifiable risk factor.

Introduction: Surgical correction of adult cervical deformity
(CD) has high rates of complication. However, patients often derive
significant benefits in functional status and quality of life from surgical
intervention despite being deemed at high risk of complication. It has yet
to be investigated whether spine surgeons are improving surgery for high
risk patients and minimizing poor outcomes. Material and
Methods: Operative CD patients ≥ 18yrs with complete pre-(BL) and
2-year(2Y) multi-center data were stratified by year of surgery from 2013 to
2018. Patients were categorized as 2013 to 2014[Early] or 2015 to
2018[Recent]. High risk [HR] patients were defined as meeting ≥ 2 of the
following criteria: 1) Baseline C2-C7 Cobb > 15° or T1S-CL ≥ 35° or C2-C7
cSVA > 4 cm or CBVA > 25° 2) being elderly [≥ 70 years], 3) severe BL
frailty [Miller frailty index], 4) CCI ≥ 1 SD above the cohort mean, 5)
undergoing 3-column osteotomy (3CO), and 6) fusion of > 10 levels, or
> 7 levels for elderly patient. Means comparison analysis assessed
differences in demographics, HRQLs, radiographic alignment, and
complications between groups. Stepwise multivariable linear regression
described associations between increasing year of surgery and complication
rates. Results: 82 CD pts met high-risk inclusion criteria
(62.11 ± 10.87 yrs, 63.7%F, BMI:29.70 ± 8.16 kg/m2, CCI: 1.07 ±
1.45), and underwent surgery (levels fused 9.4 ± 3.9, EBL: 866.51 mL). 39.0%

(p = .024). Surgically, Recent HR patients were more likely to undergo a
partial facet joint osteotomy (p = .042), though less likely to undergo a
PSO (p = .003). In terms of HRQLs, at 1Y Recent HR patients were more likely
to improve in SWAL-QOL – Communication (p = .035) and 2Y Eating Duration
domains (p = .038). By post-op complications, Recent HR patients were
significantly less likely to experience bladder incontinence at 1Y (p =
.024). Furthermore, Recent HR patients were significantly less likely to
experience any post-operative adverse events overall (p = .020), or
complications such as dysphagia (p = .045). Regression revealed increasing
year of surgery to be correlated with decreasing minor complication rates (β
= -0.166, p = .030), as well as lowered rates of DJK by 2Y (β = -0.152, p =
.048). Kaplan-Meier 2Y survival analysis revealed that of 9 Early (15.25%)
and 1 Recent (4.35%) HR patients had expired, with mean survival time was
71.56 weeks for Early HR patients, and 70.00 weeks for Recent HR patients (p
= .636). Conclusion: Over time, high-risk cervical deformity
patients have increased in frequency and comorbidity rates, yet have
demonstrated improved clinical, radiographic, and post-operative outcomes.
These findings suggest that spine surgeons have improved over time in
optimizing outcomes and patient selection, and reducing potential adverse
events associated for high-risk patients.

## 1613

## P057: Redefining cervical spinal deformity - When are sagittal plan
realignment procedures necessary?

Venu Nemani

1

, Philip Louie

1

, Caroline Drolet

1

, and John Rhee

2

1

Neurosurgery, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, Seattle, United
States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery and Neurosurgery, Emory University, Atlanta,
United States

Introduction: Cervical sagittal deformity (CSD) is an extremely
disabling condition and can be associated with concomitant myelopathy,
radiculopathy, or both. While there are radiographic parameters that define
the presence of CSD, the question remains as to whether these criteria are
sufficient to warrant a diagnosis of CSD. Further, it is unclear when a CSD
realignment procedure is warranted versus a less invasive procedure only to
address cervical myelopathy or radiculopathy, given the increased complexity
and risk of CSD realignment surgery. Material and Methods: With
these questions in mind, we conducted a REDCap survey of cervical spine
surgeons to determine if there is a consensus as to 1) the definition of a
cervical sagittal plane deformity, and 2) when a cervical sagittal plane
deformity merits a sagittal realignment procedure with its associated risks.
The survey was distributed to 82 surgeons with differing experience,
training background (neurosurgery vs orthopaedic surgery), and practice
environment (University setting vs private or hospital employed). The
questions were designed to determine whether the current published
radiographic criteria were sufficient alone to establish a diagnosis of CSD
or whether other clinical and physical exam factors were also thought to be
necessary in the diagnosis of CSD. We presented clinical vignettes to
determine which radiographic parameters would require correction in the
setting of clinical signs and symptoms such as radiculopathy, myelopathy,
axial neck pain, and difficulty holding head upright, and when a more
extensive “deformity” procedure was warranted. Results: We
received responses from 41 surgeons (33 orthopaedic surgeons, 8
neurosurgeons) with 93% working in an academic environment. 41% of surgeons
had 6-15 years of experience and 59% had 16+ years of experience. 80% of the
surgeons devote greater than 50% of their surgical practice to treating
patients with cervical spine disorders. 93% of the surgeons perform a
realignment procedure for CSD at least once every three months. There was no
consensus on whether isolated radiographic abnormalities previously defined
as associated with the need for cervical deformity surgery or a history of
difficulty holding one’s head upright was sufficient to establish a
diagnosis of CSD. However, when one or more of these radiographic criteria
were also associated with a clinical history of difficulty holding one’s
head upright, 29% of surgeons felt this was sufficient establish a diagnosis
of CSD. Surgeons generally felt that a CSD realignment procedure was more
necessary in patients presenting with cervical myelopathy compared to
cervical radiculopathy. While there was no clear consensus on what
radiographic criteria needed CSD correction in patients with myelopathy, the
most common parameters deemed important were C2-C7 SVA and C2-C7 kyphosis.
Conclusion: Despite numerous published studies, there is no
consensus amongst a diverse group of cervical spine surgeons as to what
radiographic and/or clinical criteria are necessary to define the presence
of CSD. Surgeons are more apt to perform CSD realignment procedures in
patients with myelopathy versus those with radiculopathy alone. More work is
necessary to refine the definition of CSD and what patients will benefit
from a sagittal plane realignment procedure.

## P058: Are two surgeries necessary for correction of one deformity -
Cervical kyphosis in neurofibromatosis? A rare case report

Jayprakash Modi

1,2

 and Pratikkumar Prajapati

2

1

Orthopaedic, Nutan Medical College, Mehsansa, India

2

Orthopaedic, B J Medical College, Ahmedabad, India

Introduction: Dystrophic neurofibromatosis type I, involving
upper cervical spines, is rare, which can cause serious complications.
Myelopathy develops due to compression of the cord posteriorly. Surgical
correction has its inherent risks and difficulties because of poor bone
quality, difficult anterior approach because of bizarre deformities, and the
necessary manipulation, which might cause more cord damage and ischemia.
Anterior decompression with alignment correction was an early popular
choice. But without posterior shortening, the technique proved
unsatisfactory in restoring normal alignment. It tended to expose the graft
bone at increased risk of insufficient union or extruding. So a combination
of anterior decompression and posterior correction was generally
recommended. Materials and Methods: This is a rare case study
of a patient operated at tertiary care centre having non-traumatic
involvement of spinal cord affecting neurology with history, clinical and
radiological features suggesting Cervical Nuerofibromatosis as the cause of
compression. This report describes surgical technique applicable to cases of
severe cervical kyphosis using only anterior approach. Result:
A 13-year-old boy, a case of neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with neck
pain, and bilateral upper limb radiculopathy for 2 months with affected
daily living, with intact neurology. Imaging demonstrated 46° kyphosis
(C3-C5),marked dystrophic changes of the C4 and C5, extreme dorsal
angulation indenting the cord. Anterior surgery was planned for the patient
with neuro-monitoring. Through left anterior approach, total C3, C4 and C5
corpectomy was accomplished, keeping the PLL intact. The defect was filled
with a fibular cortical graft which was stabilized with 48 mm cervical screw
plate, showing full correction of kyphosis postoperatively. At the follow-up
6 months postoperatively, lateral plain radiograph showed stability of the
cervical spine fusion without correction loss. The patient had full relief
from tingling and numbness with no neurological deficit and could resume his
daily duties. Patient is asymptomatic at 2 years follow up.
Conclusion: Only anterior decompression and fusion are
effective in satisfactorily correcting cervical kyphosis in cases of
neurofibromatosis without neurologic compromise and avoids the risk of
damage to vital neurovascular structures because of pedicle or lateral mass
screw fixation.

## P060: Comparison of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) correction-open

, and Eeric Truumees

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United

Introduction: Both open and minimally invasive surgery (MIS)

loss (EBL) and hospital length of stay (LOS). Aim: We report
the surgical and deformity corrections outcomes in matched cohorts of
Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) patients with similar Lenke types that
had undergone either open or MIS at 2 years follow-up at one institution.

were 76.4% (±8.1%) and 76.8% (±7.4%) respectively. The differences in
correction did not reach statistical significance. Mean 1- and 2-years
post-op VAS scores for MIS and open groups were 3.3 and 3.6, and 3.3 and
3.8, respectively (p > 0.05). For MIS and open group, mean 1- and 2-years
post-op ODI scores were 6.4 and 10, and 4 and 8, respectively (p > 0.05).
Mean 1- and 2-years post-op SRS scores for MIS and open groups were 4.3 and
4.1, and 4.6 and 4.2, respectively (p > 0.05). Conclusions:
In these specific curve types, our cohort data indicates that MIS technique
for scoliosis correction is a viable option and can attain corrections
equivalent to open surgery with lower EBL and shorter LOS. Additionally,
patient reported outcomes over 2 years follow up, as indicated by VAS, ODI
and SRS were comparatively better in the MIS over the open group.

## P061: Does a minimally invasive surgical technique affect intraoperative
and post-operative blood glucose levels in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
correction?

Matthew Geck

1

, Devender Singh

1

, Ashley Duncan

1

, John Stokes

1

, and Eeric Truumees

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Surgical intervention induces trauma and
stimulates the neuroendocrine stress response, releasing a cascade of
hormones ultimately resulting in hyperglycemia. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia
has long been associated with increased risk of surgical site infections and
complications with wound healing. Aim: To examine if a
minimally invasive surgical (MIS) technique influences perioperative blood
glucose levels of patients undergoing surgical correction for Adolescent
Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). Materials and Methods: The charts
of 35 patients undergoing surgical correction for AIS were reviewed.
Patients were divided into two cohorts based on surgical approach, open or
MIS. Variables including blood glucose levels at preoperative,
intraoperative, and post-operative day three were collected. Average
Intraoperative Blood Glucose was the mean of three blood glucose levels
taken from intraoperative blood gases. The presence of endocrine pathology
was defined broadly but included diabetes as well as abnormal vitamin D
levels (< 30 nmol/L). Results: The open cohort was comprised
of 18 patients, and the MIS included 17. 24% of the open were male, in
comparison to 6% of the MIS. Mean age and Body Mass Index were similar in
both groups. Overall presence of an endocrine issue was 60%. Of these, 95%
were abnormal vitamin D levels (8 deficiency, 12 insufficiency) and one
patient had a diagnosis of hypothyroidism. The incidence of endocrine issues
varied significantly in the open (n = 14) versus the MIS (n = 7). Mean
preoperative glucose was 89.3 ± 13.1 mg/dL, with no significant difference
between MIS and Open. Three blood glucose levels were averaged from blood
gases samples taken intraoperatively, with a mean of 90.7 ± 7.9 mg/dL. There
was no significant difference in mean intraoperative blood glucose levels
between MIS (89.7 ± 8 mg/dL) and Open (90.4 ± 11.8 mg/dL). Blood glucose
levels were highest on postoperative day 1 (POD1), mean 117.1 ± 12.5 mg/dL,
and consistently decreased over postoperative days 2 and 3, 106.6 ± 16.3
mg/dL and 99.3 ± 8.4 mg/dL respectively. There was no significant difference
in postoperative blood glucose levels between the two groups.
Conclusion: Though there was a significantly higher
incidence of endocrine issues in the open, there was no statistical
difference in blood glucose levels at any of the defined intervals between
the two groups. Blood glucose was the highest on POD1 in both groups and
tapered down each subsequent postoperative day in alignment with literature.
Though this sample population did not demonstrate significant differences
between groups, a larger prospective study to better understand the role of
endocrine issues and glucose levels on the risks and outcomes of AIS
correction is still warranted.

thromboelastography (TEG: G, K, angle), total bleeding volume and

correlation between bleeding and clinical variables with level of
significance set at α = 0.05. Results: In this cohort, mean
patient age was 17 years (11-48 years) with 94% of female patients. Mean BMI
was found to be 19.8 (±3.2). Curves were classified as: 42 Lenke 1A, 13
Lenke 1B, 4 Lenke 1C; 8 Lenke 5C. Mean TEG values were within normal range
in both males and females. Mean Hb, platelet count and fibrinogen
concentration were 11.12 (±1.3) g/L, 238.24 (±72.18) (x109/L) and
216.4 (±33.6) g/dL, respectively. Mean total bleeding was 152 ± 75 ml.
Pre-op fibrinogen did not correlate significantly with the total bleeding (r
= 0.34, p > 0.05). Other variables such as OR, PT, aPTT, INR, TEG and
platelet count did not correlate significantly with fibrinogen (p >
0.05). Total bleeding volume correlated significantly with cell saver (r =
0.687, p < 0.05). None of the other variables correlated significantly
with total bleeding volume (p > 0.05). Conclusions: Our
cohort analysis indicates that pre-op fibrinogen concentration does not
correlate significantly with the total bleeding volume in patients
undergoing AIS reconstruction using MIS technique. However, there was a
strong positive relationship between the total bleeding volume and
transfusion requirements.
