## P063: Does Cobb angle correlate with self-reported outcomes of patients
undergoing adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) reconstruction?

Matthew Geck

1

, Devender Singh

1

, Ashley Duncan

1

, John Stokes

1

, and Eeric Truumees

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Cobb Angle is widely used to quantify the
magnitude of spinal deformity. Clinicians use this tool to track the degree
of scoliosis correction following surgical interventions. Aim:
This study investigates the correlation between Cobb angles and
self-reported outcomes of patients undergoing minimally invasive surgical
(MIS) stabilization of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS).
Materials/Methods: 67 consecutive patients undergoing MIS
correction of AIS were prospectively studied. Age, Body mass index (BMI),
Lenke curve, preoperative (pre-op) and postoperative (post-op) Cobb angles,
Scoliosis Research Society-22r (SRS-22r), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) were evaluated. Mean (standard deviations)
were calculated. Surgical technique was uniform in all patients using two or
three para-midline incisions. At different pre-op and post-op time periods,
linear regressions were conducted in which the Cobb angle was the
independent variable and outcome scores were the dependent variables.
Results: Mean patient age was 16.5 years (11 - 47 years).
Mean BMI was found to be 21.5 (±1.9) Curves were classified as: 42 Lenke 1A,
13 Lenke 1B, 4 Lenke 1C; 8 Lenke 5C. Mean flexibility index of main curve
was 54.46% (±10.43%). Pre-op VAS and ODI were weakly correlated with pre-op
Cobb Angles with r2 = 0.05 and 0.110, respectively. At 2 weeks, 6
months, 1 year and 2 years post-op, the correlation between post-op Cobb
angles and VAS gradually improved from weak to moderate with r2 =
0.0027, 0.0067, 0.085 and 0.404, respectively. Similarly, post-op Cobb
angles and ODI at 2 weeks, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years follow-ups were
consistently correlated weakly with r2 = 0.118, 0.112, 0.091 and
0.118, respectively. SRS-22r and post-op Cobb angles at 1- and 2-years
follow-ups were weakly correlated with r2 = 0.028 and 0.035,
respectively. Conclusions: Our cohort’s data indicate that Cobb
angle and self-reported patient outcomes are weakly correlated. There is no
gold standard to measure the surgical outcomes in MIS; rather clinicians
should rely on combination of tools varying from radiographic evaluations,
patient reported outcome measures to their own clinical judgments.

## P064: Posterior vertebral tethering as an outpatient surgical option for
select cases of pediatric scoliosis: a case series

Kira Furie

1

, Hao-Hua Wu

2

, and Mohammad Diab

3

1

School of Medicine

2

Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Harvard Medical School/ Massachusetts
General Hospital & Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, United
States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, United
States

Introduction: Surgical treatment for scoliosis is typically an
inpatient procedure. Posterior vertebral tethering (PVT) is a novel
fusionless surgery that can be performed as an outpatient procedure in
select patients. The purpose of this case series is to describe outpatient
PVT and to report on minimum 12-month follow-up. Material and
Methods: In this retrospective case series, skeletally immature
patients diagnosed with idiopathic scoliosis who underwent outpatient PVT
performed by a single surgeon at an academic medical center from 2018-2022
were included. The primary outcome was no significant progression of Cobb
angle ± 5° for measurement error. Cobb angles were measured and recorded for
the most recent preoperative visit and all postoperative visits. Surveys
were administered via phone to assess for pain, satisfaction, and return to
activities. Pain ratings were given on a visual analogue scale (VAAS) from
0-10. Results: Four patients (mean age 12 ± 1.2 years) were
enrolled with mean 24.3 ± 10.2 months follow-up. Patients had a 17.8 ± 5.4°
reduction in Cobb angle that was significant at most recent postoperative
visit (p = 0.03). Patients reported lower current pain compared to
preoperative pain (1.5 ± 1.91 vs. 6.0 ± 0.82, p = 0.005). There were no
complications, revisions, or readmissions. All four patients discharged on
the same day of index operation. Additionally, all patients (100%) reported
their back feeling normal during both daily life and sports. Patients took
on average 2.8 ± 1.0 weeks to return to school and 14.0 ± 6.9 weeks to fully
return to sports. All patients (100%) reported having no stiffness,
instability, or decreased range of motion. All four patients (100%) reported
they were satisfied with the operative treatment and would elect to have the
procedure again. Conclusion: This is the first paper to
describe outpatient PVT. At minimum 12 months postoperatively, PVT patients
had significantly reduced Cobb angles, no complications, no revisions, and
reported being able to return to both daily life and sport. This may be a
less morbid surgical approach to pediatric scoliosis.

## 165

## P065: Posterior scoliosis surgery method that preserves motion by curve
correction and fusion within the major curve(s) and by posterior vertebral
tethering

Saechin Kim

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Harvard Medical School - Massachusetts General
Hospital, Boston, United States

Introduction: The surgical goals for pediatric scoliosis are to
arrest curve progression, create a balanced/stable spine, and preserve
spinal motion by fusing fewer levels, especially in the lumbar spine. In
standard posterior surgery, spinal fixation is applied above, within, and
below the curve and after corrective maneuvers, the levels are fused. In
doing so, levels where the disc angle fully corrects or reverses on side
bending are also fused. We describe a posterior scoliosis surgical method
that can change the disc angle at each individual level and allow the
surgeon to either capture the change with rod for fusion or with polyester
fiber for non-fusion or tethering. Our hypothesis is that this method is
safe and effective and can preserve motion. Material and
Methods: The novel technique is based on the observation that
manipulation of rods placed intravertebral interpedicle (IVIP) in two
adjacent vertebrae can directly change the disc angle between the vertebrae.
In this IVIP method, IVIP constructs with open lateral offset connectors
correct the deformity at the apex of the major curve(s) and the correction
is captured by placing rods into the open tulips of the constructs. IVIP
constructs with closed lateral offset connectors correct the deformity along
the convexity of the major curve(s) above or below the apical fusion or of
the minor compensatory curve and the correction is captured by polyester
fiber bands for IVIP tethering. This prospective study presents the first
ten consecutive cases by a single surgeon using this IVIP method (min 1 yr
f/u). The number of levels fused is compared to matched standard posterior
surgery controls. Radiographic measurements from xrays at first and final
f/u assess for adding on phenomenon (AO) and from side bending xrays at
preop and 1 year f/u determine lateral range of motion (ROM) at the tethered
lumbar levels. Results: The IVIP group included 8 patients with
adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Lenke classification: 1 1A, 1 1B, 2 1C, 2
3C, 1 4C, and 1 5C), 1 with tethered cord syndrome and 1 with tuberous
sclerosis (female:male 9:1, avg age = 16 yrs, range 13-19). 4 to 10 fewer
levels were fused in the IVIP cases compared to the control cases (p =<
0.0001). There was no adding on phenomenon and no reoperation. 4 patients
had at least 2 lumbar levels with IVIP tethering that would have been fused
in standard posterior surgery and side bending xrays showed increase in the
lateral lumbar ROM post op compared to preop by 18%, 22%, 43%, and 50%; in
standard posterior surgery, these lumbar levels would have been fused
resulting in significantly decreased lumbar lateral ROM.
Conclusion: IVIP method is safe and effective and can
preserve motion by fusing fewer levels at 1 year f/u. A concern with fusing
fewer levels is the risk for spinal decompensation (SD) such as AO that may
lead to worse outcome. IVIP tethering may prevent SD while preserving motion
even in skeletally mature adolescents. Further studies are needed to show
the long-term effectiveness of this IVIP method.

## P066: Changes in curve between 40 degrees and 50 degrees in adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis after skeletal maturity: over 5-year follow-up

Yunjin Nam

1

, Young Bin Lee

1

, Young Ha Kim

1

, Jungwook Lim

1

, Seong Chul Park

2

, Hong Jin Kim

3

, Dong-Gune Chang

3

, Jae Hyuk Yang

2

, and Seung Woo Suh

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Korea University Guro Hospital, Seoul,
South Korea

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Korea University Anam Hospital, Seoul,
South Korea

3

Department of Orthopaedics, Inje University Sanggye Paik Hospital,
Seoul

Introduction: Although adolescent idiopathic scoliosis rarely
causes clinical symptoms, it causes cosmetic and emotional effects and can
cause pulmonary complication with severe deformity. Female, large magnitude
of curvature, and skeletal immaturity are known to be the risk factors for
progression of curve. Surgical treatment is recommended if curvature is
larger than 50 degrees even after skeletal maturity or if curvature is
larger than 40 degrees with remaining growth potential. However, few
articles have reported on progression of curve between 40 and 50 degrees
after skeletal maturation. Material and Methods: This study is
a single center, retrospective study using medical record. From 1999 to
2016, 87 patients were included. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i)
skeletally matured patients who diagnosed with adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis, (ii) who have curve between 40 and 50 degrees, and (iii) who
followed up more than 5 years after initial period without surgical
treatment. Skeletal maturation was defined as Risser stages 4 and 5. The
initial period was defined as the first time point that satisfies both (i)
and (ii). The sex, age, magnitude of curve, location of apex, Risser stage,
height and weight were measured at initial period. The age, magnitude of
curve, height and weight were also measured at end of follow-up. A change in
the magnitude of curve, magnitude of curve per a year, height and weight
were measured. More than 5 degrees of progression in curve was defined as
significant curve progression. Results: A total of 97 curves
were observed in 87 patients (19 male, 69 female). Mean follow-up period was
97 months. The mean age was 14.6 years at initial period and 22.6 years at
the end of follow-up. Initially, 65 patients had Risser stage 4 and 32
patients had Risser stage 5. The mean magnitude of curve was 42.6 degrees at
initial period and 45.1 degrees at the final follow-up. The mean change in
curve was 2.7 degree and the annual change was 0.35 degrees. Progression in
curve more than 5 degrees were observed in 38 cases (39.2%). In 24 cases
(24.7%), the magnitude of curve reached 50 degrees at the end of follow-up.
There was a difference only in the age (13.9 vs. 15.0 years, p = 0.004) and
Risser stage (stage 4: 47.7% vs. stage 5: 5.21%, p = 0.014) between the
group with a significant curve progression or not. Risser stage (p = 0.05)
and magnitude of curve at initial period (p = 0.045) showed significant
difference between the group of curve size reached 50 degrees or not.
Conclusion: In patients with AIS, significant curve
progression was observed at 39.2% even after skeletal maturation. Younger
age and Risser stage 4 were risk factors of curve progression. Larger
initial curve and Risser stage 4 were risk factors of curve progression over
50 degrees.

## P067: The accuracy and safety of a pedicle screw using the freehand
technique in minimally invasive scoliosis surgery

Yunjin Nam

1

, Dong-Gune Chang

2

, Sangmin Lee

1

, Young Ha Kim

1

, Jungwook Lim

1

, Seong Chul Park

3

, Hong Jin Kim

2

, Jae Hyuk Yang

3

, and Seung Woo Suh

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Korea University Guro Hospital, Seoul,
South Korea

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Inje University Sanggye Paik Hospital,
Seoul, South Korea

3

Department of Orthopaedics, Korea University Anam Hospital, Seoul,
South Korea

Introduction: The safety and clinical usefulness of minimally
invasive scoliosis surgery (MISS) has been reported in various studies.
However, freehand pedicle screwing in MISS remains technically challenging.
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the accuracy and safety of pedicle
screw placement using the freehand technique in adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis (AIS) patients treated with MISS compared to conventional open
scoliosis surgery (COSS). Material and Methods: We included 76
patients who underwent deformity correction for AIS. CT scans were used to
assess screw violations divided into two groups according to the surgical
technique: MISS or COSS. Anterior violations were classified into Grade 0, 1
(no contact with internal organs), and 2 (contact with internal organs).
Medial and lateral violations were classified into Grade 0, 1 (< 2 mm),
and 3 (≥ 2 mm). Grade 2 were considered critical violations.
Results: A total of 630 and 634 pedicle screws were
inserted in the MISS and COSS groups, respectively. The overall critical
violation rates of the MISS and COSS groups were 16.8% (106 screws) and
14.0% (165 screws) (p = 0.116). Medial critical violations on the left side
in the middle thoracic region frequently occurred in the MISS group compared
to the COSS group (p = 0.003). There were no statistical differences in the
complications. Conclusion: Pedicle screw placement using the
freehand technique in MISS for AIS patients provided similar accuracy and
safety compared to COSS. Pedicle screws inserted on the left side of the
middle thoracic region, exhibited more medial critical violations in the
MISS group.

## P068: Substantial mismatch of skeletal maturity assessment between Risser
sign and Simplified Skeletal Maturity Scale (SSMS) / Thumb Ossification
Composite Index (TOCI) in patients with adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis

Masaaki Chazono

1

, Takashi Inoue

2

, and Shintaro Obata

2

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Utsunoimya National Hospital, Utsunomiya,
Tochigi, Japan

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Jikei University School of Medicine, Minato-ku,
Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: The Risser sign (RS) has been used as a primary
skeletal maturity marker in patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
(AIS) for more than half a century. However, there is considerable argument
about the ambiguous visibility of iliac apophyseal ossification, decreased
intra- and inter-rater reliability, and the insensitivity of the Risser sign
in predicting the timing of peak height velocity (PHV) and estimating the
remaining growth potential. Additionally, PHV and two-thirds of pubertal
growth typically have passed before the first stage of RS. Nevertheless, it
is still commonly used to manage the evaluation of skeletal maturity of AIS
patients in clinical practice. Currently, there are several radiograph-based
skeletal maturity scoring systems used to gauge the amount of childhood
growth and determine the timing of PHV. In particular, hand skeletal
maturity systems such as the Simplified Skeletal Maturity Scale (SSMS) or
the Thumb Ossification Composite Index (TOCI) are popular in the attempt to
predict the occurrence of PHV in adolescents. This study aims to compare the
frequency of the mismatch in estimation of HV between Risser sign (RS) and
SSMS/TOCI stages in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) patients.
Material and Methods: One hundred twenty-six female
patients with AIS were included. The mean age of the patients was 12.9
years. A whole spine and hand X-rays were obtained to establish skeletal
maturity stage according to RS, SSMS, and TOCI systems. A mismatch resulting
in overestimation (MOE) with RS compared to SSMS/TOCI was defined as the
combination of RS 2-4/SSMS 3-5 or RS 2-4/TOCI 4-6, whereas a mismatch
resulting in underestimation (MUE) with RS and SSMS/TOCI was defined as RS
0-1/SSMS 6-7 or RS 0-1/TOCI 7-8. Height velocity (HV) was compared between
MOE/non-MOE and MUE/non-MUE groups. Results: Between RS and
SSMS, the rates of the MOE and MUE groups were 9.3% and 1.6%, respectively.
Between RS and TOCI, rates were 7.1% and 1.6%, respectively. With the
combination of RS and SSMS stages, an estimate of HV of 5.6 cm/year in the
MOE group was significantly larger than that of 2.9 cm/year in the non-MOE
group, and 3.7 cm/year in the MUE group was significantly smaller than 6.7
cm/year in the non-MUE group. Likewise, with the combination of RS and TOCI
stages, an estimate of HV of 5.6 cm/year in the MOE group was significantly
greater that of 2.8 cm/year in the non-MOE group, and 3.7 cm/year in the MUE
group was significantly smaller than 6.7 cm/year in the non-MUE group.
Conclusion: The present study showed that approximately 10%
of mismatch of those skeletal maturity assessments in RS/SSMS and RS/TOCI
groups occurred. Given those results, the authors advocate that either SSMS
or TOCI classification rather than RS should be used for managing patients
with AIS.

## P070: Hybrid posterior instrumentation and mini-open anterior release for
treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a retrospective
analysis

Vijay Kumar Loya

1

 and Charanjit Singh Dhillon

2

1

MRMCW, Orthopaedics & Spine, Hyderabad, India

2

MIOT International, Spine, Chennai, India

Objective: A retrospective analysis of the role of hybrid
instrumentation, mini-open anterior release in the treatment of adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis. Methods: Medical records and imaging of
43 patients operated between January 2008 to June 2014 were retrospectively
analyzed. Subgroup analysis was done for patients managed with mini-open
anterior release+ posterior instrumentation [APSF](13 patients) vs. all
posterior approach [PSF] (30 patients). Hybrid instrumentation was used
involving the use of hooks and sublaminar wires in conjunction with pedicle
screws. A mini open thoracotomy (< 10 cm incision) was used for anterior
release. The free-hand technique was used to insert all the pedicle screws.
Stagnara wake up test was used after correction maneuvers. Appearance scores
were collected before and after the surgery. Results: The mean
age of operated cases was 15.2 (range 10-28) years, and majority cases were
females (86.05%). The average follow-up time was 46.86 months. Lenke 1 was
the most common curve pattern [74.42%]. Significant correction was achieved
and maintained at the end of the follow-up period for all the curve patterns
[PT 66.67%, MT 75.20%, DL/L – 70.83%]. The sagittal plane alignment was
maintained in all but one patient. Mean [81.25° vs. 49.16°] and bending
[66.89° vs. 32°] Cobb angles were significantly higher in the APSF group.
Improvement in the appearance scores was significant for both the groups
[APSF - 25 vs. 10.78, PSF - 18.9 vs. 9.03]. Two of the APSF patients had
prolonged ICU stay. Two patients required secondary suturing for wound
dehiscence. One case had chylothorax, which was medically managed. One
patient required revision surgery for hook pull-out after 34 months of index
surgery. There were no neurological deficits, vascular or visceral injuries.
Conclusion: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis represents a
different set of challenges in developing nations with limited re- sources.
Hybrid instrumentation with the use of sublaminar wires is still an
effective and valid strategy to reduce the cost of spinal deformity
surgeries. A mini-open anterior release, along with the use of posterior
hybrid instrumentation, helps achieve optimal coronal and sagittal
correction, especially in bigger and stiffer curves, compared to all
posterior hybrid constructs. A decision tree is provided to guide the
treatment selection for the adolescent idiopathic scoliosis cases.

## P071: Medium term outcomes in early onset scoliosis patients who have
graduated from magnetically controlled growing rods to final fusion

Henry Turner

1

, Robin McManus

1

, Flavia Alberghina

1

, Jim Kennedy

1

, Jacques Noel

1

, and Patrick Kiely

1

1

Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgery, Children's Health Ireland (CHI) at
Crumlin, Dublin, Ireland

Introduction: There is paucity in the literature regarding
outcomes in patients with early onset scoliosis (EOS) who have graduated
from magnetically controlled growing rods (MCGR) to final fusion (FF). We
present our findings analyzing EOS patients who graduated to FF from MCGR.
Material and Methods: All EOS patients who had FF after
MCGR treatment and had a minimum follow-up time of 1 year were included. The
outcomes included additional unplanned surgeries (AUS), pre-and
post-operative Scoliosis Major Cobb (MCA) and Major Kyphosis (MKA) angles,
space available for lung ratios (SALR), T1- T12 and T1-S1 heights. Results
are presented as means with standard deviation (SD) and 95% Confidence
interval (CI). Results: 16 patients (9 Females and 7 Males)
were included. C-EOS classification breakdown was as follows: 1 Congenital,
6 Idiopathic, 4 Syndromic and 5 Neuromuscular patients. 14 patients were
excluded due to insufficient follow-up time. The mean age at index MCGR
surgery was 9.8 years (SD ±2.2, CI 8.6 - 10.9) and the mean implant time of
MCGR instrumentation was 38 months (SD ± 15, CI 30 - 46). The mean follow-up
after FF was 27 months (SD ±15, CI 20 - 37). Two (12.5%) patients needed
unplanned additional surgery after FF complications. All complications were
related to wound breakdown and infection. The preoperative and latest MCAs
post MCGR insertion were 73° (SD ±13, CI 66-80) and 51° (SD ±14, CI 44 -
59), respectively. The final MCA after FF was 30° (SD ±12, CI 25 - 38). The
preoperative and latest MKAs post MCGR insertion were 37° (SD ±25, CI 24 -
50) and 33° (SD ±25, CI 24 - 42) respectively. The final MKA after FF was
38° (SD ±19, CI 29 - 50). This is a significant final decrease of 59% (p
< 0.001) in the MCA but not in the MKA (p = 0.54). The preoperative and
latest SALRs post MCGR insertion were 90% (SD ± 113, CI 83-96) and 98% (SD
±5, CI 96-101), respectively. The final SALR after FF was 99% (SD ±7, CI
94-103): a final significant increase of 9% (p < 0.001). The preoperative
and latest T1- T12 heights post MCGR insertion were 184mm (SD ±22, CI 169 -
199) and 224 mm (SD ±35, CI 205-243) respectively. The final T1- T12 height
is 245 mm (SD ±33, CI 224-264), indicating a final increase of 33% (p <
0.001). The preoperative and latest T1-S1 heights post MCGR insertion were
291 mm (SD ±54, CI 262-320) and 354 mm (SD ±62, CI 321 - 387), respectively.
The final T1- S1 height after FF is 378mm (SD ±60, CI 343 - 413), showing a
total increase of 30 % (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Our findings
show that EOS patients who have graduated to final definitive fusion (FF)
from magnetically controlled growing rods (MCGR) can achieve satisfactory
outcomes over the short to medium term. Our study also shows that there is
potential for further deformity correction when progressing to FF from MCGR.
It must be noted that additional surgery may be required after FF in some
cases.

## P072: Nonunion and implant failure following kyphectomy for severe

Rohan Parihar

1

, Samir Dalvie

1

, Kshitij Chaudhary

1

, and Pramod NK

1

1

Spine, P.D. Hinduja Hospital, Mumbai, India

Introduction: 15% of patients with open neural tube defects
develop severe kyphosis requiring kyphectomy, a high-risk surgery .50% cases
develop non-union and implant failure. We presented an unreported cause of
non-union at the rudimentary L5-S1 disc following a kyphectomy. Also, we
describe preoperative planning using 3D printed spine model of patient.
Materials and Methods: 10-year-old girl, previously
operated for meningomyelocele closure at age 6 months, presented with a non

cause of nonunion at the rudimentary L5-S1 disc (S1 sacralized). During
surgery, special attention should be given to fusion of all disc levels,
including rudimentary disc that lie within the fixation levels. 3D printed
model are of enormous help in planning this complex surgery.

## P073: Interobserver findings in the validation process of an smartphone
application as a tool for screening patients with scoliosis

Andre Castilho

1

, Pedro Torres

1

, Asdrubal Falavigna

2

, Henrique Darmstadter

1

, Orlando Righesso

2

, and Kamila Rayane Campos Lopes

1

1

Spine Surgery, Hospital Unimed, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

2

Health Science Postgraduate Program, Universidade de Caxias do Sul
(UCS), Caxias do Sul, Brazil

Introduction: Scoliosis is a spinal condition that is common
among children, adolescents, and young adults, affecting approximately 1%-4%
of children and adolescents worldwide. Most patients with scoliosis have a
mild abnormal curvature of the spine and the curvature does not progress in
adulthood. However, a more pronounced curvature and a late diagnosis can
lead to reduced quality of life of patients. Early diagnosis of scoliosis
allows treatment in its initial stages and avoids surgical treatment and
deformity progression. The present study aims to analyze the best correlated
clinical parameters among examiners using an application for smartphone
developed for screening of idiopathic scoliosis and to evaluate the friendly
use of this application. Material and Methods: This study
assesses a smartphone mobile application that analyzes several clinical
parameters related to the changes observed in scoliosis. Comparative
analyses between medical and non-medical examiners were performed to define
parameters with the greatest inter- observer correlation.
Results: 89 participants. None of the parameters between
ExL and Ex1 achieved almost perfect concordance. Substantial concordance was
noted in reduced lordosis and mid-thoracic scoliometer. Fair agreement was
achieved in increased kyphosis, presence of a hump and waist asymmetry. All
the other parameters had slight or poor agreement. The presence of a hump,
scapular asymmetry, and waist asymmetry were statistically significant
changes found between examiners. In subjects diagnosed with shoulder
asymmetry, scapular, waist and pelvic, ribcage asymmetry was found between
ExL and Ex1 with statistical difference. None of the parameters between Ex1
and Ex2 achieved almost perfect and substantial concordance. Moderate
concordance was noted in pelvic asymmetry. Ribcage asymmetry and pelvic
asymmetry had fair concordance. In subjects diagnosed with shoulder
asymmetry, scapular, waist and pelvic, ribcage asymmetry had statistically
significant concordance between them. The results of the app friendly use
evaluation showed complete satisfaction of users in effectiveness, easiness
to learn, productive possibility and system interface satisfaction. The
worst results in the evaluation were easiness to use and capacity of solving
problems by the system and the user. Conclusion: This study is
the first to evaluate almost all the parameters in the physical examination
between medical and nonmedical examiners to improve the screening of
adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Our findings showed that reduced lordosis,
mid thoracic scoliometer, presence of hump, waist asymmetry, increased
kyphosis, ribcage asymmetry and pelvic asymmetry had substantial to fair
concordance. Shoulder asymmetry, one the parameters used as an alert in the
app showed a poor interobserver correlation. The inclusion of several
physical examination parameters of a patient with scoliosis will allow an
evaluation of which parameters present the greatest agreement, while
outpatient assessment by a spine specialist will permit the validation of
the application as a screening tool. In our initial results reduced
lordosis, mid-thoracic scoliometer and pelvic asymmetry had better agreement
between examiners. These parameters needed to be checked in outpatient
assessment to be validated. The main objective of the study is to create a
simple and effective tool for the screening of adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis by non-medical professionals, especially in the school
environment.

## 621

## P074: Is shoulder imbalance a useful parameter in the screening of
idiopathic scoliosis? A preliminary study

Pedro Torres

1

, Andre Castilho

1

, Asdrubal Falavigna

2

, Orlando Righesso

2

, David Israel

1

, and Kamila Rayane Campos Lopes

1

1

Spine Surgery, Hospital Unimed, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

2

Health Science Postgraduate Program, Universidade de Caxias do Sul
(UCS), Caxias do Sul, Brazil

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a structural,
lateral, rotated curvature of the spine that arises in otherwise healthy
children at or around puberty. It is the most common spinal disorder in
adolescents, with a prevalence of 1-4%. Early diagnosis of scoliosis allows
timely treatment of the condition in its initial stages, further avoiding
surgical treatment and deformity progression. Consequently, scoliosis
screening has been advocated for early detection of reversible spinal curves
before their progression. Screening of idiopathic scoliosis is widely
discussed in medical literature. It involves different types of assessment
methods, including appearance inspection, forward bending tests, scoliometer
measurements, and individual Moiré topography, which are direct and easily
accessible. Main findings of scoliosis on physical examination are asymmetry
of the shoulders, scapulae, pelvis, trunk, and ribcage. Adam's forward bend
test is used to assess the presence of a hump and quantify the lateral
curvature; it is considered essential for the screening of scoliosis in
schools. In The Netherlands and Singapore, countries with strong scoliosis
screening program, the most frequent parameter are the Adam’s forward
bending test and the measuring of trunk rotation using a scoliometer.
Between all parameters on physical examination, shoulder imbalance has
received a great deal of attention among spine surgeons and researchers. The
normal healthy population is considered to have level shoulders. In any
measured biological parameter, it is of prime importance that the
variability of what is classified as ‘normal’ is known, especially if
surgery is planned to correct that parameter from what is judged as
‘abnormal’ back to being ‘normal’. To define what is normal, Kuklo et al.
proposed shoulder balance as a less than 1 cm side-to-side difference
between the shoulders on clinical examination in adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis patients. The deficiencies of traditional assessment methods in
screening scoliosis remain unresolved. Regardless, a most effective method
is still crucial for reducing morbidities associated with scoliosis. The
present study aims to analyze the use of shoulder imbalance as a parameter
for scoliosis screening and its relationship with other parameters of
physical examination. Material and Methods: This study assesses
a smartphone application that analyzes several parameters of the physical
examination in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Medical and non-medical
examiners applied the screening tool in students in a public school and in a
sports club. After data collection, interobserver correlation was done to
verify shoulder imbalance and to compare shoulder imbalance with Adam’s
bending test and with trunk rotation. Results: 89 participants
were examined, 18 women and 71 men. The mean age of subjects from the public
school was 11.30 years and from the sports club was 11.92 years. The
examiners had poor to slight interobserver concordance on shoulder asymmetry
in the anterior and posterior view. No significant statistical correlation
was found between shoulder asymmetry and positive Adam’s forward bending
test. Conclusion: Our preliminary study shows that the shoulder
asymmetry has a poor correlation with Adam’s forward bending test and
measuring trunk rotation using a scoliometer. Therefore, the use of shoulder
imbalance might not be useful for idiopathic scoliosis screening.

## 628

## P075: Surgical treatment of severe adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
through one-stage posterior-only approach: systematic review and
meta-analysis

Giovanni Viroli

1

, Matteo Traversari

1

, Marco Manzetti

1

, Francesca Barile

1

, Fabio Vita

1

, Tosca Cerasoli

1

, Azzurra Paolucci

1

, Alberto Ruffilli

1

, and Cesare Faldini

1

1

1

st

Orthopaedic and Traumatologic Clinic, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico
Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Severe adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a
complex, stiff, three-dimensional spinal deformity whose treatment remains
controversial. Historically, severe AIS has often been treated with combined
anterior release, followed by posterior correction and instrumentation,
resulting in good three-dimensional curve correction, but with high risk of
pulmonary complications. Some authors have also used preoperative traction
or internal distraction as a part of a staged correction, in order to
achieve better correction and shorter fusion. However, pre-operative
traction implies an increased risk of perioperative complications such as
pin loosening, pin tract infection and cranial nerve palsies. Combined
anterior and posterior or all-posterior vertebral column resection has also
been used to treat severe and rigid scoliosis, but this demanding procedure
is affected by a considerably high rate of perioperative complications.
Then, the introduction of all pedicle screws constructs allowed the
all-posterior procedures to gradually gain popularity due to the high
reliability of three-columnar fixation systems. In fact, powerful corrective
forces were exerted and spine mobilization through anterior release was not
necessarily needed. Aim of this metanalysis is to systematically review the
literature and analyse the results of one-stage all posterior fusion for
severe adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Material and Methods: A
systematic search of articles about one stage posterior spinal fusion for
severe adolescent idiopathic scoliosis was conducted according to the PRISMA
guidelines. Studies were included if they involved patients affected by
severe adolescent idiopathic scoliosis who underwent surgical correction
through one stage posterior-only approach [variably combined with posterior
column osteotomies (PCOs), maximum grade 2 S] and if they described
perioperative outcomes including correction rate and complications. Only
articles in English who met the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison
and Outcomes) criteria on systematic reviews were included. Randomized
controlled trials (RCTs), prospective and retrospective cohort studies (PCS
and RCS) and case series (CS) were considered for inclusion. Data about
population, pre and postoperative radiographical data, surgical procedure
details and complications were extracted. Metanalyses were performed with
the application of a random effect model. Results: Thirteen
studies (613 patients) were included. The mean Cobb angle of the major curve
varied from 80.0° ± 7.3 to 110.8° ± 12.1. Meta-analysis showed a
comprehensive coronal correction rate of the major curve of 58.6%, a
comprehensive operative time of 252.1 min and a comprehensive EBL of 866.5
mL (95% CI 659.3 - 1073.6, I2≈0%). A total of 47 complications
(5.4%) were reported. Overall metanalysis showed a major complication rate
of 4%. In 6 cases revision surgery was needed. Conclusion: Our
results suggest that posterior-only approach (eventually combined with PCOs)
offers enough corrective power to effectively treat severe scoliosis curves,
with acceptable blood loss and complications rate. Further, it allows to
avoid possible adverse events and pulmonary function impairment related to
anterior approaches. Moreover, it is not burdened by the high complications
rate of VCR.

## 671

## P076: Correlation between single pulse and pulse train stimulation during
neuromonitoring of thoracic pedicle screws in scoliosis surgery

Luiz Eduardo Almeida

1

 and Luis Eduardo Carelli Texeira da Silva

2

1

Spine Surgery, Children’s State Hospital, Rio de Janeiro,
Brazil

2

Spine Surgery, National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics,
Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Introduction: The use of thoracic pedicle screws (TPSs) during
scoliosis surgery entails an inherent risk of neurological deficit.
Triggered electromyography (t-EMG) is an accurate neuromonitoring test for
detection of malpositioned TPSs. However, single-pulse (SP) t-EMG
stimulation has shown variable capability for detecting medial
pediclebreaches, while pulse-train (PT) t-EMG could be more accurate. The
aim of this study was to analyze the correlation between SP t-EMG and PT
t-EMG. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included
20 patients who underwent scoliosis correction with 294 TPSs placed. A total
of 588 tests with both SP t-EMG and PT t-EMG were performed, analyzed, and
compared. The results of both t-EMG techniques were stratified into 3
different groups according to threshold obtained: group 1 (≤ 6 mA), group 2
(6.1–11.9 mA), and group 3 (12 mA). A generalized linear modelwas used to
analyze the correlation between the methods. Results: SP t-EMG
elicited response in 5 screws (1.7%) at ≤ 6 mA, 28 screws (9.5%) at 6.1-11.9
mA, and 261 screws (88.8%) at 12 mA. PT t-EMG elicited response in 16 screws
(5.4%) at ≤ 6 mA, 30 screws (10.2%) at 6.1-11.9 mA, and 248 screws (84.4%)
at 12 mA. There is a strong positive and significant association between SP
t-EMG and PT t-EMG with a decrease ratio of 2% (95% confidence interval 1%
to 3%). Conclusion: SP t-EMG and PT t-EMG stimulation
techniques had similar results when the stimuli were applied to TPSs, but PT
t-EMG may have better efficacy in low-threshold group.

## 706

## P077: Minimally invasive surgery vs standard posterior approach in the
treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a two years follow up
retrospective study

Giovanni Ciani

1

, Francesco Vommaro

1

, Chiara Cini

1

, Bruna Maccaferri

1

, Luca Boriani

1

, Elisa Carretta

2

, and Alessandro Gasbarrini

1

1

Spine Surgery

2

Medical Statistics, Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna,
Italy

Study Design: Monocenter retrospective control study.
Purpose: To compare the safety and efficacy of posterior
minimally invasive surgery (MIS) to standard posterior spinal fusion (PSF)
surgery in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Methods: We
retrospective collected 111 patients with Lenke type 1-6 AIS with Cobb angle
curve ≤ 70° who treated with MIS (n = 47) or PSF (n = 64) between February
2018 and February 2020. All of them attempted an outpatient follow-up
consisting of clinical and radiological evaluation for at least two years
from surgery. We collected values of Cobb angles degrees to study the
correction rate of the structural major curve. MIS technique was applied via
2 midline noncontiguous skin incisions. Smaller incisions and
muscle-spearing approach could reduce the blood loss significantly. We
obtained an RD maneuver that takes advantages of the flexibility resulting
from the rising of the level arm and the consequent force exerted at the
caudocranial edges using MIS. Level of apical and distal fusion, operative
time, preoperative hemoglobin and second postoperative day hemoglobin, full
length of hospitalization and time to accomplish verticalization were
recorded. NRS medium score was assessed immediately after surgery and during
the whole physiotherapeutic treatment. Complications recorded included:
temporary or permanent nerve lesions, intraoperative or postoperative nerve
lesions, fever, surgical wound dehiscence and infection, mechanical
complication and postoperative pain assessment. Results: There
was no significant difference between the 2 groups in terms of radiographic
and clinical features. The correction rates of the structural curve were not
observed to be significantly different between group 1 (MIS) and 2 (PSF)
(64.6% ± 11.7 vs 60.9% ± 13.2) as for the correction rate of secondary curve
(59.1 ± 13.2 vs 59.2 ± 12.4). The two groups had non significantly longer
operative time (209.9 ± 34.8 min vs 215.2 ± 45.2). The MIS group had a
significantly lower decrease of postoperative hemoglobin in comparison to
PSF group (2.8 ± 1.3 vs 4.3 ± 1.5) (p < 0.001). The evaluation of pain
using NRS score showed a lower score in MIS group (1.8 ± 0.8 vs 2.8 ± 0.9).
PSF group was observed to have significantly lengthier time of
hospitalization (5.2 ± 1.4 vs 6.3 ± 2.9) (p = 0.02) than MFS group.
Complications were more frequent in PSF group rather than in MFS group (11
vs 3), with no infectious complication in MIS group and 6 events of post
operatory infections in PSF group. Only one mechanical complication
(breakage of rod) was observed in MSF group. The mechanical complication
recorded was successfully treated with a surgical approach.
Conclusion: Posterior MIS is a safe and capable alternative
to standard open approach for Lenke Type 1-6 AIS patients with curves <
70°, with analogue capacity of scoliosis correction. The average number of
fusion segments in MIS group was lower than in PSF group (9.1 vs 10.2). For
these reasons MIS technique could reduce the risk of post-operative
adding-on and permits to spare motion segments. Even though there were no
difference in term of operative time between MIS and PSF, our results showed
that MIS had the advantages of less blood loss, length of stay and pain.

## 786

## P078: Experience using internal distraction systems for scoliosis
correction between surgical stages

Andres Reinoso

1

, Fernando Alvarado Gómez

1

, Nahala Aborashed-Amador

1

, Martha Cecilia Santos-Barros

1

, Maria Garcia-Rueda

1

, Maria Camila Giraldo Bernal

1

, Mario Herrera Méndez

1

, and Carlos Montero-Silva

1

1

Instituto Roosevelt, Bogota, Colombia

Introduction: In the surgical treatment of severe scoliosis, the
risk of neurological injury increases when definitive correction is
attempted in a single stage. For this reason, devices like the gravitational
traction halo have been widely used over the years to partially and
progressively correct the deformity between surgical stages in an attempt at
improving lung capacity and reducing the risk of spinal cord ischemia.
However, this treatment is not risk-free. Complications have been described,
including transient nystagmus, osteitis, upper limb paresthesia and
myelopathy progression in up to 27% of cases. In 2006, Buchowski et al.
described the use of internal distraction as a method for temporary
correction in order to reduce deformities on the coronal and sagittal planes
before definitive fusion. Material and Methods: Retrospective
case series including 9 patients in total, with 7 patients requiring a
two-stage procedure and 2 requiring three stages. Patients considered for
more than one surgical stage in whom the internal distraction system was
used between surgeries were included. Demographic, clinical, radiological,
and surgical variables, as well as associated complications, were assessed.
Results: Average blood loss at the time of definitive
fusion was 911 ml, approximately. The mean number of osteotomies was 4.1,
the most frequently used being Ponte osteotomy. Additional techniques
included oblique osteotomy and corpectomy. The distraction system was used
during a mean of 11,11 days. Pre-operatively, average Cobb angle was 88°;
with the distraction system, the size of the curvature diminished by 30.6%
in average, with a residual deformity of 32° (36.4% of the initial curve).
Complications included one catheter-associated bacteremia, one urinary tract
infection, two cases of durotomy, and one case of phlebitis. No surgical
site infection complications occurred and there was no loss of somatosensory
evoked potentials. Conclusion: The use of internal distraction
systems in the intervening time between surgical procedures for the
correction of severe scoliosis has been shown to diminish the complexity and
number of osteotomies required to restore coronal balance. This technique is
associated with lower bleeding rates and a lower risk of nerve damage.

## 833

## P079: Tranexamic acid reduces preoperative blood loss in pediatric spinal
deformity surgery - a retrospective analysis in non-idiopathic scoliosis
patients

Anna Bichmann

1

, Ali Güven

2

, Edda Klotz

1

, Thomas Ocker

1

, Pumberger Matthias

2

, and Friederike Schömig

2

1

Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Surgery, Charité - Universitätsmedizin
Berlin, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Posterior spinal fusion in scoliosis patients is
associated with high volumes of perioperative blood loss and transfusion
requirements. Even though it has previously been shown that patients with
non-idiopathic scoliosis tend to lose higher blood volumes and more often
require allogenic blood transfusions perioperatively compared with
idiopathic scoliosis patients, there is a lack of studies investigating the
effect of tranexamic acid (TXA) in this patient group. We therefore analyzed
the efficacy of TXA in reducing perioperative blood loss and blood
transfusion requirements in non-idiopathic scoliosis patients undergoing
primary posterior spinal fusion. Material and Methods: We
retrospectively included patients who underwent primary posterior fusion for
non-idiopathic scoliosis between November 2014 and December 2020. Patients
were assigned to the TXA- or No-TXA-group depending on intraoperative
administration of TXA. Perioperative data including demographic and
laboratory data, spinal levels operated on, surgical duration, hemodynamic
parameters, administration of blood products, crystalloid fluids, and
catecholamines as well as radiographs were reviewed. Descriptive summaries
for the TXA- and No-TXA-groups were analyzed using Pearson Chi-squared test,
Student t-test, or Mann-Whitney-U-test. Changes in laboratory data were
compared using the two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
The influence of different variables on the estimated blood loss was
calculated by multiple linear regression. The association of various
parameters with surgery duration was analyzed by calculating Spearman’s rank
correlation. Results: Sixty-six patients were included, 35 of
which received intravenous TXA intraoperatively. Demographic and
preoperative laboratory data did not show significant differences between
the two groups. Surgical duration (p = 0.009) and number of levels fused (p
= 0.004) were significantly higher in the TXA-group. Estimated blood loss (p
= 0.531) and administration of allogenic packed erythrocytes (p = 0.508) did
not differ significantly. TXA administration had a significant negative
effect on estimated blood loss (B = -510.98, p = 0.020). Postoperative
Hb-levels were significantly higher in the TXA-group (9.13 ± 1.27 g/dL)
compared with the No-TXA-group (8.41 ± 1.47 g/dL) on the first postoperative
day (p = 0.038). There were no postoperative thromboembolic events prior to
patient discharge in either group. Other postoperative complications
including systemic inflammatory response syndrome (p = 0.818), hypovolemia
(p = 0.177), pneumonia (p = 0.628), pleural effusion (p = 0.177), urinary
tract infection (p = 0.628), and gastrointestinal complications (p = 0.209)
did not differ significantly between the two groups.
Conclusion: Despite longer surgical durations and more
spinal levels fused, patients receiving TXA when undergoing primary
posterior spinal fusion for non-idiopathic scoliosis had similar estimated
perioperative blood loss and allogenic transfusion rates as patients who did
not receive TXA. We show that TXA has a significant negative effect on
estimated blood loss in non-idiopathic scoliosis patients. Thus, as already
practiced in idiopathic scoliosis surgery, TXA should be considered to be
part of blood management strategies in non-idiopathic scoliosis surgery as
well.

• Verified acquired etiology of the primary disease.

mm. Conclusions: The freehand technique is a safe and effective
method of instrumentation of pedicle screws for the correction of AIS,
having a high rate of precision in screw placement, however the factors that
modify the success results such as the Cobb angle, pedicle dysplasia must be
taken into consideration for the success of surgery.

## 894

## P083: Outcome of surgical treatment of scoliosis with navigation and
neuromonitoring description of surgical technique

Ziad Mohamed

1

, Mohamed Zayan

1

, Loay Abukwedar

1

, and Antony Michael

1

1

Neuro Spinal Hospital, Dubai, United Arab Emirates

Introduction: Scoliosis is a spinal deformity that comprises a
lateral curvature and rotation of the patient’s vertebrae .The most
prevalently employed method of scoliosis correction surgery is posterior
fusion with instrumentation, representing the current gold standard
approach. Novel adaptations to this method have been made in recent years
resulted in enhanced correction and a reduced number of complications.
Improved intraoperative navigation permits a higher surgical accuracy during
spinal surgery and addresses limitations. Navigation and intraoperative
neuromonitoring represent novel technologies that can be employed in
scoliosis correction surgeries to optimize surgical outcomes due to enhanced
patient safety and improved surgical accuracy. In this study we evaluated
the clinical and radiologic outcome of using navigation and intraoperative
neuro-monitoring in scoliosis correction surgeries. Methods: In
this retrospective study, 24 patients with scoliosis who underwent scoliosis
correction surgery under navigation and intraoperative neuromonitoring. The
procedure in these patients was after positioning the patient in prone,
pressure areas padded, warming and calf pumps applied, a baseline spinal
multimodal monitoring recorded. Followed by Level check with x-ray to
identify the upper instrumented vertebrae(UIV) and lower instrumented
vertebrae (LIV). Posterior midline incision, bilateral sub-periosteal
dissection from transverse process. Furthermore, X-ray to confirm levels of
UIV and LIV. Followed by O-arm run in 2 stages for navigation installing,
pedicle screws inserted under navigation guidance. Screws stimulation are
carried out at this stage to check the screws insertion at 15mA and Checking
the insertion by X-ray. Then spinal releases done by inferior facetectomy
and superficial flavectomy, spinous processes and transverse processes

correction achieved by final x-ray and final spinal multimodal monitoring

(range,10-35). The mean preoperative Cobb angle of major curve in coronal
plane was 61.4° (range, 50°-92°) changed post operatively to 17.2° (range,
5°-50°) with mean correction rate of 72.5% (range, 45.6% – 90.9%). The total
number of screws inserted was 413 screws with mean of 17.2 (range, 10-21)
and the total number of instrumented segments was 283 segments with mean of
11.7 (range, 5-15). The mean operation time was 336 minutes (range, 240 m -
453 m), while the mean hospital stay was 9 days, (range, 4 d-32 d). In the
all patients there was no intraoperative complications inform of alerts in
INM, Dural tear and bleeding. There were no perioperative neurologic
deficits or mal-positioned screws requiring reoperation. The percentage of
other post-operative complications was 8.33% (2 patients).
Conclusion: Combinations using of navigation and
intraoperative neuromonitoring can provide better safety for the patients,
however, long-term data are needed.

## P084: Selective anterior scoliosis fusion is comparable to vertebral body
tethering

Edward King

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

movement are required. Anterior Fusion surgery can be considered in cases
where the patient may not be eligible for VBT.

## 957

## P085: A comparative study of anterior thoracic and anterior thoraco
columbar surgeries

Edward King

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

, Zion Hwang

1

, Bisola Ajayi

1

, Emily Tsang

1

, Darren Lui

1

, Jason Bernard

1

, and Timothy Bishop

1

1

St George's, University of London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Five decades ago Anterior Scoliosis Surgery was
the favoured approach compared to posterior. Limitations in instrumentation
for posterior surgery meant that limited derotation control was possible.
Harrington Rod surgery utilised level selection based on vertebra in the
midline with parallel discs to the floor. Anterior instrumentation allowed
shorter fusions and improved derotation and correction of kyphosis. They
also had their limitations with hardware failure and large incisional
approaches. With the advent of pedicle screw technology both monoblock and
then polyaxial, control of scoliosis improved and posterior surgery became
the modern gold standard. Vertebral body tethering (VBT) has ushered in a
return to the era of Anterior Screw placement and VBT has limited scope in
limited patient groups. Further improved hardware such as staples and HA
coated screws straight inner shanks and techniques have improved the failure
rates. We examined our group of Selective Anterior Thoracic Fusion (SATF)
and Selective lumbar-thoracic Anterior Fusion (SLAF). Methods:
Retrospective review of Anterior scoliosis fusion cases between 2017 and
2020. Analysis of radiographs and electronic patient records were conducted
as well as British spinal registry. Results: There were 56
anterior fusions. 71.4% were SATF and 28.6% were SLAF. The mean levels for
SATF were 7.6 and 3.8 for SLAF. Screw density was segmental in each group.
The average blood loss was 400ml per case. The Hospital length of stay was
5.8 days for SATF vs 6.1 days for SLAF, the mean stay in PICU was 1.4 days
for SATF vs 1.5 days for SLAF. Conclusion: SATF and SLAF in our
instituion are in vogue again. In patients that are not suitable for VBT an
anterior fusion may have advantages for cosmesis and smaller fusion levels
compared to posterior surgery. There is a mean blood loss of 400mls. Fusion
levels are low compared to posterior surgery in the literature but similar
to VBT. HLOS is 5.8 days for SATF and 6.1 for SLAF and is comparable to our
previously reported posterior cases. There were no unplanned return to
theatre incidents. We conclude that anterior fusions can play a safe role
again in the correction of scoliosis with advantages over other techniques
particularly in lower fusion levels preserving more mobile segments.

## P086: The rate of major complications after Lenke 5 and 6 adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis deformity correction is low, but back pain is
common

Josephine Coury

1

, Zeeshan Sardar

1

, Yong Shen

1

, Mark Ren

, Michael Vitale

1

, and Lawrence Lenke

1

1

Och Spine Hospital, Columbia University Medical Center, New York,
United States

Introduction: Lenke Type 5 and 6 adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
(AIS) curves are less common than the main thoracic curve subtypes. Few
studies have outlined the long-term outcomes and complications after
surgical correction of major thoracolumbar curves. In this study, we
investigated the incidence and type of complications associated with all
posterior deformity correction for Lenke type 5 and 6 curves. Material
and Methods: A retrospective review of prospectively collected
multicenter data was performed. 193 patients were identified, 191 with
2-year and 93 with 5-year follow up were included in the final analysis. All
radiographic and clinical complications were recorded at 1, 2, and 5 years
postoperatively. All analyses were performed with SAS and alpha was set at p
< 0.05 to declare significance. Results: Lenke type 5CN (n =
147) was the most common curve type. T10 to L4 were the most frequently
fused levels (n = 54) followed by T11 to L3 (n = 38) and T9 to L3 (n = 34).

nonoperatively. Other complications included surgical site infection (n =

other neurologic complaints (n = 6). Conclusion: The rate of
revision surgery was low at 3.6% after posterior based surgery for Lenke
type 5 and 6 curves. Persistent low back pain after surgery was the most
common complication at 9.4%. The rate of symptomatic PJK within 2 years was
only 2.1%.

## 961

## P087: Upper instrumented vertebra within 3 levels of the thoracic apex is
the most significant risk factor for proximal junctional kyphosis in Lenke
type 5 and 6 adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients

Josephine Coury

1

, Zeeshan Sardar

1

, Yong Shen

1

, Mark Ren

1

, Michael Vitale

1

, and Lawrence Lenke

1

1

Och Spine Hospital, Columbia University Medical Center, New York,
United States

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is a known
complication of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) deformity correction
surgery. In specifically Lenke type 5 and 6 curves, the rates of PJK are
reported as high as 18 to 50%. Previous smaller studies have identified high
pelvic incidence, elevated preoperative proximal junctional angle (PJA), and
increased thoracic kyphosis (TK) as possible risk factors for developing PJK
in Lenke type 5 and 6 curves. In this study, we investigated multiple
factors for PJK in a multicenter cohort of patients following surgical
correction for Lenke type 5 and 6 AIS patients. Material and
Methods: A retrospective review of prospectively collected
multicenter data was performed. 193 patients were identified, 191 with
2-year and 93 with 5-year follow up were included in the final analysis.
Radiographic clinical parameters were measured preoperatively and at
postoperative year 1, 2, and 5. Radiographic measurements were performed and
confirmed by three authors. PJK was defined as the proximal junctional angle
from the UIV and 2 levels cephalad to the UIV of at least 10° and 10°
greater than preoperative measurement. All analyses were performed with SAS
and alpha was set at P < 0.05 to declare significance.
Results: Lenke type 5CN (n = 147) was the most common curve
type. T10 to L4 were the most frequently fused levels (n = 54) followed by
T11 to L3 (n = 38) and T9 to L3 (n = 34). 17 patients (8.9%) developed
radiographic PJK; 1 at 1 year, 7 at 2 years, and another 9 at 5 years. All
17 patients had an upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) within 3 levels or less
caudal of the thoracic kyphosis apex (the most horizontal vertebra on the
sagittal); no patient with a UIV 4 or more levels from the thoracic apex (n
= 96) developed PJK (X2 = 13.03, p < 0.001). Higher preoperative PJA,
pelvic incidence, thoracic kyphosis, hooks, BMI, and the Roussouly
classification were all not found to be significant predictors of PJK. Total
SRS-22 scores were significantly worse at postoperative years 2 and 5 in
patients who developed PJK (2 years: PJK 4.16 ± 0.58 vs. 4.45 ± 0.43, p =
0.018; 5 years: 3.96 ± 0.42 vs. 4.37 ± 0.48, p = 0.021). At 2 years, SRS-22
pain and general function categories were significantly lower in PJK
patients. At 5 years, SRS-22 pain, self-image, and general function
categories were significantly lower in PJK patients. Between postoperative
years 2 and 5, the PJK patients overall had lower scores, in particular
self-image significantly lowered (p = 0.0499). Conclusion: In
Lenke 5/6 Curve Types, UIV selection 4 or more levels caudal to the apex of
the thoracic kyphosis resulted in no PJK up to 5 years postop. UIV within 3
or more levels caudal to the thoracic apex was the most significant factor
leading to development of radiographic PJK. This is the first study to
demonstrate significantly worse SRS-22 scores in AIS patients with
radiographic PJK.

## 966

## P088: The spinal appearance quetionnare is a valid instrument for the
evaluation of congenital scoliosis patients over 10 yeras old

Mohammad Fanid

1

, Dilek YAPAR

2

, Aliekber Yapar

3

, İsmail Daldal

4

, Mehmet Cetinkaya

5

, Alim Can Baymurat

1

, and Alpaslan Senkoylu

1

1

Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Gazi University Faculty
of Medicine, Ankara, Turkey

2

Gazi University Faculty of Medicine, Ankara, Turkey

3

Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Health Sciences
University, Antalya Education and Research Hospital, Antalya,
Turkey

4

Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Ankara Lokman Hekim Akay
Hospital, Ankara, Turkey

5

Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Istanbul Basaksehir Pine
and Sakura City Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul,
Turkey

Introduction: The spinal appearance questionnaire (SAQ) was
developed by Sanders in 2007 out of the Walter Reed Visual Assessment Scale,
a visual test consisting of seven questions on spinal deformity, and its
validity and reliability were tested. When the overall literature was
reviewed, no disease-specific scale/questionnaire was developed to evaluate
body perception and the expectations of congenital scoliosis patients. We
aimed to evaluate the validity and the reliability of the Turkish version of
the SAQ questionnaire in Turkish patients over 10 years of age with
congenital scoliosis by assessing construct and convergent validity,
analyzing internal consistency, and test-retest validity. Hypothesis:
Evaluating the validity and reliability of the spinal appearance
questionnaire (SAQ) for congenital scoliosis patients. Study
Design: Prospective questionnaire validation study.
Material and Methods: Applied to 52 patients with
congenital scoliosis, the SAQ was applied to the same patients for the
second time with an average interval of 14.9 ± 0.9 days. Construct validity
was evaluated using factor analysis. SRS-22 was used to test the convergent
validity of SAQ. Internal consistency analysis and test-retest reliability
was evaluated to show the reliability of SAQ. Results: A
two-factor structure with eigenvalues greater than one, namely “6.1” and
“2.6” belonging to the SAQ, was obtained. The total variance of the factors
is 62.1%. The factor load of each item in the first-factor ‘Appearance’
domain varies between 0.7 and 0.8. The second-factor ‘Expectations’ consists
of four items. The factor load of each item varies between 0.7 and 0.8. A
significant negative correlation was found between the SAQ appearance score
and the self-image/appearance score of SRS-22 (r = -0.5; p < 0.001).
Cronbach alpha for SAQ was found to be 0.9. The intraclass correlation
coefficient (ICC) calculated for test-retest reliability was 0.991.
Conclusion: Previous validity and reliability studies of
SAQ have been performed in idiopathic scoliosis patients. This is the first
study containing patients diagnosed with congenital scoliosis. In this piece
of work, the 2-factor structure of the SAQ consisting of 14 items was found
to be valid and reliable in patients over 10 years of age with a diagnosis
of congenital scoliosis.

## 970

## P089: Decreasing the rate of unnecessary pediatric deformity surgery
allogenic blood transfusions

Josephine Coury

1

, Taylor Paskey

1

, Lawrence Lenke

1

, and Michael Vitale

1

1

Columbia University Medical Center, Morgan Stanley Children's
Hospital, New York

Introduction: Spinal deformity surgery is associated with a high
perioperative blood loss and risk for allogenic blood transfusion (ABT).
Previous studies have shown ABT has an increased risk of surgical site
infection, acute hemolytic reaction, and transfusion-related lung injury.
During our yearly review, our institution was noted to have a high rate of
ABT compared to others in the United States. In this study, we examined the
strategies taken to decrease our transfusion rate. Material and
Methods: Patients included had a diagnosis of AIS, underwent
posterior instrumentation and fusion (PSIF), were between ages 10-18, and
had a major cobb angle between 45 to 70 degrees. Interventions to reduce ABT
included a meeting with the postoperative care units where scoliosis
patients recovered, a change in our protocol template stating “notify spine
surgery team if transfusion is considered”, and a review of transfusions
that occurred. Results: A total of 197 patients met criteria
over 3 years. The rate of ABT from January 2019 to 2020 was 19.5% (15/77)
and from January 2020 to 2021 13.3% (8/60). The interventions to reduce ABT
rates were implemented between November 2020 to January 2021. From January
2021 to November 2021 only 5% (3/60) of patients received an ABT,
representing a significant decrease from 2020 to 2021 (p < 0.01). No
significant difference in demographics between groups existed including
gender or age. Conclusion: The rate of ABT at our institution
was significantly lowered from 13.1% to 5% by increasing scrutiny prior to
transfusion, including meeting with the postoperative care units and change
in our protocol template, and after transfusion, including a review of
transfusions that occurred.

## P090: Risk factors associated with intraoperative blood transfusion in
adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Robert Koucheki

1,2

, Andrew Howard

3,4

, Mark McVey

5

, David Levin

5

, Conor McDonnell

5

, and David Lebel

3,4

1

Temerty Faculty of Medicine - University of Toronto, Toronto,
Canada

2

Biomedical Engineering, University of Toronto, Toronto,
Canada

3

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, The Hospital for Sick Children,
Toronto, Canada

4

Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Toronto, Toronto,
Canada

5

Department of Anesthesia and Pain Medicine, The Hospital for Sick
Children, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Adolescents Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) surgeries
are associated with significant blood loss requiring high rates of blood
transfusion. This study aimed to identify factors associated with increased
allogenic blood transfusion (ABT) rates in patients with adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) treated with posterior spinal fusion. We
hypothesized that in addition to patient and scoliosis characteristics,
non-patient factors, including peri-operative practices, influence
transfusion rates in AIS surgery. Material and Methods: A
retrospective case-control study was performed for AIS patients treated at a
large children’s hospital between August 2018 and December 2020. All
patients who underwent surgical repair for AIS were evaluated. Data on
patient demographics, AIS, and transfusion parameters were collected. We
conducted multivariate logistic modelling and calculated odds ratio (OR) and
confidence intervals (CI) to identify risk factors associated with requiring
transfusion. Results: A total of 157 AIS patients were
included, of whom 56 (35.7%) were transfused RBC units (cases), and 101
(64.3%) did not receive any RBC transfusion (controls). Intraoperative care
was provided by three surgeons and thirty anesthesiologists. Multivariate
logistic regression demonstrated pre-operative hemoglobin of 130-139 g/L (OR
0.18), pre-operative hemoglobin of > 140g/L (OR 0.04), number of
scoliosis cases done by the attending anesthesiologist (OR 9.1), and
influence from individual surgeons (OR 3.8) as significant contributors to
ABT (p < 0.0001). Conclusion: In this cohort, we
demonstrated that higher pre-operative hemoglobin was protective against
ABT. Patients with hemoglobin of more than 140, had a lower odds of
receiving ABT (approximately 95% less likely). In addition, we identified
contributions from individual provider practice preferences. Although
further studies are required to better understand non-patient factors
contributing to transfusion in AIS patients, we suggest standardized,
peri-operative evidence-based strategies to potentially help reduce
variations due to individual provider preferences.

## 1079

## P091: Congenital failure of formation of the anterior column: is a VCR
always needed?

Alfredo Guiroy

1

, and Jahangir Asghar

1

1

Spine Surgery, Elite Spine Health and Wellness Center, Fort
Lauderdale, United States

Introduction: Congenital failure of formation of the anterior
column of the spine is uncommon pathology but often leads to focal deformity
of the vertebrae and severe neurological deficits. The objective of this
study is to describe and analyze the author’s experience treating this
infrequent pathology and to evaluate if a Vertebral Column Resection (VCR)
is always needed for the treatment. Material and Methods: We
reviewed the charts and imaging of patients treated for the deformity from
2010 to 2020. Demographic data, neurological status, type of deformity
(sagittal, coronal or both), kyphosis angle, scoliosis angle, defect
location operative treatment performed and complications were recorded. A
descriptive statistical analysis of the variables was done and the results
were expressed as mean and percentages. Results: We analyzed 13
patients who were operated on for congenital failures of the anterior spine
(8 male, 5 female). Mean age of diagnosis was 19 months. Three were thoracic
(from T1-T10), 6 were thoracolumbar (from T10-L2) and 4 were lumbar
dislocations. Ten had some neurological impairment pre-operatively and 5 of
those had shown progression of their impairment. Seven patients had evidence
of low lying conus and 4 underwent detethering prior to surgical
intervention. The mean age at surgery was 6 years (range: 24 months to 12
years). All the patients were treated posterior only with decompression,
deformity correction and instrumented fusion. Five had vertebral column
resection for kyphosis and the remaining 8 had posterior column osteotomies
(PCO) only. The percent correction of kyphosis for VCR patients was 42% and
for PCO it was only 44%. In 2 cases there was acute worsening of
neurological status in the immediate postoperative setting with 1 returning
to baseline and the other showing continued improvement greater than
baseline; 10 patients showed significant improvement postoperatively.
Complications involved 3 incidental durotomies and 3 cases returned to OR in
a 90-day time period: 1 for hardware revision, 1 for progression of
neurology and 1 for Irrigations and debridement. Mean follow up was 38
months (range: 11-72 months). Conclusion: Congenital failure of
formations of the anterior spine has a high rate of intraspinal pathology,
neurological deficit, and deformity progression. In certain cases
decompression and posterior only fusion may be sufficient for a good
neurological outcome.

## 1083

## P092: Evaluation of complications related to prolonged use of
halo-gravitational traction in spinal deformity surgeries

Igor Ebert Cechin

1

, Gabriel Alves

1

, Luis Eduardo Carelli Texeira da Silva

1

, and Alderico Girão Campos de Barros

1

1

Instituto Nacional de Traumatologia e Ortopedia Jammil Haddad
(INTO), Coluna, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Introduction: To evaluate the complications related to the
prolonged pre and interoperative use of halo-gravitational traction (HGT) as
an adjuvant method in the treatment of severe spinal deformities.
Material and Methods: We evaluated 27 patients who
underwent surgical treatment using pre- or interoperative HGT, between May
2014 and August 2020, through a database consultation. Inclusion criteria
were the presence of severe deformity (>100 degrees) in the coronal
and/or sagittal plane and permanence with HGT for a minimum period of 7
days. A division into 2 subgroups was performed: patients with severe
deformity in the sagittal plane accompanied by coronal deformity (11);
patients with severe deformity only in the coronal plane (16). Clinical data
were analyzed retrospectively by consulting medical records, incorporating
the variables: age, sex, diagnosis, traction time and Cobb angle. The
radiographic evaluation was retrospective by visualization in a specific
program. Results: Among the 27 patients, 13 (48%) were male and
14 (52%) were female. The age at the time of surgery ranged from 6-47 years,
with a mean of 19.6 years. The initial diagnosis was idiopathic scoliosis in
14 patients, syndromic scoliosis in 5, neuromuscular scoliosis in 3,
congenital scoliosis in 3 and 2 cases of neurofibromatosis. In the subgroup
of patients with severe deformity only in the coronal plane, the mean Cobb
angle was 123.4 degrees (100-153). The subgroup of patients with combined
deformity had a mean value of the Cobb angle for the coronal deformity of
123.6 degrees (71-159), and in the sagittal plane a mean value of 125.3
degrees (100-178). In 26 cases, 4 pins were used for cranial fixation, and
in only 1 case, 6 pins. Patients remained under traction for an average of
27 days (7-108). The mean percent correction was 17.8% in the coronal plane
and 18.4% in the sagittal plane in the subgroup with deformity in both
planes, and 23.6% in the subgroup with coronal deformity. The overall
complication rate was 37%. The incidence of complications in the subgroup
with severe sagittal deformity was 54.5%, while in the subgroup with severe
coronal deformity it was 12.5%. There were 5 complications related to the
pins, with 4 loosening treated with retightening, and 1 case of local
infection. Three patients developed less severe neurological conditions
attributed to the use of traction – two cases of diffuse paresthesia in the
limbs and one patient with blurred vision, which resolved after decreasing
the load. Two patients complained of neck pain in which traction had to be
provisionally discontinued, with complete improvement. No serious
complications related to pins and traction were identified.
Conclusion: Halo-gravitational traction has been shown to
be an important adjunctive method in the treatment of severe spinal
deformities. Despite having a considerable complication rate, there were no
serious events.

## 1087

## P093: Neural arch posterior vertebral column resection (NA-PVCR): a new
technique for angular kyphotic deformity treatment

Francisco Del Pont

1

, Igor Ebert Cechin

2

, Alderico Girão Campos de Barros

2

, and Luis Eduardo Carelli Texeira da Silva

2

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Fleni, Buenos Aires, Argentina

2

Instituto Nacional de Traumatologia e Ortopedia Jammil Haddad
(INTO), ARCOL, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Introduction: Posterior Vertebrectomy is a highly complex and
helpful tool used in the treatment of severe and rigid spine deformities,
but neurological complications are not infrequent. Changes in the position
of the spinal cord during bone resection, throughout correction maneuvers
and even after correction can generate neurological deficits.
Meningovertebral ligaments (MVL) and its biomechanical properties has been
increasingly studied in the last years, being tensioned in kypshosis and
keeping the attachment of the dural sac to the posterior arch. We believe
that the partial preservation of the neural arch (supra and interspinous
ligaments, ligamentum flavum, laminae, spinal process and part of facet
joints) in the Neural Arch Posterior Vertebrectomy (NA-PVCR) technique
maintains the MVL functions preventing spinal cord shift, with other
theoretical advantages: mechanical protection of the posterior aspect of the
spinal cord, additional surface for bone fusion and less bleeding from the
epidural space. The objective of this paper is to describe the NA-PVCR
technique and analyze the results of a initial cohort of kyphotic patients.
Material and Methods: Neural Arch Posterior Vertebrectomy
technique description. Retrospective analysis and presentation of
10 patients with acute sagittal spine deformity treated
with this technique. Results: Between February 2020 - July
2022, 10 patients underwent correction of acute sagittal spine deformity
with the use of NA-PVCR technique. Seven patients were adults and the other
three ranged from 11 to 16 years old. The diagnosis was active infection in
three patients, sequelae tuberculosis in two patients and congenital
kyphosis in the other five. Two patients were submitted to removal of one
vertebral segment, and one had an asymmetrical resection of one segment. In
five patients two vertebral segments were removed, in one three segments and
another case five segments were removed. There were no postoperative new
neurological alterations and two patients with preoperative neurological
deficits partially recovered during follow-up assessments. Pseudoarthrosis,
loss of correction, titanium mesh cage collapses, dural tear or implant
failures were not detected. Conclusion: NA-PVCR showed to be an
effective and safe technique for the treatment of angular kyphotic
deformities. Even though there was no circumferential decompression of the
spinal cord, there was no limitation to the correction or neurological
damage. This is a description of an initial cohort of kyphotic patients,
therefore, future studies will be necessary for a better evaluation.

## 1197

## P094: Effect of non-fusion anterior scoliosis correction (NFASC) on
thoracic and lumbar sagittal parameters in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
(AIS): is it detrimental?

Umesh P. Kanade

1

, keyur Akbari

1

, Vignesh Badikillaya

1

, and Sajan Hegde

1

1

Orthopaedics, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, India

Introduction: The gold standard for surgical management
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients remains spinal fusion. Surgical
treatment of Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) has experienced some
innovations in recent years particularly with regard to treatment of growing
spine. Non-fusion anterior scoliosis correction (NFASC) is a new, fusionless
revolutionary motion preserving treatment method for surgical management of
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Non-fusion anterior scoliosis correction
(NFASC) has been successful in correcting coronal deformity in patients with
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, there is paucity of literature on its
effect on sagittal parameters. We present our series of 40 patients with a
minimum follow up of 2 years. 72.5% of patients had a physiological sagittal
profile after NFASC, while 27.5% had physiological profile before NFASC. Age
and curve magnitude did not influence postoperative thoracic kyphosis (TK)
and lumbar lordosis (LL). This study evaluates the effects of non-fusion
anterior scoliosis correction on sagittal parameters of spine.
Material and Methods: It is a retrospective cohort study.
Data of 40 Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients treated with NFASC at a
single Centre with a minimum of 2 years of follow up were analysed. Coronal
cobbs’ angle, Thoracic kyphosis (TK), Lumbar Lordosis (LL), Pelvic Tilt (PT)
and Pelvic Incidence (PI) preoperatively, immediate post op and at final
follow up were measured. A Post hoc analysis following repeated measures
ANOVA test was used to examine statistically significant trends.
Results: 40 AIS patients (39 female,1 male). The mean age
was 14.57 ± 1.98 years (Range 13-18 years). The mean Risser score and
Sanders’s score was noted to be 4.22 ± 0.6 and 7.15 ± 0.59 respectively. The
cohort included 14 Lenke type 1, 3 type 3, 18 type 5, and 5 type 6. On
average 7.3 vertebrae were instrumented. Mean pre operative (pre-op)
thoracic and thoracolumbar/lumbar cobbs were 51.05 ± 7.1 °and 50.96 ± 12.07°
respectively. Mean pre-op, immediate post-operative(post-op), and at 2 years
Thoracic kyphosis were 27.20 ± 8.20, 30.83 ± 5.85 and 31.09 ± 6.06
respectively. Mean pre-op, immediate post-op, and at 2 years lumbar lordosis
were 48.92 ± 8.41, 47.23 ± 7.58 and 48.32 ± 6.06 (p > 0.05) respectively.
There was no significant change in Pelvic incidence and Pelvic tilt
preoperatively and at 2 years follow up. (p > 0.05).
Conclusion: Non-fusion anterior scoliosis correction
surgery offers fusionless correction with a positive influence on thoracic
kyphosis without having any detrimental effect on lumbar lordosis. As a
result, most of the patients achieved normal physiologic kyphosis, where as
some maintained their pre-operative alignment. There was no kyphotic effect
on lumbar spine. Non-fusion anterior scoliosis correction surgery offers
fusionless correction of deformity with positive effect on sagittal
parameters.
