## P095: Deformity correction of congenital thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis
presenting with neurological deficit

Kang Kai Lim

1

1

Orthopaedic Spine Unit, Hospital Kuala Lumpur, Kuala Lumpur,
Malaysia

A 10-year old male presented to our outpatient clinic with spine deformity
which was first detected when he was 8-year old. The thoracolumbar deformity
gradually worsened as he grew, and he subsequently developed bilateral lower
limb neurological deficit during his clinic surveillance visit at age
14-year old. Radiographic examination showed T12 hemivertebra with conus
medullaris effacement. An urgent T6 to L3 Posterior Spinal Instrumented
Fusion with 4-rod technique, T11 to L1 decompressive laminectomy, and T12
hemivertebrectomy and Harm’s cage insertion was performed. Post-operatively
his neurological deficit gradually improved and at 5 year follow up he had
good fusion mass and normal daily function with no neurological deficit.

## P096: Vertebral body tethering for immature adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis: a retrospective review of 2 to 5 years postoperative
follow-up

Meric Enercan

1

, Hamisi Mraja

1

, Celaleddin Bildik

1

, Halil Gok

1

, Ayhan Mutlu

1

, Onur Levent Ulusoy

1

, Tunay Sanli

1

, Selhan Karadereler

1

, and Azmi Hamzaoglu

1

1

Scoliosis-Spine Center Istanbul, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Anterior vertebral body tethering (VBT) has become
a popular growth modulation technique that allows spontaneous curve
correction with spinal growth in skeletally immature AIS patients.
Overcorrection and cord rupture have been reported as the most common
mechanical complications in the previous series. The aim of this study was
to evaluate the curve behaviors, mechanical complications and assess the
efficacy of vertebral body tethering technique in patients who had more than
2 years f/up. Methods: Skeletally immature patients AIS
patients with Sanders score < 4 who underwent VBT and had min. 2 years
f/up were included. Preop, first erect and latest follow-up radiographs were
reviewed and correction rates were noted. SRS-22r was used for clinical
assessment. Results: 15 patients (14F, 1M) with mean age 12,1
(10-14) and f/up 37,2 (24-62) months. There were 10 patients with Sanders
score 3 and 5 patients with Sanders score 2. A mean of 9,2 (6-13) level was
tethered. 8 patients had undergone thoracic-VBT, 2 patients had undergone
TL/L-VBT and 5 patients had undergone double VBT for both MT and TL/L
curves. Mean MT curve 58° was corrected to 22° at first erect (64%
correction rates) and 16° at latest f/up with 72% correction rates. Mean
TL/L curve 61° was corrected to 20° at first erect (68% correction rates)
and 12° at last f/up with 80% correction rates. Mechanical complications
were observed in 3 (19%) patients (2 tether breakage with a single cord, 1
overcorrection). All 3 patients had > 75% correction rates at the first
erect. None of the patients require revision surgery for tether breakage or
overcorrection. On the latest f/up, 93% of the MT curves and all (100%) of
the TL/L curves were below 30°. SRS-22r subtotal score increased from a mean
of 3.8 to 4.39 with a mean satisfaction score of 4.75 over 5 at the latest
f/up. Conclusion: Vertebral body tethering is an effective
growth modulation technique that provided satisfactory clinical and
radiological results at the end of a mean 3 years f/up. The success rate was
93% for MT and 100% for TL/L curves. Tether breakage (13%) and
overcorrection (6%) rates were lower than the previous series. Estimation of
the remaining growth is challenging, curve correction should not be more
than 60-70% at the index surgery in immature AIS to avoid overcorrection.
Double cord fixation can minimize tether breakage. Patient satisfaction
(4.75/5) was high at the latest f/up.

## P097: Restoration of ideal sagittal alignment in AIS with thoracic
hypokyphosis/lordosis with hybrid technique: combination of posterior
thoracic fusion with non-fusion thoracolumbar/lumbar vertebral body
tethering

Meric Enercan

1

, Hamisi Mraja

1

, Tunay Sanli

1

, Onur Levent Ulusoy

1

, Halil Gok

1

, Celaleddin Bildik

1

, Ayhan Mutlu

1

, Selhan Karadereler

1

, and Azmi Hamzaoglu

1

1

Scoliosis-Spine Center Istanbul, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Restoration of the ideal sagittal alignment is
essential in AIS deformity correction. We introduced Hybrid technique
including posterior surgery with or without Ponte osteotomy in order to
restore sagittal alignment better and thoracolumbar/lumbar (TL/L) vertebral
body tethering (VBT) with Double Screw-Double Cord fixation in order to
preserve lumbar flexibility and motion. The aim of this study to evaluate
the efficacy of hybrid technique for the restoration ideal sagittal
alignment in patients with double major curves with thoracic
hypokyphosis/lordosis. Methods: 24 AIS patients who had double

deformity correction, restored TL/L alignment, preserved flexibility and
motion of lumbar spine without cord rupture.

## 1502

## P098: Severe kyphoscoliosis in non-ambulatory patients with type II
spinal muscular atrophy and concomitant serious respiratory restriction: a
novel surgical strategy to correct spinal deformity and pelvic
obliquity

Tianyuan Zhang

1

, Wenyuan Sui

1

, Jingfan Yang

1

, Yaolong Deng

1

 and Junlin Yang

1

1

Spine Center, Xinhua Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School
of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: To propose a novel surgical strategy to correct
severe kyphoscoliosis and pelvic obliquity in non-ambulatory patients with
type II spinal muscular atrophy and concomitant serious respiratory
restriction. Material and Methods: Type II SMA patients with
severe kyphoscoliosis and concomitant serious respiratory restriction who
underwent posterior spinal fusion in our center from January 2019 to
December 2021 were retrospectively reviewed. A novel surgical strategy based
on alternate distraction on the concave side between a Domino connector and
distal screws was proposed to correct spinal deformity and pelvic obliquity.
Patients’ demographics and clinical data were detailed, including
anthropometric parameters, nutrition status, pulmonary function and surgical
outcomes. The scoliosis curve, kyphosis curve and pelvic obliquity were
measured before and after surgery. The ability of sitting balance was
evaluated during follow-up. Complications were also recorded.
Results: 20 patients (9 males and 11 females) with type II
SMA were included in this study. The average age at surgery was 18.7 ± 6.1
years (range, 11-30 years). Average body mass index (BMI) was 18.47 ± 4.68
kg/m2 and 60% (12/20) patients were with poor nutrition. The
mean percentage forced vital capacity (FVC%) and forced expiratory volume in
one second (FEV1%) was 35.3% ± 12.8% and 37.3% ± 13.8%,
respectively, indicating serious respiratory restriction. Severe
kyphoscoliosis was developed for all patients with highly rotated vertebra,
deformed chest wall and pelvic imbalance. No one was able to sit
independently without hands supporting and six patients was bound to bed
preoperatively. All patients underwent one-stage posterior spinal fusion,
instrumented from the upper thoracic vertebra to the pelvis. Multiple rods
construct with a Domino connector was installed on the concave side to
alternately distract collapsed trunk and achieve pelvic balance. The main
scoliotic curve, kyphotic curve and pelvic obliquity averaged 120.6° ±
17.0°, 116.8° ± 25.6° and 36.5° ± 13.6° respectively before surgery. After
surgery, it decreased to 57.7° ± 19.5°, 47.0° ± 15.0° and 15.5° ± 7.3°
respectively. The mean operation time was 351.3 ± 64.5 mins (range, 240 to
525 mins). The mean blood loss was 1377.5 ± 1107.9 ml (range, 300 to 4500
ml). 13 (65%) patients were extubated in the operating room postoperatively
and the average extubation time was 6.75 ± 11.2 hours for all. After
surgery, they stayed in ICU for mean 2.5 ± 1.6 days (range, 1 to 7 days).
The mean duration of hospital stay was 22.3 ± 9.4 days. As for postoperative
complications, only 3 patients happened pneumonia and no one needed
re-intubation due to respiratory problems. The sitting ability was recovered
with balanced pelvis and all patients could sit independently during
follow-up. Conclusions: This article presented the
characteristics of non-ambulatory type II SMA patients with severe
kyphoscoliosis and seriously restricted pulmonary function. Our novel
surgical strategy could provide substantial correction and recover patients’
sitting balance, while limited the risks of respiratory complications. Its
safety and effectiveness needed to be evaluated for severe neuromuscular
scoliosis in the future.

## 1591

## P099: Scoliosis in cerebral palsy patients. Fusion to the fifth lumbar
vertebra, the sacrum or the ilia?

Ib Green Petersen

1

, Luigi Magnano

2

, Anastasios Charalampidis

3

, and Paul Gerdhem

4

1

Karolinska University Hospital, Dep of Surgery, Sweden

2

Enna Hospital, Sicily, Italy, Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics,
Italy

3

Karolinska University Hospital, Dep of Acute Surgery, Trauma and
Orthopaedics, Sweden

4

Uppsala University, Dep of Surgical Sciences, Uppsala,
Sweden

Introduction: There is no consensus on the lowest level of
fusion in patients with cerebral palsy treated surgically for scoliosis,
although some previous studies have suggested a better radiological outcome
after fusion to the pelvis in individuals with various types of
neuromuscular scoliosis. We compared complications, reoperations and
radiological outcome in individuals with cerebral palsy fused to the fifth
lumbar vertebra (L5), the sacrum, or the ilia. Material and
Methods: 208 individuals with cerebral palsy undergoing surgery
for scoliosis aged 10 through 25 years were identified in the national
quality registry Swespine. Lowest level of fusion was L5 in 58, the sacrum
in 92, and the ilia in 58 individuals. The Cobb method was used for curve
size analysis and the Maloney method for pelvic obliquity analysis.
Reoperations were collected from the registry. An analysis on 58 matched
pairs operated to L5 or the pelvis (sacrum = 42, ilia = 16) with similar
pelvic obliquity (± 5°) was also performed. Statistics was performed with
the Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests.
Results: The median (interquartile range) follow-up for the
last radiograph was 1.7 (1.7) years and for reoperations 6.0 (5.9) years.
Preoperatively, the median Cobb angle of the major curve was 65° (23°) in
the L5 group, 68° (28°) in the sacrum group, and 78° (25°) in the ilia group
(p = 0.006). Preoperative median pelvic obliquity was 16° (19°), 21° (13°),
and 27° (28°), respectively (p = 0.004). Immediate postoperative Cobb angles
were 28° (18°), 28° (16°), and 32° (25°), respectively (p = 0.11). Immediate
postoperative pelvic obliquity was 7° (10°), 7° (8°), and 8° (10°),
respectively (p = 0.28). The median change in pelvic obliquity from the
first to the last postoperative radiograph was -5° (7°), -3° (6°), -3° (6°),
respectively (p = 0.55). 7 (12%), 11 (12%), and 7 (12%) patients required at
least one reoperation (p = 1.0), respectively. In the matched analysis based
on pelvic obliquity, no significant differences in the radiological outcomes
were found (all p > 0.38).
Conclusion: Both fusion to L5, the sacrum, and the ilia
results in sustained curve and pelvic obliquity correction, with no
significant difference in reoperation rates. This indicates that choice of
distal fusion level can be individualized in individuals with cerebral
palsy.

## 1616

## P100: The intervention effect of serial growing rod procedure on shoulder
balance in EOS patients and analysis of risk factors for final shoulder
imbalance

Ziyang Liu

1

 and Yong Hai

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: To analyze the risk factors for final shoulder
imbalance, observe shoulder balance changes during growing rod (GR)
treatments in early-onset scoliosis (EOS) patients, and evaluate the
satisfaction of families of patients with shoulder balance after GR
treatment. Material and Methods: 24 consecutive EOS patients
treated with GR at our institution from March 2008 to August 2018 were
studied. Demographic data, surgical-related factors, and radiographic
parameters were analyzed to identify the risk factors for final shoulder
imbalance in 'growing-rod graduates', and the shoulder balance changes from
GR implantation to the last follow-up after fusion were analyzed. The
radiographic shoulder balance parameters included the radiographic shoulder
height (RSH), clavicle angle (CA), and T1 tilt angle (T1T). The satisfaction
of EOS patients' parents was evaluated by an adapted questionnaire.
Results: Early postoperative shoulder imbalance (p = 0.015;
odds ratio (OR): 19.500; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.777-213.949) was
an independent risk factor for shoulder imbalance at the last follow-up.
Radiographic shoulder height (RSH) was significantly improved after GR
implantation (p = 0.036), further improved during the post-fusion period (p
= 0.021), and through the whole treatment period (p = 0.011). The changing
trend of CA was similar. RSH of patients with prefusion shoulder imbalance
was significantly improved after final fusion (p = 0.045), and there was no
significant difference in the RSH value at the early after fusion and the
last follow-up compared with that of the prefusion shoulder balance group.
The parents (100%) were satisfied with the final shoulder condition and the
entire serial GR treatment. Conclusion: Growing rod surgery
improved shoulder balance. However, shoulder balance status after GR
implantation did not determine the final status. Final fusion could further
adjust the shoulder balance of patients with prefusion shoulder imbalance.
For patients with early shoulder imbalance after final fusion, there was a
high probability of shoulder imbalance at the final follow-up.

## P101: Hoursfield unit for assessing asymmetric loss of vertebral bone
mineral density and its correlation with curve serverity in AIS

Yunzhong Cheng

1

, Honghao Yang

1

, and Yong Hai

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Low bone mass concomitantly occurs in patients
with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) and can persist until skeletal
maturity. The purpose of this study was to assess the asymmetrical loss of
vertebral bone mineral density (vBMD) and its correlation with curve
severity in patients with AIS using Hounsfield unit (HU) values were
measured from computed tomography scans. Methods: A total of 93
AIS patients were retrospectively recruited. The HU values of the vertebral
body (VB-HU) and pedicle screw trajectory (PST-HU) were measured from four
vertebrae above (Apex − 4) to four below (Apex + 4) the apical vertebra
(Apex) of the major curve. The VB-HU and PST-HU at the upper-end vertebra,
Apex, and lower-end vertebra within the concave and convex sides of the
major and minor curves and stable vertebrae were obtained.
Results: A significant correlation was found between the
Cobb angle and VB-HU at the periapical levels of the major curve. VB-HU and
PST-HU at periapical levels were significantly greater within the concavity
than the convexity of both major and minor curves. The asymmetric ratios of
VB-HU and PST-HU were significantly correlated with the major curve Cobb
angle, peaked at the apex, and gradually diminished from the apex to the end
vertebrae. The asymmetrical loss of vBMD aggravated with the progression of
curve severity, presenting as VB-HU, significantly decreased within the
convexity and insignificantly decreased within the concavity of the major
curve. Conclusion: The asymmetrical loss of vBMD was associated
with the progression of curve severity in AIS. For patients with severe AIS,
the distraction of the pedicle screws at the concave side should be a
priority in correcting the major curve, and supplemental anchors and
larger-sized screws should be placed within the convex side around the apex
of the major curve to reduce the risk of screw loosening after surgery.

## P102: Halo-pelvic traction combined with staged correction surgery for
the treatment of extrem severe and rigid kyphoscoliosis

Lijin Zhou

1

 and Yong Hai

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Severe and rigid spinal deformities are real
challenges for us with unfavorable correction and a high rate of
complications. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of halo-pelvic traction
(HPT) combined with staged corrective surgery in the treatment of extremely
severe and rigid scoliosis (Cobb’s angle > 140°), a retrospective study
was conducted. Materials and Methods: Twelve consecutive cases
of extremely severe rigid kyphoscoliosis were treated with one-stage HPT
traction and a staged posterior procedure was included in the study. There
were five males and seven females with an average age of 24.3 years. All
underwent staged correction surgery. The patient had a major coronal curve
or kyphosis > 140° and flexibility < 30%. The patient’s height, main
curve, the height difference between the two shoulders, the height
difference between the two iliac, and C7PL-CSVL distance were evaluated
before traction, after HPT, as well as after correction surgery.
Results: All patients underwent HPT traction and posterior
surgery safely. The average time for HPT traction was 13.2 weeks. None of
the patients underwent high-grade osteotomy. The main curve or kyphosis was
improved from (162.5 ± 17.3)° before the operation to (75.7 ± 14.3)° after
HPT, and to (57.7 ± 16.1)° after correction surgery. The corrective rate was
64.5%. The height, shoulder height difference and C7PL-CSVL distance of
patients after HPT and correction surgery were also significantly improved
compared with those before traction. One patient developed C5 root palsy
during traction, one patient developed skin ulceration infection, one
patient developed cerebrospinal fluid leakage during correction surgery, and
one patient developed transient lower extremity paralysis. Complications in
all patients were relieved after treatment. Conclusions: The
combination of HPT and correction surgery is a safe and effective method for
the treatment of extremely severe rigid scoliosis with Cobb’s angle >
140°, with less severe complications, and can avoid high-grade osteotomy
during the procedure.
Key words: Traction; Scoliosis; Orthopedic procedures

## P103: The efficacy of pre-operative halo-gravity traction for severe
kyphoscoliosis surgery on radiographic outcme and pulmonry function

Jianqiang Wang

1

, Yong Hai

1

, and Lijin Zhou

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Halo-gravity traction (HGT) has been proven that
can decrease the severity of the curve in the process of correction before
surgery. Currently, few studies have evaluated the efficacy of HGT on the
pulmonary function of the patient. Our study was to evaluate the efficacy of
preoperative Halo-gravity traction in treating severe spinal deformity on
both radiographic outcome and pulmonary function. Materials and
Methods: This study retrospectively included 30 consecutive
patients (male 8, female 22) with severe kyphoscoliosis who were admitted to
our department from April 2018 to January 2022 and underwent HGT before the
correction surgery. The average age of patients was 17.79 ± 7.96 years old
and the average of the pre-operative main curve was 120.66 ± 3.89°. There
were 17 patients with AIS, 11 with congenital and 2 with NF-I. The change of
radiographic outcome of deformity and pulmonary function tests (PFTs) were
analyzed before and after HGT. Results: After an average of 122
± 58 days traction, with 44.2 ± 12.7% of body weight, the main curve was
corrected from an average of 112.42 ± 34.53° to 87.15 ± 27.77° (22.5%, p
< 0.05); PFTs also showed a significant increase in FVC%, FEV1%, and MEF%
after traction [42.82 ± 15.03% VS. 45.75 ± 15.82%;40.71 ± 13.77% VS. 44.21 ±
15.20%; 40.78 ± 17.15% VS. 45.49 ± 19.14%, p < 0.05]. No significant
difference was found in deformity correction and lung function improvement
between patients with traction for more or less than three months (p >
0.05). Two patients developed brachial plexus palsy during traction and
recovered after decreasing of the traction weight. No other complication
occurred during the traction period. Conclusions: Halo gravity
traction can partially correct spinal deformity and improve pulmonary
function. It could be used as a preoperative adjuvant treatment for severe
spinal deformity. But traction for more than three months might not be
necessary, according to the present study.

## P104: Clincal application of individualized digital surgical planning and
precised execution for severe complex spinal deformity correction

Hongtao Ding

1

, Yong Hai

1

, Chaofan Han

1

, and Yangpu Zhang

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Severe rigid adult deformities are composed of the
characteristics of the complexity of anatomy, rigidity, and severe kyphosis
or scoliosis, with or without neurological dysfunction, which may lead to
physical disability or even death. The treatment strategy for such severe
deformities is comprehensive. Different levels of spinal osteotomy have been
developed and applied rapidly with good correction outcomes. However, due to
the complex anatomy of spine structure, the screw insertion, vertebrae
osteotomy, correction, and decompression procedures increase the incidence
of intra- or postoperative neurological complications significantly. This
study is to report the preliminary outcomes utilizing of Individualized
pre-operative digital planning and three-dimensional printing (3DP) guidance
template in the treatment of severe and complex spinal deformity.
Materials and Methods: After being approved by the
Institutional Review Board of our hospital, 8 adult patients with severe
rigid kyphoscoliosis were included. Based on the preoperative radiological
data, the surgery planning was simulated by software, and screw insertion
and osteotomy guidance templates were designed and manufactured utilizing 3D
printing techniques. The designed osteotomy and correction surgeries were
performed utilizing the guidance templates. The perioperative, and
radiological parameters and complications were collected and analyzed,
including surgery duration, estimated blood loss, pre-and post-operative
cobb angle, trunk balance, the ratio of osteotomy simulation and execution,
screw accuracy, etc. Results: Of the 8 patients, the primary
pathology consisted of 2 adult idiopathic scoliosis (ADIS), 4 congenital
scoliosis (CS), 1 ankylosing spondylitis (AS), and 1 kyphosis secondary to
tuberculosis (TB). There are 5 kyphoscoliosis and 2 kyphosis regarding
deformity characteristics. The pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) in 3
patients and vertebral column resection (VCR) osteotomies in 5 patients were
performed with the application of the guidance templates. The average
surgical duration is 361.25 mins, average blood loss of 800 ml, and no
surgery and instrument-related complications occurred. The main cobb angle
was corrected from 99.33° to 34.17°, the kyphosis was corrected from 110.00°
to 42.00°. The match ratio of osteotomy simulation and execution was 94.67%.
The average screw accuracy rate was 93.04% in the cohort.
Conclusions: The clinical application of individualized
digital surgical planning and precise execution and 3D printing guidance
templates in the treatment of severe adult rigid deformity is feasible,
effective, and easy to promote. The preoperative osteotomy simulation is
executed with high precision by utilizing the described guidance templates.
It could be used to reduce the surgical risk and difficulty of screw
placement and high-level osteotomy.

## P105: Operative considerations for surgical management of scoliosis in
GGPS1, a rare muscular dystrophy: a rare disease operative case
report

Matt Bellamy

1

, Raveen Jayasuriya

1

, Edward Bayley

1

, Ian Scivill

2

, and Robert John

3

1

Paediatric Orthopaedics and Trauma

2

Department of Neurophysiology

3

Department of Anaesthetics, Sheffield Children's Hospital,
Sheffield, United Kingdom

Background: GGPS1 is a rare variant of the geranylgeranyl
diphosphate synthase gene. GGPS1 causes a genetic muscular dystrophy which
is associated with progressive scoliosis, osteoporosis, and hearing loss.
This commonly results in early wheelchair dependence by the 2nd
decile of life. Of the 21 globally reported cases, 15 have undergone spinal
fusion surgery at a mean age of 14 years. There is no published literature
on spinal management or surgical considerations to guide preoperative
planning. Methods: A rare disease case study of an 8-year-old
girl with GGPS1 and rapidly progressing left thoracic scoliosis who failed
full time rigid bracing, and subsequently underwent T2-L3 posterior spinal
fusion. This report focuses on intra operative learning points to optimise
surgical management and early post-operative results. Results:
Preoperatively this patient mobilised independently, with no history of low
energy mechanism fractures, and required nocturnal non-invasive ventilatory
(NIV). Due to her early onset of rapid curve progression and curve size,
early onset scoliosis deformity correction and fusion was considered with
the aim to protect her ambulatory status and pulmonary function. Prior to
surgery the patient had normal motor function, thus full sensory-motor
neuromonitoring was expected prior to proceeding with surgery.
Intraoperative monitoring was adjusted from 1mS (standard for adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis) to 4mS interstimulus interval to achieve adequate,
repeatable, morphology and amplitude of MEP waveforms. Sub cortical and
cortical responses for SEPs were obtained. No indications of metabolic bone
abnormalities had been identified prior to surgery. However very poor bone
quality was clinically evident intraoperatively, prompting a change to a
higher instrumentation density (1.5) construct that originally planned. Full
correction was not attempted due to risk of screw displacement. This
achieved acceptable coronal plane correction from 65 degrees to 29 degrees.
Probing pedicle screw holes was highly haemorrhagic, resulting in estimated
blood loss of 750 mls (80% of circulating volume), with 303ml returned by
cell salvage and 166mls of donor blood. Surgical progress was paused whilst
fluid resuscitation with blood products reinstated haemodynamic stability.
Neurological function was normal postoperatively and no further blood
products required. Length of stay was 13 days due to slow wean off daytime
NIV on the critical care unit. Discussion: Learning points:1)
Fusion surgery may be necessary at a younger age due to rapidly progressing
scoliosis neuromuscular scoliosis. 2) Neuromonitoring needs adapting in view
of GGPS1 neuromuscular pathology. 3) Consider DEXA scan and metabolic bone
specialist involvement preoperatively 4) High implant density required, 5)
Prepare for high volume blood loss with pause for resuscitation and
cross-matched donor blood.

2Ar, 9B and 1C) and 4% were Lenke 2. Preoperatively, 14 (64%) patients were
premenarchal (median Sanders: 3 (1-7), median Risser: 0 (0-5)). A median of
7 (7-9) levels were tethered. Mean surgical time was 245 ± 75 (123-360)
minutes. Patients grew 7 cm on average; height measurements showing
significant increase at each follow-up timepoint (p < 0.001). All
patients reached skeletal maturity at final follow-up. Upper Thoracic (UT),
Main Thoracic (MT) and Thoracolumbar/lumbar (TLL) curves showed significant
decrease in each follow-up timepoint. No significant changes were noted in
kyphosis and lordosis (p < 0.05). Pulmonary, mechanical and curve
behavior complications rates were 13%, 22% and 35%, respectively. 2 (8.7%)
patients were converted to fusion. At final follow-up, 91% patients had ≤ 3
0° residual curve. SRS-22 MH, SI and subtotal scores increased
significantly. Conclusions: This study reports a single
European center experience on 23 consecutive patients with ≥5-years
follow-up who had undergone thoracic-only VBT surgery. Surgical correction
was followed by growth-dependent correction attained during follow-up.
Spontaneous correction in the non-operated upper thoracic and thoracolumbar
levels were also noted. Thoracoscopic VBT surgery prevented fusion following
≥5-years after surgery in 91% of the patients. 90% of patients that are not
converted to fusion had good radiographic and clinical outcomes at latest
follow-up; however, it is not without complications. Some complications may
be avoided with a better understanding of the growth modulation and
advancement of technical skills and technology.

## P108: Comparison of patient-reported outcomes after vertebral body
tethering and posterior spinal fusion

Altug Yucekul

1

, Gokhan Ergene

2

, Sahin Senay

3

, Sule Turgut Balci

4

, Pinar Yalinay Dikmen

5

, Caglar Yilgor

1

, and Ahmet Alanay

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology

2

Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University Vocational School of Health
Sciences, Department of Operating Room Services, Istanbul,
Turkey

3

Department of Cardiovascular Surgery

4

Anesthesiology Service, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University
Maslak Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

5

Department of Neurology, Acibadem Mehmet Ali Aydinlar University
School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Posterior spinal fusion (PSF) is the standard
surgical approach in the treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Vertebral body tethering (VBT) emerged as an alternative minimally invasive,
non-fusion, growth modulating technique. The aim of this study was to
compare the patient-reported outcomes of patients who had undergone PSF and
VBT. Materials and Methods: Matched cohorts were created among
patients having main thoracic curves ranged between 40⁰-70⁰ and having ≥ 2
years follow-up. Double-curve VBT and thoracolumbar PSF surgeries where
lumbar curves were also instrumented were excluded. Demographic data, and
preoperative radiographic measurements were compared to confirm matching.
Early and latest follow-up radiographic measurements and SRS-22r scores were
used as outcome measures. Results: 16 PSF and 18 VBT patients
(30F, 4M) were included. The mean age and the follow-up were 13.4 (10-17)
years and 25.7 (24-32) months. Preoperative proximal thoracic (28.6° vs
29.6°), main thoracic (MT) (56.8° vs 51°), and thoracolumbar (TL) curves
(32.5° vs 37°) were similar among groups (p = 0.732, p = 0.126 and p =
0.088). The surgical correction percentage in the MT curve was greater in
the PSF group (84% vs 53%, p < 0.001), while the overall correction
percentages at 2-years were similar (80 vs 76%, p = 0.616). For both PSF and
VBT groups, self-image and subtotal scores significantly increased at
2-years compared to preoperative values (p < 0.001, p = 0.037 and p <
0.001, p = 0.016), while pain, function and mental-health did not show
significant pre-to-post changes (p > 0.05 for all comparisons).
Self-image scores were improved at 6-months and were maintained in PSF
group, while they incrementally increased in the VBT cohort. SRS function
scores were higher in VBT group both at 6-months and 2-years (p = 0.027, p =
0.027) compared to PSF group. SRS pain and subtotal scores were found to be
worse in PSF group at 2-years (p = 0.020, p = 0.036) in comparison to VBT
group. Conclusions: PSF and VBT resulted in similar main
thoracic and thoracolumbar curve correction rates 2-years after surgery. PSF
resulted in earlier improvement in self-image scores while latest follow-up
scores were similar. VBT resulted in better patient-reported function and
pain scores. Further studies in larger patient cohorts with longer follow-up
are warranted.

## P109: Overcoming the challenges in management of neglected and severe
spine deformities: our case series and strategies

Harvinder Singh Chhabra

1

, and Anuj Gupta

2

1

Spine Service, Indian Spinal Injuries Centre, New Delhi,
India

2

Spine Service, Max Super Speciality Hospital, Noida, India

Introduction: Severe deformity of the spine is defined as Cobb
angle more than 90 degrees. The term neglected spinal deformity has not
formally defined but most surgeons consider it if age is more than 16 years
and no treatment has been sought till then Patients with neglected severe
scoliosis may have very low pulmonary reserve along with cosmetic deformity.
Moreover, there can be neurological compromise due to compression on spinal
cord. The challenges associated with the surgery in these patients are
rigidity of the curve, poor pulmonary reserve and compromised spinal cord in
patients with neurological deficit. The objective of our study was to assess
the outcomes of correction of severe deformities in our series and to
compile the strategies to overcome the challenges in management of neglected
and severe spine deformities. Materials and Methods: This is a
single centre retrospective study. Patients with Cobb angle >
900, flexibility on bending radiographs < 30% and age >
16 years were included in the study. 14 patients were managed in single
stage (vertebral column resection with posterior instrumentation and fusion)
and 06 in two stages (Halo-pelvic distractor application and later posterior
instrumentation and fusion). We collected data for all patients which
include age, sex, type of surgery, pre and post-op Cobb angle, T1-T12, T1-S1
length, Sagittal & Coronal alignment, Apical vertebral translation and
SRS-22 score. Results: Total of 20 patients were included in
the study. The aetiology included Congenital (12), Neuromuscular (5),
Idiopathic (2) and syndromic (1). The mean duration of follow-up was 38.6
months. The mean pre-op Cobb angle was 99.75 (50-180) in coronal plane and
60.8 (10-93) in sagittal plane. The mean post-op Cobb angle was 46.85
(22-66) in coronal plane and 35.9 (10-48) in sagittal plane (p < 0.005).
The mean pre-op and post op coronal and sagittal alignment were +4.96 cms
& +4.35 cms +2.52 cms and +2.06 cms respectively (p < 0.005). The
mean pre- and post-op apical vertebrae translation was 7.38 cms and 3.33 cms
respectively (p < 0.005). The mean pre- and post-op T1-T12 length was
15.8 cms and 21 cms respectively (p < 0.0001). Similarly, the mean pre-
and post-op T1-S1 length was 31.1 cms and 37.7 cms respectively (p <
0.0001). In our patients, there was significant improvement in all aspects
of functional scores with p value < 0.001. There were 6 patients with
pulmonary compromise pre-op and after surgery there was significant
improvement in both FVC and FEV1. We experienced no major complications like
implant failure, infection or neurological deficit. 7 patients had
incomplete neurological deficit pre-op which improved after surgery. We also
have compiled 10 strategies which can be used for management of such
deformities. Conclusion: The management of Neglected Severe
Spinal deformities may be very challenging. However, the successful outcome
after planned surgical treatment is a life changing event with improvement
in thoracic height, pulmonary function, and a profound effect on cosmesis
and self-image.

## P110: Structural scoliosis secondary to thoracic osteoid osteoma: a case
report of delayed diagnosis

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Mohamed Zairi

2

, Eya Chahed

, Sofiene Bouali

1

, Ahmed Msakni

3

, Mohsni Ahmed Amine

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,

2

Orthopedics

3

Tunisia

Introduction: Osteoid osteoma (OO) is a small benign bone tumor
that is primarily localized in long bone; lumbar osteoid osteoma combined
with scoliosis has rarely been reported. The aim of this case report is to
show that a late diagnosis of vertebral osteoid osteoma gives rise to
structural scoliosis, which can require long-term management.
Materials and Methods: We report a case of an osteoid
osteoma in the thoracic spine associated with structural scoliosis. We
describe a 14-year-old boy who complained chronic nightly left back pain and
scoliosis. Spine’s X-ray reported thoraco-lumbar scoliosis without bone
lesion. Results: MRI as well as technetium-99m total body bone

superior articular process of T11 vertebra consistent with the diagnosis of
Osteoid Osteoma. Anatomopathological study of the resection piece confirmed
the diagnosis. Surgical excision of the tumor resolved pains, but scoliosis
needed a non-operative treatment for one year. Conclusion:
Through this case, it has been demonstrated that late diagnosed vertebral
Osteoid osteoma can be the cause of structural scoliosis. Clinical and
radiological results indicate that OO resection is an effective and safe
method of treatment.

## P111: Single centre experience of intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM)
in pediatric scoliosis deformity correction surgeries

Umesh P. Kanade

1

, Sharan Achar T

1

, Harith Reddy

1

, Keyur Akbari

1

, Vignesh Badikillaya

1

, Appaji Krishnan

2

, and Dr Sajan Hegde

1

1

Orthopaedics, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, India

2

Orthopaedics, SIMS Hospitals, Chennai, India

Introduction: Neurological deficit following surgical correction
of spinal deformity is a major concern for any surgeon. Intraoperative
neuromonitoring (IONM) in the form of Somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP)
and Transcranial motor evoked potential (TcMEP) are real-time assessment
tools to decrease the likelihood of iatrogenic neurological injuries. We aim
to present our experience of multimodal IONM in pediatric scoliosis surgery.
Methods: Prospective analysis of 121 consecutive scoliosis
patients who underwent posterior scoliosis correction with IONM at our
institute between January 2015 to July 2018. All surgeries were monitored by
an experienced neuromonitoring specialist and were performed under total
intravenous anesthesia. Alerts were described as a decrease in amplitude by
50% or greater in SSEP, TcMEP, or both. Results: There were 91
females and 30 males with a mean age of 15 years 5 months. 11 patients (9%)
had positive neuro alerts of which 7 (63%) of alerts were due to
intraoperative traction, 2 (18%) were due to mean arterial pressure, 1 was
due to screw placement and 1 was due to correction of the curve. We observed
10 true positives, 1 false-positive, and 1 false-negative alert for TcMEPs
with sensitivity of 90.9% and specificity of 99%. The sensitivity and
specificity of SSEP was 18% and 100% respectively. 2 cases had postoperative
neurological deficit which recovered over time. Conclusion: Our
results support the use of IONM as a standard of care during pediatric
deformity correction surgery. The combined use of TcMEP and SSEP is a
valuable tool for improving intraoperative safety and postoperative
outcomes.

## P113: Type 3 bone-disc-bone osteotomy combined with pre-surgical
halo-traction: a safe and effective solution to correct severe angular-like
kyphoscoliosis

Tianyuan Zhang

1

, Wenyuan Sui

1

, Jingfan Yang

1

, Yaolong Deng

1

, and Junlin Yang

1

1

Spine Center, Xinhua Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School
of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Treatment of severe angular-like kyphoscoliosis is
a technically demanding surgical challenge and often requires high-risk
vertebral column resection (VCR). Bone-disc-bone osteotomy (BDBO) refers to
the resection of disc and adjacent vertebral endplates and has 3 different
types according to different ranges of resection. The resection ranges of
type 3 BDBO contains three parts: (i) partial vertebral body (includes
pedicles); (ii) superior intervertebral disc; (iii) superior partial
vertebral body (not includes pedicles). For the first time, this study
proposes a novel method that combines type 3 BDBO with pre-surgical
halo-pelvic traction (HPT) and evaluates its safety and effectiveness to
correct severe angular-like kyphoscoliosis. Material and
Methods: Patients with severe angular-like kyphoscoliosis who
underwent pre-surgical HPT and type 3 BDBO from 2017 to 2019 were
retrospectively reviewed. Patients’ demographics and clinical data were
recorded. The coronal Cobb angle and sagittal Cobb angle were measured in
the pre-operation, post-traction, post-operation, and final follow-up.
Complications were also recorded. Patients’ health-related quality of life
was compared by SRS-22 questionnaire. Results: Thirty patients
(18 females and 12 males) were included with an average age of 20.2 years
(range, 13–33 years). The mean preoperative coronal and sagittal Cobb angle
was 123.1° ± 16.4° (range, 90°-155°) and 120.3° ± 19.9° (range, 90°-156°).
After 2.9 ± 0.7 months of (range, 2-4 months) HPT, the coronal and sagittal
Cobb angle decreased significantly to 81.9° ± 13.2° and 76.0° ± 12.6°.
Postoperatively, the scoliotic and kyphotic angle further decreased to 42.4°
± 12.2° and 33.9° ± 8.8°. After mean follow-up of 2.93 ± 1.05 years, the
correction rates maintained at 64.3% ± 10.6% and 70.5% ± 6.3%, respectively,
without obvious correction loss. The mean operative time was 410.8 ± 126.2
minutes (range, 220-660 min), and average estimated blood loss was 1364.2 ±
619.8 mL (range, 600-3000 mL). There were nine patients encountering
positive evoked potential events during surgery. After surgery, five
patients demonstrated different degrees of transient neurological deficits,
including two with lower limbs numbness and three with lower limbs weakness.
All of them recovered within 1 to 6 months of rehabilitation. Respiratory
complications, including 4 pneumonia and 6 pleural effusions, happened. One
patient had surgical site infection postoperatively and we performed
irrigation and debridement. One patient encountered leakage of cerebrospinal
fluid and we performed dural repair. During follow-up, two patients had
unilateral rod fracture but no obvious correction loss, so revision surgery
was not performed. The SRS-22 scores were calculated and compared between
pre-operation and last follow-up. The scores of self-images were
significantly improved from 2.66 ± 0.27 to 3.36 ± 0.23 (p < 0.001). Other
scores showed slightly improvement but with no statistical significance.
Conclusion: This study proposed a novel strategy to correct
severe angular-like spinal deformities. The combination of pre-surgical HPT
and type 3 BDBO achieved substantial correction and satisfactory aesthetic
outcomes. No permanent neurological deficits and serious complications
happened postoperatively. Comparison of this technique with VCR was needed
to further evaluate its efficiency in the future.

## P114: Clinical and radiographic outcomes in the treatment of patients

Matthew Geck

1

, Devender Singh

, John Stokes

, Ashley Duncan

, and Eeric Truumees

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United

Introduction: Scheuermann Kyphosis (SK) is one the leading

the clinical and radiographic outcomes of patients with SK who underwent

Society-22r (SRS-22r), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Visual Analogue
Scale (VAS) and complications were evaluated. Matched pair t-tests were
conducted for statistical significance (α = 0.05). Results:

was 24.7 (± 5.3). Mean sanders score was 7.5 (± 1.0). Most treated spinal

the last visit was 47.1% (± 13%). Similarly, LL were 69.3° (± 7.8°) and
50.2° (± 7.4°), respectively (p < 0.05) with mean correction of 26.9° (±

27.3° (10.9°), respectively. Post-op last visit mean PI, PT and SS were
38.7° (± 8.4°), 9.7° (± 8.4°), respectively. Nine patients underwent
additional scoliosis correction with mean pre-op and the last visit of 27.5°
(± 10.1°) and 8.4° (± 4.5°), respectively. Mean TPA were 0.9° (± 8.3°) and
8.3° (± 4.2°), respectively. Pre-op mean VAS and ODI scores were 3.4 and
18.1 and 1.9 and 11.3 at the last visit post-op. The mean SRS-22r scores
were 3.7 (± 0.47) and 4.3 (± 0.7), respectively. One patient developed acute
hypercapnic respiratory failure post-op which was associated with
anesthesia/narcotics. Two patients underwent revision: one due to distal
segment breakdown and other developed proximal junction kyphosis/ligamentous
injury. No other complications or revisions were observed in our cohort.
Conclusions: Our cohort data showed that adequate
correction with well-balanced spine can be achieved while preserving the
motion segments and reducing the risk of junctional failure with posterior
instrumented fusion. Patient reported outcomes improved over long run as
indicated by VAS, ODI and SRS scores.

## P115: Predictive models to assess risk of extended length of stay in
adults with spinal deformity and lumbar degenerative pathology: development
and internal validation

Ayush Arora

1

, Joshua Demb

2

, Daniel Cummins

1

, and Alekos Theologis

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, San
Francisco, United States

2

Department of Medicine, Division of Gastroenterology, University of
California, San Diego, United States

Introduction: Post-operative recovery after adult spinal
deformity (ASD) operations is arduous, frought with complications, and often
requires extended hospital stays. A need exists for a method to rapidly
predict patients at risk for extended length of stay (eLOS) in the
preoperative setting. The purpose of this study is to develop a machine
learning model to preoperatively estimate the likelihood of eLOS following
elective multi-level lumbar/thoracolumbar spinal instrumented fusions (≥ 3
segments) for ASD. Material and Methods: Data were collected
retrospectively from a state-level inpatient database hosted by the
Healthcare cost and Utilization Project (HCUP). Included for analysis were
patients of age ≥ 50 with ASD undergoing elective lumbar or thoracolumbar
multi-level instrumented fusions. Predictive variables consisted of
demographics, comorbidities, and operative information. The primary outcome
was eLOS (> 7 days). Significant variables from univariate and
multivariate analyses were used to develop a logistic regression-based
predictive model that utilized six predictors. Model accuracy was assessed
through area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity.
Results: 8,866 patients met inclusion criteria. A saturated
logistic model with all significant variables from multivariate analysis was
developed (AUC = 0.77), followed by generation of a simplified logistic
model through stepwise logistic regression (AUC = 0.76). Peak AUC was
reached with inclusion of six selected predictors (combined anterior and
posterior approach, surgery to both lumbar and thoracic regions, ≥ 8 level
fusion, malnutrition, congestive heart failure, and academic institution). A
cutoff of 0.18 for eLOS yielded a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 68%.
Conclusion: This predictive model can facilitate
identification of adults at risk for eLOS following elective multi-level
lumbar/thoracolumbar spinal instrumented fusions for ASD. With a fair
diagnostic accuracy, the predictive calculator will ideally enable
clinicians to improve preoperative planning, guide patient expectations,
enable optimization of modifiable risk factors, facilitate appropriate
discharge planning, stratify financial risk, and accurately identify
patients who may represent high-cost outliers.

## P116: Risk factors for extended length of stay and non-home discharge in
adults treated with multi-level fusion for lumbar degenerative pathology and
deformity

Ayush Arora

1

, Aboubacar Wague

1

, Matt Callahan

1

, Thomas Peterson

1

, Alekos Theologis

1

, and Sigurd Berven

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, San
Francisco, United States

Introduction: Surgical intervention for adult spinal deformity
(ASD) patients often necessitates considerable time for recovery in the
hospital and after discharge. Extended length of stay(eLOS) and discharge to
a rehabilitation center following operations for multi-level instrumented
spinal fusions are important outcomes that are significantly associated with
complications and higher costs. There is thus a need to accurately identify
granular risk factors pre-operatively associated with eLOS and non-home
discharges for patients undergoing multi-level fusions for ASD and lumbar
degenerative pathology. The purpose of this study is to identify independent
risk factors, including the Risk Assessment and Prediction Tool (RAPT)
score, associated with eLOS and non-home discharge following elective
multi-level instrumented spine fusion operations for diagnosis of adult
spinal deformity and lumbar degenerative pathology. Material and
Methods: Adults who underwent multi-level (≥3 segments)
instrumented spine fusions for ASD and lumbar degenerative pathology at a
single institution (2016-2021) were reviewed. Presence of a pre-operative
RAPT score was used as an inclusion criterion. Excluded were patients who
underwent non-elective operations, revisions, operations for trauma,
malignancy, and/or infections. Outcomes were eLOS (>7 days) and discharge
location (home vs. non-home). Predictor variables included demographics,
comorbidities, operative information, Surgical Invasiveness Index (SII), and
RAPT score. Fisher’s exact test was used for univariate analysis, and
significant variables were implemented in multivariate binary logistic
regression, with generation of 95% percent confidence intervals (CI), odds
ratios (OR), and p-values. Results: Included for analysis were
355 patients. Post-operatively, 36.6% (n = 130) had eLOS and 53.2% (n = 189)
had a non-home discharge. Risk factors significant for a non-home discharge
were older age (> 70 years), SII > 36, pre-op RAPT < 10, DMII,
diagnosis of depression or anxiety, and eLOS. Risk factors significant for
an eLOS were SII > 20, RAPT < 6, and an ASA score of 3.
Conclusion: The RAPT score and SII were most important
significant predictors of eLOS and non-home discharges following multi-level
instrumented fusions for lumbar spinal pathology and deformity. Preoperative
identification of patients with the significant risk factors identified in
this study is important for financial risk minimization, patient informed
choice, preemptive administration action, and better shared decision-making
ability. Preoperative optimization of the RAPT’s individual components may
provide a useful strategy for decreasing LOS and modifying discharge
disposition.

complications are similar between these 2 groups. These findings suggest

## P118: Effect of transverse process hook of UIV instruments on prevention
of re-operation associated myelopathy following adult spinal deformity
surgery

Sun Joon Yoo

1

, Kyung-Hyun Kim

1

, Jeong-Yoon Park

1

, Dongkyu Chin

1

, Keun-Su Kim

1

, and Yong-Eun Cho

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Gangnam Severance Hospital, Yonsei
University, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is widely known
as complication after adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery, and myelopathy
with PJK is the factor that causes re-operation. Less-rigid fixation using
transverse process hooks in UIV is thought to best prevent myelopathy in ASD
surgery. The aim of this study was to compare the incidence of reoperation
associated myelopathy between pedicle screws (PS) and transverse process
hooks (TPH) at uppermost instrumented vertebra (UIV) following ASD surgery.
Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed
radiographic and clinical data of 90 consecutive patients (mean age, 68.8
years; mean follow-up period, 24.5 months) who underwent instrumented fusion
from sacrum to thoracic spine for the treatment of ASD with a minimum
24months follow-up. Radiologic outcomes including the incidence of PJK and
clinical outcomes including the presence of postoperative myelopathy were
compared between 33 patients with TPH group and 57 patients with PS group.
Results: The myelopathy did not occur in the TPH group but
occurred 38.6% in the PS group (p < 0.001). In the TPH group, UIV hook
dislodgement in one patient, sacral fracture in one patient, and rod
fracture in one patient. In the PS group, reoperation was performed in
sixteen patients. The change in proximal junctional angle (PJA) pre- and
post-operation were lower in the TPH group (0.2 ± 6.7) than in the PS group
(6.6 ± 10.0, p = 0.002). The surgical outcome was almost same results at
each groups, except back VAS and SRS-22 domains including pain and
satisfaction. The post-operative VAS in the TPH and PS groups were 3.5 and
4.1, respectively (p = 0.010). The pain domain and the satisfaction domain
in SRS-22 were significantly difference in the TPH and PS groups (3.3 vs.
2.9; p = 0.033, 3.7 vs. 3.3; p = 0.041). There was no intergroup difference
in the SF-36. Conclusion: Our results show that using TPH as a
UIV implant can prevent the progress of PJK, reduce the pain, and increase
the patient satisfaction after surgery. The TPH of UIV level can prevent
post-operative myelopathy and prevent the accompanying re-operation.

## P119: Retrospective case series of expandable meshed bag for vertebral
osteomyelitis interbody fusion and vertebral compression fractures

Zachary Crawford

1

, Brian Johnson

1

, Kellsa Mbah-Feng

1

, Nihar Shah

1

, and Anthony Guanciale

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Cincinnati College of Medicine,
Cincinnati, United States

Introduction: There are multiple techniques and approaches for
insertion of interbody cages to promote fusion, restore alignment, and
support posterior instrumentation. Patients with history of osteoporosis,
end plate injury, or irregular end plates, all of which may limit implant
contact area and stress, are at risk for subsidence and failure of fusion.
OptiMesh deployable grafting system (Spineology Inc., Saint Paul, MN, USA)
has been previously used for interbody fusion, traumatic injuries, and
vertebral compression fracture without subsidence of graft. The objective of
this retrospective case series is to evaluate the need for revision surgery
and post-operative outcomes associated with use of the OptiMesh grafting
system in the setting of vertebral osteomyelitis and traumatic vertebral
compression fractures. Methods: Electronic health record was
queried for patients with OptiMesh implant by orthopaedic spine surgeon.
Patients were included if they underwent vertebroplasty or interbody fusion
with OptiMesh at our institution by an orthopaedic spine surgeon. General
demographic information including age, gender, medical comorbidities,
smoking status, and infectious disease information were collected from
retrospective chart review. The primary outcome was revision surgery.
Secondary outcomes included post-operative infection, any return to the
operating room, and any post-operative complications. Results:
Twenty-five patients underwent vertebroplasty or interbody fusion with
OptiMesh during the study period. The average age was 61.3 years (range
31.7-87.6 years) with 16 males (64%) and 9 females (36%). Nineteen patients

cohort that required a return to the operating room for graft failure or
revision. There were 3 patients with complications of post operative
surgical site infection requiring 4 operative irrigation and debridement.
There were no additional complications. Conclusion: The use of
OptiMesh has previously been studied for vertebral compression fractures and
interbody fusion for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Our limited, case
series retrospective review utilizing this product for vertebral compression
fracture and interbody fusion in the setting of vertebral osteomyelitis has
shown to be a valuable option with limited complications and no revision for
graft subsidence.

## P120: Is sexual dysfunction an issue after undergoing a C2-sacrum
posterior spinal fusion?

Justin Mathew

1

, Joseph Lombardi

1

, Hannah Lin

1

, Nathan Lee

1

, Venkat Boddapati

1

, Zeeshan Sardar

1

, Lawrence Lenke

1

, and Ronald A. Lehman

1

1

Columbia University, Irving Medical Center, New York, United
States

Summary: Patients who have undergone C2-sacrum posterior spinal
fusion (PSF) generally continue to be sexually active, though nearly all
note some physical limitations during sexual activity.
Hypothesis: Patients who have undergone C2-sacrum PSF
experience postoperative sexual dysfunction. Study Design:
Consecutive case series of open posterior spinal instrumented fusion from
C2-sacrum. Introduction: Patient who have undergone C2-sacrum
posterior spinal fusion (PSF) comprise a poorly studied population.
Limitations in sexual function are unreported in the literature among those
with any major spinal reconstruction. While many of these patients resume
hobbies and activities, they will often query surgeons preoperatively about
their postoperative sexual function. The ability to adequately counsel this
patient population is hampered by the dearth of literature on this subject.
Methods: 25 patients who had undergone C2-sacrum PSF at a
single institution were contacted by email and telephone. A standardized,
validated questionnaire (ASEX) was administered, as well as specific
questions addressing arousal, physical limitations during sex, and sexual
satisfaction. Responses were assigned numerical values and assessed using
descriptive statistics and student’s t test. Sexual dysfunction was defined
as an ASEX score > 19. Results: Of 25 patients who had
undergone C2-sacrum PSF, 60% (15/25) responded. 48% (12/25) were able to
complete to the questionnaire. 8% (2/25) had never had sex (before or after
surgery) and were excluded. 4% (1/25) had an underlying medical condition
and felt unable to answer the questionnaire. The average follow up time was
3.3 ± 1.2 years. Over 90% of respondents had more than two years follow up
since their C2-sacrum PSF. Of those who responded, 33% (4/12) experience
sexual dysfunction as defined by ASEX > 19. Though the ASEX questionnaire
generally addresses arousal, the responses did not differ significantly from
the responses to our tailored questions (p = 0.28). Of the patients who
reported being in the upper quartile of difficulty with physical limitations
(discomfort, muscle tightness, or motion restriction), only one had sexual
dysfunction. 92% of the respondents report return to sexual activity
following C2-sacrum PSF. Conclusion: This is the first study to
evaluate sexual dysfunction after a C2-sacrum fusion. Interestingly, 92% of
those who underwent C2-sacrum PSF report a return to sexual activity, with
only 33% demonstrating sexual dysfunction.
Take Home Message: Nearly all patients who have undergone C2-sacrum PSF
remain sexually active, though with limitations and changes in their sex
lives.

## 816

## P121: Skin adhesive tapes are an effective wound closure method for
percutaneous vertebral body stenting: a retrospective cohort study

Cassie Yang

1

, Theophilus Qiu

2

, Reuben Soh

1

, and Youheng Ou Yang

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Singapore General Hospital,
Singapore, Singapore

2

Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore,
Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Percutaneous Vertebral Body Stenting (VBS) is
performed via a balloon-expandable metallic stent introduced through a stab
incision. It aims to reduce and maintain the reduction of vertebral body
fractures, as well as minimise bone cement extravasation. The delivery of
the balloon and stent implant requires the insertion of a larger access kit
as compared to traditional vertebroplasty (PVP) systems (4.7 vs 2.59mm
diameter, 330% increase in surface area). The larger skin incision, soft
tissue disruption and pedicle bore tract with exposed raw bone increases the
risk of bleeding and wound complications. Skin Adhesive Tapes (SATs) are
effective in treating small non-gaping wounds and have been used as a method
of wound closure for PVP. This study aims to evaluate the use of SATs in
closure of larger VBS wounds. Methods: A retrospective cohort
of patients who underwent percutaneous VBS (DePuy Synthes, USA) was obtained
from electronic medical records of patients treated at a tertiary hospital
from May 2019 to March 2021. Data was collected for wound closure method
(conventional non-absorbable suture closure, SAT closure), number of
operative levels and postoperative skin-related wound complications, wound
dehiscence, wound infection, postoperative bleeding, symptomatic haematomas
and return to operating theatre. At clinic follow-up post-discharge, the
wounds were also reviewed for complete healing and unsightly scarring
requiring wound revision. SAT closure was performed by applying 3 strips of
SATs to loosely oppose the wound edges. Results: 36 patients
were identified with 45 levels of VBS performed. 3 (8.3%) patients received
conventional suture closure, 33 (91.6%) received SAT closure. Conventional
suture closure was performed in view of ongoing bleeding at the wound site
for 2 patients who had coagulopathy. The remaining patient received a
planned suture closure in view of surgical expediency as part of a staged
procedure. 32 (97.0%) of SAT closures were uneventful. 1 (3.0%) patient
developed blood soaked dressings that required early removal and
reapplication of the SATs at the ward a day later with uneventful recovery
thereafter. No patient with SAT closure developed any surgical site
infection, wound dehiscence, symptomatic haematoma or required return to
theatre. All SAT closure patients had complete wound healing at outpatient
follow up with no wound revision for cosmesis. Conclusion: SATs
are a simple, safe and effective means of wound closure for the majority of
percutaneous VBS procedures. Patients who could not undergo SAT closure had
pre-existing coagulopathy or had been planned for additional procedures.

## P122: No significant radiological signs of adult spinal deformity

Peter Brumat

, Janez Mohar

, Nikša Hero

, and Matevž Topolovec

Department of Spine Surgery, Valdoltra Orthopaedic Hospital,

Introduction: Instrumentation with Harrington rod used to be the
standard of care for scoliosis treatment in children. Such a method of

sagittal malalignment in adults. The adult spinal deformity can be managed
with nonsurgical methods or surgical treatment. Surgical correction for
Harrington rod instrumentation sequelae presents a challenge in adult spinal
deformity surgery due to complex conditions involving residual structural

osteotomies, with the high surgical risk involved. Although surgical

spinal deformity after Harrington rod removal, whereby no patient consented

of 11 years of follow-up following Harrington rod instrumentation removal,
with a minimum 1 year of follow-up. Preoperative and most recent

compared, along with baseline demographics. Results: The
average age of patients (all females) at the time of instrumentation removal

angle (proximal (p = 0.488), main thoracic (p = 0.130) and lumbar (p =
0.317)). Conclusion: This study suggests that adults with no
significant change in coronal or sagittal parameters following Harrington
rod instrumentation removal may be amenable to conservative management of
residual spinal deformity if surgical correction of spinal deformity is not

0.001). Pain, function, and satisfaction domains of the patients reached
satisfying levels according to normative data of SRS-22. On the other hand,
the means of mental health and self-image domains were fall short of the
mark. Conclusion: In the study, it was observed that the use of
a brace in the conservative treatment of AIS was effective in controlling

## P125: Comparison of posterior vs double appoach in the treatment of adult

Clauio Mauricio Uribe Alpizar

1

, Alejandro Reyes-Sánchez

1

, and Carla Garcia Ramos

1

1

Orthopedic, National Institute of Rehabilitation, Mexico City,

Introduction: An increase in the adult population is currently
occurring worldwide. World literature has identified that the prevalence of
scoliosis increases with age and that curvatures may appear in a previously
aligned spine, unlike idiopathic scoliosis in young people, it presents with
pain and disability in adults. Currently, a prevalence in the population of
2 to 32% is reported in those over 50 years of age and up to 60% in those
over 60 years of age. Given that its main symptom is pain, this condition
has an impact on the quality of life of those who suffer it, limiting their
personal and work activities, becoming disabling. It is most frequently
observed in adult patients of productive age, progressing with disability.
Previous studies have shown that scoliotic curvature correction is over 70%
with a double approach vs. 44% with a posterior approach. Controversy exists
regarding lordosis, complications, pseudoarthrosis and complication rate.
This research proposes to carry out a comparative study between the
clinical, radiological and functional results of two surgical techniques and
their variants, as well as to establish if there is correspondence between
the radiographic changes and the clinical situation of the patient. The
number of studies comparing the posterior approach with a dual approach for
management of adult degenerative scoliosis is minimal. When searching with
the search terms: "surgery" + "degenerative scoliosis" + "double approach"
search in PubMed, Google Scholar, Ovid, Cochrane we obtained a total of 11
references, however, when we searched the Mexican literature, we did not
find any reference to the subject. Therefore, we conclude that there is no
precedent where the results of double surgical treatment in patients with
this disease are analyzed in our country. Material and Methods:
Prospective, longitudinal, comparative controlled study with two-year
follow-up, In adult degenerative scoliosis, divided into two groups Group I
treated with posterior approach and Group 2 treated with double approach. 43
patients with an average age of 63.2 years, 30 women (69.76%), with curves
with magnitude from 10 to 42°. 35 were subjected to a posterior approach,
while 8 were treated with a double approach (ALPA + posterior).
Results: The Roland-Morris scale in group 1 was 13.17
(0-22), and at 2 years 9.75 (0-22) for group 2 with a preoperative mean of
14.71 (8-20) and 7.28 (0-14) at 2 years. No statistical significance between
groups (p = 0.356). The Oswestry in preoperative group 2 patients was 49.71
(26-74); 2 years in 21.85 (2-44). For group 1 in 54.27 (18-82), and 35.51
(2-82) in 2 years. Pelvic parameters have no difference and only correction
of scoliosis and sagittal balance was better in the double-approach group.
Conclusions: The ALPA + posterior approaches, compared to
only the posterior approach, have an advantage in reducing the magnitude of
scoliosis and restoring sagittal balance. In terms of quality of life and
perception of pain, both approaches show to be equally effective.

## P126: Surgical treatment of ankylosing spondylitis complicated with
thoracolumbar sagittal-coronal deformity

Tao Xu

1

, Xiaoyu Cai

, Jarkenay Abudulayi

2

, and Weibin Sheng

Introduction: To investigate the incidence and clinical

complicated with thoracolumbar sagittal coronal deformity. Material
and Methods: The case data of 22 patients (17 males and 5

corrected from 10.07 ± 6.68 cm to 3.21 ± 2.01 cm and 3.33 ± 2.0 cm. CIA
improved from 18.16 ± 5.23° to 6.11 ± 3.78° and 5.99 ± 3.74°. C7-SVA was
corrected from 24.38 ± 8.65 cm to 10.7 ± 5.15 cm. GK was corrected from
61.52 ± 15.38° to 24.66 ± 13.24°. TLK was corrected from 54.99 ± 11.73° to
19.68 ± 12.19°. TK was corrected from 56.64 ± 6.54° to 41.51 ± 9.9°. LL was
corrected from 12.56 ± 8.57° to -32.64 ± 18.21°. PI was corrected from 44.64
± 8.57° preoperatively to 45.56 ± 9.5°. PT was corrected from 35.39 ± 9.59°
to 27.65 ± 6.98°. SS was corrected from 14.12 ± 8.63° to 17.97 ± 9.36°.
Significant differences were observed between the postoperative and
preoperative deformities except for PI and SS. At the last follow-up, the
correction rates of CBD, CIA, C7-SVA and GK were 80.2%, 76.2%, 76.1% and
58.9%, respectively. The mean VAS score of 22 patients was (7.42 ± 1.37)
preoperative and (4.22 ± 0.98) at the last follow-up with significant
difference (t = 20.249, P = 0.000). The average ODI was 58.68% ± 7.45%
preoperative and 26.52% ± 4.21% at the last follow-up significantly (t =
42.543, P = 0.000). The mean score of SRS⁃22 was 9.62 ± 3.06 preoperatively,
which was improved to 22.84 ± 3.15 at the last follow-up significantly (t =
25.023, p = 0.000). Perioperative complications occurred in 7 patients
(32%). Conclusion: A distance of more than 3cm between the C7
plumb line and the sacral midline was used as a diagnostic criterion for
coronal disequilibrium. Asymmetrical PSO osteotomy was used to correct
coronal imbalance at the apex of coronal imbalance, and CWO osteotomy was
used to correct kyphosis at the apex of sagittal kyphosis. For type A
patients with single-segment PSO osteotomy, asymmetrical COWO osteotomy was
used to correct both sagittal and coronal imbalance at the apex of sagittal
and coronal imbalance. The evaluation of intraoperative coronal balance by
point-line method can effectively reduce the incidence of postoperative
coronal imbalance in patients with AS complicated with sagittal and coronal
imbalance.

## P127: Physiotherapy scoliosis specific exercise improves pelvic obliquity
in adults with idiopathic scoliosis

Charles Impey

, Georgina Frere

, Erika Maude

, Emily Tsang

, Priyanshu Saha

, Bisola Ajayi

, Timothy Bishop

1

, Jason Bernard

1

, and Darren Lui

1

1

St George's University Hospital, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Pelvic obliquity (PO) contributes to altered gait
patterns, causing asymmetrical loading, increased muscular work, and
prolonged activation of lumbar muscles. It can cause waistline asymmetry
which is a well-documented complaint in scoliosis. This study aimed to
determine the effects of an intensive course of Physiotherapy Scoliosis
Specific Exercise (PSSE) on PO in patients with idiopathic scoliosis (IS).
Method: Consecutive patients with IS with primary
thoraco-lumbar or lumbar curvatures completing an intensive course of PSSE
over a 4-week timeframe between April 2019 and December 2021 were recruited.
Patients who had undergone bracing treatment or surgery for scoliosis were
excluded. All patients were routinely scanned using a Formetric Scanner pre-
and post-treatment. The PO, expressed in millimetres, was documented. Adults
(>17 years old) (group 1) and children (group 2) were analysed
separately. Results: In Group 1 (n = 19) the ages ranged from
18 to 73 with a median age of 25. 89.5% were female. The average Cobb angle
was 36.3°. There was a 35% improvement in PO from 6.63mm (SD = 4.3)
pre-treatment to 4.32mm (SD = 10.23) post-treatment (p < 0.05). In Group
2 (n = 31) the ages ranged from 8 to 16 with a median age of 14. 90% were
female. The average Cobb angle was 31.3°. There was a 23% improvement in PO
from 4.68mm (SD = 4.14) pre-treatment to 3.58mm (SD = 2.51) post-treatment
(p = 0.09). Conclusion and Significance: An intensive course of
PSSE has shown to improve PO in adult patients with IS. This can contribute
to improving the patients’ biomechanics and self-image and therefore
health-related quality of life.

## 1133

## P129: Analysis of the difference in sitting ability based on fusion level
in patients with adult spinal deformity corrective surgery

Jaeyoung So

1

 and Kyung-Hyun Kim

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Spine and Spinal Cord Institute, Gangnam
Severance Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: There is still debate how surgeons could decide
treatment methods for adult spinal deformity, operatively or not. There was
lack of information how long level fusion impacts daily activities,
especially sitting ability. The primary goal of surgical arthrodesis is to
eliminate the motion of spinal segments in an effort to alleviate pain,
improve deformity, and reduce disability. However, decreased spinal mobility
may impair performance of activities of daily living due to the resulting
stiffness or the lack of mobility of the fused segment. We aimed to assess
the sitting ability in patients undergoing adult spinal deformity corrective
surgery, comparing L4-5 or L3-4-5 fusion, L4-5 or L4-5-S1 lumbar fusion
surgeries through a patient-reported outcome questionnaire measuring the
impact of lumbar stiffness. Materials and Methods: A total 113
patients, who underwent adult spinal deformity corrective surgery, 1 or 2
levels of fusion including L4 and L5 without sacropelvic fixation (L4-5 or
L3-4-5 fusion), and 1 or 2 levels of fusion including L5 and S1 with
sacropelvic fixation (L5-S1 or L4-5-S1 fusion) in our neurosurgery clinic.
Data of the patients were obtained from electronic patients records and
Sitting ability questionnaire. Patients were divided into three groups, each
consisting of 47 patients, who underwent L4-5 fusion or L3-4-5 fusion (L4-5
Group), 33 patients who underwent L5-S1 fusion or L4-5-S1 fusion (L5-S1
Group) and, 33 patients who underwent adult spinal deformity corrective
surgery (Deformity Group). We investigate the basic demographics (age,
gender, follow duration, etc.), Sitting ability score and Lifestyle through
Sitting ability questionnaire. The factors affecting sitting ability were
also investigated. Results: The average sitting ability score
was 80.67 ± 14.28 for L4-5 Group, 79.48 ± 16.25 for L5-S1 Group, 60.70 ±
19.75 for Deformity Group, respectively. There was no significant difference
between L4-5 Group and L5-S1 Group (p = 0.753). There were significant
differences between L4-5 Group and Deformity Group (p < 0.0001), between
L5-S1 Group and Deformity Group (p < 0.0001). The mean follow-up duration
was 70.25 ± 38.80 months for L4-5 Group, 75.27 ± 59.53 months for L5-S1
Group, 40.86 ± 20.80 months for Deformity Group, respectively and there was
significant difference among these groups. (p < 0.0001).
Conclusion: Multilevel lumbar fusion significantly limits
the lumbar mobility and affects the ability to compensate postural changes.
Reducing the fusion segments as much as possible is of particular value in
preserving lumbar mobility and maintaining the compensatory mechanism of
spinopelvis. Not only the fusion level, but also the sitting ability will be
different with the difference of UIV and LIV level, so this should be
considered during lumbar fusion surgery.

## 1196

## P130: Unplanned reoperation and readmission following adult spinal
deformity surgery: an analysis over 8,500 spinal deformity patients

Daniel Gallagher

1

, William Huffman

2

, Jacob Harris

2

, Rex Marco

3

, Paul Holman

3

, and Comron Saifi

4

1

Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University, New
Brunswick, United States

2

Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania,
Philadelphia, United States

3

Department of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine

4

Spine Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United
States

Introduction: It was estimated that 30-day readmissions across
all specialties resulted in $41.3 billion in hospital costs in 2011.
Unplanned reoperations require additional resources and add further
financial strain on the healthcare system and patients. The utilization of
Adult Spinal Deformity (ASD) surgery has been rapidly growing but, the
complication rate remains high. Although prior research has identified
factors associated with adverse outcomes of spinal deformity surgery, the
few studies that have evaluated factors predictive of reoperation and
readmission rates included fewer than 800 patients, limiting their
statistical power to detect infrequent predictors. The purpose of this study
is to use the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality
Improvement Program (ACS NSQIP) to identify risk factors associated with
unplanned reoperation and readmission within 30 days following surgical
correction of ASD with ≥ 7 levels of correction. A reoperation rate of 5%
and a readmission rate of 10% were hypothesized based on prior literature.
Materials and Methods: A retrospective observational study
was conducted using the ACS-NSQIP database for patients undergoing ASD
surgery from 2010 to 2019. The NSQIP database collects more than 150
variables from over 600 participating hospitals in the United States. Each
participating site has a trained and certified surgical clinical reviewer to
extract preoperative to 30-day postoperative data for randomly assigned
patients. The NSQIP has developed multiple processes to optimize accuracy
and reliability of data collection, including an inter-rater reliability
audit of selected sites. Using the ACS-NSQIP participant user file, patients
from participating institutions, aged 18 years and older having surgical
correction of ASD with ≥ 7 levels of correction, were identified using
Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes 22843 and 22844. Methods were
conducted in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of
Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines.
Results: 8,533 patients met the inclusion criteria, with a
mean age of 62 years and a female predominance (55%). The 30-day unplanned
reoperation and readmission rates were 7.55% and 9.72%, with 13.43% having
either an unplanned reoperation or readmission. Independent predictors of
both reoperation and readmission were African American race, bleeding
disorders, and chronic steroid use. Independent predictors of unplanned
reoperation alone included >10% loss of body weight in last 6 months and
emergency cases. Independent predictors of readmission alone included
disseminated cancer, partially dependent functional status, and totally
dependent functional status. The most frequent reoperation was incision and
drainage (8.07%). The most common causes of readmission were surgical site
infection (SSI) (16.89%) and wound disruption (4.70%).
Conclusion: Patients undergoing spine surgery for adult
spinal deformity with >6 levels of instrumentation had an 8% and 10% rate
of unplanned reoperation and readmission, respectively. There was a 13% rate
of either unplanned reoperation or readmission. African American race,
bleeding disorders, disseminated cancer, immunosuppressant use for a chronic
condition, and lower functional status were the most significant predictors
of 30-day unplanned reoperation or readmission. These individual factors
were associated with increases in the rates of reoperation or readmission of
36-152%. SSI was the most common reason for both reoperation and
readmission.
