## P131: The summit versus the base: which aspect of the construct has more
influence on the development of proximal junctional kyphosis following adult
spinal deformity surgery?

Peter Passias

1

, Tyler Williamson

1

, Bailey Imbo

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Kimberly McFarland

1

, Jamshaid Mir

1

, Andrew Schoenfeld

2

, Stephane owusu-saprong

1

, Jordan Lebovic

1

, Shaleen Vira

3

, Bassel Diebo

4

, Justin Smith

5

, Virginie Lafage

6

, and Renaud Lafage

6

1

NYU Langone Medical Center, New York, United States

2

Brigham and Women’s Hospital/Harvard Medical Center, Boston, United
States

3

UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, United States

4

SUNY Downstate Medical Center, New York, United States

5

University of Virginia, Charlottesville, United States

6

Lenox Hill Hospital, New York, United States

Purpose: Evaluate the surgical technique that has greatest
influence on the rate of junctional failure following ASD surgery.
Introduction: Due to the severity and complexity of adult
spinal deformity (ASD), differing presentations may influence the extent of
surgical intervention and use of prophylaxis at the base or the summit of a
fusion construct to influence junctional failure rates. It is unclear
whether interventions at the base, summit or both are needed to effectively
mitigate junctional failure. Methods: ASD patients with 2Y data
and at least 5-level fusion to pelvis were included. Patients were divided
based on UIV: [Longer Construct: T1-T4; Shorter Construct: T8-T12].
Parameters assessed included matching in age-adjusted PI-LL or PT, aligning
in GAP-Relative Pelvic Version or Lordosis Distribution Index. Combination
of realigning the two parameters with the greatest minimizing effect of PJF
constituted a Good Base. Good Summit defined as having all 3: 1) prophylaxis
at UIV (tethers, hooks, cement), 2) no lordotic change (under-contouring)
greater than 10° of the UIV during surgery, 3) preoperative UIV inclination
angle < 30°. Multivariable regression analysis assessed effects of
junction characteristics and radiographic correction individually and
collectively on development of PJK and PJF in differing construct lengths,
adjusting for confounders. Results: 261 patients were included,
with 38% developing PJK, 10% developing PJF. The cohort that had summit and
base addressed had lower odds of PJK (OR: 0.5, [0.2-0.9]) and PJF was less
likely (OR: 0.1, [0.0-0.7]; p = .014) in the presence of a Good Summit.
Normalizing pelvic compensation had the greatest radiographic effect on
preventing PJF overall (OR: 0.6, [0.3-1.0]; p = .044). Stratifying by UIV,
114 were Longer Constructs, 147 Shorter Constructs. In Shorter Constructs,
realignment had greater effect on decreasing the odds of PJF (OR: 0.2,
[0.02-0.9]; p = .036). With Longer Constructs, a Good Summit lowered
likelihood of PJK (OR: 0.3, [0.1-0.9]; p = .027). Good Base had reducing
effects on PJF (0% vs. 20%, p < .001). In patients with severe
frailty/osteoporosis, a Good Summit lowered rates of PJK (20.0% vs. 39.3%, p
= .017) and PJF (4.0% vs. 13.4%, p = .020). Conclusion: To
mitigate junctional failure, our study demonstrated the utility of
individualizing surgical approaches to emphasize an optimal basal construct.
Achievement of tailored goals at the cranial end of the surgical construct
may be equally important, especially for higher risk patients with longer
fusions.

## 1316

## P132: Maintenance of pelvic tilt normalization following adult spinal
deformity corrective surgery: analysis of prevalence, timing, and predictors
influencing occurrence

Peter Passias

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Jamshaid Mir

1

, Kimberly McFarland

1

, Andrew Schoenfeld

2

, Bassel Diebo

3

, Renaud Lafage

4

, Virginie Lafage

4

, and Shaleen Vira

5

1

NYU Langone Medical Center, New York, United States

2

Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, United States

3

Warren Alpert Medical School, Providence, United States

4

Lenox Hill Hospital, New York, United States

5

UT Southwestern, Dallas, TX, United States

Introduction: Increasing pelvic tilt (PT) is a primary
compensatory mechanism in adult spinal deformity (ASD). Some ASD patients
improve their PT following ASD correction, while others do not. The driving
forces behind this lack of PT-response are not well defined.
Hypothesis: To determine the surgical and
radiographic parameters associated with and predict maintaining PT
normalization after ASD corrective surgery.
Methods: ASD patients fused to S1/pelvis with
full preoperative data as well as preoperative (BL), 6-week (6W), and 2-year
(2Y) post-op PT measurements were included. Patients were stratified into
four groups based on PT measurements at 6 week and 2 year follow-up: Early
Normalization with PT < 20° by 6 weeks (PTNorm6w); Delayed Normalization
with PT < 20° by 2 years (PTNorm2y); Non-normalized with PT >20° by 2
years (Non); Reversal Normalization with PT < 20° by 6 weeks and PT
>20° by 2 years (RevNorm). Univariate analyses were used to compare
normalized (PTNorm6w and PTNorm2Y) and non-normalized (Non and RevNorm) in
terms of postoperative alignment (PI-LL, SVA, and GAP score) and clinical
outcomes (complication rates, HRQL). Multivariable logistic regression were
used to develop a model consisting of significant predictors for 6 week and
2 year normalization. Results: 253 ASD patients met inclusion
criteria (64.6 ± 9.06 years, 79% female, BMI 27.9 ± 5.57 kg/m2, CCI: 1.9 ±
1.6, levels fused 11.8 ± 4.4, EBL: 1841.6 mL, op time: 449.6 min). Mean PT
was as follows: BL: 30.5°, 6W: 22.5°, and 2Y: 25°. By SRS-Schwab criteria
(Normal: PT < 20°; Moderate: PT 20-30°; Severe: PT > 30°), 56.5% (n =
143) had a moderate pelvic tilt at baseline and 43.5% (n = 110) had severe
pelvic tilt at baseline. 37.9% (n = 96) were normalized at 6 weeks and 6.3%
(n = 16) normalized between 6 weeks and 2 years, with a total of 43.1% (n =
109) normalized by 2 years. 33 (13%) had reversal of normalization at 2
years. PT6WNorm and PT2YNorm groups were more likely to be overcorrected in
radiographic goals including PI-LL, SVA, and PT at 6 weeks (p < .05). GAP
score at 6 weeks (.55 vs 1.34, p = 0.08) was greater for non-normalized
patients. RevNorm patients had significantly lower PI (56.5 vs 61.6, p <
.05) and GAP score (1 vs 1.5, p < .05) compared those achieving
normalization at 2 years. Compared to non-normalized patients, those
achieving normalization by 2 years had lower rates of implant failure (8.9%
vs 19.5%, p < .05), rod breakage (1.3% vs 13.8%, p < .05) and
pseudoarthrosis (0% vs 4.6%, p < .05). Total complication rate was
significantly lower for those achieving normalization (56.7% vs 66.1%, p =
.02). No significant difference in ODI, EQ5D, or SRS22 Pain scores.
Multivariate regressions used to create a model for normalization showed 88%
of patients achieved significantly greater normalization with lower baseline
and 6 week PI-LL (OR .82 [.7 - .95], p < .05).
Conclusion: PT normalization following ASD
correction occurred in almost 40% of patients by 6 weeks and 43% by 2 years
after surgery. Normalization was more likely to occur in patients where
reconstruction addressed lumbopelvic mismatch and extended above the apex of
the thoracic kyphosis. PT normalization and maintenance remains an important
factor for improved post-surgical outcomes.

## 1327

## P133: Incremental benefit of revision surgery after adult spinal
deformity corrective surgery: at what point does the value of multiple
revisions diminish in ASD corrective surgery and does it depend on
etiology

Peter Passias

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Kimberly McFarland

1

, and Jamshaid Mir

1

1

NYU Langone Medical Center, New York, Unitede States

Introduction: Incidence of revision surgery after
surgical correction of ASD remains high. However, the benefits of multiple
revision surgery on patient outcomes are not well-defined.
Hypothesis: To assess impact of revision
surgery on surgical outcomes, alignment, and HRQLs.
Methods: ASD patients with BL, 2Y data, and ≥
1 revisions included. Patients were stratified by number of revisions (R1,
R2, or R3 defined as > 2 revisions). Baseline demographic and surgical
details were taken from visit prior to revision surgery. Differences between
groups were assessed using ANOVA. Follow-up was based on timepoint 2Y after
final revision. 3 revision groups were propensity score matched (PSM) using
many-to-one matching, while adjusting for differences at baseline.
Radiographic parameters SVA, PI-LL, and PT were used to assess alignment
post-revision via ANOVA. MVA assessed differences in outcomes after final
revision surgery while controlling for relevant covariates.
Results: 252 patients included (R1: 108; R2:
108; R3: 36). Baseline demographic and surgical differences found no
significant differences between cohorts. Revision baseline
deformity (as defined by radiographic alignment measures SVA, PI-LL, PT)
showed no significant differences between groups (all
p>.05). 2 years after final revision surgery, ANOVA
showed significant differences between R1 and R3, and R2 and R3, with those
undergoing greatest number of revisions R3 demonstrating less improvement in
deformity measures (all p < .001). Pre-revision ODI scores for each group
showed a decline with increasing revision number. Of note, R1 and R2, as
compared to R3, had greater difference between baseline and 2 year ODI
scores, indicating a sustained benefit to revision surgery (-13.0 vs -13.9
vs -9.7). Percentage of those reaching SCB in ODI from pre-revision baseline
to years were R1 71.3%, R2 60.2%, and R3 38.9%, with significant difference
found between R1 and R3, and R2 and R3 (all p < .05). The percentage of
patients reaching MCID in ODI for each cohort was 35.2% R1, 25.9% R2, and
13.9% R3. MVA demonstrated a significantly lower odds of reaching MCID in
ODI for R2 and R3 compared to R1. Overall, patients undergoing
multiple revision surgery were 25% less likely to reach MCID in ODI as
compared to R1 group. Despite the inferior functional outcomes as measured
by ODI scores, patient satisfaction measured by SRS scores were maintained
from baseline to 2 years between revision groups. The rates of complications
increased with revisions, with R3 having the greatest overall complication
rate compared to R1 and R2. Overall, surgical indications for revisal
increased with number of revisions: R3 had significantly greater percentage
of surgical and mechanical complications leading to revision as compared to
R2 and R1. Conclusion: This study attempted to
quantify the impact of multiple revision surgeries by comparing patient
alignment and outcomes after each revision. Patients requiring multiple
revision surgeries had lower odds of reaching minimal clinically important
difference in ODI scores as well as maintaining clinical benefit. Despite
inferior functional outcomes, alignment improved, and patient satisfaction
was maintained across revision groups. These results suggest that surgical
correction may still maintain benefit with the appropriate indication.

## 1343

## P134: Disparities in recovery and survival rates in cervical versus
thoracolumbar spinal deformity patients are attributable to frailty status
at presentation

Peter Passias

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Jamshaid Mir

1

, Bailey Imbo

1

, Tyler Williamson

1

, Zach Thomas

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, and Kimberly McFarland

1

, Rachel Joujon-Roche

1

, Shaleen Vira

2

 and Bassel Diebo

3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, NYU Langone Orthopedic Hospital,
New York, United States

2

UT Southwestern, Dallas, United States

3

SUNY Downstate, New York, United States

Introduction: Previous studies have demonstrated relatively
higher risk of death in CD surgeries, yet there remains a paucity of
literature comparing and contrasting the comorbidities and predictive
factors associated with death in ASD vs CD surgery. Methods:
Operative CD patients ≥ 18yrs with pre-(BL) and up to two-year (2Y) data
were included. Group differences were assessed via means comparison
analysis. Backstep logistic regression identified mortality predictors.
Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed survivorship of expired patients. Cox
regression assessed survivability adjusting for BL frailty status. Log rank
analysis determined differences in survival distribution groups.
Results: 625 total patients were included (417 ASD, 208
CD). Within 5Y, 12 ASD patients (2.88% of ASD cohort) and 16 CD patients
(7.69% of CD cohort) expired (p = 0.004). At baseline, ASD and CD patients
differed significantly in BL Frailty score (0.29 vs 0.41, p < .001),
though not in age, gender, nor BMI (all p > .05). The most common
self-reported comorbidities in ASD patients were: arthritis (46%),
hypertension (31%), and anemia (23%); in CD patients: osteoporosis (50%),
previous myocardial infarction (17%), and any cancer (17%). No significant
differences in major, minor, nor intraoperative complications between living
or expired ASD or CD patients were observed (all p > .05). Accounting for
age, BMI, and gender, regression revealed only frailty status remained a
significant predictor of death overall (p = .047). Mean survival time for
ASD was 84.11 weeks versus 65.17 in CD patients (χ2(1) = .748, p = .387).
Conclusion: Total two-year all-cause mortality in adult
spinal deformity and cervical deformity patients remains below 3% despite
high rates of comorbidities, suggesting rigorous patient selection criteria
plays an important role in maintaining patient safety. While cervical
deformity patients demonstrate greater incidence of death post-operatively,
increased baseline frailty status may be the principle cause of such results
and should be considered when assessing surgical risks versus benefits.

School of Medicine, Durham, United States

16

Department of Orthopaedics, Lenox Hill Hospital, Northwell Health,
New York, United States

17

Department of Spine Surgery, Denver International Spine Clinic,
Presbyterian St. Luke's/Rocky Mountain Hospital for Children, Denver,
United States

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and failure
(PJF) development remains a major concern after adult spinal deformity (ASD)
corrective surgery. There remains a paucity of literature utilizing
contemporary alignment metrics and novel prophylaxis measures to predict
occurrence of PJK and PJF. Material and Methods: Operative ASD
patients with complete baseline (BL) and 2-year (2Y) postoperative
radiographic data were included. PJK was defined as ≥ 10° measure for the
sagittal Cobb angle between the inferior endplate of the UIV and the
superior endplate of the UIV+2. PJF was defined as meeting Lafage et al. PJF
criteria by 2Y. Baseline demographic, clinical and surgical information were
used to predict the occurrence of PJK and PJF using backstep binary logistic
regression analysis. Internal cross validation of the model was performed.
Receiver operating characteristic curve determined area-under-curve (AUC).
Conditional inference tree (CIT) analysis determined thresholds at (α =
.05). Odds ratio (OR) < 1.0 represents protection against PJK/PJF.
Results: 779 ASD patients (59.87 ± 14.24 years, 78% female,
27.78 ± 6.02kg/m2, mean CCI: 1.74 ± 1.71) were included. 60.5% of
patients (n = 471) developed PJK, and 10.5% (n = 82) developed PJF by their
last recorded visit. Significant predictors assessed at BL included: age,
osteoporosis, arthritis, lower extremity paresthesia, Passias et al. frailty
categorization, TS-CL, PI-LL, sagittal age-adjusted score (SAAS) modifiers,
BL maximal kyphosis at thoracic apex (MaxTK), levels fused, upper
instrumented vertebra (UIV), and PJK prophylaxis techniques: cement, hooks,
percutaneous screw fixation, or hybrid measures (hybrid), rod diameter, and
rod composition (all p < .05). The six most significant demographic,
radiographic, surgical, and post-operative predictors of PJK/PJF were: BL
age ≥ 74 (OR: 1.06 [1.014 – 1.107], p = .005), BL SAAS T1PA modifier >1
(OR: 0.352 [0.169 - 0.733], p = .004), BL SAAS PT modifier > 0 (OR: 0.547
[0.344 – 0.870], p = .008, levels fused > 16 (OR: 1.139 [1.022 – 1.269],
p = .015), use of prophylactic hooks (OR: 0.122 [0.040 – 0.372], p <
.001), and 6W SAAS PI-LL modifier > 1 (OR: 3.604 [1.840 – 7.061], p <
.001). Overall, the predictive model was deemed significant (p < .001),
and internally validated ROC analysis returned an AUC of .923, indicating
robust model fit. Conclusion: Proximal junctional kyphosis and
failure remain critical concerns in adult spinal deformity surgery, and
efforts to reduce the occurrence of PJK and PJF have resulted in the
development of novel prophylactic techniques and enhanced clinical and
radiographic selection criteria. This study demonstrates a validated model
incorporating such techniques that may allow for the prediction of
clinically significant PJK and PJF, and thus assist in optimizing patient
selection, enhance intraoperative decision making, and reduce post-operative
complications in ASD surgery.

## P136: Effects of bone cement augmentation for uppermost instrumented
vertebra on adjacent segment degeneration in lumbar fusions

Young-Hoon Kim

1

, Sang-Il Kim

1

, and Hyung Youl Park

2

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Seoul St. Mary's Hospital, The Catholic
University of Korea, Seoul, South Korea

2

Orthopedic Surgery, Eunpyong St. Mary's Hospital, The Catholic
University of Korea, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Bone cement-augmented screw is one of the
techniques used to reduce early mechanical failure in multilevel lumbar
fusions, especially in the elderly. However, there is little information
regarding the long-term effects. This retrospective study is designed to
investigate the effects of bone cemented augmentation on adjacent level
degeneration. Material and Methods: Fifty one patients who
underwent more than three levels of lumbar fusion were divided into two
groups according to bone cement-augmented screw fixation involving the upper
instrumented vertebra (UIV): 22 patients (cemented group, group I) and 29
patients (non-cemented group, group II). The analysis of radiographic
adjacent segment degeneration (ASD) involved patients with lumbosacral
fusion showing a similar degree of osteoporosis. Radiologic ASD was defined
as more than two UCLA grades of progression at 2 years postoperatively.
Other radiographic parameters including sagittal profiled and preoperative
MR Pfirrmann grades for adjacent level were analyzed. Results:
Even when no significant differences existed in preoperative demographic and
radiographic parameters between the two groups, the postoperative kyphotic
changes at 3 months were higher in the non-cemented group. In terms of
long-term effects, radiologic ASD (20 patients (95.2%) in group I; 15
(53.6%) in group II) was significantly higher in the cemented group.
Logistic regression analysis of radiologic ASD including other clinical and
radiological parameters, postoperative PI-LL mismatch (OR 5.201, 95% CI
1.123-24.090, p = 0.035) and cement augmentation (OR 20.193, 95% CI
2.195-185.729, p = 0.008) showed a significant correlation with the
development of radiologic ASD at postoperative 2 years.
Conclusion: Although bone cement-augmented screw
implantation can prevent kyphotic deformation at the proximal junction of
UIV in early postoperative stages of multi-level lumbar fusion, a discreet
selection of patients is required due to possible accelerated degeneration
of adjacent segments.
Keywords: adjacent segment degeneration; bone cement
augmentation; spinal fusion; sagittal alignment

## P137: Distal junctional failure after corrective surgery without pelvic
fixation for thoracolumbar junctional kyphosis due to osteoporotic vertebral
fracture

Yoshifumi Kudo

1

, Ichiro Okano

1

, Hiroshi Maruyama

1

, Ryo Yamamura

1

, Chikara Hayakawa

1

, Yushi Hoshino

2

, and koutaro tsuchiya

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Showa University, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo,
Japan

2

Orthopedic Surgery, Asahi University Hospital, Japan

Objective: Thoracolumbar junctional kyphosis (TLJK) due to
osteoporotic vertebral fracture (OVF) had a substantially negative impact on
quality of life. The necessity of pelvic fixation in correction surgery for
TLJK due to OVF remains controversial. The aims of this study are: 1) to
evaluate the surgical outcomes of major corrective surgery for TLJK due to
OVF, and 2) to identify the risk factors for distal junctional failure (DJF)
to identify potential candidates for pelvic fixation. Methods:
The records of patients with TLJK due to OVF who underwent surgical
correction (fixed kyphotic deformity >40°, OVF located at T11–L2, the
lowermost instrumented vertebra (LIV) at or above L5) were retrospectively
reviewed. Spinopelvic parameters such as sagittal vertical axis (SVA),
pelvic tilt (PT), pelvic incidence (PI), thoracic kyphosis (TK), lumbar
lordosis (LL: L1-S1), local kyphosis (LK) and lower lumbar lordosis (LLL:
L4-S1) were assessed. Proximal and distal junctional kyphosis (PJK/DJK), and
proximal and distal junctional failure (P/DJF) were evaluated. Demographic
data and pre/postoperative spinopelvic parameters were compared between DJF
and non-DJF patients. Results: Thirty-one patients (the mean
age 72.3 ± 7.9) were included in the final analysis. PJK was observed in
five patients (16.1%), while DJK was observed in 11 (35.5%). The main cause
(15/16 cases, 93.8%) of PJK/DJK was vertebral fracture. 12 cases (38.7%)
were categorized as failure. Among the patients with PJK, there was only one
patient (20%) categorized as PJF and required an additional surgery.
Contrary, all of eleven patients (100%) with DJK were categorized as DJF,
among whom six (54.5%) required additional surgery for pelvic fixation. In
comparisons between DJF and non-DJF patients, there was no significant
difference in pre/postoperative LK (pre/post, p = 0.725, p = 0.950).
However, statistically significant differences were observed in the
following preoperative alignment parameters: SVA (p = 0.014), LL (p =
0.001), LLL (p = 0.006), PT (p = 0.003), and PI-LL (p < 0.001).
Conclusions: Spinopelvic parameters, which represent the
compensatory function of lumbar hyperlordosis and pelvic retroversion, have
notable impacts on surgical outcomes in correction surgery for TLJK due to
OVF. To recognize the potential risks of DJF and revision surgery, surgeons
should pay attention not only to the local angles but also to the whole
spinopelvic alignment and consider each patient’s compensatory function when
choosing a surgical approach.

## P138: Where is the point of inflection from thoracic kyphosis to lumbar
lordosis in a multi-ethnic population of asymptomatic volunteers

Zeeshan Sardar

1

, Matan Malka

2

, Meghan Cerpa

2

, Jean Charles Le Huec

3

, Stephane Bourret

3

, Kazuhiro Hasegawa

4

, Wong Hee Kit

5

, Gabriel Liu

5

, Denni Hey

5

, Hend Riahi

6

, Michael Kelly

7

, and Lawrence Lenke

1

1

Spine Unit, Och Spine Hospital at New York Presbyterian/Allen, New
York, United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Columbia University Medical Center, New York,
United States

3

CHU de Bordeaux, Bordeaux, France

4

Niigata Spine Surgery Center, Niigata, Japan

5

NUH University Spine Center, Singapore

6

Kassab Institute, Manouba, Tunisia

7

Washington University School of Medicine, Saint Louis, United
States

Introduction: The point of inflection (POI) between the Thoracic
Kyphosis (TK) and the Lumbar Lordosis (LL) is an important consideration for
treatment of spinal deformity. Previous literature has shown that the
classically accepted POI of L1 is not constant among the population. The
purpose of this study is to show the population variance in POI and its role
in defining the maximum TK and LL. Material and Methods:
Asymptomatic adult volunteers between the ages of 18-80 years were enrolled
prospectively across 5 different countries/centers (France, Japan,
Singapore, Tunisia, and United States) forming the MEANS cohort. Volunteers
included in the study reported no significant neck or back pain (Visual
Analog Scale≤2), nor any known spinal disorder(s), and had no history of
prior surgical or non-surgical treatment for a spine related disorder. All
volunteers underwent a standing full body or full spine low dose
stereoradiograph (EOS imaging, Paris, France) for enrollment in the study.
Following exclusion, a total of 468 volunteers were included in MEANS. Basic
demographic data included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and ethnicity.
One more patient was removed from the data analysis because the POI was
missing. The data from the 467 patients was then evaluated. In order to find
parameters that correlate with the location of the POI as well as a possible
linear regression model predicting the POI, a new numbering system of the
vertebrae and discs was created in the following manner: C7 was given the
numerical value of 0, T1 was 1, with T1T2 being 1.5, etc.
Results: The overall mean POI was found to be 12.44
approximately corresponding to T12L1 with the median being 12.50 (also
T12L1). The patient population was then stratified by sex and ethnicity but
no significant difference was found in POI between all the groups. Though
the ranges of the POI are different among the population stratifications,
the mean and median POI’s remain relatively around T12L1. The mode POI was
L1. However, the POI varied from T8 to L4. No strong correlation was found
between POI and age, LL, Sacral Slope, or PI. Conclusion: The
most common POI was L1. However, POI ranged from T8 to L4 with the mean
being around T12-L1. A strong correlation between POI and any of the
demographic or radiographic parameters was not found. The variation in POI
should be taken into account when planning a reconstructive surgery.

## 1511

## P139: Diastematomyelia: a study of 15 cases

Sliti Firas

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Nessrine Nessib

1

, Alaa Belhadj

1

, Sofiene Bouali

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Diastematomyelia is a rare congenital spinal
malformation consisting of two spinal cords separated by a bony,
cartilaginous or fibrous septum on one or more segments. It has a good
prognosis when diagnosed and treated early. Material and
Methods: We collected the cases of diastematomyelia operated
between 2009 and 2019 at the neurosurgery departments of the National
Institute of Neurology and the Center of Traumatology of Ben Arous Tunisia.
Results: Our series consisted of 13 patients, including 9
children and 4 adults. The mean age in children was 6 years, and in adults
58 years. The sex ratio was 0.44. Clinical signs were represented by
scoliosis (7 cases), motor deficit (7 cases), skin signs (6 cases) including
hairy patch (hypertrichosis) (4 cases), urinary disorders (4 cases) and
spinal and radicular pain (4 cases). All patients underwent a radiological
study by spinal MRI and CT scan. We identified 10 cases of type I
diastematomyelia and 3 cases of type II. Associated dysraphic disorders were
present in 10 cases. There were 4 cases of postoperative complications: 1
case of anemia due to intraoperative hemorrhage, 1 case of CSF leakage, 1
case of wound infection and 1 case of transient motor deficit. Motor deficit
and pain improved in all patients. Two patients recovered completely from
their deficit. Sphincter disorders improved in only one case.
Conclusion: Diastematomyelia, also known as a split cord
malformation, is a rare occult spinal dysraphism, which is easy to diagnose
given the frequent cutaneous signs and neuro-orthopaedic syndrome. Surgery
is indicated to avoid irreversible neurological sequelae.

Introduction: Melorheostosis is a medical developmental disorder
and mesenchymal dysplasia in which bone cortex widens and becomes hyperdense
in a sclerotomal distribution. Most of the cases reported till now are
confined to appendicular skeleton, rarely affecting spine. It is well known
by its characteristic appearance of “melting wax flowing down a candle” on
radiographs. Materials and Method: This is a rare case study of
a patient operated at tertiary care centre having non-traumatic involvement
of spinal cord affecting neurology with history, clinical and radiological
features suggesting melorheostosis as the cause of compression.
Result: Here we report a rare case of melorheostosis of
thoracic spine in a middle‐aged male patient with features of myelopathy
treated by early decompression surgery, leading to complete relief of
symptoms postoperatively. Final follow‐up was of 2 years. It is a very rare,
benign and disabling entity, and the diagnosis Is primarily a radiological
one. Conclusion: Early diagnosis and decompression surgery
leads to dramatic improvement in clinical outcome and prevents unwarranted
biopsy.

Introduction: Although appropriate pain control is a critical
aspect of patient management, past few decades have been associated with
major increases in opioid-related overdoses and addiction treatment. Current
literature focuses on chronic back pain and degenerative conditions and
information regarding long-term opioid use following adult spinal deformity
surgery is limited. This study aims to analyze factors associated with
minimum 5-year postoperative continued opioid use in patients who underwent
surgical treatment for adult spinal deformity. Materials and
Methods: This was a retrospective analysis of a prospectively
collected data of patients undergoing elective spinal deformity surgery.
Patients with ≥ 4-levels fusion and ≥ 5y follow-up were included. Analgesic
use was divided into 4 groups: No Analgesics; Non-Opioid Analgesics; Weak
Opioids and Strong Opioids. Clinically-relevant 6 scenarios were
investigated: Pre-op use; 6 weeks use; Continued use at 6 months and beyond;
Opioid cessation; Restart on opioids and Persistent use at 5 years and
beyond. A total of 37 factors comprising patient characteristics,
radiographic measurements, operative details, preoperative and early
postoperative opioid use, and mechanical complications and revisions were
analysed in a univariate-multivariate setup to determine risk factors for
pre-op, 6-months and ≥ 5-years post-op usage. Results: 265
patients (215 F, 50 M) from five sites were included. The mean follow-up
duration was 68.4 ± 11.7 (60-102) months. On average, 10.6 ± 3.5 levels were
fused. Preoperatively, 64 (24.2%) patients were using opioids. The rate of
opioid users increased to 33.6% at 6 weeks and decreased to 21.5% at 6
months. During follow-up, there were patients who discontinued opioids,
while others have started and/or restarted using opioids. As a result, 59
(22.3%) patients were still on opioids at the latest follow-up. Multivariate
analyses showed that factors independently affecting opioid use at an
average of 68 months postoperatively, in order of significance, were opioid
use at sixth weeks, preoperative opioid use and opioid use at sixth months
with the odds ratios of 2.88, 2.51 and 2.38 respectively. At these time
points, factors such as age, number of comorbidities, tobacco use, the time
of the last prior spine surgery and postoperative sagittal plane alignment
affected opioid usage rates. Conclusions: Approximately 15% of
patients who received no preop opioids ended up receiving long-term (5+
years) postop opioids. Of the preop opioid users, only 56% could quit.
Opioid usage at six weeks was found to be more predictive of long-term
opioid use compared to preoperative use. Among identified risk factors,
sagittal plane correction seems to be the only parameter that is directly at
the surgeon’s discretion. Observed differences among sites can point towards
a room for improvement. Identifying patients at higher risk for opioid use
at different time points and discussing their long-term expectations may be
beneficial in the shared decision-making process. Current global efforts on
preventing chronic opioid use warrants further research to better understand
the cascade of events in order to determine actionable items.

## P142: Loads at adjacent segment level before and after surgery: combined

Dominika Ignasiak

, Ahmet Alanay

, Caglar Yilgor

9

, Stephen Ferguson

1

, and Markus Loibl

5

1

Institute for Biomechanics, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

2

Department of Teaching, Research and Development

3

4

6

Spine Unit, Hospital Vall d'Hebron, Barcelona, Spain

Department of Spinal Surgery Unit 1, Bordeaux University Hospital,

8

Spine Surgery Unit, La Paz University Hospital, Madrid,
Spain

9

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Acibadem Mehmet Ali
Aydinlar University School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Sagittal malalignment is a risk factor for
mechanical complications after surgery for adult spinal deformity (ASD).
Mechanical complications – caused by continuous or repetitive mechanical
stress – are estimated to affect 28-61% of ASD patients with longer fusion
constructs. Spinal loads, modulated by sagittal alignment, may explain this
relationship. The aims of this study were to investigate the relationships
between: (1) postoperative changes in loads at the proximal segment and
realignment, and (2) absolute postoperative loads and postoperative
alignment measures. Materials and Methods: A previously
validated musculoskeletal (AnyBody) model of the whole spine, including
articulated thorax with ribcage, was applied to study a clinical sample of
205 ASD patients. The data were collected within a multicenter study group.
The dataset included patient demographic parameters, surgical treatment
details, prior fusion, occurrence and type of mechanical complications, as
well as sagittal alignment measures obtained from preoperative and 6 weeks
postoperative long lateral radiographs. Based on clinical and radiographic
data, patient-specific sagittal spinopelvic alignment profiles were
represented in the musculoskeletal spine model. Pre- and postoperative
patient-specific alignments were simulated to predict loads at the proximal
segment adjacent to the spinal fusion. To allow between-subjects
comparability, the loads were normalized to individual body mass.
Results: The mean age (and standard deviation) was 52.1 ±
19.2 years (range 18-84 years), mean BMI was 25.7 ± 5.1 kg/m2
(range, 13.4-44.6 kg/m2). The sample included both primary (72%)
and revision (28%) surgery cases, representing a variety of fusion lengths
(median number of fused motion segments = 9, range 3-16), and upper (T2-L3)
and lower (T12- pelvis) instrumented levels, with T10-pelvis fusion being
the most common (13%). Weak-to-moderate associations were found between
pre-to-postop changes in lumbar lordosis, LL (r = -0.23, r = -0.43; p <
0.001), global tilt, GT (r = 0.26, r = 0.38; p < 0.001) and the Global
Alignment and Proportion score, GAP (r = 0.26, r = 0.37; p < 0.001), and
changes in compressive and shear forces at the proximal segment. GAP score
parameters, thoracic kyphosis measurements and the slope of upper
instrumented vertebra were associated with changes in shear. In patients
with T10-pelvis fusion, moderate-to-strong associations were found between
several postoperative sagittal alignment measures and compressive and shear
loads, with GT showing the strongest correlations (r = 0.75, r = 0.73, p
< 0.001). Conclusions: Spinal loads were estimated for
patient-specific full spinal alignment profiles in a large cohort of
patients with ASD pre- and postoperatively. Loads on the proximal segments
correlated with sagittal alignment measures. In a subset of T10-pelvis
fusion cases, postoperative GT, UIV slope, GAP, and T10-L2 angles were
associated with both postoperative compressive and shear loads. Broader
analysis of larger clinical samples should be performed in the future to
unravel whether or not (or to what degree) spinal loads provide a causal
mechanism explaining the previously reported association between sagittal
alignment and mechanical complications.

## 1644

## P143: The reliability of computer-assisted 3D surgical simulation of
posterior osteotomies in

Yiqi Zhang

1

 and Yong Hai

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital
Medical University, Beijing, China

Background: Correction surgery for patients with thoracolumbar
kyphosis secondary to ankylosing spondylitis (TLKAS) is desired with the aim
to restore the normal sagittal balance and generally performed with
posterior osteotomies including pedicle subtraction osteotomy,
Smith-Petersen osteotomy (SPO), and Ponte osteotomy. A precise and flexible
surgical planning is required for osteotomy strategy. The study was aimed at
investigating the reliability of computer-assisted three-dimensional
surgical simulation (CA3DSS) of posterior osteotomies in TLKAS patients.
Methods: Eligible TLKAS patients who underwent posterior
correction surgery with posterior osteotomies were consecutively included.
Simulated posterior osteotomies were performed in Mimics and 3-Matic Medical
software. Coronal and sagittal angle and alignment parameters were measured
in preoperative full-length X-ray, preoperative original 3D spine (Pre-OS),
simulated 3D spine (SS), and postoperative original 3D spine (Post-OS).
Reliability was tested by both intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs)
and Bland-Altman analysis. Results: A total of 30 TLKAS
patients were included. Excellent consistency of radiological parameters was
shown between preoperative X-ray and Pre-OS model. In SS and Post-OS models,
excellent reliabilities were shown in global kyphosis (ICC 0.832, 95% CI
0.677-0.916), thoracic kyphosis (ICC 0.773, 95% CI 0.577-0.885), and lumbar
lordosis (ICC 0.896, 95% CI 0.794-0.949) and good reliabilities were
exhibited in the main curve (ICC 0.680, 95% CI 0.428- 0.834) and sagittal
vertical axis (ICC 0.619, 95% CI 0.338-0.798). ICCs of correction angle
achieved by pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) was 0.754 (95% CI
0.487-0.892), and that of posterior column osteotomies (PCO) was 0.703 (95%
CI 0.511- 0.829). Bland-Altman analysis also showed good agreement for both
Cobb angle and distance measurements in Pre-OS and SS models, and good
reliabilities were shown in PCO and PSO in real spine and SS models.
Conclusions: CA3DSS can provide an accurate measurement,
and it is a reliable and effective method to conduct proper simulation for
correction surgery with posterior osteotomies in TLKAS patients.

## P144: Human recombinant bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) injection
into the uppermost instrumented vertebra (UIV) reduced the acute bony
failure type proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) in adult spinal deformity

Ho-Joong Kim

1

, Ohsang Kwon

1

, and Junyoung Choi

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Seoul National University Bundang Hospital,
South Korea

Introduction: Numerous attempts on reducing the proximal
junctional kyphosis (PJK) and thus proximal junctional failure (PJF) have
resulted in substantial but yet not complete resolution of the troublesome
complication. We attempted local transpedicular injection of human
recombinant bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) into the uppermost
instrumented vertebra (UIV) for prevention of bony failure type PJK in adult
spinal deformity (ASD) correction surgery. Material and
Methods: A mixture of 1mg rhBMP-2 and 0.5g β-tricalcium phosphate

patients (12%) in the control group and all of them were bony failures. PROM
at 6 months after surgery were significantly better in the study group. The
Hounsfield unit of the UIV significantly increased at 6 months after surgery
than the preoperative scan and the increment at the UIV was also
significantly greater than that of the UIV-1. Conclusion:
Intraoperative transpedicular injection of rhBMP-2 into the UIV reduces the
PJK and PJF rate at 6 months after surgery, by diminishing the occurrence of
bony failure. The Hounsfield unit at the UIV increased significantly which
might be interpreted as a sign of new bone formation.

Department of Orthopedics, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, United
States

2

Department of Spine Surgery, Swedish Neuroscience Institute, United
States

3

Department of Neurosurgery, Houston Methodist, Houston, TX, United
States

Introduction: As the number of spinal fusion procedures has
risen over the past few decades there has also been a reported decrease in
the utilization of three column osteotomies. Many surgeons are familiar with
the traditional posterior spinal osteotomy classification; however, a
lesser-known osteotomy, the bone-disc-bone osteotomy, exists outside of this
classification. We present the “intradiscal osteotomy” (IDO) technique, a
type of bone-disc-bone osteotomy that utilizes expandable interbody devices
to achieve all-posterior correction of complex spinal pathology.
Materials and Methods: A fresh-frozen cadaver was prepared
for demonstration of the IDO technique in the mid-lumbar spine. The
procedure was documented through serial, high-resolution photographs in
stepwise progression. Standard fluoroscopy was used to document the
procedure’s corrective ability. Additionally, a narrative case series was
chosen from within a single institute to demonstrate the procedure’s utility
and feasibility in a variety of complex spinal clinical scenarios.
Results: Intradiscal osteotomy with the use of expandable
interbody devices was successfully demonstrated on a cadaveric model. A
high-resolution technique guide was produced through serial photographs. Our
narrative case series demonstrates the IDO’s utility and feasibility in
complex spinal pathology; specifically, correction of cervicothoracic and
thoracolumbar adult spinal deformity (ASD), proximal junctional failure
(PJF), distal junctional failure (DJF), isthmic spondylolisthesis, and
pseudarthrosis. We additionally demonstrate its feasibility in iatrogenic
flat-back syndrome through an all-posterior, attritional release of the
anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL). Conclusions: The
intradiscal osteotomy combined with expandable interbody devices can achieve
powerful correction without the use of conventional three column
osteotomies. Surgeons may find this technique desirable and rapidly
adoptable due to its similarity to a traditional transforaminal interbody
fusion. Our technique guide and narrative case series is meant to assist
surgeons looking for alternatives to traditional three column
osteotomies.

## P146: Postoperative complications of Schwab-Grade-I versus
Schwab-Grade-II posterior column osteotomies (PCOs) in treating severe rigid
kyphoscoliosis patients: a minimum 2-year follow-up comparative
outcome

Nicholas Van Halm-Lutterodt

1,2,3

, Aixin Pan

3

, Ziyang Ye

2,4

, Yangpu Zhang

3

, Tie Liu

3

, Lijin Zhou

3

, Sunny Kim

2

, Yuzeng Liu

3

, Jincai Yang

3

, and Yong Hai

3

1

School of Professional Studies, Brown University, Providence, United
States

2

Department of Orthopedic and Neurosurgery, Inspired Spine Health,
Burnsville, United States

3

Department of Orthopedics Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital
Affiliated-Capital Medical University, Beijing, China

4

Department of Data Science and Analytics, University of Chicago,
Chicago, United States

Background: Smith-Petersen osteotomy, [SPO], (Schwab-grade-I)
and Ponte osteotomy, [PO], (Schwab-grade-II) are narrowly akin and
collectively appreciated as posterior column shortening osteotomies (PCOs).
The former is considered as a more gentler osteotomy grade than the latter.
In the spine literature, little information is provided on their comparison
regarding perioperative complications and major curve correction rates. A
clinical study to evaluate the perioperative complication incidence and
major curve corrective rates between these two osteotomy techniques would be
pragmatic in highlighting their safety and efficacy outcomes and inform the
spine practice of their value-based impacts in indicated deformity patients.
Methods: Following approval by the institutional review
board (IRB) of Beijing Chaoyang Hospital-Affiliated Capital Medical
University in Beijing, a pool of 38 propensity-matched adult (≥ 18 years)
severe rigid scoliosis or kyphoscoliosis patients (curved ≥ 80o)
who underwent spinal deformity primary corrective surgery were
retrospectively evaluated. The patients were dichotomized into two (2)
osteotomy technique groups: Smith-Petersen osteotomy (SPO-treated), (i.e.,
Schwab-grade-I PCO) and Ponte osteotomy, (PO-treated), (i.e.,
Schwab-grade-II PCO). The minimum follow-up period was 2 years. Primary
outcomes included baseline and clinical features between the two osteotomy
groups. Secondary outcomes included perioperative [intraoperative,
immediate, and within 2-year postoperative] complication rates between the
two types of osteotomies. Tertiary outcomes included preoperative and final
follow-up ODI and SRS-22 scores. Statistical analyses were carried out by
Student t-test and Pearson’s Chi-squared test (Fisher’s Exact Test), through
Python statistical software package. Statistical significance was set at p
< 0.05. Results: Of the 38 matched severe rigid scoliosis or
kyphoscoliosis patients, 55.30% (n = 21) were SPO-treated and 44.70% (n =
17) were PO-treated patients, respectively. The overall average age of
patients was 23.97 years, with a female incidence of 76.32%. Major curve
correction rates were 49.19% and 57.40% in SPO-treated and PO-treated
patients, respectively, (p > 0.05). Immediately following surgery,
comparable overall complication rates of 28.57% (n = 6/21) vs 29.41% (n =
5/17) were observed in the SPO-treated and PO-treated patients,
respectively, (p = 0.726). We observed 9.52%, (n = 2/21) vs 5.88%, (n =
1/17) incidence of surgical intensive care unit (SICU) admission and 4.76%,
(n = 1/21) vs 5.88%, (n = 1/17) incidence of cardiopulmonary events in
SPO-treated and PO-treated patients after surgery, respectively, (p =
0.679). Neurological deficits incidence in the SPO-treated and PO-treated
patients were respectively, 14.29%, (n = 3/21) vs 17.65%, (n = 3/17)
immediately following surgery, (p > 0.05) and 0.00%, (n = 0/21) vs
17.65%, (n = 3/17) at ≥ 2 years postoperative, (p < 0.05), but there was
only 5.88% (n = 1/17) new incidence of neurological deficits in the
PO-treated patients at ≥ 2 years postoperative, ( p > 0.05). The ODI
score in the PO-treated group was significantly inferior at minimum 2-year
follow-up, (p < 0.05), while preoperative and postoperative SRS-22 scores
were comparable in both patient groups, (p > 0.05).
Conclusion: In the current study, both SPO-treated and
PO-treated patients demonstrated comparable surgical complication rates
immediately following corrective surgery whereas PO-treated patients showed
an increased tendency of accruing postoperative neurological sequela. To
achieve value-based and effective outcomes in these severe rigid scoliosis
or kyphoscoliosis patients, prudence in patient selection, enhanced patient
management protocols and technical sophistication are profoundly critical to
maximizing safety outcomes with Schwab-grade-I or -II PCO.

Introduction: Wound closure and perioperative antibiotic use are
practiced by all surgeons involved in surgery, but methods can vary widely
depending on surgeon preference, country, and social context. The purpose of
this study is to conduct a survey of AO spine members involved in Adult
Spinal Deformity (ASD) surgery in two categories: 1. developing and
developed countries, 2. orthopedic surgeons and neurosurgeons.
Material and Methods: One hundred and sixty-four members
from 49 countries were included. The evaluation items included method of
skin closure, method of dressing, type of drain, type and duration of

doctors in the developed country group and 31 doctors in the developing

the intraoperative use of vancomycin powder was significantly higher among
neurosurgeons.

## P149: Treatment of a thoracic fracture-dislocation with a posterior only
approach

Joana Tavares

1

, Ana Luís

1

, and Diogo Morgado

1

1

Neurosurgery, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisboa,
Portugal

Introduction: Fracture-dislocations of the thoracic and lumbar
spine are highly unstable injuries, frequently resulting in neurologic
injuries. The primary goals in its surgical treatment when there is complete
spinal cord transection are the reduction of deformity and rigid spine
stabilization with fusion. The current treatment of vertebral
fracture-dislocation when there is partial or total telescoping of the
involved vertebrae is combined anterior-posterior approach with corpectomy,
anterior support implant and further posterior instrumentation. These
procedures may require two surgical teams, longer operating times and
greater risk of surgical complications related to the anterior approach, and
commonly entail longer postoperative care before discharge. A viable
alternative is opting for treatment from a posterior approach alone: with
partial vertebrectomy shortening (resection of the upper part of the lower
vertebra involved, the posterior arch and the disc), which results in
apposition of two flat surfaces of healthy bone; reduction and fixation
using long segment posterior transpedicular constructs. Material and
Methods: The authors report a case of a low thoracic
fracture-dislocation (T-11/T-12) treated with a partial vertebrectomy from a
posterior approach. Results: A 26 year-old male presented to
our emergency room after being evacuated from Cape Verde, with a complete
thoracic spinal cord section as a result of a car accident 1 month earlier.
Computed tomography scan revealed an AOSpine T11-T12: C (B3) with severe
antero-posterior dislocation. Briefly: Through an open posterior approach
pedicle screws were inserted, under fluoroscopic guidance, in
T9-T10-T11-L1-L2-L3 bilaterally; posterior arches of T11 and T12 (including
bilateral locked facets), were removed. Right laminectomy of T10, bilateral
laminectomy of L1 and partial laminectomy of L2 were preformed The dura
mater was surrounded by a dense fibrous tissue but no CSF leak was observed.
Total discectomy of T11-T12 disc was done, as well as partial T12’s
corpectomy (using an ultrasonic device), reducing to half the height of
T12’s body. Titanium bars were place to allow compression and apposition of
T11 with the rest of T12’s body. After this, the patient was repositioned to
promote additional reduction (both on the sagittal and coronal axes), the
rods were fixed and a cross-link was applied. Autologus bone was used for
postero-lateral fusion. The immediate postoperative image showed adequate
realignment of the thoracic spine. Conclusion: To date, there
is no conclusive clinical studies available to help spine surgeons decide on
the optimal surgical treatment of thoracic fracture-dislocations.
Nonetheless, a posterior-only approach may be used safely and effectively
minimizing the disadvantages associated with the anterior approach.

## P150: External validation of the global alignment and proportion (GAP)
score as a prognostic tool for corrective surgery in adult spinal deformity:
a systematic review and meta-analysis

Julian Gendreau

1

, Nolan Brown

1

, Andrew Nguyen

1

, Neal Patel

1

, Alexander Lopez

1

, Chenyi Yang

1

, Noah Pierzchajlo

1

, Shane Shahrestani

1

, Gaston Camino-Willhuber

1

, Stephen Albano

1

, Michael Oh

1

, and Martin Pham

2

1
Neurosurgery, UC Irvine, United
States
2
Neurosurgery, UC San Diego, United
States
Introduction: The Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) score
has been previously touted as an improved method for predicting mechanical
complications following adult spinal deformity (ASD) correction surgery when
compared to pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis (PI-LL) mismatch parameters.
Since its proposal, the GAP score has been the topic of several external
validation studies, which have yielded conflicting results. Given the lack
of consensus regarding this prognostic tool, the authors aim to assess the
accuracy of GAP scores in predicting mechanical complications following ASD
correction surgery by reviewing all evidence in the published literature to
date. Materials and Methods: A systematic search was performed
using PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library for the purpose of identifying all
trials evaluating the GAP score as a predictive tool for mechanical
complications. Study quality was assessed according to Newcastle-Ottawa
criteria. GAP scores were pooled using a random-effects model to compare
patients reporting mechanical complications after surgery versus those
reporting no mechanical complications. Where receiver operator curves (ROC)
were provided, the area under the curve (AUC) was pooled. All statistical
analyses was performed using R software. Results: A total of 15
studies featuring 2,092 patients were selected for inclusion in the
analysis. Qualitative analysis using Newcastle-Ottawa criteria revealed
moderate quality among all included studies (5.99/9). With respect to sex,
the cohort was predominantly female (82%). The pooled mean age among all
patients in the cohort was 58.55 years, with a mean follow-up of 33.86
months after surgery. Upon pooled analysis, we found that mechanical
complications were associated with higher mean GAP scores, albeit minimal
(mean difference = 0.571 [ 95% CI: 0.163-0.979]; p = 0.006, n = 864).
Additionally, age (p = 0.136, n = 202), levels of fusion (p = 0.207, n =
358) and body mass index (BMI) (p = 0.616, n = 350) were similar among all
patients, irrespective of complication status. Pooled AUC revealed poor
discrimination overall (AUC = 0.69; n = 1206). There was no indication of
publication bias. Conclusion: GAP scores may have a
minimal-to-moderate predictive capability for mechanical complications
associated with ASD correction.

## P151: Whole-transcriptome sequencing identifies key differentially
expressed circRNAs/IncRNAs/mRNAs and linked ceRNA networks in adult
degenerative scoliosis

Xin Shi

1,2

, Panpan Li

1,2

, Xiang Wu

1

, Zhihua Wang

1

, Gang Zhao

1

, Yinglan Wang

3

, and Jun Shu

1

1

The Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University,
Kunming, China

2

Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital of Cologne, University
of Cologne, Cologne, Germany

3

Shangqiu First People's Hospital, Shangqiu, China

Background: With an increasing elderly population, adult
degenerative scoliosis (ADS), is forecast to be a prevalent disabling
condition in an aging society. Universally, its pathogenesis is perceived as
intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD), which does not differ from other
degenerative spinal disorders. However, a thought-provoking issue is why
precisely a subset of patients with disc degeneration develop ADS. Exploring
the diversities between common disc degeneration and ADS would contribute to
unraveling the etiological mechanisms of ADS. Although the function of
ncRNAs in ADS has been proposed, crosstalk between the various transcripts
has not been systematically investigated. Therefore, we aimed to integrate
the circRNA, lncRNA, miRNA, and mRNA expression profiles from normal adults
(Normal), patients with disc herniation (LDH), and ADS by whole
transcriptome sequencing, which identifies key functional ncRNA and ceRNA
networks. Methods: The fresh whole blood samples (n = 3/group)
were collected from ADS patients (asymmetric disc degeneration, ADS group),
LDH patients (symmetric disc degeneration, LDH group), and healthy
volunteers (non-degenerative changes, Normal group), which were examined for
mRNA, miRNA, lncRNA, and circRNA expression and screened for differentially
expressed (DE) RNAs. Then, Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG analyses were
performed for gene annotation and enrichment pathways on the DE RNAs, which
were constructed as a lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA network. Eventually, DE RNAs were
validated by qRT-PCR targeting disc nucleus pulposus tissue in ADS and LDH
group (n = 10 / group). Results: Compared to the LDH group, we
identified 3322 DE mRNAs, 221 DE lncRNAs, 20 DE miRNAs, and 15 DE circRNAs
in the ADS. In contrast to Normal, 21 miRNAs and 19 circRNAs were
differentially expressed in the ADS. The expression of multiple
differentially expressed ncRNAs was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis to be
consistent with the sequencing results. In addition, GO and KEGG analysis
demonstrated that most DE mRNAs and ncRNAs target genes are involved in
various biological processes, including Endocytosis, Apoptosis, Rap1
signaling pathway, Notch signaling pathway, and others. The constructed
lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA co-expression network was primarily related to
angiogenesis and regulation. Conclusion: By focusing on
comparing asymmetric and symmetric disc degeneration, whole-transcriptome
sequencing and bioinformatics analysis systematically screened for key
ncRNAs in the development of ADS, which provided an abundance of valuable
candidates for the elucidation of regulatory mechanisms. The DE ncRNAs and
the lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA network are intrinsically involved in the regulation
of mediator and angiogenesis, which may contribute to the insight into the
pathogenesis of ADS.

## P151.1: What is the value of measuring intraoperative coronal alignment for
adult spinal deformity patients with coronal malalignment?

Nathan Lee

1

, Michael Fields

1

, Fthimnir Hassan

1

, Christopher Mikhail

1

, Stephen Stephan

1

, Joshua Baksheshian

1

, Andrew Platt

1

, Joseph Lombardi

1

, Zeeshan Sardar

1

, Ronald A. Lehman

1

, Lawrence Lenke

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Columbia University, Och Spine Hospital, New York,
United States

Introduction: Optimizing coronal alignment is an important goal for
adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery. Recently, the horizontal distance from C7
to the Central Sacral Pelvic Line (CSPL = line bisecting the sacrum and
perpendicular to the line touching the acetabular sourcils) measured on
intraoperative prone radiographs was introduced as an accurate target for
postoperative coronal alignment, particularly for patients without leg length
discrepancy. However, the clinical utility of this intraoperative measure in
predicting patient reported outcomes and postoperative lower extremity (LE)
compensatory changes have not yet been described. Material and
Methods: ASD patients with minimum 6 level fusion (including pelvic
fixation), preoperative coronal malalignment (CVA≥3cm), no LLD (<1 cm), and
minimum 2 year follow up were reviewed. Patient demographics, comorbidities,
baseline PROs, surgical factors, and radiographic factors (both coronal and
sagittal) were collected. The intraoperative distance (cm) from C7 to CSPL was
measured for each patient. The outcome of interests included the minimum
clinically important difference (MCID) for ODI/SRS and postoperative LE changes
(pelvic obliquity>1deg, asymmetric knee bending, LE mechanical axis
difference (LMAD)>2deg) at 2 years postop. Bivariate and multivariate
logistic regression were performed to determine the independent factors for the
outcomes of interest. Results: 76 patients (age 58.3 ± 13.7, female
77.6%, levels fused 14.1 ± 3.9) with preop/2yr CVA 5.0 ± 1.9/2.1 ± 1.8 cm and
SVA 5.7 ± 6.0/3.0 ± 3.9 cm were reviewed. Preop/2yr ODI 39.3 ± 17.5/18 ± 17, SRS
function 3.2 ± 0.9/3.8 ± 0.8, SRS pain 2.7 ± .9/3.8 ± 1.1, and SRS appearance
2.4 ± 0.8/4.0 ± 0.9. The rate of preop LE changes was 57.9% (pelvic obliquity PO
= 2.4⁰, LMAD = 4.2⁰, and 27% had asymmetric knee bending). The rate of 2yr LE
changes was 26.3% (pelvic obliquity PO = 2.0⁰, LMAD = 3.9⁰, and 42.9% had
asymmetric knee bending). The mean error between intraop C7-iCSPL and 2yr CVA
was 0.5 ± 1.3 cm. Worse C7-iCSPL was associated with higher risk for LE changes
(2.9 vs. 1.9 cm, p = 0.04) and remained significant in the multivariate (OR 3.0,
p < 0.01). Lower C7-iCSPL was associated with improved 2 year ODI MCID (1.8
vs. 3.2cm, p = 0.03), but did not remain significant in the multivariate.
Instead, patients with LE changes was the strongest independent predictor for
worse ODI MCID (OR 15.9, p < 0.01). Conclusion: For ASD patients
with coronal malalignment, optimizing intraoperative coronal correction may
reduce iatrogenic LE compensation, which was found to significantly contribute
to worse patient reported outcomes at 2 years.

## P152: Laminoplasty for the treatment of multi-level cervical
radiculopathy; clinical outcome

Min-gu Jang

1

 and Woo-jin Shin

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Konyang University Hospital, Seo-gu, Daejeon,
South Korea

Introduction: To evaluate the improvement of surgical outcome of
open-door laminoplasty for multilevel cervical radiculopathy. Material
and Methods: This study was conducted on 36 patients who
underwent laminoplasty surgery from January 2014 to December 2020. As
inclusion criteria, only patients with multilevel cervical radiculopathy
symptoms were included, patients with a modified JOA of 16 or higher and
Nurick grade 1 or lower were included, and patients with multilevel spinal
stenosis confirmed by MRI were included. All patients had mild to moderate
central stenosis, with or without neural foraminal stenosis. Patients who
also had myelopathy symptoms such as hand clumsiness, numbness, gait
disturbance, dysdiadokinesia, imbalance, hyperreflexia, or positive
Hoffman's reflex were excluded. To confirm the surgical outcome, the pain
severity, patient satisfaction, neurologic outcome, functional status, and
ADL, VAS and NDI were measured. As a surgical technique, a double-bent
mini-plate fixation after open-door laminoplasty was used through a
posterior approach. Results: The average age of the patients
was 62 years old. There were 25 men and 11 women. The average follow-up
period after surgery was 13 months. There were 13 cases with symptoms on the
right side, 14 cases with symptoms on the left, and 9 cases on both sides.
The level where the patient complained the most was C3456, and the level
that showed the most spinal stenosis in MRI was C34567. Considering the
patient's pain symptoms and MRI, the most frequently performed laminoplasty
level was C3456. Additional surgeries were C2 domeplasty (6 cases), C6
domeplasty (1 case), C7 domeplasty (5 cases), and unilateral foraminotomy (4
cases). VAS, pain severity, satisfaction, neurologic outcomes, functional
status, ADL, and NDI all showed statistically significant improvement
immediately after laminoplasty surgery and final follow-up compared to
before surgery. Conclusion: Open-door laminoplasty may be a
useful treatment option for patients who have multilevel radiculopathy with
mild to moderate spinal stenosis on MRI without myelopathy symptoms.

## P153: Incidence and risk factors for dysphagia following anterior or
posterior cervical spine surgery: a prospective study - interim
analysis

Vache Hambardzumyan

1

, Ryan Smith

1

, Tyler Pease

1

, Alexandra Thomson

1

, Ivan Ye

1

, Eugene Koh

1

, Daniel Gelb

1

, Steven Ludwig

1

, and Daniel Cavanaugh

1

1

Orthopaedics, University of Maryland, Spine Division, Baltimore,
United States

Introduction: Postoperative dysphagia is a well-known
complication following anterior cervical spine surgery, which includes
anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion (ACDF) and cervical disc replacement
(CDR). The reported incidence varies widely from 4-71% with an estimated
12-14% of patients experiencing persistent dysphagia after 1 year. Dysphagia
after posterior cervical decompression with or without fusions has been
reported to range in incidence from 9-11%. This study compares the incidence
of dysphagia following anterior and posterior cervical spine surgery.
Materials and Methods: Consecutive adult patients
undergoing primary, elective anterior or posterior cervical spine surgery
were included in this prospective observational study. The incidence of
dysphagia was determined by the Bazaz Dysphagia Scoring System and HSS
Dysphagia and Dysphonia Inventory (HSS-DDI) preoperatively, and at 2 weeks,
6 weeks, and 12 weeks postoperatively. The incidence of new onset
postoperative dysphagia was compared between the anterior and posterior
cervical spine surgery cohorts. Results: Currently 54 patients
have been enrolled in this study. A total of 46 patients underwent anterior
cervical spine surgery and 8 underwent posterior cervical spine surgery. The
mean age of all patients enrolled is 56.5 years old with 48.1% female. Using
the Bazaz grading, at the two-week follow-up 14 patients (35.0%) of the
anterior cohort and 1 patient (20.0%) in the posterior cohort experienced
moderate dysphagia. At the six-week follow-up, 9 patients (25.7%) in the
anterior cohort and 1 patient (14.3%) in the posterior cohort had moderate
dysphagia. At the twelve-week follow-up, 4 patients (16.0%) in the anterior
cohort and no patients in the posterior cohort reported moderate dysphagia.
There was no significant difference between the two cohorts using the Bazaz
grading. Using HSS-DDI, at the two-week follow-up, the anterior and
posterior cohorts experienced equivalent declines in HSS-DDI scores (101.7
vs. 105.6, p = 0.600). At six-week follow-up, the anterior and posterior
cohorts recovered to similar HSS-DDI scores (110.2 vs. 115.0, p = 0.825). At
twelve-week follow-up, there was no difference in the average HSS-DDI score
between the anterior and posterior cohorts (108.2 vs. 117.6, p = 0.351).
Conclusions: The preliminary results of this study suggest
there is no difference in the incidence of postoperative dysphagia between
patients undergoing anterior and posterior cervical surgery.

## P154: Using machine learning to identify patients likely to choose
surgery for one level anterior cervical disc herniations

Eeric Truumees

1

, Devender Singh

1

, Jeremiah Alexander

2

, Calvin Chandler

2

, Ashley Duncan

1

, Matthew Geck

2

, and John Stokes

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

2

Orthopedics, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, United
States

Introduction: While machine learning has shown great value in
medical diagnostics, its potential in assisting treatment decision making
continues to be explored. Aim: This study aims to investigate
if machine learning can identify factors associated with the likelihood of a
patient will ultimately choose surgical intervention for one level cervical
disc herniation? Materials/Methods: 130 retrospective chart
reviews were conducted on patients who presented with cervical disc
herniations causing radiculopathy to non-operative spine care providers at
an interdisciplinary clinic between 2015-2021. A course of non-operative
care was undertaken, however, if significant symptoms remains, surgical
consultation was offered. 88 patients were ultimately included in the
analysis, and 18 independent variables were collected across demographic,
clinical and patient reported outcome domains. Values were encoded using
one-hot encoding techniques, analyzed and subject to logistic regression
using SKLean, StatsModel and Logit models, with a focus on the recall
metric. By focusing on the recall metric, we aim to reduce the number of
false positives, or Type II errors in the model. Models were further
optimized by assessing multicollinearity of independent variables and
employing Area Under the Curve/Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUC-ROC)
and Precision-Recall threshold techniques. Results: Overall,
27.3% of the patients eventually choose surgical intervention with median
time to surgery 17 weeks from intake appointment. Sex was the only
demographic factor to have a significant impact on surgical intervention.
While the ratio of male to female patients was almost equal, 51% to 49%, 38%
of males underwent surgery compared to 16% of females. Body Mass Index
(BMI), smoking status and comorbidities did not significantly influence the
decision to have surgery, nor did any specific non-operative treatment
modality (physical therapy, prescriptions, epidural steroid injections). The
final optimized model yielded a test recall of 0.73. Three variables
significantly impacted the odds of surgical intervention. Male sex increased
the odds ratio of surgical intervention by 3.2 (p = 0.003); left symptom
laterality increased the odds ratio of surgical intervention by 3.2 (p =
0.01); and, interestingly, an increase in baseline Oswestry Disability Index
(ODI) score decreased the odds of surgical intervention marginally by 0.4 (p
= 0.02), although mean ODI scores were slightly higher in surgical patients
compared to non-operative patients(30 and 28, respectively).
Conclusions: Male gender and left symptom laterality
increased the odds of surgical intervention, while increase in baseline ODI
decreased the odds of surgical intervention in this data set. This may be
due in part to the use of ODI, which is typically used to determine
disability for low back pain, instead of the Neck Disability Index, which is
tailored to cervical spine symptoms. Sample size and variability between
physicians’ treatment protocols for acute cervical radiculopathy are
limitations of this study. A larger, prospective study would be the next
step in utilizing machine learning to predict which patients are most likely
to report satisfaction and a successful outcome.

## P155: An evaluation of the effects of surgical approach for cervical
degenerative disease on postoperative opioid use

Tariq Issa

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Gregory Toci

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Yashas Reddy

1

, Sebastian Fras

1

, Skylar Nahi

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Posterior cervical fusion (PCF) and anterior
cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) are two main surgical management
options for the treatment of cervical spondylotic myelopathy. While ACDF is
less invasive than PCF which should theoretically reduce post-operative
pain, it is still unknown whether this leads to reduce opioid use in
patients with similar construct lengths. Therefore, the primary objective of
this study was to evaluate whether PCF increases post-operative opioid use
compared to ACDF for patients undergoing 2-4-level fusion. Material
and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of all patients
who underwent 2- to 4-level ACDF or PCF at an urban academic medical center
and our affiliated sites from January 2017 to August 2021. Our state’s
prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) was queried for filled opioid
prescriptions, using milligrams morphine equivalents (MME). Prescriptions
filled up to two months prior to surgery were identified to determine the
number of patients taking opioids pre-operatively. Post-operative opioid
prescriptions were evaluated for 1-year post-operatively. Univariate
analysis was utilized to compare PCF and ACDF cohorts. Multivariate linear
regression was performed to assess independent predictors of short-term
(0-30 days), subacute (30-90 days), and long-term (3-12 months) opioid
prescription habits. Results: A total of 239 patients
undergoing ACDF and 101 patients undergoing PCF who could be identified in
the PDMP were included in this analysis. Patients undergoing PCF were older
(61.5 vs. 57.8 years, p = 0.0049) and more likely to have more levels fused
(3.08 vs. 2.45, p < 0.001). While a similar percent of patients were
using opioids both 1-2 months and 0-30 days pre-operatively, patients
undergoing PCF refilled greater MMEs during both time periods.
Post-operatively, patients undergoing PCF refilled more MMEs in the first 30
days (127.4 vs 86.4, p = 0.0001) and refilled a non-significantly greater
quantity from 30-90 days (39.3 vs 23.7, p = 0.086) and 3-12 months (105.3 vs
60.2, p = 0.059). A similar percent of patients in both groups had refilled
at least one prescription after 90 days (42.6% vs 36.0%, p = 0.252). On
multivariate linear regression, PCF (β = 33.9, p = 0.003), 30-day
preoperative MMEs (β = 0.17, p = 0.029) and a history of depression (β =
39.4, p = 0.001) predicted increased 30-day post-operative MMEs. Only 30-day
preoperative MMEs predicted opioid prescriptions filled from 30-90 days (β =
0.31, p < 0.001) and 3-12 months (β = 1.15, p < 0.001).
Conclusion: Posterior cervical fusion independently
predicted increased short-term opioid usage up to 30-days post-operatively
irrespective of other patient risk factors, but these effects did not
persist. However, short-term pre-operative opioid prescription MMEs were
independently predictive of the quantity of opioids refilled and persistent
long-term opioid use up to 1 year post-operatively. Providers should
carefully consider prescribing opioids pre-operatively as it may impact
long-term patient reliance on opioids for pain relief.

## P156: Retro-odontoid pseudotumor in tourette Syndrome a case
report

Felipe Mourao

1

, Juan Aquino

1

, and Felipe Sanchez Ribeiro

1

1

Neurosurgery, Nova Neuro, Nova Iguaçu, Brazil

Introduction: A retro-odontoid pseudotumour compressing the
spinal cord and causing myelopathy is often associated with an inflammatory
condition such as rheumatoid arthritis. A degenerative non-inflammatory
retro-odontoid pseudotumour responsible for clinically relevant spinal cord
compression is a rare condition described in small clinical series and is
likely associated with craniovertebral junction hypermobility or instability
– like conditions. Tourette syndrome is a disorder that involves repetitive
movements or unwanted sounds (tics), including offensive words, that can be
difficult to be controlled. Males are about four times more likely than
females to develop this disorder. Tics are sudden, brief and intermittent
movements and the hallmark sign of Tourette Syndrome. The head jerking is a
common motor tic of patient that have the Tourette Syndrome. Patient that
have repetitive movement of the head like in the Tourette Syndrome have a
higher risk to develop chronic atlanto-axial instability and form retro
odontoid non-neoplasic mass (pseudotumor) that can cause myelopathy.
Material and Methods: A 63 year old male with more than 40
years of head jerking tics caused by Tourette Syndrome, began in 2019
feeling numbness in upper extremity and difficult to walk. Examination
showed that he had marked spastic tetraparesis, with muscle power of at
least Grade 4 in the right upper and lower extremities. Sensory disturbance
in a distal (stocking-glove) distribution and bilateral clumsiness of the
hands were observed. There was hyperreflexia throughout the upper and lower
extremities. He did not show any evidences of rheumatoid arthritis that met
the criteria of the American Rheumatism Association and bone scintigraphy
study was negative for any malignancy disorder. Magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) showed a large and smooth mass behind the odontoid process compressing
the spinal cord. The density of the mass was intermediate on T1-weighted
images and low on T2-weighted images with a intramedullary T2 hyperintense
signal in the same level. Results: A posterior surgical
approach was used, the patient was undergone to a Goel and Harms technique
of stabilizing C1C2 and the posterior arch of atlas was resected. In a
segment MRI in five months after the surgery the retro odontoid mass have
reduced and have no more compression of the spinal cord at that level.
Conclusion: For several years, direct removal of the lesion
through an anterior or lateral approach has been advocated as the best
surgical option. However, in the last decade the posterior approach to the
craniovertebral junction, to perform C1-C2 fixation and C1 laminectomy
without removal of the retro-odontoid tissue, has demonstrated its efficacy
in reducing retro-odontoid pannus as well as in obtaining improvement of
myelopathy.

## P157: Is there an association between rotator cuff tear and cervical
spine pathology? A single-center retrospective study

Filipa Cordeiro

1

, Sérgio Pita

2

, Ana Ribau

1

, Sara Diniz

1

, and Pedro Neves

3

1

Ortopedia, Centro Hospitalar Universitário do Porto, Porto,
Portugal

2

Ortopedia, Centro Hospitalar Baixo Vouga, Aveiro, Portugal

3

Hôpital Privé Arnault Tzanck Mougins-Sophia Antipolis, Mougins,
France

Introduction: Patients with rotator cuff tendinopathy normally
present shoulder pain and weakness. These symptoms are similar to those
presented by some patients with cervical radiculopathy, making the
differential diagnosis sometimes difficult. Since the innervation of
shoulder girdle musculature is provided by cervical roots (C4, C5 and C6),
the aim of this study was to investigate if there is a correlation between
cervical neurological compression and rotator cuff degenerative pathology.
Material and Methods: It was conducted a single center
retrospective study through the analysis of all shoulder Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI) performed between 2017 and 2021, in a total of 1129 patients.
Patients with non-degenerative rotator cuff pathology were excluded (285
patients). In 175 of the remaining 844 patients, a cervical MRI was
performed in relation to cervical and/or radicular symptoms. Patients were
grouped in 6 categories based on shoulder MRI findings: no injuries,
calcifying tendinopathy, tendinosis, partial tear, complete tear and massive
rotator cuff tear. With regards to cervical MRI, patients were grouped in
seven categories: no degenerative changes, C3-C4 central compression, C4
foraminal compression, C4-C5 central compression, C5 foraminal compression,
C5-C6 central compression and C6 foraminal compression. A statistical
analysis was performed to study the correlation between rotator cuff
pathology and cervical radiculopathy. Results: A total of 175
patients were included in this study, 121 females (69%) and 54 males (31%).
The mean age was 56 years-old (SD 11.5). Sixty-six of these patients
presented with tendinosis (38%), 49 with partial tear (28%), 32 with
complete tear (18%), 9 with calcifying tendinopathy (5%) and 9 with massive
tear (5%). The remaining patients had no rotator cuff lesions (6%).
Concerning the cervical MRIs, 54 patients (31%) had no radicular or cord
compression. The most affected levels were C5 and C6, with 14 patients with
foraminal compression of C6 (8%), 11 with C5-C6 central compression (6%) and
9 with foraminal compression of C5 (5%). From the statistical analysis, it
was found that men presented with a significant higher cervical pathology -
88,9% (p < 0.01). Advanced age was also associated with more cervical
lesions – mean age with lesions was 58 years (SD 10.6) vs. mean age with no
lesions was 49 years (SD 12), p < 0.01. There was no statistically
significant correlation between degenerative findings in cervical MRI and
shoulder MRI (p = 0.870), namely the association between C4, C5 and C6 and
rotator cuff pathology. Conclusion: Despite the anatomical
relationship between shoulder musculature and cervical roots, it was not
possible to establish a correlation between rotator cuff injury patterns and
cervical neurological compression.
Based on this study, we cannot affirm that central or foraminal compression
predispose or potentiate rotator cuff tears.
