## P158: Myoarchitectonic spinolaminoplasty using hydroxyapatite spacer
versus new titanium plate

Seishi Matsui

1,2

 and Naoki Shinohara

2

1

Neurosurgery, Kajiura Hospital, Matsuyama City, Japan

2

Neurosurgery, HITO Hospital, Shikokuchuo City, Japan

Introduction: Myoarchitectonic spinolaminoplasty (MSLP) is an
effective spinous process-splitting double door laminoplasty for compressive
cervical myelopathy. It preserves all musculoskeletal attachments of the
posterior neck, so that it could prevent postoperative neck pain and loss of
cervical lordosis. In the procedure of MSLP, an original hydroxyapatite (HA)
spacer is usually utilized as a substitute for the spinous process, which is
fixed to the laminar flaps and the spinous process flaps with surgical
sutures. The authors, however, have used a newly designed titanium plate
(Baslet2) instead of the original HA spacer since 2018. The Basket2 is fixed
to the laminar flaps with titanium screws and to the spinous process flaps
with surgical sutures. The fixation with the titanium screw must be more
rigid and technically easier than the fixation with the surgical suture.
This study aimed to compare the operative time, the clinical and
radiological outcomes of MSLP using the HA spacer and the Basket2 in
patients with compressive cervical myelopathy. Material and
Methods: 52 patients with compressive cervical myelopathy who
underwent MSLP in three or four laminae were enrolled. 28 patients (19 males
and 9 females, a mean age of 65.8 years) with the use of the HA spacer were
classified as HA group and 24 patients (12 males and 12 females, a mean age
of 63.6 years) with the Basket2 were as B2 group. The operation time was
assessed. Preoperative and two-year follow-up evaluations included the
Neurosurgical Cervical Spine Scale (NCSS, full score 14 points) for
neurological condition and radiological analysis including C2-C7 lordotic
angle in neutral position (LA), flexion-extension range of motion for C2-C7
(ROM) and C2-C7 sagittal vertical axis (SVA). Results: The mean
operative time was 150 minutes in HA group and 112 minutes in B2 group,
while the mean number of treated laminae was 3.6 in both groups. Mean NCSS
was improved from 8.5 to 12.5 in HA group and from 9.5 to 12.9 in B2 group.
Mean LA increased from 4.8° to 8.2° in HA group and from 6.0° to 10.1° in B2
group. Mean ROM decreased from 31.5° to 20.5° in HA group and from 35.0° to
26.1° in B2 group. Mean SVA extended from 18.5 mm to 21.6 mm in HA group and
from 23.4 mm to 24.7 mm in B2 group. As a result, significant differences
between the two groups were observed in operative time and ROM at two-year
follow-up. Conclusion: In MSLP, the Basket2 was more useful
than the HA spacer in terms of shorter operative time and less postoperative
ROM loss. It was speculated that the differences of material, profile,
fixation method between these two spacers were involved in the results.

## 653

## P159: Is plating necessary in two-level ACDF surgery? Prospective
controlled study

Velmurugan Kandasamy

1

 and Sathish Muthu

2

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Government Royapettah Hospital, Chennai,
India

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Dindigul,
India

Introduction: Anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF)
surgeries are one of the most commonly performed spinal procedures. Despite
its frequent usage, there is no consensus among surgeons on the usage of
implants to achieve fusion when performed at two levels. We aim to
investigate the necessity of an additional anterior cervical plate over the
cages used in two-level ACDF surgery concerning the clinical and
radiological outcomes. Methods: We performed a prospective
comparative controlled clinical trial among 48 patients who underwent
two-level ACDF surgery for degenerative conditions of the spine with a
minimum follow-up of 1 year. The patients received either standalone cages
(SAC) or cage with plate (CP) constructs to achieve fusion at the two levels
operated. Clinical outcomes such as neck disability index (NDI) and visual
analog scale (VAS) score for pain were assessed at preoperative, 3,6, and 12
months post-operative period along with complications. During the
above-mentioned visits, radiological parameters such as fusion status,
subsidence, C2-C7 lordosis angle, fusion segment angle, and adjacent segment
disc space narrowing were analyzed. Results: The mean age of
the population included in the study was 49.4 ± 4.5 years with 14 females in
each group. In comparison to the CP construct for two-level ACDF surgery,
the SAC group demonstrated better NDI scores at 3, 6, and 12 months
follow-up but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.070).
We did not note any significant difference in the VAS scores between the two
groups (p = 0.208). At 1 year follow-up, we noted significant cage
subsidence in 33% of patients in the SAC group and while subsidence was
noted only in 16.6% of patients in the CP group (p = 0.021). However, none
of the patients with subsidence reported any symptoms that required revision
surgery. We noted a significant increase in post-operative dysphagia in the
CP group compared to the SAC group (p < 0.001). We also did not note any
significant difference in the other radiological parameters such as C2-C7
lordosis or fusion segment angle or adjacent segment disc space narrowing.
We did not note any significant difference in the fusion rate at one year
for both SAC (91.6%) and CP (95.8%) constructs of two-level ACDF surgery (p
= 0.32). Conclusion: The use of plating in two-level ACDF
surgery significantly reduced the incidence of asymptomatic cage subsidence
compared to the SAC group along with a significant increase in the incidence
of postoperative dysphagia. We did not find any other additive advantage
with the use of an anterior cervical plate over a cage construct in
two-level ACDF surgeries to recommend its routine use.

## P160: Laminectomy alone for cervical spondylotic myelopathy: a CSORN
study

Mathieu Laflamme

1

, Nicolas Dea

2

, and Greg McIntosh

3

1

Division of Neurosurgery, CHU de Québec - Université Laval, Québec
City, Canada

2

Neurosurgery, University of British Columbia, Vancouver,
Canada

3

Canadian Spine Outcomes and Research Network, Markdale,
Canada

Introduction: Most posterior cervical decompression is
supplemented by instrumentation and fusion in North America. However,
laminectomy alone remains a common procedure in certain parts of the world,
including Europe. Results comparing these two interventions are
contradictory in the literature. Our objectives were 1) to better defined
the cervical myelopathy population who are treated with a decompression
alone; 2) to assess the outcome of patient treated with a decompression
alone and 3) to compare their outcomes to a cohort of posterior
decompression and fusion patients. Methods: The Canadian Spine
Outcomes and Research Network (CSORN) is a multicenter national prospective
registry. Patients with CSM who underwent laminectomy without
instrumentation as their index surgery were identified from this registry.
Clinical, surgical and radiological data were extracted at baseline and
post-operatively. A propensity match analyses was conducted with patients
from the same registry who underwent decompression and instrumentation.
Groups were matched according to age, mJOA, C2-7 Cobb angle and number of
levels decompressed on 1:1 ratio. Primary outcome was the Neck Disability
Index (NDI) at 1 year post-operatively. Secondary outcomes included
reoperation, SF-36, post-operative cervical alignment, neck and arm pain and
satisfaction at 1 year. Results: From the 274 patients enrolled
in the registry, 34 met inclusion criteria. The mean age was 66.12 years and
28 (82.4%) were males. The mean mJOA at baseline was 13.15 and the mean Cobb
angle (C2-7) was -7.70° (lordotic). These two baseline parameters were
significantly different from the rest of the cohort (240 patients) who
underwent posterior instrumentation with a mJOA of 11.82 and a Cobb angle of
2.57°. There was no significant difference at baseline between the cohorts
for PROs (Neck pain, NDI, SF-36). The number of levels involved (3.77 vs
2.06), the operative time (174 vs 102 min) and the estimated blood loss (330
vs 184 ml) were significantly higher in the instrumented group, but length
of stay (6.42 vs 4.67 days) was similar. At 12 months, there was no
significant difference for NDI mean change between the laminectomy alone
(-14.07) and the laminectomy with fusion (-11.90). There was also no
difference at one year for mean change in mJOA and SF-36.
Conclusions: In this population of Canadian patients who
underwent posterior surgery for CSM, patients selected for a laminectomy
alone had a better mJOA score and a more lordotic alignment at baseline.
Laminectomy alone involved less decompressed levels, shorter operative time
and decreased blood loss. The improvement in mJOA and PROs was not different
at one year post-operatively between the laminectomy alone group and the
laminectomy with fusion. In a carefully selected population, a simple
decompression is a good treatment alternative.

## P161: Application of posterior endoscopic cervical foraminotomy (PECF)

(ACDF) surgery

Se-yi Chen

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF)
surgery is a standard treatment for cervical spondylosis myelopathy or
radiculopathy disease. Though the outcome of ACDF is quite satisfactory,
recurrent radiculopathy due to re-stenosis or adjacent degeneration are
inevitable. We applied posterior endoscopic cervical foraminotomy (PECF) as
salvage surgery after ACDF in 10 patients (14 levels). Material and
Method: We performed PECF in 10 patients (14 levels) in the past
5 years for recurrent radiculopathy after ACDF. The time to developing
recurrent radiculopathy ranges from 8 months to 3 years. Mostly were
unilateral radiculopathy and single level. Before surgery intervention, all
patients were treated with adequate medication and rehabilitation. Routine
image study include bilateral oblique view X-ray, computed tomography (CT)
and magnetic resonance image (MRI) of cervical spine. Result:
Only one of the 10 patients didn’t response immediately but showed gradual
subtle recovery after decompression surgery in the following 6 months.
There’s another 1 patient showed good sensory function recovery, but
transient motor palsy for 2 weeks. Otherwise, all the other patients showed
motor or sensory function recovery, without symptom deterioration. None of
these patients presented instability or mechanical pain after operation.
None of these patient need repeat anterior surgery. Conclusion:
PECF, a minimal invasive posterior cervical surgery, serves as an efficient
and effective salvage surgery for re-stenosis after ACDF. This procedure
prevents the patients and surgeons suffering from scarring trajectory and
longer fusion levels.

## P162: Forestier's disease presenting as dysphagia and Dysphonia - a rare
case report

Dr Sajan Hegde

1

, Sharan Achar T

1

, Vigneshwara Badikkilaya

1

, and Umesh Kanade P

1

1

Orthopaedics, Apollo Hospitals Chennai India, Chennai,
India

Introduction: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) or
Forestier’s disease is a common, but under reported disease affecting the
elderly population. It is characterized by the ossification of soft tissues,
primarily of ligament, tendon, or joint capsule insertion, and can cause
back pain and spinal stiffness. Exuberant osteophyte formation of the
anterior longitudinal ligament of the cervical spine can cause dysphagia,
most frequently and dysphonia very rarely. In this study we report one such
rare case. Material and Method: A 77 years old male K/C/O DM,
HTN, BPH, CAD, suffering from progressive dysphagia since 1 year and acute
onset dysphonia since 10 days. Semi-solid as well as liquid diet caused
aspiration necessitating ryle’s tube usage. After thorough evaluation by
otolaryngologist, neurologist, Large anterior cervical osteophytic spur at
C6 vertebrae level was detected on x-ray and computed tomography (CT)
compressing oesophagus with impingement of right recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Results: Patient was operated for DISH through anterior
Smith Robinson’s approach and the C6-7 osteophyte complex was excised. The
patient’s symptoms gradually improved and the same was confirmed by
resolution of the protruding submucosal mass, edema and inflammation along
the posterior pharyngeal wall by fiberscope examination.
Conclusions: Forestier’s disease is currently a growing
source of complications in elderly, mostly dysphagia and less commonly upper
respiratory airway obstruction and dysphonia. Surgical intervention is a
good way to relieve these symptoms. We rarely see the symptoms of dysphonia,
and the management of this complication requires a multidisciplinary team
and thorough approach, with spine surgeons, otolaryngologist and
dieticians.

development, mainly in its use at the lumbar spine level. In fact, its use
to treat cases of degenerative cervical pathology refractory to conservative
treatment has been increasing and following this paradigm in recent years.

and the clinical advantages that can arise from its development are
notorious. In fact, this technique has very gratifying clinical results that
have encouraged investment and development, particularly in the cervical
region, with promising prospects for the future.

## P164: Predisposing factors for dysphagia after anterior cervical

Tuna Pehlivanoglu

levels (C2-3 or C3-4) were predisposing factors to dysphagia after ACDF.
However, even persisting dysphagia was noted to be resolved at the last
follow-up. It was also reported that, ACDF procedure was providing

## P165: Posterior cervical decompression and fusion - is there an advantage
of going to C2? - a retrospective data base review

Anna Rienmueller

, Thorsten Jentzsch

is a common procedure to treat patients with multilevel degenerative
cervical myelopathy (CM). Standard of care includes decompression and fusion
of spinal levels involved, which is most often C3-6. Adjacent segment
deterioration at the upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) C3 due to construct
failure and loss of deformity correction might lead to increased strain on
the spinal cord and its clinical implications within follow-up time. We
hypothesize that loss of deformity correction and revision surgery in
patients undergoing PCDF can be avoided with inclusion of C2 in comparison
to ending the fusion at C3. Methods: In a retrospective
database review, we included all patients who underwent multilevel (minimum
3 level) primary PCDF for CM with an UIV of C3 or C2 between July 2005 and
December 2018. Patients with incomplete clinical and radiological data as
well as follow up < 1 year were excluded. Intraoperative parameters such
as surgical time, blood loss and complications as well as follow up and
revision surgeries were compared. C2-C7 lordosis, T1 slope, proximal and
distal lordosis, as well as proximal and distal anterolisthesis were
measured on pre-, post-op and follow-up radiographs and compared. To compare
between groups the Wilcoxon rank sum and chi-square tests were used. A
logistic regression model accounted for the a priori confounder age and the
confounder levels fused. Results: A total of 91 patients were
included, 33 with an UIV of C2 and 58 ending at C3. Although no difference
in number of levels fused the surgical time (215 min versus 185 min, p =
0.017) and blood loss (650ml versus 500 ml, p = 0-042) was significantly
higher in the UIV C2 group, no difference was found for complications.
Clinical outcome represented by the neck disability index (NDI), number of
revisions, and reason for revision showed no difference between the two
groups. Post-op proximal lordosis was significantly greater in the UIV C2
group (p = 0.001), change of overall lordosis was significantly higher in
the UIV C2 group (0.020). Discussion: We didn’t find a
statistically significant difference in clinical outcome between PCDF UIV C2
and UIV C3. Surgical time and blood loos very significantly higher. Ending
the fusion construct at C2 lead to higher proximal lordosis as well as
significantly higher change in overall lordosis in the UIV C2 group. Further
prospective studies including longer follow-ups will have to prove if better
biomechanical alignment is necessary to avoid clinically relevant adjacent
segment degeneration at C2/3.

## P166: Anomalous vertebral artery course causing radiculopathy: a case
report and review of relevant literature

Hussam Jabri

1

, Kuo-Tai Chen

2

, Sagar Sharma

3

, Yanting Liu

4

, and Jin-Sung Luke Kim

4

1

Neurosurgery/Spine, Prince Sultan Military Medical City, Riyadh,
Saudi Arabia

2

Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Chia-Yi, Taiwan

3

Smt. SCL General Hospital, Smt NHL Municipal Medical College,
Ahmedabad, India

4

Seoul St. Mary Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

We present a case of cervical radiculopathy caused by an abnormal vertebral
artery course. Ectatic vertebral artery course remains one of the rare
causes of cervical radiculopathy. Therefore, overlooking this anomaly might
lead to vertebral artery injury during cervical radiculopathy surgery. We
include a review of all 18 surgically treated cases present in literature to
date; and their relevant clinical course.
Discussion: Cervical radiculopathy is commonly caused by
degenerative/discogenic herniated disc. However, other rare causes like
ectatic vertebral artery course, congenital lesions, arteriovenous
malformation, and tumors should be ruled out, especially when no disc
herniation is identified on imaging. Most surgeons should continue to locate
the vertebral artery and its course during the preoperative evaluation for
anterior or posterior cervical spine surgery, as this is a crucial step to
avoid iatrogenic injury to these vessels. As previously mentioned, the
prevalence of vertebral artery loop formation (VALF) in a cadaveric study of
222 cervical spines was 2.7%.In another series of cervicobrachial pain
without disc pathology, 13 out of 173 patients had VALF, suggesting that the
incidence is around 7.51%.The etiology of this loop formation remains
unknown but congenital abnormality, or as postulated degenerative theory,
might be implicated. Oga et al., concluded after reviewing 22 cases that the
extent of tortuosity is correlated with the severity of cervical
spondylosis. This degenerative theory was also backed by Sakiadia et al.,
who postulated that the initial step in a process which is flowed by
pulsatile pressure leads to migration and erosion of the adjacent
structures. This theory might be supported by the higher occurrence of this
pathology in older population. Clinical presentation of cases with VALF
varies based on pain, radiculopathy, myelopathy or a combination of
symptoms. Most patients may be asymptomatic and only diagnosed incidentally
during imaging for trauma or other purposes. In neurologically symptomatic
cases, X-ray demonstrates an enlargement of the foramen transversarium with
an erosion of the adjacent bone and sclerotic margins related to pulsatile
arterial pressure. These bony details are better appreciated in axial and
reconstructed CT images. Contrasted CT and MRI show signal void in the
foramen with nerve compression. Other radiologic examinations such as CT,
MRI, and MRA might also be equally informative in demonstrating the course
and exact location of tortuosity. Furthermore, Doppler ultrasonography can
help intraoperatively in confirming the location of artery. Intraoperative
indocyanine green video angiography could be utilized; however,
interpretation of the signal intensity should be carefully monitored, which
varies with bolus timing, artery distance from the periosteal sheath, and
presence of robustious venous plexus. The ultimate surgical goal is freeing
the compressed neural structure. Although, the anterior approach that
exposes and frees the vertebral artery carries the risk of recurrent
laryngeal nerve and carotid artery injuries. Exposure carried out using
laterally passed longus colli to expose the transverse process might damage
the sympathetic nerves and may lead to Horner’s syndrome. The vessel loop
can also be relocated, but the anterior approach is not possible above C3
level.

## P167: Anterior cervical surgery for non-contiguous, "skip-level" cervical
degeneration: a PRISMA systematic review

Jerry Robinson

1

, Kortnie Broschinsky

2

, David Gendelberg

3

, Andrew Chung

4

, Jose Jimenez-Almonte

5

, Babak Khandehroo

1

, Sheila Kahwaty

1

, Neel Anand

1

, Rod Oskouian

6

, and Jens Chapman

6

1

Department of Orthopedics, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles,
United States

2

Department of Orthopedics, Summa Health System, Akron, United
States

3

Department of Orthopedics, San Francisco Orthopedics Trauma
Institute, University of California, San Francisco, United
States

4

Banner Health, Department of Orthopedics, Pheonix, AZ, United
States

5

Department of Orthopedics, Central Florida Bone & Joint
Institute, Orange City, FL, United States

6

Department of Spine Surgery, Swedish Neuroscience Institute,
Seattle, WA, United States

Introduction: Non-contiguous, “skip-level” cervical degeneration
is a phenomenon where two degenerative cervical discs are separated by a
normal, intermediate cervical disc. Skip-level degeneration presents an
interesting challenge to the spine surgeon because there is not a clear
consensus regarding optimal treatment. To date, no systematic review has
assessed the literature for guidance on this condition. Materials and
Methods: We conducted a search of the PubMed, Cochran, and OVID
databases through February 2022 using the Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We limited the
search to include full-text, English language publications that had any
reference to “non-contiguous” or “skip-level” cervical pathology to answer
the following questions: (1) What is the incidence of non-contiguous,
“skip-level” cervical degeneration? (2) What biomechanical data exists
regarding anterior cervical ‘skip-level” constructs? (3) What does the
clinical data suggest regarding outcomes for anterior cervical “skip-level”
surgery? Results: Our initial PRISMA search yielded 861
publications, which resulted in 21 unique publications after application of
inclusion/exclusion criteria. The first question resulted in one unique
publication describing the incidence of non-contiguous, “skip level”
cervical degeneration ranging from 1.6% to 22% depending on the number of
cervical levels involved. For question two, the biomechanical data is
conflicting. Cadaveric models may indicate that skip-level constructs result
in an equal distribution of forces to the remaining cervical segments, while
finite element analyses indicate that the distribution of forces may depend
on the specific “skip-level” construct. For the last question, the clinical
data suggests that any anterior surgical construct alters the normal
biomechanics of the cervical spine and can lead to adjacent/intermediate
degeneration; however, constructs including arthroplasty might alter the
normal biomechanics to a lesser degree. Conclusions: There
remains a significant deficit of quality publications regarding
non-contiguous, “skip-level” cervical degeneration. Spine researchers may
benefit from radiographic reports that specifically name and innumerate the
incidence of non-contiguous, “skip-level” cervical degeneration. Due to
discrepancy in biomechanical data, further publications regarding the
biomechanics of skip-level anterior cervical constructs are necessary. The
literature may benefit from non-contiguous anterior cervical clinical
studies that differentiate post-operative intermediate disc degeneration
rates from adjacent level degeneration rates.

## P168: Diagnosis of C4 radiculopathy

Yasuhisa Tanaka

1

1

Orthopaedics, Tohoku Central Hospital, Yamagata, Japan

Introduction: Cervical nerve root compression causes neck and
scapular pain, and its location indicates the affected root. Furthermore, C5
to C8 radiculopathy is usually accompanied by specific neurologies. However,
features of C4 radiculopathy are not well-known. Material and
Methods: We retrospectively studied patients who underwent
posterior foraminotomy of the unilateral C3-4 intervertebral level between
2012 and 2018 and showed improvements within 1 month after surgery. We
collected data on symptom duration, site of neck pain, Spurling test,
imaging findings, selective root block (SRB) effect, and surgical results
using a cervical radiculopathy scoring system (normal = 20 points).
Results: In total, eight patients were included, with mean
age of 73 (range, 52-83) years, and mean follow-up of 2 years. Symptom
durations were 3 months to 5 years and exceeded 1 year in five patients. All
patients reported unilateral nape pain of the suboccipital and upper
trapezius region. Spurling test elicited reproduction or increase of nape
pain in every patient. Plain radiographs showed facet joint hypertrophy and
foraminal stenosis at C3-4 level on the symptomatic side in every case.
Those findings were also clear on magnetic resonance imaging and computed
tomography scans. In five patients who underwent SRB, pain reproduction and
its temporary relief were obtained. Cervical radiculopathy scores ranged
from 9 to 15 points before surgery, and from 16 to 20 after surgery. Mean
improvement rate was 90%. Conclusion: Elderly patients
suffering for long time from unilateral nape pain with positive Spurling
test may have C4 radiculopathy.

## 1106

## P170: Predictors of patient satisfaction following laminoplasty and
posterior cervical fusion for degenerative cervical myelopathy

Justin Vickery

1

, Mitchell Bowers

1

, Andrew Croft

1

, Anthony Steinle

1

, Wilson Vaughan

1

, Jacquelyn Pennings

2

, Claudia Davidson

2

, Raymond Gardocki

1

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,3

, Amir Abtahi

1,2,3

, and Byron Stephens

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Research

3

Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most
common cause of spinal cord dysfunction. Symptom onset is usually insidious
in nature and can vary widely in clinical severity. Surgical management
options include decompression through either an anterior or posterior
approach. The two most common posterior operations are laminectomy and
fusion (LF) and laminoplasty (LP). While both LF and LP are appropriate
treatments for DCM, there is a paucity of data to identify patient
characteristics associated with patient satisfaction following these
procedures. To improve this knowledge gap, we conducted a retrospective
review of a large multi-center prospective spine outcomes registry
investigating which patient characteristics accurately predict patient
satisfaction following either LF or LP for DCM. Material and
Methods: The Quality Outcomes Database, a national prospective
spine surgery registry, was queried for patients who underwent LF or LP for
DCM. Included were 88 LP and 976 LF patients who received surgery between
04/2013 and 07/2019. The primary outcome was the North American Spine
Surgery patient satisfaction ordinal questionnaire, which is measured on a
4-point scale (1 = surgery met my expectations and 4 = I am the same or
worse as compared to before surgery), but we converted it to a dichotomous
outcome of being satisfied (1 or 2) or not (3 or 4). Pearson chi-square
tests, unpaired t-test, and Mann Whitney U test were used to assess initial
differences in demographics, clinical characteristics and satisfaction based
on surgical technique. A multivariate logistic regression model was
conducted to assess the association of surgical technique (LF vs LP) with
patient satisfaction, controlling for baseline demographics and clinical
characteristics. Results: No statistically significant
differences in patient satisfaction were found between LF and LP (78.3% vs
76.1%, p = 0.642) at 12-month follow-up. LP patients had significantly
higher proportions of advanced education, worse myelopathic symptoms,
private insurance, absence of depression/anxiety, and absence of adjacent
segment disease. Length of stay (LOS), neck disability index (NDI), and
baseline arm/neck pain were significantly worse in LF patients. In the
regression model, procedure type was not significantly associated with
patient satisfaction when adjusting for demographic and clinical
characteristics. Symptom duration > 3 months, increasing LOS, and race
(non-white) were significant predictors of decreased patient satisfaction in
both groups. Conclusion: Our present study found that patients
achieve equal satisfaction following either procedure at 12-month follow-up.
Symptom duration of less than 3 months, decreased length of hospital stay,
and identifying as white race were all significant positive predictors of
patient satisfaction. LP patients were better educated, less
anxious/depressed, and were more commonly privately insured than LF
patients, which highlights an important inequity in the socioeconomic access
to LP. Additionally, further research investigating the satisfaction
disparity between white and non-white patients is a critical area of future
research. As with all elective spine surgeries, proper surgical indication
and establishing post operative expectations is critical to successful
outcomes. The data from our study will aid surgeons when counseling patients
regarding satisfaction following LP and LF.

## P171: Comparative effectiveness of laminoplasty and laminectomy and
fusion for the treatment of cervical myeloradiculopathy

Justin Vickery

1

, Mitchell Bowers

1

, Anthony Steinle

1

, Wilson Vaughan

1

, Andrew Croft

1

, Jacquelyn Pennings

2

, Claudia Davidson

2

, Raymond Gardocki

1

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,3

, Amir Abtahi

1,2,3

, and Byron Stephens

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Research

3

Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Cervical myeloradiculopathy is the clinical
manifestation of degenerative cervical spine disease resulting in
concomitant central and foraminal stenosis. Surgical treatment options
include both anterior and posterior approaches. The most commonly utilized
posterior surgical option is laminectomy and fusion (LF). While laminoplasty
(LP) is commonly utilized to treat myelopathy alone, debate exists regarding
the efficacy of LP with respect to adequate treatment of radicular
complaints in patients with myeloradiculopathy. To improve this clinical
knowledge gap, our study investigated the efficacy of LP in improving
radicular symptoms and how that change compares to the improvement seen with
posterior cervical fusion. Additionally, we investigated which patient and
operative characteristics were associated with arm pain scores at 12 months.
Material and Methods: The Quality Outcomes Database, a
multi-center national prospective spine surgery registry, was
retrospectively queried for patients with myeloradiculopathy who underwent
LF or LP from 4/2013 and 07/2019. The primary outcome was Numeric Rating
Scale (NRS) arm pain, which asks the patient to rate their arm pain on a
scale of 0-10 in the past seven days. Patients who reported a preoperative
NRS arm pain score of 0 (no pain) were excluded. Differences in patient
demographics, clinical characteristics, and PROs were assessed between the
LP and LF groups (chi square/parametric and nonparametric t-tests). Changes
in NRS arm pain from preop to 12 months postop were assessed for both groups
(nonparametric paired t-tests). Linear regression was used to model
predictors of 12-month arm pain based on type of procedure (LP vs LF),
controlling for baseline arm pain and other demographic and clinical
variables. Results: There were no significant differences in
arm pain scores at 12 months between LF and LP (2.9 vs 2.0, p = 0.100), and
both demonstrated similar significant improvements in arm pain over that
time period (p < 0.001). Patients undergoing LF had significantly higher
levels of preoperative arm pain compared to LP (p = 0.003). Type of
procedure (LP vs LF) was not a significant predictor of arm pain at 12
months when adjusting for preoperative arm pain. Higher preoperative arm
pain, increased hospital length of stay, and increased neck disability index
were all significant predictors of increased arm pain at 12 months, even
when controlling for other factors. No factors were found to be significant
in predicting the change in arm pain from baseline to 12 months in LP or LF
patients. Conclusion: Laminoplasty has been questioned as an
appropriate treatment for patients with myeloradiculopathy. While
laminoplasty has been shown to adequately decompress the central canal in
myelopathic patients, uncertainty exists regarding its ability to provide
adequate decompression of the neural foramen and therefore relief of
concomitant radicular pain. These data demonstrate that patients with
myeloradiculopathy undergoing posterior cervical fusion or laminoplasty
experienced similar levels of arm pain improvement. Additionally, the type
of decompression performed was not a predictor of arm pain at 12 months.
These findings demonstrate that in patients with myeloradiculopathy,
laminoplasty is a viable treatment option for both the myelopathic and
radicular complaints.

## 1250

## P174: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusions are associated with
greater subsidence when compared to anterior cervical corpectomies for
degenerative pathology

Spencer Raub

1,2

, Caroline Drolet

1

, Jesse Shen

1,3

, Nicole Vivelo

1

, Michelle Gilbert

1

, Kellen Nold

1

, Venu Nemani

1

, Jean Christophe Leveque

1

, and Philip Louie

1

1

Neurosurgery, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, Seattle, United
States

2
School of Medicine, University of Washington,
Seattle, USA

3

Université de Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) or
anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion (ACCF) surgery has been demonstrated
to be an effective surgical treatment for degenerative cervical conditions.
ACCF, when directly compared to ACDF, has been described as the more
invasive of the two procedures, but may be more effective to improve
anterior-based stenosis that is present posterior to a vertebral body,
rather than at the disc spaces themselves. Graft subsidence is a known
complication of both procedures, but no study has compared the subsidence
rates and risk factors between these two procedures performed for
degenerative pathology utilizing the same surgical techniques. We sought to
compare subsidence, based on interscrew distance and height between ACCF and
ACDF, with a specific focus on the impact of screw-to-vertebral body ratio
and change in angle of variable screws placed at the cephalad and caudal
aspects of the construct. Material and Methods: A retrospective
cohort analysis was performed on consecutive patients who underwent a
2-level ACDF (allograft) or 1-level ACCF (titanium expandable cage) for
degenerative pathology between January 2017 and June 2021 with 6 months
follow-up. Procedures were performed by 3 spine-fellowship trained surgeons
who perform both procedures with the same surgical technique. Pre- and
6-month post-operative radiographic assessment included height
(ant/mid/post), intervertebral screw distance, and screw-vertebral body
ratio of the cephalad and caudal screws. Demographic information, operative
times, complications, and re-operation data was obtained. All analyses
predict subsidence change scores (ant/mid/post height, interscrew distance)
from screw angle change (cephalad or caudal depending on top or bottom),
postop screw angle, screw-to-vertebral body ratio, ACDF vs ACCF, postop
subsidence measurement and demographic variables (age, sex, BMI, CCI). Screw
angle change was included as an intermediate variable and was predicted by
postop screw angle, screw to vertebral body ratio, and demographic
variables. Results: In total, 65 ACDF patients and 13 ACCF
patients fulfilled inclusion criteria. There were no significant differences
between the demographics of both groups. Dysphagia requiring consultation
were similar between both groups (15.4% ACDF, 17.6% ACCF; p > 0.05).
Across all 4 measurements of subsidence, ACDF procedures resulted in greater
subsidence than ACCF (p < 0.05). Additionally, greater screw-to-vertebral
body ratio was associated with less subsidence (p < 0.05). Overall, no
re-operations were performed for subsidence-related pathology. Three ACDF
patients underwent re-operation for pseudarthrosis. One ACCF underwent
re-operation for early-onset adjacent segment pathology.
Conclusion: At a single center with similar surgical
techniques, ACDF procedures were associated with greater subsidence when
compared to ACCFs when performed for degenerative pathology. Greater
screw-to-vertebral body ratio may be protective against radiographic
subsidence. The clinical impact of these subsidence differences require
further evaluation.

Dysphagia after the anterior cervical approach has been reported in up to 60%

Candidates for surgical management with anterior cervical approach.
They have signed informed consent.

Exclusion criteria

History of previous cervical surgery.
ASA III and IV.
BMI > 30.
Presence of dysphagia prior to surgery
History of diseases in the esophagus and/or laryn
Results: The values showed a normal distribution according to
the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. A sample of 52 patients who met the inclusion
criteria was obtained, the average age was 63.17 ± 9.57 years old, 40.4%
(21/52) of the sample were male and 59.6% (31/52) The sample had homogeneous

## P176: Pack years of tobacco cigarette smoking as a predictor of bony
fusion following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion surgery

Marissa Kruk

1

, Mohamed Soliman

1,2

, Alexander Aguirre

1

, Cathleen Kuo

1

, Nicco Ruggiero

1

, Andrea Kassay

1

, Asham Khan

1

, Moleca Ghannam

1

, David Smolar

1

, John Pollina

1

, and Jeffrey Mullin

1

1

Neurosurgery, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, United States

2

Neurosurgery, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt

Introduction: Smoking tobacco cigarettes negatively impacts the
process of bone healing after spinal fusion surgery. Patient smoking history
is often assessed based on current smoker, former smoker, and nonsmoker
status. However, few studies quantify smoking history in terms of pack years
to estimate lifetime exposure and assess its effects. This study aimed to
investigate the influence that smoking history quantified in terms of pack
years has on bony fusion following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
(ACDF) surgery. Material and Methods: A retrospective chart
review was conducted to identify patients who had undergone prior ACDF

predictor of non-fusion (b-coefficient, -0.00424; 95% Confidence Interval,
[0.991,0.999], p < 0.05). Conclusion: A greater estimated
lifetime exposure to tobacco smoking, quantified in terms of pack years,
increases the risk of non-fusion following ACDF surgery.

## P178: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with ventral plate:
Influence of preoperative and postoperative sagittal balance on re-operation
rate

Magnus Michaelis

1,2

, Martin Erhard

1

, Anna C. Rienmüller

3

, Bernhard Mayer

4

, and Yu-Mi Ryang

5

1

Department for Neurosurgery, Klinikum rechts der Isar (TUM), Munich,
Germany

2

Department for Orthopedics, Sportsmedicine and Traumasurgery,
München Klinik Bogenhausen, Munich, Germany

3

Department for Orthopedic Surgery and Trauma Surgery, Medical
University Vienna, Vienna, Austria

4

Department for Neurosurgery, Klinikum Rechts der Isar der
Technischen Universität München, Munich, Germany

5

Neurosurgery, Helios Klinikum Berlin Buch, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF)
with ventral plate is a common way to treat several cervical degenerations.
Adjacent segment disease (ASD) and instability are frequent postoperative
complications, that lead to re-operation. We therefore investigated if
parameters of the cervical sagittal balance correlate with the number of
re-operations caused by ASD and instability. Material and
Methods: All Patients who underwent ACDF with ventral plate
between 2010-2016 at our institution were included and a retrospective
analysis to evaluate reoperation-rate due to ASD and instability was
performed. Cervical lordosis, k-line, segmental lordosis, T1-slope, C2
sagittal vertical axis (SVA), C7 SVA and Center of gravity (COG) SVA were
measured on preoperative and postoperative x-ray images. A binary logistic
regression analysis was performed to evaluate possible mechanical and osseus
risk factors for re-operation. Results: 155 patients were
included (86 men, 69 women; mean age: 68.8 ± 14.4). 25 out of 155 patients
(16.1%) underwent re-operation. 17 (68%) due to ASD, 8 patients (32%) due to
instability. On preoperative x-ray images correlation was found for T1-slope
(OR = 0.920; p = 0.067). Re-operated patients had a smaller T1-slope
preoperative. On postoperative x-ray images correlation was found for
segmental lordosis (OR = 1.074; p = 0.063) and C2 SVA (OR = 1.169; p =
0.115). Re-operated patients had a larger segmental lordosis and a larger C2
SVA after the first surgery. Conclusion: A smaller T1-slope
preoperative seems to increase the risk of re-operation caused by ASD and
instability after ACDF with ventral plate. A larger segmental lordosis and a
larger C2 SVA after first surgery seem to increase the risk of re-operation
as well. Although none of these correlations was significant, the direction
of our results matches with common literature. Further investigations are
necessary in order to verify our results and to find out more about the
influence of the sagittal balance on re-operation-rate.

## 1490

## P179: Autologous clavicle graft for anterior cervical discectomy and
fusion

Mandar Borde

1

, K Venugopal Menon

1

, Akash Mane

1

, and Sangram Rajale

1

1

Spine Surgery, Bharati Vidyapeeth (deemed to be University) Medical
College and Hospital, Pune, India

Introduction: Iliac crest has been the most common source of
autologous bone grafting for anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF).
Donor site complications like postoperative persistent pain and
paraesthesia, hematoma, infection, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury,
peritoneal perforations, iliac fractures and pelvic instability have been
reported with an incidence of 10-39%. To avoid occurrence of such
morbidities, alternative sources for autologous bone graft like sternum,
patella, fibula and rib have been tried but haven’t become popular. We
present a series of 25 cases with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
using autologous cancellous graft from medial end of the clavicle and
polyetheretherketone (PEEK) cage. Material and Methods: Between
January 2020 and January 2021, 25 patients and 33 levels (21 males and 4
females), ranging in age from 31 to 65 years underwent single-level (17
patients) or two-level (8 patients) anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
using this technique. Nine patients presented with radiculopathy, 6 had
myelopathy, 5 presented with myeloradiculopathy and 5 patients had traumatic
disc herniations with varying degrees of neurological deficit (4 patients
were ASIA A; 1 patient was ASIA B). Surgical decision was made after
thorough assessment of the preoperative clinical and radiological
examinations. The cervical discectomy was performed using the standard
Smith- Robinson technique. The bone graft was obtained by doing a small
corticotomy at the medial end of clavicle about 2.5 cm lateral to the
sternoclavicular joint and scooping out the cancellous bone with a curette.
A PEEK cage filled with the cancellous bone graft was fit in the discectomy
defect. Results: Clinical and radiological evaluation of all
the patients was done at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months after
the surgery. All patients showed significant improvement in their clinical
symptoms and showed radiographic evidence of solid bony fusion between 6-9
months. The mean Visual Analogue Score (VAS) at the end of 1-year was 0.2.
Radiological assessment involved anteroposterior and lateral radiographs and
lateral view radiographs in flexion and extension. Amongst the 5 patients
with neurological deficit, at the end of 1 year, 4 patients improved from
ASIA A to ASIA C while patient with ASIA B improved to ASIA D. Twenty-four
patients were highly satisfied by the cosmetic appearance of the scar at 1-
year follow up. One patient developed a keloid-like scar but was not
concerned by the cosmetic appearance. Conclusion: Cancellous
bone from the medial end clavicle is a safe, reliable, and technically easy
source of autologous bone graft that yields optimal fusion rates and patient
satisfaction with ACDF surgery. The advantages are easy access as the medial
end of clavicle lies in close proximity to the surgical field and does not
require any additional preparation or draping, no donor site pain and a
cosmetic scar; its disadvantages being the less volume of available graft
and a lack of structural support.

## P180: Degenerative cervical pathologies on magnetic resonance imaging:
retrospective analysis of prevalence in a single centre

Arkaprabha Banerjee

1

, Oliver Mowforth

2

, Mark Kotter

2

, Virginia Newcombe

3

, and Benjamin Davies

2

1

School of Clinical Medicine

2

Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge,
United Kingdom

3

Addenbrooke's Hospital, Division of Anaesthesia, United
Kingdom

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is a
condition of symptomatic spinal cord compression secondary to various
cervical spine degenerative pathologies. A diagnosis of DCM requires
degenerative cervical pathology, cord compression and myelopathic symptoms.
We studied the prevalence of degenerative pathologies in a cohort of 133
patients with asymptomatic cord compression. The objective was to compare
this cohort to previously studied asymptomatic cord compression and DCM
cohorts to identify if previously determined trends of DCM pathology applied
to our cohort. Methods: Radiological reports of cervical MRI
scans conducted at a tertiary neurosciences centre between January and
December 2015 were screened for degenerative cervical spinal changes. Of the
total 1123 cervical MRI scans screened, 133 met the inclusion criteria.
Degenerative pathology was classified into key categories. Prevalence of
each category and accompanying 95% confidence interval was calculated and
compared to asymptomatic cord compression and DCM cohorts. Within the
cohort, age and gender were used for subgroup analysis. Mean age (55.69
years) was used to dichotomise the cohort into two age-based subgroups;
patients < 55 years old and patients
> 56 years old to allow for effective
comparison of relatively younger and relatively older patients. 95%
Confidence Intervals were calculated and a Fisher’s Exact Test was carried
out for sub-group analysis. Results: The most prevalent
pathology was degenerative multilevel disc pathology (73.7%, 95% CI
66.2-81.2%), followed by degenerative single level disc pathology (23.3%,
95% CI 15.9-30.1%). Enlargement of ligamentum flavum (ELF) had a prevalence
of 9.8% (95% CI 4.7-14.8%) and spondylolisthesis/subluxation had a
prevalence of 9.8% as well (95% CI 4.7-14.8%). Congenital stenosis was the
fifth most prevalent pathology (3.8%, 95% CI 0.5-7.0%). Cranio-cervical
joint abnormalities and KFS both had prevalence values of 2.3% (95% CI
0.0-4.8%). OPLL had a prevalence of 0% (95% CI 0.0-2.7%). Non-lordotic
cervical alignment in our cohort was found to have a prevalence of 30.1%
(95% CI 22.3-37.9%). Comparison to the asymptomatic cohort revealed the
local cohort to have greater prevalence of single-level disc pathology.
Comparison to the symptomatic cohort revealed a significant increased
prevalence in multilevel disc pathology, OPLL and ELF in symptomatic
patients compared to our cohort, while our cohort at a greater prevalence of
single-level disc pathology. Given the high baseline prevalence of
multilevel disc pathology, however, this is most striking for OPLL and ELF.
Conclusion: OPLL and ELF are rare in asymptomatic
populations. Their further targeted investigation may have relevance to
exploring the natural history of DCM, a global research priority.

## 1577

## P181: Respiratory dysfunction in degenerative cervical myelopathy: a
systematic review

Lorcan Elliott

1

, Oliver Mowforth

1

, Aref-Ali Gharooni

1

, Mark Kotter

1

, and Benjamin Davies

1

1

Neurosurgery, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom

Introduction:
Degenerative cervical myelopathy is a condition of
symptomatic cervical spinal cord compression secondary to a
range of degenerative spinal pathology. Respiratory dysfunction has been
described in several cohort studies and shortness of breath is not
uncommonly reported by people with DCM. The objective of this systematic
review was therefore to synthesise current evidence on the relationship
between DCM and respiratory function. Material and Methods: The
review was registered on PROSPERO and followed PRISMA guidelines. Ovid
MEDLINE, and Embase were searched to 24th September 2022. DCM
studies reporting any respiratory measure, including spirometry and outcomes
relating to respiratory disease were eligible. Reference lists were hand
searched. Title and abstract and full text screening, risk of bias and GRADE
assessments was completed in duplicate. A quantitative synthesis is
presented. Results: A total of 517 studies identified by
literature searching; 14 met inclusion criteria, including 3 cohort studies,
5 case control studies and 6 case studies. There was conflicting evidence
across 2 cohort studies and 5 case/control studies as to whether surgical
decompression for DCM was associated with improvements in spirometric
measures such as FEV1 and FVC. Similarly, there was inconsistency in
differences in FEV1 reported between DCM patients and controls. FVC, vital
capacity and peak expiratory flow rate were consistently reported to be
lower in patients than controls. Higher spinal compression was associated
with more significant respiratory impairments than more caudal lesions. One
cohort study reported a higher prevalence of cervical spondylosis in
patients with obstructive sleep apnoea. All case reports described
respiratory dysfunction in DCM patients, some of which showed improvements
following management of ventilation or diaphragmatic function.
Conclusion: DCM may be associated with respiratory
dysfunction; however the current quality of evidence is poor. Further work
should address aetiology, such as disruption to diaphragmatic innervation by
cervical spine nerve roots or projections from brainstem respiratory
centres.

## P182: How do patient comorbidities affect the choice of osteobiologics
for anterior cervical discectomy and fusion?

Stipe Corluka

1

, Michael Collins

2

, Aidin Abedi

2

, Timothy S. Yoon

3

, Meisel Hans-Jorg

4

, Jeffrey C. Wang

2

, Zorica Buser

5

, and AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative

6

1

Spinal Surgery Division, Traumatology Department, University
Hospital Centre Sestre Milosrdnice, Zagreb, Croatia

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Southern
California, Keck School of Medicine, United States

3

Department of Orthopaedics, Emory University, Atlanta, United
States

4

Department of Neurosurgery, Bergmannstrost Hospital, Halle,
Germany

5

Gerling Institute, New York, United States

6

AO Foundation, AO Spine, Davos, Switzerland

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is
a well-known, effective, and frequently performed surgical technique in the
treatment of cervical spine degenerative conditions. Fusion can be promoted
and achieved by several biomaterials with the autologous bone graft (ABG)
still being the gold standard because of its osteogenic, osteoinductive and
osteoconductive properties. The acute and chronic donor-site complications
have been reported as a postoperative complication. Therefore, utilization
of allogenic graft materials has gained interest. Although ACDF commonly
necessitates short hospital admission and is well-tolerated by most
patients, surgical delays, complications, and increased length of stay can
be influenced by identifiable risk factors, but long-term impact on fusion
rate is not observed. Pseudoarthrosis after ACDF surgery represents a
challenging complication and the aim of the current study was to determine
the impact of patient comorbidities on choice of osteobiologic use.
Material and Methods: This systematic review was designed
based on the PRISMA methodology by electronic literature searches on MeSH
terms. The search phrases were formulated to capture the studies on
‘anterior cervical spine’ AND ‘decompression/fusion’. To be included in the
final review, studies needed assess the factors affecting the choice of
osteobiologics in adult patients undergoing a one- to four-level ACDF.
Results: Search string resulted in 5012 records which were
screened based on title/abstract sections. At the end 68 studies were
included for full-text assessment and finally, 0 studies evaluated how
patient comorbidities (osteoporosis, smoking, history of RA, history of
steroid use, obesity, etc.) affected the choice of osteobiologics used in
elective ACDF surgery. Conclusion: Lack of studies meeting the
criteria of the review reflect the paucity of the literature on patient
comorbidities. This is particularly critical given the increased choice of
available osteobiologics and very limited evidence to support their
extensive use.

The incidences of other CDArelated complications in Pretic-I group were also
well-accepted, comparable to the Discover group, without significant
differences. Conclusion: CDA with Pretic-I demonstrated a
well-accepted and sustained clinical outcome, with a significantly lower
incidence of high-grade HO. This newly designed prosthesis is expected to
become an alternative choice for cervical disc prosthesis in the future.

disease, Heterotopic ossifcation

## P184: Acute quadriplegia and death following a routine MRI for
undiagnosed degenerative cervical myelopathy

Cylene Yang

, Oliver Mowforth

, Benjamin Davies

, and Rodney Laing

1

1

Neurosurgery, Addenbrookes, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Bilateral upper limb paraesthesia and pain are common symptoms of
degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM). Such symptoms instigate
investigation by cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This was
the case for patient AB, who was an otherwise fit male in his early
seventies. During the scan AB unfortunately developed sudden onset
quadriplegia secondary to an intervertebral disc prolapse. This necessitated
intubation due to respiratory failure and urgent transfer to the
neurosciences critical care unit at a tertiary neurosciences centre. Despite

## P185: 23 hour stay anterior cervical discectomy and intervertebral
fusion

Kathryn Kneale

1

 and Timothy Woodacre

1

1

Neurosurgery, University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust, Plymouth,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and interbody fusion
(ACDF) is a commonly performed operation, with a mean length of stay of two
days. There has been a drive to increase Day Case surgery within the NHS to
increase efficiency, reduce costs and improve the patient experience. Our
Trust introduced a new 23 hour stay pathway for suitable ACDF patients, to
be discharged from the Day Case Unit by 9am (thus avoiding impacting the
functioning of the Unit), following the successful implementation of a Day
Case pathway for lumbar microdiscectomy patients. We modified practice by
introducing specific patient selection criteria, educating patients
preoperatively, changing operative scheduling and standardising the
postoperative management including analgesia. We aimed to ascertain if this
was a feasible pathway, if patients were satisfied with their experience and
how we could improve it. We also wanted to see what is required to move to
same day ACDF surgery. Material and Methods: All patients who
had undergone ACDF on this pathway under a single surgeon cohort were
identified and demographics and operation details recorded. They were
contacted to complete a telephone survey about their experience, including
the quality/quantity of information given pre and postoperatively, adequacy
of analgesia on discharge, and their overall experience. Results were
analysed. Results: A total of 17 patients underwent ACDF on
this pathway between July 2021 to September 2022. Of these, 13 were
contactable, and completed the survey. There were eight males and five
females. The average age was 48 years (39-64 years). All patients rated it
as a positive experience, with six (46%) rating it very good, and the
remaining seven (54%) good. Three patients (25%) felt there was a lack of
information on the postoperative course/poor communication postoperatively,
and two patients (15%) reported inadequate analgesia. There were two
complications with one patient requiring a washout at two weeks and another
patient who represented with neck swelling which resolved spontaneously.
Conclusion: Overall patients in this small cohort reported
a positive experience. This suggests it is feasible to adopt this pathway
for suitable patients, and we encourage other surgeons in the Trust to use
it. Ways of improving it would be to do a more detailed patient information
leaflet on the postoperative course, and an educational video for those who
cannot read well. Limitations of this study are a small sample size and
recall bias when answering questions. We plan to develop this to offer same
day ACDF surgery to selected patients.

0.727), or BMI (p = 0.892). Using these matched cohorts, the rate of early
reoperation for ASD was 8.0 % in the PI-LL mismatch cohort and 9.1% in the
normal PI-LL cohort (p = 0.805) with a mean time to reoperation of 1.28 and
1.33 years, respectively. Conclusions: After propensity score
matching, PI-LL mismatch was not associated with early reoperation for ASD
in patients undergoing 1-to-2 level lumbar fusions for degenerative
conditions.

## P188: The role of machine learning in surgical decision making for lumbar
disc herniation

Devender Singh

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

, Jeremiah Alexander

2

, Calvin Chandler

2

, Ashley Duncan

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, and John Stokes

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

2

Orthopedics, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Current care pathways recommend exhausting all
non-operative measures for at least six weeks in patients presenting with
uncomplicated lumbar disc herniation. Intent to treat analyses suggest that
overtime, the advantages of surgical intervention decline relative to
non-operative care, further complicating surgical decision making.
Aim: Using machine learning identify factors associated
with the likelihood of a patient will choose surgical intervention for
lumbar disc herniation. Materials and Methods: 300
retrospective chart reviews were conducted on patients who presented from
January 2019 to January 2021 with lumbar disc herniation. 27 independent
variables were collected across various domains including demographic,
medical history, clinical presentation, patient-reported outcomes, and
encoded using one-hot encoding techniques. The encoded data was analyzed and
subject to logistic regression using SKLean, StatsModel and Logit models,
with a focus on the recall metric. By focusing on recall, we aim to reduce
the number of false positives, or Type II errors in the model. Models were
further optimized by assessing multicollinearity of independent variables
and employing Area Under the Curve/Receiver Operating Characteristic
(AUC-ROC) and Precision-Recall techniques. Results: Overall
surgical rate was 25.3%, with median time to surgery eight weeks from intake
appointment. Demographic factors did not have a statistical impact on
surgical intervention, although men chose surgery at a higher rate than
women (29% vs 21.2%) Comorbidities and clinical presentation were not found
to have an effect on odds of surgical intervention. The median patient
reported back/leg pain and disability scores were higher in patients that
did have surgery (38 vs 34 and 7 vs 6, respectively), but this was not
statistically significant. The final optimized model yielded a test recall
of 0.4. In the end, only three variables were found to impact the odds of
surgical intervention. Patients who received a prescription for non-narcotic
medication and had at least one epidural injection, increased the odds of
surgical intervention by 3.4 and 2.6, respectively. Prescribing opioids
decreased odds of surgical intervention by 0.37. Conclusion:
Non-narcotic medication and injections increased the odds of later surgical
intervention. Given the current standard of care, this is not surprising as
one should exhaust all non-operative measures before culminating in surgical
intervention. Prescribing opioid medications during this minimal six-week
time frame lowered the odds of surgical intervention. This could be due to
the fact that opioids were prescribed to patients that had comorbidities or
other factors that do not lend themselves to the preferred physical
rehabilitation plan of care. These patients would already be unlikely
surgical candidates due to increased risk associated with medical
comorbidities. Limitations include variability between physicians’ practice
and sample size. A larger, prospective study would be the next step in
utilizing machine learning to predict which patients are most likely to
report satisfaction and a successful outcome.

## P189: Perioperative and radiographic outcomes between single position

Introduction: Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion (LLIF) and

degenerative lumbar pathologies. Dual position (DP) lumbar surgery involves
repositioning the patient from the supine or lateral decubitus position to
prone for posterior fixation. Single-position (SP) lumbar surgery (LS) is
commonly performed nowadays, minimally invasive alternative performed

## P190: Intravenous corticosteroid therapy for acute lumbar radicular
pain

Oded Hershkovich

1

 and Raphael Lotan

1

1

Edith Wolfson Medical Center, Holon, Israel

Introduction: The efficacy of pharmacological interventions for
acute lumbar radicular pain (ALRP) is limited, and systemic steroid use
remains controversial. We evaluated the effectiveness and tolerance of
systemic steroid use in a cohort of patients with ALRP.
Methods: A retrospective cohort of 56 patients (24 females)
admitted with intractable ALRP resistance to conservative treatment of
NSAIDs and opiates between the years 2016-2018. Medical records were studied
for demographics, physical examination findings, Visual Analogue Score
(VAS), IV steroids side effects, and recent imaging findings. All patients
received a daily dose of IV 24 mg Dexamethasone until discharge, SNRB or
Surgery. Results: The average IV Steroid treatment was 3.9 (±
2.8) days, with most patients showing significant pain relief to allow
discharge (69.7%). SNRB was required in 19.6% and surgical intervention in
10.7% within the same admission. Multivariate analysis did not find any
parameter to predict treatment failure (Age, gender, motor/sensory deficit,
CT/MRI findings). The motor deficit, positive Straight leg raising (SLR) and
dural sac compression on CT were higher in the intervention group but did
not reach statistical significance. One patient required discontinuation of
IV steroids due to elevated blood pressure. Conclusion: Despite
the insufficient evidence in the literature, IV steroid treatment is still a
viable option in ALRP treatment, with pain relief allowing discharge in 70%
of patients and a low complication rate. Our study found daily 24mg IV
dexamethasone for ALRP to be an effective treatment and helpful in most
patients admitted. This study supports the common practice used by spine
units.
Keywords: Sciatica; Radiculopathy; Herniated disc; Steroid treatment;
Pharmacotherapy
Synonyms: ALRP = Acute lumbar radicular pain, SNRB = Selective nerve root
block, SLR = Straight leg raising

## P191: Is stabilisation of contralateral side necessary while using
unilateral approach in lumbar fusion surgery at 2 adjacent levels?

Sathish Muthu

1,2

 and Girinivasan Chellamuthu

2

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Dindigul,
India

2

Department of Spine Surgery, Orthopaedic Research Group, Coimbatore,
India

Introduction: Generally, fusion supplemented with bilateral
pedicle screw fixation is the widely accepted method of stabilisation to
create an ideal environment for fusion of the unstable and the degenerated
disc area. Rigid internal fixation by bilateral pedicle screw fixation has
its shortcomings in the form of adjacent lumbar segment degeneration and
implant-related osteoporosis. Moreover, bilateral fixation was associated
with longer surgical time, greater blood loss and involving greater costs. A
relatively less rigid fixation in the form of unilateral pedicle screw
fixation could reduce the stress shielding and adjacent intervertebral disc
degeneration caused by bilateral pedicle screw fixation. Biomechanical
studies supported his concept stating that unilateral pedicle screw fixation
was sufficient to maintain the stability of the spine. We performed this
meta-analysis to compare the safety of unilateral with bilateral
instrumented fusion in two-level degenerative disorders of lumbar spine.
Materials and Methods: We conducted independent and
duplicate electronic database search including PubMed, Embase and Cochrane
Library till January 2020 for Randomised Controlled Trials(RCTs) comparing
unilateral pedicle screw fixation with bilateral pedicle screw fixation for
multi-level lumbar degenerative disorders. Fusion and complication rates
were the primary outcomes analysed. Analysis was performed in R platform
using OpenMeta[Analyst] software. Results: 5 RCTs including 215
patients (Unilateral/Bilateral = 106/109) were included in meta-analysis.
There was no significant difference between the two groups regarding fusion
rate, complication rate, blood loss, duration of hospital stay, functional
outcome scores like Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index
(ODI) and Short-Form health survey (SF-36) at final follow-up. Unilateral
pedicle screw fixation was associated with a significant reduction in
operation time (p < 0.001). Compared to open approach, minimally invasive
approach showed significant difference in terms of factors like operative
time, blood loss, hospital stay, VAS and ODI (p = 0.004).
Conclusion: Our meta-analysis establishes the immediate
safety and significant lesser operative period of unilateral pedicle screw
fixation in lumbar fusion. However, due to lack of evidence on complications
like cage subsidence and adjacent segment disease, unilateral pedicle screw
fixation cannot be recommended as an alternative to bilateral pedicle screw
fixation for two-level degenerative spinal disease. Our analysis established
the lacunae in literature for high-quality evidence on the subject hence we
recommend further large multicentre studies with longer follow-up to arrive
at a conclusion.

## P192: Management of discal cyst: case report and narrative review

Pedro Torres

1

, Andre Castilho

1

, Rodrigo Cruzeiro

1

, and Henrique Darmstadter

1

1

Spine Surgery, Hospital Unimed, Brazil

Introduction: Lumbar discal cyst (LDC) is a rare clinical entity
with unclear etiology. First described by Chiba et al. in
2001, is believed to be originated from the disc material and as a result of
previous disc injury. LDC is defined as an intraspinal extradural cyst with
distinct communication with the corresponding intervertebral disc. Clinical
history is similar to patients with disc herniation, manifesting as a
unilateral single nerve root lesion with neurologic deficits corresponding
to the involved nerve root. Discal cyst is one of the different types of
cysts that can exist extradurally in the lumbar spine, specifically in the
spinal canal and neuroforamen. Imaging nuances such as the location of the
cyst, bony changes on CT, contrast filling with discography or myelography,
and MRI characteristics can be useful to differentiate between different
types of cysts. LDC is almost always located behind the posterior vertebral
body, which is also a typical location for herniated discs. On MRI, LDC
appears as hypointense on T1-weighted image and hyperintense on T2-weighted
image and enhances homogenously after gadolinium. There are no guidelines
regarding the best treatment option for LDC. Therefore, we present a case of
LDC who underwent surgical treatment and try to identify evidence-based
treatment strategies for patients diagnosed with discal cyst. Material
and Methods: We report a case of a 21-year-old man with
radiculopathy of L5 root in the left side. The MRI showed a left-sided
extradural cyst at the level of L4/5. The cyst was hypointense and
hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, respectively. After 4 weeks of
conservative treatment without good outcomes, the patient underwent
microscopic surgery. The literature listed in MEDLINE/PubMed was reviewed to
identify related articles using the terms “Disc cyst AND treatment NOT disc
herniation”. We also made a manual search, and 15 papers were included in
this review. Results: At the first appointment the VAS was 9
and the L5 motor grade was 5. The patient was submitted initially to
conservative treatment with physical therapy and analgesic drugs. After 04
weeks of treatment the pain increased (VAS 10), ODI was 40% and L5 motor
grade was 3. During surgery, the cist capsule was at intimate contact with
the L5 root and with a hemorrhagic content. After surgery, patient sciatica
had a great reduction (VAS 3). After 6 months of surgery the ODI score was
0% and the motor grade of strength was 5. The histopathologic analysis
described simple fibrous tissue corresponding to capsule. No atypia was
found. Conclusion: Despite numerous reports, the explicit
pathophysiology of intraspinal discal cysts remains obscure. MRI is both
noninvasive and sensitive in diagnosing discal cysts and identifying
surrounding structures. For patients with mild to moderate symptoms,
conservative treatment can be successful, even inducing spontaneous
regression. Low grade evidence suggest that surgical treatment is the best
option for discal cysts. Excision of the cyst alone without excision of the
corresponding intervertebral disc could be considered as an option for
surgical treatment. Endoscopic surgery could also be a safe and promising
treatment.

## P193: Stand-alone lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) in patients with
aborted second-stage procedures: a case series

Benjamin Catoe

1,2

, David Barnes

3

, Cameron Kersey

2

, Sohrab Vatsia

2

, L. Erik Westerlund

2

, and Douglas Pahl

2

1

Orthopedic Surgery Residency Program, Jack Hughston Memorial
Hospital Phenix City, AL, United States

2

Hughston Clinic, Columbus, GA, United States

3

St. George Orthopedic Spine, St. George, UT, United States

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF), has gained
significant popularity over the last decade. LLIF is typically supplemented
with posterior or lateral fixation and decompression when necessary. We
hereby report a case series of patients who underwent stand-alone LLIF as
part of the first of a two-stage procedure whose second stage was
subsequently aborted due to risks of anesthesia or patient preference.
Material and Methods: Patients who had an aborted second
stage with a resulting stand-alone LLIF between 2014-2020 at our institution
were retrospectively identified. Chart and radiograph review were utilized
to evaluate for evidence of fusion, implant migration, implant subsidence,
minor and major complications, revisions, and symptom resolution. Oswestry
Disability Index (ODI) and Visual Analog Score (VAS) were assessed at the
initial and one-year interval follow-up visits postoperatively.
Results: Seventeen cases, involving 31 levels, were
identified with at least 12 months of follow up. At final follow up, 28
levels (90.3%) have shown radiographic evidence of fusion with evidence of
cage migration in one case (3.2%). The average disc height increased by
25.6%. Twenty-four levels (77.4%) demonstrated Grade 0 (0-24%) subsidence
and four levels (12.9%) had Grade I (25-49%) subsidence. There were no
revisions, no major complications, and no additional procedures were
recommended. Pre- and post-operative VAS and ODI were 6.4/3.5 (p <
0.0001) and 39.9/24.8 (p < 0.032). Conclusion: Stand-alone
LLIF is a viable option in patients with refractory back and leg pain due to
a lumbar spine condition and should be considered for patients with
significant risk factors to decrease anesthetic time and perioperative
complications.

## P196: An analysis of out of hours referrals for cauda equina syndrome in

## P197: Radiographic robustness of lumbar interbody fusion
techniques

Alice Bouchard

1

, Jeffrey Mun

1

, Frank Vazquez

1

, Alex Tang

2

, Edward DelSole

3

, Russell Strom

4

, and Tan Chen

3

1

Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine, Scranton, United
States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Geisinger, Northeast Residency, Wilkes-Barre,
United States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery

4

Neurosurgery, Geisinger Medical Center, Danville, United
States

Introduction: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) can be achieved with
various techniques, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.
Differences in long-term radiographic outcomes remain unclear. The purpose
of this study was to (1) evaluate the changes in sagittal parameters in the
preoperative, immediate post-operative, and latest follow-up phase, and (2)
to evaluate the radiographic maintenance of these parameters over time.
Material and Methods: Patients who had undergone single
level anterior (ALIF), lateral (LLIF), posterior (PLIF), or transforaminal
(TLIF) lumbar interbody fusion in an integrated health system from 2007 to
2022 were identified. Orthopaedic spine and neurosurgical patients were
included. Exclusion criteria included a non-degenerative diagnosis,
inadequate radiographs, multilevel and revision surgery, and postoperative
follow-up less than one month. Retrospective chart review was conducted to
collect patient demographics and diagnosis at time of surgery. Upright
lumbar radiographs taken prior to surgery, at the time of surgery, and at
most recent follow-up were analyzed. Each radiograph was measured for pelvic
incidence (PI), lumbar lordosis (LL), segmental lordosis (SL), posterior
disc height (PDH), and foraminal height
(FH).Results: A total of 158 patients met
inclusion criteria. There were 24 ALIFs (follow-up = 27.2 mon), 14 LLIFs
(follow-up = 14.0 mon), 74 TLIFs (follow-up = 12.8 mon) and 46 PLIFs
(follow-up = 26.4 mon). Differences were found in patient age, gender, and
BMI between cohorts. PDH and FH spinal parameters increased immediately
following ALIF (ΔPDH = +5.3 mm ΔFH = +3.7 mm p < 0.0001), LLIF (ΔPDH =
+4.1 mm ΔFH = +4.2 mm p < 0.01), TLIF (ΔPDH = +3.5 mm ΔFH = +3.6 mm p
< 0.001), and PLIF (ΔPDH = +4.7 mm ΔFH = +4.2 mm p < 0.0001). SL
changed immediately only for ALIF (ΔSL = +5.7deg, p = 0.002) and LLIF (ΔSL =
+4.4deg, p = 0.0002). Compared to the immediate post-operative phase, PDH
and FH decreased at latest follow-up for ALIF (ΔPDH = -1.9 mm p = 0.005, ΔFH
= -1.2 mm p = 0.16), LLIF (ΔPDH = -0.9 mm ΔFH = -1.9 mm p < 0.05), TLIF
(ΔPDH = -1.1 mm ΔFH = -2.3 mm p < 0.001), and PLIF (ΔPDH = -1.0 mm ΔFH =
-1.8 mm p < 0.01). SL decreased for ALIF (ΔSL = -5.4deg, p = 0.0005),
LLIF (ΔSL = -0.8deg, p = 0.34), TLIF (ΔSL = -1.1deg, p = 0.04), and PLIF
(ΔSL = -1.5deg, p = 0.07). LL did not change at any time point
postoperatively across techniques. Accounting for interobserver reliability,
no significant differences in the change in radiographic parameters was
noted across all techniques at final follow up (p > 0.05).
Conclusion: Lumbar interbody fusion, regardless of
technique, was shown to provide significant radiographic changes in
posterior disc height and foraminal height. Techniques utilizing larger
intervertebral cage sizes (ALIF and LLIF) improved segmental lordosis.
Single level LIF did not affect overall lumbar lordosis. Over time, all LIF
techniques demonstrated a degree of loss of correction and radiographic
settling. No LIF technique demonstrated superior radiographic robustness
over time. A limitation of this study was that ALIF and LLIF were not
subdivided into standalone LIF versus LIF supplemented with posterior
instrumentation. Further studies are warranted to study the relationship of
these parameters to the degree of indirect decompression, as well as its
relationship to clinical outcomes.

## P199: Decompression with fusion versus decompression alone in patients
with degenerative spondylolisthesis. A systematic review and
meta-analysis

Pravesh Gadjradj

1

, Fabian Sommer

1

, Jake Goldberg

1

, and Roger Hartl

1

1

Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell, New York, United
States

Introduction: Surgical decompression is standard care in the
treatment of degenerative spondylolisthesis in patients with symptomatic
stenosis, but there remains controversy over the benefits of adding fusion.
The persistent lack of consensus on this matter and the availability of new
data warrants a contemporary systematic review and meta-analysis of the
literature. Material and Methods: Multiple online databases
were systematically searched up to August 2022 for randomized controlled
trials (RCTs) and prospective studies comparing outcomes of decompression
alone versus decompression with fusion for lumbar spinal stenosis in

95% confidence intervals (CI) at two-year follow-up. Results:
Of the identified 2403 studies, eventually five RCTs and two prospective
studies were included. Overall, most studies had a low or unclear risk of
selection bias and most studies were focused on low grade degenerative
spondylolisthesis. All patient-reported outcomes showed low statistical
heterogeneity. Overall, there was high quality evidence suggesting no
difference in functionality at two years of follow-up (SMD -0.02, 95% CI
-0.22 to 0.18). Furthermore, there was high quality evidence of no
difference in leg pain (SMD -0.11, 95% CI -0.30 to 0.07) or back pain (SMD
-0.11, 95% CI -0.30 to 0.07) between patients undergoing decompression vs.
decompression with fusion. Pooled surgical outcomes showed less blood loss
after decompression only, and similar length of hospital stay and
reoperations compared to decompression with fusion. Conclusion:
Based on the current literature, there is high quality evidence of no
difference in functionality after decompression alone compared to
decompression with fusion in patients with degenerative lumbar
spondylolisthesis at 2 years of follow-up. Further studies should focus on
long-term comparative outcomes, health economic evaluations, and identifying
those patients that may benefit more from decompression with fusion instead
of decompression alone.
This review was registered at Prospero (CRD42021291603).
