## P200: Risk factors for ambulatory surgery conversion to extended stay
among patients undergoing posterior lumbar decompression

Yusuke Dodo

1,2

, Ichiro Okano

2

, Neil Kelly

3

, Leonardo Sanchez

3

, Haffer Henryk

1

, Maximilian Muellner

1

, Erika Chiapparelli

1

, Lisa Oezel

1

, Jennifer Shue

1

, Darren Lebl

1

, Frank Cammisa

1

, Federico Girardi

1

, Alexander Hughes

1

, Gbolabo Sokunbi

1

, and Andrew Sama

1

1

Spine Care Institute, Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United
States

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Showa University Hospital,
Shinagawa, Japan

3

Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, United States

Introduction: Ambulatory surgery (AMS) is becoming increasingly
common in the U.S. because it is associated with a similar or even higher
quality of care compared to inpatient surgery, significant cost reduction,
and patients’ desire to recuperate at home. However, there are instances
when AMS patients may be subjected to extended hospital stays. Unanticipated
extension of hospitalization stays can be a great burden not only to
patients, but to medical providers and insurance companies alike. Our study
aimed to investigate the factors associated with the conversion of patient
status from AMS to observation service (OS) (fewer than 48 hours) or
Inpatient (greater than 48 hours). Material and Methods: One
thousand and ninety-six patients underwent one- or two-level lumbar
decompression AMS at a single orthopedic specialized hospital between
January 1, 2019 to March 16, 2020 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients
were categorized in three groups based on length of stay: 1) AMS, 2) OS, or
3) Inpatient. Demographics, comorbidities, surgical information, and
administrative information such as operation start time were collected.
Simple and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted
comparing AMS patients and OS/Inpatient as well as OS and Inpatients.
Results: Of the 1,096 patients, 641 (58%) patients were
converted to either OS (n = 486; 44%) or Inpatient (n = 155; 14%) status.

DM, hypothyroidism, steroid use, dural tear, drain use, and laminectomy for
spinal stenosis. Conclusion: Several surgical factors along
with patient specific factors were significantly associated with AMS
conversion. Addressing modifiable surgical factors, such as blood loss,
surgery duration time, post-operative pain management, operation start time,
and drain use, might reduce the AMS conversion rate and be beneficial to
patients and facilities.

## P201: Management of osteoporotic vertebral fractures adjacent to

Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

1,2

, Hamdan Abdelrahman

1,2

, Drazen Prsa

1

, and Ali Ezzati

1

1

Spine Center, Helios Klinikum Erfurt, Erfurt, Germany

2

Department of Orthopaedics and Trauma, Assiut University Hospitals,
Assiut, Egypt

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures adjacent or
subjacent to degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosis or spondylolisthesis
represents a clinical challenge. Patients commonly present with combined
symptoms of low back pain as well as radicular or claudication pain. The
main options for treatment include conservative treatment, cement
augmentation (kyphoplasty/vertebroplasty), or cement augmentation and
decompression fusion surgery. Patients and Methods: Between
January 2018 and December 2021, ten patients with acute or subacute
osteoporotic vertebral fractures adjacent or subjacent to lumbar spinal
canal stenosis or degenerative spondylolisthesis were operated upon in our
center. Six patients were operated upon after failure of the conservative
treatment: two patients with kyphoplasty and decompression, four patients
with interbody fusion surgery and cement-augmentation of the screws.
Results: Of total ten patient, 4 women and 2 men were
operated upon. The mean age was 79.2 years. Two patients received
Kyphoplasty with decompression (mean operative time 75 minutes, mean blood

mean VAS of back pain improved from 7.2 ± 2 preoperatively to 2 ± 1.8, VAS

vertebral fractures adjacent to lumbar spinal canal stenosis. In cases with
spondylolisthesis, fusion surgery with cement augmentation of the screws is
recommended. Both achieved good clinical and radiographic outcomes.

## 583

## P202: Modified pedicle screw insertion technique at the lumbosacral
junction

Hamdan Abdelrahman

1

, Ali Ezzati

1

, and Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

1,2

1

Spine Center, Helios Klinikum Erfurt, Erfurt, Germany

2

Orthopaedics and Trauma, Assiut University Hospitals, Egypt

Introduction: Instrumented fusion of or extended to the
lumbosacral junction is a common surgical procedure indicated for different
pathological conditions affecting the lumbar and lumbo-sacral junction. A
high incidence of pseudoarthrosis and screw loosening is well described in
this junctional zone. Given the specific anatomical and biomechanical
characters of the L5 and S1 pedicles, optimal positioning of pedicle screws
is sometimes challenging due to the wide interpedicular distance and the
need to medialize the tip of the screw to get optimal projection of the S1
screw. We modified L5 and S1 screw insertion technique to get the optimal
trajectory and length of the screw aiming to reduce the incidence of screw
loosening. Materials and Methods: In patients indicated for
instrumented fusion including L5 and S1, a modified technique was used.
After standard posterior approach to the lumbosacral junction, the L5 or S1
entry points were identified. Excessive soft tissue dissection was avoided
though doing an extra postero-lateral 1.5 cm skin incision. The site of the
incision was usually about 5 cm from the midline and about 3 cm cranial to
S1. The paravertebral muscles were bluntly separated to allow for the
introduction of the awl and then the cannulated pedicle finder. The pedicle
was prepared, then the trocar of the pedicle finder was removed, and a guide
wire was inserted. 3D image intensifier scan was then conducted, and the
position of the wires was controlled. Once the wires position is accepted,
the screw was then inserted over the wire. Results: We operated
450 patients. In 350 cases instrumentation was extended to S1, most of the
cases were operated due to degenerative spine diseases. In all cases,
bi-cortical purchase was achieved. The mean screw diameter was 7 mm and the
length varied between 50 to 60 mm. There were no re-operations due to screw
malposition in these patients. Six Patients had wound healing problems; four
needed wound revisions. Conclusion: The modified pedicle screw
insertion through additional postero-latero-cranial skin incision achieved
optimal screw trajectory and longer screws aiming to reduce screw loosening
in area with high incidence of pseudoarthrosis. It avoids excessive soft
tissue dissection especially in muscular and fatty patients.

## P203: Randomized clinical trial evaluating 2 closure techniques in lumbar
spine surgery (SCAR - Spinal Closure Aesthetic Reconstruction Trial) - Pilot
study

Juan Del Castillo-Calcáneo

1,2

, Ezequel Rodriguez-Talavera

1

, and Guy Gilbert Broc - Haro

1,2

1

Neurosurgery, ISSSTE - Hospital Regional Adolfo Lopez Mateos, Mexico
City, Mexico

2

Neurosurgery, ABC Medical Center, Mexico City, Mexico

Introduction: Low back pain is the main cause of loss of years
due to disability throughout the world. The global rate of lumbar spine
surgery increased by 54% from 1999 to 2013, from 78 to 120 per 100,000
population. Various methods of closing surgical wounds in the lumbar spinal
region have been used finding that there is no increased incidence of
complications between them. Currently, there is no consensus on which method
of skin closure is the most appropriate for patients undergoing lumbar spine
surgery using the posterior approach. One of the main complaints of patients
in the postoperative period is the notoriety of the scar caused by this type
of surgery. In this study we made a comparison between two closure
techniques, evaluating the aesthetic result and the rate of complications in
each group. Material and Methods: In this pilot study, we
evaluated the aesthetic result between two types of skin closure for
posterior lumbar spine surgery (subcuticular suture (group 1) and simple
running suture (group 2)), randomly assigned, using the Patient and Observer
Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS) at 24 hours, 2 weeks, 1 month and 3 months.
Likewise, the rate of complications in each group was determined as well as
their general information. Results: A total of 10 patients
undergoing lumbar spine surgery by posterior approach were randomized (5 men
and 5 women), with an average age of 60.7 years (40-73 years). Of all the
cases, only one had a complication by the presence of seroma but did not
required additional intervention, this subject belonged to group 2. The
result on the POSAS scale at 24 hours was 120 in group 1 and 241 in group 2.
2 weeks: group 1 of 107 and group 2 of 244. At one month: group 1 of 107 and
group 2 of 188. At 3 months: group 1 of 90 and group 2 of 159. The average
time for closure with subcuticular technique it was 10.4 minutes and 8.8
minutes for the simple running suture group. The average time for removal of
the suture material was 10 seconds for group 1 and 72 seconds for group 2.
No subjects with cerebrospinal fluid leak were identified.
Conclusion: Our pilot study suggests that subcuticular
closure in posterior lumbar surgery, in addition to being accompanied by a
better aesthetic result, does not increase the rate of complications
compared to the simple running suture technique. The time for removal of
suture material is significantly shorter in the subcuticular closure
group.

## P204: A retrospective observational study to evaluate adjacent segmental
degenerative change with the dynesys-transition-optima instrumentation
system

Chiruei Li

1

, Hsi-Kai Tsou

2,3,4

, Shih-Hao Chen

5

, Chung-Yuh Tzeng

6

, and Wen-Hsien Chen

7

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Neurological Institute

2

Functional Neurosurgery Division, Neurological Institute

3

College of Medicine, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung City,
Taiwan

4

Nursing and Management, Department of Rehabilitation, Jen-Teh Junior

5

Department of Orthopaedics, Tzu Chi General Hospital at Dalin and
Tzu Chi University, Taiwan

6

Department of Orthopaedics

7

Department of Radiology, Taichung Veterans General Hospital,
Taiwan

Introduction: In clinical scenarios, adjacent segmental disease
(ASD) is problematic because further surgical management might be necessary
and adverse effects on functional outcomes might be encountered in those
patients who received lumbar spine operation. Hybrid dynamic stabilization
technique with Dynesys-Transition-Optima (DTO) seems to be a practicable
answer for ASD. The purpose of this retrospective observational study was to
evaluate the adjacent segmental degenerative change with instrumentation
method of DTO system. Material and Methods: One hundred and
fourteen lumbar spinal stenosis patients complicated with spondylolisthesis
that refractory to nonsurgical management were recruited. These patients
received dynamic stabilization with DTO system in a single medical center by
a single neurosurgeon between 2012 to 2020. Initially 33 patients were
excluded that received more than 1 segment fusion or additional

patients that received rigid fixations applied at the L4-5 segment only with
complete postoperative data. Finally, 32 patients were enrolled into our
study. Follow-up visit was planned after 6, 12, and 24 months
postoperatively. Radiologic assessment included disc height, listhesis

segments. In the assessment of motion angular change, only the L3-4 segment
revealed significant decrease between the preoperative and 2-year
postoperative data. Conclusion: Regarding our study, disc
height decreased and listhesis distance revealed the minor trend and later
ASD change in the index level compared to the L2-3 and L5-S1 levels. Less
angular change occurred at the index level while in motion is also noted in
our study. Although evidence in ASD prevention did not show significant
differences compared with other clinical studies, the minor and delayed
index level degeneration still showed optimistic results. As mentioned
above, this dynamic stabilization technique could be a promising surgical
strategy for delaying ASD.
Keywords: adjacent-segment disease, dynamic stabilization,
dynesys-transition-optima, lumbar spinal fusion, motion preservation,
degenerative disc disease, loading force sharing

## P205: Clinical outcomes of lumbar interbody fusion combined with cortical
bone trajectory screw fixation technique

Jong Tae Kim

1

1

Neurosurgery, The Catholic University of Korea, Incheon Saint Mary's
Hospital, Incheon, South Korea

Introduction: Cortical bone trajectory (CBT) pedicle screw
fixation is alternative new technique, and some biomechanical or anatomical
studies, which demonstrate the priority of pullout strength of CBT screws
comparing to the conventional pedicle screws, especially in osteoporotic
patients have been reported. And also several clinical reports have been
published recently in terms of the benefit as well as lessening of the
complications of the CBT screw method. We report, the clinical and
radiological results of the short level lumbar interbody fusion with CBT
pedicle screw insertion. Material and Methods: 21 patients (8
males and 13 females) with at least 6months follow-up were enrolled, who
were underwent single or two levels lumbar interbody fusion using PLIF or
TLIF using CBT screw fixation method in single hospital, between October
2014 and August, 2015. All CBT screws were inserted by one surgeon under
intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopic guidance. The medical records and pre- and
postoperative imaging studies were reviewed retrospectively. Mean age of the
patients was 63 (range: 49-81) and the mean follow-up period was 28.9 months
(range 7-69 months). The 9 cases (42.9%) were revisional surgery. All
patients was underwent interbody fusion, and the total number of interbody
fusion level was 21 (12 single level, 9 two levels). Interbody fusion
methods were PLIF, TLIF, or OLIF (16, 12 and 1, respectively). A total
number of 104 CBT screws were analyzed radiologically. Results:
Average T-score of BMD was -2.0 SD. Preoperatively mean VAS score was 7.5(SD
± 1.12), and postoperative mean VAS score was 2.8 (SD ± 0.93). Mean
operation time for the single level fusion and two level fusion was 209 (SD
± 45.5) and 267 (SD ± 35) minutes respectively, and the estimated blood loss
was 496ml (SD ± 150) and 722ml (SD ± 380). Postoperative CT was conducted
immediately after surgery, except for two patients among the 21 patients. In
the 96 screws analyzed, 14 screws (14.6%) were not inserted correctly, but
there was no case of the violation or compromise of the neural foramen. In
one patient, intraoperative dura injury was developed. Postoperative screw
loosening or halo was detected in the 3 patients (6 screws). In the
follow-up period, the posterior displacement of the interbody cage was
detected just 4 weeks after surgery, in a case of severe osteoporosis
patient (T-score -5.0). Nevertheless, in most of patients (17/21), favorable
surgical results were achieved. Conclusion: The CBT screw
fixation is a good alternative method, especially in the case of
osteoporosis, and this technique has several advantages that minimize
paraspinal muscle disruption and decrease operation time, as well as that
allows to avoid exposure or injury of the adjacent facet joint. However,
some limitations and possible disadvantages reside simultaneously.
Comparative or controlled study and larger numbers of patients with longer
durations of follow-up will be need for the universal use of the CBT screw
method.

## P206: Comparative evaluation of transforaminal lumbar endoscopic
discectomy versus open microdiscectomy for lumbar disc herniation: a
retrospective analysis of 885 cases

Nikolaos Gkantsinikoudis

1

, Christos Siopis

1

, and Stylianos Kapetanakis

1,2

1

Spine Department and Deformities, Interbalkan European Medical
Center, Thessaloniki, Greece

2

Department of Minimally Invasive and Endoscopic Spine Surgery,
Athens Medical Center, Athens, Greece

Introduction: Lumbar Disc Herniation (LDH) represents a
frequently encountered clinical entity and the leading etiology of low back
pain in young and middle-aged individuals in recent years, being unfavorably
associated with considerable morbidity and mortality. Open Microdiscectomy
(MD) represents the current gold standard for surgical management of LDH.
Transforaminal Lumbar Endoscopic Discectomy (TLED) constitutes a novel,
full-endoscopic, minimally invasive technique that is increasingly recruited
for surgical management of LDH in a worldwide basis in recent years.
Published data regarding comparison of these two techniques remain limited
in current literature. Hence, we hereby present our experience from
conduction of TLED versus MD for surgical treatment of patients with LDH.
Material and Methods: Eight-hundred and eighty-five (885)
patients with symptomatic LDH according to clinical and radiologic criteria
were retrospectively evaluated. All patients fulfilled established
indications for surgical treatment. Enrolled individuals underwent surgical
management either with TLED (TLED group) or with MD (MD group) from the same
experienced spine surgeon in two distinct tertiary centers in the period
2013-2019. Medical archives were searched for predetermined demographical
and clinical data as well as for assortment of values of standard primary
and secondary outcome measures. Primary outcome measures were operation
time, length of incision, timing of postoperative mobilization,
hospitalization duration and specific patient-reported outcome measures as
Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Short-Form
36 (SF-36) Medical Health Survey Questionnaire. Secondary outcome measures
were recorded complications and recurrence rates. Retrieved data were
derived from conducted evaluation on an outpatient basis at specific
intervals preoperatively and at 6 weeks, 3, 6, 12 months and at 2 and 5
years postoperatively. Results: All patients were subjected to
uneventful TLED or MD, exhibiting no major perioperative complications.
Demographical data were not significantly differentiated in the two groups.
Primary outcome measures analysis demonstrated that operation time, length
of incision as well as timing of postoperative mobilization and
hospitalization duration were statistically significantly ameliorated in
TLED group (p < 0.05). Furthermore, self-reported outcome measures (VAS,
ODI, SF-36) featured a statistically significant amelioration at each
follow-up intervals in comparison with preoperative values in both groups,
demonstrating albeit no statistically significant differentiation between
them at determined intervals. Moreover, incidence of recorded complications
and recurrences was not found to be significantly differentiated between the
two groups. Conclusion: In this retrospective analysis, TLED
was demonstrated to be non-inferior in terms of clinical efficacy in
comparison with conventional MD, alongside exhibiting relative superiority
in terms of operation time, length of incision and postoperative
mobilization-hospitalization time. Our results advocate that TLED should be
considered as a beneficial alternative for surgical management of LDH,
concerning, however, the relatively high and steep learning curve that may
crucially compromise favorable clinical outcomes, especially for beginner
spine surgeons.

## P207: Correction of spinal sagittal alignment after posterior lumbar
decompression: does severity of central canal stenosis matter?

Delano Trenchfield

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Nick D'Antonio

1

, Sydney Somers

1

, John Paulik

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, Chris Kepler

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Maintaining a balanced posture is essential in
patients with lumbar central canal stenosis and understanding sagittal
spinopelvic alignment is necessary to achieve that. A previous study has
shown that central canal stenosis severity is associated with greater
preoperative sagittal misalignment. However, no study has evaluated
postoperative differences. Our study aims to identify if there is a
difference in the degree of correction of spinal sagittal alignment between
severe and non-severe central canal stenosis. Materials and
Methods: Patients undergoing < 4 level posterior lumbar
decompression were retrospectively identified. Patients were excluded if
they had no preoperative MRI or if there was inadequate visualization of the
femoral head and lumbar spine on lateral x-ray. Patients were divided into
two cohorts based on the Lee MRI grading system: Grade 3 (severe) central
canal stenosis and Grades 0-2 (non-severe) central canal stenosis. Patient
demographics, surgical characteristics, clinical outcomes, and sagittal
measurements were collected and compared using independent t-tests,
Mann-Whitney U tests, and Pearson’s chi-square tests. A multivariable
logistic regression model accounting for age, sex, BMI, CCI, and
preoperative MRI Grade 3 stenosis was performed to measure their effects on
preoperative, postoperative, and delta pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS),
lumbar lordosis (LL), and pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis (PI-LL).
Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.
Results: Of 153 patients, 40 had severe stenosis, and 113
had non-severe stenosis. Patients with severe stenosis were older (67.0 ±
12.9 vs. 54.4 ± 13.7, p < 0.001) with higher CCIs (3.00 ± 1.50 vs. 1.42 ±
1.37, p < 0.001), operative times (123 ± 39.5 vs. 89.8 ± 32.2 minutes, p
< 0.001), lengths of stay (1.68 ± 1.54 vs. 0.64 ± 0.94 days, p <
0.001), and levels decompressed (2.40 ± 1.10 vs. 1.42 ± 0.76, p < 0.001).
There were no significant differences in 90-day readmission or revision
rates. Patients with severe stenosis demonstrated lower preoperative SS and
LL but higher PI-LL (p < 0.05). Postoperatively, SS and LL remained lower
in patients with severe stenosis (P < 0.05). Postoperative PT and PI-LL
trended towards being higher in severe stenosis but were not statistically
significant (p = 0.051 and p = 0.058, respectively). Both groups showed
improvement in sagittal balance postoperatively but there were no
significant differences in delta LL (1.40 o ± 7.15 o
vs 2.37 o ± 6.68 o, p = 0.44), SS (0.96 o ±
4.65 o vs 1.07 o ± 5.38 o, p = 0.91), PT
(-0.18 o ± 5.84 o vs 0.55 o ± 7.60
o, p = 0.583), or PI-LL (-1.40 o ± 7.15
o vs -2.37 o ± 6.68 o, p = 0.440)
between the groups. Multivariate logistic regression found no significant
predictors of delta LL, SS, PT, or PI-LL. However, severe stenosis was
predictive of a lower preoperative LL (estimate = -5.403, p = 0.031), and a
higher preoperative PI-LL (estimate = 6.853, p = 0.12), postoperative PT
(estimate = 3.751, p = 0.033), and postoperative PI-LL (estimate = 5.903, p
= 0.033). Conclusions: Severe stenosis was associated with
greater spinopelvic mismatch preoperatively. Sagittal balance improved in
patients with severe and non-severe central canal stenosis after posterior
lumbar decompression. However, the degree of correction is not statistically
different, and differences in sagittal parameters remain
postoperatively.

## P208: Association between preoperative lumbar fat infiltration and

Filipa Cordeiro

, Tiago Barbosa

, and Ricardo Rodrigues-Pinto

Unidade Vertebro-Medular (UVM), Porto, Portugal

Introduction: The lumbar musculature is a fundamental stabilizer
of the spine, and the relationship between chronic low back pain and
paraspinal muscle atrophy has been well established. In several studies, fat
infiltration has been associated with low back pain and lower limb pain.
Thus, the preoperative condition of the lumbar musculature may interfere
with the results of the surgical treatment. The aim of this study was to
assess whether there is an association between preoperative fat infiltration
and clinical outcomes after posterolateral lumbar fusion. Material and
Methods: All patients who underwent elective posterolateral
lumbar fusion between 2014 and 2019 were retrospectively evaluated. The
classification of fat infiltration was performed through the analysis of
preoperative Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and the correlation with the

persistence of low back pain and/or lower limb pain and Visual Analogue
Scale (VAS). Results: A total of 64 MRI were evaluated, most of
which (89.1%) belonged to patients undergoing surgery for spondylolisthesis.

higher levels of preoperative fat infiltration and worse ODI scores.

infiltration and clinical outcomes after posterolateral fusion. Further
studies are needed to validate a possible correlation.

## P209: Fatty infiltration of paraspinal muscle served as an independent

supra-adjacent paraspinal muscle was strongly associated with bone nonunion
and cage subsidence after single level anterolateral lumbar fusion surgery.
Patients with more than 35-40% FI of supra-adjacent PM may result in
nonunion and cage subsidence. Therefore, appropriate intraoperative endplate
preparation and close following-up the fusion outcome after surgery are
important.

## P211: Transpsoas versus ante-psoas technique in lateral approaches: pros
and cons

Alessandro Longo

1

, Federica Penner

1,2

, Mario Allevi

2

, Armando Massara

2

, and Alessandro Ducati

1

1

Spine Surgery Unit, Humanitas Cellini, Turin, Italy

2

Department of Neurosciences “Rita Levi Montalcini”, Neurosurgery
Unit, Neurosurgery, University of Turin, Turin, Italy

Introduction: The lateral transpsoas approach (LLIF) is the most
commonly used among the minimally invasive technique for degenerative spine
diseases and is supported by several recognized advantages over posterior
interbody fusion, such as lower post-operative pain, greater disk removal,
better footprint, good indirect foramen and central canal decompression and
lower adjacent segment disease rates. The oblique lumbar interbody fusion
(OLIF) technique is an ante-psoas approach which brings all the advantages
of an anterior approach and other benefits when compared to the transpsoas
technique, such as excellent visualisation of anterior longitudinal
ligament, avoiding muscular trauma and lumbar plexus injury risk, cost
reduction due to the possibility of not using a monitoring system for lumbar
plexus, no need to use jack knife position. Furthermore using the orthogonal
manoeuvre ante-psoas cage insertion can reach a favourable angle to correct
coronal imbalance and scoliosis. The increased vascular injury risk is the
main drawback of the OLIF technique. The aim of this study is to compare the
LLIF and OLIF techniques focusing on intraoperative challenges and
complications. Material and Methods: The authors performed a
retrospective review on 199 consecutive patients treated over a 4-year
period for lumbar degenerative disease and adult scoliosis. We implanted 59
cages through the OLIF approach. 38 patients underwent single level surgery,
14 patients underwent double level surgery and 7 patients also implanted
other cages through mixed approaches (such as TLIF). We also implanted 198
cages through the LLIF approach. 62 patients underwent single level surgery,
62 patients underwent double level surgery and 7 patients also implanted
other cages through mixed approaches. Results: Our experience
showed 19 (9,6 %) intraoperative complications during cage implants in the
LLIF group (such as subsidence, anterior longitudinal ligament rupturing and
anterior cage migration), while only 3 (5,1 %) intraoperative complications
during cage implants in the ante-posas group (one peritoneum rupturing, one
cage rotation, one cage subsidence). Conclusion: The ante-psoas
technique is a valuable alternative to the transpsoas approach. We
identified several advantages and some cons of using the ante-psoas approach
instead of the transpsoas technique, and different rates of intraoperative
complications. In our experience we observed that the two techniques could
be complementary and they should be performed according to the specific
patient anatomy and clinical needs.

## P212: The intersection of perioperative polypharmacy and surgical
outcomes after lumbar spinal fusion: a retrospective cohort study

Cathleen Kuo

1

, Mohamed Soliman

1,2

, Alexander Aguirre

1

, Marissa Kruk

1

, Joseph Iskander

1

, Hannon Levy

1

, Asham Khan

1

, Moleca Ghannam

1

, Patrick Jowdy

1

, John Pollina

1

, and Jeffrey Mullin

1

1

Neurosurgery, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, United States

2

Neurosurgery, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt

Introduction: Spine fusions are one of the most common
procedures in elderly patients. Among this group, these patients typically
also balance a multitude of other medical conditions that can require a
delicate management of medications. The objective of this study was to
identify the impact of an increased number of medications, polypharmacy, and
its impact to various postoperative outcomes. Material and
Methods: A retrospective review of patient charts was completed.
Data collection included the number of pharmaceutical drugs a patient was
actively taken, as self-reported by the patients. Polypharmacy was defined
according to previous literature as the patient taking five or more drugs at
a single time. Other data collection included patient demographics,
preoperative comorbidities, intraoperative outcomes, and postoperative
outcomes. Uni-variate analysis was utilized to identify potential
differences between groups. Results: A total of 713 patients
were identified. Among these patients 539 (75.6%) of patients utilized five
or more drugs at a single time. Preoperatively, the polypharmacy group had
significantly higher history of illicit drug abuse (p = 0.003), increased
American Association of Anesthesiologist (ASA) scores (p < 0.001),
increased Charlson Comorbidity index scores (p < 0.001) and were
significantly older (p = 0.01). In the operating room polypharmacy patients
required a larger number of fusion levels (p = 0.01), had greater estimated
blood loss (p < 0.001), and increased length of stay (p = 0.01). The
polypharmacy group also had significantly greater estimated blood loss (p
< 0.001) and longer hospital stay (p = 0.01). Conclusion:
Polypharmacy is an extremely common before and after spine fusions, which
leads to an increased rate of adverse perioperative outcomes.

## P213: Preoperative degrees of fat infiltration, intervertebral disc
degeneration and Modic changes do not influence the outcomes of lumbar
fusion

Filipa Cordeiro

1

, Tiago Barbosa

1

, João Seixas

1

, and Ricardo Rodrigues-Pinto

1

1

Orthopaedics Department, Spinal Unit, Centro Hospitalar
Universitário do Porto, Portugal

Introduction: The lumbar musculature is a fundamental stabilizer
of the spine. Several studies have associated fat infiltration, especially
of the multifidus and erector spinae, to
low back pain and radiculopathy. In addition, discogenic low back pain has
been described as the most common cause of chronic low back pain. Thus, the
preoperative condition of the lumbar spine may interfere with the results of
its surgical treatment. The aim of this study assess the influence of the
degrees of pre-operative fat infiltration, intervertebral disc degeneration
and MODIC changes on the clinical status of patients submitted to lumbar
fusion. Material and Methods: A retrospective study with
patients submitted to lumbar fusion between 2014 and 2019 was performed. The
preoperative degree of fat infiltration was measured and the degree of
intervertebral disc degeneration was analyzed using the Pfirmann and Modic
classifications, and then correlated with the postoperative clinical
results, using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Visual Analogue Scale
(VAS) and subjective improvement of low back pain and radicular pain.
Results: One hundred thirty-nine patients were included, of
which 64 were submitted to posterolateral fusion (PLF) and 75 to interbody
fusion (51 via transforaminal - TLIF - and 24 via posterior - PLIF). The
most frequent surgical indication was spondylolisthesis (77%). Patients
undergoing interbody fusion reported greater subjective improvement in low
back pain and radicular pain when compared to patients undergoing PLF (p
< 0.05), regardless of the degree of fat infiltration. No statistically
significant association was found between the type of surgery (interbody
fusion vs. PLF) with ODI (30.32 vs. 31.70), VAS for low back pain (5.4 vs.
4.2), for radicular pain (4.1 vs. 2.8), respectively. No relation was found
between previous disc status with ODI, VAS low back pain/radicular pain or
return to work. An association was found between patients with a greater
degree of fat infiltration and greater persistence of postoperative
radicular pain (p = 0.041). There was no association between the degree of
fat infiltration and other postoperative clinical parameters, such as ODI,
VAS low back pain/radicular pain or return to work. Conclusion:
Results in this study failed to identify an association between the degree
of intervertebral disc degeneration or fat infiltration and the
postoperative clinical outcomes of lumbar fusion, regardless of the surgical
technique utilized.

## P214: Comparison of unilateral versus bilateral instrumentation in

Dr Sajan Hegde

, Sharan Achar T

, Vigneshwara Badikkilaya

1

, and Umesh Kanade P

1

Orthopaedics, Apollo Hospitals Chennai India, Chennai,
India

Introduction: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) has
become gold standard technique for management degenerative lumbar disc
disease, traditionally performed with bilateral pedicle screw fixation.
Alternatively, Unilateral instrumented in TLIF has been reported to be
effective. This study compares the clinical and radiological outcomes in a
select series of patients treated with Unilateral versus Bilateral Pedicle
Screw instrumented TLIF (UPSF vs BPSF TLIF). Materials: Single
center, Single surgeon, retrospective study with minimum 2-year follow up.
Retrospective cohort study including 806 patients with 396 patients operated
with UPSF TLIF compared to 410 patients with BPSF TLIF with at least 2 years
follow-up. Demographic data, operative time, blood loss, hospital stay,
implant costs, complications were evaluated. Functional outcome assessed
using Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Short-Form health survey (SF-36) and

of patient-reported clinical outcomes, fusion rates, and complication rates
with the additional benefits of less operative time, less blood loss,
shorter hospitalization, and less cost in selective cases.

## P215: Comparison of total health operational cost for 1-stage vs 2-stage
anterior lumbar interbody fusion procedures

Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Som Singh

1

, Michael Olufawo

1

, Samuel Brehm

1

, Abby Carey-Ewend

1

, Karma Barot

1

, Ahmed Hanafy

1

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Matthew De la Paz

1

, Raj Lavadi

1

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, Julio Jauregui

2

, and Camilo Molina

1 2

1

Neurosurgery, Washington University, St. Louis, United
States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University, St. Louis, United
States

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusions (ALIF) are a
common operative procedure for the management of degenerative lumbar spinal
pathology. Anatomically, an ALIF techniques allows for midline workflow of
disc space and endplate preparation which can maximize surface area during
fusion-based restoration. Let alone, the widespread practice of ALIF has
increased compared to its posterior, transforaminal, lateral, and oblique
lumbar fusion cohorts. This has led to ALIF often being among the highest
Medicare reimbursement expenditures over the past 2 decades. As healthcare
utilization and expenditures continue to rise within spinal surgery, there
becomes more of an imperative need to evaluate lumbar interbody fusion
approaches for value-based care when determining approaches between levels.
The aim of this study is to describes the costs of operations between
1-level and 2-level ALIF surgeries being performed as 1-stage vs 2-stage
procedures. Material and Methods: This was a single
institutional retrospective cohort study of 212 patients who underwent
spinal fusion surgeries at Barnes Jewish Hospital in Saint Louis from
January 2021 to January 2022. Among this cohort, patients who underwent
1-level or 2-level ALIF were evaluated for medical billing costs incurred
during their individual operating room (OR) and hospital courses (HC). All
Hospital Costs (HC) incurred for 18 functional areas were obtained from
Hospital billing for each patient’s surgical admission. We performed
comparisons of ancillary costs (AC) and operating costs (OC) across the
1-level or 2-level ALIF procedures. We used tableau desktop and R Studio for
data visualization and statistical analyses. Cost distributions were
compared using the non-paired samples Wilcoxon rank sum test. Descriptive
statistical analysis was performed using tableau desktop and R studio for
both cohorts. Additionally, the distribution of costs were compared using
independent U tests. Statistical significance was established as p <
0.05. Results: A total of 16 1-level or 2-level ALIF surgeries
were identified in the database. 7 cases were 1-Stage and 9 were 2-Stage
surgeries. The mean OR time of 1-stage surgeries was 403 min (CI
365.59-440.69) and for 2-stage procedures was 530 min (CI 424.85-636.65).
The mean LOS of 1-stage surgeries was 2.86 days (CI 1.61-4.1) and for
2-stage procedures was 4.13 days (CI 2.75-5.5). Neither group developed
complications during the hospital course. In terms of total operational cost
(including ancillary, hospital stay and operating room cost), the median
cost was 50203.14 USD (SD 8012.21) for 1-stage surgeries and 60849.22 USD
(SD 11744.04) for 2-stage procedures. The differences in OR time, LOS and
total operational cost were not statistically significant.
Conclusion: This study establishes economic profile of
medical costs associated with 1-level and 2-level ALIF among patients with
degenerative disease. Based on the data distributions of the total
operational cost total, it seems 1-stage procedures are able to provide more
efficiency in terms of resource utilization for equitable patient outcomes
compared to 2-stage procedures. However, this study failed to showed a
statistically significant difference. Validation with a larger cohort of
patients will help to determine the most cost-effective ALIF approach.

## P216: Radiographic outcomes for bilateral versus unilateral cages in
TLIFs

Jeremy Heard

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Nicholas D'Antonio

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, John Bodnar

2

, Gregory Schneider

2

, Evan Bloom

2

, Parker Brush

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, The Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas
Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States

2

Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: While unilateral cage placement likely confers
less surgical risk to the patient than bilateral cage placement, there is
limited and conflicting literature regarding surgical outcomes when
comparing bilateral and unilateral cages. There is little published
literature comparing radiographic parameters following unilateral and
bilateral cage placement, which may allow us to understand whether one
technique is superior in its restoration of sagittal alignment, disc space
distraction, or endplate obliquity. There is no clear evidence to dictate
whether bilateral or unilateral cages promote superior radiographic or
surgical outcomes in posterior-based spinal fusions. Our study aims to (1)
compare radiographic outcomes between unilateral and bilateral cage
placement in transforaminal lumbar interbody fusions (TLIF) and to (2)
determine if the rate of fusion at the one-year postoperative point was
different between patients who received bilateral versus unilateral cages.
Methods: Patients > 18 years of
age who underwent primary one- or two-level TLIFs at our institution were
identified and propensity matched in a 3:1 fashion (unilateral compared to
bilateral). Patient demographics, surgical characteristics, and radiographic
outcomes including vertebral endplate obliquity, segmental lordosis,
subsidence, and fusion status were compared between groups. Multivariable
regression analysis was performed. Significance was set to p < 0.05.
Results: Of 184 patients included, 46 received bilateral
cages. Bilateral cage placement was associated with greater subsidence (1.06
± 1.25 vs. 0.59 ± 1.16 mm, p = 0.028) and enhanced restoration of segmental
lordosis (5.74o ± 14.1o vs. -1.57o ±
10.9o, p = 0.002) at the one-year postoperative point, while
unilateral cage placement was associated with an increased correction of
endplate obliquity (-2.02o ± 4.42o vs.
0.24o ± 2.81o, p < 0.001). Bilateral cage
placement was significantly associated with radiographic fusion on bivariate
analysis (89.1% vs. 70.3%, p = 0.018) and significantly predictive of
radiographic fusion on multivariable regression (1.35 [1.51 - 12.05], p =
0.010) analysis. Conclusions: In comparing unilateral and
bilateral TLIF procedures, TLIFs with bilateral cages resulted in greater
improvements in segmental lordosis and bony arthrodesis. Unilateral cages
were more likely to affect endplate obliquity. Given that this is one of the
few studies comparing radiographic between unilateral and bilateral cages in
patients undergoing TLIF procedures, additional high-quality prospective
studies are needed to verify the results of the present study and add
further context to whether the improvements in segmental lordosis and
endplate obliquity result in greater long-term clinical outcomes.

## P217: Titanium coated PEEK interbody fusion device performance for
treatment of degenerative spine conditions

Madilyn Riegel

1

, Jillian Mohn

1

, Matthew Gary

2

, Joseph Lee

, Safdar Khan

4

, Elizabeth Yu

4

, Benjamin Chen

5

, and Hallie Murray

1

1

Tyber Medical, LLC, Clinical Affairs, Bethlehem, United

2

Neurosurgery, Emory Spine Center, Atlanta, United States

3

Orthopedic Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopedics, Tarrytown, United

4

Orthopedic Spine Surgery, The Ohio State University, Columbus,
United States

5

Orthopedic Spine Surgery, MultiCare Institute of Research and
Innovation, Puyallup, United States

Introduction: Interbody fusion devices designed using an
integrated technology consisting of an organic thermoplastic polymer,
polyetheretherketone (PEEK), and a porous titanium coating (ProTi) are FDA
cleared and CE marked to treat patients with lumbar degenerative spine
conditions. These degenerative spine conditions include, but are not limited
to, degenerative disc disease, stenosis, and radiculopathy. The objective of
this research is to examine the clinical outcomes and time to fusion for
patients who have received the ProTi interbody fusion devices to evaluate
the device’s performance in treating these degenerative spine conditions.
Material and Methods: Approval from the Institutional
Review Board was obtained to gather clinical and radiographic outcomes on
patients treated retrospectively and prospectively for one-level lumbar
fusion with a ProTi interbody fusion device to correct degenerative disc
disease or other spinal deformities. The ProTi interbody fusion device is
designed with pyramidal teeth to resist expulsion in all directions, tracks
on the surface to lead and turn the spacer into position, and a
self-distracting bullet-nose to allow easy insertion. The subjects in this
study were evaluated by using patient reported outcome measurements
including the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and the Visual Analog Scale

an average score of 24.23 at 12-month follow-up (p = 0.053). These results
demonstrated the ability of ProTi devices to successfully alleviate pain
caused by a degenerative spine condition managed through spine fusion.
Conclusion: The preliminary analysis for this on-going
study was the most recent to evaluate the clinical outcomes and time to
fusion of one-level lumbar fusion using a ProTi interbody fusion device for
the treatment of degenerative disc disease and other degenerative spine
conditions. Study results demonstrated significant improvements in reported
pain that resulted from the degenerative spinal deformities patients
presented with prior to surgery and proved successful in obtaining solid
bony fusion in one-level lumbar spine fusion procedures. Additional research
will need to be done to fully evaluate the performance of ProTi interbody
fusion devices.

## P218: Evaluating 5-years outcomes of interlaminar devices as an adjunct
to decompression for symptomatic lumbar canal stenosis

Naresh Kumar

1

, Andrew Thomas

1

, Meetrra Seyher

1

, Kasia Chua

1

, Sean Lee

1

, Liang Shen

2

, and Laranya kumar

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Medical Statistics, National University of Singapore, Singapore,
Singapore

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis(LSS) is a common spine
condition encountered in clinical practice, having an increasing prevalence
especially with an ageing population. The SPORT trial established that
surgical treatment of spinal stenosis yields greater improvement in pain and
function. Currently, the gold standard of treatment of symptomatic LSS is
open decompression and fusion, but it has several drawbacks such as
increased soft tissue morbidity and adjacent segment degeneration. As such,
the interlaminar device (ILD) has been proposed as an alternative solution
that allows for a less invasive procedure with dynamic stabilisation, thus
reducing surgical morbidity. Current literature on the effectiveness of ILD
for patients with symptomatic LSS is limited to short term studies only. Our
study is the first to assess and compare 5-year outcomes following
non-instrumented spinal decompression with and without an ILD insertion to
determine if there was a statistically significant improvement in clinical
outcomes and radiological parameters. Materials and Methods: A
retrospective review of prospectively collected data under a single surgeon
cohort study, consisting of 116 patients who underwent spinal decompression
with and without an ILD insertion between 2007 - 2015 was performed.
Patients who met the study criteria were offered the choice of an ILD device
insertion. Those who accepted an ILD insertion were placed in the D+ILD
group (n = 61) and underwent an additional step involving the insertion of
an ILD (Coflex or Stenofix) at the involved level through the same surgical
incision; while those opting for decompression alone were placed in the DA
group (n = 55). All patients in both groups received the same postoperative
care. Clinical outcomes such as the Oswestry disability index, EuroQoL-5d
(Eq5d), VAS-back pain & VAS-leg pain, and SF-36 scores were measured
while radiological indices comprising of the anterior disc height, posterior
disc height and foraminal height were assessed both preoperatively and up to
5-years postoperatively. Results: Both arms of our study showed
statistically significant (p < 0.001) improvement in all clinical outcome
indicators measured at all time points as compared to their preoperative
state. However, the D+ILD group achieved and maintained significant
radiological correction in posterior disc (p < 0.01) and foraminal height
(p < 0.01) at all time points measured while the DA group did not attain
this. This is in concordance with existing literature that supports the
adjunct use of an ILD for its increased stability in extension and reduction
in intradiscal pressure which translates into better clinical outcome scores
for axial back pain and preservation of radiological parameters at varying
time points. There were no major complications in both groups.
Conclusion: The use of an ILD in conjunction with spinal
decompression in patients with symptomatic LSS has been shown to offer
positive clinical outcomes with reproducible correction in radiological
parameters as compared to decompression alone.

## P219: Predict the culprit segment in percutaneous transforaminal
endoscopic surgery (PTES) under local anesthesia for surgical treatment of
lumbar degenerative disease: radiologic images or patient's
symptoms?

YuTong Gu

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Zhongshan Hospital Fudan University, Shanghai,
China

Objective: Percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic surgery (PTES)
is a novel minimally invasive technique that has been used in the treatment
of lumbar degenerative diseases (LDDs). It is very important to predict the
culprit segment in surgical treatment of LDDs. Generally, we predict the
culprit segment according to lumbar degenerations and neurologic compression
on MRI and CT. Additionally different lumbar nerve root being compressed can
lead to the pain in special place of buttock and leg, and the culprit
segment can be predicted according to the position of leg pain. When
radiologic images are not in accordance with neurologic symptoms, how to
predict the culprit segment? PTES under local anesthesia was performed to
treat the culprit segment of LDDs predicted by radiologic images or clinical
symptoms, and the efficacy, security and feasibility were evaluated.
Methods: 87 cases of LDDs with nerve root symptoms, which
were not consistent with lumbar degenerative levels and degree on MRI and
CT, were treated with PTES under local anesthesia in day surgery ward from
Jan 2015 to Dec 2019. 42 patients, whose culprit segment was predicted by
radiologic images are included in group A. The other 45 patients, whose
culprit segment was predicted by clinical symptoms are included in group B.
Leg pain VAS and ODI before and after surgery are recorded. The outcome is
defined according to MacNab grade at 2-year follow-up. Postoperative
complications are recorded. Results: In group A, 2 patients
underwent PTES for 1 segment, 37 patients for 2 segments and 3 patients for
3 segments. One of 1-segment PTES had no relief of symptoms and underwent
another PTES for other culprit segment 3 months after surgery. In group B 44
of 45 patients were treated using PTES for 1 segment and 1 patient for 2
segments. Group B showed significantly less operative duration, less blood
loss and less fluoroscopy frequency than group A (p < 0.001). VAS score
of leg pain and ODI significantly dropped after operation in both groups (p
< 0.001). The leg pain VAS of group B was significantly lower than that
of group A immediately, 1 week, 1 month, 2 months and 3 months after surgery
(p < 0.001), but there was no statistical difference between two groups 6
months, 1 year, 2 years after surgery. Five patients (11.9%, 5/42) in group
A and one patient (2.2%, 1/45) in group B had rebound effect of leg pain.
VAS score of these patients rose 1 week after surgery and got relieved
within 2 months. The excellent and good rate was 97.6% (41/42) in group A
and 100% (45/45) in group B at 2-year follow-up. There was no statistical
difference in ODI and the excellent and good rate between two groups. No
complications such as wound infection, permanent nerve injury were observed.
Conclusion: It is much more accurate to predict the culprit
segment according to clinical symptoms than radiologic images in PTES under
local anesthesia for surgical treatment of LDDs, which can decrease
operative duration, blood loss, fluoroscopy frequency, and postoperative
rebound effect of leg pain.

## P220: Evaluating 5-year outcomes of between the use of Coflex compared to

Naresh Kumar

Objective: Literature on benefits of interlaminar devices (ILD)

parameters for quantifying patients with positive surgical outcomes have
been correlated. First, to assess and compare 5-year outcomes following the
use of the Coflex device compared to the Stenofix device as an adjunct to
spinal decompression. Second, to determine whether improvement in
radiological indices correlated with clinical outcomes.
Methods: We conducted a prospective single surgeon cohort

to 51.8 at 5 years postoperative respectively. For the VAS score, Coflex had
a greater improvement than Stenofix (p = 0.03) from 6.0 to 1.0 compared to
6.2 to 2.3 at 5 years postoperative respectively. There was no significant
difference in the remining clinical outcomes between the groups.
Conclusions: Interlaminar device insertion with spinal
decompression in symptomatic LSS with up to grade I spondylolisthesis offers
good clinical outcomes as compared to decompression alone with sustained
radiological correction. Our study highlights that in the treatment of
symptomatic LSS (with up to grade I spondylolisthesis), the use of the
Coflex device is superior to the Stenofix interlaminar device with greater
improvement in posterior disc height and clinical outcomes such as SF-36 MCS
and VAS overall.

## P221: Comparing TLIF vs PLF for patient reported outcomes, complications,
readmissions, and revisions

Anthony Steinle

1,4

, Raymond Gardocki

1

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,3

, Amir Abtahi

1,2,3

, and Byron Stephens

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Research

3

Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

4

Atrium Health Neurosciences Institute & Department of
Neurosurgery, Carolinas Medical Center, Charlotte, NC, United
States

Introduction: Elective lumbar fusion is commonly used to treat
various lumbar pathologies when conservative therapy fails. Two common
approaches for posterior lumbar fusions include transforaminal lumbar
interbody fusion (TLIF) and posterolateral fusion (PLF) alone without an
interbody. Whether TLIF or PLF leads to better patient-reported outcomes
(PROs) and reduced complications remains an area of active research. The
current study sought to compare TLIF vs PLF alone in regard to 1) patient
reported outcomes (PROs), and 2) rates of complications, readmissions, and
reoperations. Material and Methods: The Lumbar Module of the
Quality Outcomes Database (QOD), a national multi center prospective spine
registry, was queried between 04/2013-06/2019 for patients older than 18
years of age who underwent TLIF or PLF. Patients with previous lumbar
surgery and all minimally invasive, multi-stage, and revision cases were
excluded. Covariates included age, BMI, race, education, smoking status,
comorbidities, primary spine diagnosis, number of levels fused, ASA grade,
and baseline PROs. 12-month PROs included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI),
North American Spine Society (NASS) patient satisfaction index, numeric
rating scale (NRS) back and leg scores, and Euroqol 5-Dimension (EQ-5D).
Other outcomes included 30-day complications, 30-day reoperations, 3-month
readmissions, 12-month return to work (RTW), and 12-month return to
activities. For most outcomes of interest, multivariate regression analysis
was run controlling for covariates and the baseline measure of the outcome
when applicable. Unadjusted univariate analysis was performed to evaluate
12-month RTW, 3-month readmission, and 30-day reoperation outcomes due to
the low frequency of these outcomes in the PLF group. Results:
3,318 patients met inclusion criteria. 3,101 patients underwent TLIF while
217 patients underwent PLF. Patients with TLIF were more likely to have a
single level fused vs multiple levels fused when compared to patients who
underwent PLF (64.1% vs 51.2%, p = .001). No differences were found for the
other baseline covariates or any demographic variable. Unadjusted univariate
regression revealed no significant differences between the TLIF and PLF
groups for the following outcomes: 12-month RTW (p = 0.2113), readmissions
within 3 months (p = 0.4610), and reoperations within 30 days (0.8247). The
adjusted multivariate analysis demonstrated no significant differences
between TLIF and PLF groups for all 12-month outcomes including ODI, NRS
back pain, NRS leg pain, EQ-5D and NASS patient satisfaction. Additionally,
TLIF was not a significant predictor of 12-month return to activities (p =
0.0523) or 30-day complication rates (p = 0.8026). Conclusion:
In summary, there were no discernible differences in 12-month PROs, 30-day
complication or reoperation rates, or 3-month readmission rates in patients
undergoing TLIF vs. PLF alone in elective lumbar fusion. Though long-term
follow up is needed, these data add to the growing body of evidence that
interbody fusion does not offer superior benefit with respect to outcomes
following lumbar fusion for degenerative spine conditions. Given the
additional concerns with increased time of procedure and potential
complications raised by previous studies, surgeons should carefully select
which patients would potentially benefit from transforaminal lumbar
interbody fusion.

## P222: Observational prospective study of predictors of clinical and
neurological recovery in operated degenerative lumbosacral spine
disorders

Ankit Singh

1

 and Nishat Goda

Introduction: Majority of the elderly population deal with
nagging backache and claudication resulting in disability and poor quality
of life. Surgical intervention employed in patients not amenable to
conservative management not only decreases chronic pain but prevent dreaded
complication of instability and neurodeficits. Assessing the clinical and
neurological outcomes of operated patients enable us to dictate predictors
thereby improving patient selection and thus the outcome. Material and
Methods: Consecutive 30 patients with diagnosed degenerative
lumbosacral spine diseases not showing improvement to conservative treatment
for 6 weeks were subjected to surgical intervention. Clinical history,
demographics and examination findings with relevant radiographic parameters
were recorded. Clinical examination findings, VAS (Visual analogue scale)
score, Roland Morris disability questionnaire (RMDQ), Oswestry disability
index (ODI) and radiological findings were assessed at 3 months,6 months and
9 months’ follow up after surgery. Counselling regarding compliance was

classified then into successful v/s unsuccessful based on pain scale,

improving by 45.1% and 47.70% respectively. 81% were classified as
successful outcomes. Conclusion: With the increasing longevity
of the population, the incidence of degenerative spine disease is
increasing. Proper selection of patients subjected to surgery often show
improvement maximally after 12 weeks post surgery. Age < 60 years, lower
duration of symptoms less than 9 months and lower number of levels are
positively correlated with better results.
Keywords: clinical, degenerative, lumbo-sacral spine, neurological recovery,
predictors

## P223: Effect of timing of total joint replacement on elective lumbar
surgery outcomes

Anthony Steinle

1

, Alex Volkmar

1

, Hani Chanbour

2

, Eric Dilbone

1

, William Waddell

1

, Andrew Croft

1

, Wilson Vaughan

1

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,2

, Byron Stephens

1,2,3

, Ryan Martin

1

, and Amir Abtahi

1,2,3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Department of Neurological Surgery

3

Center for Musculoskeletal Research, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center,Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Concurrent hip/knee and spine pathology is common
in the elderly population, and many patients require both total joint
arthroplasty and lumbar spine surgery. It is unknown whether the timing of
total joint arthroplasty in relation to lumbar surgery affects lumbar
surgery outcomes. The aim of the current study was to determine whether
lumbar surgery outcomes differed between patients who underwent THA/TKA
before or after lumbar spine surgery. We hypothesized that patients who
undergo THA/TKA before lumbar spine surgery will have better lumbar spine
surgery outcomes due to improved hip/knee range of motion and reduced
hip/knee pain at the time of lumbar surgery. Material and
Methods: A retrospective cohort study was performed utilizing
data from a prospectively collected registry. The registry was queried for
patients who underwent THA/TKA and lumbar surgery within a 3-year timeframe.
THA/TKA revisions, lumbar disc herniations, lumbar revisions, and lumbar
deformity cases were excluded. Patients were dichotomized into: 1) THA/TKA
before lumbar surgery and 2) THA/TKA after lumbar surgery. Covariates
included age, gender, BMI, type of joint replacement (unilateral vs
bilateral), spine pathology, spine approach, number of operated spine
levels, length of hospital stay, and discharge disposition. Outcomes
included 1) 3- and 12-month numeric rating scale (NRS) back pain, NRS leg
pain, Oswestry Disability Index, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
scores and North American Spine Society patient satisfaction scores, 2)
Length of hospital stay and discharge disposition, and 3) 3-month rate of
complications, readmissions, and revisions. Three separate analyses were
performed: THA/TKA grouped together, THA alone, and TKA alone.
Results: Of 108 eligible patients, 52 underwent THA/TKA
before lumbar surgery, while 56 underwent THA/TKA after lumbar surgery.
There were no significant differences in any demographic or baseline
variable. Bivariate analysis showed no differences in spine surgery outcomes
between groups. Multivariate regression showed timing of THA/TKA in relation
to lumbar surgery was not associated with a change in any 3- or 12-month
PROs or complications. A sub-analysis consisting of only THA patients
included 34 patients, of which 17 underwent THA before lumbar surgery and 17
underwent THA after lumbar surgery. Bivariate analysis showed no differences
in any spine surgery outcome. Multivariate regression showed THA after spine
surgery was associated with higher/worse 12-month PHQ-9 scores (p <
0.001). A sub-analysis consisting of only TKA patients included 74 patients,
of which 35 underwent TKA before lumbar surgery and 39 underwent TKA after
lumbar surgery. The group that underwent TKA after lumbar surgery had higher
baseline NRS leg pain scores (p = 0.046). Bivariate analysis showed no
differences in any spine surgery outcome. Multivariate regression showed TKA
after lumbar surgery was associated with lower/better 12-month PHQ-9 scores
(p = 0.043). Conclusion: These results suggest that timing of
THA and TKA in relation to lumbar surgery was not associated with a change
in clinical outcomes following lumbar surgery with the exception of PHQ-9
scores in the individual THA and TKA sub-analyses. Thus, we recommended that
the severity of symptoms as well as patient preference dictate surgical
order for patients with concomitant hip/knee pathology and degenerative
lumbar spine disease.

## 1224

## P224: Predictive factors for discharge disposition after surgery for
degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis

Anna Filley

1

, Avionna Baldwin

1

, Khuzaima Rangwalla

1

, Faisal Bawahab

1

, Ashraf El Naga

1

, David Gendelberg

1

, and Sigurd Berven

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, United
States

Introduction: Early discharge planning is important for reducing
length of hospital stay, minimizing unnecessary utilization of inpatient
resources, and optimizing the cost-efficacy of surgical treatment.
Particularly for orthopaedic surgical patients, a period of rehabilitation
or additional assistance may be required in the immediate postoperative
period, making an accurate assessment of each patient’s functional needs
crucial for facilitating a safe, efficient discharge from the hospital. The
purpose of this paper is to identify medical and socioeconomic factors that
may impact discharge disposition. Material and Methods:
Retrospective study of 184 consecutive patients who underwent elective
surgical treatment of symptomatic degenerative spondylolisthesis at our
institution between January 2016 and June 2020. The primary outcome was
discharge disposition, either to home (with or without additional services)
or to a non-home location (acute rehab or skilled nursing facility).
Bivariate analysis was used to compare patient groups by preoperative
demographics, medical comorbidities, and surgical characteristics in order
to identify factors associated with discharge disposition.
Results: Eighty-eight patients (47.6%) were discharged to
home, 60 (32.4%) home with additional support services, 17 (9.2%) to acute
rehab, and 19 (10.3%) to a skilled nursing facility (SNF). Among all
patients, those who were not partnered (single, divorced, or widowed) had
greater odds of a non-home discharge (OR: 3.57, p = 0.001) than those who
were partnered (married or with significant other). Compared to patients
discharged home, those discharged to acute rehab were also more likely to
identify as black or multi-racial (OR: 4.88, p = 0.0049). Despite undergoing
similar procedures (operation type, surgical invasiveness index, procedure
duration, blood loss), patients with a non-home discharge had a
significantly longer length of hospitalization than those discharged home (p
< 0.0001). A non-home discharge was also associated with older patient
age, lower baseline functional status, and a greater number and severity of
comorbidities. Conclusion: Patient age, race, relationship
status, baseline functional capacity, and comorbidities are predictive of
discharge disposition following surgical treatment of degenerative lumbar
spondylolisthesis. Attention to these factors may assist with early
discharge planning and identification of patients who may need additional
assistance postoperatively.

Introduction: Lumbar fusion has shown to be an effective
surgical management option when indicated, improving patient outcomes and
functional status. However it produces abnormal mechanical conditions at
mobile segments above or below the site of spinal disorders and is
clinically referred to as adjacent segments disc disease (ASDD) or
transition syndrome in the case of a previous surgical treatment.
Methods and Designs: It’s a retrospective descriptive study
of 32 patients who had undergone decompression and instrumented lumbar
fusion of two or more vertebrae over 8 years. The parameters studied were -
after an initial arthrodesis - clinical signs including pain, use of

age, weight, extent of arthrodesis and its level and surgical technique.

about the incidence or risk factor to ASDD.

## P226: International validation of the SORG machine learning algorithm for
predicting prolonged opioid prescriptions in opioid-naive lumbar spine
surgery using 2,795 patients from Taiwan

Shin-Fu Chen

, Chih-Chi Su

, Yin-Tien Kao

, Hung-Kuan Yen

, Chih-Wei Chen

, Juin-Jen Yang

1

, Mao-Hsu Yen

1

, Jorrit-Jan Verlaan

2

, Joseph Schwab

3

, Tze Hong Wong

1

, Shu-Hua Yang

1

, and Ming-Hsiao Hu

1

1

National Taiwan University Hospital, Taiwan

2

University Medical Center Utrecht

3

Introduction: Identifying patients at risk of prolonged opioid
use after surgery could lead to appropriate prescription and more
personalized treatment plans. The Skeletal Oncology Research Group machine
learning algorithm (SORG-MLA) had been developed to predict the risk of
prolonged opioid use in opioid-naive patients after lumbar spine surgery.
However, its utility in a geographically and medicolegally distinct country
remains unknown. Therefore, we sought to externally validate the SORG-MLA in
a Taiwanese patient cohort undergoing lumbar spine surgery. Material
and Methods: This is a retrospective study at a large academic
medical center in Taiwan. Overall, 2,795 patients were included who were 20
years or older undergoing a primary procedure for lumbar decompression
surgery from 2010 to 2018. The outcome of interest was prolonged opioid
prescription defined as sustained prescription opioid use exceeding 90 days
after surgery Discrimination (area under received characteristic operating
curve [AUROC] and area under precision-recall curve [AUPRC]), calibration,
overall performance (Brier score), and decision curve analysis were used to
assess the performance of SORG-MLA in the validation cohort.
Results: Among 2,795 patients, the prolonged opioid
prescription rate was 5.2%. The validation cohort differed with the
developmental cohort on several variables, such as older age, more impatient
disposition, and more common pharmaceutical history of NSAIDs. Despite the
differences, the SORG-MLA provided a good discriminative ability (AUROC of
0.71 and AURPC of 0.36), a good overall performance (Brier score of 0.044
compared to that of 0.039 in the developmental cohort). However, the
probability of prolonged opioid prescription tended to be overestimated
(calibration intercept of -0.07 and calibration slope of 1.45. Decision
curve analysis suggested greater clinical net benefit in a wide range of
clinical scenarios. Conclusion: The SORG-MLA retains good
discriminative abilities and good overall performances despite being applied
in a medicolegally different region. It is validated for use in Taiwan to
predict high-risk patients preoperatively. Future studies should test this
model in real clinical practice by targeting high risk patients with
instrumentations.

1

Neurosurgery, Yonsei Okay Hospital, Gyeonggi do, South

Objective: Conventional fusion extension surgery has long been
considered the treatment option for symptomatic adjacent segmental disease
(ASD) after lumbar interbody fusion surgery. However, extensive muscle
dissection and revision of previous operation scar were problems of fusion
extension surgeries. If we used endoscopic assistant procedure of fusion
extension, extensive muscle dissection and skin incision may be reduced and,
it might be easier to achieve fusion extension which relieves the rigors of
open surgery. The purpose of our study is to introduce our technique of
endoscopic fusion extension surgery using biportal endoscopic systems with
video clips. Material and Method: From December 2019 to June
2020, 8 patients underwent fusion extension surgery for symptomatic ASD
using the new-designed biportal endoscopy assisted surgical technique. As
with primary endoscopic fusion surgery, this technique allows for the entire
operation, including the removal of old screws and rods, through small skin
incisions for percutaneous screws insertion. Old screws and rods were able
to be removed under endoscopic guidance through the small step wounds over
the pedicles. Interbody fusion procedures of ASD level were achieved by
usual biportal endoscopic fusion approach. Thus, there is no need to
periosteal dissection on the previously operated area with encountering
serious surgical adhesions. Postoperative Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
were taken routinely to measure the area of muscle damaged. Functional
outcomes were evaluated using Oswestry Disability Index score, and Visual
Analogue Scale, respectively. Results: We successfully
performed biportal endoscopy assistant fusion extension surgery in 8
patients. There were no complications related with surgery. VAS and ODI were
significantly improved after surgeries (p < 0.05). The mean operation
time and estimated blood loss per one level extension were 216.3mins
(185-250) and 163.8 cc (150-200). Conclusion: This procedure
may be a safe and efficacious treatment option for revisional lumbar fusion
extension with less morbidity than open surgery. Thus, this new-designed
endoscopic based technique could be a feasible alternative to conventional
fusion extension surgery, although more cases and long-term follow up
studies are needed to obtain accurate clinical results.

## 1488

## P230: Predictive factors of lumbar pseudarthrosis following primary
lumbar fusion

Hania Shahzad

1

, Moizzah Ahmad

2

, Nazihah Bhatti

1

, Elizabeth Yu

1

, Frank Phillips

3

, and Safdar Khan

1

1

Wexner Medical Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, United
States

2
The Ohio State University, Columbus, United
States

3

Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, United States

Introduction: A common iatrogenic complication of lumbar fusion
is pseudarthrosis which commonly presents with worsening back pain
necessitating surgical intervention. Results for such revision surgeries
have been relatively poor historically. Identifying demographic comorbid
characteristics that are predictive of developing pseudarthrosis can enable
physicians to optimize care for potentially high-risk patients. The
objective of this study is to identify predictors that may be associated
with a higher risk of developing pseudarthrosis in patients that undergo
lumbar fusion surgery for the management of degenerative spinal diseases.
Material and Methods: The PearlDiver database over 92
million MEDICARE and MEDICAID patients was utilized to identify patients who
underwent lumbar spinal fusion. Patients were further grouped into those
that had a claim for pseudarthrosis and those who did not within the 10-year
interval following the initial lumbar spinal fusion. The primary outcome was
the odds of selected demographic/comorbid factors in patients who were
grouped under the claim of pseudarthrosis within 10-years following lumbar
spinal fusion. Univariable model results were reported as odds ratios (OR)
and 95% confidence intervals (CI). All data were analyzed in aggregate form
using R Statistical Software version 4.1.0 in the PearlDiver Software.
Results: The results of the query revealed a total of
304,627 patients who had undergone spinal fusion in the period 2010 to 2021.
Out of the total patients, 11,401 (3.74%) received the diagnosis of
pseudarthrosis following their primary surgery while 293,226 (96.26%) had no
associated claim of pseudarthrosis following 10 years of their primary
lumbar fusion. The average time from the first procedure to the diagnosis of
pseudarthrosis was 2.5 years (SD 2.36). Chi-square analysis and univariable
regression modeling revealed the factors that were associated with patients
who developed pseudarthrosis. A significantly lower proportion of patients
who developed pseudarthrosis were 65 years or older (OR: 0.78 [0.75, 081],
p-value < 0.001). For all comorbid conditions, a significantly higher
proportion of patients who developed pseudarthrosis were male (OR:1.06
[1.02, 1.10], p-value < 0.001), had a CCI score of 2 or more (OR: 1.25
[1.20, 1.30], p-value < 0.001), a prior diagnosis of alcohol abuse (OR:
1.86 [1.72, 2.00], p-value < 0.001), tobacco use (OR: 1.85 [1.78, 1.93],
(p-value < 0.001), a positive history of opioid use (OR: 3.18 [2.77,
3.66], p-value < 0.001) a positive history of cannabinoid use disorder
(OR: 1.72 [1.46, 2.02], p-value < 0.001), a prior diagnostic claim of
osteoarthritis (OR: 1.58 [1.52, 1.64], p-value < 0.001), diabetes (OR:
1.24 [1.19, 1.30], p-value < 0.001), vitamin D deficiency (OR: 1.50
[1.43, 1.56], p-value < 0.001), and claims of a wound infection within 30
days of the primary surgery (OR: 1.45 [1.35, 1.56], p-value < 0.001).
These comorbidities were only included if their claims were made before the
primary lumbar fusion surgery on the patient record.
Conclusion: Pseudarthrosis is a common complication of
lumbar spine surgery. Our analysis outlines potential demographic and
co-morbid risk factors that are associated with the development of
pseudarthrosis. In these patients, physicians should optimize the modifiable
risk factors while counseling the patients for the potential development of
pseudarthrosis, especially in patients at higher risk.

the pelvis for adult deformities, open 1-to-2 level fusions, minimally
invasive 1-to-2 level fusions or open 3-to-5 level fusions for degenerative
conditions. Participants were then asked about the type of post-operative
dressing usually employed, timing of initial dressing removal and type of
subsequent dressing applied. Chi-squared test was performed to evaluate
statistical significance. Results: A total of 280 participants
from North America (18.21%), Latin America (14.29%), Europe & Southern
Africa (36.07%), Middle East & North Africa (8.21%), Asia Pacific
(23.21%) completed the survey. Most surgeons were male (94.64%), aged
between 35 and 44 (42.14%), and practicing for at least 5 years (84.29%).
Most respondents were orthopaedic surgeons (75%), practiced in and academic
hospital (46.43%), completed a spine surgery fellowship (64.29%) and
operated between 50 and 150 cases per year (48.21%). Following lumbar spine
surgery, 71.42% utilized a dry dressing, 24.60% a plastic occlusive
dressing, 5.55% applied glue, 5.95% used the DERMABOND™ PRINEO™ Skin Closure
System, 3.17% an incisional wound vacuum, and 4.19% other dressings. Initial
dressing was removed either on postoperative day 1 (11.63%), 2 (39.22%), 3
(20.25%), 4 (1.72%), 5 (4.31%), 6 (0.43%), 7 or later (12.5%), or depending
on drain removal (9.91%). Following initial dressing removal, 75.86% applied
a dry dressing, 17.67% a plastic occlusive dressing, 1.29% glue, while
12.06% used no dressing. No statistically significant differences were found
when comparing type of initial dressing, timing of dressing removal and type
of subsequent dressing with the type of surgery performed (i.e., length of
fusion, deformity vs. degenerative cases, open vs. minimally invasive).
Conclusion: Most spine surgeons utilized a dry or a plastic
occlusive dressing initially applied at the end of surgery. The first
dressing tended to be changed during the first 3 post-operative days and
replaced with the same type of dressing in the majority of cases. However,
no significant differences regarding the type of dressing and timing of
dressing change were reported taking into account the length of fusion or
the use of either an open or minimally invasive approach.

## P232: Clinical outcomes of percutaneous endoscopic lumbar annuloplasty
and nucleoplasty for discogenic low back pain: meta-analysis

Saran Pairuchvej

1

 and Jatupon Kongtharvonskul

1

Orthopedics Department, Queen Savang Vadhana Memorial Hospital,

2

Orthopedics Department, Faculty of Medicine Ramathibodi Hospital,

Objective: Percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy and
annuloplasty (PELDA) and nucleoplasty (PELAN) is a minimally invasive spinal
technique for relief back pain in lumbar disc herniation and chronic,
non-radicular, and discogenic low back pain (DLBP). The aim of the present
article is to present the outcomes of the systematic review and
meta-analysis regarding the short-term outcomes of this surgical technique.
Methods: We searched all prospective and retrospective

reviewers. A meta-analysis was applied to assess treatment outcomes.
Results: 13 cohort studies (N = 708 patients) met inclusion

Macnab’s criteria showed an excellent and good outcome, with a success rate
