herniation. The prevalence of complication including dura tear and nerve
root injury and reoperation of PELAN in Lumbar disc herniation were 0.116
(95%CI: 0.020 to 0.212) and 0 respectively while in chronic discogenic back
pain were 0.064 (95%CI: 0.022 to 0.106) and 0.045 (95%CI: 0.017 0.106)
respectively. Conclusions: Percutaneous endoscopic lumbar
discectomy and annuloplasty and nucleoplasty provides favorable outcomes for
carefully selected groups of patients with lumbar disc herniation and
chronic discogenic back pain.
Keywords: annuloplasty, nucleoplasty, PELD, Percutaneous endoscopic lumbar
discectomy, ODI, VAS

## 1694

## P233: The impact of diabetes on lumbar spinal stenosis

Peter Udby

1

, Søren Ohrt-Nissen

2

, and Thomas Vestergaard

1

1

Spine Surgery and Research, Zealand University Hospital, Køge,
Denmark

2

Spine Unit, Rigshospitalet, København Ø, Denmark

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a condition with a
severe impact on walking distance and exercise capacity. Reduced physical
activity due to LSS can increase the risk of obesity and diabetes. Diabetes
(DM), an autoimmune and lifestyle disease, has been associated with a less
successful outcome and increased risk of complications after spine surgery.
The question is what impact Diabetes has on spine degeneration and Patient
Reported Outcomes (PROs) before and after surgery in LSS patients?
Material and Methods: We performed a cohort study over a
nine-year period (2010-19) on patients undergoing lumbar decompression
surgery due to LSS. All patients were registered in the Danish National
spine registry (DaneSpine). Prospective data were collected preoperatively
and at two-year follow-up. Primary outcomes were the Oswestry Disability
Index (ODI), back- and leg pain scores on the visual analog scale (VAS), and
quality of life (QOL) measured by the European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions
(EQ-5D) index score. Results: A total of 362 patients were
included, 311 patients without Diabetes (-DM) and 51 with Diabetes (+DM).
The DM+ group had significantly worse disability scores and reduced QOL
compared to the -DM group preoperatively (p > 0.05). Both groups obtained
significant improvement in all primary outcomes at two-year follow-up (p
> 0.01). The improvement was similar for both groups (ΔODI and ΔEQ-5D, p
< 0.05). At two-year follow-up, the +DM still had significantly worse ODI
and EQ-5D-scores compared to the -DM group (p > 0.05). Pre- and
postoperatively back and leg pain scores including Δ-values were similar for
the two groups (p < 0.05). Conclusion: Patients suffering
from LSS and DM have significantly worse QOL and disability both
preoperatively and at two-year follow-up compared to patients without DM.
Both groups of patients experience a significant improvement in disability,
QOL, and pain scores at two-year follow-up. Physical exercise is important
in the management of DM. Therefore, we advise that additional focus is
directed at the identification and treatment of LSS patients with
concomitant DM.

## P234: Surgeon preferences in peri-operative drain utilization in open 1-
or 2- level fusion surgery for lumbar degenerative pathologies

Juan P. Cabrera

1

, Timothy S. Yoon

2

, Matthew Gary

3

, Ho-Joong Kim

4

, Jeffrey C. Wang

5

, Samuel Cho

6

, Zorica Buser

7

, Patrick Hsieh

8

, and AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative

9

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Hospital Clínico Regional de Concepción,
Concepción, Chile

2

Department of Orthopedics

3

Department of Neurosurgery, Emory University, Atlanta, United
States

4

Spine Center and Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Seoul National
University Bundang Hospital and Seoul National University College of
Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

5

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine,
University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

6

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount
Sinai, New York, United States

7

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, NYU Grossman School of Medicine,
New York, United States

8

Department of Neurological Surgery, Keck School of Medicine,
University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States

9

Research Department, AO Spine International, Davos,
Switzerland

Introduction: Avoiding wound-related complications
in open fusion surgery for degenerative lumbar conditions is critical to
patients and surgeons. The variation in peri-operative management can be
associated with differences in the incidence of such complications,
including post-operative drain use. Therefore, this study aims to analyze
the surgeon preferences related to drain utilization and the factors
influencing drain use and management. Material and Methods: A
survey was distributed to AO Spine members worldwide to elucidate the
variation in drain use and management around the globe. Surgeon demographics
and factors related to peri-operative drain use in 1 or 2-level open fusion
surgery for lumbar degenerative pathologies were collected. In addition, we
conducted a comparative analysis between surgeons that use peri-operative
drain (DG) and surgeons that do not use drains (ND) with univariate and
multivariate analysis using binary logistic regression.
Results: 231 surgeons responded to the survey, including
220 males (95.2%) and 11 females (4.8%) between the ages of 25 and 44. There
were 100 responses (43.3%) from Europe, 83 from (35.9%) Southern Africa, and
50 responses (21.6%) from the Asia Pacific. Most surgeons are orthopedics
(178, 77.1%), and almost half of the respondents are in
academic/university-affiliated practices (114, 49.4%). The survey revealed
that the overwhelming majority of surgeons worldwide utilize drains in their
surgery for degenerative lumbar conditions (186, 80.5%). In comparison, less
than 20% of surgeons do not use drains (45, 19.5%). In addition, almost all
surgeons prefer to place subfascial drains (178, 77.1%). Drain duration
after placement is variable, with drain removal on day 2 for 33.3% of
surgeons, while 29.4% of surgeons based their decision on drain duration
outputs. 15.6% of surgeons remove drains when output is < 50 mL per 24
hrs, while 10% remove drains when the output is between 50 to 100 mL in 24
hrs. On multivariable analysis, significant predictors of drain use were age
35 - 44 (OR = 11.9, 95% CI = 1.2-117.2, p = 0.034), age 45 – 54 (29.1,
3.1-269.6, p = 0.003), age 55 - 64 (8.9, 1.4-56.5, 0.019), and wound closure
using Steri-Strips (6.0, 1.2-29.0, p = 0.025). Conclusion: The
majority of spine surgeons worldwide prefer to place a post-operative drain
for open lumbar fusion surgery. Subfascial drain placement is preferred by
most, but drain duration after surgery varies widely based on surgeon
preference. Finally, the choice for peri-operative drain placement is
significantly associated with the surgeon's age and the use of Steri-strips
for wound closure.

## 1824

## P235: Cauda equina syndrome following decompression for spinal stenosis.
A very rare yet fearsome complication in a very common spinal
procedure

Mariano Vitelli

1

, Giovanni Barbagli

1

, Elisabetta Peppucci

1

, Nicoletta Gargiuoli

1

, Alexander Evins

2

, Alessandro DiChirico

1

, and Sandro Carletti

1

1

Neurosurgery, IFCA Firenze, Italy

2

Weill Cornell Medical College, Neurosurgery, New York, United
States

Introduction: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is one of the fearest
complication of lumbar disc herniation; however, a cauda equina syndrome
(with or without motor symptoms) is a very rare complication following a
spinal decompression procedure for spinal stenosis. When this complication
occurs surgical exploration remains the prevailing type of management. In
this study we describe a case of post-operative partial cauda equina
syndrome, without motor dysfunction, following decompression for spinal
stenosis. Material and Methods: We present a case of a 47 years
old man admitted at our institution for a Adjacent Segment Disease (ASD) at
L3-L4 following a L4-L5 posterior lumbar fixation (PLF) in another hospital.
Physical Examination (PE) at admission showed back pain with bilateral
radicular pain at lower legs. The patient underwent a L3-L4 decompression
with posterior screw fixation in order to connect this segment to the one
already fixed. The decompression was achieved under the guidance of the
operative microscope. The procedure has been reported uneventful and blood
loss was less than 100 mL. On the post-operative day 1 (POD) patient
developed a pinpoint anesthesia in the perineal area (encompassing the
entire scrotal area and the penile surface) without any sensitive or motor
deficits at the lower limbs. Patient underwent imaging studies (CT scan and
MRI) that showed no extrinsic compression or alteration to the neural
structures. Patient underwent intermittent catheterization and start to
recover spontaneously both the sensation and the urinary retention from the
POD 5. Authors carried out a complete literature review examining the
current data on PubMed and MEDLINE. Results: The literature
about this tricky situation lacks of sources; however, a cauda equina
syndrome following spinal decompression for spinal stenosis is somewhere
reported. The literature shows that the incidence ranges from 0.08-2%, and
the principal factors implicated are compressive lesions such as epidural
hematomas, fat pad grafts or gel foam. In rare cases there is no evidence of
extrinsic compression at imaging studies. In our belief, according with the
Parke's neuro-ischemic theory, it might depend on scarce blood supply below
the conus medullaris. Moreover, the chance to get a CES following a spinal
decompression could be related to the severity of the stenosis and
consequent edema at the decompression. We should also consider that, in our
case, the stenosis was not related to arthrosis yet was due to a ASD which,
as well known, is an even more stressful situation for the neural
structures. Conclusion: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) following a
spinal decompression for lumbar stenosis is a very rare yet frightful
complication. The vast majority of cases solve spontaneously in weeks but
not all patient completely recover from it. Further studies, as clinical
series or meta-analysis of current literature are needed to provide more
awareness of this serious complication.

## 1829

## P236: Anterior lombar interbody fusion (ALIF) surgery - the first seven
consecutive cases

Ricardo Sousa

1

, Pedro Batista

1

, Raquel Ricardo

1

, Bárbara Costa

1

, Filipe Castelo

1

, and Alfredo Carvalho

1

1

Orthopaedics, Centro Hospitalar Universitário Cova da Beira,
Covilhã, Portugal

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) surgery,
though introduced in the mid 20th century, has only been universally
accepted in recent years. This approach allows direct access to the anterior
spinal column through the abdomen, hence mitigating the potential for severe
neurological lesions. Injury to the iliac vessels and hypogastric plexus are
the primary concerns. The present study aims to describe the initial
experience and outcomes with ALIF surgery in a district hospital.
Material and Methods: By review of patients’ medical files,
questionnaires and direct examination, we analysed seven individuals with a
mean age of 50 years (range 42 to 63 years), 29% males and 71% females. All
seven patients presented L5-S1 degenerative disc disease, four of which
additionally suffered from instability. Therefore, all patients underwent
ALIF surgery with further posterior percutaneous screw fixation in those
cases of instability. All procedures were performed by the same surgical
team with both the abdominal approach and lumbar exposure beeing carried out
by general surgeons. The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
and Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) for both lower back
and radicular pain were applied. We also registered post-operative
complications and established a timeline between the patients’ first
symptoms, the surgery and the final interview. Additionally, patient’s
satisfaction levels regarding the treatment were surveyed.
Results: An overall positive response to the treatment was
clear. Apart from mild constipation felt in some cases, major surgical
complications were not reported and the postoperative period was uneventful.
After a minimum follow-up of six months, all seven patients were
experiencing either minimal or moderate disability (ODI) and only one had
more than mild pain (NPRS). At the final interview, all patients showed
elevated levels of satisfaction regarding the surgical outcome.
Conclusion: We conclude that ALIF surgery can be a safe,
well-tolerated, effective technique in carefully selected cases. Convincing
results were obtained even in the early stages of the learning curve. Thus,
it should be considered as a viable alternative to other conventional
approaches in the treatment of L5-S1 degenerative disc disease, particularly
if spondylolisthesis is present or previous posterior surgery was
performed.

## P237: Degree of fat degeneration of preoperative paraespinal muscles as
prognostic factors of clinical outcomes in post-operated patients with l4-l5

Saul Solorio Pineda

, Alejandro Reyes-Sánchez

1

1

Spine Surgery Department, Instituto Nacional de Rehabilitacion,
Mexico City, Mexico

Background: The multifidus muscle is the most important
stabilizer of the lumbar spine, spanning the lumbosacral junction and having
a prominent influence on sagittal alignment. Defects of the paraspinal
muscles cause degeneration of the intervertebral disc. Its size is reduced
in patients with chronic low back pain compared to healthy individuals.
Objectives: To evaluate the influence of the degree of
fatty degeneration of the preoperative paraspinal muscles on the clinical
results of lumbar spine surgery. Material and Methods: A
retrospective, observational and descriptive analysis of 53 patients aged 30
to 59 years with a diagnosis of lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis,
operated on fixation and posterior lumbar L4-L5 arthrodesis at the National
Institute of Rehabilitation "LGII" in a period of 5 years was carried out.
January 2015 to December 2020. An analysis of the epidemiological, clinical
and post-surgical variables of interest was performed. Preoperative
T2-weighted images (T2WI) axial fast spin-echo sequence spin-echo magnetic
resonance imaging examinations of the lumbar spine were reviewed, evaluating
the volume and degree of fatty degeneration of the paraspinal muscles at the
L4-L5 level by 2 Independent observers, these results were correlated with
the aforementioned variables as well as with the pre- and post-surgical
functional scales (VAS, ODI, Roland-Morris and SF36 physical/mental).

(36/53) belonged to female patients. The age at the time of surgery was

80 – Maximum 480); Bleeding in milliliters 437.92 ± 322.18 (Minimum 100 –
Maximum 1600). Correlations were made using the Pearson test, between the
degree of clinical improvement using scales (VAS, Oswestry, Roland-Morris
and SF36 physical/mental) and fatty degeneration. For this purpose, groups 1
and 2 were joined under the term "mild degeneration" and groups 3 and 4
under the term "severe degeneration". It was determined if the degree of
fatty degeneration influenced bleeding, surgical time, presence of
complications without finding any association between the variables. Just as
the rest of the correlations and associations did not show differences
between other factors, such as gender or the rest of the comorbidities, no
factor was associated with complications. Conclusion: With the
present study we determined that the fatty degeneration of the paraspinal
muscles does not influence the clinical results at one year of follow-up in
patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis L4-L5.
Keywords: Degenerative spondylolisthesis, fatty muscle degeneration, low back
pain

## P238: Intradural lumb disc herniation

Eya Chahed

1

, Sliti Firas

1

, Nessrine Nessib

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, and nadhir karmani

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunisia

Although lumbar disc herniation is very common, intra dural lumbar discal
hernia is one of its rare complications. Less than 100 cases have been
documented to this day. The frequency of intra dural lumbar discal hernia is
very low. The most common level is L4-L5. Research have proven that it is
mainly seen in men. Age is approximatively around 40-60. Symptoms vary
between acute cauda equine syndrome and simple radiculalgia. Sciatic pain
evolving for many years before the diagnosis is very usual. In 26% of cases
there is a spinal intervention during the weeks preceding the diagnosis. MRI
is the modality of choice for the diagnosis. It shows the intra dural hernia
and even some epidural bone fragments. Enhancement on Gadolinium injection
in T1 weighted sequences can indicate an arachnoiditis. We present the
description of two cases of two male patients who were operated at the
National Institute of Neurology in Tunisia. The first one is 42 years old,
who came for sciatica and urinary incontinence. The exam showed a
neurological L5 deficit. Lumbar CT scan showed a rounded intra canal lesion
in L5S1 suggesting a neuroma. MRI however proved that it was in fact an
excluded hernia at the level of L5-S1. The patient had a laminectomy of L5
and S1 and we discovered disc material on the posterior surface of the dura
mater. Post operatively, the patient recovered from his neurological
deficit. The second patient is a 36 year old male who presented for
lumbosciatalgia that has been evolving for 7 years and urinary impetuosity
evolving for 3 months. The exam objectified a L5 band hypoesthesia. Lumbar
MRI showed a mediane disc herniation in L3-L4 migrated upwards conflicting
with the 2 L4 roots and the contents of the dural sheath. He also had a
laminectomy of L3 and L4. During surgery, we discovered disc material on the
anterior surface of the dura mater. Postoperative course was uneventful. In
conclusion, intra dural lumb disc hernia is a rare pathology. In most cases,
it translates as an acute cauda equine syndrome or a lumbar radicular
syndrome. MRI is the modality of choice for the diagnosis. Prognosis in
uncertain.

showed 15% complication rate. Conclusion: Patients treated with

## P240: Mini open SA-ALIF with hyperlordotic cages in surgical treatment of

visual analogue scale (VAS) for back and leg pain and Oswestry Disability
Index (ODI) scores. Global fusion rate and main complications were
collected. Preoperative dynamic X-Ray, CT scan with venogram, bone density

single level surgery based on preoperative planning. This technique permits
to obtain an optimal LL distribution and a solid anterior column support,
with lower complications and higher fusion rates when compared to posterior
approaches. Using a hyperlordotic cages is a milestone for improving the
postoperative results.

## P241: Association between preoperative paraspinal muscle mass and
quality, and clinical outcomes after lumbar spinal fusion: an observational
cohort study

Esther Janssen

1,2

, Bart Bongers

3

 and Paul Willems

1

1

Orthopaedics, Maastricht UMC+, Maastricht, The Netherlands

2

VieCuri MC, Orthopaedics, Venlo, The Netherlands

3

School of Nutr and Transl Res in Metab, Maastricht University,
Maastricht, The Netherlands

Introduction: Patients suffering from a spinal disorder may show
a reduction of muscle mass (atrophy) and increased fat infiltration
(myosteatosis) in the paraspinal muscles on MRI. Studies have identified
that muscle atrophy and myosteatosis in the paraspinal muscles is predictive
of morbidity and mortality after major abdominal surgery. As lumbar spinal
fusion (LSF) is major surgery, atrophy and myosteatosis of the paraspinal
muscles may also be predictive of outcomes after LSF. If so, preoperative
MRI results can be used as a predictor to aid the surgeon in calculating a
patient’s expected outcome and risk for complications after surgery.
Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate whether muscle atrophy
and myosteatosis in paraspinal muscles, is associated with complications,
length of stay (LoS), functional recovery, and one-year postoperative
reduction in pain in patients undergoing elective LSF. Material and
Methods: Patients undergoing elective 1-3 level LSF because of a

retrospective cohort. Patients filled out the visual analogue scale (VAS)

between pre- and one-year postoperative VAS was used as a dependent
variable. Functional recovery was measured using the modified Iowa level of
assistance scale (mILAS). To measure muscle atrophy, the cross-sectional
area (CSA) was calculated. To determine myosteatosis, the functional
cross-sectional area (FCSA) was measured. The amount of fatty infiltration
(lean muscle ratio) was measured by calculating a ratio of FCSA divided by
CSA. Measurements were taken from the transversal coupes of L5 from the
preoperative MRI scan. To determine the association between muscle atrophy,
myosteatosis and lean muscle ratio, and surgical outcomes, a Pearson’s or
Spearman’s correlation was calculated. Results: 130 patients
were eligible, of which 12 were excluded as their MRI-scan showed
scattering. Eighteen patients (15,2%) had a complication of which 11 were
minor. Mean LoS was 7.02 days (SD ± 3.02) and the mean functional recovery
time was 5.33 days (SD ± 2.70). Analysis of the complications, LoS and
functional recovery time in relation to the CSA, FCSA, and lean muscle ratio
of the paraspinal muscles showed no correlation (r: -0.417 to 0.124). The
difference between one-year postoperative and baseline pain also showed
there was no correlation between any of the dependent variables with the
CSA, FCSA, or lean muscle ratio of the paraspinal muscles (r: -0.190 to
0.377). Conclusion: Muscle atrophy, myosteatosis, and lean
muscle ratio of the paraspinal muscles on preoperative MRI showed no
association with any of outcome after LSF. These parameters measured at a
single time point may therefore not be predictive of clinical outcome after
LSF. However, these parameters do not consider individual changes in muscle
over time. Moreover, we did not explore the association with physical
functioning. Therefore, a next step would be to study the relation between
paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration over time and functional
outcomes after LSF.

## P242: Role of pedicle screw augmentation in decreasing the reparations

Pablo Mendivil

1

1

Neurocirugía, Unidad de Cirugía Espinal Compleja y Minimamente
Invasiva - Neurocentro Salta - IMAC Instituto Medico de Alta
Complejidad, Salta, Argentina

Objective & Background: Posterior spinal arthrodesis is the
most commonly used spinal fusion procedure. The main middle and long-term
causes of reoperation are adjacent segment disease and screw loosening. The
objective of the present work is to determine the relevance of pedicle screw
loosening in the reoperation rate after lumbar interbody fusion, identify
risk factors and incidence, and assess the impact of pedicle screw
augmentation. Methods: We analyse retrospectively the data of
318 patients, mean age 54 years (± 9.6, range 18 to 84) who underwent

fusion. Revision because wound or deep infection was excluded. The main
reoperation causes were ASD (13 patients /3.73%) and screw loosening (24

essential when indicating surgery and informing the patient of its risks.

complication, as lumbar interbody fusion is increasingly common in
osteopenic or osteoporotic patients due to the aging of the population.
Pedicle screw augmentation decreases significantly the screw loosening and

## P243: Utilizing viseon camera for minimally invasive lumbar decompression
surgery in low and middle-income countries: a technique and feasibility
study

Costansia Bureta

1

, Francois Waterkeyn

2

, Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi

2

, Fabian Sommer

2

, Hamisi Shabani

1

, and Roger Härtl

2

1

Neurosurgery, Muhimbili Orthopedic and Neurosurgery Institute,
Bujumbura, Republic of Burundi

2
Neurological Surgery, New York Presbyterian
Hospital/Och Spine, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York United
States
Introduction: Minimally invasive spinal surgery (MISS) offers
better outcomes and quality of life than traditional methods. However, MISS
is yet to be adopted in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) owing to
limited knowledge and resources, such as a lack of access to endoscopes or
microscopes, which are cumbersome, expensive, and require specific
maintenance. Objective: We aim to describe our initial
experience utilizing the Viseon MaxView camera system for MISS at Muhimbili
Orthopedic Institute, highlighting this system's safety, feasibility, and
applicability. Methods: We report four cases of unilateral
laminectomy for bilateral decompression (ULBD) using the Viseon Max camera
system in a resource-constrained setting. The Viseon MaxView System is a
novel visualization system that utilizes a miniature, single-use camera
attached to a tubular retractor and projects 4K resolution images onto a
head-up display. Data on the surgery duration, blood loss, perioperative
complications, and technique mishaps were collected. Short-term clinical
outcome was assessed using the visual analog scale (VAS) and the Oswestry
disability index (ODI). Result: Four patients, two male, and
two females, with a mean age of 62 years, had severe radicular pain that was
worse on the left, and mild back pain. Additionally, two patients had severe
claudication, and another had a motor deficit. The duration of symptoms of
the patients was, on average, 49 months. Magnetic resonance imaging showed

and easy and did not require any assistance from the company. The image
quality was very sharp but could not offer 3D visualization. The average
duration of surgery was 146 min, with an average blood loss of 63 mls. All
patients were ambulant on the first-day post op with no post-op
complications. The average time from admission to surgery was four days.
Conclusion: Despite the lack of depth perception and a few
episodes of frozen images while using monopolar, the Viseon MaxView camera
system appears to be a feasible solution for MISS cases for patients in LMIC
countries, and could be used an alternative to the surgical microscope.

## P244: Risk factors for additional lumbar fusion surgery at the index
level after posterior decompression surgery for lumbar canal
stenosis

Tetsuryu Mitsuyama

1

 and Kaiji Ota

2

1

Neurosurgery

2

Orthopedic Surgery, Shinagawa Shishoukai Hospital, Tokyo,
Japan

Introduction: It has been reported that decompression plus
fusion surgery does not result in better clinical outcomes than
decompression surgery alone among patients with lumbar spinal stenosis.
However, some patients require additional lumbar fusion surgery due to
symptomatic foraminal stenosis after posterior decompression for lumbar
canal stenosis. The aim of this study is to investigate predictable factors
of additional fusion surgery after decompression surgery alone for lumbar
canal stenosis. Methods: Fifty-four consecutive patients
undergoing posterior central decompression for lumbar canal stenosis by a
single surgeon from 2016 to 2019 were retrospectively analyzed. Age, sex,
range of posterior decompression and preoperative radiological findings at
the decompressed levels were compared between patients with and without
additional lumbar fusion surgery at the index levels. Predictive risk
factors of additional fusion surgery after central decompression for lumbar
spinal stenosis were determined with multivariate logistic regression
analyses and Mann-Whitney U tests. Results: Seven patients
(13%) underwent additional lumbar interbody fusions for symptomatic
foraminal stenosis at the decompressed levels. Five of them (9%) had
additional fusion surgery within two years after initial decompression
surgery. Significant risk factors for additional fusion surgery were
intervertebral disc wedge angle over 5 degrees (OR = 9.11, 95% CI =
1.62-51.1, p < 0.012), posterior spondylolisthesis over 5 mm (OR = 6.3.
95% CI = 1.08-36.7, P = 0.041) and intradiscal vacuum phenomenon on X-ray
(OR = 5.63 95% CI = 1.07-29.7, P = 0.042). Range of posterior decompression
was significantly larger in patients with additional fusion surgery (mean
2.6 levels) than in patients without additional fusion surgery (mean 1.9
levels). On analyses of additional fusion surgery within two years,
significant risk factors were also intradiscal vacuum on X-ray (OR = 17.8.
95% CI = 1.77-17.9, p = 0.015), posterior spondylolisthesis (OR = 13.2. 95%
CI = 1.76-98.9, p = 0.012) and disc wedge (OR = 9.0. 95% CI = 1.27-63.9, p =
0.028). Discussion: This study demonstrated that 9% of patients
with posterior decompression surgery alone for lumbar canal stenosis
required additional lumbar fusion surgery for symptomatic foraminal stenosis
at the index levels within two years. Intradiscal vacuum phenomenon on
X-ray, posterior spondylolisthesis over 5 mm and intervertebral disc wedge
angle over 5 degrees were predictive risk factors for such additional lumbar
fusion surgery. Lumbar interbody fusion surgery may be indicated for
patients with all of above radiological findings.

## P245: Effects of social determinants of health on preoperative
presentation of patients who underwent operative management of degenerative
spondylolisthesis

Avionna Baldwin

1

, Anna Filley

1

, Khuzaima Rangwalla

1

, Ashraf El Naga

1

, David Gendelberg

1

, and Sigurd Berven

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, United
States

Introduction: Degenerative spondylolisthesis (DS), is one of the
most common causes of back pain and disability worldwide. Recent data has
supported the role of surgical intervention for improving outcomes in
symptomatic DS. As we study DS treatment efficacy, it is important to look
at populations’ access to surgical care. The purpose of this study was to
investigate the relationship between social determinants of health (SDoH)
and the clinical presentation of patients with operative DS in order to
better understand factors influencing patient access to surgical care.
Methods: Retrospective study of 184 consecutive patients
who underwent surgical treatment of symptomatic DS at UCSF, January 2016 and
June 2020. Primary outcomes were duration of baseline, worsening, and
severity symptoms at first consultation, time from referral to surgical
consultation and time from consultation to surgical procedure. Univariate
analysis was used to assess the influence of SDoH on these outcomes.
Results: Patients with estimated median income in the
lowest two quartiles had a significantly longer duration of baseline (112.4
vs 54.5 months, p = 0.00139) and worsening symptoms (17.4 vs 9 months, p =
0.0262) and waited longer for surgical consultation after initial referral
(52 v 35 days, p = 0.0143) than those in the top two quartiles. Patients
living > 50 miles from UCSF had a significantly longer duration of
baseline symptoms (104 vs 61 months p = 0.018) and waited longer for
surgical consultation after initial referral (53 vs 34 days, p = 0.0086).
Following surgical consultation, patients with public insurance waited
longer for procedures than those with private insurance (440 vs 251 days; p
= 0.046). Conclusion: Low income was a risk factor for worse
preoperative presentation. In order to ensure equitable access to
appropriate surgical care, SDoH must be considered as these are modifiable
risk factors to improve patient outcomes. By understanding factors that may
predispose patients to presenting in a worse clinical state prior to
surgery, we can not only increase access, but also improve surgical
outcomes.

## 73

## P246: The legal and socioeconomic considerations of spine telemedicine in
Canada

Jessica Jung

1

, Shawn Baldeo

2

, Markian Pahuta

3

, Sunjay Sharma

4

, and Daipayan Guha

4

1

Faculty of Health Sciences

2

Department of Psychiatry, University of Toronto, Canada

3

Department of Orthopedic Surgery

4

Department of Neurosurgery, McMaster University, Hamilton,
Canada

Introduction: While the COVID-19 crisis had accelerated the use
of telemedicine in Canadian healthcare, there remains significant
uncertainty as to its efficacy and future directions. There are inherent
challenges to telemedicine, including questions of clinical reliability and
privacy, balanced against the possibility of efficiency and increased access
to specialists. Here, we review the current landscape of telemedicine in
Canadian healthcare, with applications to spine surgery. Material and
Methods: This narrative review provides an overview of both the
pragmatic elements of conducting virtual assessments in spinal surgery,
along with a synthesis of its legal implications. This review was supported
by a search of the Lexis Advance Quicklaw database to evaluate the
prevalence of medical negligence lawsuits in Canada. Results:
The Canadian healthcare system poses significant challenges in the
evaluation and systemic implementation of telemedicine, given the lack of a
national legal framework and separate provincial or territorial regulation
systems across the country. Telemedicine is of a particular interest to
spinal surgeons, given the prevalence, morbidity, and economic costs
associated with spinal pathologies. Despite perceptions of increase
liability, to date, there have not been any malpractice suits specifically
related to the use of virtual care or telemedicine. Conclusion:
The role of telemedicine in Canada continues to evolve with the dynamic
aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. Its ability to expedite access to
medical care makes it a valuable resource, particularly given the health
disparities across geographically isolated regions in Canada. However, there
are significant challenges navigating the widespread upstart of
telemedicine, given the lack of a national legal framework and the inherent
difficulties of navigating individual provincial systems. Without a unifying
policy, there is uncertainty regarding best practice policies, along with
unclear legal implications of confidentiality and privacy, which may serve
as a barrier for clinicians to integrate telehealth into their practice.

## P247: Bone turnover markers in the preoperative assessment of bone
quality - A prospective investigation of bone microstructure and advanced
glycation endproducts in lumbar fusion patients

Henryk Haffer

1,2

, Maximilian Muellner

1

, Erika Chiapparelli

2

, Yusuke Dodo

2

, Jiaqi Zhu

2

, Yi Xin Han

3

, Eve Donnelly

3

, Jennifer Shue

2

, Andrew Sama

2

, Frank Cammisa

2

, Federico Girardi

2

, and Alexander Hughes

2

1

Center for Musculoskeletal Surgery, Charité - Universitätsmedizin
Berlin, Germany

2

Hospital for Special Surgery, Spine Care Institute

3

Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Cornell University,
New York, United States

Introduction: Effective tools to evaluate bone quality
preoperatively are scarce and the standard method to determine bone quality
requires an invasive biopsy. Therefore, a non-invasive, and preoperatively
available method for bone quality assessment would be of clinical value. We
hypothesized that bone turnover marker are associated to volumetric bone
mineral density (vBMD), posttranslational bone collagen modifications and
the bone microstructure. Therefore the study aimed to investigate the
associations of bone formation marker, serum bone alkaline phosphatase
(BAP), and bone resorption marker, urine collagen cross-linked N-telopeptide
(uNTX) to 1) vBMD, 2) fluorescent advanced glycation endproducts (fAGEs) and
3) bone microstructure. Material and Methods: A cross-secional
analysis using prospective data of patients undergoing lumbar spinal fusion
from from 2014 to 2021 was performed. The study was approved by the
institutional review board and informed consent was obtained from all
patients. BAP and uNTX were preoperatively collected. Quantitative computed
tomography (QCT) was performed at the lumbar spine (vBMD ≤ 120
mg/cm3 osteopenic/osteoporotic). Bone biopsies from the
posterior superior iliac spine were obtained and evaluated with multiphoton
fluorescence microscopy for fAGE crosslink density and microcomputed
tomography (μCT) for bone microarchitecture. Correlations between BAP/uNTX
to 1) vBMD, 2) fAGEs and 3) μCT parameters were assessed with Spearman’s ρ.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis evaluated BAP and uNTX as
predictors for osteopenia/osteoporosis. Multivariable linear regression
models with adjustments for age, sex, BMI, race and diabetes mellitus
determined associations between BAP/uNTX and fAGEs. Results:
127 prospectively enrolled patients (50.4% female, 62.5 years, BMI 28.7
kg/m2) were analyzed. uNTX (ρ = -0.331, p < 0.005) and BAP (ρ = -0.245, p
< 0.025) decreased with cortical fAGEs, and uNTX (ρ = -0.380, p <
0.001) decreased with trabecular fAGEs. BAP and uNTX revealed no significant
correlation with vBMD. ROC analysis for BAP and uNTX discriminated
osteopenia/osteoporosis with an AUC of 0.477 and 0.561, respectively. In the
multivariable analysis, uNTX decreased with increasing trabecular fAGEs
after adjusting for covariates (β = 0.923; p = 0.031).
Conclusion: This study demonstrated an inverse association
of bone turnover markers and fAGEs. Both uNTX and BAP could not predict
osteopenia/osteoporosis in the spine. uNTX reflects collagen characteristics
and might have a complementary role to vBMD, as a non-invasive tool for bone
quality assessment in spine surgery.

## P248: The Hoffmann parallax: a prospective study to determine the benefit
of Hoffmann's sign

Eric Gruenberger

1

, Sohrab Vatsia

1

, Rourke Stay

1

, Cameron Kersey

1

, Mudassar Khan

1

, and Douglas Pahl

1

1

Hughston Clinic, Columbus, GA, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most
common cause of age-related spinal dysfunction worldwide. Despite the
widespread use of provocative physical exam maneuvers in the workup of DCM,
the clinical significance of Hoffmann’s sign is controversial and its
diagnostic benefit in patients with cervical cord compression remains
unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to prospectively assess
the diagnostic performance of Hoffmann’s sign in a cohort of patients
treated by a single spine surgeon. Material and Methods:
Patients were divided into two groups in keeping with the presence of a
Hoffmann sign on physical examination. Advanced imaging studies were
independently reviewed by four raters for confirmation of a diagnosis of
cervical cord compression. Prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood,
and relative risk ratios for the Hoffmann sign were calculated, with
subsequent Chi-square and receiver operator characteristic (ROC) analysis to
further characterize correlative findings. Results: Fifty-two
patients were included in this study – of whom, thirty-four (58.6%) patients
presented with a Hoffmann sign, and eleven (21.1%) patients demonstrated
cord compression on imaging. The Hoffmann sign demonstrated a sensitivity of
20% and a specificity of 35.7% (LR = 0.32; 0.16-1.16). Chi-square analysis
revealed that imaging findings positive for cord compression were
proportionally greater for patients lacking a Hoffmann sign than those with
a confirmed Hoffmann sign (p = 0.032) ROC analysis demonstrated that a
negative Hoffmann sign performed moderately well in predicting cord
compression (AUC.721; p = 0.031). Conclusion: The Hoffmann sign
is an unreliable marker for cervical cord compression, and the lack of a
Hoffmann sign may be more predictive of cervical cord compression.

## P249: Reliability of manual intervetebral disc measurment

Philipp Schenk

1

, Nadya Guellil

2

, Ingmar Kaden

3

, Magnus Krieghoff

3

, Christian Hohaus

4

, and Hans-Jörg Meisel

5

1

Department of Science and Research

2

Department of Plastic and Hand Surgery, Burn Unit

3

Institute of Radiology and Neuroradiology

4

Department of Neurosurgery, Hospital Dessau, Dessau,
Germany

5

Department of Neurosurgery, BG Klinikum Bergmannstrost, Halle
(Saale), Germany

Introduction: Reliable methods to quantify disc degeneration are
mandatory for treatment evaluation of degenerated discs. Since MRI have been
used to diagnose vertebral diseases to objectify and quantify disc
degeneration. The aim of this study was to investigate the inter- and
intra-observer reliability (interRR, intraRR) of manual measures of disc
height and volume in healthy and degenerated lumbar intervertebral discs
(IVD) in MRI scans. In addition, the reliability of the
Pfirrmann-classification was investigated. Material and
Methods: T2w images of 60 Patients with mono-segmental lumbar
disc herniation at L4/5 (N = 10) or L5/S1 (N = 50) and healthy,
non-degenerated IVD at L3/4 were investigated in this study. IVD height were
measured using three manual methods: H1: disc height in the center of the
midsagittal layer. H2: mean of anterior and posterior disc height in
midsagittal layer. H3: mean of nine defined locations, three in the
midsagittal layer, three each in a defined left and a right layer,
respectively. IVD volume was calculated by multiplying the slice thickness
(4mm) with the sum of the measured disc areas in every sagittal layer. The
Pfirrmann-classification was determined for the degenerated IVD. Two
observers (observer1: surgeon, observer2: radiologist) carried out the
measurements. To calculate intraRR, observer1 performed the measurements two
times with an interval of 4 weeks. Intra -class-correlation coefficient
(ICC(3, 1)) was used for intraRR and interRR. The reliability of the
Pfirrmann classification was calculated using Kenadalls Tau. InterRR was
calculated two times, comparing the results of both measures from observer1
(1a and 1b) with the results of observer 2. SPSS v28 was used for
statistical analyses. Results: Data of 34 male and 26 female
patients with an age of 36 ± 10 years were analyzed. The highest intraRR for
IVD height measures was found for H3 with 0.822 for healthy and 0.910 for
degenerated IVD (healthy IVD: H1 0.815, H2 0.677; degenerated IVD: H1 0.874,
H2 0.842). For volume measures the intraRR was 0.887 and 0.913 for healthy
and degenerated, respectively. The interRR showed for the healthy IVD for H3
with 0.634 the highest and for H2 with 0.396 the lowest reliability. For the
degenerated IVD, again, H3 showed with 0.792 the highest and H2 with 0.630
the lowest interRR. The interRR of the volume measures of the healthy IVD
was 0.701 for observer1a and observer 2 and 0.728 for observer1b and
observer 2. For the degenerated IVD interRR was 0.860 and 0.791. Degenerated
IVD showed Pfirrmann-classification of Grade II (N = 16), Grade III (N =
17), Grade IV (N = 20) and Grade V (N = 7). The intra-observer reliability
(Kendalls Tau) was 0.628. The inter-observer reliability was 0.457 and
0.615. All reliability values showed a p < 0.01. Conclusion:
Overall, reliability showed values from moderate up to very height. The H3
method (9-points) showed the best reliability for IVD height measures. Using
2 Points (H2) for height measures showed the lowest reliability. The
reliability of the measures of healthy IVD was slightly lower, compared to
degenerated IVD. Studies, which address IVD height and volume, should report
the reliability of their measures.

## P250: New bone formation in ossification of the posterior longitudinal

Tran Canh Tung Nguyen

1

, Zhongyuan He

, Hiroto Makino

Introduction: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal
ligament (OPLL) is characterized by the ectopic bone formation that occurs
in the PLL due to hyperostotic changes. The pathogenesis of OPLL is
multifactorial and remained to be fully elucidated. Objectives of this study
are to clarify whether and how spinal inflammation or degeneration is
associated with the new bone formation in ossification of the posterior
longitudinal ligament (OPLL). Material and Methods: The whole
spinal computed tomography and serum high-sensitive C-reactive protein
(hs-CRP) levels were obtained in 162 patients with cervical OPLL. Patients

years) and hill-shaped groups (50 males and 28 females; mean age: 67.2
years). Sacroiliac (SI) joint changes were classified into four types and
three subtypes, as previously described. Interactions among ossification
shapes, hs-CRP levels, and morphological changes in the SI joint were
investigated. Results: The maximum ossified lesion thickness of
the Hill shape was larger and more common in the intervertebral regions

vertebral segments (59.5%). Serum hs-CRP levels in the plateau-shaped group

group (0.07 ± 0.08 mg/dL). SI joint intra-articular fusion was the main

levels compared to the anterior para-articular bridging, which more
frequently occurred in the hill-shaped group. Conclusion: OPLL
classification based on the two opposite morphological appearances may be
beneficial for understanding its underlying mechanism. Our findings indicate
that the plateau shape OPLL is similar to syndesmophyte in ankylosing
spondylitis, probably due to inflammatory pathogenesis, whereas the
hill-shaped ossification appears as a degenerative process.

## P252: Prospective clinical study of the diagnostic accuracy of

Bernhard Ullrich

, Mark Unthan

, Heinen Camilla

, Felix Kohler

2

4

Radiology, University Hospital, Friedrich Schiller University, Jena,

Introduction: The WHO defines fragility or insufficiency
fractures as injuries without adequate trauma due to reduced bone quality.
Demographic changes have resulted in an increase in pelvic ring
insufficiency fractures. These patients require special attention in
clinical care and should be considered differently than bone healthy
patients with pelvic ring fractures. When a pelvic ring insufficiency
fracture is suspected, for diagnostic purposes a native CT is employed.
However, the CT shows poorer sensitivity compared to MRI (CT: 77%, MRI:
96.3%) in the diagnosis of sacral fractures. SPECTRAL CT can visualize bone
marrow edema using different absorption spectra, similar to MRI. The study
aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of SPECTRAL CT compared to MRI in
the detection of fractures in the posterior pelvic ring. Material and
Methods: The monocentric, prospective cohort study included
patients presenting to the central emergency department with low back pain.
Patients with adequate trauma and patients younger than 55 years were
excluded. Each patient initially received a SPECTRAL CT (GE RevolutionCT,
GSI, rapid kilovolt switching), and promptly underwent a basin MRI during
the inpatient stay. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the
medical faculty of the University of Jena (2021-2124MV). The evaluation was

in musculoskeletal radiology using a standardized reporting form. Diagnostic

pelvis, which is the current gold standard. Results: To date,

shows high sensitivity (96%) and specificity (75%) in detecting pathology in
the posterior pelvic ring region. CT pelvis native shows significantly worse
sensitivity in comparison (sensitivity 70%, specificity 75%).
Conclusion: The data show a high diagnostic sensitivity of
SPECTRAL CT compared to CT pelvis. In everyday clinical practice, this
enables the correct diagnosis and classification already in primary
diagnostics, for example according to the osteoporotic fractures (OF) pelvis
or fragility fractures of the pelvis (FFP) classification. SPECTRAL CT could
thus represent a time- and resource-saving alternative diagnostic method to
the MRI.

## P253: Fracture-like lesions could potentially be a red herring for the

Greece

Introduction: Difficulties in the clinical diagnoses arise from
cases in which medical history, physical examination, imaging, and lab tests
are contradicting. Bone pain of traumatic etiology may sometimes aggravate
and consequently reveal a preexisting painless bone pathology while painful,
non-traumatic bone lesions may often present as fractures after radiographic
evaluation. Material and Methods: We present the case of a
16-year old female who was referred to our spine clinic due to persisting
and worsening neck pain that started about 6 months prior to her visit to
us. Initially, the patient presented to the emergency department (ED) as a
result of falling and landing on her head while bouncing on a trampoline.
The patient was observed for a couple of hours and was later discharged.
Since the patient had mild pain without neurological deficits, no
radiographs were ordered by the ED physician. However, the pain gradually
increased and, approximately two months after her initial injury, the
patient presented to her primary doctor for further evaluation. The primary
doctor ordered plain radiographs and referred the patient to our clinic with
the diagnosis of a pancake fracture of the C6 vertebra. The radiographs were
reviewed, but the appearance of the fracture in the context of the traumatic
circumstances raised concerns challenging the initial diagnosis.
Results: New radiographs were obtained and compared to the
previous ones. The lesion appeared worse with conspicuous erosion of the C6
endplates and loss of the vertebral height. We proceeded in ordering an MRI.
MRI revealed a lesion compatible with "Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis" and
not with a pancake fracture. The patient was immediately referred to
hematology/oncology which scheduled a bone biopsy. Bone biopsy confirmed the
MRI results. Subsequently, the patient started the indicated treatment with
excellent prognosis. Conclusion: Several times an accurate
diagnosis may be sacrificed in the altar of the "apparent or obvious."
However, a ruminative analysis of the medical history and how it relates to
diagnostic tests may unravel a camouflaged contradiction. In our case, we
speculated that a traumatic impact forceful enough to cause a pancake
fracture at one's C6 vertebra would have most likely caused more intense
pain as well as apparent neurological deficits thus prompting the ED
physician to order at least plane radiographs. Our prudent approach led to
an accurate and timely diagnosis of a sinister condition with excellent
prognosis.

## P254: Clinically significant radiologic parameter of thoracic

Hyunjun Jang

1

, Kyung Hyun Kim

1

, Jeong Yoon Park

1

, Keun Su Kim

1

, Yong-Eun Cho

1

, and Dong Kyu Chin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Spine and Spinal Cord Institute, Gangnam
Severance Hospital, Yonsei University College of Medicine, Seoul, Korea,
Rep. of South

Introduction: Thoracic ossification of the ligamentum flavum
(OLF) is one of the major cause of motor and sensory deficit of lower
extremity. Since it is hard to detect the disease unless taking MR images of
thoracic spine, it often takes time to get the final diagnosis. The purpose
of this study is to find the parameters that could be useful to screen
thoracic OLF on pre-operative lateral view X-ray. Material and
Methods: We investigated patients who underwent surgery for
thoracic OLF (n = 114) and those who had thoracic OLF but did not undergo

parameter. The optimal cut-off point was 0.42, 82% Sensitivity, and 83%
Specificity. Conclusion: A TOLF / FD of 42% or less is the best
way to diagnose clinically significant thoracic OLF on lateral X-ray. In
this case, the patient may have paralysis due to thoracic OLF, so further

## P255: Emergency decompression for spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma in
octogenarians: risk factors, clinical outcome and complications

Pavlina Lenga

1

, Guelec Gelo

1

, Karl L. Kiening

1

, Andreas W. Unterberg

1

, and Basem Ishak

1

1

Neurosurgery, Heidelberg University Hospital, Heidelberg,
Germany

Introduction: Spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma (SSEH) is a
rare but disabling disease with a high morbidity. Although several cases
have been reported in the literature, the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and
timing of treatment remain unclear, especially in patients with advanced
age. Owing to the lack of clinical evidence on this topic, we aimed to
describe the clinical outcomes of cervical SSEH in octogenarians with an
acute onset of neurological illness undergoing laminectomy, assess morbidity
and mortality rates, and determine potential risk factors for a
non-ambulatory outcome. Material and Methods: Electronic
medical records from a single institution between September 2005 and
December 2020 were retrieved. Data on patient demographics, neurological
conditions, functional status, degree of disability, surgical
characteristics, complications, hospital course, and 90-day mortality were
also collected. Results: Over a period of 15 years, 22 patients
aged ≥ 80 years with SSEH undergoing surgical decompression via laminectomy
were enrolled in this study. The mean age was 84.3 ± 3.1 years. The mean
Charlson comorbidity index was 9.1 ± 2.0, indicating a poor baseline
reserve. Cardiovascular diseases were the most prevalent comorbidity. Ten
individuals (45.5%) were taking anticoagulant agents and had a pathologic
partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 46.5 ± 3.4 s. Progressive neurological
decline, as defined by the motor score (MS) of the American Spinal Injury
Association impairment grading system, was observed on admission with a mean
score of 63.8 ± 14.0. The in-hospital and 90-day mortality were 4.5% and
9.1%, respectively. Notably, the MS (93.6 ± 8.3) improved significantly
after surgery (p < 0.05). Revision surgery was necessary in 5 cases due
to recurrent hematoma. Anticoagulant agents and pathological PTT are
significant risk factors for its occurrence. Motor weakness and
comorbidities were unique risk factors for loss of ambulation.
Conclusion: Decompressive laminectomy and evacuation of the
hematoma in octogenarians with progressive neurological decline showed
beneficial effects on the functional outcomes at discharge. Emergent surgery
seems to be the “state of the art” treatment for symptomatic SSEH even in
such a frail cohort. However, potential complications associated with
adverse prognostic factors, such as the use of anticoagulants, should be
clearly discussed with the patient and their relatives.

## P256: The role of neurophysiological monitoring during patient
positioning in cervical spine procedures

David Felzensztein

1

, Eilat Sapirstein

1

, and Eyal Itshayek

1

1

Neurosurgery, Rabin Medical Center, Holon, Israel

Introduction: IONM allows intraoperative assessment of spinal
cord function through real time feedback from sensory tracts, motor tracts,
and nerve roots. IONM assess the functional integrity of the spinal cord and
nerve roots, allowing early detection and reversal of neurological deficits.
The pattern of signal loss during monitoring is important - sudden signal
loss is associated with severe and irreversible injury, and gradual
degeneration is more likely to represent mild recoverable damage. Different
evidence exists regarding the sensitivity and specificity regarding the
detection of new neurological deficits and current studies show multimodal
ION (SSEP, MEP, and EMG) to provide a more accurate interpretation of the
information acquired. Positioning during cervical procedures is a
potentially damaging manoeuvre that may require an adequate
neurophysiological monitoring technique to prevent damage to the spinal
cord. IONM can be useful in detecting positioning-related brachial
plexopathy during cervical spine surgery and thus serves as a tool for
predicting neurological outcomes. Despite advancements in understanding IONM
and the popularity of this technique in modern spine surgery, controversies
still exist regarding its effectiveness and the necessity for its use in
routine spinal procedures. Material and Methods: We
retrospectively reviewed prospectively collected data from 2017 and
currently going. All patients who underwent cervical spine surgery with
neuromonitoring at Rabin medical center Beilinson hospital from 2017 till
current were included. Demographic data, medical history, findings at
neurological examination and imaging, electrophysiological data recorded
during surgery, and neurological outcomes were collected and analysed.
Results: Five hundred and one patients met the inclusion
criteria. Loss of potentials detected in twenty patients during patient
positioning and repositioning was performed with the aim of restoring
electrophysiological signals. In 15/20 patients, repositioning resulted in
immediate restoration of the baseline potentials. In 5/20, repositioning did
not immediately restore electrophysiological signals out of those 5, in ¼
potentials reappeared later during the decompression and in ¾ potentials had
not recovered till the conclusion of surgery. Conclusion:
According to the above data, we believe that multimodal IONM is a useful
method to prevent spinal cord injury during neck positioning in cervical
spine surgical procedures and can be used to reduce the risk of neurological
damage caused during patient positioning.

## P257: Validity of sedimentation sign of nerve root in the diagnosis of
lumbar canal stenosis

Zion Hwang

1

, Jason Bernard

2

, Timothy Bishop

2

, Jan Herzog

2

, Shahnawaz Haleem

2

, Tesfaladet Kurban

2

, Emily Tsang

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

, Bisola Ajayi

2

, Thamer Hamdan

2

, and Darren Lui

2

1

St. George's University of London, London, United Kingdom

2

Trauma and Orthopaedics, St. George's University Hospital, London,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Lumbar spine canal stenosis induces a series of
clinical features due to reduction of the lumbar spinal canal capacity which
leads to compression of the neural tissues. At present, the most promising
imaging test for diagnosis of this condition is magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI). These clinical features correlate poorly with the severity of
stenosis and the cross-sectional area of the dural sac in MRI examination.
Therefore, there is a real need to improve the ability to diagnose lumbar
canal stenosis by a special imaging findings. The sedimentation sign is a
new measurement tool that can enable physicians to objectively assess and
quantify spinal stenosis. The sign is most often present in patients who
have clinically significant lumbar stenosis and require surgery. This study
aims to evaluate the validity of the nerve root sedimentation sign in
diagnosing central lumbar canal spinal stenosis. Material and
Methods: This cross-sectional analytic study assessed the MRI of
711 patients complaining of lower back pain with or without sciatica between
1st of April 2019 and 1st of December 2020. The
patients were divided into three groups according to lumbosacral spine MRI
findings: Group I individuals with normal MRI, Group II with lumbar disc
prolapse and Group III with lumbar canal stenosis. We measured the spinal
canal and dural sac diameter at each level from first lumbar (L1) to fifth
lumbar (L5) vertebrae. We looked for the nerve root sedimentation sign above
and below these levels. Results: Positive nerve root
sedimentation sign was seen in 15.2% of normal MRI group, 50.42% of disc
prolapse group and in 86.4% of lumbar canal stenosis group. The sensitivity
and specificity of nerve root sedimentation sign for the diagnosis of lumbar
canal stenosis were 86.4% and 84.74% respectively. Conclusion:
The nerve root sedimentation sign is sensitive but not specific for
diagnosis of lumbar canal stenosis. It is unable to differentiate between
lumbar canal stenosis and other dural compressing diseases like
intervertebral disc herniation. Therefore, the authors suggest that it can
be used as an added tool to clinical examination for diagnosis of lumbar
canal stenosis and its severity but may not add specific diagnostic
information beyond the traditional clinical diagnostic standard.

## 1283

## P258: Awareness of degenerative cervical myelopathy in the primary care
setting in Portugal: results of a survey

Catarina Nogueira

1

, Carolina Luísa Lemos

1

, Oliver Mowforth

1

, Benjamin Davies

1

, and Ricardo Rodrigues-Pinto

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Centro Hospitalar Universitário do
Porto, Spinal Unit (UVM), Porto, Portugal

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most
common cause of spinal cord impairment. DCM is often misdiagnosed, and it is
not as discussed as other less debilitating diseases. As DCM might
significantly affect patients’ quality of life, there is an urgency to
detect this condition at its earliest stages. As primary care physicians
(PCPs) are often the first to assess these patients, it is imperative to
ensure a strong knowledge base of DCM amongst primary care physicians.
However, the existing literature suggests PCPs typically fail to diagnose
DCM. This study aimed to assess DCM knowledge amongst family physicians in
Portugal and to address potential factors perpetuating the present issues
regarding DCM awareness. As a secondary aim, this study intended to provide
information to family physicians that may aid them in diagnosing and
managing patients with DCM. Material and Methods: We created an
online questionnaire and shared it with registered general practitioners
(GPs), GP trainees, and physicians without a speciality that practise family
medicine. We advertised our survey via social media platforms and mailing
lists with the help of several medical institutions. An informed consent
explaining the study preceded the questionnaire. All responses were
voluntary and well-informed. All PCPs working in Portugal were considered
eligible for inclusion in this survey. At the end of the questionnaire,
respondents could leave their email if they were interested in participating
in a learning module regarding DCM. To objectively evaluate PCPs’ knowledge
of DCM, we attributed a score to some of the questions inquired. We surveyed
for almost three months. Statistical analysis of this study was conducted
using SPSS software. Results: We collected a total of 341
responses. Most participants scored Low in questions
regarding DCM presentation. The majority of PCPs disregarded lower-limb and
autonomic symptoms as possible DMC manifestations. Most participants checked
hyporeflexia as a typical sign of DCM; every other physical sign presented
in our questionnaire was much less chosen, although typically related to
DCM. PCPs recognise there is a lack of knowledge of DCM in primary care and
reported that it was mainly due to insufficient practising in DCM assessment
during speciality training. Having heard or had any teaching about DCM was
associated with Averagescores in questions related to
disease presentation. Regarding DCM management, conservative treatment was
always the first choice for almost 28% of the population. The main reason
for delaying the referral of a patient to specialist care is the long
waiting time for a specialist consultation. Conclusion: There
is a lack of awareness in primary care, and PCPs appear to mistake
myelopathy for radiculopathy. Our study reinforced the need to develop
diagnostic tools to facilitate DCM detection in primary care. PCPs
demonstrated interest in learning more about this condition.

## P259: Gait characterization for patients with cervical myelopathy using
three dimensional motion capture

Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, J.D. Peiffer

1

, Jie Fei

2

, Jennifer Lee

1

, Michele Santacatterina

3

, Ismael Seanez

2

, and Brenton Pennicooke

1

1

Neurosurgery

2

McKelvey School of Engineering, Washington University in St. Louis,
St. Louis, United States

3

Department of Population Health, New York University, New York,
United States

Introduction: Cervical myelopathy (CM) symptoms include
recognizable gait disturbances (with a wide, ataxic pattern) and balance
issues. Our current methods to assess functional status before and after
surgery rely on health-related quality of life metrics with poor sensitivity
and modest reliability. Kinematic analysis is an emerging tool in the
evaluation of movement dysfunction in neurologic populations. The purpose of
this study was to develop a gait analysis algorithm capable of
characterizing CM gait dysfunction compared to normal subjects using
objective measurements of motor function using a motion capture system.
Methods: A control subject without CM (male, height 1.75 m,
weight 76 kg) and a subject with CM underwent kinematic recordings before, 6
weeks and 3 months following a C5-C6 anterior discectomy and fusion (ACDF)
using a 10 camera motion capture system (Qualisys, Göteborg Sweden). Tasks
consisted of an 8-meter walking test completed at casual and fast speeds and
a tandem gait test. Each task was repeated three times. Kinematic metrics
including step length, step width, step height, joint flexion angles, and
normalized pelvic jerk were calculated from markerless pose estimation.
Results: Before surgery, the subject with CM had
significantly decreased step length (0.1 m/m) and increased step width
(0.015 m/m) when compared to control. In addition, the subject with CM had
increased normalized pelvic jerk while walking and during the tandem gait
task. Finally, the subject with CM had decreased joint flexion angles (12°
hip, 4° knee). The shorter and wider steps along with the decreased joint
angles could be a compensatory mechanism for gait disturbances caused by CM.
Further, the increased pelvic jerk indicates an unstable center of mass
during walking and while performing the tandem gait task. Following ACDF,
the subject’s pelvic jerk significantly decreased when compared to
preoperative data during both the walking and tandem gait tasks. This
indicates that their center of mass moved more smoothly over a step and
which indicates the efficacy of the spinal surgery to return y have returned
some balance. Step length and height increased as well, with the increase in
step height occurring at the 3-month timepoint indicating greater confidence
during walking. Conclusion: The subject with CM had significant
differences in kinematic metrics with the control subject before surgery.
Following surgery, these kinematic measures regressed towards the control
subject’s baseline values. These results establish kinematic measures
assessed via motion capture technology as a possible method to evaluate
neurological recovery and predict outcomes following spinal procedures.

## P260: Spinal adhesive arachnoiditis: an underestimated entity

Jorge Morales- del Angel

1

 and Armando Díaz

1

1

Hospital Angeles Valle Oriente, Cien, San Pedro Garza García,
Mexico

Introduction: The chronic adhesive spinal arachnoiditis is a
complex entity, with multiple radiologic findings. It was first recognized
in 1909 by Horsley. In the last 55 years around 1000 cases have been
reported. This number is dramatically underrated because of the lack of
recognition, or omission of the patient. It is of uttermost importance to
recognize the spinal adhesive arachnoidtis as a complex entity with many and
various symptoms that can cause severe neurological deficit. Material
and Methods: We present the case of a 61 year old female patient
with history of multiple falls treated with spinal injections and
physiotherapy, who underwent a craniotomy and fenestration for a left
temporal arachnoid cyst. She suffered from dorsalgia, cervicalgia, and
chronic lumbalgia. The patient also experienced a shoulder arthroscopy for
joint wear. Immediately after the procedure she complained of sudden left
arm weakness and thermoalgesic stimuli alteration with C6 hypoesthesia.
Because of these symptoms a cervical MRI was performed, showing
cervicodorsal syringomyelia. The lumbar MRI exposed radiologic features
compatible with spinal adhesive arachnoiditis, with an overt clumping and
syryngomyelia caused by a spinal cord tethering phenomenon because of the
multiple adhesions. Undergoing multiple spinal injections, as well as having
brain surgery are well known risk factor for adhesive arachnoiditis, which
may have caused subarachnoid hemorrhage at some level. Results:
We performed a L4 laminoplasty and adhesiolysis. Histopathological analysis
exposed a dense tissue associated with chronic and acute inflammation. The
patient had a great recovery with MRI imaging showing a decrease in the
syryngomielia. Conclusion: The spinal adhesive arachnoiditis is
an under diagnosed entity that causes neurological deficit that can be as
severe as cuadriparesis or tetraparesis. The importance of this case lies in
the acknowledge of this disease and to remind all spine surgeons that it is
of great importance to know how to recognize this entity.

## P261: An extremely rare case of vertebral artery dissection as the cause
of ventral spine epidural hematoma

Joana Tavares

1

, Tiago Lorga

2

, Inês Freire

2

, Cristina Branco

2

 and Ana Luís

1

1

Neurosurgery

2

Neuroradiology, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisboa,
Portugal

Introduction: Acute spinal epidural hematoma occurring in the
absence of any trauma or iatrogenic procedure is described as spontaneous
spine epidural hematoma (SSEH) and has an incidence of 0.1/100,000
inhabitants/year. The anterior location (ventral) of the hematoma is very
uncommon since the dural sac is firmly attached to the posterior
longitudinal ligament. Vertebral artery dissection (VAD) as cause of SSEH is
extremely rare with only two cases reported in the literature.
Material and Methods: We report the case of a patient with
a VAD complicated with SSEH. Results: A 31-year-old female
presented at the emergency room (ER) with a 2h history of sudden onset
cervicalgia while resting, initially radiating to her right arm but that
very quickly progressed to bilateral cervicobraquialgia and tetraparesis. In
her medical history stood out an apparently uneventful eutocic delivery with
epidural anesthesia 4 months earlier and the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2
infection at this ER admission. She denied any trauma, taking any medication
(including anticoagulants and antiplatelets) or prior neck pain. On
neurologic examination she presented neck stiffness, tetraparesis with
paraplegia and upper limbs severe paresis (grade 2/5 bellow C6), sensitive
level T2 e urinary retention. Neuro-axis CT showed a voluminous hyperdense
collection compatible with a spinal ventral epidural hematoma extending from
C2 to T10, with mass effect, especially between C5-T9. Angio-CT showed a
possible right VAD without other vascular malformations. She was submitted
to an emergent and uneventful C5-T9 laminectomy. Five days after the surgery
the patient was submitted to a digital subtraction angiography which
revealed a dissecting aneurysm of the right vertebral artery at V3 segment.
Given the previous hemorrhage the patient was proposed for endovascular
treatment with stents that took place one month after the event. The
procedure went without complications and the patient was discharged one week
later oriented to a rehabilitation center. At 3-month evaluation she
presented normal light touch and proprioceptive sensation, hypoesthesia for
thermic and pain sensation below T2, need for bladder emptying with clean
intermittent catheterisation when unsuccessful voiding attempt and
significantly improve in upper limbs muscle strength (4/5 at elbow extensors
bilaterally, 3/5 at grip and at finger extensors on the left side and 2/5 on
the right). In the lower limbs despite still not recovering useful strength,
she recovered to a grade 2/5 strength. Conclusion: VAD with
subsequent perivascular hemorrhage is one of the possible causes of SEEH,
especially, when ventrally located in the cervical and/or high thoracic
column. Hence the importance of a thorough investigation of the vertebral
arteries.

## P262: Spinal intradural arachnoid cyst: a case report

Sliti Firas

1

, Alaa Belhadj

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

, Nessrine Nessib

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Eya Chahed

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Spinal intradural arachnoid cyst is a benign
condition of uncertain pathophysiology. It is most often asymptomatic but
can cause serious neurological sequelae especially when treatment is not
initiated in time. We report the case of a 47 years old male patient treated
at the Neurosurgery Department of the National Institute of Neurology,
Tunisia. Material and Methods: We report here the case of a 47
year old man with no notable pathological history, who consulted for
continuous back pain with bilateral sciatica evolving for 3 months, the
evolution of which was marked by the onset of intermittent medullary
claudication severely reducing the walking range, as well as the onset of
urinary disorders. On clinical examination, we find a patient suffering from
pain, with a spastic paraparesis and a pyramidal syndrome, as well as a T12
sensory level. A spinal MRI revealed an elongated well-defined epidural
lesion extending from T9 to T11 with a high T2 signal and a low T1 signal
with no enhancement. The patient was operated on via posterior approach for
cyst resection with simple postoperative course. Neurological symptoms
gradually resolved. Results: Spinal intradural arachnoid cyst
is a rare cause of spinal cord compression. It can be seen at any age; its
pathogenesis is not clear and remains a subject of debate, it can be
congenital or acquired. The clinical presentation is that of a slow spinal
cord compression. Spinal MRI is therefore essential to confirm the diagnosis
of spinal intradural arachnoid cysts and to eliminate other differential
diagnoses. It is therefore the exam of choice to study the spinal content as
a whole, to characterize the cystic nature of the lesion and to better
assess the extent of the cystic and to better appreciate the spinal cord
implications. Once the diagnosis is made, surgery is the best way to restore
the normal flow of CSF by removing the compression exerted by the cyst on
the spinal cord. The prognosis is generally good. Conclusion:
Despite its high rarity, the spinal arachnoid cyst is one of the etiologies
of spinal cord compression syndrome to think about because its diagnosis
allows for a complete cure by radical surgical treatment.

## P263: Sarcoidosis inaugurated by vertebral lesion mimicking metastatic
disease

Mouadh Nefiss

1

, Mohamed yassine Belhedi

1

, ben aissa ali

, Mohamed Amine Gharbi

1

, Hedi Ezzine

, Ramzi Bouzidi

, Ezzaouia Khelil

Orthopeadic and Traumatology, Mongi Slim Hospital, Marsa,

Introduction: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease
characterized by the formation of granulomas without necrosis in various
organs, most frequently in the lungs and lymphatic system. Because of its
complexity and heterogeneous multisystem involvement, it is usually a
diagnosis of exclusion based on a range of evidence. Bone involvement is
rare (1-13%), and vertebral involvement is even rarer. Most often, this bone
lesion is either concomitant with pulmonary or lymphatic involvement or
occurs in a known patient with the disease. To our knowledge, isolated
vertebral involvement has not been described so far. We report the case of a
young Tunisian woman presenting with back pain in connection with spinal
lesions suggestive of metastatic disease. However, biopsies were consistent
with sarcoidosis. Clinical Presentation: This is a 43-year-old
Tunisian woman with no previous history of SARS-COV2 pneumonia who presented
with bilateral, poorly systematized lumbosciatic pain without neurological
signs. An MRI of the lumbar spine was requested and came back without
abnormalities. Thus the symptomatology was linked to Covid-19 and the
patient was put on symptomatic treatment. The evolution was marked by the
improvement of the lumbosciatic pain and the appearance of back pain
associated with mixed bilateral cervico-brachial neuralgia with poorly
systematized tilt without neurological signs. Moreover, the patient reported
asthenia and a weight loss of 10 kg in one year without night sweats,
evolving in a context of apyrexia. A cerebral-medullary MRI was performed

compression of the spinal cord opposite D4 and spinal cord replacement
lesions D1, D2 and D3. The metastatic origin was evoked in the first place,
from which a CT scan was requested, but no other lesion was found. This was
completed by a scannoguided biopsy of D4. Finally, the anatomopathological
examination showed epithelioid granulomatous and gigantocellular
inflammatory remodeling without caseous necrosis consistent with
sarcoidosis. The patient then received a Neofrakt brace and was referred to
internal medicine for specific medical treatment. Conclusion:
Sarcoidosis is a complex multi-systemic disease. Spinal involvement is
difficult to differentiate from metastatic lesions on MRI. Hence the
interest of biopsy and anatomopathological examination at the slightest
doubt.

## 68

## P264: Cervical intradural disc herniation: a systematic review

Qing Guan

1

1

Spine Surgery, The First People’s Hospital of Yibin, Yibin,
China

Background: Cervical intradural disc herniation (CIDH) is rare,
and diagnosis and treatment are challenging.We conducted a systematic review
and meta-analysis of the literature on the diagnosis and treatment of CIDH.
Method: The presentation, imaging manifestations,
diagnosis, management, prognosis and possible pathogenesis were reviewed
following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
guidelines. English-language studies and case reports published from
inception to recent were retrieved. Data on presentation, imaging
characteristics, diagnosis, management, outcomes and pathogenesis were
extracted. Results: Twenty articles involving 23 patients were
selected. The most common involved level was C5-6 (43.5%), followed by C6-7
(30.4%), C4-5 (13%), and C3-4 (13%). Spontaneous IDH occurred in 61% of the
patients, and relevant cervical trauma was present in 39%. Brown–Sequard’s
syndrome (56.5%), quadriparesis (34.8%), and radiculopathy (8.7%) were the
main presentations. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was the most commonly
used diagnostic technique, and the ‘‘halo” and ‘‘Y-sign” were strong
indicators of CIDH. Three (13%) patients were diagnosed as having CIDH
preoperatively, and 87% were confirmed intraoperatively. All patients
underwent surgical intervention primarily (73.9%) through an anterior
approach. Neurological function improved postoperatively in all patients but
one. Dural and arachnoid mater tears were managed by direct suture or
covering with a substitute, and only one patient sustained cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) leakage after surgery. Conclusion: IDH mostly
involves the lower cervical spine. More than half of the patients had
spontaneous CIDH, and some had a relevant cervical trauma history. BSS was
the main presentation. It is difficult to diagnose CIDH depending on
clinical presentations and radiographic findings. Surgery is an effective
treatment for CIDH and can provide a definitive diagnosis. With meticulous
management of dural and arachnoid tears, the postoperative incidence of CSF
leakage is found to be low.
