Introduction: Lumbar disc disease can prove a debilitating
injury. Typically, it is believed to be a multifactorial process inclusive
of aging, obesity and abnormal biomechanical loading patterns in the spine.
Nevertheless, traditional theories of pathophysiology may not hold true for
younger populations. That serves the premise for this study, to investigate
comparative risk factors for lumbar disc herniation (LDH) in pre- and
post-menopausal female cohorts. Materials and Methods: A
retrospective review was conducted at our institution, a national tertiary
referral centre, for female patients who underwent surgery for symptomatic
lumbar disc herniation between June 2016 and May 2020. Patients were
separated into two specific cohorts; (i) those aged < 45 years of age at
the time of injury, termed the pre-menopausal cohort and (ii) those aged ≥
45 years of age at the time of injury, termed the post-menopausal cohort.
Demographic, clinical and radiological characteristics were collected and
compared between groups. Results: 110 patients were identified
(43 pre-menopausal, 67 post-menopausal). On univariate analysis, the
pre-menopausal cohort had a significantly higher BMI (29.6 kg/m2
vs 27.1 kg/m2; p = 0.02), history of LDH (p = 0.02) history of
lumbar spine surgery (p = 0.02), greater degree of psoas fat infiltration (p
< 0.001), lumbar lordosis (p < 0.01) and proportion of distal lumbar
lordosis (p = 0.01). On multivariate analysis, only psoas fat infiltration
retained its significance (OR: 1.78, 95% CI 1.22:2.97, p < 0.01).
Conclusion: Our findings show that pre-menopausal patients
who presented with LDH were at risk of LDH due to a significantly greater
degree of psoas fat infiltration when compared to the post-menopausal group.
This may be related to a possible relationship between oestrogen, adipokines
and myokines. The authors encourage further robust studies in order to
elucidate this potential relationship.

## P266: Percutaneous laser disc decompression: a prospective study with

Marc Prod'homme

, Grasset Didier

, and Duccio Boscherini

Neuro Orthopedic Center, Clinic La Source, Lausanne,

Introduction: In case of a contained disc herniation (CDH),

microdiscectomy. Its percutaneous approach aims to decompress the bulging
disc when not yet an authenticated fragment excluded from the disc.
Computerized navigation with O-arm allows more accurate surgery with the
advantage of providing no irradiation to the surgeon. The aim of the study
is to assess O-arm PLDD in terms of clinical results and irradiation.
Material and Methods: A prospective inclusion of all
consecutive patients was performed when they presented with a lumbar CDH and
related sciatica without any neurological deficit, confirmed by magnetic
resonance imaging, showing a high intensity zone, and operated on by O-arm
PLDD. Demographic data, clinical scores such as numerical rating scale of
pain (NRS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) were recorded. Disc level of
the surgery, operative time and irradiation data were also collected.
Radiation exposure and its absolute risk of radiation-induced cancer (AR,
in%) were calculated using the dose length product (DLP) and the dose area
product (DAP) coming from the dosimetric report of the O-arm, and the
effective dose E was calculated according to the recommendations of the
International Commission on Radiological Protection. Complications were
collected. Results: 26 patients were included, with a follow-up
between 1 and 24 months. Mean age was 47 years. L4/5 and L5/S1 were the most
operated levels. Multi-level surgery was performed on 4 patients. Average
operative time was 32 minutes. NRS decreased from 7 to 4/10, p = 0.04. ODI
decreased from 51 to 20%, p < 0.01. Mean E was 4.03 mSv, with a related
AR of 2.1x10-4 %. No intraoperative complication occurred. One
patient presented with a contralateral recurrence after 10 days and another
with ipsilateral recurrence after 1 month and they were both scheduled for
microdiscectomy with good evolution. Conclusion: Clinical
results are encouraging. O arm PLDD was safe and effective and also
minimally invasive with an acceptable level of irradiation. This technique
plays a role in conditions where surgery is not mandatory and patients have
significant pain.

## P268: Predictive factors for disc degeneration at the levels above and
below instrumented posterior fusion in thoracolumbar junction
fractures

Mouldi Lamouchi

1

, Jlidi Mohamed

1

, Mohamed Hedi Gharbi

1

, Walid Bouaicha

1

, Ayachi Montassar

1

, and Selim Daas

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Hospital of Mohamed Taher
Maamouri, Nabeul, Tunisia

Introduction: Disc degeneration is a physiological aging
process. The disc above or below a spinal fixation appears to be exposed to
accelerated degeneration. The objective of our work is to determine the
predictive factors of adjacent segment degeneration after treatment of
thoracolumbar jonction fractures. The objective of our work is to determine
the predictive factors of adjacent segment disease (ASD) after treatment of
thoracolumbar junction fractures with posterior arthrodesis. Material
and Methods: We conducted a single-centre retrospective
descriptive and analytical study over a period of 10 years. The fractures
were classified according to the Magerl classification. The DSA was studied
before surgery and at the last follow-up according to the UCLA
classification. All fractures were operated on through a posterior approach.
Our patients were divided according to the number fixed vertebrae: a long
fixation (2 vertebrae above the fracture and 2 vertebrae below), a mixed
fixation (2 vertebrae above the fracture and one vertebra below) and a short
fixation (one vertebra above the fracture and one vertebra below).
Results: Our series included 120 patients with a mean age
of 48.39 years. The sex ratio was 1.6. The body mass index (BMI) was 28
kg/m2 with extremes of 20.7 kg/m2 and 38.21
kg/m2. The initial radiological control shows an average of
20.51° for the vertebral kyphosis, an average of 18.03° for traumatic
regional angulation of 18.03° and an average of 0.6 for the beck index. 57%
of the patients were grade 1 according to the UCLA classification. Type A3
according to the Magerl classification was the most frequent 54.2% of the
patients had a long fixation. 33 of our patients had a mixed fixation. The
short fixation was used with 22 patients. The average follow-up was 57
months. X-rays at the last follow-up showed an average of 13.49° for the
vertebral kyphosis, an average of 10.39° for the traumatic regional
angulation and an average of 0.77 for the beck index. 27% of our patients
were grade 3 or 4 according to the UCLA classification at the last
follow-up. The segment above the fractured vertebra is the most affected. In
a univariate study, the predictive factors for DSA were: BMI, age, female
gender, short fixation and Magerl type A3. In a multivariate study, the only
factor predicting osteoarthritic degeneration was age (p = 0.019). The
radiological parameters before and after surgery were not predictive
factors. Conclusion: ASD after treatment of thoracolumbar
junction fractures is commonly accepted despite some clinical discordance.
The frequency and main factors of ASD have been analyzed in various
biomechanical and clinical studies. The multifactorial nature of disc
degeneration is well established. The only predictive factor found in our
series was gender. BMI, type of fixation and type of fracture should be
taken into consideration in order to prevent adjacent segment disease during
thoracolumbar junction fixation.

## P269: Analysis of umbilical cord stem cell-derived microparticles effects

Julia Martins de Oliveira

1

, Lucas Seabra Fernandes

, Gustavo Ribeiro

1

, Mario Lenza

1

, Luciano Rodrigues

, Andrea Aparecida de Aro

2

, Rafael Maza Barbosa

, Alexandre Leite Rodrigues de Oliveira

2

, Eliane Antonioli

1

, and Pedro Pohl

1

1

Projeto Locomotor, Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, São Paulo,
Brazil

2

Universidade de Campinas, Campinas, Brazil

Introduction: Spinal diseases related to intervertebral disc
degeneration (IDD) represent a public health problem due to physical and
social limitation and economic losses. Researchers have demonstrated
benefits of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) over intervertebral disc cells.
Pathways of cell-cell communication were recently identified, including a
new way of cellular communication mediated by microparticles (MPs)
(microvesicles (MVs) or extracellular exosomes), that can be isolated from
conditioned media of cellular cultures. There are different sources of MSCs
and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) has got attention as a
potential cell source for regenerative medicine, as well as their MPs. Cell
free therapy is a hot topic in treatment of diseases and correlating to this
project can bring together the benefits that UC-MSCs products can provide
through their cellular microparticles. Methodology: Umbilical
cord samples will be collected for isolation of mesenchymal cells following
the protocol described. Human intervertebral disc cells will be obtained
from intervertebral disc waste material during elective spinal surgical
procedures, with the annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus being
anatomically separated, washed, fragmented and digested for 60 minutes at
37ºC in an enzyme solution with 0.2% pronase. The material will be subjected
to further digestion and incubated at 37° C in a humidified atmosphere of 5%
carbon dioxide and 20% oxygen and cultured in a monolayer until confluence
of 70-80%. MPs from UC-MSCs will be isolated from the culture medium of
UC-MSCs until the seventh passage. After 95% cell confluency, the cells will
be washed and incubated for 48h in a new medium. Confirmation of the

image, the criteria for MPS approval will be obtaining MPs with 0.1 to 1 µm,
validating the protocol, and reserved for use. The results will be evaluated
using flow cytometry to confirm and quantify the internalization of MPs
derived from UC-MSCs in intervertebral disc cells, AF and NP, using the
described technique. Controls will be performed with the supernatant and
culture medium without MPs. Gene expression analysis of key factors in the
production and maintenance of the extracellular matrix of intervertebral
disc cells exposed to UC-MSCs MPs will be performed in comparison to their
soluble products present in the supernatant and untreated controls. The
level of gene expression of extracellular matrix molecules by AF and NP
cells will be analyzed after 72h of treatment: collagen types I and II,
aggrecan and enzymes responsible for the degradation of the extracellular
matrix. Results: This is an ongoing project supported by AO
Spine Start-Up Grant. It is expected to present positive effects on IVD
cells when exposed to UC- MSCs MPs. We are analyzing the results, but they
are progressing well. We’ll have them by the Global Spine Congress.
Conclusion: We expect to find that UC-MSCs MPs will be
internalized by intervertebral disc cells, resulting in a change in their
gene and protein expression, stimulating the expression of aggrecan and
collagen and inhibiting the production of factors that favor the degradation
of the extracellular matrix.

## P270: Biportal endoscopic trans-laminar approach for the lateral recess
stenosis and scontra-lateral extraforaminal disc herniation: technical
report

Jisoo Ha

1

 and Do Hyung Kim

1

1

Neurosurgery, Yonsei Okay Hospital, Gyeonggi do, South
Korea

Objective: Biportal interlaminar approach for unilateral
laminotomy and bilateral decompression (ULBD) has long been considered the
first treatment option for symptomatic lumbar degenerative disease such as
central canal stenosis or foraminal disc extrusions and stenosis.
Interlaminar approaches. It is satisfactory for central canal stenosis.
However, limited to the contra lateral side lesion with
foraminal/extraforaminal stenosis or herniated disc. If we used
‘translaminar’ approaches. It is not difficult to perform full decompression
from the central canal to the contralateral extra foraminal area. The
purpose of our study is to introduce our technique of translaminar approach
for the lesions with contra-lateral recess stenosis and extraforaminal
stenosis at the same time. Techniques: The “trans-laminar”
approach targets lamina more directly than the “inter-laminar” approach,
which used generally in central canal decompression. It is the same
principle as the full endoscopic PSLD's keyhole laminotomy for discectomy
and the thoracic decompression technique by UBE. Since the translaminar
approaches make the portal more proximally than interlaminar approaches, the
initial point of the laminotomy would be more proximal than formar
decompression. When approaching the epidural space after sufficient bone
work, the working portal becomes parallel to the exiting root-disc level
compared to the interlaminar approach. This allows access to bony spurs,
hard disks, and even to the extraforaminal area around the exiting root.
Thus, you can achieved the contra-lateral side foraminotomy more easily.
Results: We successfully performed “translaminar approach”
for the patient who got central stenosis, traversing root compression due to
contra lateral recess stenosis and even extraforaminal stenosis. There were
no complications related with surgery. VAS and ODI were significantly
improved after surgeries. Conclusion: This procedure may be a
safe and efficacious treatment option for contralateral lesions or
multiple-sites stenosis. Thus, this new-designed endoscopic based technique
could be a feasible alternative to staged decompression surgeries for
multiple site stenosis. although more cases and long-term follow up studies
are needed to obtain accurate clinical results.

## P271: Pronostic factors for cauda equina syndrome

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Mahmoud Ben Messaoud

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Eya Chahed

1

, Nadhir Karmani

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare clinical entity
which is secondary to the compression of the cauda equina roots. It is a
diagnostic and therapeutic emergency, marked by motor, sensory and
genitourinary sequelae that may be irreversible, with a significant impact
on the patient's life and his social rehabilitation. We carried out this
study to analyze the epidemiological, clinical, para-clinical and
evolutionary characteristics and to study and identify the different
prognostic factors.
Materials and Methods: We performed a retrospective study of 54
cases of Cauda equina syndrome operated in emergency at the neurosurgery
department of the National Institute of Neurology of Tunis over a period of
10 years from 2010 to 2019. Results: The average age of our
patients was 45 years. The most represented age group was between 40 and 49
years (42.6%). Our series included 41 men (76%) and 13 women (24%). The time
course varied from one day to 6 months. Only 14.8% of the cases had a delay
of less than 48 hours. The onset was progressive in 74% of cases. The
functional signs were dominated by genital-sphincter disorders (100% of
cases). The other signs were low back pain in 79% of cases, radiculalgia in
90.7% of cases, paresthesia in 51% of cases and motor disorders in 87.1% of
cases. Perineal sensory disorders were observed in 37% of cases. Our series
included an incomplete form of cauda equina syndrome in 63% of the patients
and a complete form in 37% of the cases. Lumbar MRI, performed in all our
patients, was the examination of choice and allowed to confirm the diagnosis
and to orient the etiology. The etiological origin was dominated by lumbar
disc herniations, which were found in 87% of cases, followed by tumor causes
in 13% of cases. Urgent surgical decompression was performed in all
patients. The long-term evolution (2 years of follow-up) was stationary in
37% of the cases, favorable in 61.1% of the cases of which 33.3% had a
complete recovery, with only one case of aggravation (1.9%). Our analytical
study showed significantly a favorable evolution in the age group below 45
years. The incomplete form was significantly associated with a favorable
evolutionary prognosis. A duration of evolution lower than 48 hours is
associated with better prognosis. The presence of anaesthesia in the saddle
is a statistically significant factor of poor prognosis.
Conclusion: Cauda equina syndrome is a neurosurgical
emergency marked by severe motor and sphincter sequelae. Urgent surgical
decompression within 48 hours of the onset of signs and the incomplete form
are associated with a favorable evolution.

## P272: Mechanical characterization of flexible and reservable support
materials for tissue engineered intervertebral discs

Pravesh Gadjradj

1

, Branden Medary

1

, Alikhan Fidai

2

, Byumsu Kim

2

, Ibrahim Hussain

1

, Roger Härtl

3

, and Lawrence Bonassar

2

1
Neurosurgery, Weill Cornell Medical College,
New York, United States

2

Biomedical Engineering, Cornell University, New York, United
States

3
Department of Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell Medicine and
Och Spine, New York Presbyterian Hospital, New York,
United States
Introduction: An enduring challenge in implementing a tissue
engineered replacement for end stage intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration
is mechanically stabilizing the construct at early timepoints. Previously,
polylactic acid (PLA) cages were used to provide mechanical reinforcement
for tissue engineered intervertebral discs (TE-IVDs) in a pilot minipig
study. While these materials have properties that should far exceed those
needed to support loads in the spine, stress concentrations arising from
vertebral anatomy led to failure of these implants in vivo.
Identifying materials with sufficient flexibility is key to the successful
implementation of a support cage for TE-IVDs. FlexiFil (FormFutura) is an
elastomeric 3D printer filament that is amenable to the fabrication of
support cages, but little is known on how the mechanical performance of
FlexiFil printed cages compares to PLA. Therefore, the objective of this
study was to compare the mechanical performance of printed PLA and FlexiFil
cages and assess microscale damage as revealed by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM). Methods: To assess how TE-IVD cage materials
behave under loading, force-displacement testing was performed on PLA and
FlexiFil cages. Specifically, 3 PLA and 3 FlexiFil cages with a height of
2.5 mm were printed using a Prusa i3 MK3S+. To simulate compressive forces
arising from differences in vertebral anatomy, a flat ended indenter with a
triangular cross-section was used to load samples through the mid-plane.
Printed cages were mounted and subjected to 2 mm of indentation at a rate of
0.1 mm/s. After loading, samples were sputter coated with Au-PD and imaged
using a Tescan Mira SEM. Results: Force-displacement testing
revealed that at 2 mm of indentation, PLA cages were significantly stiffer
than FlexiFil cages (p = 0.0007) with average loads of 79.6 ± 8.9 N and 30.4
± 1.3 N, respectively. Notably, plastic deformation occurred at much lower
displacements for PLA (0.98 mm) compared to FlexiFil (1.75 mm). Consistent
with mechanical testing, SEM imaging of indented cages revealed that the PLA
samples had a wide footprint of plastic deformation, extending > 2 mm
from the indentation site. Plastic deformation of PLA samples led to
delamination of printed layers and brittle failure of the material at the
indentation site. In contrast, FlexiFil samples showed only a narrow band of
plastic deformation ∼25 µm from the indentation site with no signs of
delamination or brittle failure. Discussion: Force-displacement
testing and SEM imaging reveal early yield and mechanical failure of PLA
cages. In contrast, FlexiFil was able to withstand nearly twice the
deformation without any detrimental changes in mechanical performance and
minimal damage as seen in SEM. To fully recapitulate compressive forces seen
in vivo, future work will load TE-IVD cages in a
minipig spine ex vivo. Collectively, our studies suggest
that FlexiFil is a promising material for fabricating a TE-IVD support
structure. Significance: FlexiFil cages exhibited a wider range
of elastic behavior than PLA cages, with less microscale damage. As such,
FlexiFil is a promising candidate for fabrication of support structures for
IVD tissue engineering.

## P273: Diagnosis and management of thoracolumbar spinal disorders
presenting as cardiac, gastrointestinal, and other false pain
syndromes

Nolan Brown

1

, Angie Zhang

, Andrew Chan

, Shane Shahrestani

, Alexander Himstead

, Rohin Singh

, Alvin Chan

, and Michael Oh

Neurosurgery, UC Irvine, United States

Neurosurgery, Columbia University, United States

Neurosurgery, UC San Diego, Unite States

Introduction: Although pseudoangina is most commonly caused by
cervical disc herniation, several cases have been described where thoracic
herniation produced symptoms of pseudoangina. If thoracic herniation can
produce angina-like pain, then it is important to consider whether pathology
of the thoracolumbar spine in general can trigger false pain syndromes
distinct from pseudoangina. Materials and Methods: We seek to
provide the most comprehensive study regarding the diagnosis and treatment
of spinal conditions causing false pain syndromes. In order to accomplish
this objective, we queried the literature and systematically selected
relevant studies according to PRISMA guidelines. Results:

surgery (pancreaticojejunostomy) or other invasive procedures.
Conclusion: In spinal disorders manifesting with atypical
pain syndromes, delay in proper diagnosis and unnecessary treatments can
unfortunately cause prolonged patient suffering and increased cost of
healthcare. As a result, some have proposed that spinal screening should be
incorporated into clinical examinations involving false visceral pain
syndromes.

## P274: Comparison of opioid use and prescribing patterns among orthopedic
surgeons and other orthopedic subspecialties in the United States

Chadi Tannoury

1

, Rahul Bhale

1

, Justin Koh

1

, Aziz Saade

1

, Christopher Maatouk

1

, and Tony Tannoury

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University, Boston, United
States

Introduction: The US opioid epidemic has received particular
attention with 33091 reported deaths from narcotic overdose in 2015. A
recent survey comparing US and Japanese opioid prescribing patterns from the
AOA-JOA traveling fellows included 76 US orthopedic surgeons representing 8
subspecialties. We used this data to compare opioid prescribing patterns
among US spine surgeons to other orthopaedic subspecialties.
Methods: The survey included data based on surgeon
demographics (gender, age, years in practice), patient baseline opioid
use(pre/post-operative opioid use, types of opioid agents, duration of
opioid use), perioperative pain management (procedure/institution factors,
multimodal analgesic therapy), and responses to questions regarding opioid
use attitudes. Survey responses were recorded as either categorical or
semi-continuous variables. Statistical analysis was performed using
chi-squared analysis for categorical responses and Kolmogorov-Smirnov
testing to a statistical significance level of p < 0.05. Parameters that
trended toward significance to p < 0.10 were also recorded. Statistical
analysis was performed using Stata statistical analysis software [StataCorp,
College Station, Texas]. Results: Spine patients were more
likely using opioid medications prior to evaluation by spine surgeons
compared to non-spine patients (p = 0.029). Patients with spine pathologies
treated non-operatively were also more likely to be prescribed opioids (p =
0.006). Post-operatively, spine patients were less likely to stop opioid
prescriptions on the intended time (p = 0.046). Peri-operatively, spine
patients were more likely to be given muscle relaxant medications, and less
likely to receive local/regional anesthesia (p = 0.0025). Additionally,
spine patients showed a trend toward association for requesting additional
opioids beyond their initial prescription (p = 0.057). Spine surgeons showed
a trend toward association for choice of opioid agent prescribed-spine
patients were less likely to receive codeine/tramadol analogs (p = 0.062).
When surveyed on opinions regarding opioid use, US spine surgeons did not
show significantly different opinions regarding opioid use compared to
surgeons in other subspecialties. Conclusion: Spine patients
did demonstrate statistically significant patterns of opioid use,
particularly regarding opioid use prior to evaluation by orthopedic surgeon
and use of opioids for nonoperative pathologies. They were also less likely
to stop opioid prescriptions on time. Surgeon prescription patterns and
perceptions of opioid use were not significantly different for spine
surgeons compared to other subspecialties.

## P275: Epidemiology of work related neck pain among spine surgeons

Sameh Abolfotouh

1

, Omar Alnori

2

, Theodore Choma

3

, Don Moore

3

, and Mostafa Abolfotouh

4

1

Orthopedics Department, MEDCARE Hospital, Dubai, United Arab
Emirates

2

Orthopedics Departmen, Hamad Medical Corporation, Doha,
Qatar

3

Spine Unit, Orthopedics Department, University of Missouri,
Missouri, United States

4

King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), National Guard Health Affairs,
Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Background: Spine surgeons are at risk of musculoskeletal pain
and injuries possibly due to their work-related activities, posture and
affected body mechanics. Aims: to investigate work-related neck
pain among spine surgeons in different AO SPINE regions, by (1) estimation
of the prevalence of work-related neck pain, and (2) determination of its
predictors, its personal and occupational consequences, and the different
management methods adopted for it. Methods: A cross-sectional
survey of 411 spine surgeon members of AO spine was conducted during
March–May 2021, using the Modified Nordic Questionnaire and the Neck
Disability Index. Data on experience of neck pain during the last 12 months,
and its consequences and risk factors were collected. Logistic regression
analysis was done to identify significant predictors of neck pain.
Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05.
Results: The majority of spine surgeons were married (360,
92.3 %), and their average age was 45.31 ± 7.86 years, and average BMI was
26.95 ± 4.07 kg/m². They experienced 66.7% 1-year neck pain prevalence.
According to the Neck Disability Index, more than one-half (52.8%) of
surgeons experienced disability due to neck pain of mild (45.5%), moderate
(6.5%) and severe (0.8%) grades. Neck pain was responsible for stopping work
in 17.5% of surgeons, with a median 3.5 (IQR, 2-7.8) days off work during
the last year. One half of participants (56.3%) were treated by medical
care, 31.5% by physiotherapy, and 16.5% requested rest days and/or sick
leave. Physical stress (p < 0.001) and non-exercising (p = 0.04) were
significant predictors of neck pain, while demographics, workload-related
factors and the use of surgical magnification (Loupes and microscopes) were
not significantly associated with neck pain prevalence (p > 0.05 each).
Conclusion: The 12-month prevalence of neck pain was high
among spine surgeons, with an impact on activities of daily living, mostly
of mild degree, reported by one-half of surgeons. Physical stress was the
only significant predictors while sports practice was ta protective factor
of neck pain. Medication was the main management adopted. An increased focus
on pain prevention through improved workplace ergonomics, and sports
activity programs to reduce the risk of neck pain and arrange for proper
rest periods is recommended.

lumbopelvic alignment. We hypothesize alignment of the cervical spine can
predict lumbopelvic morphotype. Material and Methods: Healthy
volunteers (N = 497) between 20-40 years of age with no pre-existing spine
pathology were recruited. Baseline demographics, Oswestry Disability Index,
and Neck Disability Index were collected. Whole body 2D EOS imaging was
obtained for all participants. Using a semi-automated image analysis
software (KEOPS, by SMAIO), standard measures of alignment of the pelvis,
lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine were obtained. Roussouly morphotype
(RM) was identified for each participant. Principal components (PC) of
cervical vertebral body centroids were input into a support vector machine
algorithm to predict RM. Results: Average age of participants
was 28.4 ± 5.2 years. Fifty six percent of participants were female, average
BMI was 24.9 ± 4.2. Number of participants of each RM were: Type 1 = 26,
Type 2 = 126, Type 3 = 221, Type 4 = 124. When PC explaining 90% of
variability were used, RM was appropriately predicted as follows: Between
Type 1, 2, 3 and 4 = 50%, Type 2, 3, 4 = 53%, Type 2, 3 = 69%, Type 2, 4 =
47%, Type 3, 4 = 69%. Including nearly all PC (99.99% of the variance),
classification rates improved: Between Type 1, 2, 3 and 4 = 68%, Type 2, 3,
4 = 88%, Type 2, 3 = 89%, Type 2, 4 = 99%, Type 3, 4 = 99%.
Conclusion: This study demonstrates that a predictable
relationship between cervical and lumbopelvic alignment exists; this
relationship is sensitive to subtle features of cervical spine shape,
captured by higher order PCs. It provides a robust normative database for
cervical spine alignment and will provide insight into normal patterns of
lumbopelvic compensation with “abnormal” cervical spine alignment. Future
work will aim to classify patterns of cervical spine alignment, and identify
features specifically captured by each principal component, particularly the
higher components.

## P277: Level of spin in the abstracts of RCTs in spine surgery - an
ORG-LOC tool based assessment

Sathish Muthu

1,2

 and Girinivasan Chellamuthu

2

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Dindigul,
India

2

Orthopaedic Research Group, Quality Appraisal Committee,
Coimba

Introduction: There has been a massive surge in published spine
literature in the last few years. Even in highly credible research models
like Randomised Control Trials (RCTs), many pitfalls do exist that a reader
must be aware of. One common but less explored pitfall is the spin.
Particularly in the abstracts, it is a potential source of deception.
Grading of RCTs based on spin will help readers to interpret their results
better. Hence we aim to grade the RCTs of spine surgery based on spin in
their abstracts, analyze its prevalence, and highlight on the usefulness of
spin grading for any RCT. Materials and Methods: We selected
250 recent RCTs from top 5 spine journals. Baseline data were collected.
CONSORT Adherence Score (CAS) based on the adherence of the abstracts of the
RCTS to CONSORT checklist was calculated. The abstracts of the RCTs were
graded using the Level Of Confidence (LOC) grading tool developed by the
Orthopaedic Research Group. The association of spin grade with other
characteristics of the articles were analyzed. Results: The
median CAS was 11 (IQR 10-12). Only 47.6% (n = 119) articles had High LOC
with no or one non-critical spin in abstract and 12.4% (n = 31) had Moderate
LOC with more than one non-critical spin. 28% (n = 70) had at least one
critical spin and 12% (n = 30) had more than one critical flaw making their
results have Low and Critically Low LOC respectively. Of the ten variables
analyzed in multivariate regression analysis, CAS was the only significant
factor that determines the level of confidence in the abstract of RCTs.
Conclusion: Spin based grading of RCTs is the need of the
hour to aid readers to interpret the true essence of research papers. 40% of
the RCTs in top spine journals had low to critically low LOC. Structuring of
abstracts is the way forward to prevent spin.

## P278: Does English speaking status affect post-acute care in
thoracolumbar fusions? A retrospective study in a multiethnic
population

Henry Hoang

1

, Aaron Hui

1

, Dan Berman

1

, Ananth Eleswarapu

1

, Jonathan Krystal

1

, and Zach Sharfman

1

1

Orthopedics, Montefiore Medical Center, Bronx, United
States

Introduction: English speaking status is an often-overlooked
risk factor that influences the longitudinal progression of patient care.
Obstacles such as the procurement of physician appointments, comprehension
of treatment plans, misdiagnoses, and delayed treatment are all amplified in
the setting of a language barrier. Thoracolumbar fusions are indicated for
the management of degenerative disc disease, degenerative spondylolisthesis,
spinal stenosis, tumors, and fractures with more than 300,000 performed
annually. Post-operative clinical outcomes of non-English speaking patients
who undergo thoracolumbar fusion have not been thoroughly studied. A
comprehensive understanding of the post-operative sequelae of non- English
speaking and minority patients is crucial for the development of
interventions aimed at reducing complications and post-operative
readmissions. The purpose of this study is to compare rates of readmission,
complications, and treatment durations between English and non-English
speaking patients undergoing thoracolumbar fusions. Material and
Methods: A retrospective study of 301 patients who underwent a
thoracolumbar fusion at a level 1 trauma center in the Bronx from 2016 was
performed. Demographic, surgical, and post-operative measures were
collected. The primary outcome were readmission to the emergency department
(ED) within 30 days, 90 days and chief complaint. Our secondary outcome was
length of stay defined as days patient spent in inpatient admission
post-operatively. Odds ratio were calculated using SPSS to determine
differential rates of re-presentation to the ED post-operatively. An
independent-samples t-test was run to determine if there were differences in
postoperative length of stay(days) between non-English speakers and English
speakers. Results: All 301 patients who undergone thoracolumbar
fusions in 2016 were analyzed in this study, consisting of 62 non-English
speakers and 239 English speakers. There were 7 non-English patients that
returned to ED within 30-days post-operation compared to 36 English
speakers. The odds ratio of returning to the ED within 30-days
post-operation in non-English speakers versus English speakers was 1.393
(95% CI, .588 to 3.302). There were 21 non-English speakers who returned to
the ER compared to 63 English speakers. The odds ratio of returning to the
ED within 90 days post-operation was .699 (95% CI, .384 to 1.273). There was
no significant different in length of stay between non-English speakers (7.8
± 6.4) and English speakers (8.5 ± 8.8) with a difference of 1.2 (95% -3.05
to 1.67), T (299) = -.579, p = .563. Conclusion: We have
described that a large portion of patients undergoing thoracolumbar surgery
in the Bronx present back to the ED within 30 and 90 days of operation.
English speaking status was determined not to be associated with different
rates of presentation to the emergency room within 30 and 90 days of
thoracolumbar fusion, or different lengths of stay. Taken together,
English-speaking status is not evidenced to be a risk factor that influenced
post-operative readmission of patients undergoing thoracolumbar fusion.

## P279: Epidemiological features of traumatic spinal cord injury in a
tertiary hospital in Cagayan Valley: a 5-year cross-sectional study

Jake Albert Miguel

1

 and Niccolo Mamba

1

1

Orthopaedics, Cagayan Valley Medical Center, Tuguegarao,
Philippines

Introduction: Globally, the recorded prevalence and incidence of
people with Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury (TSCI) is maybe underreported due
to the lack of a national registry system for spinal cord injuries
particularly in developing countries, hindering injury prevention, health
care, and other social planning. Numerous articles on TSCI epidemiology have
been published in Europe, North America, and Australia because most Western
nations have implemented TSCI registries or databases. In the Philippines,
Cagayan Valley Medical Center (CVMC) is the largest medical facility and has
the greatest number of admitted patients in the entire region. However,
little is known and documented about the prevalence of TSCI at this time.
The overall objective of this study is to describe the epidemiological and
demographic characteristics of patients with TSCI admitted in CVMC as well
as to determine its prevalence. Material and Methods: The
researchers retrospectively reviewed the medical records of patients with
traumatic spinal cord injuries admitted in Cagayan Valley Medical Center
from 2016 to 2020. Variables included age, sex, civil status, occupation,
and the clinical profile: mechanism of injury, spinal level of injury,
American Spinal Injury Association Impairment (ASIA) Scale, imaging studies,
treatment received (conservative or surgery), and condition upon discharge.
Results: Between 2016 and 2020, a total of 145 patients had
traumatic spinal cord injuries. The mean age of the patients was 42.13
years, and 93.10% were males with a male/female ratio of 13.5:1. The
occupations with the highest risk were the unemployed (59.31%) with falls
from a height (51.72%) were the leading cause of injuries. This was followed
by motor vehicular collisions (43.45%). The most common level of spinal
injury was the cervical region, accounting for 57.24%, with the majority of
documented cases having an American Spinal Injury Association Impairment
(ASIA) Scale of A. Nonoperative management was done in most of the cases
(80%). For those operated cases, instrumented posterior decompression and
spinal fusion were done (65.52%). Most of the patient’s conditions improved
upon discharge (57.93%) Conclusion: The result of this study is
comparable to other previous literature. The majority of the patients are
typically males sustaining injuries in the cervical spine secondary from
falls from a height in the workplace. The formulation of preventive
strategies should focus on identified high-risk groups sustaining such
injuries. In addition, to precisely document the epidemiological profile of
patients with TSCI, a standardized spine trauma form should be created.
Moreover, the establishment of a national registry system will accurately
describe the incidence and prevalence of TSCI not only in CVMC but in the
entire Philippines.

## P280: Patient reported function outcomes versus objective fitness
assessments: are patients telling the truth about their fitness
level?

Fthimnir Hassan

1

, Yen-Lou Lee

1

, LaRae Klarenbeek-Mitchell

2

, David Ruderman

2

, Eric Schaum

2

, and Lawrence Lenke

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Columbia University Medical Center, The
Och Spine Hospital at New York-Presbyterian, New York, United
States

2

Department of Physical Therapy, The Och Spine Hospital at New
York-Presbyterian, New York, United States

Introduction: Adult Spinal Deformity (ASD) patients
provide subjective outcomes to assess overall fitness on various patient
reported outcomes (PROs). However, these outcomes may be subject to response
bias leading pts to answer survey questions untruthfully. This analysis aims
to determine whether pt. reported fitness outcomes correlate with the
results of objective fitness assessments. Methods: ASD patients
≥ 18 who underwent prehabilitation (prehab) fitness assessments prior to
agreeing to surgery were evaluated from 2017-2020. Prehab included a variety
of fitness tests such as 5x sit-to-stand test (5xSST), gait speed, Hand Grip
Strength, and the 6 minute walk test (6MWT). Surgical factors included
surgery type, total fusion levels (TFL), total instrumented vertebrae (TIV),
and length of stay. PROs (SRS22r and ODI) were collected at preop. Prehab
measures were analyzed alongside the SRS function domain to determine
correlation using pearson/spearman correlation coefficients and multiple
linear regression (MLR). Results: Of the 39 patients evaluated,
mean age was 52 ± 11yrs, 34 (83%) were women, 25 (61%) were revision cases,
and 34 (87%) were fused to the pelvis averaging 12 ± 5 TFL, 13 ± 4 TIV and a
length of stay of 6.4 ± 2days. Preoperatively, Mean HR, SpO2, BP were 75 ±
14 bpm, 98 ± 2%, 127/80 ± 13/9 mmMg, respectively. Mean SRS22r and ODI were
65 ± 13 and 38 ± 19, respectively, with a mean SRS function domain of 3.2 ±
1. SRS function domain correlated with the following: age (r = -0.4; p =
0.0049), 5xSTT (r = -0.6; p = 0.0001), gait speed (r = 0.6; p < 0.001),
and 6MWT (r = 0.6; p < 0.0001) demonstrating weak negative, moderately
negative, moderately positive, and moderately positive correlations,
respectively. The best fitted MLR model utilized the distance covered in the
6MWT, 5xSST, age, HR, SpO2, and lung capacity to predict the outcome of the
SRS function domain leading to an Adj-R-squared = 0.5 suggesting a moderate
effect size. Conclusion: ASD PRO’s provide a subjective value
on their overall level of function that has moderate correlation to a
variety of objective fitness tests utilized in this comparative study. Thus,
it is safe to say that ASD patients are telling the truth when reporting
functional status on the SRS outcomes instrument.

## P281: Variations in treatment for vertebral compression fractures and
impact on the incidence of subsequent hip fractures

Jennifer Bell

1

, Thomas Alter

2

, Mary Kate Erdman

1,3

, Hyunwoo Kang

1,4

, Emily Mills

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Ram Alluri

1

, and Raymond Hah

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, United States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Harborview Medical Center, University of
Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, United States

4

Orthopaedic Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical
School, Boston, United States

Introduction: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the
incidence of hip fractures following a vertebral compression fracture (VCF)
in patients treated with and without anti-osteoporotic medication and/or
surgical intervention. Material and Methods: A deidentified
patient database from a large, private insurer was utilized, identifying
patients from January 2007 to December 2016. Exclusion criteria were
patients less than 50 years of age and patients with less than one-year
follow-up. Patients were grouped based on if they received anti-osteoporotic
medication within one year prior to and following VCF, and whether or not
treatment included surgical intervention (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty).
Results: Our query resulted in 73,907 patients with VCF,
66.8% of which were female. The most common age group was 70-74 (18.0%). A
total of 9,077 (12.2%) patients received surgical treatment. At one-year and
all-time follow up, 3.5% and 9.3% of patients sustained a hip fracture,
respectively. Of the surgically treated, 4.6% and 12.7% of patients suffered
a hip fracture at one-year and all-time follow up, respectively. Older,
female patients with a higher Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI) had higher
hip fracture rates. A 1:3 match on age, gender, and ECI identified 648
patients initiated on new anti-osteoporotic medication following VCF and
1579 without anti-osteoporotic medication. Patients who were initiated on
AOT had higher rates of subsequent hip fractures (11.6% vs 9.4% at all-time
follow up). Conclusion: Our data displays higher rates of hip
fractures in patients with surgically treated VCF and patients initiated on
anti-osteoporotic medication following VCF. This may be due to the fact that
patients with more severe osteoporosis are more likely to be surgically and
medically treated. Further studies are necessary to identify if patients
with surgically treated VCF and patients initiated on anti-osteoporotic
medication following VCF have more severe osteoporosis at the time of index
VCF.

## P282: The relationship between handgrip strength and thoracolumbar
vertebral compression fracture

Hirokazu Inoue

1

, Yukinori Hayashi

2

, Hideaki Sawamura

1

, Atsushi Kimura

1

, Masayuki Masubuchi

2

, and Katsushi Takeshita

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Jichi Medical University, Shimotsuke,
Japan

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Shiobara Spring Hospital,
Nasushiobara, Japan

Introduction: As the elderly population grows, the number of
patients with osteoporosis is increasing, and the prevalence of
thoracolumbar vertebral compression fractures (VCFs) and hip fractures due
to falls is increasing. Loss of lower leg muscle mass and handgrip strength
are also risk factors for the development of VCF, and may be closely related
to the pathogenesis of sarcopenia. Handgrip strength (HGS) is easy to
measure and useful, so it has been used to predict the patient’s condition
in many studies. This study assesses the relationship between HGS and
activities of daily living (ADL), walking speed, and calf circumference for
VCF. Material and Methods: A cross-sectional study in a single
hospital was performed, and elderly patients diagnosed with VCF were
enrolled. After admission, we evaluated HGS, 10m-walk test (speed), Barthel
Index, Berg Balance Score (BBS), numerical rating scale (NRS) of body pain,
and calf circumference. We used low HGS (< 28 kg for male and < 18 kg
for female) and walking speed < 1.0 m/s to define sarcopenia in this
study, according to the 2019 Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia. A
multi-frequency validated bioelectrical impedance analysis instrument, the
Inbody S10 (Biospace, Seoul, Korea), was performed with the patient in the
supine position. Skeletal muscle mass and fat mass were also measured.
Skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) was the measured skeletal muscle mass
divided by the square of the height in meters. Results: A total
of 112 patients who admitted for VCF were included in this study (26 males,
86 females; mean age 83.3 years). The prevalence of sarcopenia according to
2019 Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia guideline was 61.6%. HGS was
significantly correlated with walking speed (p < 0.001, r = 0.485),
Barthel index (p < 0.001, r = 0.430), BBS (p < 0.001, r = 0.511), calf
circumference (p < 0.001, r = 0.491), and SMI (p < 0.001, r = 0.629).
Height, weight, age, and muscle mass were correlated with HGS, but body mass
index and NRS were not correlated with HGS. Conclusion:
Sarcopenia was 61.6% in the patients with VCF. HGS is associated with
walking speed, muscle mass, ADL such as Barthel index and BBS in the
patients with thoracolumbar VCF. HGS is suggested to be important as a
parameter of ADL as well as whole-body muscle strength.

## P283: Correlation between neurological compromise and projectile
trajectory in vertebral gunshot injuries; a case series study

Juan Mandujano-Sanchez

1

, Jose Maria Jimenez Avila

1

, Fernando Carrillo

1

, and Hao Hua Wu

2

1

Clínica de Columna, Campus Guadalajara, Instituto Tecnológico y de
Estudios Superiores de Monterrey, Zapopan, Mexico

2

Orthopaedic Spine Service, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston,
United States

Introduction: Gunshot wounds to the spine account for about 13
to 17% of spinal trauma today, being the third leading cause of spinal cord
injury only behind car accidents and fall from heights. Trajectory of the
projectile and its anatomical location infer the neurological status of the
patient and its prognosis. Material and Methods: Retrospective,
descriptive case series study which included 50 patients with spinal gunshot
wounds diagnosed by simple CT scan who arrived at a first level trauma
hospital from July 2019 to July 2021. Firearm projectile trajectory was
assessed through the GATA SMI classification. Type I: anteroposterior, type
II: Tangential to spinal canal (oblique trajectory) type III: Side-to-side
trajectory (bullet passed through both facet joints and/or pedicles) and
type IV: Tangential to vertebral column (oblique trajectory). Neurological
compromise was assessed through ASIA International Standards for
Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI). Neurological
and projectile trajectory correlation was described using correlation
charts. Results: 50 patients were included. 82% were men and
18% women, the average age was 32.66 years. Thoracic spine injuries were the
most prevalent with 46% of the total. 54% of patients had complete spinal
cord injury (ASIA A). Type III trajectory had more patients with complete
spinal cord injury with 57% of the total in ASIA A. The thoracic segment
presented a higher prevalence of complete spinal cord injury with 67% of all
patients in ASIA A. 14% presented a type I trajectory, 32% a type II
trajectory, 42% type III and 12% type IV according to the GATA SMI
classification. Conclusion: The neurological status of the
patient who presents with a gunshot wound to the spine will depend on the
trajectory of the projectile in relation to the spinal cord and the segment
of the spine affected. The thoracic segment is the segment with the highest
incidence of GS injuries and the one with the highest incidence of complete
spinal cord injury (ASIA A). The type III trajectory according to the GATA
SMI classification presented the highest incidence of patients with complete
spinal cord injury. The type IV trajectory, being a tangential lesion that
does not cross the spinal canal, presented the lowest number of patients
with spinal cord injury. None of these patients presented complete spinal
cord injury. Knowing the projectile trajectory and neurological status in
spinal GS injuries can help ER and spine doctors to determine the prognosis
and the use of future treatment algorithms for patient care.

Department of Hematology/Oncology, OLVG Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The

of which almost 20% was classified as instable, meaning a surgical
consultation is recommended. While no association between VFCs at baseline
and survival was found, the number of VFCs was associated with a more
advanced disease stage.

Introduction: Surgery for spinal deformity in the elderly can be

the EQ-5D index;(2) relative change – 15% increase in the SRS-22r sub-total
and in the EQ-5D index;(3) relative change with a cut-off in the outcome at

completed the SRS-22r and 170 patients completed the EQ-5D at baseline and 2
years postop. 74% and 75% of patients reached MCID in the SRS22r in both the
absolute and relative approaches, respectively. Patients who reached MCID
experienced more pain and worse health at baseline
(absolute:EQ-5D:0.5 ± 0.2 vs 0.6 ± 0.2, p = 0.009;
SRS-22r: 2.6 ± 0.6 vs 3.0 ± 0.6, p = 0.002; relative:EQ-5D:
0.5 ± 0.2 vs 0.6 ± 0.2, p = 0.001;SRS-22r:2.6 ± 0.6 vs 3.0 ± 0.6, p <
0.001). Baseline PRO scores and number of severe adverse events (AEs) were
the only identified risk factors (absolute: no. of AEs:OR =
0.48 [0.28 – 0.82, p = 0.044]; EQ-5D:OR = 0.01 [0.00 – 0.12], p = 0.003;
relative: no. of AEs:OR = 0.39 [0.23 – 0.69, p =
0.007]; EQ-5D:OR: 0.00 [0.00 – 0.07], p < 0.001). 51% and 62% of patients
reached MCID in the EQ-5D using the aforementioned approaches, respectively,
demonstrating similar characteristics regarding pain and health at baseline
(absolute: ODI:48.6 ± 14.1 vs 42.1 ± 15.8, p = 0.017;
relative: ODI:47.7 ± 15.4 vs 41.5 ± 14.3, p = 0.017).
Baseline PROs and number of severe AEs were identified as risk factors
(absolute: no. of AEs:OR = 0.58 [0.38 – 0.89], p =
0.024; ODI:OR = 1.05, [1.02 – 1.07], p < 0.001;
relative: SRS22r:OR = 0.31 [0.16 – 0.57], p <
0.001). In the relative/cutoff approach, 81% reached
MCID in the SRS22r. These patients experienced worse health at baseline
(EQ-5D:0.5 ± 0.2 vs 0.6 ± 0.2, p = 0.040). The number of AEs and baseline
PROs were the only identified risk factors (no. of AEs: OR = 0.44, [0.25 –
0.77], p = 0.007; EQ-5D:OR: 0.01 [0.00 – 0.22], p = 0.007). 83% of patients
reached MCID with the EQ-5D index using the same approach. Patients
experienced less AEs (1.3 ± 1.7 vs 3.1 ± 2.8, p = 0.001) and a lower number
of actions taken due to the occurrence of AEs (1.0 ± 1.2 vs 2.9 ± 2.6, p
< 0.001). The number of actions taken due to AEs (OR = 0.50 [0.35 –
0.73], p < 0.001) was found to be the only risk factor. No surgical,
clinical, or radiographic variables were identified as risk factors using
either of the aforementioned approaches. Conclusion: In this
large multicenter prospective cohort of elderly patients undergoing primary
reconstructive surgery for ASD, surprisingly no clinical, radiological, or
surgical parameters were identified as factors that can be prognostic for
reaching MCID. However, patients who experienced more pain at baseline were
more likely to reach MCID. Conversely, patients who experienced severe AEs
were less likely to reach MCID.

## P286: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on ambulatory lumbar spine
decompression surgery

Spine Care Institute, Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Showa University Hospital,
Shinagawa, Japan

3

Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, United States

Introduction: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak
spread worldwide in a rapid and unpredicted scale in the beginning of 2020.
During the height of the pandemic, the U.S. Centers for Medicare and
Medicaid Services (CMS) announced that all elective surgery should be
delayed to enhance the clinical response to COVID-19. This recommendation
led to clinical and ethical challenges for spine surgeons in deciding
practical management and triaging of patients. However, little is known on
how the pandemic affected surgeons’ and patients’ attitudes towards
ambulatory spinal surgery, including factors such as patient selection, and
hospital length of stay (LOS). This study aim to investigate patient
characteristics and hospital LOS trends during the pre-pandemic period and
three pandemic stages in patients undergoing lumbar decompression procedures
in the ambulatory surgery (AMS) setting. Material and Methods:
A total of 2670 adult patients undergoing one- or two-level lumbar
decompression surgery planned for AMS were retrospectively reviewed.
Patients were categorized into four groups: 1: pre-pandemic (before the
pandemic restriction from January 1, 2019 to March 16, 2020), 2: restricted
period (when elective surgery was cancelled from March 17, 2020 to June 30,
2020), 3: post-restricted 2020 (July 1, 2020 to December 31, 2020 before
vaccination) and 4: post-restricted 2021 (January 1, 2021 to December 31,
2021 after vaccination). Data on patient demographics, comorbidities, LOS,
admission patient class, surgical information, and administrative
information was collected. Simple and multivariable logistic regression
analyses as well as retrospective interrupted time series (ITS) analysis
were conducted comparing AMS patients in the four periods.
Results: 1096 patients were classified as pre-pandemic, 128
patients as restricted, 481 patients as post-restricted 2020, and 965
patients as post-restricted 2021. The three pandemic periods had a lower
admission rate (7.8% to 9.1%) compared to the pre-pandemic period (13.2%).
The ITS analysis demonstrated a significant drop in mean LOS at the
beginning of the restricted period. Hospital LOS gradually increased after
the sudden drop and recovered to the pre-pandemic levels in one year’s time.
Compared to the pre-pandemic period, the patients who underwent surgery
during the restricted period were younger and had fewer comorbidities. After
adjusting for these patient factors, post-restricted 2020 patients still
showed significant association with decreased LOS. Multivariable logistic
regression analyses indicated that the pandemic was an independent factor
influencing the LOS in post-restricted phases. Conclusion: Our
results suggest that spine surgery patients from the restricted period were
younger and healthier, which led to a shorter LOS. Hospital LOS that
significantly decreased in the beginning of the restricted period gradually
increased and recovered to the pre-pandemic levels in one year’s time. Since
the results might be independently influenced by the pandemic, these results
should be taken into account when interpreting the LOS of the patients
undergoing ambulatory lumbar spine surgery in post-restricted phases.

Purpose: To explore the demographics and clinical presentation
of patients with scoliosis in the United Arab Emirates.
Methods: A questionnaire was filled from the medical
records of the patients with scoliosis who had been seen in our hospital.
The questionnaire was specifically devised for this study and included
questions on patient demographics and clinical presentation. Responses were
expressed as frequencies for qualitative analysis. Results: One
hundred and forty-five patients were included in the study, of which 102
(71%) were female, and 50 (35%) were of the Emirati ethnicity. Ninety-six
patients (67%) had a neuromuscular disease, and 88 patients (61%) primarily
presented with back pain. The onset of scoliosis did not arise until after
age 10 in 115 (80%) of patients, and the degree of spinal curvature was more
than 25-degrees in 107 (74%) of patients. Conclusion: Scoliosis
is more prevalent in females and those of Emirati origin in the UAE.
Furthermore, patients with neuromuscular disease are at an increased risk of
developing scoliosis, as corroborated by the current literature, with back
pain as the primary presentation. No notable findings with regards to
delayed developmental milestones or family history were observed. Future
research should focus on quantitative outcomes and adopt a prospective or
retrospective design to yield valid and reproducible evidence.
Keywords: Scoliosis, qualitative, idiopathic scoliosis, nonidiopathic
scoliosis, UAE

Introduction: Tertiary medical centers are often located in the
middle of large metropolitan areas. The distance or access to these
institutions can be a hurdle for patients seeking surgical intervention for
spine pathology. The objective of this study was to investigate and report
the surgical outcomes of patients located in both metropolitan and
non-metropolitan areas. The objective of this study was to investigate and
report the surgical outcomes of patients located in both metropolitan and
non-metropolitan areas. Material and Methods: A retrospective
chart review was completed of 792 consecutive patients who underwent lumbar

Conclusion: Accessibility to healthcare to tertiary
hospitals that can complete complex surgical interventions is not equal in
all parts of the country, which can significantly impact the outcomes of
spine surgery.

2

Neurosurgery, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt

Introduction: The social determinants of health have long been
investigated and a strong negative association between them and the outcomes
after spinal fusions has proven significant. The impact of economic
instability has been shown to correlate with increased rates of hospital
readmission and increased length of stay (LOS). However, the current study
reports the findings between the mean household income and intraoperative
and postoperative outcomes. The current study aimed to report the findings
between the mean household income and intraoperative and postoperative
outcomes. Material and Methods: A total of 792 consecutive
patients who underwent a spine fusion were identified and then data was
collected, which included the patients’ zip code at the time of surgery and
both intraoperative and postoperative outcomes. Using the 2020 United States

was completed between the median household income quartile and perioperative
outcomes. Results: Of the 792 patients, 193 (24.4%) were in the

increased rates of the African American/Black race, women, and metropolitan
location in the lower quartiles. No rates of postoperative complications or
perioperative surgical outcomes differed significantly between quartiles.
Conclusion: While the median household income differs
significantly among patients who undergo spine fusions, the surgical
outcomes of patients are independent of the patients socioeconomic
status.

Introduction: Low back pain is part of a range of

can significantly affect people's quality of life. The diagnosis requires a
careful anamnesis and a good physical examination. The risk factors involved
are possibly linked to psychosocial, behavioral, and occupational aspects
such as high task demand, dissatisfaction with the work environment, as well
as lower socioeconomic status, obesity, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, and
sleep quality.
Objective: To determine the prevalence of low back pain and
establish a correlation with risk factors for the development of low back
pain in a Teaching Hospital in the East Zone of São Paulo.

questionnaire (ODI) and analogue pain scale (VAS) (p = 0.000).

pain among institutionalized individuals, mainly hospitalized, compared to
rates observed outside this context of hospitalization. Therefore, more
research needs to be carried out in this area, since there are difficulties
in finding systematic studies carried out in Brazil that discuss the
prevalence rates of low back pain in the population and among its
subgroups.

## P291: Underweight as a risk factor for vertebral fracture: nationwide
cohort study

Jiwon Park

1

, Joonhyeok Boo

1

, and Jae-Young Hong

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Korea University Ansan Hospital, Ansan, South
Korea

Introduction: Underweight, a known risk factor for osteoporosis
and sarcopenia that is strongly associated with vertebral fractures,
particularly in the elderly, can accelerate bone loss, contribute to
impaired coordination, and increase the risk of falls in the elderly as well
as the general population. The purpose of this study is to identify the
degree of underweight as a risk factor for vertebral fractures in the South
Korean population. Material and Methods: This study included
data from nationwide regular health checkup in 2009 conducted by the Korean
National Health Insurance Service. Participants were followed up from 2010
to2018 to find incidence of newly developed fractures. Based on their body
mass index, the study population was categorized into normal (18.50-22.99
kg/m2), mild underweight (17.50-18.49kg/m2), moderate underweight
(16.50-17.49 kg/m2), and severe underweight (< 16.50
kg/m2) groups. Cox proportional hazards analyses were
performed to calculate the hazard ratios for vertebral fractures based on
the degree of underweight with respect to normal weight to identify the
associated risk. Results: This study evaluated 962,533 eligible
participants, of whom 907,484 were classified as normal weight, 36,283 as
mild underweight, 13,071 as moderate underweight, and 5,695 as severe
underweight. The adjusted hazard ratio of vertebral fractures increased as
the degree of under weight increased. Severe underweight was associated with
a higher likelihood of occurrence of vertebral fractures. The adjusted
hazard ratio was 1.11 (95% confidence interval,1.04-1.17) in the mild
underweight group, 1.15 (1.06-1.25) in the moderate underweight group, and
1.26 (1.14-1.40) in the severe underweight group when compared with the
normal weight group. Conclusion: Underweight is a risk factor
for vertebral fractures in the general population. Furthermore, underweight
of greater severity was associated with a higher risk of vertebral
fractures, even after adjustment for other factors. Clinician can educate
the patients to gain weight through adequate nutritional support and
exercise in order to reduce the risk of the vertebral fractures in under
weight patients.

## P292: Traumatic versus non traumatic spinal cord injury: epidemiological
data from Bio Bio Province, Chile

Oscar González

1,2

, Boris Fuentealba

2

, and Cristian Flores Ferrada

2

1

Neurology, Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción,
Concepción, Chile

2

Neurosurgery, Complejo Asistencial Víctor Ríos Ruíz, Los Ángeles,
Chile

Introduction: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating
condition that can lead to significant neurological impairment and reduced
quality of life. Literature about SCI epidemiology in Chile is sparse. The
aim of the study is to describe the characteristics of patients with SCI
admitted to our Center and compare outcome for patients with traumatic
(TSCI) and non-traumatic spinal cord injuries (NTSCI) after primary
rehabilitation regarding neurological improvement, length of stay and
complications. Material and Methods: We reviewed
retrospectively 51 patients hospitalized in our center, admitted to the
neurosurgery unit over the last decade. Data was collected from their
initial admission and from follow-up and electronics records. Statistical
analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel 2010 and STATA v12.
Results: All 51 cases. Mean age was 44,2 (SD: 17 - 82)
years. 86.2% were men (44/51), 62.7% TSCI and 37.3% NTSCI. In the TSCI
group: mean age was 41.1 years, 87.5% (28/32) were men and 12.5% (4/32) were
women. In the NTSCI group: mean age was 49 years, 84.2% (16/19) were men and
15.8% (3/19) were women. The leading causes of TSCI was Diving Injuries and
Falls, follow by fire weapons injuries and traffic accidents. The main
causes of NTSCI was Tumors, follow by degenerative and infectious conditions
of the spine. Length of Hospital stays was longer in TSCI group 29.8 vs. 24
days. Urinary tract infections frequency were similar in both groups TSCI
(21.9%) vs NTSCI (21%). Pressure ulcers were more frequent among TSCI
(21.9%) vs NTSCI (5.3%). Pneumonia were more frequent in TSCI (31.3%) vs
NTSCI (5.3%). Neurogenic bladder were more frequent in TSCI (75%) vs NTSCI
(63.2%). At discharge, 56.3% in TSCI group were able to walk vs 42.1% in
NTSCI group. The rate of surgery was similar in both group TSCI (65.6%) vs
NTSCI (63.2%). 37.5% in TSCI group improve ASIA score vs 26.3% in NTSCI
Group. Conclusion: For the first time, we are able to provide
local epidemiological status on TSCI and NTSCI based on available data from
hospital registry in Biobío Province, Chile. Further studies are required to
improve the capture of TSCI and NTSCI for future studies. Patients with SCI
have a rehabilitation potential regardless of etiology. Complications are
frequent in both groups and often prolong hospitalization. Complication
patterns differ between the two groups, and specific prevention and optimal
treatment will shorten and optimize the length of primary
rehabilitation.

## P293: Familial arachnoiditis with syringomyelia: analysis of a family of
15 affected individuals and a systematic review

Ali Moghaddamjou

1

, Alex Bak

2

, Francois Mathieu

1

, Jerry Ku

1

, and Michael Fehlings

1

1

Neurosurgery, University of Toronto, Canada

2

University of Toronto, Canada

Introduction: We report a case of a 61-year-old male with
non-communicating thoracic syringomyelia living in Canada of Japanese
descent with 15 known family members with the same condition . Most cases of
idiopathic syringomyelia are sporadic, with no family history of the
disease. Familial syringomyelia is an extremely rare form of non-traumatic
spinal cord injury and is defined by the presence of syringomyelic cavities
in 2 or more patients within the same family. Our patient has been diagnosed
in 2011 and after an initial progressive phase causing significant lower
extremity spasticity, has remained clinically and radiologically stable. He
has no history of trauma, Chiari malformation or associated scoliosis. He
has been started on riluzole 50 mg b.i.d. as an off-label use since 2017. We
aim to report on our case of familial arachnoiditis with syringomyelia and
to conduct a systematic review of similar cases to provide a summary of our
current understanding of this condition. Material and Methods:
Ten keywords relating to familial trait and 23 keywords relating to
syringomyelia were used as search terms on MEDLINE, EMBASE and Cochrane
libraries. Abstracts were screened by two reviewers following the PRIMSA
checklist. Papers reporting cases of familial syringomyelia in English were
included for quantitative analysis. Results: The search
revealed 476 results of which 25 were included in the quantitative analysis.
Overall, there are 131 cases reported of which 16% had associated scoliosis
and 65% associated Chiari Malformation. Most of the patients had surgery as
a treatment (71.7%). Among reported outcomes, most patients showed
improvement in their symptoms (n = 18). This was followed by patients that
showed stable symptoms (n = 9) after treatment. Four patients showed
progression of symptoms and one patient experienced peri-operative death
after treatment for FS. Conclusion: After a systematic review
of the current English literature, we can conclude that our case is one of
the largest known family clusters of syringomyelia not associated with a
Chiari Malformation in North America. Although it is difficult to
demonstrate efficacy, we propose the off-label use of riluzole as a
potential conservative therapy. Apart from these results, there is basic
science support for the use riluzole for arachnoiditis-associated secondary
injury. Given the autosomal dominant pattern in our case, whole exome
sequencing would be an interesting avenue of investigation into the
pathophysiology of this condition. Currently there are no known genetic
causes.

## P295: A single site review of COVID-19's impact on elective spine
surgery: temporary decrease in volume, but business as usual?
Jon Raso
1
, Pramod Kamalapathy
1
, Lawal Labaran
1
, Eric Solomon
2
, Hamid Hassanzadeh
2
, and Amit Jain
2

1

Department of Orthopaedics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville,
United States

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Bethesda, United
States

Introduction: The COVID-19 pandemic has had large impacts on
patient care across all fields, including orthopaedic spine surgery. At many
institutions, elective procedures were cancelled or postponed for a time to
mitigate the risks of COVID exposure. The effects of reduced case volume and
changing practice parameters has been incompletely explored. Our goal was to
evaluate the effect of the pandemic on pre-operative characteristics and
surgical outcomes for patients undergoing elective spine surgery. We
hypothesized that patients selected for elective surgery would overall be
younger, have less comorbidity, and lower American Society of
Anesthesiologists (ASA) scores as compared to pre-COVID. Similarly, we
hypothesized that patient outcomes would not be significantly worse during
the pandemic. Material and Methods: We identified all patients
undergoing elective spine surgery at our single tertiary institution from
January 1st 2019, to December 31st 2020. All surgeries
were performed by five board certified orthopaedic spine surgeons. They were
divided into two cohorts, those receiving surgery before and after March
15th, 2020, which corresponds to the date the elective
procedure deferment was implemented. Demographic and procedural information
for each patient was collected, including age, comorbidities, ASA
classification, and procedure type. Outcomes data up to 90 days was
collected, including major and minor medical complications, reoperation and
readmission rates, length of stay greater than 3 days, and discharge
location. Results: 1545 elective spine surgeries were
identified. Of those, 957 were before March 15th, 2020
(Pre-COVID), and 588 occurred after. 266 patients underwent lumbar fusions,
149 underwent cervical fusions, and 319 underwent lumbar decompression
pre-COVID, compared to 166, 112, and 111 in the COVID cohort. Surgical
volume was lowest in March 2020, in which 34 elective cases were performed
in total- average pre-COVID volume was 69.6 cases per month. Surgical volume
returned to baseline within three months after elective surgery deferment
began, faster than anticipated by the authors. There was a significant
decrease in reoperation rates in the COVID cohort compared to pre-COVID (p =
0.006) for all procedures. When divided by procedure type, fusion patients
experienced a significant decrease in reoperation rates (p < 0.001).
Decompression patient outcomes were not statistically different across
cohorts. Discharge location (long-term care facilities, home) did not change
significantly across the study period. Rates of common post-operative
outcomes were not statistically different for all procedure types both
before and during the cutoff date. Conclusion: Our study
suggests that, despite the COVID-19 pandemic, elective spine procedures did
not carry significantly increased risk. Elective procedure volume returned
to baseline within three months. Further research assessing multiple
different surgical sites is necessary to corroborate these findings. These
findings have a positive implication for future COVID variants or
pandemics.

## P296: Demographics and economic trends in vertebral fracture surgeries
throughout the United States

Khaled Taghlabi

1

, Alexander Beschloss

2

, Daniel Rodriguez

2

, Nathan Lee

3

, Sachin Gupta

2

, Kevin Bondar

4

, Joseph Lombardi

3

, Amir Faraji

1

, and Comron Saifi

4

1

Neurosurgery

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia,
United States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Columbia University Vagelos College of
Physicians and Surgeons, New York, United States

4

Orthopaedic Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United
States

Introduction: Vertebral fractures represent a large public
health concern given the diagnostic challenge and proclivity for
re-fracture. In case of progressive neurological deficits, gross spinal
instability, or intractable pain, surgical intervention is required. Prior
studies have evaluated the costs associated with vertebral fractures;
however, there is little information about the economic and demographic
factors associated with vertebral fracture surgery. The purpose of this
study was to investigate economic and demographic trends pertaining to the
surgical treatment of vertebral fractures between 1993 and 2015 using data
from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database. The present papers tests
the hypothesis that the number of vertebral fracture surgeries and costs
increased between 1997 and 2014 due to more common operative management for
vertebral fractures. Materials and Methods: The National
Inpatient Sample (NIS) was queried for patients who underwent surgical
treatment of a vertebral fracture (ICD-9-CM-3.53) (excluding kyphoplasty and
vertebroplasty) between 1993 and 2015. Demographic data included patient
age, sex, income, insurance type, hospital size, and location. Economic data
including aggregate charge, aggregate cost, hospital cost, and hospital
charge were analyzed. Results: The number of vertebral fracture
surgeries, excluding kyphoplasty and vertebroplasty, increased 461% from
3,331 in 1993 to 18,675 in 2014. Inpatient mortality increased from 1.9% to
2.5%. The mean age of patients undergoing vertebral fracture surgeries
increased from 42 in 1993 to 53 in 2015. The aggregate cost of surgery
increased from $189,164,625 in 2001 to $1,060,866,580 in 2014, a 461%
increase. Conclusion: The increase in vertebral fracture
surgeries between 1993 and 2014 may reflect an increased rate of fractures,
an increased propensity for surgical management, or a multifactorial
combination. The increasing rate of vertebral fracture surgery, coupled with
increasing hospital costs and mortality, signifies that efficient and
effective treatment of vertebral fractures is a challenge and that further
research in epidemiology and management will be beneficial.

## P297: Time to fixation after traumatic spinal cord injury prolonged with
certain race and insurance statuses

Jon Raso

1

, Pramod Kamalapathy

1

, Eric Solomon

2

, Elizabeth Driskill

3

, Kristina Kurker

3

, Hamid Hassanzadeh

2

,
and
Amit Jain

1

Department of Orthopaedics

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Bethesda, United
States

3

School of Medicine, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, United
States

Introduction: Traumatic spinal cord injuries (TSCIs) are
potentially catastrophic injuries to the spine with historically poor
functional outcomes for patients. The management of TSCI requires prompt
evaluation and may necessitate urgent intervention to preserve neurologic
function, therefore time to fixation as a predictor of patient outcomes is
of great interest. Although the optimal timing of surgical intervention for
TSCI is somewhat controversial, early intervention has been recognized as
being beneficial in several studies. The objective of this study was to
evaluate the role of various socioeconomic factors on the time to surgical
fixation in the management of TSCI. Our primary goal was to identify
socioeconomic factors that may delay treatment. Material and
Methods: The present study utilized the Trauma Quality
Improvement Program (TQUIP) dataset to collect adult patient records from
2007-2016. Patients were divided into subgroups based on race. Patients were
also categorized by insurance type into subgroups for additional analysis.
Demographic information for each patient including patient age, gender,
presence of comorbidities, injury location and procedure type were
collected. Additional facility information was also included. Polytrauma
patients were excluded from analysis. A univariate and multivariate linear
regression analysis was used to compare time to procedure based on primary
race, and payer type while adjusting for demographic, hospital, information,
levels involved, region of the spine fixed, accident patterns, and emergency
room disposition. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Results:
8,773 patients were included in the study. The largest group was White
patients (n = 5902, 67.3%) followed by Black (n = 1217, 13.9%), Hispanic (n
= 771, 8.8%), Other (n = 545, 6.2%), and Unknown (n = 338, 3.9%). Most
patients were male (n = 6,499, 74%), and the average GCS score was 14.24 ±
2.26 for the overall group. Hispanic and Black race was associated with a
significantly increased time to fixation of 12.1 hours (95% CI 5.5-18.7, p
< 0.001), and 20.1 hours (95% CI 12.1-28.1, p < 0.001), respectively
compared to white race. Both Other and Unknown cohorts were not associated
with a statistically significant difference in time to fixation compared to
white patients (p > 0.05). Univariate analysis showed that Medicare,
Medicaid, government and military-based insurances, and self-pay were all
associated with significant increases in time to fixation compared to
private insurance (p < 0.05). However, with multivariate analysis, only
Medicaid insurance was associated with a statistically significant increased
time to fixation when compared with private insurance (11.6 hours, 95% CI
3.9-19.2, p = 0.003). Conclusion: Race and certain insurance
statuses were associated with statistically significant increases in time to
fixation following TSCI, potentially compromising quality of patient care
and resulting in poorer outcomes. More research is needed to better
understand these trends and ensure equitable care.

## P298: Prevalelence of global spinal malalignment in the sagittal plane -
A cross sectional analysis of associations with LBP and HR-QOL in a general
non-elderly population

Koichiro Okuyama

1

1

Department of Orthpaedic Surgery, Akita Rosai Hospital, Odate,
Japan

Background Context: Understanding of normal parameters’ range in
the sagittal alignment of the spine is very important to treat degenerative
spinal disorders. For Mongoloid heritage, prevalence of global spine
