clinical significance and associations between GS mal-Algin and bone mineral
density (BMD), skeletal muscle index (SMI), back muscle extensors strength
(BMES), and HR-QOL has not been disclosed enough. Purpose: To
investigate prevalence of GS mal-Algin, and the associations between BMD,
SMI, BMES, low back pain (LBP), and HR-QOL in non-elderly populations in

Patients Samples: Two hundred and sixty-three non-elderly

Outcome Measures: Sagittal parameters of the spine and the

significant differences were found between the participants with PI-LL ≧
10°and those with < 10°, PT ≧ 20° and < 20°, and SVA ≧ 40 mm and <
40mm. However, 1.5% (4/263) of the participants associated with all of PI-LL
≧ 10°, PT ≧ 20°, and SVA ≧ 40 mm had a significantly lower SF-36 mental
component score than others (p < 0.05). Conclusions: In a
general non-elderly population (18 < age < 65 years, Mongoloid
heritage in East Asia, n = 263), PI-LL ≧ 10°, PT ≧ 20° , and SVA ≧ 40 mm was
found in 10.6%, 11.8% , and 6.1%, and each mean value was 15.3 ± 5.9°, 25.1
± 4.0°, and 52.7 ± 12.2 mm. PI-LL ≧ 10° only had an association with LBP,
and it is also speculated that coexistence of PI-LL ≧ 10° plus PT ≧ 20° and
SVA ≧ 40 mm leads to a poor mental HR-QOL.

## P299: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the corrections of spinal
deformities through the posterior approach in the Unified Health System in
Brazil

Rodolfo Gomes Dias

1

 and Mohammad Zarrabian

2

1

Orthopaedic and Traumatology Department, Santa Casa de Misericórdia
de Araçatuba, Araçatuba, Brazil

2

Department of Spine Surgery, Winnipeg Spine Centre, University of
Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada

Introduction: In regards on spine deformities, scoliosis
consists of deformities that affect the spine and are characterized by
involving the three reference planes: lateral deviation in the frontal
plane, vertebral rotation in the axial plane and lordosis in the sagittal
plane (1). Data from epidemiological studies point to a high prevalence of
postural alterations in the spine of children and adolescents; presenting an
overall prevalence between 1% and 2%, where idiopathic scoliosis is the most
common subgroup (2). The pandemic caused by COVID-19 considerably affected
elective surgeries in the country, but there are no studies that show its
influence when performing corrections of spinal deformities with posterior
approach (CSDP) in the Unified Health System (UHS). Material and
Methods: This is an observational study using aggregate national
data from the Hospitals Information System (SIH/SUS) and the Brazilian
Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). These databases capture all
procedures performed in the public health care system which comprises 75% of
the Brazilian health care system. There was no need for ethics committee
approval due to the data being public. We analyzed the number of procedures,
total and mean value in Brazilian reals(R$) of CSDP procedures in 1 to 12 or
more levels in the five Brazilian. The results were organized in a
spreadsheet and then descriptive statistics were used for comparison during
the pre-and ongoing period of the pandemic, consisting of April 2018 to
March 2020 (period 1) and April 2020 to March 2022 (period 2). For the
statistical analysis, the Chi-Square test was used, considering p < 0.05
as significant. Results: In period 1, 1,379 CSDP were carried
out by the UHS, 19, 161, 670, 488 and 41, in the North, Northeast,
Southeast, South and Center-West regions respectively; at a total cost of R$
14,715,548.44 and an average of R$ 10,671.17 per procedure and
hospitalization. During period 2, 985 CSDP were carried out, at a cost of
R$11,076,589.99 at an average value of R$11,245.27; being 11, 174, 513, 243,
and 44 in the North, Northeast, Southeast, South and Center-West regions,
respectively. A reduction of: 42.105%, 23.433%, 50.205%, in the North,
Southeast and South regions respectively; and an increase of 8.075% and
7.317% in the Northeast and Midwest regions, respectively. With a cost
reduction of 24.729%. Conclusion: There was an overall
reduction of 28.571% of CSDP during the pandemic in Brazil, with the most
affected region being the South region, with a reduction of 50.205% (p <
0.05). It is extremely important to analyze these data to identify the
impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in relation to the performance of the
studied procedure. This data from this study may assist the competent
authorities in identifying and correcting discrepancies and reduction of the
procedure studied caused by the COVID-19 pandemic in different Brazilian
regions.

## 1516

## P300: 2 years of COVID-19 pandemic: current overview of the posterior
thoraco-lumbosacral fusion surgeries in the Unified Health System in
Brazil

Rodolfo Gomes Dias

1

 and Mohammad Zarrabian

2

1

Orthopaedic and Traumatology Department, Santa Casa de Misericórdia
de Araçatuba, Araçatuba, Brazil

2

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Spine Surgery Division, Winnipeg
Spine Centre, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada

Introduction: Thoraco-lumbosacral spine fusion (TLSF) is a
surgical technique widely used for the treatment of several pathologies of
the spine, including degenerative diseases, trauma and deformities. The
initial objective of this procedure is to obtain fusion between the
vertebral segments to promote the restoration of stability and alignment
lost due to pathologies that affect the spine. It is known that the pandemic
significantly affected elective medium and high complexity surgeries in
Brazil; however, there are no studies regarding its influence on the
performance of TLSF surgeries in the Unified Health System (UHS) in Brazil.
Material and Methods: This is an observational study using
aggregate national data from the Hospitals Information System (SIH/SUS) and
the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). These databases
capture all procedures performed in the public health care system which
comprises 75% of the Brazilian health care system. There was no need for
ethics committee approval due to the data being public. All one to seven
level TLSF procedures performed in pediatric and adult populations between
April 2018 and March 2020 (pre-pandemic) and April 2020 and March 2022
(post-pandemic), all five Brazilian regions were analyzed. TLSF procedures
during the pre-pandemic period were compared to the post-pandemic period in
terms of total procedures performed, as well as total and average cost in
Brazilian Reals(R$), included all direct costs to the health system such as
hospitalization and fees. For the statistical analysis, the Chi-Square test
was used, considering p < 0.05 as significant. Results: In
the pre-pandemic period, 12,645 TLSF surgeries were performed by the UHS.
Regional analysis demonstrated 456, 1,447, 4,706, 4,814 and 1,222 procedures
were performed in the Northern, Northeastern, Southeastern, Southern and
Center-West regions respectively. The total cost was R$100,087,353.45
(Brazilian reais) with an average cost of R$7,915.17 per procedure. During
the post-pandemic period 8,891 TLSF surgeries were performed with 318,
1,226, 3,546, 2,952, and 849 performed in the Northern, Northeastern,
Southeastern, Southern and Center-West regions respectively. This
represented a relative reduction of 30.3%, 15.3%, 24.7%, 38.7% and 30.5% in
the Northern, Northeastern, Southeastern, Southern and Center-West regions
respectively as compared to pre-pandemic levels. Total cost was
R$71,330,939.05 with an average cost of R$8,022.83. Conclusion:
There was an overall reduction of 29.7% in TLSF surgeries during the
pandemic in Brazil, with the most affected region being the Southern region,
with a reduction of 38.7% (p < 0.05). It is important to analyze this
data to identify the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in relation to the
performance of posterior spinal surgeries and its implications on wait lists
in the various health regions. Future projects would look for underlying
causes for the decrease in surgeries and its regional variation.

## 1568

## P301: Surgical management of compressive myelopathy due to spinal
fluorosis

Jayprakash Modi

1,2

 and Pratikkumar Prajapati

2

1

Orthopaedic, Nutan Medical College, Mehsansa, India

2

Orthopaedic, B J Medical College, Ahmedabad, India

Introduction: Fluorosis is an endemic disease of India which
causes compressive cervical and/or dorsal myelopathy. This study aims to
evaluate the role of surgical management in the crippling fluorosis along
with evaluation of radiological imaging as screening/diagnosing tool for the
disease. Materials and Methods: This is a prospective cohort
study of 33 patients operated at tertiary care center having non-traumatic
involvement of spinal cord affecting neurology with history, clinical and
radiological features (Ossified Posterior Longitudinal Ligament, Ossified
Ligamentum flavum) suggesting fluorosis as the cause of compression.
Outcomes were measured in terms of improvement in Nurick grading, Rankins
scale, spasticity, Oswestry Disability Index, modified Japanese Orthopaedic
Association scores. Results: Spinal fluorosis is a male
predominant disease affecting the elderly after years of fluorine intake.
Cervical and/or dorsal spine are predominantly involved at multiple levels
(> = 2). Diagnosis of the disease poses difficulty due to lack of
established laboratory parameters with high sensitivity, availability, and
lack of awareness among surgeons. Skeletal survey alone has > 90%
sensitivity for diagnosing the disease. Once evaluated properly,
decompression at correctly identified levels invariably improves the
spasticity and quality of life immediately post-surgery. At final follow-up,
there was on average improvement of 2 scales in Nurick grade, Rankins scale
and Ashworth grading whereas average improvement in ODI, mJOA and dorsal
specific mJOA were 52%, 3.17 points and 2.7 points respectively. However,
preoperative counselling for “apparent neurological deterioration” in
immediate postoperative period is very important. Complications like
infection and dural tear have to be prevented with special surgical tactics.
Conclusion: Skeletal survey along with computed tomography
and magnetic resonance imaging is cost-effective modality for the
screening/diagnosis for fluorosis. Once developed, surgery, either curative
or palliative, is the best treatment at crippling stage of the disease.
Keywords: Dorsal myelopathy, endemic, fluorosis, laminectomy, ossified
ligamentum flavum, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament.

## P302: A multidisciplinary approach does not discriminate based on
socioeconomic factors in patients presenting with an adult spinal
deformity

Caroline Drolet

1

, Jesse Shen

1,2

, Michelle Gilbert

1

, Kellen Nold

1

, Venu Nemani

1

, Jean Christophe Leveque

1

, Rajiv Sethi

1

, and Philip Louie

1

1

Neurosurgery, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, Seattle, United
States

2

Université de Montréal, Canada

Introduction: Adult spinal deformity surgery (ASD) is partly a
high-risk procedure due to the comorbid aging population it often affects.
Multidisciplinary approaches were developed to improve outcomes and decrease
complications and have shown their efficacy in optimizing and screening
patients. However, socioeconomically disadvantaged populations are more
burdened with comorbidities. Whether multidisciplinary teams are biased
towards healthier and more socioeconomically advantaged patients warrants
further investigation. We sought to assess whether patients received surgery
following a multidisciplinary conference review will differ by socioeconomic
status, as defined by the area deprivation index. Material and
Methods: A single-center retrospective analysis of patients
operated for ASD was performed. Patients presented at a multidisciplinary
conference for surgical clearance between August 2015 and March 2021 were
reviewed. Patients were categorized based on their operative status. Each
patient’s residence was ranked using the Area Deprivation Index based on the
Neighborhood Atlas. This index ranks every zip code based on deciles, with
one being the least disadvantaged and ten being the most disadvantaged
within a state. Using logistic regression, we examined whether demographic
variables, ADI rank for Washington (median split into low/advantaged and
high/disadvantaged), distance from the hospital, and the interactions
predicted whether patients received surgery after the conference.
Results: Our analysis identified 330 patients (209 female,
121 male; 19-86 years old, M = 64.6, SD = 12.1). Patients with a history of
psychiatric disorders were less likely to receive
surgery, p = .02. No other main effects approached
significance. There was a significant interaction between ADI and
distance, p = .04. More advantaged patients were less
likely to receive surgery if they were closer than farther from the
hospital, p = .03. Distance did not significantly
affect whether more disadvantaged patients received
surgery, p = .51. Conclusion: This
analysis suggests that a multidisciplinary approach does not discriminate
based on socioeconomic status. Further investigation is needed to understand
the relationship between distance and ADI, and their interactive effect on
surgery.

## 1607

## P303: Disparities in access to timely spine surgeon evaluation for
degenerative lumbar pathology

Karissa Yamaguchi

1,2

, Caroline Drolet

1

, Mary Kim

1,2

, Thomas Hanks

1,2

, Lisa Depledge

1,2

, Rajiv Sethi

1

, and Philip Louie

1

1

Neurosurgery, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, Seattle, United
States

2

School of Medicine, University of Washington, United States

Introduction: Studies have demonstrated the association between
race, socioeconomic status (SES),and insurance type and worse preoperative
physical and mental health at presentation in patients indicated for spine
surgery. Unfortunately, these factors negatively impact postoperative
clinical outcomes as well. Little research characterizes how race, SES, and
insurance type impact patients’ abilities to navigate the health system from
the initial referral to consultation with a spine surgeon. This study aimed
to evaluate the impact of race, SES (as measured by the Area Deprivation
Index [ADI]), and insurance type on timeliness to a spine surgeon
appointment after initial referral; specifically, evaluating patients
presenting with symptoms of lumbar radiculopathy. We hypothesized that
patients with Medicaid, living in areas of higher deprivation (thus, lower
SES), and of non-white race experience longer wait times between the initial
referral to a spine surgeon and their initial consultation presentation.
Material and Methods: This retrospective observational
study was approved by the institutional review board (IRB). New patients
evaluated for lumbar radiculopathy between March 2021 to September 2021 by
four fellowship-trained spine surgeons at a single-center outpatient clinic
were included. Patients seen as a part of the Centerof Excellence program or
for a second opinion were excluded. A review of the electronic medical
record and patient-staff communication logs obtained the following
variables: Initial referral date, initial spine surgeon visit date, type of
visit (virtual vs. in-person), symptom duration at presentation, referring
provider, referring institution (internal vs. external), and referral
timing. Demographic data including race, insurance type, zip code of
residence, and location of initial consultation were extracted last to avoid
bias in the depth of chart review. Multivariable analyses were performed to
determine if specific demographic characteristics are associated with
prolonged wait times for neurosurgery consultation. Results: Of
the 305 new patients seen for initial neurosurgery consultation, 245 met our
criteria. In our study, patients with Medicaid experienced significantly
longer wait times when compared with patients with Medicare and private
insurance (p = 0.007). Asian patients experienced the longest mean wait time
(mean = 59.1 days), followed by White patients (mean = 30.6), then Black
patients (mean = 21.3), but this was not statistically significant (p =
0.08). Living in an area of high deprivation was also not associated with
significantly prolonged wait times (R = 0.025, p = 0.696).
Conclusion: This study highlighted structural disparities
in access to timely neurosurgery evaluation. Our results indicate that a
patient's insurance status prolongs wait times for consultation. Further
qualitative research is needed to identify specific barriers contributing to
delays in care and solutions.

## P304: Scoliosis among children in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau of China: a

Lijin Zhou

1

, Yong Hai

1

, and Honghao Yang

1

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital

Introduction: The average altitude of the Qinghai-Tibetan
Plateau is 4,500 m and most of the residents are of Tibetan ethnicity. The
purpose of this study was to investigate the prevalence of scoliosis and
associated factors among children in this region through a scoliosis
screening program. Methods: A cross-sectional study was
performed between May 2020 and December 2020 in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. A
total of 9,856 children aged 6-17 years from schools and nearby villages
were screened using visual inspection, the Adams forward-bending test, the
angle of trunk rotation, and radiography. A self-designed questionnaire was
used to collect demographic data. The prevalence of scoliosis and associated
factors were analyzed. Results: The overall prevalence of
scoliosis among children in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau was 3.69%, with 5.38%
for females and 2.11% for males. The prevalence of scoliosis was 3.50% in
children who resided below 4,500 m while 5.63% in those resided above 4,500
m (p = 0.001). The prevalence of congenital scoliosis (2.14 vs. 0.42%, p
< 0.001) and neuromuscular scoliosis (0.34 vs. 0.07%, p = 0.041) were
significantly higher in the altitude above 4,500 m. 50.00% of patients
resided above 4,500m were recommended for surgery while 16.24% in those
resided below 4,500 m (p < 0.001). Independent associated factors were
detected as female (OR = 2.217, 95 CI% 1.746-2.814, p < 0.001), BMI <
18.5 (OR = 1.767, 95 CI% 1.441–2.430, P = 0.005), altitude of residence ≥
4,500 m (OR = 1.808, 95 CI% 1.325-2.483, p = 0.002), and sleep time < 8 h
(OR = 2.264, 95 CI% 1.723-2.846, p = 0.001). Conclusion: The
prevalence of scoliosis among children in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau was 3.69%.
With increasing altitudes, the prevalence of scoliosis and its major type
were different from that at lower altitudes. Female, BMI < 18.5, altitude
of residence ≥ 4,500 m, and sleep time < 8 h were independently
associated with the prevalence of this disease. Early screening should be
carried out before the age of 7 years, especially in high-altitude,
underdeveloped, and rural areas.

## P305: Differences in spinal cord astrocytoma treatment across
urbanicity

David Sykes

1

, Nancy Abu-Bonsrah

2

, Jacob Sperber

1

, Edwin Owolo

1

, Romaric Waguia Kouam

1

, Tara Dalton

1

, Mackenzie Price

1

, Quinn Ostrom

1

, Harrison Hockenberry

1

, Dana Rowe

1

, Emily Luo

1

, Corey Neff

1

, Brandon Bishop

1

, Antoinette Charles

1

, Margaret Johnson

1

, Melissa Erickson

1

, and C. Rory Goodwin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Duke University School of Medicine,
Durham, United States

2

Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine,
Baltimora, United States

Background: Spinal cord astrocytomas (SCAs) are highly
infiltrative gliomas of the spinal cord, representing the second most common
intramedullary spinal cord tumor. The management of SCAs may include
surgery, radiation therapy, and/or systemic therapy, with patient outcomes
potentially affected by their location. However, the role urbanicity in SCA
treatment remains unknown. The authors, therefore, set out to determine the
association between urbanicity and SCA outcomes. Methods: The
Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States (CBTRUS) analytic dataset,
a combination of the CDC’s National Program of Cancer Registries and NCI’s
Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results datasets, was used to identify
individuals with histopathologically-confirmed SCAs between 2004 and 2019.
US Department of Agriculture 2013 Rural Urban Continuum Code definitions
were used to classify patients as metropolitan or non-metropolitan.
Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations
between urbanicity and SCA treatments adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex,
race and ethnicity. Treatment was defined as radiation, surgery (excisional
biopsy), systemic and comprehensive (radiation, surgery and systemic). Cox
proportional hazard models were constructed to understand the effect of
treatment, urbanicity, and age at diagnosis on the survival time of
patients. Results: 2021 patients were included in this
analysis. Of these, 1744 patients lived in a metropolitan (metro) area and
277 in non-metropolitan (non-metro) area, with a median age at diagnosis of
30 years and 28 years, respectively. There was a higher proportion of White
Non-Hispanic (NH) individuals in the non-metro group (86% vs 66%, p <
0.001), and a higher proportion of Black NH individuals in the metro group
(14% vs 9.9%, p < 0.001). No statistically significant difference was
found on survival between the two groups. Non-metro group had a higher
incidence of Grade I and II astrocytoma than the metro group, (51% vs 44%, p
< 0.001) and (30% vs 19%, p < 0.001) respectively. No statistically
significant difference was found between metro and non-metro groups in
regard to treatment options. However, Hispanic ethnicity was associated with
increased odd of receiving radiation [1.5 CI (1.13; 1.99)], systemic therapy
[1.45, CI (1.07; 1.97)] and comprehensive treatment [1.64; CI (1.08; 2.43);
p = 0.018]. Conclusions: Although metropolitan patients present
with severe SCA (higher grade SCA), living in a metro or non-metro county
was not associated with decreased odds of receiving SCA treatment. Further
work is necessary to understand the role of urbanicity in outcomes of
patients with SCA.

## 1879

## P306: Pull-up bar associated spine injury: an analysis of the 2012-2021
NEISS database

Angelo Changas

1

, Sohrab Vatsia

2

, Grant Reviere

3

, Gerald McGwin

4

, Brent Ponce

2

, L. Erik Westerlund

2

, Douglas Pahl

2

, James McGrory

2

, and David Gloystein

2

1

Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine, Suwanee Campus,
Suwanee, GA, United States

2

Hughston Clinic, Columbus, GA, United States

3

Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine, Auburn Campus, Auburn,
AL, United States

4

Department of Epidemiology, University of Alabama at Birmingham,
Birmingham, AL, United States

Introduction: Interest in the use of home exercise regimens in
the United States has risen considerably in the past several years. The use
of pull-up bars allows for ease of access to strength training exercise, yet
faulty manufacturing or improper installation of such equipment has led to a
multitude of serious injuries and even litigation. Therefore, the purpose of
this study was to analyze the mechanism of spinal injuries associated with
pull-up bar usage. Material and Methods: The National
Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) database was queried to
estimate the incidence of injuries related to pull-up bar consumer products
from 2012-2021 in the United States. Resultant data was analyzed to describe
trends in demographics, incidence, and injury patterns associated with
pull-up bar usage. Results: A total of 1470 pull-up bar-related
injury cases were identified from review of the NEISS database query
resulting in a weighted estimate of 50,108 injuries from 2012-2021 in the
United States. Demographically, pull-up bar-related injuries were more
common in males (74.3%), and the highest incidence of cases was reported in
the 19-44 years old age group (50.4%) followed by the less than 18 years old
age group (36%). Additionally, injuries were 1.55 times more likely to occur
in a “Home” setting versus “Places of Recreation”. The NEISS codes for
“Neck”, “Upper Trunk”, and “Lower Trunk” were utilized to distinguish
anatomic regions of the spinal column – with a majority of cases (54.5%)
localized to the “Upper Trunk” zone. Mechanistically, “Sprain/Strain”
accounted for 24.0% of all injury cases, followed by “Lacerations” (12.5%)
and “Fractures” (10.8%). In total, there were 529 weighted cases of spinal
fracture due to pull-up bar malfunction, of which, 63 estimated “Neck”
spinal fractures all occurred secondary to pull-up bar malfunction.
Conclusion: Pull-up bar-related injuries are largely
attributed to the use of home exercise equipment. These injuries are likely
preventable, as pull-up bar malfunction injuries were 11 times more likely
to occur in the “Home” setting in comparison to all other recorded locales.
Improved product design and education underlying best practices for the use
of pull-up bars and home exercise equipment may prevent an increasingly
prevalent and deleterious mechanism of spinal injury.

## P307: Differential interspinous process device adoption and utilization
across the United States

Justin Chan

1

, Nicholas Peterman

2

, Sohaib Hashmi

1

, Yu-po Lee

1

, and Henry Hoang

3

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, Irvine Medical
Center, Orange, United States

2

Carle Illinois College of Medicine, Medicine, Urbana, United
States

3

Montefiore Medical Center, Bronx, USA

Introduction: Interlaminar/interspinous process
stabilization/distraction devices (IPDs) are relatively new treatment
options for spinal stenosis that have recently been given identifiable
billing codes by Medicare in 2017. This project utilizes publicly available
Medicare physician billing databases, among other population level
databases, to track the practice patterns, utilization, and expansion of
IPDs in the 4-year period of 2017 to 2020 and catalog potential geospatial
disparities in IPD adoption and the sociodemographics of those most
effected. Material and Methods: The yearly Medicare Physician
& Other Practitioners dataset containing all codes billed to Medicare,
the location of billing, and the quantity of reimbursement was utilized for
2017 to 2020. This dataset was filtered to contain only IPD codes 22867,
22868, 22869, and 22870 and combined with the year-matched Medicare
Geographic Variation dataset which contained the sociodemographics of the
Medicare population on a county-level. The total dataset was then merged
with the American Community Survey dataset from the United States (US)
Census Bureau to obtain county-level economic data. Moran’s I clustering
analysis was then conducted using GeoDa, a geospatial analysis software, to
identify significant, p < 0.05, hotspots and coldspots of IPD insertions
per 10,000 Medicare patients. The resulting hotspot and coldspot county
groupings were then compared for significant differences across all recorded
variables with a Mann-Whitney U Test. Results: 30,889 IPD
insertion procedures costing a total of $111,472,207 to Medicare were
captured in this analysis. 12.5% of procedures had PID insertions at two
levels. The number of IPD procedures increased by 95.5% per year while costs
increased by 132.3% per year on average across the 4-year period. 2019 was
an outlier year, with a 17.4% reduction in total procedures from 2018,
likely due to the impact of COVID on elective procedures. Cost increase was
primarily driven by increased utilization of ambulatory surgical centers
(ASCs), which Medicare reimburses at a higher rate. IPD insertion in ASCs
increased by 10.7% per year to 37.6% overall in 2020. Geospatial clustering
analysis of IPD insertions per 10,000 Medicare patients revealed hotspot
clusters of IPD adoption in Los Angeles CA, Denver CO, Las Vegas NV,
Jacksonville FL, Lincoln NE, Wichita KS, and Savannah GA. Coldspot clusters
were predominantly along the Eastern Coast and in the Midwest Region.
Compared to hotspots, coldspots were significantly more rural, whiter, less
educated, more impoverished, and with higher Medicare participation rates.
Conclusion: IPD insertion procedures have grown rapidly in
recent years as a valid treatment strategy, but this growth has not been
equally distributed across the United States. Rural, predominantly white,
areas in the Eastern Coast and Midwest have lagged behind nationally. COVID,
ASC utilization, socioeconomics, and the practice patterns of the surgeons
themselves may all play a part in the geographic disparities identified in
this work.

## P308: Subsequent fusion following multilevel lumbar decompression
surgery

Ryan Hoel

1

, Melissa Albersheim

2

, Sharon Yson

2

, Jeffrey Luna

3

, Paul Soriano

2

, Jason Haselhuhn

2

, and Jonathan N. Sembrano

2

1

Twin Cities Orthopedics, Edina, United States

2

University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

3

Minneapolis VA Health Care System, Minneapolis, United
States

Introduction: In select patients with lumbar spinal stenosis,
surgical decompression is efficacious in reducing pain and improving quality
of life. However, there is a debate about the role of posterior
decompression and the number of operative levels contributing to spinal
stability and reoperation rate. In this study, we sought to investigate the
incidence of reoperation of patients after multilevel adjacent lumbar
decompression, with a particular interest in the rate of subsequent fusion
at the previously decompressed levels. We hypothesize a moderate incidence
of subsequent fusion surgery after multilevel decompression surgery.
Materials and Methods: After IRB approval, we
retrospectively reviewed the charts of all spine surgeries performed over 15
years at a single Veterans Affairs tertiary referral hospital. We identified
patients who underwent three or more level of lumbar decompression without
concomitant fusion and determined if surgeons performed any subsequent
spinal operations. We excluded patients with less than a year follow-up
period. We attempted to contact all patients by phone for a follow-up to
inquire if they had received spine surgery outside our institution. We
determined and calculated the reoperation type and rates for each case and
the time it took before a reoperation occurred. Results:
Forty-five patients (44M:1F) with a mean age of 68 met the inclusion
criteria and were included in the final analysis. The median follow-up time
was 27 months. Three (7%) underwent subsequent fusion surgery at a
previously decompressed level at 14, 23, and 25 months. Another three (7%)
patients underwent revision decompression at previously decompressed levels
at 6, 24, and 130 months. Five (11%) other patients underwent reoperation in
the first two months for wound complications related to infection or
hematoma. One (2%) patient underwent debridement of an epidural abscess
located three levels cranial to the most proximal decompression six years
after his index surgery; the abscess was deemed unrelated to the prior
decompression. Overall, 12 patients (27%) underwent reoperation during their
follow-up period. Conclusion: Our results suggest that the need
for subsequent arthrodesis in decompressions of three or more consecutive
levels without concomitant fusion may be less than intuitively suspected and
that concomitant fusion at the time of index surgery is not warranted. We
recommend mid-term and long-term analysis of rates of subsequent fusion.
This study lends information for preoperative discussion with patients
considering the risks and benefits of decompression alone versus
decompression with fusion for multilevel lumbar surgery.

## P309: Effects of COVID-19 pandemic on spinal deformity operations and
discectomies in the Unified Health System in Brazil

Rodolfo Gomes Dias

1

 and Mohammad Zarrabian

2

1

Orthopaedic and Traumatology Department, Santa Casa de Misericórdia
de Araçatuba, Araçatuba, Brazil

2

Spine Surgery Division, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery,Winnipeg
Spine Centre, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada

Introduction: Although the COVID-19 pandemic affected elective
surgeries in Brazil there is no data on its effect on spinal surgeries. To
better understand this we analysed data on the number and costs of spinal
deformity operations and discectomy operations done from April 2018 to March
2022. These two categories were chosen for analysis as spinal deformity
operations and discectomies represent opposite ends of the spectrum in terms
of surgical risks, resource utilisation, and costs. Material and
Methods: National data from the Hospitals Information System
(SIH/SUS) and the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE)
collected. These databases capture all procedures performed in the public
health care system which comprises 75% of the Brazilian health care market.
There was no need for ethics committee approval due to the data being
public. The number of posterior spinal deformity operations (PSDO) and
cervical, lumbar or lumbo-sacral discectomies performed between April 2018
and March 2020 (period 1) were compared to the number performed between
April 2020 and March 2022 (period 2) in the five Brazilian health regions.
These procedures were analysed in terms of total procedures performed, as
well as average cost using the chi-square test with p < 0.05 considered
significant. Costs included all direct costs to the health system such as
hospitalisation and fees. Results: In period 1 1,379 PSDOs were
performed with 19, 161, 670, 488 and 41 performed in the Northern,
Northeastern, Southeastern, Southern and Centre-West regions respectively.
During period 2, 985 PSDOs were performed with 11, 174, 513, 243, and 44
performed in the Northern, Northeastern, Southeastern, Southern and
Centre-West regions respectively. The average cost of a PSDO was R$10,671.17
in period 1 and R$11,245.27 in period 2. By comparison 8,130 discectomies
were performed in period 1 with 367, 878, 4,402, 1,877 and 606 performed in
the Northern, Northeastern, Southeastern, Southern and Center-West regions
respectively. In period 2 5,696 discectomies were performed with 212, 597,
3,228, 1,150, and 515 performed in the Northern, Northeastern, Southeastern,
Southern and Centre-West regions, respectively. The average cost of a
discectomy increased from R$ 1,592.02 in period 1 to R$ 1,637.36 in period
2. Conclusion: There was a 28.6% decrease in the number of
PSDOs (p < 0.05) performed in the Brazilian public health care system
between period 1 and period 2 while the average cost per case rose. The
Southern region was the most affected with a reduction of 50.205% (p <
0.05) but the number of PSDOs in the Northeastern and Midwestern regions
paradoxically increased by 8.08% and 7.32% respectively. In comparison
nationally there was a 29.9% decrease in the total number of discectomy
operations during the same time period (p < 0.05) and costs increased.
Decreases occurred in every health region although the most affected was the
Northern region with a 42.2% decrease. Despite significant differences
between the risks, resource utilisation and costs of a spinal deformity
operations and discectomies both types of operations decreased by similar
amounts relative to their pre-pandemic levels while their costs increased.
The Northern region suffered the greatest relative reduction in spinal
surgeries.

## P310: Portal utilization in surgical spine patients: sociodemographic
factors and social determinants of health

Edwin Owolo

1

, Zoey Petitt

1

, Antoinette Charles

1

, Cesar Baeta

1

, Emily Poehlein

2

, Cynthia Green

2

, Chad Cook

2

, Jacob Sperber

1

, Melissa Erickson

3

, and C. Rory Goodwin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery

2

Department of Biostatistics and Bioinformatics

3

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Duke University School of
Medicine, Durham, United States

Summary of Background Data: Patient portals (PP) have been shown
to improve outcomes and quality of care. Engaging them requires internet
access, technological literacy, and dexterity, which may serve as access
barriers. The aim of this study is to examine patient portal use among the
surgical spine patient population across different sociodemographic groups
and assess impact of patient portal use on clinical outcomes.
Methods: After exclusion criteria were applied, the study
included data for 9,211 encounters from 7,955 patients. PP utilization was
defined as having activated and used the patient portal system, MyChart, at
least once. Sociodemographic characteristics included urbanicity, age, race,
ethnicity, language, employment, and primary insurer. Clinical outcomes
included length of hospital stay during procedure, 30-day return to the
emergency department, 30-day readmission and being discharged somewhere
other than home. Results: Being older than 65, non-White,
unemployed, non-English speaking, male, not-partnered, uninsured or publicly
insured (Medicaid, Medicare and under 65 years of age, or other government
insurance), and living in a rural environment were all risk factors for
decreased PP utilization among surgical spine patients. A one-risk factor
decrease in the number of social risk factors was associated with a 78%
increase in the odds of PP utilization [odds ratio (OR): 1.78; 95% CI:
1.69-1.87; p < 0.001]. Patients not utilizing the portal at the time of
their procedure had higher odds of 30-day readmission (OR: 1.59; 95% CI:
1.26-2.00), discharge somewhere other than home (OR: 2.41, 95% CI:
1.95-2.99), and increased length of hospital stay (geometric mean ratio:
1.21; 95% CI: 1.12-1.30) compared to those who utilized it.
Conclusions: In patients undergoing spine procedures, PPs
are not equally utilized amongst different sociodemographic groups. PP
utilization is also associated with better outcomes. Interventions aimed at
increasing PP uptake may improve care for certain patients.

## P311: Impact of measures to fight the COVID-19 pandemic on posterior

Rodolfo Gomes Dias

1

 and Mohammad Zarrabian

2

Spine Surgery Division, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Winnipeg

Introduction: The first description of a disc herniation causing

with a herniated disc, mostly resolves nonoperatively; but some patients
whose conservative management fails, surgical interventions can be
considered. The pandemic caused by COVID-19 considerably affected elective
surgeries in the country, but there are no studies that show its influence

32.005%, 26.670%, 38.732% and 15.017% in the North, Northeast, Southeast,
South and Midwest respectively. With a cost reduction of 28,731%.
Conclusion: There was an overall reduction of 29,688% of
LSPD during the pandemic in Brazil, with the most affected region being the
North region, with a reduction of 42,234% (p < 0.05). It is extremely
important to analyze these data to identify the impact of the COVID-19
pandemic on the procedure studied. This data, may assist the competent
authorities in identifying and correcting discrepancies and reduction of the
procedure studied caused by the COVID-19 pandemic in different Brazilian

## P313: Functional paraspinal muscle area at L3 in the diagnosis of
sarcopenia: establishing normative data in the Asian population and
proposing new surrogate measurements of muscle mass

Julia Ng

1

 and Jacob Oh

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Tan Tock Seng Hospital, Singapore,
Singapore

Introduction: Low back pain and sarcopenia are highly prevalent
conditions in the elderly with significant correlations. A diagnosis of
sarcopenia requires both structural and functional measurements. Our study
sought to investigate two potential estimates of sarcopenia of paraspinal
muscles from routine imaging and to establish normative data for these
indices for the Asian population. Materials and Methods: 250
consecutive non-reformatted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) lumbosacral
spine studies of patients performed at our institution from 1 October 2018
to 31 December 2018 were reviewed in the unenhanced T2 sequence in the axial
slice closest to the level of the lumbar three (L3) superior end plate. For
each patient, bilateral multifidus and erector spinae muscles were measured
using two measurements each: functional muscle area (muscle without
intra-muscular fat) and total muscle area (muscle with its intramuscular
fat) were objectively measured using Fiji, an open-source biological image
analysis software8. Two ratios relevant to functional muscle area
were obtained: functional-to-total muscle area (fCSA:tCSA), and
intramuscular fat-to-functional muscle area (IFA:fCSA; i.e. Goutallier
staging). Multiple regression analysis was done to analyse the correlation
between symptoms of low back pain and the ratios of functional muscle area
for each of the 4 muscle groups, adjusting for age and gender.
Results: 166 patients were included in the study, with 63
aged ≥ 65 years old and 110 reporting symptoms of low back pain during the
scan. Gender distribution was equal. After adjusting for age and gender, our
study found no significant correlation between the presence of low back pain
and neither the fCSA:tCSA ratio nor the Goutallier staging for all 4
paraspinal muscles studied (p values > 0.05 for all measurements). Both
age and gender were significantly correlated to both ratios for all 4
paraspinal muscles (p < 0.05 for all ratios), except for the left ES
Goutallier staging ratio, where the effect of gender was not significant (p
= 0.295). Age- and gender-specific normative data for the two ratios were
further obtained. Older females consistently had the lowest fCSA:tCSA and
highest IFA:fCSA ratios across all 4 paraspinal muscles.
Conclusion: Our study is the first to describe normative
functional paraspinal muscle area data at the L3 level for the Asian
population. We show that functional paraspinal muscle area is poorly
correlated with the presence of low back pain, but is strongly related to
both age and gender. We propose a new measurement incorporating the extent
of myosteatosis, akin to the Goutallier staging of rotator cuff muscles, as
surrogate for muscle area in the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

## P314: Utility of seated lateral radiographs for the assessment of
degenerative spondylolisthesis

Tariq Issa

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Qudratallah Qadiri

1

, Caroline Zaworski

1

, Henley Spracklen

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Gregory Schroeder

1

, and Joseph Lee

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: The clinical heterogeneity in degenerative
spondylolisthesis (DS) requires multiple imaging view to assess for the
degree of vertebral translation, loss of disc space, slip angle, and the
presence of instability. Traditional dynamic flexion and extension
radiographs have been demonstrated to have poor reliability for detection of
instability, are often pain-limited, and are not possible in patients with
limited mobility. While supine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used for
preoperative planning and traditional four view radiographs may offer
information regarding DS, traditional protocols may expose patients to
unnecessary radiation at repeated office visits. Therefore, the primary
objective of this study was to evaluate which radiographic images and are
most important for the detection of DS severity and instability.
Material and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted
of all patients who received a clinical diagnosis of DS by a single provider
from January 2021 to May 2022. All patients receive baseline standing
lateral upright, lateral flexion, and seated flexion radiographs during
their office visits. Slip measurement parameters were collected from all
radiographs and MRI, when available. Angular instability was defined as a
change of at least 10 degrees, and translation instability was defined as a
change in vertebral translation of at least 8%. DS was classified according
to Meyerding and CARDS classifications. Univariate ANOVA was utilized to
compare continuous imaging parameters between images, and paired chi-square
tests were utilized to compare categorical variables. Results:
A total of 136 patients were included in this review. Most spondylolisthesis
occurred at L4-L5 (78.7%), followed by L5-S1 (11.8%), and L3-L4 (9.6%).
Seated flexion (Si) and standing flexion (Flex) radiographs revealed the
greatest degree of slip percentage (16.0% and 16.7%), while supine MRI
revealed the lowest slip percentage (12.2%). Seated flexion and standing
flexion radiographs produced more kyphosis (4.66 and 4.97 degrees,
respectively) than standing upright and MRI (7.19 and 7.20, respectively) (p
< 0.001). Seated flexion performed similarly to standing flexion in
identifying slip percentage, slip angle, and detecting the presence of disc
space collapse or kyphotic angulation (p > 0.05). Comparable numbers of
patients were classified in each CARDS (CARDS A, 19.1%; vs 18.4% CARDS B,
21.3% vs 24.3%; CARDS C, 47.1% vs. 40.4%; CARDS D, 12.5% vs 16.9%, p =
0.602) or Meyerding subgroup. Combination of seated flexion or standing
flexion with MRI performed better in detecting translational instability
than when combined with lateral upright films (31.5% vs 20.2%, p = 0.041,
and 28.1% vs 14.6%, p = 0.014, respectively). However, there was no
difference between seated flexion or standing flexion in detecting
translational or angular instability (all, p > 0.20).
Conclusion: Standing upright films do not provide any
additional information in the detection of DS and expose patients to
unnecessary radiation. The detection of instability may be reserved for
detection using MRI that will likely be indicated pre-operatively and may
combined with a single seated flexion radiograph rather dynamic
flexion/extension radiographs.

## P315: Dynamic standing lateral X-rays used to detect instability in
patients with lumbar spondylolisthesis: how accurate is the standard
technique? A modification aimed to obtain more precise results

Tuna Pehlivanoglu

1

, Bahadir Gokcen

2

, Gorkem Muratoglu

3

, Tugay Yagci

1

, O. Nuri Eroglu

1

, and Cagatay Ozturk

1

1

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery, Liv Hospital Ulus, Liv Spine Center
certified by AOSpine, Istanbul, Turkey

2

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery, Liv Hospital Vadi, Liv Spine Center
certified by AOSpine, Istanbul, Turkey

3

Dept. of Orthopaedic Surgery, Istinye Uni. Liv Hospital, Liv Spine
Center certified by AOSpine, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Surgical decision making based on the level of
instability in patients with lumbar spondylolisthesis is of crucial
importance. However, no consensus exists in terms of the ideal radiographic
modality for the most accurate detection of instability, while standard
standing lateral dynamic (flexion-extension) X-rays (SSLDXR), which are
extremely subjective and totally dependend on patients’ physical and
cognitive abilities, are the most frequently used method to evaluate lumbar
instability. Hence, these functional X-rays might provide variable results.
The aim of the present study was to assess, if a modified version of
traditional dynamic X-rays might provide higher accuracy of instability
detection, together with more precise measurement of parameters used to
define instability (ST > 3 mm / > 8%, SA > 20°, PVO > 5°).
Methods: 37 consecutive patients with an average age of
68.7, who had a diagnosis of lumbar spondylolisthesis at the level L3-L4
were enrolled. They underwent first SSLDXR, and then the same X-rays were
taken as the patients in standing position leaned on a chair fixed to the
ground while doing the flexion and extension movements (modified standing
lateral dynamic X-Ray (mSLDXR)). Segmental angulation (SA), sagittal
translation (ST), posterior vertebral opening (PVO), lumbar lordosis and
rates of clinically detected instability were calculated and compared
between SSLDXR and its modified version. Results: Mean SA of
the SSLDXR and mSLDXR were 8.4°(3.8°-22.4°) and 14.9° (10.6°-31.2°) (p <
0.001). Mean ST of the SSLDXR and mSLDXR were 5.4% (4.3%-8.7%) and 10.2%
(7.4%-14.1%) (p < 0.001). Mean PVO of the SSLDXR and mSLDXR were
-2.7°(-6.1°-5.2°) and 5.2° (0.4°-6.8°) (p < 0.001). All parameters showed
significant difference between the two modalities. Average instability
detection rate of the SSLDXR and mSLDXR were 32.4% (12/37) and 78.3% (28/37)
(p < 0.001) underlining the superiority of the modification. Mean LL in
flexion of the SSLDXR and mSLDXR were 29.1° (15.2°-40.8°) and 18.4°
(4.6°-32.4°) (p = 0.003), while no significant difference was detected in
terms of LL in extension. As a result of the correlation analysis a
significant negative correlation was detected between LL in flexion and
differences of SA, ST and PVO, while no significant correlation was detected
between LL in extension and any of the parameters of instability.
Conclusion: Using the chair fixed to the ground a physical
assistive device and as a hinge point for lumbar flexion, provided a forced
lumbar movement, resulting in the provocation of the abnormal lumbar
mobility caused by lumbar instability due to spondylolisthesis. Hence,
radiographic parameters regarding the instability (SA, ST, PVO), which are
hindered by utilizing standard technique, are more pronounced are less
biased. This study concluded, that as compared to SSLDXR, by using the
mSLDXR technique, more precise values regarding the lumbar instability could
be obtained resulting in a superior rate of instability detection,
preventing cases that could be missed as a result of patients’ physical or
cognitive incapabilities leading to biased results if assessed for
instability with SSLDXR.

## P316: Relationship between lumbar disc herniation and sedimentation sign
in upright magnetic resonance images

Kishan Patel

1

, Seung Min Son

2

, Qiwen Zhang

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, and Zorica Buser

3

1
Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine,
Los Angeles, United States

2
Orthopaedic Surgery, Yangsan Hospital, Pusan
National University, Busan, South Korea

3

Grossman School of Medicine, Orthopaedic Surgery, New York, United
States

Introduction: The nerve root sedimentation sign is a
radiological sign that can serve as a predictor of lumbar spinal stenosis
(LSS) in symptomatic patients on supine and upright MRIs. Pathogenesis of a
positive sedimentation sign is hypothesized to occur due to compression of
the spinal canal. While the sedimentation sign has been seen in cases of
non-specific lower back pain, there are few studies determining the presence
of the sedimentation sign in other causes of spinal canal compression
besides LSS. Lumbar disc herniation can cause compression of the spinal
canal leading to radiculopathy. This study’s goal was to determine the
relationship between lumbar disc herniation and a positive nerve root
sedimentation sign on upright kinematic MRI patients. Material and
Methods: T2-weighted axial upright kMRI images were obtained of
100 patients with the presence of disc herniation in at least one lumbar
disc between L1/L2 and L4/L5. Sedimentation sign, spinal canal
anterior-posterior (AP) diameter, and disc height were measured. Size of
disc herniation, type of herniation, and zone of herniation were evaluated.
A positive sedimentation sign was defined as having either the majority of
nerve roots running ventrally or centrally in the canal or conglomeration of
the nerve roots at the mid-disc level. Herniation types were defined as
either no herniation, disc bulge, protrusion, extrusion, or sequestration.
Zones of herniation were categorized as either central, lateral, or far
lateral per MSU classification. T-test and Chi-Square test were performed to
determine measurements’ significance. Cohen’s kappa values were calculated
for intra-observer reliability. Results: The kappa value of
intra-observer reliability was 0.915. The kappa value of disc levels with a
negative sedimentation sign were seen more frequently (n = 326, 65.2%) than
those with a positive sedimentation sign (n = 174, 34.8%). A positive
sedimentation sign was seen most frequently at the L4/L5 (n = 50, 50%) disc
level. The incidence of Grade IV and V Pfirrmann grades were higher in
patients with a positive sedimentation sign at all disc levels. The spinal
canal AP diameter was found to be significantly decreased at the L3/L4 and
L4/L5 level in patients with a positive sedimentation sign. At all levels,
discs with a negative sedimentation sign were more likely to have no
herniation compared to those with a positive sign. Discs with a positive
sedimentation sign were seen to have a larger average size of disc
herniation compared to those with a negative sign at all levels. The
Chi-square statistic was significant at the L2/L3, L3/L4, and L4/L5 disc
levels for a relationship between positivity of the sedimentation sign and
type of disc herniation. No relationship was seen between herniation zones
and positivity of sedimentation sign. Conclusion: In the
current study a relationship between disc herniation and a positive
sedimentation sign in the lumbar spine was seen. Patients with a positive
sedimentation sign were seen to have larger disc herniations and more
severely degenerated discs. Further studies may elucidate if a positive
sedimentation sign indicates improved post-operative outcomes in discectomy
patients.

Retrospective chart review of consecutive charts was performed for cervical
spine MRIs at a VA medical center and its surrounding VA clinics between
January 2014 and June 2018. An American College of Radiology (ACR)
appropriateness score between 1 and 9 was determined for each MRI based on
duration and location of pain, accompanying symptoms, red flags (e.g.
incontinence, fever, chills, weight loss), and physical exam findings.
Results: 332 cases from neurologists (n = 24), orthopaedic
surgeons (n = 76), primary care physicians (n = 203), pain medicine
physicians (n = 21) and physiatrists (n = 8) were reviewed. Orthopaedic
surgeons ordered MRIs most appropriately with an average ACR appropriateness
score of 8.4 (p < 0.05). Orthopaedic surgeons had more comprehensive
physical exams, as they tested range of motion (p < 0.005) and sensory (p
< 0.005), performed a graded motor exam (p < 0.005), and utilized
provocative maneuvers such as Spurling’s test (p < 0.005) and
differentiating maneuvers such as Tinel’s test (p < 0.005) more often
than other specialties. Treatment outcomes did not vary by physician
specialty or ACR appropriateness score, except for patients of pain medicine
physicians who received interventional pain management more often (p =
0.000). Conclusion: Orthopaedic surgeons utilize MRI most
appropriately and have more comprehensive physical exams. These findings
suggest a need for increased physician education on what indicates an
appropriate MRI in order to improve the use of resources and further protect
patient risk-benefit profiles. Further research elucidating factors to
minimize negative findings in “appropriate” MRIs is indicated.

## P319: Decay variance processing for multi-echo MRI in diagnosing
intervertebral disc degeneration - First in human results

Kyle Sheldrick

1

 and Ashish Diwan

1

1

University of New South Wales, Kensington, Australia

Introduction: Intervertebral disc degeneration is a cause of
back pain, however current diagnostic techniques in clinical practice
perform poorly. The work of Corniola et al demonstrated that changes in
Pfirrmann grade using T2 weighted MRI correlates poorly with patients’ self
rated levels of pain and disability. Further it does not predict patient
response to surgical intervention. We have previously described and
published “Decay Variance”, a non-relaxometry post-processing technique for
multi-echo T2 data, which correlated strongly with histological disc
degeneration in rabbits. Here we describe the first pilot usage in humans.
Material and Methods: We performed the Decay Variance scan
in adults with back pain and healthy controls. All participants with back
pain met inclusion criteria including: meeting the NIH definition of chronic
low back pain; pain present on > 50% of days over preceding 6 months,
other potential radiologically identified causes of back pain excluded on
structural MRI performed in the previous 12 months; aged at least 18.
Results: 15 participants were recruited, 12 with back pain
and 3 without back pain, 1 to 1 age matching of controls was planned but
abandoned due to the permanent closure of our MRI provider during the
COVID-19 pandemic. Participants with higher self-rated back pain severity
had worse Decay Variance scores. Participants with severe back pain (≥ 7/10)
had worse Decay Variance scores than those without (≤ 6/10), 3.03 ± 0.58 vs
1.87 ± 0.47. Self-rated back pain also correlated moderately strongly with
Decay Variance score using a Pearson correlation co-efficient (r^2 = 0.44, p
= 0.007). Conclusion: The results of this first in human pilot
study suggest that patients with more severe back pain have worse Decay
Variance values in their intervertebral discs, however caution is needed in
interpreting the results. The selection of participants, especially given
the NIH definition of chronicity limits the generalizability of this
finding, especially in regards to effect size and coefficient of
correlation. Further a cross sectional design, especially one without
patient matching such as ours, cannot address causality and is vulnerable to
residual confounding. The small sample size makes the estimates of effect
size imprecise. We have commenced a large longitudinal cohort study, funded
by the Australian government, to overcome these limitations, expected to be
complete 2024.

## P320: Signal intensity changes of the second sacrum on MRI targeting the
lumbar spine indicate sacral insufficiency fracture

Kohei Ohta

1

, Hiroki Ikuchi

2

, Takayuki Ogawa

3

, and Akihiro Nagamachi

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Yoshinogawa Medical Center, Tokushima,
Japan

2

Orthopedic Surgery, Takamatsu Municipal Hospital, Kagawa,
Japan

3

Orthopedic Surgery, Sakaide Kaisei Hospital, Kagawa, Japan

Introduction: The incidence of sacral insufficiency fracture
(SIF) has been reported to be 1.0% to 1.8% in at-risk patient populations.
Patients with SIF most commonly complain low back pain, buttock pain, hip
pain or other symptoms similar to the lumbar spine diseases. Diagnosis of
SIF often delayed because appropriate diagnostic imaging studies sometimes
lack due to the characteristics of the symptoms. Tamaki reported signal
changes in the second sacrum on sagittal view of MRI targeting the lumbar
spine indicated SIF in 4 patients. This finding will help early diagnosis of
SIF. The purpose of this study was to clarify the clinical features of SIF
and verify the usefulness of the signal changes in the second sacrum on
sagittal view of MRI targeting the lumbar spine in diagnosis of SIF.
Material and Methods: Forty-two patient with SIF
participated in this study. There were 6 male and 36 females and their mean
age was 81 years. Mean bone mineral density was 0.681g/cm2. Cause
of injury and initial symptom extracted from the electric medical record.
Twenty-nine of 42 patients underwent MRI targeting the lumbar spine at the
first visit. We observed signal intensity changes of T1-weighted image,
T2-weighted image and Short T1 Inversion Recovery (STIR) on MRI sagittal
view. Results: The causes of injury were falling down in 28
cases (66.7%), falling in 4 cases (9.5%), farm work in 2 cases (4.8%),
massage in 1 case (2.4%) and unknown in 7 cases (16.7%). The initial
symptoms were low back pain in 27 cases (64.3%), buttock pain in 21 cases
(50%), leg pain in 6 cases (14.3%), hip pain in 8 cases (19.0%) and sacral
pain in 4 cases (9.5%). Signal intensity changes of the second sacrum on MRI
sagittal view were observed in all 29 patients. Low signal intensity of
T1-weighted image was observed in all patients. High signal intensity, low
signal intensity and both high and low signal intensity on T2-weighted
images were observed in 11 (37.9%), 14 (48.3%) and 4 patients (13.8%),
respectively. High signal intensity changes on STIR image were observed in
all 29 patients. Conclusion: Linstrom et al. reported an
anatomical and biomechanical analysis showing that the horizontal component
of the fracture seems to develop at a later stage after loss of support of
the central sacrum from the laterally positioned vertical fracture in the
sagittal plane. The loss of lateral sacral alar support causes the entire
weight of the upper body to be longitudinally transferred down the central
portion of the sacral bodies, which include the second sacrum. We consider
that signal changes at the second sacrum on lumbar MRI indicate an
insufficiency fracture or bone marrow lesion caused by this mechanism. The
initial symptoms of SIF are similar to those of lumbar spine disease. Signal
intensity changes on sagittal view of the second sacrum of MRI targeting the
lumbar spine was a valuable finding in early diagnosis of SIF.

## 1537

## P321: Discrepancies between radiologist and spine surgeon interpretations
of cervical and lumbar stenosis

Graysen Petersen-Fitts

1

, Edwin Chaharbakhshi

2

, John France

2

, Sanford Emery

2

, Shari Cui

2

, and Scott Daffner

2

1

Bluegrass Orthopaedics, Lexington, United States

2

Department of Orthopaedics, West Virginia University, Morgantown,
United States

Introduction: Previous studies have demonstrated poor interrater
reliability of imaging interpretation between surgeons of various
specialties and radiologists for a variety of pathologic conditions.
Discrepancies in radiologic interpretations can lead to diagnostic
frustration and difficulty formulating treatment plans. Moreover,
third-party payors often rely on documented radiology reports rather than
surgeons’ independent interpretation of imaging studies (and never review
the actual images), which can impact insurance authorization for surgery or
reimbursement. Ultimately, conflicting radiologic interpretations may
negatively impact patient care. The purpose of this study was to evaluate
the rate of and degree to which radiologists and spine surgeons differ in
interpreting magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in the setting of
cervical and lumbar spinal stenosis. Material and Methods: A
retrospective review was performed at a single academic institution of 100
consecutive patients undergoing decompressive surgery of either cervical or
lumbar spine in 2018. Patients’ documented preoperative MRI interpretation
from both the radiologist and the orthopaedic spine surgeon were compared.
Degree of pathology was classified as “mild,” “moderate,” or “severe.”
Demographic data was also recorded. Outcomes included the frequency of
discrepancies as well as the degree of discrepancy (ie “mild” vs
“moderate”). Chi squared analysis was performed to evaluate for differences
between observed and expected outcomes. Results: A total of 100
patients were included (49 males) including 44 cervical and 56 lumbar
studies. Discrepancies were identified in 65 cases (65%). There was no
statistically significant association between patient age, gender, or BMI
and whether a discrepancy existed. There was a trend toward discrepancies
being more common when interpreting cervical MRI than lumbar (p = 0.063).
There were 14 instances (21.5%) of two-grade discrepancy where radiologists
interpreted pathology as “mild” and the spine surgeon interpreted the same
pathology as “severe.” Conclusion: Our data found that
disagreements in MRI interpretation between orthopaedic spine surgeons and
radiologists occur more often than not. Moreover, the discrepancies were
often two-grades, with spine surgeons rating pathology as more severe.
Although this study was not designed to elucidate the reasons behind
discrepancies, we hypothesize that this is due to the spine surgeons also
having information from the physical examination of the patient when
interpreting imaging studies. Given the implications of these discrepancies
including denial or delay of care by third-party payors, we propose that
when such differences exist, payors should defer to the interpretation
provided by the physician who has actually examined the patient.

## P322: Evaluating the safe zone for lumbar pedicle screws: a 3D image
analysis using virtual screws

Tony Tannoury

1

, Henry Hojoon Seo

1

, Aziz Saade

1

, Bachir Atallah

2

, Mirna Chahine

2

, and Chadi Tannoury

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston,
United States

2

Lebanese University, Beirut, Lebanon

Introduction: Pedicle screw breach (PSB) is not uncommon
following lumbar instrumentation, and in some instances, it may lead to
vascular and/or neurologic complications. Previous literature suggested that
screws crossing the vertebral midline on an anterior-posterior (AP)
radiograph (or midsagittal on CT) are concerning for medial pedicle
breach.Our primary aim was to map out the safe zones (SZ) of bilateral
pedicle instrumentation and their relationship at each lumbar vertebral
level. Our secondary aim was to evaluate the presence of SZs’ intersection
at each lumbar level, denoting safe midline pedicle screws crossing not
otherwise associated with medial pedicle breach. Material and
Methods: CT scans of 51 patients were randomly selected from “The
Cancer Imaging Archive” (TCIA) online database for analysis. The Sectra 3D
Spine software was used to create 3D renderings, place virtual screws, and
make measurements. At each lumbar vertebra, the right and left pedicle
corridors were mapped. At each pedicle, two screw positions were templated,
the “medial limit screw” (MLS) and the “lateral limit screw” (LLS). Each
limit screw was the most extreme position that the screw could exist in
without causing a medial or lateral breach. The safe zone was defined as the
zone between MLS and LLS. Measurements were taken for each level (between
L1-L5) and side (Left, Right). Results: A total of 253 lumbar
vertebrae from 51 patients (mean age 53.1, 56.9% male) were included. Two
vertebrae from two patients were removed for poor image quality. Out of the
506 screw positions analyzed in our study, 97.4% had overlapping SZ and
crossed the midplane without medial pedicle breach. The significant factors
(p < 0.01) for safe midplane-crossing screws included: the screw length
(L1-L5); laterality of the screw entry point (L1-L4); and pedicle diameter
(L2 and L5). Conclusion: A midline crossing pedicle screw on a
lumbar AP radiograph is not necessarily indicative of a medial pedicle screw
breach. Anatomical (i.e. larger pedicles diameter) and technical (i.e.
longer screws, and lateral entry points) factors allow for safety zone
intersections and indicate safe midline crossing by pedicle screws.

## P323: Management protocol of patients with lumbar spinal stenosis, using
the qualitative grading as a tool

Jayprakash Modi

1,2

 and Pratikkumar Prajapati

2

1

Orthopaedic, Nutan Medical College, Mehsansa, India

2

Orthopaedic, B J Medical College, Ahmedabad, India

Objectives: Several parameters exist for assessment of lumbar
spinal stenosis (LSS) but these parameters lack clinical correlation. To
formulate a protocol for management of these group of patients using the
qualitative grading as a tool. Materials and methods: A
prospective study was undertaken using the qualitative grading on magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) to assess the clinical outcome of LSS at a single
level. Irrespective of the grade every patient underwent a minimum 3 months
period of conservative management after which depending on the Oswestry
disability index (ODI) and visual analogue scale (VAS) for pain he was
grouped into success or failure and the failed patients were advised for

conservative group, out of these 57 were operated of which only nine did not
match the success criteria, while the other four either refused surgery or
were lost to follow-up. In grades A1 to 3, only two patients failed
conservative trial while from A4 to D, there was a gradual decline in
success of conservative trial. Conclusion: Qualitative grading
is a useful tool in LSS and correlates with the clinical outcome and to
decision making of these patients.

## 1671

## P324: Evaluation of axonal injury with filtered diffusion weighted
magnetic resonance imaging in cervical spondylotic myelopathy

Saman Shabani

1

, Shekar N. Kurpad

1

, and Matthew Budde

1

1

Neurological Surgery, Medical College of Wisconsin, Wauwatosa,
United States

Introduction: In cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM), axonal
injury is believed to be the main correlate with functional outcome.
Although diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is sensitive to microscopic
pathologies, its utility has been limited in CSM in setting of substantial
edema or myelomalacia. The purpose of this study was to assess the spinal
cord diffusion measures in patients with CSM using a new filtered diffusion
weighted imaging (fDWI) technique that aims to reduce the confounding
effects of edema and extracellular water on the measured diffusion values.
Materials and Methods: Twenty-one patients with CSM
underwent pre-surgical fDWI and DTI scans on 3T MRI system. DTI was obtained
with 25 directions at a b-value of 800 s/mm2. fDWI employed
spinal cord-optimized diffusion weighting along 26 directions with a
“filter” b-value of 2000 s/mm2 and “probe” max b-value of 1000
s/mm2. Parallel diffusivity metrics obtained from DTI and
fDWI were compared to one another and with metrics derived from
T2-weighted MRI including relative signal changes and lesion
size. Results: The parallel apparent diffusion coefficient
(fADC||) acquired from fDWI at the level of maximum
compression (-15.16 ± 12.07%) decreased relative to most cranial slice and
had a larger change than axial diffusivity (AD) acquired by DTI (-3.18 ±
14.41%). A linear regression identified a significant relationship between
AD and T2 metrics (r2 = 0.453, p = 0.05) whereas
fADC|| was not significantly related to T2 metrics
(r2 = 0.069, p = 0.70). AD was significantly increased at
spinal cord slices with T2 intensities (t(81) = 1.65, p = 0.05) compared to
slices without T2 abnormalities, whereas fADC||was not
significantly different between spinal cord slices with or without T2
abnormalities. Conclusions: The results demonstrate that filter
diffusion encoding reduces the coupling between T2 spinal cord changes and
diffusion measurements that are presumed to reflect extracellular water and
can considerably affects DTI metrics. Future studies evaluating the
relationships with functional status and outcomes in a larger cohort of CSM
patients would be beneficial.

## P325: MRI-tractography as a method to predict neurological recovery in
patients with cervical spinal cord injury

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Ievgenii Slynko

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, and Yurii Derkach

1

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The achievement of scientific and technical
progress in recent decades, the introduction of computer and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) into clinical practice made it possible to review
both tactical approaches to the treatment of neurologically complicated
cervical spine injuries, as well as the criteria for predicting the
long-term results of therapy. Currently, MRI is the gold standard in the
diagnosis of traumatic injuries of the spinal cord in patients with
neurological deficits. This is due to the high informativeness of
visualization of soft tissue structures, in particular the spinal cord, the
possibility of detecting damage to the disc-ligamentous apparatus of the
spinal column, and the absence of ionizing radiation. However, the data of
the literature ambiguously interpret the correlation between MRI results and
the degree of neurological disorders. The idea of our study is the primary
assessment of the prognostic features of MRI tractography in patients with
severe subaxial cervical spine and spinal cord injury. Material and
Methods: The clinical group consisted of 5 patients hospitalized
in the Department of Spine Surgery Romodanov Neurosurgery Institute during
period from April to July 2019 with severe traumatic injury of the cervical
spine and spinal cord. MRI was performed in the following modes: T1W, T2W,
FLAIR, STIR, T2W FFE, CSF flow and DTI in 5-7 days after surgery. The
dynamics of neurological disorders regression were evaluated according to
the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord
Injury. The level of spinal canal traumatic stenosis of the was determined
by SCT both before and after surgical correction. Due to the small clinical
group, statistical processing of the obtained digital indicators was not
performed. The main task was to identify general patterns in order to
determine the direction of further detailed studies. Results:
Spinal cord edema at the damage level was observed in 100% of patients, that
corresponded to the level of neurological disorders. The presence of
hemorrhagic component was detected in 3 patients, while post-traumatic
spinal stenosis was: more than 50% - 1 patient, up to 50% - 1 patient and
less than 25% - 1 patient. Spinal cord parenchyma edema was accompanied by
varying degrees of compression of the cerebrospinal spaces, from subtotal to
total, with the presence or absence of a hemorrhagic component that did not
affect the intensity of cerebrospinal fluid flow disorders. Evaluation of
DTI results showed a moderate inverse relationship between fractional
anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) indicators. In 2 patients, a
regression of neurological disorders was registered. Restoration of
sensory-motor functions did not correlate with the degree of compression of
the spinal canal or the nature of changes in the parenchyma of the spinal
cord, but was noted in patients with maximum FA values and low MD.
Conclusion: Tractography is an informative predictor of the
regression of neurological disorders in patients with severe spine and
spinal cord injury. Further studies are needed to identify the optimal
timing of its implementation and to establish diagnostically significant
values of anisotropic diffusion indices.

## P326: Incidence and predictors of postoperative wound infection in the

Sameh Abolfotouh

, Mohamed Khattab

, Atiq Uz Zaman

, Omar Alnori

Study Design: Retrospective cohort study.
Objectives: This study aimed to estimate the incidence of

## P327: Intraoperative topical antibiotics administration in instrumented

multicenter comparative analysis and literature review

Giovanni Barbagli

1

, Elisabetta Peppucci

1

, Mariano Vitelli

1

, Nicoletta Gargiuoli

1

, Giulio Wembagher

2

, Matteo Capozza

, Giuseppe Cavallo

, Alexander Evins

, Alessandro DiChirico

, Stefano Romoli

, and Sandro Carletti

4

Neurosurgery, Weill Cornell Medical College, New York, United

Introduction: The use of topical antibiotic (i.e. vancomycin) in
addition to intravenous administration of antibiotics has been reported as
an effective tool in reducing the rate of surgical site infections (SSI),
which could be very serious complications, in particular in fusion spine
surgery. However, it is not widely used yet. The recent trend in fusion
surgical spine procedures carries along an increased rate of revision
surgeries that are associated with more durotomies and prolonged surgical
length. Both these factors are well-known predictors of SSI; other important
point is an increasing incidence of well-known risk factors such as obesity,
diabetes and smoking. Moreover, SSIs may require surgical debridement, which
leads to higher postoperative morbidity and mortality. The aim of the study
is to evaluate the rate of infections between different cohorts, treated in
different high-volume centers in Italy and estimate the efficacy in reducing
SSIs when a topical antibiotic is added to a routinary intravenous one.

Mann-Whitney U test with independent samples. The analysis to assess any

the two groups (p = 0.09). 71.6% of patients received intraoperative

the non-vancomycin group the rate of infection was 16%. The use of
vancomycin was found to be associated with a lower occurrence of infectious
post-operative complications, with a very high statistical significance (p =
0.001). Conclusion: The intrawound application of vancomycin
powder in addition to intravenous administration of antibiotics may
significantly reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) after
spinal surgeries. Further studies with larger sample size and high quality
are needed to provide more evidence.

and postop antibiotics, length of hospital stay (LOS), reoperation, and
mortality. Long-term antibiotics were those in use > 6 months.
Results: Ninety-six consecutive patients with hematogenous
vertebral osteomyelitis were included. The median age was 59.5 years; 64%
were male; median BMI was 27.7. Most infections occurred in the lumbar
region (44.2%), followed by the thoracic spine (37.9%), more than two spinal
regions (10%) and cervical spine (8.9%). Biopsy was performed in 94.1% of
cases and returned positive cultures in 93.4%. Of the cultures taken, MRSA
accounted for 9%; MSSA, 26%; Streptococcus species, 12%; other gram-positive
bacteria, 23%; gram-negative, 17%; fungal, 2.6%; and 11.5% of cultures
returned no growth. Sixty-one patients ultimately underwent surgery to treat
their disease. Of the 61-undergoing surgery, 41% underwent secondary
surgeries due to a heavy wound burden of necrotic tissue and pus, or the
failure of multimodal care including antibiotics and debridement. Of
these, 57% of the patients had undergone a trial of
antibiotics preoperatively, with a mean course of 37.2 ± 25.7
days. Postoperative antibiotics were prescribed to all
patients, with a mean length of 70.2 days. Mean LOS was 17.9 ± 15.3 days.
Additionally, 51.6% of the patients were prescribed long-term antibiotic
therapy. The overall mortality rate was 3.1%. All three patients underwent
surgery. Demographic and clinical characteristics of the deceased patients
include a mean age of 64 years, majority male (66.7%), who had major
comorbidities such as diabetes, anemia, obstructive lung disease and
hypertension. Major cause of death was septic shock. Major post-infection
sequelae occurred in 24.5% of patients. Patients suffering sequelae had a
mean age of 69.3 years, were mostly male (83%) and carried major
comorbidities including diabetes, anemia, hypertension and renal disease.
The most common sequelae were persistent infection, sepsis, and abscess.
Conclusions: The presence of major comorbidities (diabetes,
hypertension, and renal failure) appear to increase the risk of
post-infection sequelae and death. Our population included patients
hospitalized in a tertiary care center with spinal osteomyelitis. They were
therefore more likely to carry concomitant diagnoses such as epidural
abscess, resulting in a high rate of surgical intervention. A future study
with a larger sample size utilizing logistic regression would be able to
identify significant risk factors both for hematogenous infection itself,
and for failure of non-operative and initial operative care. In the
meanwhile, available data suggests that patients presenting with
hematogenous osteomyelitis be followed closely as failure of non-operative
management was high.
