## P330: Comparison of outcomes in thoracolumbar fusion wound closure done
by spine surgeons versus plastic surgeons in varying levels of vertebral
fusion

Jini Jeon

1

, Aaron Hui

1

, Henry Hoang

1

, Dan Berman

1

, Ananth Eleswarapu

1

, and Jonathan Krystal

1

1

Orthopedics, Montefiore Medical Center, Bronx, United
States

Introduction: Plastic surgeons are often involved in closure of
complex thoracolumbar fusion surgeries performed by spine surgeons.
Indications for plastic surgeon involvement is not standardized. A possible
indication that may be used is the number of spinal levels fused. This study
aims to further evaluate and compare outcomes for thoracolumbar fusion wound
closures performed by spine surgeons versus those done by plastic surgeons
across varying levels of total fused vertebrae. Material and
Methods: A retrospective cohort analysis of 301 patients who
underwent a thoracolumbar fusion at a single institution in the Bronx from
2016-2018 was performed. Demographic, surgical, and post-operative variables
were collected. The patients were placed into two cohorts: wound closure
done by a spine surgeon (S) and wound closure done by a plastic surgeon (P).
Cases were also categorized based on number of vertebrae fused: 1-2 levels,
3-6 levels, and ≥ 7 levels. The primary outcomes were length (days) of
postoperative hospital stay, and return to operating room for culture
positive infection and debridement. Our secondary outcome outcomes were
return to the emergency department (ED) within 90 days. An independent two
sample t-test assuming unequal variances was conducted to compare the
average length of postoperative hospital stay. A Fisher’s exact test of
independence was done to determine if there was a difference in rates of
returning to the operating room for culture positive infection and
debridement, revision and emergency room within 90 days.
Results: Three hundred and one patients were identified and
categorized into spine surgeon closure (N = 272), and plastic surgeon
closure (N = 29). In the S cohort: N= 186, 73, 13 were categorized into 1-2
levels, 3-6 levels, and ≥ 7 levels fused respectively. In the P cohort: N =
6, 13, and 10 cases were categorized into 1-2 levels, 3-6 levels, and ≥ 7
levels fused respectively. There was no statistically significant difference
in mean days of postoperative hospital stay between the S and P cohorts
across all levels of fusion. For return to OR for positive culture I&D,
there was statistical significance for 1-2 levels and 3-6 levels of fusion.
There was no significant statistical different between the two cohorts in
return to ED within 90 days of operation for any spinal level fusions.
Conclusion: Findings suggest that a plastic surgery wound
closure in thoracolumbar fusion does not reduce length of postoperative
hospital stay when compared to spine closure across all levels of vertebral
fusion. Plastic surgery closure was found to be non-advantageous over spine
surgeon closure with higher rates of return to OR due to infection in
shorter levels of fusion, which may be explained by patient factors not
explored in this study, such as age, BMI, smoking history, and degree of
complex anatomy. There was no difference in rates of return to ED within 90
days post-op between the cohorts across all levels. Additional studies may
be conducted to further evaluate different factors of complexity that
indicate for plastic surgery wound closure versus spine surgeon wound
closure, and patient outcomes.

## P331: Removal of instrumentation is not required to successfully treat
post-operative wound infections in most cases

Viral Patel

1

, Benjamin Mueller

1

, Amir Mehbod

1

, Manuel Pinto

1

, James Schwender

1

, Timothy Garvey

1

, John Dawson

1

, and Joseph Perra

1

1

Twin Cities Spine Center, Minneapolis, United States

Introduction: Recommendations for treating surgical site
infections (SSI) in instrumented spine cases include both removing the
implants and retaining the implants. In either case, successful treatment
means eradicating the infection and preventing its recurrence. Retaining the
implants may be advantageous because they help maintain stability. We
studied the persistence of SSI in relation to retaining or removing spinal
implants. Material and Methods: Spine surgery patients who
underwent irrigation and debridement (I&D) for a SSI were studied.
Persistence (recurrence or non-recurrence) of infection in relation to
implant status, fusion status, and patient reported outcomes were analyzed.
Results: One hundred thirty five patients were studied.
Implants were retained in 64% (87/135) of patients; 7% (6/87) had a
persistent infection. Implants were removed in 36% (48/135) of patients; 6%
(3/48) had a persistent infection. Thus, we detected no difference between
persistence with implants present versus implants removed (p = 1.0). Fifty
patients (37%) patients received irrigation and debridement (I&D) and
primary wound closure and 85 patients (63%) received I&D and
vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) treatment. There was no statistical difference
in SSI persistence between primary wound closure and VAC treatment (p =
0.15). Fusion status and persistent infection were unrelated. At minimum
one-year follow up, achieving a minimum clinically important difference
(MCID) for functional outcome was independent of recurrence or
non-recurrence of the infection. Conclusion: Persistent
infection was unrelated to the retention or removal of implants. Those with
a persistent infection were no more likely to exhibit pseudoarthrosis than
those with no persistent infection. All our patients' self-reported
functional outcomes were improved at minimum 1-year follow up.

## P332: Epidemiological and clinical characteristics of patients with

Taofeek Adeyemi

1

, Adetunji Toluse

, Mustapha F. Alimi

, and Babatunde A. Osundina

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Trauma, National Orthopaedic
Hospital Igbobi, Lagos, Nigeria

Background: Although Tuberculosis is one of the world’s oldest
disease, it is still a major public health issue in developing countries
with profound medical, social and economic impact. The objective of this
study was to investigate the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of
patients treated for spinal tuberculosis at a regional spine center in
South-west Nigeria. Methods: This study was a retrospective
observational study. We extracted data from the medical records of all cases
of spinal tuberculosis that presented at the hospital between January 2017
and December 2019. Epidemiological, clinical characteristics, imaging
findings, laboratory test results and treatment methods were recorded and
analyzed. Results: During this three-year period, 171 cases of
spinal Tuberculosis were identified. The patients’ mean age was 43 ± 15.7
years with a slight male predominance (56.1%). Axial pain was the main
clinical manifestation (81.9%); 51.5% presented with over 6 months of
symptoms. Prior history suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis was seen in
14%. The most common imaging technique was x-ray (94.2%), followed by
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (87.1%). Majority of the lesions involved the

age groups most. Late presentation and neurological impairment was seen in
majority of cases. Persistence of neurological impairment is a concern.

## P334: Significance of cutibacterium acnes in intraoperative cultures
during spinal instrumentation

Geno Tai

1,2

, Gina Suh

2

, Brian Lahr

3

, Paul Huddleston

4

, and Aaron Tande

2

1

Infectious Diseases and International Medicine, University of
Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

2

Infectious Diseases

3

Quantitative Health Sciences

4

Orthopedic Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, United States

Introduction:Cutibacterium acnesis a known
pathogen in spinal hardware infections. The ideal management for these cases
is unknown, and there is a lack of data on treatment outcomes. We described
the outcomes of cases with actual infections (AI) and clinically
insignificant (CI) cultures. Material and Methods: We performed
a retrospective study of patients aged 18 years or older who underwent
spinal fusion surgery with instrumentation and whose intraoperative tissue
culture specimens were positive for C. acnesbetween January
1, 2011, and December 31, 2020. We categorized the culture results as actual
infection (AI) or clinically insignificant (CI) based on a set
criterion.
Diagnostic Criteria for Actual Infection:
1. C. acnes was isolated from 
two
 intraoperative specimens obtained during primary or revision
instrumentation.
2.C. acnes was isolated from 
one
 intraoperative specimen, 
PLUS

a. Intraoperative purulence or secondary wound dehiscence with the implant
visible
b. Radiographic evidence of inflammation on x-ray, computed tomography,
magnetic resonance imaging, or radiolabeled scan with gallium or
technetium
c. Systemic signs of inflammation such as fever (> 38 °C) without other
recognized cause
d. Histopathology showing acute inflammation
We excluded cases of polymicrobial infection with virulent organisms
(e.g.,Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative bacteria) or
two non-virulent organisms (e.g., Coagulase-negative staphylococci,
anaerobes) to have homogeneity of cases.
We definedtreatment as receiving more than two weeks of
systemic antibiotics. The outcome of interest was an adverse event defined
as a post-operative diagnosis of spinal hardware infection either
with C. acnesor other microorganism/s or unexpected
surgery secondary to infection.
Results: There were 91 patients who had at least one
intraoperative culture positive for C. acnes during spinal instrumentation.
The median age was 59 years old (IQR 43-70). Monomicrobial infections
represented 73.6% (n = 67). Majority (87.9%, n = 80) were isolated during
revision surgeries (e.g., debridement, exchange/ addition/ removal of
hardware). There were 63 AI and 28 CI. Among those with AI, 49 (77.8%) were
treated for a median duration of 344 days (IQR 97-531). There were five
adverse outcomes during 68.6 cumulative patient-years of follow-up, with an
annual rate of 7.3% (95% CI 2.4% - 17.0%). The median time to event was 12.2
months (range, 1.9-14.6). In the 14 untreated patients with AI, two adverse
outcomes occurred over 23.0 cumulative patient-years (annual rate 8.7%, 95%
CI 1.1% - 31.4%). Among those with CI cultures (n = 28), half were treated
with antibiotics. No adverse outcome occurred among all patients with CI
cultures. Conclusion: We described the outcomes of cases with
positive C. acnesduring spinal instrumentation. The
rates of adverse outcomes for treated and untreated AI are almost similar.
We found that some AI cases were managed with hardware removal alone and had
favorable outcomes. In some instances, treating AI with oral antibiotics
alone is appropriate. There is no apparent advantage of treating CI
cultures. Our study was limited by the small number of events; thus, no
formal comparisons were made. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate
different diagnostic criteria to guide treatment strategies.

## P335: Pre-operative epidural steroid injections do not increase the risk
of post-operative infection in patients undergoing lumbar decompression or
fusion: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Yunsoo Lee

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Arun Kanhere

1

, Skylar Nahi

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Gregory Schroeder

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Jose Canseco

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Epidural corticosteroid injections (ESI) are one
of the mainstays of early nonoperative treatment for patients with lumbar
spine pathology. While many patients are responsive to nonoperative
treatment, a small number may progress to surgical management such as lumbar
decompression or fusion. Recent literature evaluating the risk of infection
following ESI after elective orthopedic surgery has produced conflicting
evidence, which has led to growing debate around the timing of pre-operative
ESI. Our primary objective was to review the literature and provide a larger
meta-analysis analyzing the temporal effects of steroid injections on the
risk of infection following lumbar spine surgery. Material and
Methods: We conducted a query of the PubMed, Embase, and Scopus
databases from inception until April 1, 2022 for studies evaluating the risk
of infection in the setting of prior spinal steroid injections in patients
undergoing lumbar spine decompression or fusion. Three meta-analyses were
conducted, (1) comparing ESI within 30-days to control, (2) comparing ESI
within 30-days to ESI between 1-3 months pre-operatively, and (3) comparing
any history of ESI to control. Tests of proportions were utilized for all
comparisons between groups. Study heterogeneity was assessed via forest
plots, and publication bias was assessed via funnel plots and qualitative
assessment with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results: Nine total
studies were included, five of which demonstrated a significant association
between pre-operative ESI and post-operative infection, while four studies
found no statistical significance at any evaluated time point. Most data
originated from large databases, but three studies evaluated institutional
data. Comparison of weighted means demonstrated no significant difference in
infection rates between the 30-day ESI group and control group (2.67% vs
1.69%, p = 0.144), 30-day ESI group and the > 30-day ESI group (2.34% vs
1.66%, p = 0.1655), or total ESI group and the control group (1.99% vs.
1.70%, p = 0.544). Heterogeneity was low for all comparisons following
sensitivity analyses (I2 = 0% in the first two analyses and
I2 = 32% in the third comparison). Conclusion:
Our meta-analysis suggests that current evidence does not implicate
pre-operative ESI on an increase in post-operative infection rates following
lumbar fusion or decompression. Operative treatment should not be delayed
due to pre-operative infection rates due to current evidence. There remains
a paucity of high-quality data in the literature evaluating the impact of
pre-operative ESI on post-operative infection rates.

reported on literature. Responsible for causing important morbidity and
causing serious long-term sequelae, this complication offers a intricated
challenge on how to manage patients and how to stratify the best therapeutic
strategy. Despite this there are some risk factors already identified like
obesity, alcoholism, smoking, diabetes and wound infection site. Study
design: Case Report Objective: Report a case of
management of spondylodiscitis on the adjacent level of instrumentation that

negative-pressure wound therapy. Along this period, she never manifested
clinic of infection. At 6 months after surgery, she presented with sudden
onset of low back pain without neurological commitment or fever associated
with peri-inflammatory signals on top of the surgical site with active
drainage that motivated hospitalization for study and treatment.

be insufficient to control the infection and often there’s a need for

obtaining bacteriological samples, as well as eventual decompression and
stabilization in order to control the infection spread and provide spinal
stability. Conclusion: The therapeutic and prognostic success
resides, above all, in a timely diagnosis and intervention and in the
periodic monitoring of the effectiveness of the instituted treatment.

## P338: Evaluation of percutaneous pedicle screw fixation in patient with

Katsunori Fukutake

Orthopedics, Toho University, Ota-ku, Tokyo, Japan

retrospectively reviewed 54 consecutive patients who underwent treatment in
our hospital for PS during 2005-2018 and followed up for at least 12 months.
Of those we excluded cases showed effectiveness to initial treatment (it was
defined fever relief and C-reactive protein (CRP) inversion in 3 weeks of
intravenous antibiotic) so that this study is a retrospective study in cases
showed initial treatment resistance. Finally, this study included 29 cases.
To evaluate the impact of PPS fixation, these cases divided into two groups,
the conservative group: 17 cases, and the PPS group: 12 cases. Since 2010,
PPS fixation has been relatively selected, but cases with poor general
condition have selected conservative treatment. Results: We
investigated the period from first visit to our hospital to fever relief,
CRP inversion, ambulation, and discharge or transfer. There is no
statistically significant difference in fever relief (p = 0.051) and CRP

and 1-year survival rate was 92%. In the C-group, 5cases died of
infarction-sepsis (3cases), acute myocardial infarction (1case), and
unknown(1case). 1-year survival rate was 71%. The P-group was relatively
high 1-year survival rate, but there is no statistically significant
difference (p = 0.354) between two groups. The rate of Discharge to home and
care facility is 58% in P-group, and 47% in C-group. And the rate of
Transfer is 33% in P-group, and 35% in C-group. Conclusion:
Present study shows that PPS fixation was effective to achieve shorten the
period to ambulation and discharge or transfer. But it was not effective to
infection control, such as fever relief and CRP inversion. This result
suggests that PPS fixation should be aggressively administered to patients
who can expect pain relief and early ambulation by PPS fixation in the
patient of PS showed resistance to initial treatment.

massive involvement. The 360° approach allows better surgical control of the

ensures a more stable fixation.

## P340: Risk factor for surgical site infection with spinal instrumentation
surgery

Shinji Tanishima

1

, Tokumitsu Mihara

1

, Chikako Takeda

1

, Masaki Yoshida

1

, Satoshi Fujiwara

1

, and Hideki Nagashima

1

1

Division of Orthopedic Surgery, Department of Sensory and Motor
Organs, School of Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Tottori University,
Yonago, Japan

Introduction: Surgical site infection (SSI) after spinal
instrumentation surgery is a serious complication, but its occurrence is
difficult to eliminate. This study aimed to examine the risk factors for SSI
at our institution. Subjects and Methods: A total of 483
patients aged 18 years or older who underwent spinal instrumentation surgery
at our hospital between January 2016 and March 2021 and who were available
for follow-up for at least 30 days were included in the study. The mean age
of the patients was 68.9 ± 14.3 years. Patient-related factors (age, gender,
malignant disease, diabetes, skin disease, hemodialysis, smoking, steroid
and immunosuppressive drug use, body mass index, albumin, total protein,
C-reactive protein (CRP), American Society of Anesthesiologists
classification, and nasal culture) and surgery (the same re-operation,
scheduled/emergency surgery, dural injury, vancomycin spray, operative time,
and blood loss) were analyzed. Statistical analysis was performed with a
univariate analysis of the infected and uninfected groups and multivariate
logistic analysis of factors that showed an associated trend (p < 0.2).
Results: Of the 483 patients, 11 of (2.3%) were infected,
with nine having a deep infection and two having a superficial infection. In
univariate analysis, the patient factors were albumin level (4.1 ± 0.6: 3.7
± 0.8 mg/dl) and CRP level (0.74 ± 1.8 mg/dl: 3.2 ± 5.3 mg/dl) in the
uninfected group and emergency surgery rate (27.8%: 63.6%) in the infected
group. In logistic analysis, emergency surgery was identified as a risk
factor for SSI (odds ratio: 4.6, 95% confidence interval 1.3-15.9, p =
0.016). Although this study was not statistical, once SSIs occurred, they
tended to occur sequentially within 3 months. Currently, SSI countermeasures
are strictly implemented at all facilities, and our hospital is also taking
measures to prevent SSI. As a result, infectious hosts, such as diabetes
mellitus and immunosuppressive drugs, were not risk factors. However,
emergency surgery was a risk factor, but this was thought to be due to the
lack of sufficient infection control measures in emergency situations.
Additionally, once SSIs occurred, they occurred one after another. This
suggests that SSIs occur when some problems occur in the perioperative
management. Conclusion: Although infection rates are not high
in spinal instrumentation surgery, infection rates are increasing in
emergency surgery, and more careful infection control measures are
needed.

## P341: Retrospective case series review of decompression versus

Brown University, Orthopaedic Surgery, Providence, United

Background Context: Spine infection including epidural abscess,
vertebral osteomyelitis, and diskitis is a major cause of morbidity in the
United States with potential for significant complications. Previous
literature has shown delayed diagnosis can increase mortality and patients
treated with decompression alone have higher complications including
reoperation rates. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to
further evaluate the outcomes of spine infection comparing decompression
versus decompression and fusion. Study Design / Setting: This
retrospective chart review was completed on patients presenting to a single
level 1, tertiary medical center between January 2010 and June 2021 for
osteomyelitis, diskitis, or epidural abscess. Patients were treated by
orthopaedic and neurosurgical trained spine surgeons. Patient
Sample: Patients were included for any osteomyelitis, diskitis,
or epidural abscess within the study time period. Patients were excluded if
they had isolated paravertebral abscess or soft tissue infection that did
not also include osteomyelitis, diskitis, or epidural abscess. Outcome
Measures: Outcome measures included length of antibiotic regimen,
discharge location, ED admissions, complications, and reoperations.
Methods: Electronic medical record chart review was
completed by searching for associated appropriate ICD-9 or ICD-10 codes and
CPT codes for orthopaedic and neurosurgery spine attendings during study
period. Demographic information including age, sex, insurance carrier, and
co-morbidities including history of intravenous drug use, tobacco use, and
Charleston Comorbidity Index were collected on all patients. Additional
information including levels and location of epidural abscess, deformity,
instability, serum infectious markers, and culture data were also collected.
Results: There were a total of 163 patients identified and
111 patients included for study review. There were 58 patients in
decompression alone (60% male, n = 35) and 53 in decompression and fusion
(60% male, n = 32). The average age was 54 years and 53 years respectively
in each group (p = 0.988) and there was no statistical difference in rates
of osteomyelitis, diskitis, and epidural abscess in each group.
Additionally, there was no statistical difference in instability, deformity,
and Charleston Comorbidity Index in each group. Patients in decompression
alone averaged 4.2 spine levels of epidural abscess while those in
decompression and fusion averaged 2.8 levels (p = 0.008). There was no
difference in erythrocyte sedimentation rate, c-reactive protein, or white
blood cell count levels between groups, however patients with decompression
alone were more likely to have concomitant bacteremia (n = 48, 82.7%
compared to n = 28, 52.8% in decompression and fusion, p = 0.00018). There
were 10 reoperations (17%) in decompression alone with 4 to complete fusion,
while decompression and fusion had 13 reoperations (24.5%) with 3 to extend
or revise previous fusion. Conclusions: Patients with spine
infection including osteomyelitis, diskitis, and epidural abscess have a
high morbidity with numerus complications. In this retrospective, single
center study of spine we found there was no significant difference in
outcomes between decompression versus decompression and fusion for spine
infection. Patients who underwent decompression alone were more likely to
have higher burden of infection and concomitant bacteremia compared to those
with decompression and fusion.

## P342: Preoperative epidural steroid injection does not increase infection
risk following posterior cervical surgery

Tara Shelby

1

, Emily Mills

1

, Hyunwoo Kang

1,2

, Andy Ton

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, and Ram Alluri

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical
School, Boston, United States

Introduction: ESI is a helpful tool in alleviating pain and is
often used as a diagnostic tool prior to cervical surgery. However, a recent
small-scale study found that ESI prior to cervical fusion was associated
with an increased risk of postoperative infection. The purpose of this study
was to characterize infection risk of preoperative epidural steroid
injection (ESI) in patients undergoing posterior cervical surgery.
Material and Methods: Patients from 2010-2020 with cervical
myelopathy, spondylosis, and radiculopathy who underwent posterior cervical
procedure including laminectomy, laminoforaminotomy, fusion, or laminoplasty
were queried from the PearlDiver database. Patients who underwent revision
or fusion above C2 or who had a diagnosis of neoplasm, trauma, or
pre-existing infection were excluded. Patients were then divided based on
whether they received an ESI within 30 days prior to the procedure. The two
groups were subsequently matched based on age, gender, and preoperative
comorbidities. A chi-square test was used to calculate the risk of
developing a postoperative infection within 90 days of surgery.
Results: Based on our inclusion and exclusion criteria,
82,907 patients were identified, including 991 who received a preoperative
ESI and 81,916 who did not. Matching resulted in 975 in the injected group
and 1,929 in the control group. There was no significant difference in
postoperative infection rate in those who received an ESI within 30 days
preoperatively and those who did not (3.28% versus 3.78%, OR = 0.86, 95% CI:
0.57-1.32, p = 0.494). Conclusion: Given the growing use of
steroid injections in spinal surgery, it is important to determine the
associated risk of surgical site infection. In contrast to previous
literature, the present study has found no association between preoperative
ESI within 30 days prior to surgery and postoperative infection in patients
undergoing posterior cervical surgery after matching for an extensive list
of comorbidities and a comprehensive set of exclusion criteria. Further
multicenter prospective studies are indicated to more fully characterize
infection risk post-ESI.

## P343: Cervical osteomyelitis: a rare infection

Tiago Canas

1

, Emanuel Homem

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

, João Cruz

1

, and Luis Soares

1

1

Ortopedia, Hospital Divino Espirito Santo, Ponta Delgada,
Portugal

Introduction: Vertebral osteomyelitis constitutes 1-7% of bone
infections, with the cervical area being affected in only 3-10% of cases and
is related to diabetes, and both recreational and prescription intravenous
drug abuse. Cervical spondylodiscitis is thought to carry a significant risk
for rapid neurologic deterioration with a poor response to nonsurgical
management. It is described most commonly at one level (85%), and less often
at two contiguous levels. Given the overall low quality of the available
literature, it remains difficult to determine the optimal timing of surgical
management. The authors present a case of multilevel cervical
spodylodiscitis, characterizing neurologic presentation and postoperative
neurologic outcome. Material and Methods: A 51-year-old male
patient with a history of intravenous drug abuse, presented at the emergency
department (ER) with an one-month worsening cervical pain which motivated 3
prior visits to the ER. With no past history of trauma, pain, classified as
VAS 9/10, relieved with the conservative management (NSAID and analgesic
drugs) to tolerable levels (VAS 2/10). Physical exam revealed an incomplete
neurological deficit, around C6 level, classified as ASIA B. Cervical CT and
MRI documented an infectious process of C6 and C7 vertebral bodies
conditioning retroshift of the posterior walls and consequent spinal cord
compression. Bloodworks demonstrated a leukocytosis of 17.36 x 10 3 /uL and
increased CPR of 17.9 mg/dL. Blood cultures identified a
methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. The patient
was submitted to urgent surgery: corporectomy of C6 and C7 and anterior
arthrodesis (C5-T1) with autologous tricortical graft and locked plate;
without complications. Results: The postoperative in-hospital
stay went uneventful (50 days) and the patient recovered neurologically
(classified as ASIA D), which was maintained throughout follow-up (12
months). Intra-operative biopsies isolated the same causative agent (MSSA).
Intravenous antibiotic therapy with flucloxacilin was maintained for 6
weeks, followed by 6 weeks of oral form. PCR and ESR normalized around the
4th week of follow-up and at 6 months arthrodesis was confirmed with
cervical CT. Conclusion: Cervical osteomyelitis normally
presents with nonspecific clinical picture. For that reason an interval of
around 3-4 months between the onset of symptoms and diagnosis is generally
verified. The most frequent agent is Staphylococcus aureus
and neurological injury surgery is an indication for surgery. The authors
describe a classical case of cervical osteomyelitis submitted to multilevel
anterior arthrodesis with good functional, clinical and imagiological
results.

## P344: Decompression only versus fusion in octogenarians with spinal
epidural abscesses: early complications, clinical and radiological outcome
with 2 years follow-up

Pavlina Lenga

1

, Gelo Guelec

1

, Karl L. Kiening

1

, Andreas W. Unterberg

1

, and Basem Ishak

1

1

Neurosurgery, Heidelberg University Hospital, Heidelberg,
Germany

Introduction: Despite the global trend toward increased life
expectancy due to remarkable improvements in the quality of health care, the
treatment of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis (PVO) with a spinal epidural
abscess (SEA) remains challenging, especially in patients older than 80
years. The aim of this study was to assess, exclusively in octogenarians,
the prevalence of PVO with SEA and clinical outcomes after surgical
treatment, comparing decompression only with decompression and
instrumentation. Material and Methods: A retrospective review
of electronic medical records at a single institution was conducted between
September 2005 and December 2021. Patient demographics, surgical
characteristics, complications, hospital course, and 90-day mortality were
collected. Comorbidities were assessed using the age-adjusted Charlson
comorbidity index (CCI). Results: Over a 16-year period, 35
patients aged ≥ 80 years with PVO and SEA were identified. Eighteen patients
underwent surgical decompression only (“decompression group”), and 17
underwent surgical decompression with instrumentation (“instrumentation
group”). Both groups had a CCI > 6 (8.9, SD 2.1 vs. 9.6, SD 2.7,
respectively; p = 0.065), indicating severe comorbidities. Patients from the
instrumentation group had a significantly longer hospitalization stay, but
no ICU stay. In-hospital and 90-days mortality rates were similar in both
groups (instrumentation: in-hospital = 5.6%; 90-days mortality = 23.5% vs.
decompression: 11.6%; 5.6%; p > 0.05. The mean follow-up was 26.6 months
(SD 12.4), and no further surgeries were performed. Irrespective of
treatment, the levels of infection and neurological status were improved in
both groups at discharge. At second stage analysis significant improvements
in the blood infection parameters and the neurological status were detected
solely in the decompression group. Conclusion: Patients older
than 80 years with PVO and SEA have a high risk of adverse events after
surgical procedures. Surgical decompression only might contribute to earlier
clinical recovery in elderly patients. Additionally, in terms of morbidity
and 90-day mortality, the instrumentation group had poorer outcomes, and
this is why the choice of a surgical approach should be thoroughly discussed
with the patients and carefully weighed.

## P345: Comparative analysis of mechanical complications from structural

Alderico Girão Campos de Barros

, Pedro Cardoso Afonso

, Igor Ebert Cechin

, and Luis Eduardo Carelli Texeira da Silva

Instituto Nacional de Traumatologia e Ortopedia Jammil Haddad

Introduction: To compare the mechanical complications between
patients who were submitted to vertebral body replacement using either
structural allograft (SA) or titanium cage (TC) in the management of
thoracic and lumbar tuberculosis. Material and Methods: A
longitudinal study, based on retrospective evaluation of medical records of
patients admitted through 4th tier public health system between
November 2012 and July 2021, in consecutive convenience sampling, who were
operated by the same surgical team. All patients with a confirmed
histopathological diagnosis of vertebral tuberculosis who underwent through
vertebrectomy surgery targeting decompression, debridement and deformity
correction were included in the sample. The vertebral bodies were replaced
using either SA or TC containing autologous graft, followed by posterior
arthrodesis of at least two levels above and two levels below the structural
support using pedicle screws. Results: Twenty-two cases of
vertebral tuberculosis surgically treated with vertebral body replacement

support and vertebral body replacement in tuberculosis treatment showed
similar results in postoperative correction, as well as similar
postoperative mechanical complication rates. Future studies with larger
samples and follow-up period are necessary to assess metal rod breakage
rates.

between conservative or operative treatment is debatable and not consistent.

July 2018 to July 2022 were enrolled in the study. Patients with any age and

complications such as neurological deficits, kyphosis and abscess. Despite
of decades of research and public education campaigns aimed at decreasing
patient morbidity, it is common that the treatment delay were associated
with poor clinical outcome.

## 1188

## P347: Vacuum assisted closure - A panacea in postoperative spinal
infections

Shanmuganathan Rajasekaran

1

, Sri Vijay Anand KS

1

, Ashish Naik

1

, Chandhan Murugan

1

, Rishi Kanna

1

, and Ajoy P Shetty

1

1

Dept. of Spine Surgery, Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, India

Background: Surgical site infections (SSI) following spinal
surgery are potential detrimental complications that increase
hospitalization and expenses, cause significant morbidity and adversely
affect the outcomes. Radical wound debridement, irrigation, and intravenous
antibiotics are the conventional treatments for postoperative deep surgical
site infection. Despite the best efforts, infections can persist. Our study
aims to review the efficacy of the wound vacuum-assisted closure (VAC)
system in treating deep surgical site infection after spine surgery with
instrumentation and exposed dura. Material and Methods: We
retrospectively reviewed 31 patients who underwent vacuum-assisted closure
for postoperative spinal infections following spinal instrumentation between
2016-2020. The patient’s demographic details and biochemical parameters were
noted from the hospital information system, and imaging was analysed by
PACS. Other pertinent information included bacterial culture reports and
antibiotic sensitivity patterns, duration of VAC application, number of
cycles of VAC application before final wound closure, and infection
recurrence. Results: There were 17 females and 14 males in the
study population. There were 21 lumbar spine surgeries and five thoracic and
thoracolumbar spine surgeries. Following wound debridement, VAC was applied
to all patients. A mean of 2.5 cycles of VAC application, each lasting 5-9
days, was applied before wound closure. Twenty-seven had positive bacterial
cultures, and the rest were culture-negative. Klebsiella and Pseudomonas
were the most prevalent organisms. CSF leak through the VAC was managed in
two patients who had dural repair and subsequent infection, by lowering the
suction pressure of the VAC and switching to cyclical mode. One patient died
due to an unrelated cause, and one patient with chronic viral hepatitis had
an increased blood loss following VAC. All the patients had good healing of
wounds with a minimum follow-up of 12 months with no recurrence of
infections. All patients except one had retained the implants.
Conclusion: The VAC system is a valuable tool in managing
postoperative spinal infections. It allows for the retention of the
instrumentation and eradication of infection. It does not increase the
chances of CSF leak and is safe, reliable, and easy to use.

taken to check and record the post operative change in kyphotic angle at

brace was applied for at least 6 months. Data was analyzed using SPSS 17.0.

countries.

## 1356

## P351: Risk factors for surgical site infections in operatively treated
fractures of the ankylosed spine disorders

Celeste Tavolaro

1

, Jonathan Yamaguchi

1

, Mathew Vincent

1

, Jonathan Seavey

1

, Richard Bransford

1

, and Carlo Bellabarba

1

1

Orthopaedics and Sport Medicine, Harborview Medical Center -
University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Operative management of spine fractures in
patients with ankylosing spinal disorders is associated with increased risk
for perioperative complications and 1-year mortality. Due to the rigid
nature of the ankylosed spine, these fractures are commonly treated with
posterior instrumentation (typically 3 levels above and below the level of
injury at our institution); multiple and non-contiguous fractures frequently
necessitate longer and/or multiple constructs. Surgical site infection is
one of the more common complications associated with operative treatment and
management frequently requires formal irrigation and debridement combined
with a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics. Surgical site infections
are a significant source of morbidity to the patient and cost to the
healthcare system, and identification of associated risk factors may help
guide and optimize perioperative management. To describe the incidence and
characteristics of post-operative surgical site infections in patients with
ankylosing spinal disorders undergoing surgical management of a spine
fracture and to identify risk factors associated with surgical site
infection as compared to uninfected controls. Material and
Methods: Following UW IRB approval, a total of 383 patients who
had spine fractures and ankylosing spine disorders (Ankylosing spondylitis
(AS) and diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)) over a 15-year
period were identified and analyzed retrospectively. The medical and
surgical records were reviewed. Demographic data, comorbidities, operative
data, hospital data, wound complications, and microbiology were recorded
within 90-days of the index surgical procedure. The infected and not
infected groups were analyzed using Chi-square and Student’s T-tests for
categorical and continuous variables, respectively. Results: A
total of 383 patients (55 women and 328 men) were included. The mean patient
age was 70 years old (SD ± 13.3 years). One hundred fifty-five patients had
an underlying diagnosis of AS and 228 had DISH. The mean follow-up was 6
months. Fifty-two patients (13.6%) had surgical site infections, and 48
patients (12.5%) underwent irrigation and debridement within 90 days of the
index procedure. Among all patients, a mean of 7 levels were fused (SD ± 3
levels) – with significant differences (6.36 ± 2.52 vs 7.81 ± 3.23 levels, p
< 0.001) observed between the infected and non-infected groups. The
surgical invasiveness index was also significantly higher in the infected
group 13.49 ± 5.87 vs 16.69 ± 7.54, p < 0.005). Infected patients were
also more likely to have Ankylosing Spondylitis and more multi-level
injuries. Conclusion: Surgical fixation of fractures in the
ankylosed spine is frequently complicated by surgical site infection.
Identified risk factors include longer constructs, multi-level injury and
greater levels of surgical invasiveness. Ankylosing spondylitis also appears
to be associated with a higher risk of post-operative surgical site
infection although the mechanism for this is not well-defined. Diabetes
mellitus, ASA grade and length of ICU and hospital stay were not
significantly associated with presence of surgical site infection compared
to uninfected controls.

## 1369

## P352: Relationship between degenerative disc disease and cutibaceterium
acnes: a prospective analysis

Zachary Crawford

1

, John Stout

1

, John Bonamer

1

, Brian Johnson

1

, and Anthony Guanciale

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Cincinnati College of Medicine,
Cincinnati, United States

Background: Degenerative disc disease and low back pain are
substantial causes of disability and productivity loss with significant
impact on the healthcare system. Previous literature has focused on low back
pain and degenerative changes in the lumbar intervertebral disc although
more recent literature has reported serologic evidence of gram-positive
infection in 31% of patients with radicular symptoms. Of positive disc
cultures, the most common infectious agent is Cutibacterium
acnes with animal models suggesting low grade infection can
precipitate and progressively worsen degenerative disc disease. The Purpose
of this study is to further evaluate the relationship between degenerative
disc disease and infection. Methods: This prospective study
included patients who presented to a single orthopaedic spine surgeon for
the degenerative disk disease. Patients were included if they were taken to
the operating room for decompression of herniated disc or decompression and
fusion of spine for degenerative disc disease. The disc removed was then
cultured in standard fashion based on previously reported literature.
General demographic information including age, gender, medical
comorbidities, smoking status, and infectious disease information were
collected prospectively and retrospectively from chart review. The primary
outcome was positive culture from intervertebral disc. Results:
There were a total of 85 patients and 134 levels included in analysis. The
average age was 54.71 years (±12.9) with an average BMI of 31.7 (±6.39) and
Charleston Comorbidity Index Score of 1.98 (±1.547). There were 8 patients
(9.4%) that were positive for C. acnes with one additional
patient positive for Staphylococcus aureus. There were no
significant differences between patients with and without infection in
regards to previous antibiotic use, smoking status, BMI, or previous steroid
use. The majority of the patients with culture positive disc were men, 7 men
versus 1 woman (p = 0.020). There was no significant difference in MODIC
score of patients with and without infectious degenerative disc disease.
Conclusion: Degenerative disc disease and low back pain
have considerable influence on the healthcare system and productivity in the
United States of America. There have been considerable research efforts to
define the causes of degenerative disc disease with recent literature
suggesting indolent infection from C. acnes may be a
source. Our prospective analysis of over eighty patients and 130 levels
found a significant number of patients were culture positive for C.
acnes. Further studies on associated risk factors and natural
progression of infectious degenerative disc disease are warranted to develop
new treatments or procedures.

pneumonia in February 2021 and was treated with high dose dexamethasone,
remdesivir, and tocilizumab. This was complicated by Klebsiella
pneumoniae urosepsis and disseminated intravascular
coagulopathy which was treated with meropenem, followed by clinical
recovery. Two weeks later he presented with severe back pain. MRI of the LS
spine followed by a PET-CT showed multiple lesions with increased uptake in
the entire spine, pelvis and proximal femur. A bone marrow biopsy revealed
marrow necrosis and ruled out malignancy, and he was started on a tapering
dose of steroids with good clinico-radiological improvement. A month later,
he developed severe back pain with bilateral radicular pain. MRI pelvis and
lumbar spine showed an anterior epidural collection at L4-5, and infective
foci around sacroiliac joints and left piriformis. CT guided biopsy showed
avascular osteonecrosis and grew Klebsiella sensitive to
meropenem. After 2-3 days, he progressed to develop an acute foot drop and
underwent emergency epidural abscess drainage. The intraoperative cultures
also grew Klebsiella. He was given meropenem for 6 weeks
with good clinico-radiological response. However, after 2 weeks he presented
with increased pain and the MRI showed an increase in osteomyelitis now
involving the L3-4, L4-5 and L5-S1 levels. A repeat CT guided biopsy grew
the same organism. Meropenem was restarted and continued for further 7
months. He has now completed 18 months and 15 months since the diagnosis of
COVID-19 and osteomyelitis respectively. He is pain free but his left foot
drop still persists. Conclusion: Such extensive bone marrow
necrosis following COVID-19 has not been reported in literature. We presume
that this was secondary to the hypercoagulable state induced by COVID-19
infection, sepsis and DIC. The necrotic areas were secondarily infected with
Klebsiella that lead to epidural abscess and
neurological deficit.

## P354: Improvement in ODI scores after surgical intervention in TB spine:
a 21 case series

Sushant Srivastava

1

, Paresh Bang

2

, Mohammed Faizan

2

, and Nikhil Tiwari

3

1

Orthopaedics, Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya Shatabdi Hospital, Mumbai,
India

2

Orthopaedics, NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences and Research
Centre and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur, India

3

Orthopaedics, Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences
& Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, New Delhi, India

Introduction: Tuberculosis is one of the oldest maladies
affecting mankind. Since the advent of Homo sapiens on earth, mycobacterium
tuberculosis have lived in symbiosis with humans. The most common subtype of
extra-pulmonary tuberculosis, accounting for almost 15% of cases is spinal
tuberculosis. The proximity of the infection to the spinal cord and nerves
often leads to neurological symptoms such as pain, weakness, and numbness in
the lower limbs. Spinal tuberculosis may go on to cause serious disability,
morbidity, residual neurological deficits, and severe deformities, if it
goes unattended and untreated. This chain of reactions lead to the loss of
functional capabilities, especially in terms of mobility, leading to
difficulty in walking, self-care, and management of the sphincter. The
patient’s quality of life is adversely affected due to the depreciating
physical, mental, emotional health and social trials and tribulations.
Materials and Methods: This was a single centre study and
ethics committee approval was obtained. All patients were explained about
the study and written informed consent was taken from all. The data from
consecutive spinal TB patients was prospectively collected from January 2019
to December 2019. This prospective database included 21 patients with TB of
the cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine with moderate to severe cord
compression who were surgically treated and given chemotherapy. The
diagnosis of spinal TB was based on clinical presentation, radiologic
findings [plain radiographs, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI)], and hematologic and pathological examinations.
Clinical presentation manifested as pain, night sweats, low-grade fever,
weight loss, and neurological dysfunction. The ODI scores were calculated
before and after intervention to assess the functional outcome.
Results: Epi info-7 software was used for data analysis. A
paired t-test was used to compare the pre-treatment and post-treatment,
clinical data including ODI Scores. The results are reported descriptively,
as mean ± standard deviation (SD). A P-value of less than 0.05 was
considered statistically significant. There were 3 cervical, 14 thoracic and
5 thoracolumbar cases of spinal tuberculosis out of which 9 were females and
12 males. The age group was from 18 -70 years of age. The pre-operative ODI
score was 75.61 ± 3.066 and post-operative ODI score was 38.09 ± 4.267.
Conclusion: In this study we compared ODI Scores, as
functional outcome assessment before and after surgery of spinal TB
patients. This prospective study proves that there is an improvement in ODI
Scores after surgical intervention in TB spine and the right timing of these
decisions are extremely beneficial.

## P355: Intramedullary tuberculoma: a case report

Ghorbel Mohamed

1

, Ines Cherif

1

, Daoud Ahmed

1

, Kolsi Fatma

1

, and Boudouara Zaher

1

1

Neurosurgery, Habib Bourguiba Hospital, Tunisia

Introduction: Intramedullary tuberculoma is a rare condition. It
affects mainly patients in developing countries. Diagnosis and treatment can
be challenging. Material and Methods: We report the case of a
young patient who was diagnosed with intramedullary tuberculoma and was
treated in the department of neurosurgery in the Habib Bourguiba hospital in
Sfax, Tunisia. Results: The patient was a 21-year-old female.
She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. She was admitted for walking
disturbances with sphincter dysfunction. Physical examination found a
spastic paraparesis with a T8 sensitive level. The patient had anal
sphincter hypotonia, vesical retention and bilateral Babinski sign. Spinal
MRI showed an intramedullary nodular mass at the level of T7. The patient
underwent urgent surgery. Tumor removal was not complete due to adherences.
Pathology was in favor of tuberculoma. The patient had physical therapy
along long-term antibiotics. She was symptom-free few weeks after surgery.
Conclusion: Intramedullary tuberculoma is rare. However,
such diagnosis should be considered in some contexts. Surgery when possible
followed by medical treatment is the best alternative.

## P356: Hydatidosis of the spinal column: our series and review of the
literature

Ghorbel Mohamed

1

, Mohamed Boukhit

2

, Daoud Ahmed

1

, Kolsi Fatma

1

, Ines Cherif

1

, and Boudouara Zaher

1

1

Neurosurgery, Habib Bourguiba Hospital, Sfax, Tunisia

2

Neurosurgery, Fattouma Bourguiba Hospital, Monastir,
Tunisia

Introduction: Hydatid disease is a parasitic infection which can
infect humans through the larval stage of the Echinococcus Granulosis (EG).
It’s commonly seen in the Mediterranean region, Middle East and India.
Hydatid cysts are frequently formed in the liver (60-70%), then the lungs.
Although, Bone involvement is rare with approximately 0.5% of all hydatid
cyst cases residing in the vertebrae. We report a series of spinal column
hydatid cyst, treated over a period of 16 years. This study aim to discuss
the diagnosis and the management of spinal hydatid cyst, based on a
literature review. Materials and Methods: We report a
retrospective study of 7 cases of spinal column hydatid cysts treated in the
neurosurgery department of Habib Bourguiba University Hospital of
Sfax-Tunisia, between January 2003 and December 2018. Results:
It’s about 3 males and 4 females aged from 7 to 66 years with a mean age of
36.8. The revealing clinical symptomatology was spinal cord compression,
back pain and sciatica. Weakness of the lower limbs was seen in 4 cases. We
found bowel and bladder dysfunction in 57.1% of the patients. Whole spine
MRI was done in all cases. Hydatid cysts were localized in dorsal column in
3 cases, dorsolumbar junction in 1 case, lumbosacral vertebrae in 1 case and
lumbar column in 2 cases. All the patients were operated and treated with
antihelminthic (Albendazole). Posterior approach was performed with 5 cases.
The two other patients were operated through a lateral and an anterior
approach. 5 patients had good recovery of muscle strength and resolution of
limb sensory disturbance. The evolution was marked by relapse in 3 cases,
which were reoperated. The average follow-up of patients after surgery was
6.3 years. Conclusion: Spinal hydatid cyst is a serious disease
with significant morbidity. The recommended treatment is surgery with
anterior or posterior approach and subsequent adjuvant medical therapy. The
results are rarely satisfactory and the prognosis is usually poor due to the
frequency of relapses.

## P357: Results of intervertebral fusion using autogenous tricortical
spinous process bone during surgical treatment of pyogenic
spondylits

Young-Yul Kim

1

, Jong-Beom Park

2

, and Jae-Hoon Kim

1

1

Orthopedics, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital, Deajeon, South
Korea

2

Orthopedics,
St. Mary's Hospital, Uijeonbu, South Korea

Introduction: Pyrogenic spondylitis is a rare spinal disease
that occurs in disc space. However, the incidence is increasing due to the
recent increase in treatment of epidural steroid injection. When performing
intervertebral fusion surgery during the surgical treatment of pyogenic
spondylitis, autogenic iliac bone graft is commonly used. But this
autogenous cancellous bone graft may cause problems such as loosening or
breakage of the device due to a decrease in the gap between the vertebrae
after surgery. Therefore, in this study, we evaluate results about
performing intervertebral fusion using trimming tricortical spinous process
bone by microdrill after the autogenous spinous process in the same area
where no infection occurred. Materials and Methods: A total of
9 patients with pyogenic spondylitis diagnosed in 2017-2021 who did not
respond to antibiotic treatment were targeted. All patients had MRI
evaluation preoperatively. Among the patients who observed the abscess of
disc, facet joint, and epidural space on MRI, patients who did not involve
in spinous process were targeted. The average age of the patient was 62.4
years, and the male-female ratio was 6:3. We're going to do postop x-rays,
6-month follow-up x-rays, 12 month x-rays, and postoperative 12 month
CT. The height between the vertebrae of the disc space was
compared and analyzed. In addition, the degree of clinical improvement was
measured using VAS (Visual analog scale) and ODI (Oswestry disability
index). Results: In post op x-ray, the final fusion was 11.2
cm, 6 mon 10.8, and 12 mon 10.4. The convergence period was judged to be
more than 6 months. The average VAS preoperatively cored at 8.2, it
estimated as 5.2, 4.1 at 6 months after the surgery, and finally 2.1 at 12
months. In the case of ODI, all 9 of them showed severe disability, but 6
months after the surgery, 6 of them changed to moderate. And 2 people showed
minimal disability and 1 showed severity disability, and in the 12th month
evaluation, it was shown in 7 people with minimal disability and 2 people
with moderate disability. Conclusion: In patients with
pyrogenic spondylitis, intervertebral fusion using an autogenic tricortical
spinous process bone can induce intervertebral fusion while maintaining the
height of the vertebral body. It was useful option about
pyogenic spondylitis surgery.

## P358: Infectious complications in non-instrumented lumbar spine
surgery

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Kais Maamri

2

, Mohamed Boukhit

2

, Mohamed Amine Hadj Taieb

2

, Maher Hadhri

2

, Ghassen Belkahla

2

, Atef Ben Nsir

2

, and Mehdi Darmoul

2

1

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

2

Neurosurgery, Fattouma Bourguiba Hospital, Monastir,
Tunisia

Introduction: Surgical site infection (SSI) is one of the most
serious complications after lumbar disc herniation surgery. Rates vary from
0.7% to 12.0%. Materials and Methods: This is a retrospective
study conducted between January 2008 and December 2018, to assess the
incidence of surgical site infections following non-instrumental lumbar disc
herniation surgery in adults. We present this study in order to highlight
the epidemiological, clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic characteristics of
SSI, and to identify its risk factors. Results: 869 procedures
for lumbar disc herniation without instrumentation were performed during
this period. 24 SSI were identified with an incidence of 2.76%. Superficial

days. The most frequently isolated microorganism was Staphylococcus aureus.
Several significant risk factors for SSI were identified. The prognosis and
clinical expression of SSI depend on the extent of the infection and the
time between the surgical intervention and the first symptoms. SSIs should
be treated with appropriate antibiotics associated with surgical treatment.
Conclusion: Our study determined the incidence and
identified the risk factors for SSI following lumbar disc herniation
surgery. This makes it possible to develop effective preventive
measures.

## P359: Isolated tuberculosis of the atlas

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Sliti Firas

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Nadhir Karmani

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Alaa Belhaj

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Pott's disease is still a common disease in
countries with poor socio-economic conditions. It continues to pose a public
health problem since it affects a young population in full activity, which
shows the role of prevention. The dorsolumbar spine is the preferred site.
Tuberculosis in the cervico-occipital hinge is very rare. It is estimated to
occur in only 1% of spinal locations. Materials and Methods: We
report the case of a 63-year old female treated in the neurosurgery
department at the Mongi Ben Hamida National Institute of Neurology in
Tunisia. Results: Our patient was without any particular
pathological history and without any notion of tuberculosis infection. The
patient consulted for mechanical cervical pains evolving for 1 year, of
progressive aggravation, with trismus, torticoli and dysphagia to solids.
The clinical examination revealed a significant painful stiffness of the
cervical spine and the neurological examination was normal without any sign
of spinal cord injury, fever or alteration of the general condition. The
biological workup showed a non-specific inflammatory syndrome. The CT scan
of the cervical spine showed an osteolytic lesion of the anterior arch of C1
lateralized to the left with rupture of the cortical bone. MRI showed a
lesion that fixed the contrast, rounded, left paravertebral, extended to the
adjacent soft tissues respecting the aerodigestive carrefour, whose
appearance suggests a tumoral process originating from the paravertebral
soft tissues, invading the anterior arch of C1, or an infectious process
with common or specific germs. Sputum and urine were negative for BK. TST
was negative. Wright serology and card-test negative. Needle biopsy was not
possible because of the invincible trismus, and the lesion was biopsied
surgically. Anatomopathological examination confirmed the tubercular nature
of the lesion. Under anti-tuberculosis treatment, the evolution was
favorable, both clinically and biologically. Conclusion: Pott's
disease of the upper cervical spine is a very rare condition. The diagnosis
is usually made late at the stage of neurological deficit. It should be
suspected in the presence of chronic torticoli associated with prevertebral
thickening and C1C2 lysis. MRI is of great diagnostic value and allows
monitoring of treated forms. The diagnosis must be made early ; it is
confirmed on histo-bacteriological grounds but sometimes retained on
presumptive elements. Medical treatment based on anti-tuberculosis
antibiotic therapy and immobilization of the cervical spine must be
instituted as a first-line treatment despite the extent of bone lysis.
Surgical treatment should be reserved for cases with diagnostic doubt, or in
the presence of severe nerve compression or progressive worsening with or
without respiratory disorders, or in cases of documented dynamic
instability. The evolution under treatment is usually favorable.

## P360: Central nervous system infection revealing a dermal sinus

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Nadhir Karmani

1

, Nessrine Jemel

1

, Eya Chahed

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: The dermal sinus is a congenital dysraphic anomaly
that corresponds clinically to the presence of a punctiform cutaneous
orifice of the median and posterior paramedian raphe from the occipital
region to the sacrum but often from the lumbosacral region. The main
complication of dermal sinus is central nervous system infection.
Materials and Methods: We report the cases of 3 patients
treated in the neurosurgical department at the Mongi Ben Hamida National
Institute of Neurology in Tunisia, in whom the diagnosis of dermal sinus was
made only after a severe central nervous system infection.
Results: They were two boys and one girl, aged 11 months, 3
years and 11 months, respectively. Cerebrospinal MRI was performed in two
cases for a neurological deficit in a febrile context, and in the third case
for a recurrent purulent meningitis. In all three cases, it was a lumbar
intradural abscess associated with a dermal sinus. The abscess was evacuated
with excision of the dermal sinus. Two children had sequelae. These
infectious complications are the most serious aspect of non-operated dermal
sinuses because they can lead to serious neurological sequelae, in
particular urological disorders and/or paraplegia, which will require
long-term multidisciplinary management and can compromise the functional
prognosis of these children. Conclusion: The severity of
neurological sequelae due to infectious complications of the dermal sinus
makes its detection the responsibility of any physician examining a child
and indicates its urgent prophylactic surgery.

Introduction: The Hydatid cyst infection is caused by infection
with the pathogen Echinococcus Granulosus. Musculoskeletal infection
accounts for 0.5-1 % of all cases with Spinal Hydatid cyst representing half
of those cases. The purpose of this study is to discuss the diagnosis,
Differential Diagnosis and the management of spinal hydatid cyst.
Material and Methods: Using a survey research, this study
reviews six reports of spinal hydatid disease from Tunisia during the past
30 years and the main features of the treatment. Results: The
population of our study is made of four man and two women (Sex Ratio 2:1)
with a medium age of 40 years and symptoms duration ranging from 2 days to
32 years. 2 Patients presented with back pain, 2 patients with local
swelling, 2 patients with radiculopathy and 3 patients with myelopathy.
Radiological assessment (CT for 2 patients, CT+MRI for 4 patients) showed a
dorsal spinal localization of the cyst in 4 cases, 1 case extending from
dorsal to lumbar spine and one extended from lumbar spine to sacrum, with an
associated location of pulmonary infestation in one case. Peri and
post-operative Albendazole drug treatment were given in all cases. The
initial surgery approach was a posterior one with epidural cysts removal and
spinal decompression for all the cases with a relapse rate of 5/6 of the

total spondylectomy with spinal fusion was performed to two patients who
showed No recurrence after a mean duration of 4 years.

found to show poor outcome especially in recurrent disease and a higher risk
of relapse and neurological deterioration. Combined approach (laminectomy +
Spinal fusion) may be strongly considered to maximize the chance of success
Strict follow-up is mandatory. Further studies are needed to establish
Treatment guidelines.

## P362: Has SARS-Co V-2 ( COVID-19) caused further increase on already
increasing discitis (NVO)? An observational study

Mukta Vadhva

1

 and Poorna Veerappa

1

1

Orthopaedics, Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Preston,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Bacterial native vertebral osteomyelitis (NVO),
synonymous with spondylodiscitis, is an important cause of back pain. NVO is
associated with haematogenous seeding or contiguous spread from local
infection. The literature reports 1 and 2 per 100,000 population in USA and
UK respectively. The incidence (up to 9.8/100,000 per year (Kehrer et al.,
2014) has increased (from 1-2/100,000 to 9.8/100,000 over the last 2
decades, possibly reflecting an ageing population (Kehrer et al., 2014;
Mylona et al., 2009; Akiyama et al., 2013; Loibl et al., 2014). At our
regional combined spinal surgical unit, our team suspected that there has
been a surge in discitis during the covid period compared to pre-pandemic
levels. A rapid literature search in major bio-medical databases yielded no
current publications regarding this. Material and
Methods:Type of Study: Retrospective,
observational cohort study of adult patients with bacterial NVO.
Inclusion criterion:
1. Adult (above age 18)
2. Radiology (CT/MRI +/-MRI contrast) confirmed discitis
3. No history of previous spine surgery
Exclusion criterion:
1. Non-adult population
2. People with previous spine surgery with or without fusion
Methodology: Referral databases at our tertiary spine
surgery unit, which provides service for a wide geographical area within the
northwest of England by both orthopaedic and neuro-surgical spinal surgeons,
were reviewed. The arms were divided into pre-COVID and post-COVID. Data was
collected for a seven-month period (January to July) in the two years,
namely 2017 and 2021. A total of 2000 patients were included in each limb.
Results: Review of our results showed 20 patients with
confirmed discitis in the pre-COVID study period, whereas 38 patients had
radiology confirmed discitis during the pandemic. Further analysis of our
data showed that prior to COVID-19, 68% of all confirmed cases of discitis
were in females, whereas post COVID-19 the incidence was more prevalent in
males at 79%. It was also observed in our observational study, that
pre-COVID-19 only one patient had skip lesion in the spine, whereas post
COVID-19, skip lesions were observed in a total of five cases.
Conclusion: It is our observation that there has been an
increase (almost doubling) of discitis since the pandemic. It is unclear
about the exact cause for this increase. Our study also noted that only one
patient was COVID positive when discitis was diagnosed. It is our view that
we need to have low threshold in suspecting discitis, especially in male
population presenting with back pain. Further Plan: The
observation was discussed at regional spine network, and it was deemed to
carry out a multicentric study within the Northwest region.
Acknowledgments: Neurosurgical and Orthopaedic spine department for allowing
to use the database of their patients.
Keywords: COVID-19, SARS-Co V-2, Spondylodiscitis, discitis, native vertebral
osteomyelitis

## P364: Gram-negative hematogenous spondylodiscitis. Incidence, risk
factors and outcome

Hamdan Abdelrahman

1,2

, Mootaz Shousha

, and Heinrich Boehm

3

1

Asiut University Hospitals, Egypt

2

Helios-Hospitals Erfurt, Spine Surgery, Erfurt, Germany

3

Zentralklinik Bad Berka, Bad Berka, Germany

Introduction: In recent years, the incidence of spinal
infections has raised, this has been attributed to an increasing proportion
of elderly population with predisposing factors and comorbidities. Various
studies confirm staph. aureus as the most common causative organism in
hematogenous spinal infections. Gram negative bacteria cause a significant
proportion of all these cases. The incidence seems to be increasing in the
recent years. Patients and methods: Retrospective analysis of
the prospectively collected data of all patients with spinal infection
between 2005 and 2015. The study revealed 600 patients with hematogenous
spinal infections after exclusion of the cases with postoperative, wound
infections and the cases treated for infection before this period. A
causative organism could be identified from the site of infection in 405
patients (67.5%). Gram-negative bacteria could isolated in 45 patients of
all cases (7.5%). In this study, we have collected and analysed the
demographic, clinical, radiological and laboratory data as well as the
outcome of management of those patients with gram-negative spondylodiscitis.
Results: 45 patients, 21 females and 24 males with mean age
of 66.96 ± 11.42 years 41 patients (91.1%) were older than 50 years. In
those patients, 60% of the patients had ASA- Score class III and IV. The
most common comorbidities were cardiac in 24 patients, DM in 22, renal
insuffiecncy in 20 patients. Other site of infection were found in 30
patients; the most common one was UTI in 21 of them (
p-value 0.000*
). At the time of presentation, 30 patients (66.7%) had received
antibiotic with average period of 15.9 ± 13.13 days (2-50). The pre-surgical
interval was variable and ranged between 5-120 days, neurological deficit in

culture in 8 of them) and in 6 patients septic manifestations were found at

junction in 5 cases of them. Monosegemental was the commonest in 28 patients
(62.2%), in 4 patients multifocal infection was found. The preoperative
inflammatory parameters revealed mean CRP of 88.91 ± 72.55. The most common
isolated organisms from the site of infection were E. coli in 20 patients
(44.4%). In 5 patients (11.1%) had (mixed infection) and 4 of them had bed
sore at the time of admission. One patient had pyogenic infection (in tissue
culture) on top of tuberculous lesion (histopathological). All patients have
been surgically treated; combined ventro-dorsal approach was necessary in 40
patients. In five patients, recurrence of infection has been detected and
treated surgically (11.1%). In-hospital mortality of 6.7%. The neurological
improvement rate of at least one grade reached 83%. Postoperative antibiotic
therapy had to be taken more than 8 weeks in 31 patients.
Conclusion: Gram-negative bacteria cause a significant
proportion of vertebral osteomyelitis with incidence reached 7.5% in this
study. The multimorbid elderly patients are more affected than the other age
groups. The treatment is challenging, requiring prolonged hospital stay and
multiple antibiotic regimes are often needed to prompt control of the
infection and to prevent its recurrence.

## P365: Lumbar posterior inter-apophyseal arthritis complicating jugular
catheterization

Mohamed Yassine Belhedi

1

, Mouadh Nefiss

, Chahed Houssem Eddine

1

, Hedi Ezzine

1

, Mohamed Amine Gharbi

, Ramzi Bouzidi

1

, Ezzaouia Khelil

1

, and Tborbi Anis

1

1

Orthopeadic and Traumatology, Mongi Slim Hospital, Marsa,
Tunisia

Introduction: Arthritis is defined as an acute or chronic
inflammatory disease of the synovial mucosa of one or more joints. The
etiology can be various, inflammatory, immune, or infectious. Septic
arthritis is a medical-surgical emergency that must be suspected in a
clinical context that is sometimes frustrating or in the presence of other
inflammatory arthropathies. It usually affects a peripheral joint,
particularly the knee and hip. Spinal involvement is not frequent. We report
the case of a patient who presented a septic arthritis of the posterior
lumbar inter-apophysis following the placement of a jugular catheter.

at 15 days of the symptomatology, showing a staged zygapophyseal arthritis
with intracanal diffusion. A complementary MRI scan showed an aspect in
favor of a posterior lumbar inter-apophyseal arthritis, extending from L2/L3
to L5/S1, probably of infectious origin with intra-articular effusion,
synovitis as well as collections with intracanal development without
associated discitis. The patient underwent posterior surgery. He underwent
an extended laminectomy from L2 to S1 with exploration of the destruction of
the right L4/L5 joint and the presence of staged intracanal collections
opposite L2/L3, L3/L4 and L4/L5. These collections were drained. A
superficial and deep bacteriological samples were taken and returned
negative. The patient was then put on vancomycin with good
clinico-biological evolution and total recovery of his neurological deficit.
Conclusion: The posterior inter-apophyseal joint is a rare
septic location. The clinical expression is very similar to that of a
spondylodiscitis and is marked by an important spinal stiffness and by an
inconstant febrile syndrome. MRI is the most efficient examination to make
the diagnosis, which constitutes a medical-surgical emergency.

## P366: Isolated thoracic and lumbar transverse process fractures, do they
need spine surgeon evaluation? A high volume level I trauma center
experience with cost analysis

Asa Peterson

1

, Jonathan Behrens

1

, Pooria Salari

1

, and Howard Place

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, St. Louis Univeristy, St. Louis, United
States

Introduction: Transverse process fractures (TPF) of the thoracic
and lumbar spine have become increasingly identified due to CT imaging. At
many institutions the spine service, neurosurgical or orthopaedic, is
consulted for further evaluation and management. There are several studies
that demonstrate no difference in clinical outcome with or without spine
service intervention (bracing, surgery, etc.). However, no study to our
knowledge provides an additional cost analysis. We hypothesize that isolated
transverse process fractures of the thoracolumbar vertebrae are structurally
and neurologically stable injuries. Furthermore, spine service consultation
and evaluation results in increased healthcare costs. Methods:
Patients were identified using the trauma registry data at Saint Louis
University (SLU) from January 2012 to August 2018. The registry was queried
for CPT code 22305 (closed treatment of vertebral process fracture). Chart
and imaging review was performed to determine if any additional spine
fractures were identified by the spine team which were not included in the
initial radiology report. TPF associated with other spinal injuries were
characterized by the presence of one or more thoracic and/or lumbar TPF in
addition to any other acute fracture or dislocation in the cervical,
thoracic, or lumbar spine. A separate cost analysis with
institution-specific charges was also performed. Results: Six
hundred and eighty two patients with TPF from January 2012 to August 2018
were identified. Two hundred and twenty eight patients met the criteria to
be included in this study. Of these, four hundred and seventy seven lumbar
TPFs and one hundred and three thoracic TPFs were identified. Additional
spinal pathology that was not included in the initial radiology report was
identified in 5 (2.19%) patients, none of which required surgical
intervention. These included two nondisplaced facet fractures (T6 and L3)
that were treated non-operatively, a nondisplaced C7 laminar fracture
treated with a rigid cervical orthosis, and a T3/4 widening which was
suggestive of possible posterior ligamentous injury on a subsequent MRI exam
which was treated with bracing. Cost analysis demonstrated additional costs
associated with spine service intervention totaled $1,725,360.28. Average
cost per patient in our cohort summed to $2,529.85. Conclusion:
These data support that isolated TPF of the thoracic and lumbar spine are
stable injuries that likely do not require spine service intervention and in
fact may represent unnecessary financial burden. Foregoing unnecessary
consultation can alleviate time constraints within spine service practices
and reduce health care costs by eliminating costly extraneous interventions
from the patient’s care.

## P367: A 5 year cost-utility analysis for recombinant bone morphogenetic
protein 2 (rhBMP-2) use in transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion for
degenerative lumbar pathologies

Carlos Ortiz-Babilonia

1,2

, Arjun Gupta

1,3

, Micheal Raad

1

, Miguel Cartagena

1,4

, and Amit Jain

1

1

Department of Orthopedic Spine Surgery, John Hopkins University,
Baltimore, United States

2

University of Puerto Rico Medical Sciences Campus, Department of
Orthopedic Surgery, San Juan, Puerto Rico

3

Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, Department of Orthopedic Surgery,
Newark, United States

4

Ponce Health Sciences University, Department of Orthopedic Surgery,
Ponce, Puerto Rico

Study Design: Cost-utility analysis. Objective:
This study aimed to evaluate the cost-utility of utilizing recombinant human
bone morphogenetic protein 2 (rhBMP-2) in addition to local bone graft (LBG)
in transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion surgery (TLIF) for adults with
degenerative lumbar disease compared to LBG only. Background:
Past clinical studies including cost-effectiveness analyses have shown TLIF
to be an effective treatment for degenerative lumbar pathologies in adult
patients. The utilization of rhBMP-2 has been shown to lower pseudoarthrosis
rates in the setting of TLIF, however its cost-effectiveness has not been
previously demonstrated. Therefore, in this study we attempt to evaluate the
cost-effectiveness of rhBMP-2 use as a treatment strategy in adult patients
undergoing TLIF. Methods: A decision tree comparing LBG +
rhBMP-2 use versus use of LBG alone was built for a hypothetical 60-year-old
man with degenerative lumbar pathology (DLP) requiring surgery. A
comprehensive review of the literature was performed to obtain event
probabilities, costs and health utilities. Health utilities were utilized to
calculate Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs). A base-case analysis was
carried out to obtain the incremental cost and effectiveness (QALYs) of
rhBMP-2 utilization in TLIF. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis was
performed using 1000 Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the uncertainty in
our model and obtain mean incremental costs, effectiveness, and net monetary
benefits. One-way deterministic sensitivity analyses were also performed to
identify the variables with most impact on our base-case results.
Results: TLIF with LBG + rhBMP-2 was favored on base-case
analysis. Adding rhBMP-2 to LBG in TLIF was favored in 80% of the Monte
Carlo simulations. Utilization of rhBMP-2 resulted in mean savings of
$10,024 (SD = 2,191) while gaining a mean of 0.11 (SD = 0.24) additional
QALYs compared to TLIF with LBG only. The mean cost of rhBMP-2 + LBG in TLIF
surgery was $36,400 (SD = 3034), while TLIF with only LBG resulted in
$46,424 (SD = 3814). The mean INMB and ICUR of utilizing rhBMP-2 in TLIF
surgery were found to be $20,967 (95% CI, $19,436 - $22,498) and -$34,096
(95% CI, -$75,695 - $7,501) at a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of
100,000 USD/QALY, respectively; indicating that rhBMP-2 use in TLIF is a
cost-effective strategy in comparison to TLIF with LBG alone. On one-way
deterministic sensitivity analysis, the three parameters with most effect on
the conclusions of our model were the probability of pseudoarthrosis with
LBG only, the cost of revision, and the effect of nonunion on patient
quality of life.Conclusion: Cost-utility analysis supports the
use of rhBMP-2 in adult patients undergoing TLIF for lumbar degenerative
pathologies.
