## P368: Predictors of academic productivity among spine surgeons

Mark Lambrechts

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Nicholas D'Antonio

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Payton Boere

1

, Ari Clements

1

, Zachary Crawford

2

, Patrick O'Connor

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

 and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, The Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas
Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States

2

Orthopedic Surgery, University of Cincinnati, United States

Introduction: Academic productivity of orthopaedic surgery
residency applicants has risen in importance as the field becomes more
competitive. However, the relationship between research productivity in
training and future productivity as an attending physician is not well
established in the literature nor has the impact of geographic location of
training institutions on future academic success been investigated. For
trainees interested in academic medicine, knowing these factors may help set
research goals and choose training programs. Therefore, the aim of our study
was to: (1) summarize characteristics of academically productive spine
surgeons, (2) assess the impact of academic productivity during different
training timepoints on long-term productivity, and (3) establish the impact
of geographic location on long-term academic productivity.
Methods: A query of the 2021-2022 North American Spine
Society (NASS) Spine Fellowship Directory of all orthopedic and
neurosurgical spine fellowship selection committee members for each
institution participating in the spine fellowship match. Each surgeon's
current institution of practice and medical education was recorded through
an online search of institutional websites. A search on PubMed was then used
to collect data on the number of articles published prior to residency,
during residency, during fellowship, and following fellowship determined
based on the recorded medical education history. The attending publication
rate was calculated and the author's h-index was collected
through a search of each author's Scopus profile through July 1, 2022. Data
was analyzed by residency training and attending institution geographic
location. A multivariate linear regression model was developed to determine
if pre-residency, residency, or fellowship publication rate were
independently predictive of attending publication rate or
h-index. Results: A total of 310
orthopedic and neurosurgical spine surgeons, representing 76 fellowship
programs, were identified on the NASS directory as involved in spine
fellowship mentoring. Multivariate linear regression analysis identified
that the publications during residency (p < 0.001) and during fellowship
(p<0.001) were significant predictors of an increased publication rate as
an attending surgeon. In contrast, the pre-residency publication rate (p =
0.729) was not significantly predictive of the attending publication rate.
Multivariate analysis of h-index found that residency
publication rate had a positive correlation (p = 0.031) as compared to
pre-residency (p = 0.579) or fellowship (p = 0.257). Attendings who had
attended residency in the Northeast and currently practicing in the
Northeast had a higher publication rate (p < 0.001 and p = 0.004,
respectively). Conclusion: Understanding factors important to
long term research productivity can help academic institutions hire trainees
and attendings while also assisting trainees in program selection. A higher
number of publications in residency and fellowship was significantly
predictive of an increased publication rate as an attending spine surgeon,
indicating that an emphasis on research throughout surgical training, with a
particular focus during residency, is advantageous for those interested in a
career in academic spine surgery. In contrast, pre-residency publications
may not be indicative of future academic productivity as an attending.
Location may also contribute to attending publication rate and favors those
who undergo residency training and ultimately practice in the Northeast.

## P369: Gender disparities among abstract presenters at recent Global Spine
Congress Annual Meetings

Yunsoo Lee

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Jasmine Lin

1

, Skylar Nahi

1

, Alexander Becsey

1

, Qudratallah Qadiri

1

, Preston Carey

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: The percentage of female surgeons in neurosurgery
and orthopaedic surgery has grown significantly over the past several years,
but still lags behind other fields. However, research has demonstrated that
women are less likely to have adequate mentorship, promotions to
professorship, and research productivity. We aimed describe trends in the
gender of presenters at the Global Spine Congress over the last 5 years.
Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective study
examining the annual programs of the Global Spine Congress final programs
from 2017-2022. Speaker names, institutional data, and session titles were
collated. The gender of speakers was identified through an online search of
their institutional profiles with collection of gender pronouns, when
available, or classifying individuals by their presenting gender.
Results: During the past 5 Global Spine Congress Annual
Meetings, there were a total 1,636 paper presentations. Gender information
could be identified for 1,514 (92.5%) speakers, all of whom were included in
the final analysis. Speakers were predominantly male (N = 1286, 84.9%) and
from the United States (N = 387, 25.6%). European (N = 99, 22.0%) and North
American (N = 91, 15.9%) institutions supported the most female presenters
(p < 0.001). Among other regions of the world, 12.0% of East
Asian/Pacific Islanders, 11.1% of Central/South American, 8.6% of Middle
Eastern, and only 2.4% of South Asians were female. The 2018 and 2019
meetings in Canada and Singapore had the lowest female representation (10.8%
and 12.8%, respectively) compared to those in France (16.9%), United States
(16.8%), and Italy (17.8%), although this did not meet statistical
significance (p = 0.058). Over the last 5 years, there was no significant
increase in the gender of female presenters. Conclusion:
Overall, 14.1% of presenters at the Global Spine Congress were female in
line with recent trends from other orthopaedic and neurosurgery conferences.
However, disparities exist internationally particularly among institutions
and conferences located outside of Europe and the United States. Efforts
should be established to help promote gender equity at future annual
meetings, monitor gender representation from historically less inclusive
regions of the world, and emphasize recruitment and retention efforts of
women.

## P370: The impact of COVID-19 on spine surgery

Emily Mills

1

, Ethan Faye

1

, Kevin Mertz

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, and Ram Alluri

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

Introduction: The COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact on
the healthcare system. However, only a few small scale studies have studied
the effect of COVID-19 on spine surgery volume. Therefore, the aim of this
study was to characterize the impact of COVID-19 on the rate of ten common
spine procedures as well as the percentage of outpatient procedures.
Material and Methods: The PearlDiver national database was
queried for posterior lumbar instrumented fusion (< 6 segments),
thoracolumbar intstrumented fusion (> 6 segments), posterior cervical
fusion, anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF), cervical
laminectomy, lumbar laminectomy, microdiscectomy, cervical disc
arthroplasty, cervical laminoplasty, and lumbar interbody fusion. The yearly
rates of these procedures between January 2010 through April 2021 was
recorded. Monthly trends were assessed from January 2020 through April of
2021. The years 2020 and 2021 were compared to 2019. Monthly trends
throughout 2020 and 2021 were compared to January of 2020. Inpatient versus
outpatient data was compared between 2010-2019 (pre-COVID) and
2020-2021(post-COVID). Results: Overall, there was a 4.3%
decrease in all ten procedures in 2020 compared to 2019 and a 6.3% increase
in all ten procedures in 2021 compared to 2019. March and April of 2020 had
the largest decrease in procedures, with March of 2020 seeing a 18.2%
decrease in procedures and April 2020 seeing at 51.6% decrease in procedures
compared to January of 2020. Although there were also increasing case
numbers in January of 2021, there was only a 1.8% decrease in total cases
compared to January of 2020. Later months of 2021 had an increase in total
cases, with April of 2021 increasing case volume by 138% compared to January
of 2020. Pre-COVID, outpatient procedures made up 39.7% of all spine
procedures, compared to 49.1% post-COVID (p < 0.001).
Conclusion: The greatest effect on volume in spine surgery
from the COVID-19 pandemic occurred in March and April 2020. Other than
these two months, spine procedures were either very similar or increased
compared to January of 2020. Additionally, the COVID-19 pandemic
significantly increased the volume of outpatient spine procedures.

## P371: Assessing the economic benefit of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery
(ERAS) protocols in adult cervical deformity patient outcomes: is initial
cost offset by clinical gains?

Peter Passias

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Kimberly McFarland

1

, Jamshaid Mir

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, Bailey Imbo

1

, Tyler Williamson

1

, Rachel Joujon-Roche

1

, Jordan Lebovic

1

, and Andrew Schoenfeld

2

1

Neurological and Orthopaedic Surgery, NYU Langone Health, New York
City, United States

2

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Brigham and Women's Center for
Surgery and Public Health, Boston, United States

Introduction: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) can help
accelerate patient recovery and assist hospitals in maximizing the
incentives of bundled payment models while maintaining high-quality patient
care. However, the economic benefits of ERAS protocols, nor the
heterogeneous components that make up such protocols, have been established.
Material and Methods: Operative CD patients ≥ 18yrs with
complete pre-(BL) and up to 2-year(2Y) postop radiographic/HRQL data were
stratified by enrollment in Standard-of-Care ERAS beginning in 2020,
including expedited time to ambulation, multimodal analgesia and pain
control, and early oral diet and Foley catheter removal. Differences in
demographics, clinical outcomes, radiographic alignment targets,
peri-operative factors and complication rates were assessed via means
comparison analysis. Costs were calculated using PearlDiver database
estimates from Medicare pay-scales. QALY was calculated using NDI mapped to
SF6D using validated methodology with 3% discount rate to account for
residual decline to life expectancy. Results: 270 patients were
included (58.11 ± 11.97 years, 48% female, 29.13 ± 6.89 kg/m2. Of
these patients, 54 (20.0%) received ERAS protocol recovery treatment
post-operatively. At baseline, ERAS+ had significantly higher NDI (p = .005)
and EQ5D (p = .023), and significantly lower mJOA scores (p < .001). At
BL, ERAS- patients were significantly more likely to utilize opioids than
ERAS+ patients (p = .016). Furthermore, ERAS+ patients also had
significantly lower EBL overall (583.48 vs 246.51, p < .001), and
required significantly lower doses of propofol intra-operatively than ERAS-
patients (p = .020). ERAS+ patients also reported lower mean LOS overall
(4.33 vs 5.84, p = .393), and were more likely to be discharged directly to
home (χ2(1) = 4.974, p = .028). In terms of complications, ERAS+
patients were less likely to develop neurological complications overall (p =
.025), and less likely experience thromboembolic complications or be
diagnosed with venous disease post-operatively (p = .025). Per cost
analysis, ERAS+ patients reported a significantly lower mean total 2Y cost
of 33,829 USD compared to ERAS- patients at 36,951 (p < .001).
Furthermore, ERAS+ patients trended towards greater life-expectancy 2Y QALYs
gained versus ERAS- patients (.423 vs .368, p = .051), and demonstrated
significantly lower cost of reoperation by 2Y (7050 USD vs 8110 USD, p <
.001). Conclusion: Patients undergoing Enhanced Recovery After
Surgery (ERAS) protocols experience lower operative times, length of stays,
as well as lower rates of peri-and and post-operative complications.
Subsequently, this study demonstrates that ERAS programs in ACD surgery may
lead to increased cost-effectiveness and reduced total cost by 2Y
post-operatively. Due to the potential economic benefit of ERAS for
patients, physicians and institutions should consider incorporation of ERAS
into practice for eligible patients.

## P372: Assessing the insurance deductible effect on outcomes following
elective spinal surgery

Anthony Steinle

1

, Jessa Fogel

1

, Rishabh Gupta

1

, Alicia Hymel

1

, Claudia Davidson

1

, Andrew Croft

1

, Wilson Vaughan

1

, Jacquelyn Pennings

1,2

, Kristin Archer

1,2,3

, Scott Lawrence Zuckerman

1,4

, Raymond Gardocki

1

, Amir Abtahi

1,2,4

, and Byron Stephens

1,2,4

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery

2

Center for Musculoskeletal Research

3

Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation

4

Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Many private insurers operate on a calendar
deductible system. Plans typically reset on January 1st, placing
pressure on patients and health care workers to perform medical services,
including elective spine surgeries, before the end of the year to maximize
patient savings. This insurance-driven scheduling of elective procedures
could negatively impact patient reported outcomes (PROs) due to the
increased burden placed on healthcare staff during the month of December, in
addition to potentially lowering the threshold to undergo surgery for
patients who have met their deductible. The purpose of this study was to
investigate if patients undergoing surgery in December had different
baseline characteristics and postoperative outcomes compared to the other 11
months. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective
review of data collected from The Quality Outcomes Database, a national
spine registry. The registry was queried for patients who underwent elective
lumbar or anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) surgery between
2012 and 2021 for degenerative spine conditions. Oswestry/Neck Disability
Index (ODI/NDI), EuroQol 5-Dimensions (EQ5D), EuroQol Visual Analog Scale
(EQ-VAS), numeric rating scale (NRS) leg/arm pain, and NRS back/neck pain
scores were collected at baseline and 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
Patient satisfaction scores using the NASS questionnaire were recorded at 3
and 12 months. Separate analyses were run for the lumbar and ACDF cohorts.
Three multivariable linear regression models were performed for both groups,
in which 12-month outcomes were predicted based on surgical timing. One
model included all patients, a second included patients with private
insurance, and the third included patients without private insurance.
Results: A total of 978 patients underwent ACDF in December
vs 10,526 in other months. 1,104 patients underwent lumbar fusion in
December vs 11,826 in other months. For the ACDF cohort, there was a
significantly higher percentage of patients in the December group with
private insurance (68.1% vs 60.1% p < 0.001) and employment (50.1% vs
43.5%, p < 0.001). The December group had higher 3-month EQ-5D (0.79 ±
0.18 vs 0.78 ± 0.19, p = 0.019) and baseline EQ-VAS (63.36 ± 19.53 vs 61.72
± 20.36, p = 0.016) scores. For the lumbar cohort, there was a greater
chance of undergoing surgery in December if the patient had private
insurance (56.4% vs 45.0%, p < 0.001) and was employed (38.4% vs 29.9%, p
< 0.001). NRS leg pain at 3 months was significantly higher for the
December group vs the other months (2.4 ± 2.9 vs 2.2 ± 2.7, p = 0.038). All
other PROs were similar. Results from the linear regression models showed
timing of surgery was not predictive of any 12-month outcome except for
EQ-VAS in the ACDF group with private insurance (-1.637 [95% CI:
-3.027-(-0.246)]). Conclusion: Financial pressure created by
the deductible calendar likely affects the scheduling of elective fusions,
specifically for patients with private insurance. However, patients
undergoing fusion surgeries in December did not experience any significant
clinical difference in postoperative outcomes compared to the non-December
group. These findings suggest physicians are scheduling patients
appropriately for elective fusion surgery in December despite external
pressure from insurance companies.

Introduction: Both nonoperative and operative treatments for
spinal metastasis are expensive interventions. Previous studies have

approaches, based on patients’ prognosis and walking ability. We sought to
determine the cost-effectiveness of operative and non-operative
interventions, stratified by ambulatory status and predicted probability of

## 1465

## P374: Optimizing spine surgery instrument trays to immediately increase
efficiency and reduce costs in the operating room

Setti Belhouari

1

, Jay Toor

1

, Aazad Abbas

2

, Johnathan Lex

1

, and Jeremie Larouche

2,3

1

Temerty Faculty of Medicine

2

Division of Orthopaedics, Department of Surgery, University of
Toronto, Toronto, Canada

3

Department of Surgery, Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, Toronto,
Canada

Introduction: Over-crowded surgical trays result in
perioperative inefficiency and unnecessary costs. While methodologies to
reduce the size of surgical trays have been described in the literature,
they each have their own drawbacks. In this study, we compared three
methods: 1) clinician review (CR), 2) mathematical programming (MP), and 3)
a novel hybrid approach based on surveys and cost analysis. While CR and MP
are well documented, CR can yield suboptimal reductions and MP can be
laborious and technically challenging. We hypothesized our easy-to-implement
HM would result in a reduction of surgical instruments in both the
laminectomy tray (LT) and basic neurosurgery tray (BNT) that is comparable
to CR and MP. Material and Methods: Three approaches were
tested: CR, MP, and HM. We interviewed 5 neurosurgeons and 3 orthopedic
surgeons, at our institution, who performed a total of 5437 spine cases,
requiring the use of the LT and BNT over a four-year (2017-2021) period. In
CR, surgeons suggested which surgical instruments should be removed. MP was
performed via the mathematical analysis of 25 observations of the use of a
LT and BNT tray. The HM was performed via a structured survey of the
surgeons’ estimated instrument usage, followed by a cost-based inflection
point analysis. Results: The CR, MP, and HM approaches resulted
in a total instrument reduction of 41%, 35%, and 38%, respectively,
corresponding to total cost savings per annum of $50,211.20, $46,348.80, and
$44,417.60, respectively. Conclusion: While hospitals continue
to examine perioperative services for potential inefficiencies, surgical
inventory will be increasingly scrutinized. Despite MP being the most
accurate methodology to do so, our results suggest that savings were similar
across all three methods. CR and HM are significantly less laborious and
thus are practical alternatives.

at the index level(s), significantly elevated surgical risk, a history of
drug abuse, and/or inability to take orally administered acetaminophen were
excluded from this study. Enrolled patients were randomized into either IV
or PO groups. Preoperative baseline surveys were collected. The first dose
of the assigned acetaminophen was administered within 3 hours prior to
surgery. Postoperatively, 7 additional doses were given every 6 hours.
Patients had access to supplemental opioid analgesics as needed. Analgesic
consumption and visual analog pain scale (VAS) scores were recorded daily
until discharge. Patients were followed at 6 week and 6 month
post-operatively and administered questionnaires. Pain medication usage was
recorded. Results: Daily morphine equivalent (MME) consumption
was statistically significantly lower for the IV group than the PO group (p
= 0.001) from post-operative to final administration of acetaminophen
dosage. Post regimen average daily MME was also statistically significantly
lower for IV group than PO group (p = 0.002). Average length of stay was
similar between groups. The IV group showed greater reduction in VAS and ODI
between baseline and discharge. However, VAS Back and VAS Leg scores were
similar for both groups out to 6 months post-op, but both groups showed
statistically significant differences from baseline in frequency and
intensity. ODI was also statistically lower than baseline in both groups out
to 6 months. Conclusion: In addition to an overall reduction in
opioid use, patient surveys indicate an improvement of pain management with
the use of IV acetaminophen. Our findings suggest that IV acetaminophen is a
safe and effective alternative to opioid use. The decrease in risk of side
effects makes IV acetaminophen a promising alternative to opioid use, even
despite the added cost.

Spine Surgery, UMAE Hospital de Traumatología y Ortopedia Lomas

## P377: Comparative analysis of outcomes in one to two level minimally
invasive and open transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion

Ashley Duncan

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, Devender Singh

1

, John Stokes

1

, and Eeric Truumees

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Minimally Invasive Surgical (MIS) techniques
potentially offer a less morbid alternative to traditional open surgical
techniques with shorter length of stay. Aim: This study aims to
compare the outcomes of patients undergoing minimally invasive
transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion to those that underwent the
traditional open technique. Materials and Methods: 31
Retrospective chart reviews were conducted on patients that underwent one to
two level transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion from 2020-2021. Patients
were divided into two cohorts, those that underwent the traditional open
approach and those that had a minimally invasive technique. Twelve variables
were collected across demographic, surgical, clinical, and patient reported
outcomes (PROs) (PROMIS Physical Function, Pain Interference and
Satisfaction with Social Roles; and Oswestry Disability Index) domains and
analyzed accordingly. Results: 12 patients were included in the
minimally invasive cohort and 19 were included in the open cohort. Mean age,
BMI and sex were similar in both groups. There was a significant difference
in the mean number of levels fused, 1 ± 0 in the MIS group and 1.3 ± 0.5 in
the open group (p = 0.009917). While the MIS group had lower mean
skin-to-skin surgical time, estimated blood loss and length of stay, none of
these were statistically significant. Both cohorts consistently reported
improvements in PROMIS and ODI scores across their recovery period up to one
year postoperatively, however, there were differences not only in timing,
but also in domain reported. At three months postoperative, the MIS cohort
showed significant change in PROMIS Pain Interference (59.9 ± 8.8) from
preoperative (68.4 ± 7.3) and ODI scores (27.5 ± 17.7) from preoperative
(27.5 ± 17.7). MIS patients also reported significant decrease in ODI scores
at six months postoperative, 20.2 ± 13.8 from preoperative 41 ± 15.7. Though
there were improvements in all PRO domains at nine months and 1-year
post-operative, these changes were not significant. The open cohort reported
significant change from preoperative levels in PROMIS Physical Function and
Pain Interference and ODI scores at three months, ODI scores at six months,
and PROMIS physical Function, Pain Interference and Social Roles at nine
months. Though there were improvements in all PRO domains at 1-year
post-operative, these changes were not significant.
Conclusions: The number of levels fused was the
statistically significant surgical variable between the open and MIS groups,
though surgical time, EBL and length of stay were lower in the MIS group.
The open cohort reported more statistically significant changes from
baseline PROs scores across more instruments and postoperative intervals
than the MIS cohort. However, neither group reported statistically
significant changes at one year postoperative from baseline preoperative in
any PRO instrument. This is most likely due to the limited number of
responses at one-year post-operative.

## P378: Quantitative analysis of tissue injury markers after adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) correction: a prospective study of open vs.
minimally invasive surgery

Matthew Geck

1

, Devender Singh

1

, Ashley Duncan

1

, John Stokes

1

, and Eeric Truumees

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) offers a
potentially less morbid treatment option for patients requiring
stabilization of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Aim: To
compare the tissue injury markers in AIS cohorts matched for Lenke type
curve that had undergone either open or MIS. Materials and
Methods: 39 patients who either underwent MIS or open corrections
were consecutively enrolled. MIS or open approaches were surgeon selected
based on curve magnitude, location, flexibility on bending films and the
patient’s body habitus. Enrollment criteria included: age > 10 yrs and
< 30 years; Lenke types were 1, 2 or 5; Cobb angle ranged 35°∼70°; caudal
levels for open and MIS cases were L2 or above and L3 or above,
respectively. Open approach included posterior spinal instrumentation and
fusion with posterior column osteotomy. MIS technique was uniform in all
patients using two or three para-midline incisions. The serum enzymes
representing skeletal muscle injury (creatine kinase and aldolase) were
analyzed on the day before surgery and days 1, 2, 3, 4, discharge, 3 weeks,
3 months and 6 months postoperatively. Results: MIS and open
groups comprised of 19 and 20 patients, respectively. Mean patient age was
16 years in MIS and 15 years in open group. Mean pre-op Cobb angles for MIS
and open differed significantly (52.8 ± 4.6° vs. 60.5 ± 5.8°). Number of
spinal levels treated were similar between the two groups. Mean surgical
time, blood loss and length of hospital stay were significantly greater for
the open group (p < 0.05). Compared to the baseline, mean serum aldolase
was significantly high on post-op day 2 for both the groups (MIS: 5.18 U/L
vs. 9.8 U/L; Open: 5.36 U/L vs. 13.2 U/L). For all visits, open group had
comparatively higher mean serum aldolase levels than their counterparts.
Mean serum creatine kinase for open group was significantly higher than MIS
group at post-op days 1, 2, 3, 5 and discharge (p < 0.05). For the both
groups, mean creatine kinase was highest at post-op day 2. Mean creatine
kinase and aldolase levels returned to the normal levels for both the groups
at visits 3-week, 3- and 6-months post-op. Patient-reported pain and
disability scores were similar. Both groups reported one complication each
which resolved with interventions (MIS: wound drainage; open: CSF leak and
lumbar drain). Conclusions: Our cohort data indicates that MIS
technique for scoliosis correction is a viable option and may significantly
reduce muscle injury during the acute post-op period. MIS technique may
limit post-operative surgical morbidity.

## P379: Comparative outcomes betwen percutaneous and endoscopic
radiofrequency ablation of the sacroiliac joint complex in th treatment of
sacroiliac joint pain patients: systematic review and meta-analysis

Saran Pairuchvej

1

 and Jatupon Kongtharvonskul

2

1

Orthopedics Department, Queen Savang Vadhana Memorial Hospital,
Cholburi, Thailand

2

Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Faculty of
Medicine Ramathibodi Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok,
Thailand

Introduction: The sacroiliac joint (SIJ) is a junction between
the spine (sacrum) and the pelvis (ilium). The SIJ complex is one of the
sources of chronic low back pain compromising between 15 and 25% of cases.
The treatment of SIJ pain is challenging with no easy solution. Percutaneous
radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a common practice. However the limitation
of this treatment due to no visualization of the medial branch at the facet
joint L5/S1 resulting in different area is commonly targeted. Recently,
endoscopic RFA of SIJ allows better visualization nerve and the surrounding
ligamentous tissue. But there is no current consensus regarding which method
is the most suitable. Therefore we conducted a systematic review and
indirect meta-analysis to compare the post-operative outcomes among SIJ
treatment and identify which method is the best for surgical treatment of
SIJ pain patients. Material and Method: We searched all
prospective and retrospective studies that reported post-operative outcomes
of percutaneous and endoscopic RFA for surgical treatment of SIJ from the
PubMed and Scopus databases up to 5 January 2022. Data were independently
extracted by two reviewers. An indirect meta-analysis was applied to assess
treatment outcomes. Results: 18 cohort studies (N = 734
patients) met inclusion criteria. Interventions were endoscopic (N = 70
patients) and percutaneous RFA (N = 664 patients). A direct meta-analysis
showed that the UMD of pain (numeric rating scale) after surgery in
endoscopic RFA were significantly difference of -3.5 (95%CI: 4.34 to2.67),
-4.76 (95%CI: -6.43 to -3.10), -4.33 (95%CI: -6.60 to -2.06) scores at 1, 3,
6 months while percutaneous RFA groups were significantly difference of
-4.19 (95%CI: -5.21 to -3.18), -3.56 (95%CI: -3.95 to -3.17), -3.62 (95%CI:
-4.23 to -3.00) and -3.42 (95%CI: -4.07 to -2.76) scores at 1, 3, 6 12
months when compared to before surgery. The UMD of Oswestry Disability Index
(ODI) score after surgery were better of -9.20 (95%CI: -11.70 to -6.70),
-19.51 (95%CI: -40.25 to 1.22) and -24.04 (95%CI: -51.54 to 3.45) scores at
1, 3, 6 months while percutaneous RFA groups were significantly difference
of -8.66 (95%CI: -14.74 to -2.58) and -7.17 (95%CI: -9.95 to -4.39) at 3 and
6 months when compared to before surgery. For indirect meta-analysis showed
that effects of pain of endoscopic RFA were -0.69 (95%CI: -4.89 to 3.51)
scores, 1.22 (95%CI: -0.13 to 2.58) scores and 0.77 (95%CI: -1.25 to 2.79)
scores at 1, 3 and 6 months when compared to percutaneous RFA group. While
the ODI of endoscopic RFA were -9.70 (95%CI: -56.40 to 36.99) and -17.15
(-87.27 to 52.97) at 3 and 6 months when compared to percutaneous RFA group.
There have no statistically significant differences between endoscope and
percutaneous RFA in all outcomes. In term of complications, there have no
complications of both groups. Conclusions: Although there was
no significant difference in pain and disability scores between endoscopic
and percutaneous RFA, the superiority of surgical time, cost of surgery,
wound size and technical demand indicated that percutaneous RFA offer more
effective therapy for SIJ pain than endoscopic RFA surgery.

## P380: Footdrop and spine endoscopy: is the future here?

Emanuel Homem

1

, Joana Rodrigues

1

, Tiago Canas

1

, João Cruz

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

, and Luís Soares

1

1

Hospital do Divino Espírito Santo, Ponta Delgada, Portugal

Introduction: Acute and progressive foot drop are well-known
entities. The most common cause is degenerative lumbar spinal disease (with
52% of causes secondary to disc herniation and 35% to spinal stenosis). The
inability of ankle dorsiflexion may lead to multiple falls and injuries,
resulting in substantial impairment and decreased quality of life.
Percutaneous endoscopic discectomy is being increasingly used as solution
for this condition. The authors describe a case of acute right foot drop
caused by a L3-L4 disc herniation with lumbar canal stenosis treated with
percutaneous endoscopic transforaminal. The goal is to highlight the ease of
access and great outcome to support minimally invasive solution for these
cases. Material and Methods: A 40-year-old male presents with
sudden onset of severe back pain (VAS 10/10) with right foot drop while
getting up from a chair. He has past medical history of progressive left
footdrop due to paramedian L4-L5 herniated disc already submitted to
percutaneous translaminar and transforaminal treatment with good functional
outcome. On examination, the patient had a positive straight leg test at 30°
with right ankle and toe extension’s muscle strength of 1/5 and hypoesthesia
of right L4 dermatome. Deep tendon reflexes were normal and without
cerebellar signs. He had previous decreased contralateral ankle strength
(4/5) and no other neurological deficits. His bladder function was normal
with intact perianal sensation. MRI diagnosed a disc herniation at right
L3-L4 level (inferior migrated) with spinal canal stenosis due to ligamentum
flavum hypertrophy. Next day, patient underwent percutaneous transforaminal
endoscopic foraminotomy, discectomy and lumbar decompression at L3-L4 level
by an 1cm incision. Results: Postoperative period was
uneventful: the patient was mobilized on the same day of operation and
discharged the next day with the improvement of ankle and toe dorsiflexion
to 4/5 muscle strength and slight hyposesthesia. At 3 months follow-up, his
muscle strength was recovered and hyposthesia resolved near completely.
Conclusion: Lumbar disc herniation with canal stenosis
should be considered in patients presenting with foot drop. Early surgery
may prevent severe late neurological consequences and has a favorable
outcome. The objective of using endoscopy is to provide a safe and minimally
invasive approach, even to address multiple lumbar levels with early
postoperative mobilization and faster return to work.

## P381: Full-endoscopic foraminotomy in stable lytic lumbar listhesis. A
multicenter case series and data analysis

Facundo Van Isseldyk

1,2

, Javier Quillo-Olvera

3

, Cristian Ricardo Correa Valencia

1

, Jung-Hoon Kim

4

, Yanting Liu

4

, David Del Curto

1

, and Jin-Sung Luke Kim

4

1

Latinamerican Endoscopic Spine Surgery Society (LESSS)

2

Hospital Privado de Rosario, Neurosurgery, Rosario,
Argentina

3

Anahuac University, School of Medicine, H+ Hospital, Querétaro,
Mexico

4

Spine Center and Department of Neurosurgery, Seoul St. Mary’s
Hospital, College of Medicine, the Catholic University of Korea, Seoul,
South Korea

Introduction: Lytic lumbar spondylolisthesis (LLS) affects 8.2%
of the worldwide population. Although commonly associated in the surgical
community with segmental instability , only a small percentage of cases
demonstrate actual radiological instability. However, even in stable cases
neurological symptoms can occur as a result of radicular compression in
lateral recess or foraminal area. Open foraminal decompression usually
requires a concomitant fusion due to the muscular, osseus and ligament
disruption caused by the surgical approach. In this setting, full-endoscopic
approaches could decompress the affected root while preserving segmental
stability, avoiding the need for instrumented fusion. Material and
Methods: We present a case-series of 17 consecutive patients with
low-grade, stable LLS and concordant symptomatic radiculopathy, treated with
full endoscopic foraminotomy. Patients baseline and imaging characteristics,
as well as preoperative back pain VAS, leg pain VAS and ODI were obtained.
Included patients were treated by four of the authors with endoscopic
foraminotomy according to the “module-based” approach previously published.
Surgery planning and execution was performed following the selected modules.
Degree of intervertebral disc breach during surgical procedure was also
recorded. Outcome variables included back pain VAS, leg pain VAS and
ODI. Postoperative CT scans and dynamic X-Rays were obtained to assess the
amount and precision of bony resection and segmental stability. Follow-up
consultation was performed every 6 months. Paired T-Test was used for
normally distributed variables, while the remaining was analyzed with
Wilcoxon’s sum rank test. Results: 9 male patients and 8 female
were included. The mean age was 68 years. In 76% of the patients a
transforaminal approach was used, while the remaining 24% had an
interlaminar contralateral approach. 76.5 % of patients had high Pfirmann
values (4-5). Postoperative values of ODI, leg pain VAS and back pain VAS
showed statistically significant reduction compared with preoperative
values. No intraoperative or postoperative complications were observed. One
patient had high-level disc breach during surgical procedure (wide
annulotomy and intersomatic discectomy) and subsequently developed
radiological instability that required lumbar fusion as a separate
procedure. No leg pain recurrence was observed in the follow up period.
Conclusion: In the present series, full-endoscopic
foraminotomy allowed to successfully control radicular symptoms in patients
with LSS, while preserving segmental stability in the great majority of
cases. Only one patient developed postoperative instability and required
subsequent fusion, possibly related to high-level disc space breach. This
is, to our knowledge, the first case series of patients with LSS treated
with full-endoscopic foraminotomy ever published.

## P382: How can cement leakage be prevented in kyphoplasty? Technical
report and clinical study

Inan Uzunoglu

1

, Gokhan Gurkan

2

, Ceren Kizmazoglu

3

, Rafet Ozay

1

, Murat Sayin

2

, and Nurullah Yuceer

2

1

Neurosurgery, Ankara Diskapi Yildirim Beyazit Training and Research
Hospital, Turkey

2

Neurosurgery, Izmir Katip Celebi University, Ataturk Training and
Research Hospital, Ankara, Istanbul

3

Neurosurgery, Dokuz Eylul University Medicine Faculty, Izmir,
Turkey

Introduction: Vertebral compression fractures can occur due to
many different reasons. Kyphoplasty is at the forefront in the treatment of
these fractures. The most worrying complication of kyphoplasty is cement
leakage. We wanted to share the effectiveness of the technique we used in
our series in preventing cement leakage. Material and Methods:
300 patients were retrospectively screened in our clinic. While group A (150
patients) was operated on with classical kyphoplasty techniques, while group
B(150 patients) used similar methods before cement injection, the
suitability of cement fluidity for injection is determined by pushing cement
fillers and forming a ring on itself. After reaching this consistency, it is
sent to the corpus bilaterally or unilaterally. At this stage, the corpus is
divided into three equal areas in the craniocaudal plane on the lateral
x-ray, and the operation is terminated if the cement passes into the most
posterior area. Results: While some of our patients were
treated with a single vertebra in the same session, some of our patients
were treated with 4 vertebrae in the same session. Cement leakage was
detected in 123 (30.8%) of 400 operated vertebrae. Of these 123 vertebrae,
16 (13%) were in Group B and 107 (87%) were in Group A, a statistically
significant difference was found (p < 0.001). Epidural leakage in 5
(4.1%) vertebrae in total were detected in 3 vertebrae in Group A and 2
vertebrae in Group B. While intradiscal leakage was detected in 44 (35.8%)
vertebrae, all of them were in Group A. Extracorporeal leak was detected in
62 (50.5%) vertebrae, while only 8 of them were in Group B. Intravasal leak
was detected in only 12 (9.8%) vertebrae, equally in both groups. There was
a statistically significant difference in terms of cement leakage between
vertebrae whose posterior wall was not intact and the others (p < 0.05).
At the same time, statistically significant differences were found in A3 and
A4 fractures according to the AO spine classification compared to other
fractures and in patients who underwent more than one vertebra operation in
the same session (p < 0.05). Between Group B and Group A, the dose of
scope was statistically significant in favor of Group B (p < 0.05). In
Group B, there was a statistically significant difference between cement
viscosity, fracture type and etiology, trauma-operation time, type of
balloon used, type of intervention, and cement amount. no significant
differences were found (p > 0.05). However, in cases where the amount of
injected cement exceeded 7cc, it was statistically revealed that cement
leakage could increase in both groups (p < 0.05).
Conclusion: Kyphoplasty is an effective treatment method
for vertebral fractures, but a simple surgical procedure can turn into a
very catastrophic one after cement leaks may develop. There are techniques
described in the literature to prevent cement leakage. however, none of them
have been fully successful. In the literature, cement leakage ranges between
5-87%. In our study, it was determined that it could be applied as an
effective technique, with a rate of 7.7%.

## P383: When to consider stand-alone lateral lumbar interbody fusion: is

Cristiano Magalhães Menezes

, Erica Godinho Menezes

Orthopedics, Columna Institute, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

3

Orthopedics, Hospital Español, Mendoza, Argentina

Introduction: Degenerative disc disease is one of the most
common conditions treated by spine surgeons and is a common cause of
dysfunction with a negative impact on quality of life. Lateral lumbar
interbody fusion (LLIF) is a minimally invasive technique proven to be
useful for indirect decompression of the spinal canal and foramina with high
fusion rates and a very low risk of complications. The objective of this
study is to perform a comprehensive review of the literature about the role
of stand-alone lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF). Material and
Methods: A MEDLINE review was conducted including studies about
stand-alone LLIF for any condition. The opinions of the authors were also

articles of interest for the objective of this review were analyzed.
Recommendations based on the literature were made. Although most of the
recommendations in the literature were about augmentation with pedicle
screws, there may be a role for stand-alone LLIF in some particular cases.
Specific technical aspects should be considered to reduce the failure rate.
Conclusion: Although there might be some specific
indications for stand-alone LLIF, but despite the high subsidence rate and
low fusion rates, it should be considered an exception rather than the
rule.

## P384: Single position spine corpectomies. A multicentric study

Alfredo Guiroy

, Cristiano Menezes

, J. Alex Thomas

, Ashish Patel

, Gaston Camino-Willhuber

, Michael Galgano

Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

6

Neurosurgery, University of North Carolina, North Carolina, United

Elite Spine Health and Wellness Center, Fort Lauderdale, United

Introduction: Single position spine surgery for disc pathologies
has been gaining momentum as it has proven to reduce operative time, blood
loss and hospital length of stay with similar or better outcomes than
traditional dual-position surgery. The objective of this study is to
describe and discuss a multicentric case series of patients treated by
single position corpectomy (SPC). Material and Methods:
Multicenter retrospective study of patients treated using a single position
corpectomy (SPC) of the thoracic or lumbar vertebra. The following data was
collected from each center involved: demographics, diagnosis (trauma, tumor
or infection), neurological status, comorbidities, surgical approach and
procedure (single position lateral or prone lateral), number of instrumented
levels, intraoperative parameters (length of surgery, estimated blood loss,
transfusion), postoperative parameters (time to mobilization, length of
stay, days spent in the Intensive care unit), complications, reoperation and
readmissions and radiological variables. The minimum follow-up for inclusion
was six months. Results: 34 patients were included (24 males,
10 females), with a mean age of 51.2 years. The diagnosis that motivated the

complications we had 2 returns to the operating room (1 persistent stenosis
and 1 wound infection). Conclusion: This is the first
multicentric series of patients that underwent single position corpectomy
and fusion. This technique has shown to be safe and effective to treat a
variety of spinal conditions with a relatively low rate of complications.
More series are required to validate this technique as a possible standard
approach when thoracolumbar corpectomies are indicated.

using a microscope. The objective of this study was to introduce an
effective and safe surgical approach for up migrated LDH by UBE translaminar
keyhole approach. Material and Methods: Twelve patients with
high-grade and very high-grade up LDH treated with a UBE translaminar
keyhole approach between March 2021 and February 2022 were reviewed in this
study. Clinical outcomes were assessed including preoperative, immediately
postoperative and one-month follow up visual analog scale (VAS) for back and
leg pain and MacNab Criteria. Results: Nine male and three
female patients underwent surgery using UBE translaminar keyhole approach.
Seven patients showed high-grade up migrated LDH, and five patients showed
very high-grade up migrated LDH (above the pedicle level). In all cases, the
migrated LDH was removed successfully confirmed by postoperative magnetic
resonance imaging. The improvements of VAS for back pain were 4.5 (SD = 3.1)
to 2.0 (SD = 1.0) and 1.0 (SD = 1.0) for immediately postoperative and
one-month follow-up, showing a statistically significant difference (p <
0.001). Improvements of VAS for leg pain was 6.5 (SD = 2.5) preoperatively
to 2.3 (SD = 1.1) and 0.8 (SD = 0.4) immediately postoperative and one-month
follow up respectively, showing a significant difference (p < 0.001).
According to MacNab criteria, we observed excellent outcomes in 66.6% and
good outcomes in 33.3%. Conclusion: Translaminar discectomy
using UBE is a minimally invasive surgical technique that embraces the
advantages of biportal endoscopy and translaminar approach to treat uo
migrated LDH. It could be considered as a feasible alternative surgical
options to treat high-grade up migrated LDH.

## P387: Technique notes and preliminary outcome of transforaminal approach
by unilateral biportal endoscopic spinal surgery for lumbar extraforaminal
disc herniation

Chih-ying Wu

1,2

 and Cheng-Di Chiu

3,4

1

Neurosurgery, China Medical University Hsinchu Hospital, Hsinchu,
Taiwan

2
Graduate Institute of Integrated Medicine
3
Neurosurgery, China Medical University Hospital, Taichung,
Taiwan
4
Graduate Institute of Biomedical Science,
China Medical University, Taichung, Taiwan
Introduction: Lumbar extraforaminal disc herniation (LEFDH)
accounts for approximately 7-12% of all lumbar herniation discs. It can
cause severe radiculopathy and disability. Unlike the posterolateral lumbar
dis herniations, midline approach for LEFDH is challenge due to the bone
restriction. Minimally invasive spine surgery has seen a breakthrough
progress in recent decades. The purpose of minimally invasive spine surgery
is to reduce normal tissue damage, preserve normal anatomical structures,
decrease patient stress, and achieve the same or better prognosis as open
surgery. At present, the tools of minimally invasive spine surgery are
microscopes and endoscopes. Endoscopic spine surgery included uniportal and
biportal endoscope. Both have their advantages and advocates. According to
the current literature, there seems to be no significant difference in the
comparison of operation time and patient prognosis. However, there was two
advantages of biportal endoscopic spinal surgery (BESS). The first is using
of conventional spine surgical instruments like open surgery. Second is
protecting the neural structures by assistant retractor is safer than the
uniportal endoscopic spine surgery. Hence, in this article, we evaluate the
clinical outcome of LEFDH removal by transforaminal approach of unilateral
BESS. Material and Methods: We collected 13 patients with LEFDH
from January 2021 to August 2022. All patients scheduled transforaminal
approach of unilateral BESS performed by one single neurosurgeon. The BESS
surgical steps are as follows: First, we identified the surgical level and
the tips of transverse processes (TP) under C-arm fluoroscopy guiding. Two
skin incisions were made at the tip of TP on the ipsilateral side. Then the
two portal surgical instruments are inserted into the base of the TP
respectively. The surgical space is enlarged and identified the Kambin's
triangle, lateral border of isthmus and superior articular process.
Foraminoplasty may be performed with drilling and Kerrison punch if
necessary. Then, we could remove the LEFDH safely by assistant retractor. We
recorded the operation time, the number of operation level, complications,
and hospital days. Visual analog scale (VAS) was measured pre- and
postoperatively. After discharge, Modified Macnab criteria was analyzed for
outcome evaluation. Results: The mean age of the patients was
68.7 ± 8.8 years old. There were 8 males and 5 females. The mean operation
time was 97.8 ± 26.3 min. The mean follow-up time was 229.9 ± 8186 days. The
average length of hospital stay was 3.5 ± 0.8 days. Pre- and postoperative
VAS were 7.5 ± 80.8 and1.8 ± 81.1, respectively (p value < 0.001). The
Modified Macnab criteria after discharge: excellent 23.1%, good 69.2%, fair
7.7%. Only one complication is dura tear but no neurological deficit.
Conclusion: BESS requires experienced and skillful surgical
technique for nerve root protection and herniation disc removal. According
to our statistical results, the transforaminal approach of unilateral BESS
is quite effective, safe, and alternative method for the treatment of
LEFDH.

## P388: Minimally invasive TLIF options for lumbar
spondylolisthesis

Gabriel Tender

1

1

Neurosurgery, Louisiana State University, New Orleans, United
States

Introduction: Previous studies have shown that minimally
invasive spinal techniques result in shorter hospital stays and quicker
recovery. Minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MI
TLIF) has become the preferred fusion method for the L5-S1 and / or L4-5
levels at our institution. However, patients with spondylolisthesis may
represent a challenge, due to the distorted anatomy. Material and
Methods: We review our experience with MI and standard open TLIF
for patients with spondylolisthesis within the past 4 years.
Results: A total of 75 patients underwent MI TLIF at our
institution between Jan 2016 and Dec 2020, whereas 27 patients underwent
standard open TLIF. 45 of the MI TLIF patients (60%) had radiographic signs
of spondylolisthesis. The majority exhibited grade 1 spondylolisthesis (33,
44%), with the remainder being grade 2 (12, 16%). One patient in the MI TLIF
spondylolisthesis group had an S1 pedicle fracture after a fall and had to
have that screw repositioned. Of the 39 patients in the MI TLIF group (52%)
who presented for their 1-year follow-up CT, 37 (94%) had a solid fusion,
with one patient in each group not showing bridging bone through the treated
interspace. Similarly, 19 of the 20 patients (95%) in the standard open TLIF
group who presented for the 1-year follow-up CT showed a solid fusion.
Conclusion: MI TLIF for patients with grade 1 or 2
spondylolisthesis yields comparable fusion results with the standard
techniques, with shorter hospitalization and quicker recovery. Certain
surgical maneuvers may help improve fusion rates and screw placement
accuracy.

## P389: Cage positioning significantly impacts lumbar lordosis and disc
space restoration following minimally invasive lateral lumbar interbody
fusion

Tariq Issa

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Khoa Tran

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Sebastian Fras

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Division of Spine Surgery, Rothman Orthopaedic Institute,
Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) offers the
reliability of lordotic correction seen in anterior lumbar surgery while
also supporting a minimally invasive approach that can reduce complications.
While cage geometry and cage placement have been suggested to play an
integral role in radiographic outcomes in various interbody fusion
approaches, the role of these parameters remains unclear in LLIF procedures.
The objective of our study was to evaluate patient and surgical factors that
predict increased overall lumbar lordosis and segmental lordosis correction
following an LLIF. Material and Methods: A retrospective review
was conducted of all patients who underwent 1- or 2-level LLIF.
Pre-operative, initial post-operative, and six-month post-operative
measurements of lumbar lordosis, segmental lordosis, anterior disc height,
and posterior disc height were collected from standing lateral radiographs
for each patient. Cage placement was measured utilizing center point ratio
(CPR) on immediate post-operative radiographs. Spearman correlations were
used to assess associations between cage lordosis and radiographic
parameters. Multivariate linear regression was performed to assess
independent predictors of outcomes. Results: A total of 105
levels in 78 unique patients were included. Most procedures involved fusion
of one-level (N = 50, 64.1%), most commonly at L3-L4 (46.2%). Despite no
differences in baseline segmental lordosis, patients with anteriorly or
centrally placed cages experienced the greatest segmental lordosis
correction immediately (anterior: 4.81 mm and central: 4.46 mm vs.
posterior: 2.47 mm, p = 0.0315) and at six-months post-operatively, and
patients with anteriorly placed cages had greater overall lordosis
correction post-operatively (6.30 deg, p = 0.0338). At six-month follow up,
patients with anteriorly placed cages experienced the greatest increase in
anterior disc height (anterior: 6.24 mm vs posterior: 3.69 mm, p = 0.0122).
Cages placed more posteriorly increased the delta posterior disc height
post-operatively (posterior: 4.91 mm vs anterior: 1.80 mm, p = 0.0001) and
at six-months (posterior: 4.18 mm vs anterior: 2.06 mm, p = 0.0255). There
were no correlations between cage lordosis angle and outcomes. On
multivariate regression, anterior cage placement predicted greater six-month
improvement in segmental lordosis, while posterior placement predicted
greater six-month improvement in posterior disc height. Percutaneous screw
placement, cage lordosis angle, and cage height did not independently
predict any radiographic outcomes. Conclusion: LLIF procedures
reliably improve lordosis and increase intervertebral disc space. Anterior
cage placement improves lordosis angle greater than posterior placement,
which better corrects sagittal alignment, but there is still a significant
improvement of lordosis even with a posteriorly placed cage. Posterior cage
placement provides greater restoration in posterior disc space height,
maximizing indirect decompression, but even the anteriorly placed cages
provided indirect decompression. Cage parameters including cage height,
lordosis angle, and material do not impact radiographic improvement.

## P390: An effective treatment option for nonuion of Kummell's desease
after treated with PKP

Hui Liu

1

 and Deqing Luo

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, The Affiliated Southeast Hospital
of Xiamen University, Zhangzhou, China

Introduction: Percutaneous kyphoplasty (PKP) has been widely
used to treat Kummell’s disease and provides good results in patients with
persistent pain and an intact posterior wall. However, intravertebral
nonunion between the cement and bone, like a ball socket effect after
percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP), can cause persistent severe pain and
sagittal kyphosis, even neurological dysfunction. The optimal treatment for
nonunion of Kummell’s disease treated With PKP remains controversial and
unclear. The purpose of this study was to investigate the efficacy of staged
anterior and posterior minimal invasive approach (OLIF and multifidus
approach) in treating nonunion of Kummell’s disease treated with PKP.
Method: We retrospectively evaluated all patients who
underwent nounion of Kummell’s disease after treated With PKP with between
January 2019 and June 2022. Patients with a minimum follow-up of 12 months
were included. The patients were treated with SRS 2-3 osteotomy and long
segment fixation with screw augmentation through posterior multifidus
approach firstly, secondly expandable mesh cage reconstruction of anterior
column were carried out through OLIF approach. Anterior edge height of
injured vertebrae, kyphosis Cobb angle were measured to evaluate the
radiological result. Patient clinical outcomes were quantified via Oswestry
Disability Index (ODI), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) Back, preoperatively and
postoperatively and at 3, 6, and 12 months follow-up. Analyses were
performed using IBM SPSS Statistics software, v24.0 (IBM SPSS, Chicago, IL).
Results: All patients were followed up 12-28 months, with
an average of 15.3 months. The average operative duration was 126 ± 25
minutes(posterior) and 115 ± 17 minutes(anterior), and the average
intraoperative blood loss was 245 ± 45 mL (posterior) and 168 ± 27
minutes(anterior). ODI, anterior vertebral heights, and kyphotic Cobb angles
were improved significantly at 1 week after surgery compared the
preoperative examinations, and were well maintained at the final follow-up
evaluation. There was no instrumentation failure in our study during
follow-up. Conclusion: staged anterior and posterior minimal
invasive approach (OLIF and multifidus approach) is a safe and effective
surgical option for treating nonunion of Kummell’s disease treated with
PKP.

## P391: Transforaminal lumbar endoscopic surgery on the limits: experience
from extreme cases management in a single tertiary center

Nikolaos Gkantsinikoudis

1

, Christos Siopis

1

, and Stylianos Kapetanakis

1,2

1

Spine Department and Deformities, Interbalkan European Medical

2

Department of Minimally Invasive and Endoscopic Spine Surgery,
Athens Medical Center, Athens, Greece

Introduction: Transforaminal Lumbar Endoscopic Decompression
(TLED) constitutes a novel, minimally invasive and atraumatic technique
recruited for surgical management of a plethora of spine ailments. Principal
indication for TLED conduction is Lumbar Disc Herniation (LDH). However,
considering the substantial advantages of technique in comparison with
conventional open surgical methods, spectrum of TLED indications has been
demonstrated to constantly widen in recent literature. Recruitment of TLED
for surgical management of extreme cases of foraminal stenosis (FS)
encountered in the framework of Adult Degenerative Scoliosis (ADS), Adjacent
Segment Disease (ASD) post previous fusion surgery and postoperative
Recurrent Foraminal Stenosis (RFS) after open decompression surgery
represents a feasible strategy according to current literature reports,
demonstrating promising clinical outcomes. Hence, we hereby present our
experience with management of extraordinary cases of FS with TLED surgery.
Material and Methods: Twenty-one (21) individuals with
clinically remarkable secondary FS on the ground of ASD (n = 7), ADS (n = 6)
and previous open decompression surgery (n = 8) were included in this
prospective investigation. After meticulous clinical and radiologic
investigation, all enrolled patients underwent TLED (outside-in technique)
in 2018-2019. Postoperative evaluation was conducted in predetermined
follow-up intervals via clinical examination and performance of specific
patient-reported outcome measures as Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), modified
McNab criteria and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). All patients were
followed-up for an at least 1-year period (mean: 1.4 years).

in all cases. Operated segments were L3-L4 (19.0%), L4-L5 (52.4%) and L5-S1
(28.6%). VAS and ODI measures demonstrated a statistically significant (p
< 0.05) improvement in all patient immediately postoperatively, which was
constantly observed until the end of follow-up. Overall clinical outcomes,
as analyzed with modified MacNab criteria, were depicted to be excellent in
12 patients, good in 6 and fair in 3 patients. Conclusion:
According to our results from this limited case-series analysis, TLED
represents a safe and effective surgical alternative for management of
patients with secondary FS on the ground of ADS, ASD post fusion surgery and
postoperatively after previous open decompression surgery.

Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgery has grown
exponentially in recent years, with the development of new techniques and
suitable surgical instruments. This has become advantageous in the treatment
of degenerative spinal pathology, as it allows to minimize possible surgical
complications associated with age and comorbidities of the patient, compared
to the conventional “open” surgery. The aim of this study was to evaluate
the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing treatment for lumbar disc
herniation via endoscopic transforaminal approach. Material and
Methods: A retrospective study of all patients consecutively
submitted to endoscopic transforaminal lumbar discectomy by the same surgeon
between September 2018 and May 2021 was performed. Results: A
total of 40 patients were included (24 (60%) men, 16 (40%) women). The mean
age was 55 years. The mean follow-up period was 17 months [12-36 months].
Most patients (82%) had a herniated disc in a foraminal location, 57% at
L4-L5, 25% at L3-L4 and 18% at L5-S1. A statistically significant clinical
improvement was recorded postoperatively compared to preoperatively on the
Oswestry Disability Index (23 ± 3.6 vs 62 ± 3.3; p < 0.005) on the Visual

underwent surgical revision via an “open” approach within an average period
of 11 months after the endoscopic procedure. Conclusion:
Transforaminal endoscopic surgery is a safe and effective alternative in the
treatment of patients with foraminal lumbar disc herniation. Studies with a
longer follow-up period and with a greater number of patients are needed to
validate the results of this procedure.

## 908

## P394: Endoscopic treatment of symptomatic lumbar epidural cysts

Karel Willems

1

 and Fred Ruythooren

1

1

Orthopedie, AZ Delta Roeselare, Roeselare, Belgium

Introduction: Lumbar epidural cysts are a rare cause of spinal
cord or nerve root compression. Conventionally, symptomatic cases are
treated by open surgical decompression or percutaneous infiltration
techniques. However, we believe the rise of full endoscopic spinal surgery
offers a sage and reliable alternative to conventional methods due to its
minimal invasive nature, maintaining the ability to directly visualize the
underlying pathology. Materials and Methods: We describe the
resection technique of the three most commonly epidural lumbar cysts: facet
cysts, flavum cysts and blaastrup cysts. Results: Each type of
the cysts need a different type of endoscopic treatment. Flavum cyst is
localised more lateral, adherent at the facet joint. Partial resection of
the medial part of the facet joint is started, followed with peeling the
cyst wall of the adjoining dura/radix. The more dorsal located flavum cysts
are peeled off the dura and resected as the are not as densely adhered to
the thecal sac. Blaastrup cyst needs a spacious central decompression,
achieved by a partial resection of the lamina and the base of the spinous
process. Conclusion: Full endoscopic surgical decompression
offers a safe, reliable and minimal invasive alternative in the treatment of
symptomatic lumbar epidural cysts.

, Katsunori Fukutake

, and Hiroshi Takahashi

Introduction: Minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody

focused on adjacent segment degeneration (ASD). Material and
Methods: A retrospective analysis of prospectively collected

evaluated according to the Japanese Orthopedic Association score (JOA

due to ASD. Radiographic ASD and multifidus muscle atrophy was assessed
using flexion-extension radiographs and MRI. MIS-TLIF was performed via a

and post- radiographic sagittal spinopelvic parameters (PT, PI-LL) between
the two groups. The mean JOA scores in MIS group and C group were both
significantly improved to 25.3 and 24.5 respectively at the latest follow-up
with no significant difference. Clinical ASD was observed in 3 cases with
MIS and in 11 cases with C (p = 0.04). Radiographic ASD was observed in 17
cases with MIS group and in 23 cases with C group (p = 0.36). Postoperative
multifidus muscle atrophy in MIS group was significantly less than C group.
Conclusion: This study demonstrates that MIS-TLIF obtained
the same clinical improvements as C-TLIF over ten years period. Preservation
of posterior elements using MIS technique including minimizing approach
related soft tissue trauma, posterior bony structures can reduce adjacent
segment disease.

bowel incontinence. Patient has significant cardiac history of ischemic
heart disease and atrial flutter for which patient was started on an oral
anticoagulant two weeks prior to onset of symptoms. Magnetic resonance
imaging showed a large extradural mass compressing the cauda equina causing
severe stenosis at the level of lumbar four to five. Patient underwent
minimally invasive transforminal Lumbar four to five decompression and
instrumented fusion. A facet cyst containing gross blood products was
excised during the lumbar decompression and fusion surgery. Post operatively
patient symptoms of lower back pain as well as bladder and bowel
incontinence improved. Results: We conducted a review of the
literature which revealed that predominately patients’ present with leg
pain, lower back pain, weakness and sensory deficits such as numbness,
tingling and paresthesia. Urinary and bowel incontinence is rarely reported
except in two previous cases reports. However, both cases were not
associated with use the anticoagulation. Hence, this case report documents
the first case of hemorrhagic facetal cyst secondary to oral anticoagulant
use causing cauda equina compression presenting with bowel and urinary
incontinence. Conclusion: This is the first case report of
lumbar four to five hemorrhagic facetal cyst secondary to oral
anticoagulant, resulting in cauda equina compression.

## P399: Laparoscopic aided interlocking screw removal for symptomatic leg
pain after anterior lumbar interbody fusion technique

Michael Rogers

1

, Ashish Patel

1

, Jahangir Asghar

2

, and Alfredo Guiroy

2

1

Spine Surgery, Duly Health and Care, Naperville, United
States

2

Spine Surgery, Elite Spine Health and Wellness, Plantation, United
States

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) has become
a standard procedure in the repertoire of a minimally invasive spine surgeon
and will likely be performed more often as the incidence of adult
degenerative spinal disorders in the United States increases. It is
beneficial for spine surgeons to be aware of technical considerations
associated with an ALIF and how to prevent complications to ensure complete
surgical proficiency. We report 2 cases of an uncommon complication
associated with an S1 compression neuropathy due to deep left-sided sacral
screw placement using a four-hole implant. Material and
Methods: This case study included two patients who underwent a
standalone ALIF with a four-hole implant for lumbar degenerative disease.
Both patients had full strength and were ambulatory. Both patients had
persistent intermittent numbness and aching in the S1 distribution that
promoted evaluation via a CT scan. Results: CT scan
demonstrated the left-sided screw was prominent into the left S1 foramen.
The imaging correlated with the patient's symptoms and both patients elected
for screw removal. Both patients underwent a novel laparoscopic assisted
method for screw removal. In both cases, the screws were removed
uneventfully with complete resolution of leg symptoms in both patients.
Conclusion: Our report describes a novel laparoscopic
method for ALIF screw removal in the event of a prominent screw into the
sacral foramen. Furthermore, we outline the considerations of selecting
screw length in each hole when using this four-hole ALIF implant.

## 1121

## P400: Comparison of postoperative bone healing in patients with UBE or
conventional lumbar discectomy

Jaeyoung So

1

 and Jeong-Yoon Park

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Spine and Spinal Cord Institute, Gangnam
Severance Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: In unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE)
discectomy, as opposed to conventional discectomy, continuous irrigation
lowers the temperature thereby reducing bone damage and promoting bone
healing. The purpose of this study was to investigate the difference of bone
healing at the postoperative laminectomy site in patients who underwent
unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) or conventional discectomy.
Materials and Methods: From January 2018 to June 2021, 66
patients who underwent laminectomy in our institute were retrospectively
reviewed. All patients were matched with sex, age, BMI, BMD, and F/U
duration by a 1:2 matching ratio and were divided into the “UBE” group (UBE,
22 patients) and the “conventional” group (44 patients, conventional
discectomy). We investigate the site of laminectomy shown in pre- and
postoperative x-ray images through scientific image analysis software
(ImageJ). The factors related with bone healing were also investigated.
Results: The average bone healing area of the UBE group was
69.59 mm2, and that of the conventional group was 44.56
mm2, a significant difference (p = 0.022). The remaining
laminectomy area was significantly lower in the UBE group than in the
conventional group (13.91 mm2 vs. 53.84 mm2, p <
0.001). The bone recovery ratio in the UBE group was 85.42%, compared to
51.33% in the conventional group, a significant difference (p < 0.001).
Primary laminectomy area, bone healing during 6 months, and clinical
outcomes were not significantly different between the two groups.
Conclusion: Compared with the conventional group, the UBE
group had greater bone healing area and higher bone recovery ratio for
patients with lumbar discectomy. These findings suggest that it is more
feasible to preserve the normal structure during UBE than during
conventional surgery.

## 1191

## P402: Comparison of clinical outcomes after single, double and multilevel
ELIF

Carlos De La Torre

1

, Darren Lui

1

, Bisola Ajayi

2

, and Khai Lam

1

1

Orthopaedics, London Bridge Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

2

Orthopaedics, NHS St George's Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

Introduction and Purpose: The minimally invasive extreme lateral
interbody fusion (ELIF) has increasingly gained importance in the treatment
of lumbar spine pathology. The purpose of this study was to compare surgical
outcomes and complications of single, double and multilevel fusion in
patients who underwent ELIF. Materials and Methods: Between
January 2013 and July 2021, we identified 95 patients undergoing ELIF for
lumbar pathology. Patients were divided into groups based on number of
levels fused during their procedure (1,2, or 3 or more) Patient related
outcome measures (PROMS) were collected preoperatively, and up to 12 months
postoperatively. PROMS included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Visual
Analog Scale (VAS) for both back (BP) and leg pain (LP) and EQ5D.
Results: There were 55% female and 45% male patients with a
mean age of 55 (26-84) years. 73 patients underwent single-level fusion, 12
underwent two level fusion and 10 underwent 3 or more levels fusion. For
ODI, statistically significant mean improvements from pre-operative to last
follow-up were 29.5± 2.4 (p < 0.001) for single-level, 15.4 ± 8.2 (p <
0.05) for double-level and 17 ± 5.5 (p < 0.01) for multi-level fusion.
For VAS BP, significant mean improvements from pre-operative to last
follow-up were 5.1 ± 0.34 (p < 0.001) for single-level, 3.9 ± 1.2 (p <
0.009) for double-level and 3.5 ± 0.8 (p < 0.001) multi-level. For VAS LP
the mean improvements were 4.6 ± 0.37 (p < 0.0001) for single-level, 2.9
± 1.1 (p < 0.05) for double-level and 4.5 ± 0.8 (p < 0.001) for
multi-level. For EQ5D the mean improvements were 23 ± 2.5 (p < 0.0007)
for single-level, 14.4 ± 6.7 (p < 0.05) for double-level and 21 ± 6.5 (p
< 0.01) for multi-level fusion. Five patients (6%) developed an adverse
event in the single-level group, 2 in the double-level (16%), and 2 in the
multi-level group (20%). The mean retraction time was 24, 36 and 56 minutes
for the single, double and multi-level groups respectively, the mean length
of stay was 3.6, 6.7 and 7.3 days for single, double and multi-level groups
respectively. All groups had an estimated blood loss of less than 100 ml.
Based on a previous study the percentage of patients that met the MCID for
ODI was 76%, 50% and 70% for single, double and multi-level fusion
respectively. For VAS BP was 82%, 66% and 80% and for VAS LP was 74%, 58%
and 80%. Conclusions: Our analysis showed that patients in
double and multilevel ELIF experienced less improvement in all aspects of
PROMS, had more complications, and had a late discharge home compared to
single-level ELIF. These findings are important for operative planning, for
setting appropriate preoperative expectations, and for risk stratification
in patients undergoing ELIF.

## 1236

## P403: Comparison of clinical outcomes between lumbar levels for
single-level extreme lateral inter body fusion

Carlos De La Torre

1

, Darren Lui

1

, Bisola Ajayi

2

, and Khai Lam

1

1

Orthopaedics, London Bridge Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

2

Orthopaedics, NHS St George's Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

Introduction and Purpose: The minimally invasive extreme lateral
interbody fusion (ELIF) has gained importance in the last decade. This
approach has differing complication profiles because of the inherent
anatomical differences encountered on each lumbar level. The purpose of this
study was to evaluate surgical outcomes and complications of single-level
ELIF comparing L4/L5 fusion with any other level fusion. Materials and
Methods: Between January 2013 and August 2021, we identified 76
patients undergoing single-level ELIF. Patients were divided into two
groups: L4/L5 level fusion group and other level fusion group. Patient
related outcome measures (PROMS) were collected preoperatively, and up to 12
months postoperatively. PROMS included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI),
Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for both back (BP) and leg pain (LP) and EQ5D.
Perioperative and postoperative data included retraction time (RT),
estimated blood loss (EBL), length of stay (LOS) and adverse events (AE).
Results: There were 58% female and 42% male patients with a
mean age of 54 (26-82) years. 60 patients underwent single-level fusion at
the L4/L5 level and 16 patients underwent single-level fusion at other level
(11 at L3/L4, 5 at L2/L3). For ODI, statistically significant mean
improvements from pre-operative to last follow-up were 31.2 ± 2.6 (p <
0.001) for L4/L5 fusion, and 24.1 ± 5.1 (p < 0.001) for other level
fusion. For VAS BP, significant mean improvements from pre-operative to last
follow-up were 5.1 ± 0.3 (p < 0.001) for L4/L5 fusion, and 4.5 ± 0.7 (p
< 0.001) for other level fusion. For VAS LP the mean improvements were
4.5 ± 0.4 (p < 0.001) for L4/L5 fusion, and 4.5 ± 0.7 (p < 0.001) for
other level fusion. For EQ5D the mean improvements were 23.3 ± 2.9 (p <
0.001) for L4/L5 fusion, and 19.8 ± 3.9 (p < 0.001) for other level
fusion. Four patients (6%) developed an adverse event in the L4/L5 fusion
group, 2 of them had urinary retention and improved after conservative
treatment, one developed an infection at the navigation pin insertion site,
improving after antibiotic therapy, and one developed radiculopathy which
required posterior revision. Two patients (12%) presented an adverse event
in the other level fusion group. One developed a pedicle fracture which was
treated with exchange of posterior screws, the other patient had
postoperative back and sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain, which was treated with
SIJ and epidural injections. The mean retraction time was 24 minutes in both
groups, the mean length of stay was 4 days in both groups. All groups had an
estimated blood loss of less than 100 ml. Conclusions: It has
been previously proposed that ELIF at the L4/L5 level carries a higher risk
of postoperative motor deficit due to nerve injury. Our analysis showed that
patients who underwent ELIF approach at the L4/L5 level did not experience
increased incidence of complications compared to other level fusion surgery
and they all experienced similar clinical outcomes. Therefore, we consider
that ELIF at L4/L5 level is a reasonable and effective fusion technique.
