## P404: Comparative analysis of prone lateral versus lateral decubitus
positioning in achieving optimal outcomes and reducing complication rates in
single-position minimally invasive spine surgery

Peter Passias

1

, Peter Tretiakov

1

, Jamshaid Mir

1

, Pooja Dave

1

, Kimberly McFarland

1

, Rachel Joujon-Roche

1

, Tyler Williamson

1

, Bailey Imbo

1

, Zach Thomas

1

, Stephane owusu-saprong

1

, Jordan Lebovic

1

, Shaleen Vira

2

, and Bassel Diebo

3

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, NYU Langone Orthopedic Hospital,
New York, United States

2

UT Southwestern, Dallas, United States

3

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, SUNY Downstate, New York, United
States

Introduction: Recent literature has pointed to the rising use of
prone lateral versus lateral decubitus positioning in Minimally-Invasive
Spine Surgery (MISS) as a method to reduce operative time, increase patient
safety, and aid in surgical accessibility. However, there is a paucity of
literature as to how prone lateral and lateral decubitus positioning
compares in terms of reaching optimal postoperative outcomes and reducing
complication rates. Materials and Methods: MISS patients with
baseline (BL) and 2-year (2Y) postop radiographic/HRQL data were included.
Patients positioned in the Prone Lateral (PL) or single-position Lateral
Decubitus (LD) position were isolated. At 2Y, an optimal outcome score was
calculated using 4 equally weighted criteria: 1) achieving ideal PT per
SRS-Schwab at 2Y, 2) Achieving ideal PI-LL per SRS-Schwab at 2Y, 3) No
complication requiring reoperation 4) Achieving NRS MCID by Salaffi et al.
criteria; optimal score threshold was set at meeting 2 of 4 criteria. Means
comparison analysis assessed differences in radiographic and clinical
outcomes at BL and 1Y post-op. ANCOVA assessed estimated marginal means
adjusting for BL age and revision status. Results: 34 Prone
Lateral and 36 Lateral Decubitus patients were included (54.40 ± 12.49
years, 40% female, 30.93 ± 6.52 kg/m2, mean CCI: 2.23 ± 1.55)
were included. At baseline, patients were comparable in age, gender, BMI,
and CCI (all p > .05). Peri-operatively, PL patients demonstrated
significantly lower operative time (200.09 vs 284.54 min, p = .007) and EBL
(332.35 vs 192.05 mL, p = .027). Though optimization scores were equivalent
between groups (p = .160), PL patients demonstrated significantly lower
peri-operative complication rates (p = .012), neurological complication
rates (p = .006), and had a fewer number of total complications by 2Y (p =
.014). When controlling for BL age and revision status, the PL patients
demonstrated consistently lower intra- and peri-operative complications as
well (both p < .015). In terms of patient-reported outcomes, PL patients
also demonstrated significantly improved NRS-Leg scores compared to LD
patients by 1Y (p = .038). Conclusions: Patients placed in the
Prone Lateral position during minimally invasive adult spinal deformity
surgery demonstrate decreased mean operative times and decreased
intraoperative invasiveness and blood loss versus patients operated on via
single-position Lateral Decubitus positioning. Though overall rates of
achieving optimal outcome remain comparable, Prone Lateral approach should
be considered as there may be significant additional benefit in reducing
peri- and post-operative complications by 2Y.

## 1364

## P405: Perioperative glucose response in diabetic patients with lumbar
spinal stenosis treated with biportal endoscopic decompression

Javier Quillo-Olvera

1

, Javier Quillo-Reséndiz

1

, and Michelle Barrera-Arreola

1

1

Spine Center, Hospital Angeles Centro Sur, Querétaro,
Mexico

Introduction: Physiological stress hyperglycemia is observed in
more than 40% of critically ill patients and 32% of patients undergoing
elective surgery. This phenomenon is usually transient in non-diabetic
patients and is defined as blood glucose > 140 mg/dL and severe
hyperglycemia > 180 mg/dL; the last one is associated with attenuation of
the basophil count, T cells, and monocytic function, leading to decreased
postoperative immunity and a high risk of infections. In diabetic patients,
severe perioperative hyperglycemia is common and associated with poor
postoperative results after spinal surgery. Therefore, we hypothesize that
the perioperative glycemic response of controlled diabetic patients
undergoing biportal endoscopic decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis is
similar to that of non-diabetics. Material and Methods: A
comparative study with prospective data acquisition and retrospective review
was performed. Controlled diabetic patients with a < 7 g/dL HbA1c and
non-diabetics with single-level lumbar spinal stenosis, radicular pain, or
neurogenic claudication consistent with radiological findings were treated
through unilateral biportal endoscopic access and bilateral decompression
(UBE-ULBD). Patients were divided into diabetic and non-diabetic cohorts.
Demographics, perioperative characteristics, and clinical outcomes were
compared and analyzed between groups. Preoperative, intraoperative, and
postoperative at 12 and 24 hours blood glucose measurements were obtained in
all patients to observe glucose response to surgical treatment.
Results: Two groups with 18 patients were made up. The mean
age in the DM2 group was 65.83y (±9.2), while the non-diabetic group was
52.67y (±19.8). L4-L5 was the most decompressed level; 88.9% of diabetic
patients were discharged the next day, while 11.1% on postoperative day 2.
All non-diabetic patients were discharged the next day. The mean operative
time in the DM2 group was 74.28 min (±26.87), while in the non-diabetic was
76.83 min (±29.22). The average EBL in the DM2 group was 29.44mL (±9.98),
while the non-diabetic group was 33.3 mL (±11.88). The mean HbA1c in DM2
group was 6.436 mg/dL (±0.43), and 5.261 mg/dL (±0.23) in non-diabetics. A
statistically significant decrease (p < 0.005) between preoperative and
postoperative pain and disability scores in both groups was observed. The
mean preoperative blood glucose was 136.5 mg/dL (±25.091) in DM2 group and
101.11 mg/dL (±10.255) in non-diabetics. The mean intraoperative glucose in
diabetics reached 170.22 mg/dL (±27.627), while non-diabetics it was 125.50
mg/dL (±19.847) (p = 0.007). The postoperative glucose at 12 and 24 hours
was 130.89 mg/dL (±23.552) in DM2 group and 106.89 mg/dL (±11.591) in
non-diabetics, and 136.06 mg/dL (±11.032) in DM2 group and 105.39 mg/dL
(±10,331) in the non-diabetics respectively (p = 001).
Conclusion: The present study reported that biportal
endoscopic surgery was associated with increased intraoperative glucose in
both groups, much higher in diabetic patients. Therefore measures for its
reduction should be considered during the surgery to avoid sustained
hyperglycemia and the known associated risks. However, postoperative glucose
at 12 and 24 hours did not show a trend of severe hyperglycemia when the
biportal endoscopic technique was used in diabetic patients.

## 1412

## P406: The implementation of minimally invasive spine surgery at a UPMC
peripheral community hospital

Yunting Tang

1

, Anthony Oyekan

1

, Jonathan Dalton

1

, Dominic Ridolfi

1

, and Vivek Sharma

1

1

University of Pittsburgh, 200 Lothrop Ste BST E 1640, Pittsburgh,
United States

Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) techniques
were developed to address several challenges with traditional approaches to
decompression and fusion, including extensive muscular dissection and
subsequent postoperative back pain and prolonged recovery.1,2
Since the introduction of a tubular distraction system for use in
microendoscopic diskectomy in 1997, MISS has undergone a rapid technological
evolution, including major improvements to endoscopy, robotic-assisted spine
surgery, and navigation.3 The implementation of MISS comes with
challenges including cost and learning curve. Thus, we aimed to study the
initial clinical experiences of a spine surgeon performing unilateral lumbar
laminectomy with bilateral decompression (ULLBD) via MISS at a UPMC
peripheral community hospital with no previous in-house spine service. We
hypothesized that a minimally invasive spine surgery program may be safely
implemented at a peripheral community hospital and will allow most patients
to have a rapid recovery with discharge to home. Material and
Methods: A retrospective review of a prospectively collected
database was performed with University of Pittsburgh review board approval.
We initially identified 131 elective ULLBD cases by a single
fellowship-trained orthopedic spine surgeon, from October 2019 to March
2021, at a non-teaching UPMC community hospital with no previous in-house
spine coverage. The minimum postoperative follow-up was 1 year. Data points
collected include patient demographics, diagnoses, discharge date, discharge
disposition, and narcotic use. Patients who underwent ULLBD were indicated
for instrumented posterior spinal fusion by pre-operative dynamic
instability and iatrogenic instability associated with the decompressive
procedure. Differences in patients who underwent fusion and those who did
not undergo fusion were compared using Chi-squared, Fischer’s exact test,
and two-tailed unpaired t-tests analysis. A p < 0.05 was considered
significant. Results: 55 patients were included in the analysis
(32 F, 23 M; age 65 ± 17 years, BMI 30.0 ± 6.1). 51 (92.7%) patients were
discharged on postoperative day 1, 3 (5.5%) patients were discharged on
postoperative day 2, and only 1 (1.7%) patient was discharged after
postoperative day 2. 53 (96.3%) patients were discharged to home and only 2
(3.6%) required a skilled nursing facility. Instrumented posterior spinal
fusion for ULLBD was generally performed in older patients with
spondylolisthesis and required greater OR time, radiation dose, blood loss,
and narcotic prescription doses than patients without instrumented fusion
Notably, all patients on chronic narcotics had no change in their
preoperative prescriptions despite continued clinical improvement. There
were no complications that required re-operation. Conclusion:
ULLBD via MISS may be safely performed at a MISS-naïve peripheral community
hospital with excellent outcomes. Implementation of a minimally invasive
spine surgery program in such a setting is safe, feasible, and allows for
optimal clinical outcomes. ERAS protocols may improve perioperative
restrictions, pain control, and rehabilitation. Considerations include
equipment needs, personnel training, and surgeon experience.

## 1471

## P407: Short-term clinical and radiological outcome of intradiscal
condoliase injection in lumbar disc herniation

Akihiro Nagamachi

1

, Hiroki Ikuchi

2

, Kohei Ohta

1

, and Takayuki Ogawa

3

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Yoshinogawa Medical Center, Tokushima,
Japan

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Takamatsu Municipal Hospital, Kagawa,
Japan

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Sakaide Kaisei Hospital, Kagawa, Japan

Introduction: Condoliase has high substrate specificity for
chondroitin sulfate and hyaluronic acid, which are glycosaminoglycans of
proteoglycans abundant in the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc.
Condoliase has been used to treat lumbar disc herniation (LDH), however
there is a paucity of evidence in clinical outcome of intradiscal condoliase
injection. In this prospective study, we investigated clinical and
radiological outcome of intradiscal condoliase injection. Material and
Methods: A total of 32 patients with LDH underwent intradiscal
condoliase injection at our hospital. All patients had clinical symptoms of
LDH and confirmed herniated disc on lumbar spine MRI. There were 25 male and
7 female and their mean age was 45 years (16 ∼ 85 years). Affected
intervertebral disc were 2 at L1-2, 1 at L2-3, 16 at L4-5, 13 at L5-S1.
Intradiscal condoliase injection was performed under fluoroscopic guidance.
A single 1 mL dose of condoliase (1.25 U/mL) was injected into the center of
the affected intervertebral nucleus pulposus using a 21-gauge puncture
needle. Patient was hospitalized in one day to observe adverse events.
Clinical and radiological assessments were conducted before, 1 week, 4
weeks, 3 months and 6 months after the injection. Clinical outcome was
measured using Japanese Orthopaedic Association Back Pain Evaluation
Questionnaire (JOABPEQ) and Visual analog scale (VAS, 0 to 100 mm) of
buttock and leg pain. Patient improved without additional surgery was
defined as responder and patient needed additional surgery because of
remained symptoms was defined as non-responder. All patients underwent
lumbar spine MRI. Axial and sagittal MRI were used to classify herniation
types; subligamentous extrusion (Sub), transligamentous extrusion (Trans)
and sequestration (Seq). Herniated disc area was measured on axial section.
All responders completed the minimum follow-up period of 6 months,
non-responders dropped out of this study at when additional surgery was
performed. Results: There were 26 responders and 6
non-responders. Number of patients of Sub, Trans and Seq were 23, 5 and 3,
respectively. Percentage of responders in Sub, Trans and Seq were 75%, 100%
and 0%, respectively. In responders, all item score of JOABPEQ were improved
after the injection. Mean VAS of responder before injection, 1 week, 4
weeks, 3 months and 6months were 68.0, 37.9, 25.0, 14.5 and 16.1,
respectively. On the other hand, mean VAS of non-responders before, 1 week
and 4 weeks after the injection were 82.2, 56.1 and 58.3, respectively.
Herniated disc area before and 6 months after the injection in responders
were 64.0 mm2 and 29.2 mm2, respectively.
Conclusion: Response rate of intradiscal condoliase
injection was 81.3% in this study. Therapeutic effect of condoliase is
confirmed only in Sub type herniation in clinical trial, however, response
rate was 100% even in Trans type in this study. Based on this result, we
indicate intradiscal injection of condoliase for patients with Sub and Trans
type. Non-responder did not improve at 1 week after the injection. Clinical
outcome at 1 week after the injection might give valuable information to
change treatment plan for non-responders.

## P409: Comparative outcomes of transcorporeal versus transdiscal anterior
endoscopic dissectomy for cervical radiculopathy: meta-analysis

Gun Keorochana

1

 and Jatupon Kongtharvonskul

1

1

Orthopedics Department, Faculty of Medicine Ramathibodi Hospital,
Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand

Objective: In recent years, the application of spinal endoscopy
has become more prevalent. At present, percutaneous endoscopic cervical
discectomy (PECD) is mainly divided into the anterior transdiscal approach
and the posterior interlaminar approach. Although the anterior transdiscal
approach can provide direct decompression for central or paramedian cervical
disc herniation, the iatrogenic disc damage may result in decreased
intervertebral space when compared to posterior interlaminar access.
Anterior transcorporeal approach under endoscopy could enable an individual
and adjustable trajectory within the vertebral body under different
conditions of disc herniation preserving the motion of adjacent segment,
especially in a migrated or sequestered lesion. But there is no current
consensus regarding which method is better. Therefore this systematic review
and meta-analysis of transdiscal and trancorporeal PECD was conducted with
the aim of updating the comparison of the two for post-operative outcomes
(neck pain arm pain (VAS), disabilities (NDI), modified Macnab criteria,
complications and reoperations) for treatment of cervical intervertebral
disc herniation. Methods: This systematic review was conducted
according to the PRISMA guidelines. Relevant studies that reported pain,
disabilities, modified Macnab criteria, complications and reoperations of
either technique were identified from Medline and Scopus from inception to
September 4th, 2022. Results: eleven studies were
included for the analysis of transdiscal(Td) PECD, 17 studies were included
for analysis of transcorporeal (Tc) PECD and one comparative study were
included for compared TdPECD to TcPECD. Overall, there were 1503 patients
(978 in the TdPECD group and 525 in the TcPECD group). A pooled UMD of
post-operative neck pain, arm pain (VAS), disabilities (NDI) scores of
TdPECD and TcPECD were -4.48 (95%CI: -5.28 to -3.68), -6.03 (95%CI: -7.29 to

-2.44), -5.96 (95%CI: -6.80 to -5.12), -27.38 (95%CI: -52.77 to -1.99) when
compared to before surgery. The pooled prevalence of having excellent and
good in modified Macnab criteria, complications and reoperation of TdPECD
and TcPECD were 0.89 (95%CI: 0.77, 1.00), 0.024 (95%CI: -0.030 to 0.078),
0.03 (95%CI: 0.003 to 0.051) and 0.75 (95%CI: 0.61 to 0.88), 0.005 (95%CI:
-0.005 to 0.015), 0.016 (95%CI: 0.002 to 0.032). Indirect meta-analysis,
TdPECD provided better postoperative neck and arm pain (VAS), disabilities

-13.98 (95%CI: -40.42 to 68.39) when compared to TcPECD technique, but there
were not significant difference between two techniques. While the chance of

reoperations in the TcPECD group were lower of 0.84 (95%CI: 0.67 to 1.05),
0.19 (95%CI: 0.01 to 3.00) and 0.58 (95%CI: 0.16 to 2.08) times when
compared to TdPECD. Conclusion: In post-operative outcomes 3 up
to 4 years follow-up, there is no significant difference in all clinical
outcomes between the 2 approaches. Although TdPECD have better arm pain,
neck pain and neck disabilities scores when compared to TcPELD, however,
TcPELD have lower chance of having complications and reoperations when
compared to TdPELD.
Keywords: percutaneous endoscopic cervical discectomy; PELD; transcorporeal;
trandiscal; disc herniation

Introduction: Surgical treatment of the degenerative disc

## P411: Early experience with single paraspinal incision, single-level
minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MITLIF) with 3D
printed titanium cage and unilateral pedicle screw construct

Yunting Tang

1

, Anthony Oyekan

1

, and Vivek Sharma

1

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Pittsburgh,
Pittsburgh, United States

Introduction: The implementation of MISS presents challenges
including cost and learning curve. This study aimed to characterize initial
clinical experiences with minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody
fusion (MITLIF) at a University-Affiliated community hospital. We
hypothesized that MITLIF with a 3D printed titanium cage and unilateral
pedicle screw construct may be safely implemented in single-level lumbar
spine fusions with favorable clinical outcomes. Material and
Methods: With review board approval, a retrospective review of a
prospectively collected database was performed. We reviewed initial
consecutive cases of single-level MITLIF using 3D printed titanium cages
with a unilateral pedicle screw construct performed by a single
fellowship-trained orthopedic spine surgeon from October 2019 to March 2021.
The minimum postoperative follow-up was 1 year. Data points collected
include patient demographics, diagnoses, comorbidities, operating time,
fluoroscopy time/dose, EBL, hospital length of stay (LOS), discharge
disposition, 30-day and 90-day readmissions and narcotic use (per the
Pennsylvania Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, PDMP). The MITLIF
protocol included a single paraspinal incision, non-expandable 18/22mm
beveled slotted tubular retractors, an operating microscope, fluoroscopy,
neurophysiologic monitoring, and an ERAS perioperative plan.
Results: 47 patients were included - 25 F/22 M, age 67 ± 12
years, BMI 31.7 ± 5.7. Average operating time was 120 ± 18 min, fluoroscopy
time 0.93 ± 0.41 min, radiation dose 3.80 ± 2.51 rad, and EBL 65 ± 35 cc.
BMI directly affected radiation dose but had no effect on OR time or EBL.
Patients were prescribed 28 ± 24 outpatient narcotic doses for 8 ± 6 days.
All patients on chronic narcotics had no prescription changes pre- versus
postoperatively, despite achieving their desired outcomes. One patient had
hardware displacement requiring revision surgery, no other complications
were reported. Four patients were readmitted at 30-days, and one at 90-days.
Forty-three patients were discharged on POD1, 3 on POD2, and 1 after POD2.
All patients were discharged home; 21 required home health assistance.
Conclusion: MITLIF with 3D printed titanium cages and a
unilateral pedicle screw construct may be a viable option for minimally
invasive single-level lumbar spine fusions with favorable outcomes. This
technique may help reduce hardware density and surgical footprint. It may
also have future cost benefits and applications in the treatment of lumbar
adjacent segment disease. However, further studies are needed to investigate
these potential applications. Considerations include need for special
equipment, personnel training, surgeon experience, technique proficiency and
diligent patient selection.

## 1551

## P412: Out-patient minimally invasive spine surgeries during the COVID-19
pandemic - A retrospective analysis of 164 consecutive cases

Benjiang Ma

1

 and Aaron Smith

1

1

West Palm Beach, Spine and Orthopaedic Specialists, Florida, United
States

Introduction: Cervical and lumbar spine intervertebral disc
(IVD) disease is the leading cause for neck or back pain. The most common
mechanism of injury during non-fatal motor vehicle accidents is cervical or
lumbar disc herniation and spine instability. Surgery is the last resort if
all conservative measures failed. Here we share the retrospective analysis
of the patient data and our surgical experiences from a single spine surgeon
group utilizing minimally invasive procedures performed in the outpatient
setting at the ambulatory surgery centers (ASC) during the COVID-19
pandemic. Material and Methods: Anterior cervical discectomy
and fusion (ACDF), anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF), minimally
invasive laminotomy and discectomy (MILD), percutaneous endoscopic
laser-assisted discectomy (PELD) and percutaneous kyphoplasty (PK) were
performed on carefully selected patients at multiple ambulatory surgery
centers (ASCs) with appropriate protective measures. Results:
From January 2020 to December 2021, our group performed 164 consecutive
cases on 153 patients involving a total of 249 IVD levels. Of these
surgeries, 116 cases (70.73%) from 114 patients (74.51%) were cervical,
predominantly ACDF, and 48 cases (29.27%) were lumbar. Notably, 8 of these
patients had both cervical and lumbar procedures (single or multi levels) in
a single anesthetic session (SAS) and were discharged on the same day. The
most affected IVDs in cervical spine were at the C4-C5 and C5-C6 levels,
which comprised 92.17% (106) of the ACDF cases and 76.04% (146) of the total
IVD levels. Of the 40 cases of lumbar decompression/fusion procedures
combined, 38 (95.0%) were at lower lumbar levels (L4 to S1). Six (6) cases
(15.0%) involved 2 lumbar levels including L3-S1 IVDs. In sharp contrast, 6
out of 8 kyphoplasties (75.0%) involved lower thoracic/higher lumbar
vertebral columns (T11 to L2) and only 2 were at the lower lumbar L4 level.
Conclusion: With appropriate precautions, we have safely
performed various cervical and lumbar spine surgeries in the ASCs amid
COVID-19 pandemic, including patients that underwent combined multi-level
cervical and lumbar spine procedures in a SAS with no complications and
achieved the same day discharge (SDD). Analysis of our data demonstrated
that, in non-fatal trauma during MVAs, mid-lower cervical (C4 to C6) and
lower lumbar (L4-S1) IVDs were the most vulnerable levels. Clinical
relevance: Our experience could be the valuable reference for
fellow spine surgeons to increase their level of comfort to perform more
skill-demanding surgeries in outpatient settings to reduce the cost in the
today’s rising healthcare expenditures. Enhanced safety measures need to be
investigated to protect the aforementioned skewed vulnerable cervical and
lumbar spine levels from injury during MVAs.
Keywords: intervertebral disc, spine surgery, minimally-invasive, ambulatory
surgery center, single anesthetic session, same day discharge, motor vehicle
accident

## 1580

## P413: Technique for spondylolisthesis reduction and segmental lordosis
optimization in lateral lumbar interbody fusion with percutaneous pedicle
screw fixation: a case series

Paul Soriano

1

, Jason Haselhuhn

1

, and Jonathan N. Sembrano

1

1

University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion with percutaneous
pedicle screw fixation (LLIF-PPS) is a circumferential minimally-invasive
procedure designed to minimize morbidity and enhance recovery after lumbar
surgery. There has been increasing emphasis on restoring optimal segmental
sagittal alignment, even in single-level fusion procedures. We described a
technique to optimize segmental lordosis (SL) and reduce spondylolisthesis
in LLIF-PPS and analyzed radiographic results in a series of patients on
whom this technique was used. The objective of this study was to evaluate
the effects of introducing an angled-up position of distal screws and
hyper-contouring of rods before the final tightening of instrumentation
("novel reduction technique") on lumbar lordosis (LL) in patients with
spondylolisthesis undergoing LLIF-PPS fixation. Methods: After
IRB approval, we reviewed consecutive cases of single-level LLIF-PPS for
degenerative spondylolisthesis from January 2016 through December 2021. In
all patients, after the pedicle screws were placed percutaneously and after
passing the rods, the caudal screw extenders were tilted caudally, and
caudal set plugs were tightened. This locks the screw heads in place and
leaves the rostral end of the rods sticking up dorsally relative to the
cephalad screw heads. Because the caudal screw heads were already locked,
gradual reduction of the rods to the cephalad screw heads resulted in
spondylolisthesis reduction and SL increase without needing rod compression.
We measured the SL on operative levels in intraoperative images at every
step of the surgery (before cage placement, after cage placement, after
repositioning, and after posterior instrumentation). We measured pelvic
incidence (PI), pelvic tilt, and LL in preoperative and postoperative
standing x-rays. Ideal lumbar lordosis (ILL) was calculated using the
formula: ILL = 0.5 (PI) + 28. Results: We
included 16 patients (7 male; 9 female) in the final
analysis. Five were done in a single position (lateral decubitus), while the
rest were repositioned (lateral then prone). The average age was 60.4 years
(SD ±9.7) and BMI 33.6 (SD ±8.9). The average segmental lordosis change was
4.4°, broken into 2.4° after cage placement and an additional 2.0° after
posterior instrumentation. The percentage of preoperative and postoperative
patients with > 10° difference between measured and ideal LL is 18.8%
(3/16) and 25.0% (4/16), respectively. Conclusions: Together
with interbody cage placement, the described instrumented reduction
technique resulted in increased operative level segmental lordosis (average
4.4°). Although no posterior column osteotomies were performed, 75.0% of
patients who underwent single-level LLIF-PPS using this technique ended
within 10° of patient-specific ideal lumbar lordosis.

## P414: Short-term clinical and radiological outcome of full-endoscopic
lateral lumbar interbody fusion via Kambin's triangle in degenerative lumbar
diseases

Akihiro Nagamachi

1
, Hiroki Ikuchi
2
, Kohei Ohta
1
, andMasatoshi Morimoto
3

1

Yoshinogawa Medical Center, Orthopedic Surgery, Tokushima,
Japan

2

Takamatsu Municipal Hospital, Orthopedic surgery, Kagawa

3

Tokushima University, Orthopedic Surgery, Tokushima, Japan

Introduction: Kambin reported the concept of percutaneous
posterolateral nucleotomy in 1973. Since then, minimally invasive procedure
using transforaminal approach has been developed. Full-endoscopic lateral
lumbar interbody fusion via Kambin’s triangle (KLIF) offers several
advantages over open methods like protection of posterior ligamentous and
bony structures and paraspinal musculature. The purpose of this study was to
evaluate early clinical results of degenerative lumbar diseases treated with
KLIF. Material and Methods: Nine patients with degenerative
spondylolisthesis (6 cases), spondylolytic spondylolisthesis (1 case) and
degenerative lumbar scoliosis (2 cases) were participated in this study.
There were 5 male and 4 female and their mean age was 63 years ranged from
34 to 77 years. All patients underwent CT and MRI to observe bony union and
decompression of spinal canal 6 months and 1 year after the surgery.
Clinical result was evaluated by Japanese Orthopaedic Association Back Pain
Evaluation Questionnaire (JOABPEQ) and visual analog scale (VAS). Mean
duration of observation was 21 months ranged from 6 to 36 months. Wilcoxon
signed-rank sum test was used for statistical analysis. KLIF using a
transforaminal approach was performed under general anesthesia with patient
in a prone position on a radiolucent table, combined with motor evoked
potential monitoring. After percutaneous pedicle screws were placed under
fluoroscopic guidance, an endoscope was inserted in the superior articular
process (SAP) through 8 mm skin incision created around 80 mm from the
midline. The exposed SAP was removed using a 3.5 mm diameter high speed
drill to expose disc space adequately. After the disc space was cleaned up,
autologous milled bone and an expansion cage were inserted by using
originally designed instruments. Mean duration of operation was 201 minutes
and mean amount of blood loss was 45.5cc. No neural injury and deep surgical
site infection was observed. Results: Union rate of the fused
level was 100%. Among mean JOABPEQ item scores, pain related disorders sore,
social life dysfunction score and psychological disorders score were
significantly improved postoperatively. Lumbar spine dysfunction score and
gait disturbance score did not have statistically significant improvement,
however, p value were 0.058 and 0.059, respectively. We thought that those
may have statistically significant value if the number of patient will
increase. There were statistically significant improvement in mean VAS of
LBP, buttock and leg pain. Conclusion: Open posterior interbody
fusion inevitably causes paraspinal muscle injury. It is usually limited to
the lower lumbar level. It has an increased risk of durotomy, especially
during the revision surgery. Oblique lumbar interbody fusion and Lateral
lumbar interbody fusion are suitable for degenerative lumbar diseases
including sagittal and coronal deformity. But those carry the risk of
vascular injury and intestinal injury. Zhao compared 40 cases of the
endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion group (ETLF) and the 38
cases of Minimally invasive trans foraminal interbody fusion group. He also
reported that ETLIF may be efficient alternative surgery for degenerative
lumbar spinal stenosis. KLIF was safe, effective and minimally invasive
technique in treatment for degenerative lumbar disc diseases.

## P415: Anatomical and technical considerations of transiliac endoscopic
assisted intraforaminal lumbar inter body fusion: A cadaveric study

Jose Miguel Sousa

1,2

, Hugo Ribeiro

1

, João Gamelas

1

, and Jose Consciência

2,3

1

Orthopaedics, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisboa,
Portugal

2

Comprehensive Health Research Center, NOVA Medical School, Lisboa,
Portugal

3

Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Pre and Pos Graduation
Department, Lisboa, Portugal

Introduction: Endoscopic spine surgery has gained wide
popularity among spine surgeons over the last decade. The adoption of this
surgical technique is backed up by recent meta-analyses that favor lumbar
endoscopic discectomy over microdiscectomy in clinical outcomes, duration of
surgery, length of hospital stay, and lower risk of complications. Initially
seen as a tool for treating lumbar disc herniations, the range of
applications for spine endoscopy expanded, namely to the cervical and
thoracic spine. Its use in the treatment of foraminal, lateral recess, and
central stenosis is increasingly common. However, the benefits of an
endoscopic approach go beyond decompression surgeries. Initial reports on
endoscopically assisted fusion date back to the mid-1980s. A recent
meta-analysis comparing endoscopic assisted intraforaminal lumbar interbody
fusion (iLIF) and minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion
(MI-TLIF) has shown that for the treatment of lumbar degenerative diseases,
iLIF has significantly less intraoperative blood loss and reduced length of
hospital stay. Although the iLIF technique has been gaining traction in L4L5
and the upper lumbar spine, the unique anatomy of L5S1 has put some
limitations to the expansion of the technique in this segment. To overcome
some of these limitations, a transiliac approach has been described to
address disc herniations and stenotic pathology. However, its reference to
the iLIF technique is anecdotic. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate
the feasibility of a L5S1 iLIF transiliac approach and to characterize the
anatomic correlations of the endoscopic transiliac track. Material and
Methods: Ten transiliac iLIF and ten suprailiac iLIF were
performed bilaterally at L5S1 in five randomly selected fresh-frozen human
cadavers. The following measurements were recorded: distances from the
transiliac track to the iliac crest, posterior superior iliac spine, and
superior gluteal neurovascular bundle; pelvic parameters; approach angles;
cage’s lateral and AP center point ratio (CPR); percentage of the cage
crossing the midline in the AP and lateral views. Endplates integrity was
assessed through endoscopic visualization. Facet joint, sacroiliac joint,
iliolumbar ligament, exiting, and traversing nerve roots were checked for
integrity through anatomic dissection. Results: In the
transiliac technique, the axial and coronal approach angles were
significantly decreased by 13,5° (95%CI -15.5; -11.5; p value < 0.001)
and 13.2° (95%CI -15.3; -11.1; p value < 0.001), respectively, the
sagittal approach angle was significantly increased by 5,4° (95%CI 1.8, 8.9;
p value = 0.008), and the AP CPR was significantly higher (MD 0,16; 95%CI
0.12,0.20; p value < 0.001). The percentage of the cage crossing the AP
view’s midline was increased by 31.6% (95%CI 19.8, 43.4; p value <
0.001). Integrity of endplates, facet joints, sacroiliac joints, iliolumbar
ligament, exiting, and traversing nerve roots was maintained.
Conclusion: L5S1 transiliac iLIF is a feasible surgical
technique. It allows a more centrally placed interbody cage in the coronal
plane without compromising the anterior position in the lateral plane. The
integrity of the major anatomic structures at risk was preserved.

## 1678

## P416: Clinical outcomes, complications and fusion rates in endoscopic
assisted intraforaminal lumbar inter body fusion (iLIF) versus minimally
invasive transforaminal lumbar inter body fusion (MI-TLIF): systematic
review and meta-analysis

Jose Miguel Sousa

1,2

, Hugo Ribeiro

2

, João Luis Silva

2

, and Jose Consciência

1,3

1

Comprehensive Health Research Center, NOVA Medical School, Lisboa,
Portugal

2

Orthopaedics, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisboa,
Portugal

3

Pre and Pos Graduation Department, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa
Ocidental, Lisboa, Portugal

Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgeries intend to
reduce tissue trauma, decrease complication rates, and improve functional
recovery. Advances in endoscopic spine surgery made way for new
opportunities to minimize tissue aggression further. Recently published
meta-analyses regarding the treatment of lumbar disc herniations favored
endoscopic discectomy (ED) over microdiscectomy (MD) in clinical outcomes,
duration of surgery, length of hospital stay, and lower risk of overall
complications. These results opened the perspective that ED could take over
the place of MD as the gold standard of care in the management of lumbar
disc disease. Technological innovations in endoscopic spine surgery have
widened its range of applications beyond lumbar disc herniations. Endoscopic
treatment of central and lateral recess stenosis, as well as endoscopic
assisted lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) for degenerative lumbar diseases, are
increasingly common. The benefits of an even less invasive technique than
minimally invasive TLIF (MI-TLIF) would be further improvement in the
advantages over open TLIF. Encouraged by the success of ED, endoscopic
assisted intraforaminal LIF (iLIF) has been increasing its popularity. Even
though several surgical techniques have been described, Kambin’s triangle
approach through an intraforaminal facet sparing technique is the most usual
and the one that has greater potential to reduce iatrogenic soft and bone
tissue trauma. Recent studies have shown promising results regarding reduced
blood loss, decreased length of stay, clinical outcomes, complications and
fusion. However, the comparison between MI-TLIF and iLIF is sparse in the
literature, and concerns about the safety and effective benefits of the
endoscopic technique remain unanswered. This systematic review and
meta-analysis of MI-TLIF and iLIF were conducted to synthetize and compare
the available data in the literature on clinical outcomes, complications and
fusion rates. Material and Methods: The MEDLINE, Embase, and
Cochrane Library databases were searched. The inclusion criteria were: five
or more consecutive patients who underwent iLIF or MI-TLIF for lumbar
degenerative diseases; description of the surgical technique; clinical
outcome measures, complications and imaging assessment; minimum follow-up of
12 months. Surgical time, blood loss, and length of hospital stay were
extracted. Mean outcome improvements were pooled and compared with minimal
clinically important differences (MCID). Pooled and direct meta-analysis
were evaluated. Results: We identified 42 eligible studies. The
iLIF group had significantly lower mean intra-operative blood loss (UMD
110,61mL; 95%CI 70.43, 150.80; p value < 0.0001), and significantly
decreased length of hospital stay (UMD 2,36; 95%CI 1.77,2.94; p value <
0.0001). VAS back, VAS leg and ODI baseline to last follow-up mean
improvements were statistically significant (p value < 0.0001), and
clinically important for both groups (MCID VAS back > 1.16; MCID VAS leg
> 1.36; MCID > 12.40). There was no significant difference in
complication nor fusion rates between both cohorts. Conclusion:
Interbody fusion using either iLIF or MI-TLIF leads to significant and
clinically important improvements in clinical outcomes for lumbar
degenerative diseases. Both procedures provide high rates of fusion at 12
months or later, without significant difference in complication rates. iLIF
is associated with significantly less intraoperative blood loss and length
of hospital stay.

## 1692

## P417: Is narrow oblique corridor a contraindication for oblique lumbar
interbody fusion?

Weerasak Singhatanadgige

1

, panupong chatareeyagul

1

, Vit Kotheeranurak

1

, and Worawat Limthongkul

1

1

Orthopedics, Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok,
Thailand

Introduction: Evaluation of the pre-psoas oblique corridor is
generally recommended before performing Oblique Lumbar Interbody Fusion
(OLIF) procedure. Narrow corridor especially at L4-5 is one of the
constraints to perform OLIF due to the increasing risk of major vessel
injury. The aim of this study is to investigate if there was a difference in
functional outcome and operative complication between narrow and wide
corridor size patient operated with OLIF at L4-5. Material and
Methods: Retrospective study of patients who had undergone OLIF
surgery at least one level which include L4-5 from 2017 and 2020. The
patients were divided into three groups by size of the corridor; not more
than 10mm, between 10 to 20 mm, and 20 mm or more. We collected and reviewed
VAS score, ODI score, complication and radiographic findings in each group
for up to one-year follow-up. Results: Eighty patients were
divided into three groups from the size of the corridor (0-10 mm, 11-20 mm
and more than 21 mm). No significant difference of VAS score, ODI score and
complication between each group. The radiographic findings including
position of the cage, anterior and posterior disc height, segmental angle
and foraminal height were recorded and found no significant difference
between each group. The only radiographic finding that has significant
difference between each groups is the angle of the cage. In the group of
more than 20mm corridor had found significantly less degree of angle than
the other two groups. (p-value = 0.01). There was no recorded incidence of
major vascular complication. Conclusion: Narrow or wide
corridor does not affect functional outcome and radiographic finding
including position of the cage, anterior and posterior disc height,
segmental angle and foraminal height after OLIF procedure at L4-5 level.
Only angle of the cage that were affected by the size of corridor. Thus,
narrow corridor should not be the contraindication to perform OLIF
procedure.

were assessed with Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Visual Analog Scales

pre and post operative MRI images using the Schizas classification for LSS
and Meyerding classification for lumbar Spondylolisthesis. Level - The L4L5
level was most discussed in this series, 6 cases, 3 in L5S1 and 1 in L3L4.
Schizas – 5 cases grade B, 3 grade C and 2 grade D. Meyerding – 8 cases
grade 1 and 2 cases grade II. Results: All patients reported
significant improvement in axial and radicular pain symptoms as well as
classic neurogenic claudication in LSS cases, documented by the ODI and VAS.
Int 9 of 10 cases, was improvement related to the Schizas. There was no
difference in relation to the pre and post op Meyerding classification.
Conclusion: In this series of cases, full endoscopic
decompression associated with posterior percutaneous stabilization proved to
be affective for the treatment of LSS with DS with favorable clinical and
radiological outcomes, in addition to the advantages of a minimally invasive
surgery.

## P422: Advantages of 4K 3D exoscope in thoracic and thoracolumbar MIS
approaches

Joseph Aferzon

1,2

1

Neurosurgery, Hartford Hospital, Hartford, United States

2

Neurosurgery, University of Connecticut, Farmington, United
States

Introduction: With advent of new MIS techniques, visualization
of deep structures through a narrow portal can be challenging. All
traditional means of visualization present shortcomings. Current
Microscopes are too bulky and with limited focal depth they
presents very restricted working space, particularly when using long
instruments. Additionally, steep working angles require surgeons to stand in
awkward position while trying to look "down the scope". Surgical
Loupes provide limited magnification and require additional means
of illumination. Additionally, surgical loupes are an ergonomic disaster,
particularly for long cases. Endoscope technologies may solve
some of these issues but they do not provide 3D depth perception, which I
believe has contributed to its limited use in high precision surgery. The
new exoscope technology has the potential to address all of the
above shortcomings. Material and Methods: Author has extensive
experience with advanced MIS surgery for thoracic and thoracolumbar
pathology, with over 200 cases performed successfully. He has traditionally
used surgical loupes and microscope when feasible. Author presents his
experience using novel Mantis 3D 4K exoscope (1) for deep MIS thoracic and
thoracolumbar exposures for decompression, fusion and fixation.
Results: Exoscope provides improvement over loupes and
microscope. Because of the longer focal distance and smaller profile it
dramatically increases working space compared to the microscope. Because of
decoupling between image acquisition and visualization it significantly
improves ergonomics during surgery particularly noticeable during long
procedures. It offers excellent depth perception, therefore overcoming the
limitations of an endoscope. This exoscope provides a unique opportunity for
teaching surgical techniques through real time sharing of 3D images as well
as 3D replay after the surgery. This Exoscope use has a learning curve of 5
to 10 cases based on surgeons prior experience with technique and
technology. Conclusion: Exoscope overcomes many limitations of
traditional intraoperative visualization solutions. It is particularly well
suited for deep approaches through a narrow corridor. This technology should
facilitate adoption of advanced minimally invasive techniques.
(1) Mantis Health, Stamford CT USA

lumbar disease. Material and Methods: In this retrospective
study, plain radiographs and three-dimensional computed tomography were

loosening were pedicle screw depth and severe multifidus atrophy.

## P424: Clinical evaluation of computerized modified paramedian approach
technique (CMPAT) and conventional midline approach (MAT) of lumbar

Yuan-Dong Zhuang

, Yi-Ze Chen

, Qi-Ying Lin

, Si-Qi Zhong

2

Basic Medical College, Fujian Medical University, Fuzhou,

Introduction: Lumbar puncture (LP) technique is one of the
commonly used clinical treatment methods in the neurological system and is
of great value in the diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases. The
traditional LP technique is the midline approach technique - lumbar puncture
(MAT-LP), which has various problems such as low success rates, many
complications and crude learning methods. Compared with MAT-LP, paramedian
approach technique - lumbar puncture (PAT-LP) has the advantages of low
puncture failure rate, low number of puncture attempts, and low incidence of
post-LP headache. The various reported PAT-LP puncture methods have not yet
been unified, and previous studies on PAT-LP lacked intelligent global
analysis and three-dimensional multi faceted analysis. Therefore, based on
digital avatar and computer simulation technology, our study has proposed a
evaluation of Computerized Modified Paramedian Approach Technique (CMPAT) in

and success rate. Accordingly, the purpose of the present study is to to
compare the effects of CMPAT and MAT lumbar puncture in patients requiring
lumbar puncture. Material and Methods: The trial plan included
84 patients, aged 18-99 years, from multiple study centers requiring LP with
Fujian Medical University's Union Hospital as the group leader, randomly and
equally divided into 2 groups of 42 patients each, with CMPAT-LP in group A
and MAT-LP in group B. The patients were followed up on postoperative days
1, 3 and 7. The primary observation of the study was the number of punctures
attempted by the surgeon at the time of successful lumbar puncture; the
secondary observation was the pain in the head, back, hind legs after lumbar
puncture, and pain assessment was performed before, during, and 30 minutes
after the operation, 6 hours after the operation, day 1, day 3, day 7, and
day 30 after the operation, all using the pain numerical rating scale (NRS)
scoring. The study complied with the requirements of the Declaration of
Helsinki established by the World Medical Association. Participants gave
informed consent to the trial content and treatment procedure and signed an
informed consent form. Discussion: The trial expects to
demonstrate thatCMPAT-LP has a higher success rate, lower pain scores and
fewer complications than MAT-LP.

## P425: Comparison of clinical effect of percutaneous endoscopy through

herniaion

Yizhou Xie

1,2

, XiaoHong Fan

1

, and Yang Yu

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional
Chinese Medicine, Chengdu, China

2

Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell Medical College-New York
Presbyterian Hospital, New York, United States

Study Design: Retrospective Cohort Study.
Objectives: To compare the clinical effect of percutaneous
endoscopic through lateral approach and posterior approach treating the
shoulder type of L5/S1 lumbar disc herniation (LDH). Methods:
Each 30 cases diagnosed in shoulder type of L5/S1 LDH who received
percutaneous endoscopy through lateral approach and posterior approach were
collected and divided into: the lateral approach group and the posterior
approach group. Clinical evaluation was performed at preoperation and
postoperative 3rd day, 1st month and 1st
year in each group. The indicators involved include VAS, ODI, operation
cost, operation time and fluoroscopy time. Results: In
contrast, the posterior approach group showed shorter mean operation time
and fewer mean intraoperative radiation (p < 0.05). However, compared
with posterior approach group, lateral approach group was more economical (p
< 0.05). In terms of VAS and ODI, the difference between two groups is
not significant in preoperative and postoperative 3rd day, 1st
month and 1st year (p > 0.05). On the other hand, mean VAS and
ODI of two groups acquired by three postoperative follow-up phases were
significantly improved compared with preoperation (p < 0.05). No
statistical significance was observed in pairwise comparison among three
postoperative follow up phases in two groups (p > 0.05).
Conclusion: In treating shoulder type of L5/S1 LDH, both
the lateral approach and the posterior approach for percutaneous endoscopy
are effective. Compared with the lateral approach, the posterior approach
has the advantages of fewer intraoperative X-ray radiations and less
operation time. However, the lateral approach is less costly than the
posterior approach.

## P426: Biportal endoscopic revision operation of postoperative cage

Yizhou Xie

1,2

, XiaoHong Fan

1

, and Yang Yu

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional
Chinese Medicine, Chengdu, China

2

Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell Medical College-New York
Presbyterian Hospital, New York, United States

Background: Postoperative cage migration is a catastrophic
operational complication after a spine surgery which could cause severe
clinical symptoms. Its revision operation using endoscope has rarely been
reported in the literature so far. This is a case report of a 48-year-old
female occurring postoperative cage migration in the 3rd days
after a biportal spinal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion. Case
Presentation: A 48-year-old female patient presented with a left
L4-5 radiculopathy with medical imagining and physical sign corresponded. A
biportal spinal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion was then performed using

at once to get it well managed ultimately. After surgery, the patient's
symptoms were greatly relieved until he was discharged in the
15th days postoperatively. Conclusion:
Postoperative cage migration in spinal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion is
a rare complication. But endplate damage and the undersized cage with
posteriorly placement are more prone to developing this complication.
Endoscopic revision operation is an optimal surgical intervention that worth
considering.

## P427: Comparison of the safety and efficacy of unilateral biportal
endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion and uniportal endoscopic lumbar interbody
fusion: a 1-year follow up

Yizhou Xie

1,2

, XiaoHong Fan

1

, and Yang Yu

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional
Chinese Medicine, Chengdu, China

2

Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell Medical College-New York
Presbyterian Hospital, New York, United States

Objectives: To compare the short-term outcomes of unilateral
biportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (BLIF) and uniportal endoscopic
lumbar interbody fusion (ULIF). Methods: Sixty patients
diagnosed with L4/5 spinal stenosis who underwent BLIF and ULIF were
included (30 in each group). Clinical evaluation was performed
preoperatively and postoperatively in the 1st week,
1st month, and 1st year. Factors such as the
visual analogue score (VAS), Oswestry disability index (ODI), operative
time, surgical complications, and radiological outcomes (fusion rate, screw
loosening, and cage subsidence) were compared between the two groups.
Results: All patients showed improved mean VAS and ODI at
all three postoperative follow-ups, and no statistically significant
differences were detected between the BLIF and ULIF groups. The mean
operative time in the BLIF group was shorter than that in the ULIF group.
Nerve root injury occurred in two patients in the BLIF group, while leakage
of cerebrospinal fluid occurred in one patient in the ULIF group. All
adverse events were treated adequately prior to discharge. The fusion rates
with definite and probable grades were significantly higher in the BLIF
group than that in the ULIF group. One case of cage subsidence with no screw
loosening occurred in each group. Conclusion: Both BLIF and
ULIF are safe and effective surgical techniques. Compared with ULIF, BLIF
has the advantages of shorter operative time and a higher fusion rate. Other
merits of BLIF include a wider surgical field, greater maneuverability of
instruments, visibility during cage implantation, and transverse orientation
of the cage.

## P428: The impact of 2 expandable TLIF cage design types on geometry of
the lumbar spine - preliminary results of case series

Pravesh Gadjradj

1

, Fabian Sommer

1

, Ibrahim Hussain

1

, Jacob Goldberg

1

, Sertac Kirnaz

1

, Branden Medary

1

, Rodrigo Navarro-Ramirez

1

, and Roger Härtl

1

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell Medicine and New
York Presbyterian Hospital - Och Spine, New York, United States

Introduction: Tubular MIS TLIF is a widely used procedure for
lumbar spine fusion. One limitation of this technique is the amount of
segmental lordosis that can be achieved with interbody cages. Recently, a
variety of expandable, lordotic cage designs have been developed that allow
cage height and lordosis adjustment. The RISE ® cage has a fixed
lordosis of 8 degrees and can be expanded in height. The SABLE ®
cage can have lordosis of up to 15 degrees after which the height can be
expanded. It is unclear as to how these cage designs affect lumbar lordosis
postoperatively. We present a case series evaluating short term radiographic
outcomes using this device. Methods: A prospective study of
consecutive patients undergoing one-level tubular MIS TLIF with either a
RISE® or SABLE® expandable cage was performed.
Pre- and postoperative day 1 radiographs were compared, measuring anterior
and posterior disc height, lumbar lordosis, segmental lordosis, and pelvic
incidence. Perioperative data was also collected including operative time,
blood loss, length of hospital stay, and procedure-related complications.
Results: A total of 77 patients were included: 40 with
RISE® cages, and 37 with SABLE® cages. There was a
decrease in overall lumbar lordosis and an increase in posterior disc height
from pre-operation to post-operation for both RISE® and
SABLE® groups, with no difference between segmental lordosis.
There were no differences between RISE® and SABLE®
groups at pre-operation and post-operation overall. In the preoperative low
lordosis group, the segmental lordosis showed a statistically significant
increase compared to preop independent of the type of cages used. The mean
segmental lordosis either stabilized or slightly decreased after surgery in
patients with preoperative segmental lordosis from 16 degrees or higher.
Overall segmental lordosis for RISE® and SABLE® cages
went from 16.9 ± 10.7 to 17.0 ± 8.4 (p = 0.95) and 16.6 ± 8.9 to 15.2 ± 7.8
(p = 0.53) respectively. Overall lumbar lordosis for RISE® and
SABLE® cages significantly decreased from 48.0 ± 19.0 to 44.0
± 17.4 (p = 0.005) and from 35.3 ± 37.1 to 28.1 ± 35.0 (p = 0.002). Finally
posterior disc height for RISE® and SABLE® cages
significantly increased from 4.8 ± 2.7 to 8.7 ± 2.2 (p < 0.001) and from
4.3 ± 2.1 to 8.2 ± 2.8 (p < 0.001). Conclusion: In this
large prospective case series between two expandable cage designs used
during TLIF, there were no differences between RISE® and
SABLE® cages after surgery in terms of radiological spinal
parameters. More patients are needed to make definitive conclusions.

## P429: Does the use of robotic guidance system in spine surgery increase
the safety and accuracy of implant placement? Assessment of 450
cases

Sajan Hegde

1

, Appaji Krishnan

1

, Vigneshwara Badikkilaya

1

, Sharan Achar T

1

, Umesh Kanade P

1

, and Harith Reddy

1

1

Orthopaedics, Apollo Hospitals Chennai India, Chennai,
India

Introduction: The placement of pedicle screws in complex and
deformed spines is a challenging task with increased demand on the operating
surgeon to be safe and accurate. The need to do minimally invasive surgery
entailing radiation hazards to the operating room personnel necessitates a
system to guide screw placement safely, accurately and with reduced
radiation exposure. The Renaissance and Excelsius GPS robot helps in guiding
the placement of pedicle screws in deformities and for various minimally
invasive procedures. The objective of this study is to study and analyse
efficacy of the robotic guidance system in pedicle screw placement in spinal
deformities and minimally invasive spine surgery for degenerative and
infective conditions. Material & methods: Prospective case
series of 450 patients with a mean age of 42 yrs (Range: 7-78yrs) were
operated for various indications as spinal deformities in 88 patients
(Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis-46, Neuromuscular Scoliosis-18, Congenital
Scoliosis-10, Ankylosing Spondylitis-2, Congenital Kyphosis-6,
Degenerative-2, Post-traumatic-2, Failed/revision-2), degenerative
conditions (single/ double/ multilevel (3-4) lumbar disc disease with
stenosis and/or degenerative listhesis - 336), dorsal stabilisation for
infection/ malignancy- 22 and 4 vertebral body lesions biopsy.
Parameters such as operating time, radiation exposure, screw accuracy and
complications were calculated. Results: In the deformity group
all the screws were found acceptable as per intraoperative fluoroscopy. One
screw was misplaced laterally as a result of ‘Skiving’ but without any
adverse neural or vascular effect. In the Minimally Invasive group, per
operatively 89 guide wires were not as per planning on fluoroscopic check
and needed repositioning. All the screws were found to be acceptable
intraoperatively as per fluoroscopy. Postoperative CT scan analysis of screw
accuracy by an independent radiologist and one of the authors showed that
all screws except 42 had screws placed as per the pre-operative planning,
resulting in an accuracy of 98.9. There were no adverse vascular or
neurological events intra-operatively. The average radiation exposure per
screw was 0.98 seconds in the deformity patients and 1.595 seconds in the
MIS group. The operating time was comparable to standard open procedures and
there was a significant reduction (40%) in operating time in the second half
of cases with respect to the first half, showing an attainable learning
curve. Conclusion: Robotic guidance helps in increasing the
safety and accuracy of the pedicle screw placement in various spinal
disorders especially in obese degenerative disc disease and paediatric
deformity patients.

## P430: Pain outcomes in minimally invasive surgery for palliative
treatment of spinal metastases

Nolan Brown

, Chenyi Yang

, and Michael Oh

3

Introduction:Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) of the spine has
emerged as an established component of the spine surgeon's armamentarium.
MIS comes with the advantage of reduced surgical insult, conferring
particular benefit to patients undergoing palliative treatment who have
metastatic spinal tumor burden. Materials and Methods:The
present study aims to assess the safety, efficacy, and impact on quality of
life of MIS of the spine for palliative treatment of spinal metastases by
analyzing complication rates and visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores. A
systematic literature search was performed from January 22, 2002 to January
22, 2022 searching for all articles of patients undergoing MIS for spinal
metastases. All studies reporting clinical data and surgical complications
were included. Results:Five studies reporting on 62 metastatic
spinal tumor cases were included. There were 35 males and 27 females. Of the
included studies, China had the most studies (40%) with Germany, Canada and
The United States reporting one study each (20%). The mean age of
participants was 58.1 years. The most common tumor location was in the
thoracic spine (60.5%), while the most common sources of spinal metastasis
included cancers of lung (32.3%), bone marrow (myeloma) (21.0%), and breast
(11.3%). The mean preoperative VAS score was 7.1 ± 1.1 while the mean
postoperative score VAS was 1.2 ± 1. There was an average reduction in VAS
scores across all 5 studies of 6.4 ± 1.0. Mean follow-up time was 9.25
months in the four articles reporting this data. Average complication rate
was 9.26% with a range between 0-32% with zero perioperative deaths
recorded. The most common complication mentioned was cement leakage.
Conclusion:Minimally invasive approaches for palliative
surgical management of spinal metastases are associated with improved VAS
scores. In addition to favorable pain outcomes, complications appear to be
minimal; these approaches therefore represent a viable option for palliative
pain management that can improve quality of life.

, Alexander Himstead

1

1

1

Neurosurgery, UC Irvine, Irvine, United States

Introduction:As patient demand for minimally invasive SIJF has
increased, non-surgeons (including pain management physicians) have begun to
perform a growing number of minimally invasive posterior SIJF procedures,
even though these have traditionally been reserved for spine surgeons, whose
extensive training renders them experts in spinal instrumentation and
biomechanics. Materials and Methods:In November 2021, a
PubMed/Medline search and initial screen yielded 11 studies that were
subjected to full text analysis. Using the list of SIJF devices obtained
from these studies, additional searches were conducted using the National
Institute of Health (NIH) Clinical Trials website and FDA 510(k), among
others, yielding 6 unique devices that can currently be used by non-surgeons
in the posterior SIJF approach. Results:Spine surgeons
generally perform lateral or posterolateral MIS SIJF. There are 11 unique
FDA-approved devices and a total of 33 SIJF devices overall. 10 of these
devices have been described in numerous reports within the peer-reviewed
medical literature. For example, Titanium Triangular Implants (lateral) are
described in 11 retrospective studies (level 4 evidence), 2 level 2
prospective studies, and 2 level 1 prospective studies. By contrast,
non-surgeons have only investigated the use of posterior allograft devices
in 2 studies. One of these studies (PainTEQ) is featured on
ClinicalTrials.gov. The other is a systematic review citing 6 studies on
posterior SIJF performed by non-surgeons. However, 2 of these 6 studies are
conference abstracts and therefore cannot be assigned meaningful levels of
evidence. Conclusion:Instrumentation of the spine requires
extensive surgical training such as that completed by spine surgeons. There
is an increasing body of evidence in the literature supporting the
performance of MIS SIJF.

## 115

## P433: Influence of navigation on pedicle screw malpositions depending on
the vertebral segment supplied

Pascal Beuting

1

1

Trauma, BG Bergmannsheil Bochum, Bochum, Germany

Introduction:Misplacement of pedicle screws can have significant
impact on the postoperative outcome after dorsal spinal fusion. Various aids
such as fluoroscopy and navigation are available to improve the screw
position. The aim of the present study was to clarify to which extent the
supplied spinal column segment has an influence on the selection of the aids
and misalignment of the pedicle screw. Method: This
retrospective CT-based cohort analysis (2016 to 2020) included 631 patients
(m 341/f 293) who underwent surgical treatment in the thoracic and lumbar
area due to their vertebral body fractures. Fractures in the area of the
cervical spine were excluded. The pedicle diameters were measured in all
patients and the surgical treatment was evaluated based on the pedicular
screw position. For this purpose, the distance between the outer edge of the
screw and the pedicle cortex was measured. Based on the measured distance,
the screw position was divided into three stages (< 2 mm, 2-4 mm, > 4
mm overhang). A perforation of the pedicle of the screw > 2 mm was rated
as an incorrect position. Results: The area with the highest
rates of screw misplacement was the middle thoracic segments, where the
smallest pedicle diameters were also measured. Th5 showed the highest
misalignment rate of misplacement 21% (n = 31). Similar misalignment rates
were also found in the adjacent segments. The pedicle screws at T6 16% (n =
26), T7 20% (30) and T8 17% (n = 28) were > 2 mm outside the pedicle. In
the cranial thoracic vertebral segments (Th1-3), malposition rates of 5%
(Th1; n = 1) to 15% (Th2; n = 9) were found. In the area of the
thoracolumbar transition and especially the lumbar spine (Th12 - L3), 3%
(L2; n = 15) to 5% (Th12; n = 25) of the pedicle screws showed a
misplacement of > 2 mm. A comparison of the use of navigation shows that
it was used particularly in the area of the upper and middle thoracic spine.
Looking at the navigated screws in isolation, the malpositions in the area
of the segments T4 to T8 can be seen with 25% (T4; n = 9) to 33% (T7; n =
10). In the area of the cranial thoracic vertebral segments, in which the
navigated method was often used, misalignment rates of 6% (Th1; n = 1) to
16% (Th2; n = 5) are impressive. In the S1 segment, 4% (n = 1) of the
pedicle screws showed a breach. Conclusion: The results of the
present study show that the navigated procedure was used in particular in
the areas of the cranial and middle thoracic spine as well as in the area of
the lower lumbar spine. This can be explained on the one hand by the smaller
pedicle diameter in the thoracic spine and by the more difficult
accessibility of the caudal lumbar spine. In the thoracolumbar transition
and in the area of the upper lumbar spine, due to the larger pedicle
diameters, a low misalignment rate can also be achieved by conventional
insertion of the pedicle screws, and thus the higher time expenditure of the
navigated procedure may not be justified here.

## P434: iCT-based navigation vs CBCT-based navigation for percutaneous
pedicle screw placement in the thoracic spine: a cadaveric study

Antonia Medrow

1,2

, Eric Mandelka

1

, Jula Gierse

1

, Felix Zimmermann

1

, Paul Alfred Grützner

1

, Jochen Franke

1

, and Vetter Sven

1

1

Department of Trauma Surgery and Orthopedics, BG Klinik
Ludwigshafen, Ludwigshafen, Germany

2

Medical Faculty Heidelberg, University of Heidelberg, Heidelberg,
Germany

Introduction: Pedicle screw placement is considered a standard
procedure in thoracolumbar spine surgery for a variety of indications. 3D
navigation guidance is increasingly used as the accuracy has proved to be
more accurate compared to both fluoroscopic guidance and freehand screw
placement. While different imaging and navigation devices can be used for
intraoperative imaging and navigation, there are few studies comparing these
under similar conditions. The aim of this study was to compare iCT-based
navigation and a novel navigation system for 3D C-arm Cone Beam Computed
Tomography (CBCT)-based navigation under standardised, experimental
conditions in human specimens. Material and Methods: The study
was performed on 4 fresh-frozen torsos. The combinations of imaging device
and navigation system investigated were the iCT (Airo, Brainlab, Munich,
Germany) with Curve navigation (Brainlab, Munich, Germany) and a latest
generation flat-panel mobile 3D C-arm CBCT (Cios Spin, Siemens, Erlangen,
Germany) with the Pulse navigation platform (NuVasive, San Diego, CA, USA).
After obtaining referencing scans, the image data was transferred to the
navigation system and unilateral navigated percutaneous pedicle screw
placement (Reline MAS, Nuvasive, San Diego, CA, USA) was performed by an
experienced spine surgeon on levels T2 to T12. Subsequently, referencing
scans were performed using the second image device and navigated screw
placement was performed on the contralateral side. Finally, a control scan
was performed to allow for screw accuracy assessment which was performed by
to blinded observers (Obs1 and Obs2) using Gertzbein and Robbins grading
system. Grades A (no pedicle breach) and B (perforation < 2 mm) were
deemed acceptable, while perforations of ≥ 2 mm (grades C to E) were deemed
inacceptable. Accuracy between the different combinations was compared using
Chi2 test with a significance level of p < 0.05. Interrater agreement was
calculated using kappa (κ) as suggested by Landis and Koch.
Results: Overall, 87 pedicle screws were placed in the 4
specimens. In the iCT navigation group, one screw could not be placed due to
technical issues and a second screw could not be assessed because of poor
image quality. For iCT-based navigation, the accuracy rate was 85.7% (Obs1)
and 83.3% (Obs2) while using CBCT-based navigation reached an accuracy rate
of 95.5% (Obs1) and 93.2% (Obs2). However, the difference between the
combinations was not statistically significant (p = 0.152 for Obs1 and p =
0.191 for Obs2, respectively). Interrater agreement for screw accuracy being
acceptable or not was moderate (88.1%; κ = 0.545) for iCT-based navigation
and fair (93.2%; κ = 0.365) for CBCT-based navigation.
Conclusion: Percutaneous pedicle screw placement in the
thoracic spine proved to be accurate with both iCT- and CBCT-based
navigation, however, accuracy with CBCT-based navigation tended to be
higher. Further studies are needed to investigate if the results of the
navigation system used with the CBCT can be transferred to clinical
practice.

## P435: 3D custom modelled navigation jigs in posterior spinal fusion: a
retrospective case series

Libby Gooda

1

, Emily Tsang

1

, Bisola Ajayi

1

, Jason Bernard

1

, Timothy Bishop

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

, Zion Hwang

1

, and Darren Lui

1

1

Trauma & Orthopaedics, St. George's University Hospital, London,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Navigation of the spine is an established
technique to improve accuracy of pedicle screw placement. Intra-operative CT
is often required, and sometimes two scans are required depending on the
length of fusion, which can increase intra-operative time that the spine and
metalwork are exposed with potential for infection. The use of 3D printing
in spinal surgery is a growing technique. In the past, this was limited to
use as a pre-operative visual aid, however, in recent years it has been used
to create intra-operative patient specific screw jigs. A whole spine, low
dose, 1mm axial cut CT scan is used to create a 3D model of the spine, to
which 3D custom modelled navigation jigs (3DCMNJ) are created unique to each
vertebra. This allows for accurate and precise techniques for pedicle screw
insertion. Material and Methods: The British Spine Registry and
ICLIP were used to identify all scoliosis patients who underwent posterior
spinal fusion using 3DCMNJ from 22/09/2020-09/12/2021 at a South London
tertiary medical centre and a London private hospital. Data was then
collated regarding age, gender, time for screw insertion, blood loss during
screw insertion, and screw density. Results: Data was collected
on 25 patients. There was an average age of 16.16 (SD ± 1.95), N = 97. There
was a higher proportion of female patients at 68% female, 32% male. The
average time for screw insertion was 83 minutes (± 45), N = 20. The average
blood loss during screw insertion was 153.1ml (± 159.21), N = 10. Screw
density was 1.60 (± 3.50), N = 25. Two patients returned to theatre, one due
to a spinal cord monitoring event, and one due to wound dehiscence.
Conclusion: The use of 3DCMNJ in posterior spinal fusion
allows for the rapid insertion of pedicle screws, thus limiting blood loss
during this phase. Preoperative low dose CT allows for reduced operating
time compared to intra operative CT for navigation or robotic pedicle screw
entry. Less time of spine or metal work exposure could lead to decreased
risk of infection. Further research is required to compare to standard
posterior spinal fusion.

## 915

## P436: Comparison of 3D custom modelled navigation jigs with freehand
pedicle screw insertion for posterior spinal fusion in scoliosis

Libby Gooda

1

, Emily Tsang

1

, Bisola Ajayi

1

, Timothy Bishop

1

, Jason Bernard

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

, Zion Hwang

1

, and Darren Lui

1

1

Trauma & Orthopaedics, St. George's University Hospital, London,
United Kingdom

Background: Scoliosis is characterised by a curvature of the
spine. Significant curvature of the spine is often treated with spinal
fusion. There are many different approaches to spinal fusion, with freehand
pedicle screw insertion being the most common. However, this has inherent
inaccuracies and a greater danger of spinal cord injury due to
mispositioning. In more recent years, a new navigation technique has arisen.
This technique utilises 3D printing technology to create unique, custom made
patient-specific screw jigs, that fit onto each vertebra, allowing for
accurate and precise pedicle screw insertion. Material and
Methods: The British Spine Registry and ICLIP were used to
identify all scoliosis patients who underwent posterior spinal fusion from
16/01/2017-09/12/2021 at a South London tertiary medical centre and a London
private hospital. Data was then collated regarding age, gender, diagnosis,
duration of surgery, estimated blood loss, screw density, hospital length of
stay (HLOS), SRS-22 scores, and whether patients returned to theatre.
Results: The average age was 17.94 (SD ± 3.77) N = 72, for
freehand patients, and 16.16 (SD ± 1.95) N = 25, for 3DCMNJ patients. Both
the freehand group and 3D custom modelled navigation jigs (3DCMNJ) groups
had a greater proportion of female patients, at 74% and 68% respectively.
Patients comprising the 3DCMNJ group had a higher screw density (SD ± 1.95,
N = 57) when compared to the freehand group (1.60 ± 3.50, N = 25). 77.8% of
the freehand patients were classed as having adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
(AIS). The remainder: syndromic scoliosis (11.1%), secondary scoliosis
(2.78%), cerebral palsy (2.78%), adult idiopathic scoliosis (1.39%),
neurofibromatosis (1.39%), idiopathic kyphosis (1.39%), unknown (1.39%).
76.0% of the 3DCMNJ patients were diagnosed with AIS. The remainder:
Scheuermann’s kyphosis (8.0%), unknown (8.0%), idiopathic kyphosis (4.0%),
and congenital scoliosis (4.0%). Duration of surgery and estimated blood
loss did not appear to differ significantly between the two groups. There
also did not appear to be any significant differences in HLOS, nor
post-operative SRS-22 scores. In the 3DCMNJ group, there was a return to
theatre rate of 8% (4% spinal cord monitoring event, 4% wound dehiscence).
In the freehand group, there was a return to theatre rate of 11.1% (5.56%
due to failure of metalwork, 1.39% spinal cord monitoring event, 1.39% due
to infection, 1.39% wound dehiscence, and 1.39% post-operative haemothorax).
Conclusion: The use of 3DCMNJ does not lead to significant
differences compared to freehand pedicle screw placement with respect to
operating time, blood loss, HLOS, or SRS-22 scores. However, the 3DCMNJ
group had a higher screw density when compared to the freehand group which
may account for similar operative times and blood loss. Previous research
has shown 3DCMNJ leads to shorter time and low blood loss during screw
insertion. 3DCMNJ assisted spinal fusion patients may have a reduced return
to surgery rate, but a larger study group is needed.

## P437: Navigation trends in lumbar spine surgery

Tara Shelby

1

, Emily Mills

1

, Matthew Chen

1

, Hyunwoo Kang

1,2

, Andy Ton

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, and Ram Alluri

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical
School, Boston, United States

Introduction: Intraoperative computer-assisted navigation (CAN)
has fostered the growth of minimally invasive techniques and improved
anatomical characterization. Using CAN minimizes intraoperative risks, as it
allows for greater surgical precision. As such, CAN utilization has seen a
steady increase over the past decade within cervical and thoracic spine
procedures. Studies investigating CAN specifically in the context of the
lumbar spine, however, remain sparse. Given the high prevalence of
degenerative lumbar pathologies, this study aims to define CAN utilization
trends in the top 10 lumbar spine procedures for treatment of degenerative
conditions. Material and Methods: Patient data from 2010 to
2021 was accessed through the querying of the national insurance database
PearlDiver using ICD-9, ICD-10 and CPT codes. After first identifying the
top five lumbar degeneration codes, the top ten lumbar spine CPT procedure
codes associated with these diagnoses were isolated to create a cohort of
patients. This cohort was then split into the patients who had the procedure
along with one of the top five computer navigation procedure codes and those
that didn’t. Temporal analysis was then conducted on each cohort to identify
the trend of incidence in each group overtime. Results:
Querying PearlDiver found a total of 1,234,493 patients underwent one of the
top ten lumbar spine procedure for lumbar degeneration pathology from 2010
to 2021, with 10,760 (0.87%) and 1,223,733 (99.13%) patients undergoing
procedures performed with and without CAN. Comparing 2010 to 2021
demonstrated a significant increase in the use of CAN with lumbar spine
procedures (p < 0.001), increasing from 0.553% (556 patients) to 2.187%
(769 patients). Trends in CAN utilization was relatively steady from 2010 to
2015, with a decrease from 2015 (0.763%, 933 patients) to 2016 (0.483%, 541
patients), before linearly increasing from 2016 to 2021 (2.187%, 769
patients). Conclusion: The current analysis has demonstrated in
lumbar spine procedures what has been shown previously in cervical and
thoracic procedures: the use of computer assisted navigation has been
increasing in use overtime. We intend to next compare demographic variables
and outcomes between the two cohorts, as well as conduct multivariate
analyses adjusting for patient age, ECI score, insurance, hospital region
for all primary outcomes.
