## P438: Optical navigation in spine surgery an in vivo study

Josh Schroeder

1

, Leon Kaplan

1

, and hmed Shawan

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Hebrew University Hadassah Medical Center,
Jerusalem, Israel

Introduction: Surgery and spine surgery specifically are using
increasing amounts of ionizing radiation in order to allow tracking and
navigation during surgery. This increase in harmful radiation increases the
risk of cancer for both the patients and the surgical staff. In addition, in
cases in which the spine is mobile, the vertebras move during the case
causing decreased accuracy as the case progress. In light of these issues,
research into optical imaging and navigation has been conducted to allow a
radiation-free solution. Materials and Methods: Using a
specialized high definition 3D camera, augmented technology for optical
imaging and AI software allowing radiation free matching of the preoperative
imaging to the real anatomy of a patient, pedicle screws were planned and
lamina anatomy were navigated in lumbar cases (both female and male). Real
time tracing and imaging was tested in all cases. Results: Real
time tracking with optical navigation between L1 and S1 vertebrae was
performed in ten patients, using the real-time tracking software. Spine
anatomy including spinous process, lamina, pars intra-articularis and
transverse process was identified correctly in real time. Real time tracking
and imaging was tested and successful throughout the cases.
Summary: Optical navigation is an emerging new technology
that provides a safe solution for a radiation free spine surgery. As this
technology continues to evolve allowing sub-millimeter accuracy and real
time imaging, it shall be able to decrease the need of intraoperative
imaging for patients. Continues testing is needed to translate this
promising technology to everyday practice.

Introduction: This study is to evaluate that the C-arm installed
with multi-angle lasers assistant device whether can promote the efficiency
of X-ray fluoroscopy in lumbar spine surgery or not for beginners.

two groups (n = 10): experimental group (group A) and control group (group

by subjective questionnaire survey after the experiment.

0.162) in group B. Group A was more accurate (67.36%) than Group B. In the
above three indexes, group A was better than group B, and the difference was
statistically significant (p < 0.05). The results of the questionnaire
show that the scores of comfort, interest, efficiency of self-learning
operation, and mastery of relevant operation knowledge in group A were
higher than those in group B, and the difference was statistically
significant (p < 0.05). Conclusion: Multi-angle lasers
assisted C-arm can significantly improve the beginners efficiency of X-ray
photography during lumbar surgery, and also have significantly higher
satisfaction, which shows that the new technology is well worth
spreading.

, Devender Singh

, and Eric Mayer

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United

Introduction: Fewer studies in the literature have examined the

the PT group may experience comparatively better functional and pain

database of patients undergoing 1-2 level lumbar fusion surgery for
degenerative disease was assembled. Demographic and outcome scores such as

rehabilitation may benefit the majority of adult patients undergoing lumbar
fusion surgery for a degenerative indication. Prospective studies with

## 155

## P443: Determining what markers increase the odds of successful
non-operative treatment of lumbar disc herniation

Eeric Truumees

1

, Devender Singh

1

, Jeremiah Alexander

2

, Calvin Chandler

2

, Ashley Duncan

1

, and Eric Mayer

1

1

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

2

Orthopedics, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Treatment selection for acute lumbar disc
herniation remains uncertain due to reports of similar outcomes with
surgical and non-operative management over long-term follow-up. Current care
pathways recommend non-operative measures for six weeks before considering
surgical intervention, in the absence of neurological deficits.
Aim: This study aims to identify factors predictive of
successful non-operative treatment. Materials and Methods: We
reviewed 157 charts of patients for lumbar disc herniation. Inclusion
criteria consisted of encounters with ICD10 code M51.26 (other
intervertebral disc displacement, lumbar region), three months of follow-up
care, pre and post treatment ODI scores and non-operative care only.
Independent variables collected consisted of age, smoker status, presence of
comorbidities, antidepressant and opioid use, length of symptoms, treatment
prescribed (Physical Therapy, prescription and opioids, epidural steroid
injections (ESI)) baseline and three-month Oswestry Disability Index (ODI).
Categorical variables were then coded as discrete values, 0 for “no”, 1 for
“yes”; or in the case of smoking status 1 = never, 2 = former, 3 = current.
In regard to change in ODI score between baseline and three months, a
successful treatment was defined as a decrease in ODI of at least 10 points
and encoded as “1”. Treatment failure was defined as any increase in ODI or
a decrease of less than 10 and encoded as “0”. Multinomial logistic
regression was conducted on the encoded data. Results: Mean age
at appointment was 50.6 years. Most patients (81%) were never smokers, while
13% were former smokers and 6% were current smokers. 139 (89%) patients had
the presence of a comorbidity, and 16% were being treated with
antidepressants for anxiety/depression and 15% were already taking opioids
at the time of the first encounter. Mean duration of symptoms was 78.3 weeks
± 26.8. 95% of patients received a prescription, 69% had at least one ESI,
50% went to physical therapy and 16% received a prescription for opioids.
Results of the logistic analysis demonstrated only injection therapy and
opioid treatment were significant predictors of treatment success with odds
of 2.8 and 3.9, respectively. As expected, smoking and presence of
comorbidities decreased the odds of successful non-operative treatment by
1.1% and 28.1%, respectively. Interestingly, the logistic analysis of this
data showed that for each unit increase in age, the odds of successful
outcome increased by 2.5%. Conclusions: ESI and opioid therapy
were the only variables that significantly impacted the odds of successful
non-operative treatment on lumbar disc herniation at three months. The
positive impact of opioid prescription (290.3%) was surprising, given the
small number of occurrences in this population and the mechanism of action,
with no known local oranti-inflammatory properties. Increased age was also
positively correlated with treatment success, although non-significantly.
This contradicts the theories that increasing age becomes a liability and a
risk in the healing process and treatment decision making process. The
impact of opioid and age on treatment success in this analysis begs the
question of what psychological factors impact the patients’ determination of
a meaningful, successful outcome.

Introduction: Nearly 90 % of cases of coccygiodynia can be

## P445: Anti-osteoporotic medication prescription patterns in patients with
vertebral compression fractures

Jennifer Bell

1

, Thomas Alter

2

, Mary Kate Erdman

1,3

, Hyunwoo Kang

1,4

, Emily Mills

1

, Andy Ton

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Ram Alluri

1

, and Raymond Hah

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, United States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Harborview Medical Center, University of
Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, United States

4

Orthopaedic Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical
School, Boston, United States

Introduction: The purpose of this study was to (1) report
prescribing patterns of anti-osteoporotic medication in patients diagnosed
with a vertebral compression fracture (VCF) and (2) evaluate the influence
of surgical management on anti-osteoporotic prescribing patterns.
Material and Methods: A large de-identified patient
database from a private insurer was utilized. Patients diagnosed with a VCF
from January 2007 to December 2016 were identified. Exclusion criteria were
patients less than 50 years of age and patients with less than one-year
follow-up. Patients were grouped based on whether or not they received an
anti-osteoporotic medication within one year prior to or following the VCF,
and whether or not treatment included surgical intervention.
Results: A total of 73,907 patients sustaining VCF were
identified, of which 66.8% were female. The highest rate of VCF were
reported in patients between 70-74 years of age. Prior to the indexed VCF,
13,219 (17.8%) patients received anti-osteoporotic medication. A total of
60,688 (82.1%) patients were not prescribed anti-osteoporotic medications
prior to sustaining a VCF. Of these 60,688 treatment naïve patients, 9.6%
were prescribed an anti-osteoporotic medication within 1-year of the VCF.
The frequency of initiation in surgical and non-surgical patients was 18.4%
and 8.4%, respectively. For the 60,688 (82.1%) treatment naïve patients,
females between 70 and 84 years of age, were most likely to be initiated on
new anti-osteoporotic medications following a VCF. 9,077 (12.3%) patients
were treated surgically, of which 1,490 (16.4%) were treated with
anti-osteoporotic medication prior to index VCF. Conclusion:
Our data displays similar rates of anti-osteoporotic medication prior to VCF
in both operative and non-operative patients. Older female patients are more
likely to be treated prior to an event in comparison to their younger male
counterparts. Lastly, the prescribing patterns for anti-osteoporotic
medication after VCF, with or without surgical treatment, are low.

## 478

## P446: Clinical outcome of a conservative treatment protocol for lumbar
canal stenosis

Sai Viksheth Raj Basani

1

, and Harvinder singh Chhabra

1

1

Spine Services, Indian Spinal Injuries Centre, New Delhi,
India

Introduction: The management of Lumbar Spinal Stenosis begins
with nonoperative treatment, such as neurotropic medication like membrane
stabilizing agents (MSEs), NSAIDs, epidural steroid injections, and physical
therapy. Surgery is deferred until the failure of conservative treatment or
the appearance of red-flag signs. Unfortunately, most clinicians fail to
concur on what constitutes a fair conservative trial and the duration
required for eliciting the response. So, an urgent need exists to provide an
evidence-based protocol for clinical practice. Material and
Methods: A prospective cohort study was conducted at an Indian
tertiary spine care center. A total of 410 patients were recruited who
presented with neurogenic claudication and had a JOA’s LSS-DST score of 7 or
more. They were managed by a multimodal conservative protocol, consisting of
dose escalation and combination protocol of MSA’s/anti-depressants, NSAIDs,
methylcobalamin, TENS therapy, local heat/ice packs, counterirritants,
general conditioning with stretching exercises and patient education for
lifestyle modification. Those who didn’t respond within three to six weeks
were offered up to three TFESI at weekly intervals or surgery was suggested
when canal morphology is not amiable for TFES (i.e., Schizas’ Grade C and
D). The subjects were analyzed using Claudication distance, VAS score for
the leg and back, ODI score and SF36 score at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months
and 1-year intervals. Results: 387 patients completed the
study, while 23 were lost to follow-up. The mean age of the study population
was 61.36 years, with 15% being younger than 50 years. Schizas MRI grades B
and C accounted for 36% of subjects. Neurotropics were well tolerated, with
drowsiness and peripheral oedema reported in 23% of patients requiring dose
modification. No other untoward complication was noted. A total of 15
patients responded to TFES, and 7 others needed it twice; the response
didn’t correlate with MRI grade. A total of 57 patients required surgery. 14
of them had complications ranging from SSI to pyogenic spondylodiscitis. All
outcome variables showed a gradual improvement with time. Claudication
distance revealed a significant difference between MRI grades A1, A2 and
Grade C, D. While grade A1 stenotic patients had a significantly better SF36
score at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months, but at 12 months, there was no
difference in scores among various grades. Similarly, patients on
conservative treatment had better scores at 1st, 2nd,
and 3rd follow-up than operated patients. However, there was no
difference between the endpoint groups at the final follow-up. There was no
significant correlation between baseline variables and outcome. 81.5% of
patients who were advised surgery elsewhere responded to our conservative
protocol. Successfully conserved patients were more likely to be satisfied
with our protocol than those being operated on. Conclusion: Our
study demonstrated encouraging results with multimodal conservative protocol
and a decreased need for surgery. As no baseline variable can successfully
predict the response to our protocol, it is advisable to start an initial
conservative approach for all patients, and those with an unsatisfactory
result can be treated surgically later with a good outcome.

## P447: The effectiveness and longevity of epidural steroid injections in a
single center retrospective cohort

Annabel Kim

1

, Joshua Sanchez

2

, Marc Abdou

2

, Zorica Buser

3

, David Cheng

1

, and Gene Tekmyster

1

1

Keck Hospital of USC, Los Angeles, United States

2

Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, United States

3

Gerling Institute, New York, United States

Introduction: Low back pain and associated radicular syndromes
are significant health and socioeconomic issues that account for over 100
billion dollars annually in the United States. Epidural steroid injections
(ESIs) are a common method for relieving radicular pain from lumbar spine
etiologies. The current ESI literature is unclear due to the variability in
indications, injection techniques, number of allowed injections, and the
lack of standard and objective outcome measures. Thus, we evaluated the
changes in Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) scores for pain from lumbar spine
ESIs and their specific effectiveness in preventing a subsequent lumbar
spinal fusion procedure within a year follow-up period. Material and
Methods: Keck Hospital patients who received lumbar ESIs by a
single interventional physiatrist from 2018 to 2019 were identified using
Discern Reporting Portal. The electronic health record was used to verify
that their first ESIs were between January 2018 and April 2019, they had
one-year follow-ups, and there were no prior surgeries (foot, ankle, knee,
or hip). Patients whose back pain was instigated by a traumatic incident
were also excluded. All patients had a primary diagnosis of lumbar
radiculopathy (M54.16 ICD-10 code) and received transforaminal ESIs. The
first three ESIs received within the period were included. Collected
variables included demographics (age, gender, BMI, smoking status),
comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, pulmonary
conditions, cardiovascular conditions, renal conditions, and/or mental
illness), prior and concurrent opioid use, ESI injection levels and
laterality, NRS pain scores, and conversion to lumbar spine surgery. The
Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare NRS score change from pre-ESI
to post-ESI time points. Results: A total of 46 patients with
1-year follow-ups were identified. The average age was 55.1 ± 16.5. 54.3% of
the patients were male, and 45.7% were female. The most prevalent
comorbidities for the population included hypertension (32.6%),
hyperlipidemia (19.6%), and mental health diagnoses (23.9%). 15 patients
(32.6%) used opioids prior to their first ESI, and 8 (17.4%) used opioids
during their ESI treatment. The average pre-ESI NRS was 6.54 ± 2.64. The
most significant change in NRS scores from baseline was observed 6-month
post-ESI with an average decrease of 3.79 ± 3.75 (p = 0.005). At the 1-year
point, the average decrease in NRS score was 2.5 ± 2.81 (p = 0.02). 35
(76.1%) patients did not undergo lumbar surgery after ESI. In contrast, 11
(23.0%) patients underwent lumbar spine surgery within a year of their first
ESI. Conclusion: ESIs appear to be most effective at the
6-month mark and taper off at the 1-year point. Of the 11 patients that
converted to surgery, the majority (6) received two ESIs prior to surgery. 3
received one, and 2 received at least three ESIs prior to surgery. The
majority of patients (76.1%) did not convert to surgery. However, the
largest mitigating factor to this study is the small sample size, which
affected the ability to accurately determine the surgery conversion
rate.

## P448: Factors affecting brace adherence in adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis - a qualitative application of protection-motivation
theory

Raveen Jayasuriya

1

, Paul Norman

2

, Daniel Hind

3

, and Ashley Cole

1

1

Paediatric Spinal Surgery, Sheffield Children's Hospital, Sheffield,
United Kingdom

2

Department of Psychology

3

Clinical Trials Research Unit, University of Sheffield, Sheffield,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Full-time brace treatment to prevent the need for
spinal surgery (where 18 - 20 hours of brace wear is required) has been
shown to be adherence dependent in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Adherence to bracing however is variable between individuals. The factors
affecting health related behaviour in bracing have not been evaluated in a
structured theory-based framework. Material and Methods: This
study explores patient and parent perspectives and psychological effects of
bracing through semi-structured interview dyads. The interview topic guide,
and directed content analysis of transcripts, were performed utilising
protection-motivation theory as the underpinning psychological framework.
Results: Fifteen patients and nineteen parents
participated. For approximately half of the participants, appraising the
threat of the diagnosis was not possible as scoliosis was an unknown.
Following information given by surgeons, and independent research, most
participants had consistent perception of the severity of their scoliosis
and their vulnerability for future prognosis. The overwhelming content of
interviews focussed on the coping appraisal of bracing and the response cost
of treatment adherence; this was also consistent between participants,
despite good belief in the response efficacy of bracing. The self-efficacy
strategies that patients employed to increase adherence, and the maladaptive
response rewards of poor adherence, was variable between participants.
Conclusion: This qualitative semi-structured dyadic
interview study demonstrates that PMT provides a coherent psychological
framework with which to explore the factors affecting brace adherence in
patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Wearing the brace at school
poses a great challenge to patients in full-time bracing, causing anxiety
and stress; from worrying about how peers at school will perceive them, to
the limitations of how to make the brace less visible with clothing choices,
and coordinating extra-curricular activities around brace wear, all whilst
still adhering to the required brace wear hours. This study highlights both
the circumstances under which patients would choose not to wear the brace,
and the self-efficacy strategies employed to maintain adherence. This study
provides valuable data for the development of adherence prediction tools for
screening and stratifying. It also offers clinicians a framework with which
to augment information provided to patients thus maximising
protection-motivation behaviour for optimum brace adherence.

## 822

## P449: Spinal motion and low back pain - prospective analysis of the
association between lumbar movement and the occurrence of chronic back
pain

Friederike Schömig

1

, Luis Becker

1

, Pumberger Matthias

1

, Lea Cordes

2

, Georg Duda

2

, and Hendrik Schmidt

2

1

Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Center for Musculoskeletal
Surgery, Berlin, Germany

2

Berlin Institute of Health, Julius Wolff Institute, Berlin,
Germany

Introduction: Despite the increasing prevalence of chronic low
back pain (LBP), therapeutic management of LBP remains challenging, which is
mainly due to a lack of understanding of the underlying mechanisms of pain
development. While in the past, adaptations of spinal motion in the presence
of LBP have been increasingly studied, to date little is known about the
quantitative analysis of lumbar movements. Thus, we investigated movements
of the lumbar spine of both asymptomatic participants and LBP patients in
their daily lives for the first time. Material and Methods: We
prospectively included asymptomatic participants as well as patients who had
been suffering from LBP for at least twelve weeks. A body-mass-index (BMI)
of > 26 kg/m2 was an exclusion criterion. All asymptomatic
participants and LBP patients were measured for 24 hours during their daily
lives using the Epionics SPINE System with the standing position as a
reference. Lumbar movements of over 5° were recorded independently from the
movement’s starting position and were grouped into movements of >15°,
10-15°, and 5-10°. For statistical analysis, the Student’s t-test, analysis
of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni post-hoc test, and the Spearman
correlation coefficient were used. Results: A total of 208
asymptomatic participants and 106 LBP patients were included. While the
groups did not differ significantly in the distribution of sexes or in their
BMIs, the group of LBP patients was significantly older (50.9 ± 13.6 vs.
40.3 ± 14.0 years, p < 0.001). We found significantly fewer small,
medium, and large movements in the sagittal plane (total movement count
15,564 ± 8,078 vs. 20,521 ± 7,160, p < 0.001) in the group of LBP
patients. In the axial plane, LBP patients were shown to perform
significantly fewer small movements (total movement count 7,317 ± 5,881 vs.
11,106 ± 5,134, p < 0.001). There was a weak but significant correlation
between age and the number of sagittal (r = -0.179, p = 0.010) as well as
axial (r = -0.172, p = 0.013) movements shown for the group of asymptomatic
participants, while in LBP patients this correlation was only found for
sagittal movements (r = -0.290, p = 0.003). Conclusion: Our
results show that in addition to a significantly reduced total amount of
lumbar movements in LBP patients compared to asymptomatic participants,
there are significant differences between men and women especially regarding
large sagittal movements. We also found a reduction in lumbar movement with
increasing age, the correlation of which, however, was only weak. While it
remains unclear whether the shown changes in spinal motion are cause or
effect of pain development, the association between movement adaptations and
chronic LBP needs to be considered in the optimization of motion-based
conservative treatment strategies and therefore needs to be further
investigated.

## 1057

## P450: Efficacy of nucleoplasty for radiculopathy caused by foraminal
cervical disc herniation: clinical results of case series and technical
note

Pius Kim

1

1

Neurosurgery, Chosun University Hospital, Gwangju Metropolitan City,
South Korea

Introduction: Percutaneous cervical nucleoplasty (PCN) is a
minimally invasive technique used for the treatment of cervical disc
herniation. However, if the lesion is located at the neural foramen,
complete access and effective neural decompression are often challenging
because of the special anatomical condition of the uncovertebral joint,
osteophyte, and facet joint of the cervical foraminal space. In this
presentation, when performing PCN for foraminal cervical disc herniation
(FCDH), the technique for overcoming those anatomical difficulties is
described, and the study results of analyzing the clinical effects are
reported. Material and Methods: This study included 44 patients
with radiculopathy caused by FCDH who were treated with PCN. Visual analog
scale (VAS) scores, preoperative, 1 week and 3 months postoperatively, and
at the last follow-up, as well as the MacNab criteria, were used to evaluate
clinical outcomes. A paired t-test was used to compare the preoperative and
follow-up VAS scores. The percentage of patients with VAS score ≤ 3 at each
follow-up time point was also investigated. Statistical significance was set
at p < 0.05. Results: Twenty-seven men (62.4%) and 17 women
(38.6%) were enrolled in this study. The mean age was 54.5 years (range
31-81). The average follow-up period after the operation was 15.4 months
(range 3.7-30.8). The mean preoperative VAS was 7.50 ± 1.21. The VAS scores
at 1 week, 3 months, and the last follow-up were 4.36 ± 2.46, 3.20 ± 2.58,
and 2.91 ± 2.74, respectively, showing a significant improvement in pain
compared to before the operation (p < 0.001 for all). The number of
patients (percentage) with a VAS score of ≤ 3 was 20 (45.5%), 28 (63.6%),
and 31 (70.5%) of 44 patients at 1 week, 3 months, and the last follow-up,
respectively. The number of patients (percentage) with excellent, good,
fair, or poor satisfaction according to the MacNab criteria was 17 (38.6%),
9 (20.5%), 8 (18.2%), and 10 (22.7%) of 44, respectively. No patients
experienced postoperative complications. Conclusion: Although
PCN for radiculopathy caused by FCDH is thought to have limitations because
of the surrounding bony structure, the clinical outcome seemed favorable. If
PCN is not contraindicated, it may be a viable treatment option for CR due
to FCDH.

## P451: The impact of physical therapy after lumbar fusion surgery

Jeremy Heard

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Nicholas D'Antonio

1

, Nicholas Siegel

1

, Tariq Issa

1

, Yash Reddy

2

, Sanath Patil

2

, Caroline Purtill

2

, John Bodnar

2

, Sydney Somers

2

, Delano Trenchfield

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, The Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas
Jefferson University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States

2

Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Literature on the efficacy of physical therapy
(PT) after lumbar fusion surgery is mixed and limited guidance on PT
interventions after lumbar surgery exists. Given the prevalence of PT
referrals and lack of high-quality evidence, there is a need for additional
studies investigating the efficacy of PT after lumbar fusion surgery to aid
in developing robust clinical guidelines. Thus, our objectives are to (1)
determine if PT attendance after lumbar fusion impacts PROMs and (2)
determine if PT attendance after lumbar fusion affects readmission or
revision rates. Methods: We retrospectively identified patients
receiving lumbar fusion surgery by current procedural terminology codes and
separated them into two groups based on whether PT was prescribed.
Electronic medical records were reviewed for patient and surgical
characteristics, PT utilization, and surgical outcomes. Patient reported
outcome measures (PROMs) were identified and compared preoperatively to one
year postoperatively. Multivariable regression analysis was performed.
Significance was set to p < 0.05. Results: Our methodology
identified 323 patients that attended PT and 400 patients that did not. In
comparison to patients that did not attend PT, those that attended PT had
similar patient characteristics and comorbidities. Patients that attended PT
had significantly more fused levels (1.41 ± 0.64 vs. 1.32 ± 0.54, p =
0.027), longer operative durations (234 ± 96.4 vs. 215 ± 86.1 minutes, p =
0.012), and lengthier postoperative hospital stays (3.35 ± 1.68 vs. 3.00 ±
1.49, p = 0.004). There were no significant differences between readmission,
complications, and revision rates. Bivariant analysis of PROMs demonstrated
that physical therapy attendance did not confer significant benefits to
overall clinical improvement at the one-year postoperative: MCS-12 (2.88 ±
12.1 vs. 3.52 ± 10.3, p = 0.739), PCS-12 (11.5 ± 11.8 vs. 8.82 ± 11.2, p =
0.171), ODI (-25.50 ± 21.0 vs. -19.16 ± 18.1, p = 0.071), VAS Back (-3.68 ±
3.60 vs. -2.87 ± 3.19, p = 0.175), and VAS Leg (-4.69 ± 3.67 vs. -4.40 ±
3.54, p = 0.644). Multivariable analysis showed that PT was not
significantly associated with PROM improvement postoperatively both at three
months and one year. Conclusion: Our study found there was no
significant benefit to postoperative physical therapy after lumbar fusion
with regards to improvements in three-month or one-year patient reported
outcome measures. In addition, PT attendance did not impact 90-day
readmission rates. Given the current conflicting literature on the topic, at
this time it is difficult to recommend for or against PT after lumbar fusion
surgery. As PT is costly to the healthcare system, however, stronger
recommendations are needed to guide treatment and physicians should use
their discretion when prescribing PT.

## 1148

## P452: Acceptance and commitment therapy screening model for patients
undergoing spinal surgery

Happy Kumar

1

, Alex Coffman

2

, Natalie Glass

2

, Valerie Keffala

2

, Cassim Igram

2

, Andrew Pugely

2

, and Catherine Olinger

2

1

University of Iowa Carver College of Medicine, Iowa City, United
States

2

Department of Orthopedics & Rehabilitation, University of Iowa
Hospitals & Clinics, Iowa City, United States

Introduction: Chronic pain is an issue that affects over 100
million Americans daily. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) has been
found to be beneficial for patients with chronic pain by focusing provider
efforts to teaching coping mechanisms for pain instead of eliminating the
pain entirely. Data collected post-operatively indicates ACT benefits
patients with 64.8% improving in at least one key domain in a longitudinal
study by Vowles et al. 2011. Presently the University of Iowa does not have
a strict standard protocol for referring patients to ACT with the Department
of Orthopedic Surgery Pain Psychologist. The aim of the study is to evaluate
the effectiveness of PCS as a screening tool for ACT in the spine patient
population at the University of Iowa Hospitals & Clinics Department of
Orthopedics & Rehabilitation. This study will determine whether the PCS
is effective at identifying patients who would benefit from ACT.
Materials and Methods: Every patient that presented to
spine clinic at University of Iowa Hospitals & Clinics (UIHC) from
February 2022 to June 2022 was surveyed using the Pain Catastrophizing Scale
(PCS). Patients indicated for spinal surgery were reviewed retrospectively.
The patient list was filtered down to 600 adult spinal patients with
pre-operative and post-operative PCS scores. 200 patients were chosen via a
random number generator and additional information, such as the patients’
History of Present Illness, Visual Analog Scale Scores, PROMIS-CAT Pain
Interference Scores, and status of opiate usage were collected and presented
to UIHC Orthopedic Spine Surgeons. Surgeons were blinded to the PCS Cutoff
Scores. The UIHC Orthopedic Spine Surgeons then identified which patients
they would indicate for ACT and their reasoning. Surgeon referral was then
compared to referral based on the PCS score of the same patients to evaluate
the accuracy of the PCS scoring tool. Results: Effectiveness of
this screening tool was based on frequency at which the surgeons and PCS
score were complimentary. ROC Curve demonstrated an area under the curve of
0.7784 with a Sensitivity of 0.68 and a Specificity of 0.79. Cut-point
according to Youden’s index is 35. Conclusion: The data showed
that the PCS is moderately accurate in its ability to distinguish between
patients who should and should not be referred for ACT. The adjusted
cut-point indicates that patients above a PCS of 35 should be deemed at-risk
and referred the department pain psychologist for evaluation for ACT while
those below a PCS score of 35 should not be referred. The goal following
this study is to perform future investigations regarding PCS and ACT with
patients regarding chronic opioid use and post-operative outcomes. Patients
who were referred for help with chronic opiate use would be compared to
PCS-referred patients and non-referred patients. Pre-operative ACT would be
compared to patient outcomes post-operatively. The aim is to evaluate if
PCS-referred patients have better pain management post-operatively as
compared to the control and opiate-referred patients.

## 1230

## P453: Changes in M.multifidus cross sectional area, muscle thickness and
echogenicity measured via ultrasound during an isolated lumbar extension
resistance exercise (ILEX) rehabilitation programme in a sample of chronic,
neuropathic and specific low back pain patients

Bruno Domokos

1

, Ettinger Julia

2

, Raschka Christoph

1

, and Spang Christoph

2

1

Institute of Sport Science, University of Wuerzburg, Wuerzburg,
Germany

2

Private Spine Center Dr Alfen, Würzburg, Germany

Introduction: Paraspinal muscle atrophy and increased muscle fat
fraction are well documented pathological changes in chronic, specific and
neuropathic low back pain (LBP) conditions (Hodges & Danneels, 2019).
Studies have highlighted the benefits of addressing these muscles in
conservative treatment approaches including post-operative rehabilitation
(Hodges & Danneels, 2019). Machine-based ILEX adapted to the
individual’s pathology has shown good clinical outcomes for patients with
spinal disorders like disk herniations and radiculopathy (Steele et al.,
2015; Golonka et al., 2021). However, morphological adaptations of the
M.multifidus muscle during a rehabilitation process have not been assessed
yet. Material and Methods: In this ongoing prospective study,
ultrasound imaging was used to assess cross-sectional area (CSA), muscle
thickness (MT) and echogenicity in the M.multifidus muscle (right and left
side) of 14 patients (7 women, 7 men) suffering from chronic low back pain
(duration > 3 months) with previously diagnosed specific lumbar spine
pathologies including disc herniations, spondylarthritis, spondylolisthesis
and other degenerative conditions. All patients underwent an ILEX-based
exercise protocol consisting of 18 sessions (9 weeks) within a
diagnose-based range of motion. One set of ILEX was performed per session
with the resistance progressively increased during the protocol. Imaging was
conducted at four time points (t1 = pre-interventional;
t2 = 3 weeks; t3 = 6 weeks; t4 = 9
weeks) using the Logic S7 Expert (GE Healthcare, Munich, GER) ultrasound
device with a linear transducer. Pain and disability levels were documented
with the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index
(ODI). For statistical analysis, Friedman test (with Bonferroni correction)
and Pearson coefficient was used. Results: A substantial
progressive linear decrease in mean pain levels and disability was found
during the process of rehabilitation. Significant differences were
especially observed between t1 (VAS: 50.5 (mean) ± 19.4 (standard
deviation, SD); ODI: 17.9% ± 8.6) and t4 (VAS: 20.2 ± 14.0, p
< 0.001; ODI: 7.3% ± 5.2, p < 0.001). 13/14 patients reported an
improvement in pain and functional score. Concerning muscular adaptations,
CSA increased progressively in a linear manner (7.44 cm2 ± 1.98
(t1) vs. 8.09 cm2 ± 1.91 (t4); p <
0.001). Furthermore, there was a non-significant increase in MT (3.06 cm ±
0.58 (t1) vs. 3.08 cm ± 0.57 (t4); p = 0.194). No
changes were measured for echogenicity and side differences for MT and CSA.
Before the programme, there was a correlation (r= -0.557, p < 0.05)
between CSA (per kg bodyweight) and ODI scores. Conclusion: To
the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to analyse morphological
effects of heavy loaded ILEX in patients with chronic, specific LBP
conditions. The results indicate that clinical improvement is accompanied by
substantial structural improvements of the M.multifidus. At baseline, there
was a correlation between high CSA and better functional scores which
further highlights atrophy of the M.multifidus in the pathogenesis of
chronic spinal pain conditions. Deriving from the results, ultrasound
imaging is a useful method to be applied for the process and results
evaluation following surgery, conservative rehabilitation or for preventive
purposes in population groups at risk for the development of LBP (e.g. due
to inactivity).

## P454: Prognostic significance of lab data and performance comparison by

retrospective study aims to investigate the prognostic impacts of laboratory
data and to compare the performances of Metastases location, Elderly, Tumor
primary, Sex, Sickness/comorbidity, and Site of radiotherapy (METSSS) model,
New England Spinal Metastasis Score (NESMS), and Skeletal Oncology Research
Group machine learning algorithm (SORG-MLA) for SM. Materials and
methods: From 2010 to 2018, patients who received radiotherapy
(RT) for SM at a tertiary center were enrolled and the data were
retrospectively collected. Multivariate logistic and Cox-proportional-hazard
regression analyses were used to assess the association between laboratory
values and survival. The area under receiver-operating characteristics curve
(AUROC), calibration analysis, Brier score, and decision curve analysis were
used to evaluate the performance of SPMs. Results: A total of
2,786 patients were included for analysis. The 90-day and 1-year survival
rates after RT were 70.4% and 35.7%, respectively. Higher albumin,
hemoglobin, or lymphocyte count were associated with better survival, while
higher alkaline phosphatase, white blood cell count, neutrophil count,
neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, or
international normalized ratio were associated with poor prognosis. SORG-MLA
has the best discrimination (AUROC 90-day, 0.78; 1-year 0.76), best
calibrations, and the lowest Brier score (90-day 0.16; 1-year 0.18). The
decision curve of SORG-MLA is above the other two competing models with
threshold probabilities from 0.1 to 0.8. Conclusion: We
demonstrated the clinical impact of selective laboratory values such as
serum albumin level, hemoglobin level, and lymphocyte count on survival
prediction in patients receiving radiotherapy for spinal metastases.
SORG-MLA, incorporating laboratory values and the flexible modeling
technique, accurately predicts 90-day and 1-year survival for the
radiotherapy cohort. SPMs integrated into patient decision aids for shared
decision-making present opportunities for individualized patient-centered
care in the future.

100%. Conclusion: Target-oriented lumbar percutaneous

discogenic back pain with relatively well-maintained disc heights, which is
the case of the modified Pfirmann classification graded 3 to 6. A successful
outcome depends upon proper patient selection and correct trajectory.

## P456: Ultrasound-guide pulsed radiofrequency of cervical nerve root for

trial

Weerasak Singhatanadgige

1

, poornpan Chalermkitpanit

1

, and Vit Kotheeranurak

1

1

Orthopedics, Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok,
Thailand

Introduction: Pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) on cervical DRG for
pain management in cervical radicular pain is mostly performed via
transforaminal approached under fluoroscopic guidance. Ultrasound-guidance
periradicular cervical nerve root intervention raises concern in the
neuromodulatory effect. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and
duration of pain relief between PRF treatment and steroid injection on the
cervical nerve roots. Material and Methods: Forty-two patients
presented with chronic cervical radicular pain were prospectively randomized
into pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) group and steroid group. Patients in the
PRF group received PRF treatment at 42 degrees Celsius for 4 minutes
followed by the injection of 2% lidocaine 1.5 ml with dexamethasone 10 mg to
the targeted cervical nerve root. The steroid group received the same

pain intensity and neck functional assessment before and after the
procedure. The duration of pain reduction at least 50% was recorded up to

and 20 patients receiving pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) and steroid treatment,
respectively. At 3-month post procedure, patients in PRF group had
significantly less pain (NRS 2.8 ± 2.7) than patients in steroid group (NRS

sole steroid injection. The duration of pain relief at least 50% was
significantly longer in patients received PRF treatment (6.0 ± 4.1 months)
compared to those in the steroid group (2.3 ± 2.1 months) (p < 0.01). The
vascular puncture did not occur in both study groups.
Conclusion: Ultrasound-guided periradicular cervical nerve
root PRF exhibited neuromodulatory effect and was considered a safe and
effective treatment for patients with cervical radicular pain. It provided
longer duration of pain relief and the improvement of neck function up to 6
months.

## P457: Comparison of healing rates between rigid and semi-rigid bracing in
adolescent lumbar pars bone stress injuries

Paul Licina

1

, Patrick Beaumont

2

, and Mark Young

2

1

Faculty of Health, Exercise and Nutrition Science, Queensland
University of Technology, Kelvin Grove, Australia

2

Spine Surgery, Brisbane Private Hospital, Brisbane,
Australia

Introduction: Adolescent athletes are predisposed to lumbar bone
stress injuries of the pars interarticularis (pars stress injuries or PSIs).
These injuries are the most common cause of significant adolescent low back
pain and may progress to chronic disability, non-union and isthmic
spondylolisthesis. They are heterogenous and may be acute or chronic, and
unilateral or bilateral, and the injury grade may be a stress reaction, an
incomplete fracture, or a complete fracture. MRI can identify the chronicity
and grade of the lesion by measuring bone marrow oedema (BMO) and
visualising the fracture. Bracing has been proposed as a treatment for acute
PSIs. It not only relieves pain but has been previously shown to increase
the likelihood of bony healing, reducing the risk of progression. The
lumbosacral brace may be a rigid custom-made Boston brace-type orthosis or a
semi-rigid off-the-shelf brace. The objectives of this study were to
quantify the types of PSIs, to determine the bony healing rates after 12
weeks of bracing, and to compare healing rates between rigid and semi-rigid
braces. Materials and Methods: We performed a retrospective
analysis of adolescents with acute PSIs (as defined by a bone BMO ratio ≥ 2)
who wore either a rigid or semirigid brace for 12 weeks. All participants
underwent an MRI scan prior to bracing and at 12 weeks, to assess the degree
of BMO and the injury grade. From this, it was determined whether the BMO
had resolved (ratio < 2) and whether the fracture had healed during the
bracing period. Results: We identified 88 patients with an
acute PSI treated in a brace. Overall, 14 worsened, 12 remained unchanged
and 62 improved (i.e., had resolution of BMO). Of those that improved, 25
also showed fracture healing. 49 were unilateral acute PSIs, 4 of which had
a contralateral chronic complete fracture. Of the 45 unilateral acute PSIs
without a contralateral chronic fracture, 32 improved with 17 of those
healed. However, all 4 patients with a contralateral chronic fracture
worsened. 39 were bilateral acute PSIs, and in this group, 30 improved with
8 of those healed. Of the 88 patients, 42 used rigid orthoses and 46 used
semi-rigid braces. There was no significant difference between rigid and
semirigid bracing in overall improvement or healing.
Discussion: We demonstrated that the use of bracing in
acute PSIs led to a 70% rate of resolution of BMO and a 28% rate of fracture
healing at 12 weeks with only 16% worsening. We found that bracing is
significantly more effective in unilateral only and bilateral acute PSIs,
compared to unilateral acute PSIs with a chronic contralateral fracture,
questioning the role of bracing in this subgroup. We were unable to
demonstrate that bracing was superior to non-bracing but there are
considerable ethical challenges in withholding treatment in an adolescent
population where the intervention is relatively benign and has previously
been demonstrated to be effective. Off-the-shelf semirigid braces are more
convenient and less expensive, and in our study showed similar efficacy in
BMO resolution and bony healing.

Elie Najjar

Introduction: Long level pedicle screw placement requiring

95CI: 0.63). Conclusion: Full power assisted pedicle screw

## P459: Clinical application of new concept of rod connector; connector for
simultaneously fixing screw head and rod (for ASD operation)

Moon-Kyu Kim

1

1

Neurosurgery, Gangneug Asan Hospital, Gangwon-do, South
Korea

Introduction: With the development of pedicle screw system and
spinal deformity surgery, spinal fixation surgery is gradually increasing.
Accordingly, surgery for adjacent segments after spinal fusion is also
increasing. Due to the adjacent segment diseases (ASD), incision of all
previous surgical ranges during surgery has a wide range of surgery and
concerns about damage to muscle soft tissue due to revision, therefore,
several connectors (open connectors) have been developed as results of
effort to minimize revision surgeries. However, these type connectors are
mainly connected only to rods (rod to rod) and single connector is
mechanically weak when they are use alone, thus multiple connectors are used
to get enough strength to extend fusion levels. Therefore, authors developed
a connector capable of extended fusion by combining the top load fixation
type screw head and rod simultaneously to strengthen the connection
structure, exposing only the top-level screw head during adjacent segment
surgery, and applied it to clinical practice. Methods: The
basic concept was prepared in 2016 and patented in 2019 (application in
2017). The clinical device (Qnector) using this concept started development
in 2017 and was completed in 2019, passed KFDA in 2020, and applied to
clinical trials in 2021. The basic concept is that the connector is fixed to
the rod and the screw head located at the end of the existing surgical
instrument at the same time, and a new rod is connected to this connector.
This structure compensates for the vulnerability to rotation based on the
rod direction by fixing it with the screw head, so Qnector has the effect of
using only one connector instead of using multiple open connectors.
Results: Between March 2021 and June 2022, Qnectors were
applied to 9 patients who developed ASD after the previous multilevel level
fusion, and showed a stable and good clinical course without hardware
failure and were enough strong to endure rod bending after connection by in
situ benders. The screws previously operated were different types, but all
were applicable to Qnectors. Discussion: The new concepted
connector can be developed in various shapes other than the one developed
this time. It can be developed in various forms, and could be supposed to
open the horizon for a new concept of connectors that can affix the screw
head and rod simultaneously. Conclusion: A powerful connector
that connects the screw head and rod at the same time could minimize the
re-opening of the previous surgical site, improving the patient's recovery
after surgery and lowering the operator's surgical difficulty.

## P460: ALL repair and disc replacement for hyperextension injuries -
extending the indications for motion preservation in the cervical
spine

Adrian Cavalcanti Kußmaul

1

, Titus Kuehlein

1

, Becker Christopher

1

, Bruder Jan

1

, Woiczinski Matthias

1

, Kistler Manuel

1

, Böcker Wolfgang

1

, and Greiner Axel

1

,
Sandy Walter

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics and Trauma Surgery, Musculoskeletal
University Center Munich (MUM), University Hospital, LMU, Munich,
Germany

Introduction: Anterior tension band injuries are usually the
result of high impact hyperextension trauma. However, these injuries can be
increasingly observed in geriatric patients based on the current demographic
change. Surgical treatment includes anterior plating bearing the risk of
soft tissue irritation, such as esophageal dysphagia or rupture, and
degeneration of adjacent cervical segments or implant failure due to an
iatrogenic spondylodesis. Tape suture constructs, reenforcing ligamental
stability while permitting physiological micro mobility of the affected
motion segment, are already established for ligamental injuries in ankle,
knee or shoulder surgery. Recently, a biomechanical in vitro study was
further able to demonstrate the feasibility of this flexible osteosynthesis
technique for the treatment of AO type B3 injuries. Consequently, this in
vivo study aims to examine the biomechanical properties of tape suture
constructs for the treatment of AO type B3 injuries in cadaver specimens.
Materials and Methods: The anterior longitudinal ligaments
(ALL) and the cervical disc of 16 human cadaver C5/6 segments were
dissected, simulating an AO type B3 injury. Then, two groups were formed and
treated either with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) (anterior
4-hole-plate, DePuy Synthes®) or a cervical total disc
replacement (CTDR) (Prodisc®- C Vivo) combined with a tape suture
construct, similar to the SpeedBridgeTM (Arthrex®),
which was implanted ventrally according to the anatomical course of the
disrupted ALL. The specimens were then mounted onto a biomechanical testing
machine in a neutral position and biomechanical forces were applied through
a lever arm until a force of 15N was reached in the sagittal plane,
simulating extension and flexion. Next rotational forces to both directions
were applied until cervical resistance resulted in a rotational force of
2N/m. Implant failure was defined as a dislocation exceeding 25mm for
extension and 7° for rotation. For statistical analysis, the dislocation (°)
and its corresponding force (N) of each specimen was measured and compared.
Results: Preliminary results show a higher range of motion
for the tape suture construct in all motion planes with the tape suture
construct however consistently staying below physiological mobility. No
specimen suffered from implant failure. Detailed evaluation among the
specimens is currently in progress and will be completed in time for the
congress. Conclusion: The tape suture combined with CTDR
provides sufficient biomechanical stability for the treatment of AO type B3
injuries compared to anterior plating. Preliminary results display a
sufficient limitation of movement in the sagittal plane, especially
regarding cervical extension, which’s limitation is crucial for ligamental
healing. The rigid ACDF highly compromises cervical rotation and lateral
bending, which are usually not affected in a hyperextension injury, while
the tape suture and CTDR approach the physiological range of motion.
Consequently, the tape suture construct is a promising alternative to the
current gold standard of anterior plating for the treatment of AO type B3
injuries based on its excellent biomechanical results and its preservation
of cervical micro mobility with a concomitant prevention of an iatrogenic
spondylodesis.

## P463: Knowledge gaps in biophysical changes after powered robotic
exoskeleton walking by individuals with spinal cord injury - a scoping
review

Christopher Yip

1

, Chor Yin Lam

2

, Kenneth Man Chee Cheung

2

, Yat Wa Wong

2

, and Paul Koljonen

2

1

The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong

2

Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, The University of Hong
Kong, Hong Kong

Introduction: In addition to helping individuals with spinal
cord injury (SCI) regain the ability to ambulate, the rapidly evolving
capabilities of powered robotic exoskeletons provide an array of secondary
biophysical benefits which can reduce the complications resulting from
prolonged immobilization. This scoping review seeks to provide an overview
on the known effects of overground exoskeleton use, on the prevention of
secondary health complications, changes to the QOL, and their effect on the
independence of SCI individuals in the community settings. Moreover, the
intent of the review is to identify gaps in the literature currently
available, and to make recommendations on focus study areas and methods for
future investigations. Material and Methods: The reporting of
methods and results in this scoping review follow the Preferred Reporting
Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews
(PRISMA- ScR) guidelines. The framework by Arksey and O’Malley has been
referenced for the protocol of this scoping review. PubMed, Cochrane, and
EMBASE were searched for relevant articles from database inception to June
19, 2021; the bibliographies of included articles were screened. The search
term used included “exoskeleton,” “spinal cord injury,” and related
keywords, both as the free-text keywords and controlled vocabulary of their
respective databases (e.g., MeSH for PubMed and Cochrane Library). The
refinement of protocol was done after the initial search, with focus placed
on a defining eligibility criterion with specific attention to the list of
biophysical characteristics to include. The final selection of studies was
separated into individual groups based on the type of biophysical
characteristic that was evaluated; studies that measured more than one
biophysical characteristic were included more than once across different
tables. Data extraction templates were generated a priori,
with minor modifications done after the initial search, and the data
elements extracted included: study, intervention, number of training
sessions, ASIA grade, number of subjects, time-points during trial when
specific relevant measurements were taken, outcome metrics used in the
study, and the presence of any control arms. Results: 654
articles were found in the initial search, 231 of which were found to be
duplicate; 329 articles were excluded during the screening of the titles and
abstracts, and a further 52 were eliminated after screening the full texts.
In the final analysis, 42 papers were included from the initial search,
combined with an additional 8 from scanning through the reference lists of
relevant studies. 50 unique studies were included in the charting process.
Detailed results will be presented in this abstract.
Conclusion: This scoping review the most robust systematic
review performed on this topic to date. It has identified various focus
areas in the need of further investigation, such as CVS health, BMD, body
composition changes, and independence and functional applications for
exoskeletons. Detailed analysis on each domain were performed and presented.
We have identified pitfalls, such as heterogeneous methodologies, disparate
study populations, and dissimilar training programs, which need to be
overcome in future studies.

## P464: Smartphones, wearables, and digital biomarkers: the evolution of
spine care outcomes research

David Kurland

1

, Christina Bi

1

, Roee Ber

1

, Douglas Kondziolka

1

, Darryl Lau

1

, Donato Pacione

1

, Anthony Frempong-Boadu

1

, Ilya Laufer

1

, and Eric Oermann

1

1

Neurosurgery, NYU Langone Health, New York, United States

Introduction: Over the past generation, outcomes research in
spine care has evolved from reliance on clinician-reported assessment toward
a recognition of the importance of the patient’s perspective, and the wide
incorporation of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). While PROMs are
now considered an integral component of outcomes assessments, they cannot
wholly capture the state of a patient’s functionality. The pervasiveness of
smartphones and wearable devices in modern society, which passively collect
data related to health, has ushered in a new era of spine care outcome
measurement – and in some respects, a return to objectivity. The patterns
emerging from these data, so-called “digital biomarkers,” can accurately
describe characteristics of a patient’s health, disease, or recovery state.
Material and Methods: PubMed was queried for the following
terms on July 20, 2022: (smartphone OR wearable OR mobile device) AND (spine
OR spine surgery OR spinal fusion OR spinal decompression OR spinal
deformity). Two authors (DBK and CB) independently screened each record.
Clinical articles reporting the use of smartphones and wearable devices in
objective spine care outcomes research were eligible for inclusion in this
review. Pertinent topical review articles were also evaluated separately for
content. Non- or pre-clinical studies were excluded, as were reports on
devices that were prototypes or in pre-commercialization stages. We also
excluded manuscripts that described smartphone or wearable applications
strictly designed for use by a provider in a clinical or office setting.
Results: The initial search returned 437 unique results. Of
these, 330 were readily deemed ineligible based on subject matter. Of the
remaining 107 sought for retrieval, 37 were excluded based on the exclusion
criteria described above. A total of 70 manuscripts (46 clinical studies and
24 pertinent topical reviews) published between 2015 and 2022 met inclusion
criteria, and were reviewed in detail. The current applications of digital
biomarkers are manifold and include: 1) surgical decision making, 2)
diagnosis and disease severity stratification, 3) remote pre- and
post-operative symptom monitoring, as well as 4) remote
care/self-management. These applications and concepts have been successfully
applied to patients with chronic low back pain, lumbar stenosis,
degenerative disc disease and cervical stenosis. Conclusion:
Digital biomarkers and continuous passive monitoring have a number of
currently validated applications in the field of spine care, as well as
tremendous potential to expand into the field of personalized medicine.
Smartphones and wearable devices increase the accessibility of mobility
measures previously confined to the clinical or laboratory setting.
Continuous collection of mobility data can improve symptom and disease
progression monitoring, detect deterioration or functional decline, and
improve perioperative care. The pervasiveness of smartphones and wearables
naturally increase patient compliance and have the potential to further
involve patients in their own care, creating a deeper collaboration between
patient and care providers. More extensive data collection of mobility and
gait metrics, both on a population and an individual level, will allow for
the utilization of digital biomarker measures in a more personalized way,
allowing for more appropriate treatment decisions, more accurate prognostic
measures, and more efficient resource allocation.

## P465: The efficacy of stand-alone spacers in comparison to conventional
cage and plate in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion surgery: a

outcomes

Jake McDonnell

1

, Salma Youssef

2

, Gráinne Cunniffe

1

, Stacey Darwish

1

, and Joseph Butler

1

1

National Spinal Injuries Unit, Mater Misericordiae University
Hospital, Dublin, Ireland

2

School of Medicine, University College Dublin, Dublin,
Ireland

Background: ACDF is commonly performed with cage and plate
constructs to provide stability to the diseased or injured cervical segment.
Despite it being a commonly performed procedure, there are notable rates of
associated morbidity reported in the literature. Anchored stand-alone
spacers represent a novel form of instrumentation to conventional cage and
plate constructs. However, little is known regarding their collective
comparative evidence versus cages and plates. This serves the premise for
this study. The objective of this study is to elucidate if anchored spacers
have improved operative characteristics and postoperative outcomes in
anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) cohorts when compared to
traditional cage and plate, and can be inferred as efficacious as
conventional instrumentation in the management of cervical spine disorders.
Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was
conducted of PubMed/Medline, Embase and Google Scholar databases per the
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and
Meta-Analyzes (PRISMA) guidelines. Studies of interest included
comparative (conventional cage and plate) instrumentation versus anchored
stand-alone spacers for patients undergoing ACDF. Pre- and post-operative
clinical and radiological outcomes were collated and compared for
significance between cohorts. Results: 10 RCTs were identified
and included with 779 patients total. Mean age of the entire cohort was 50.1
years (range 30-78 years). 62% (483/779) of the cohort were male, while 38%
(296/779) were female. 384 patients underwent ACDF with stand-alone cage,
while 395 had ACDF with conventional cage and plate. Stand-alone spacers
significantly outperformed conventional instrumentation in terms of
estimated blood loss (p < 0.01), total postoperative complications (p
< 0.01), dysphagia rates (p = 0.04) and adjacent segment disease (p =
0.04). Non-inferiority was evident in both patient reported outcome measures
and radiological outcomes. Conclusion: The results of this
meta-analysis highlight the efficacy of stand-alone spacers for the
management of primarily cervical spondylitic disease for both single-level
and multi-level pathology, and thus present an attractive alternative to
conventional instrumentation for patients undergoing ACDF surgery.

## P466: Medical grade, operating theatre, HEPA and UV light air filter
effectively reduce air particles with implied viral sterilisation

Angelo Fragkakis

1

, Zion Hwang

2

, Jason Bernard

1

, Timothy Bishop

1

, Jan Herzog

1

, Shahnawaz Haleem

1

, Tesfaladet Kurban

1

, Bisola Ajayi

1

, Emily Tsang

2

, Priyanshu Saha

2

, and Darren Lui

1

1

Trauma and Orthopaedics, St. George's University Hospital, London,
United Kingdom

2

St. George's University of London, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: SARS-CoV-2 has become a worldwide threat exposing
patients and physicians to significant risks. The virus starts primarily as
a respiratory infection and has airborne capabilities with a 60–140nm
diameter transmissible through droplet particles of Ø 0.3-10µm.
Aerosol-generating procedures can increase the particles’ transmission risk,
therefore neutralisation methods become paramount. Studies show that the
success of ultraviolet (UV) light disinfection warrants greater research
into its utility within clinical settings. Only recently, UV light has been
paired with HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters. This innovative
technology could have the potential to aid prevention of viral and bacterial
nosocomial infection and its associated morbidities. Therefore, this study
aims to assess whether Illuvia® HUAIRS, a medical-grade HEPA and
UV light air recirculation system, can reduce the airborne particle count,
and thus potentially reduce the spread of nosocomial infection.
Material and Methods: This prospective pilot study
conducted in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a tertiary UK hospital
(2020-2021) assessed the impact of Illuvia® HUAIRS, filtering
41.8m3/min of air. The air particles concentration was
measured with a validated and published particle counter (HT9600; Dongguan
Xintai Instrument Co. Ltd.). As a surrogate measure for an infectious
bioaerosol carrying COVID-19, 0.3μm, 2.5μm and 10μm particle sizes were
considered. In a 150m2 ICU, with 14 patients and 20 staff, 7
consecutive time-points (T0-T7) were collected 12-hourly over a 4-days
period, from 32 established locations and compared against baseline
samplings. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05.
Results: A statistically significant improvement was
registered 24 hours after the activation of Illuvia® HUAIRS at
Nurse Stations (NS, 37% and 59%) and Patients’ areas (PT 27% and 52%), for
0.3μm and 2.5μm, respectively. 10μm particles were not detected.
Illuvia® HUAIRS had a clear impact in reducing the pollution
between gates’ and patients’ areas from 2.3-folds to 1.8-folds. No
statistical significance between nursing station/patients nor side-rooms was
identified. Conclusion: The Illuvia® HUAIRS could
represent a potential adjuvant solution in reducing the bioaerosol
particles, making the environment safer for patients and staff. Also, given
the well-established relationship between airborne pathogen levels and
healthcare-associated infections, this technology could be further utilised
on other clinical/surgical areas.

## P467: The impact of robotic lumbar spine surgery on 90-day
outcomes

Nicholas D'Antonio

1

, Jeremy Heard

1

, Yunsoo Lee

1

, Mark Lambrechts

1

, Caroline Purtill

2

, John Bodnar

2

, Patrick Fitzgerald

2

, Dominic Farronato

2

, Josh Pezzulo

2

, John Paulik

2

, Tariq Issa

1

, Parker Brush

1

, Sebastian Fras

2

, Jose Canseco

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, and Gregory Schroeder

1

1

The Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas Jefferson University
Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery, Philadelphia, United States

2

Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Robot-assisted spine surgery has become an
increasingly popular option for spinal fusion and instrumentation
procedures. Although there is promise in the literature regarding robotic
surgery, hesitancy around the widespread adoption of robotic spine surgery
still exists. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to (1) evaluate the
surgical outcomes of robotic surgeries compared to nonrobotic surgeries and
(2) determine trends regarding robotic surgery usage for spine surgery.
Methods: Patients > 18 years of
age who underwent primary lumbar fusion surgery at our institution were
identified and propensity matched in a 1:1 fashion based on use of a robot
during surgery. Patient demographics, surgical characteristics, and surgical
outcomes including 90-day all-cause readmissions and 90-day surgical
readmissions were collected. Multivariable regression analysis was
performed. Significance was set to p < 0.05. Results: Of 830
patients included in the analysis, 415 patients (50.0%) had a robotic lumbar
fusion. Cases with the robot were less likely to be revisions (5.54% vs.
17.1%, p < 0.001) but more likely to have a longer operative duration
(287 vs. 205 minutes, p < 0.001) and more than one incision made during
the operation (30.6% vs. 3.13%, p < 0.001). Intraoperative durotomies
were more common in cases where the robot was not used (14.9% vs. 3.37%, p
< 0.001). On bivariant analysis, compared to patients with a robotic
fusion, those without a robotic fusion had a significantly higher rate of
all-cause 90-day readmissions (14.0% vs. 8.92%, p = 0.029) but no
significant difference in 90-day surgical readmissions (10.6% vs. 8.67%, p =
0.410). A bivariant subanalysis of one to two level fusions demonstrated
all-cause 90-day readmissions (p = 0.024) and intraoperative durotomy (p
< 0.001) were significantly more likely in the nonrobotic fusion group.
However, surgical readmission rate and etiology were not significantly
different between groups. A multivariable analysis of the entire cohort
revealed that robotic fusion was not a significant predictor of all-cause 90
day readmissions (OR = 0.768 [0.47-1.24], p = 0.283) or all-cause 90 day
readmissions (OR = 1.03 [0.64-1.79], p = 0.784). An additional multivariable
analysis those with one to two level fusions demonstrated that robotic
surgery was not a predictor of surgical or all-cause 90-day readmissions.
Conclusion: Our study suggests that robotic-assisted and
nonrobotic-assisted lumbar fusions are associated with a similar risk of
90-day all-cause and surgical readmissions. Robotic surgery may result in
fewer intraoperative complications but increased time under anesthesia.
High-quality prospective studies are needed to add context to the literature
studying the impact of robotic lumbar fusion surgery on readmissions.

## 1180

## P468: A biomechanical analysis of a novel spinolaminar plate construct
for posterior lumbar fusion compared to traditional pedicle screw
fixation

Dimitriy Kondrashov

1,2

, Amit Piple

2

, Victor Ungurean

2

, and Oluwatodimu Raji

1,2

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, St. Mary's Medical Center, San Francisco,
United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, The Taylor Collaboration, San Francisco, United
States

Introduction: Bone anchors in osteoporotic patients are prone to
failures, both acute and delayed. In orthopaedic trauma surgery, locking
plates, which utilize locking screws and pre-threaded plates, have
revolutionized the fixation of osteoporotic fractures. We sought to combine
the traumatology principle of locking plate fixation using fixed angle
constructs with the spine principles of segmental fixation.
Methods: A novel pre-contoured spinolaminar locking plate
with a polyaxial saddle was designed based on morphometric anatomic studies
of human thoracolumbar vertebrae. The plates were fixed to an osteoporotic
cadaveric human lumbar spine and connected to form a 1-level L4-L5 construct
using 10-16mm and 3.5mm locking screws and 3.5mm locking plates. An
analogous 1-level T12-L1 construct was made using conventional pedicle screw
fixation. In total, 1 spinolaminar and 1 pedicle screw construct were
designed from the same cadaveric specimen (age: 69 years old, sex: female).
Pure moment testing was performed to assess range of motion
(flexion/extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation) after 30,000 cycles
of combined flexion-compression-anterior shear at 17Nm-400N-200N,
respectively. Evidence of construct failure was assessed every 5,000 cycles
with fluoroscopy. Static load-to-failure was performed under combined
flexion-compression-anterior shear moment. Fixture pullout strength was
assessed by applying a continuous axial tensile force oriented to the
principal axis of the pedicle until pullout was observed.
Results: The pedicle screw construct failed by a windshield
wiper mechanism due to vertebral body fracture along the midplane of the
pedicle at approximately 12,000 cycles. The spinolaminar plate construct
completed cyclic loading with no evidence of failure. Post fatigue range of
motion was observed to be 7.1 degrees in lateral bending, 1.7 degrees of
axial rotation, and 1.7 degrees of flexion/extension for the spinolaminar
plate. Upon static load-to-failure testing, the spinolaminar construct
failed at 41Nm-928N-473N of combined flexion-compression-anterior shear.
Static failure of the spinolaminar construct was due to separation of
proximal non-instrumented vertebral level from upper instrumented vertebra
via dislocation of the posterior elements while the plate, rods and screws
remained intact and fixed.The maximum pullout strength of the spinolaminar
plate was 590N while the maximum pullout strength of the pedicle screw
construct was 424N. Discussion: The spinolaminar locking plate
maintained adequate fixation post-fatigue, particularly in flexion/extension
and axial rotation. Moreover, spinolaminar plates may be superior to pedicle
screw fixation with respect to cyclic fatiguing and pullout strength.
Further testing should be performed on additional cadaver spines to validate
these findings; however, our novel spinolaminar plates appear to be a viable
instrumentation technique for posterior lumbar fusion in osteoporotic
spines.

## P469: Digital neurocognitive monitoring in patients undergoing opioid
medication after spinal surgery: a feasibility study

Vicki Butenschön

1

, Ferdinand Wriedt

1

, Bernhard Meyer

1

, and Sandro M. Krieg

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Technical University Munich, Munich,
Germany

Introduction: Patients undergoing spinal surgery usually require
postoperative pain management to alleviate wound pain. Pain medication
includes WHO grade 1 analgesic but also potent opioids, potentially leading
to severe side effects such as fatigue, nausea and cognitive decline. Up to
now, the cognitive impairment due to postoperative pain protocols is only
poorly studied. Methods: We performed a prospective monocenter
feasibility study enrolling patients before undergoing spinal surgery.
Cognitive testing was performed using a tablet-based application before
surgery (baseline), as well as on day 2 after surgery (intravenous opioids),
before discharge (oral opioids) and at follow-up. We recorded the exact pain
medication and other side effects from the medication. Potential risk
factors for postoperative decline in cognition were age, high-dosed opioid
application, length of surgery and blood loss. Results: We
included 20 patients in our study. Median age was 67 years. Baseline
assessment revealed no cognitive impairment before surgery. All patients
underwent a dorsal instrumentation in our neurosurgical department for
degenerative (60%), osteoporotic fracture (15%) or tumor (25%) indication.
Cognitive testing after surgery showed a significant decline under
intravenous opioid therapy including short time and delayed recall word
listing as well as logic testing including arithmetic fluency (p <
0.001). Cognitive performance significantly improved with recovery until
follow-up and opioid discontinuation. Conclusion: Cognitive
assessment in patients undergoing spinal surgery with postoperative opioid
medication revealed a postoperative impairment under intravenous medication.
Side effects should be monitored closely, and cognitive decline should be
considered in follow-up operation informed consent.

## P470: Pioneering robot-assisted spine surgery in the United
Kingdom

Carlos De La Torre

1

, Darren Lui

1

, Bisola Ajayi

2

, and Khai Lam

1

1

Orthopaedics, London Bridge Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

2

Orthopaedics, NHS St George's Hospital, London, United
Kingdom

Introduction: The placement of a large interbody implant allows
for a larger fusion area. Retroperitoneal approaches facilitate the
placement of these implants. At the same time, robot-navigation facilitate
complex posterior screw fixation. This is a single-surgeon, single-centre
report of the first procedures ever performed for navigated robot-assisted
spine surgery in the United Kingdom. Materials and Methods:
Between October 2019 and May 2021, we identified 34 consecutive patients who
underwent robot-assisted spine surgery. The demographic, intraoperative, and
perioperative data of the 34 patients were reviewed. Technique:
With the patient positioned in the lateral or dorsal decubitus position, a
routine anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) and/or an extreme lateral
interbody fusion (ELIF) is performed. In a second stage, with the patient in
a ventral decubitus position, a dynamic reference base and a surveillance
marker are put in place, an intraoperative CT scan is obtained and the
images are transferred into the robotic positioning system. Pedicle screw
trajectories are planned and saved. A surgeon-controlled foot pedal
activates and positions the robot arm to the planned pedicle trajectory.
Stab incisions are made on the skin where the pedicle screws are inserted
using navigated instruments guided by the robotic arm. This sequence will be
repeated until all pedicle screws had been placed. Rods will then be placed
in a standard fashion and locking caps will be set once the rods are in
their proper position. If needed, one can also insert the pedicle screws
using an open or a transmuscular technique or consider performing a single
position lateral (SPL) approach with a single stage procedure.
Results: Of the 34 patients, 65 levels were treated in
total (204 screws). 21 patients (60%) underwent single-level fixation, 14 of
them (67%) were treated at the L5/S1 level, 3 at L3/L4, 3 at L4/L5 and 1 at
L2/L3 level, 13 patients (40%) underwent multi-level fixation, with 4 of
them treated for adult scoliosis. Eight patients underwent a supine ALALIF
approach and one a lateral decubitus AL-ALIF, 7 had a pure ALIF approach, 8
patients underwent combined XLIF and AL-ALIF approach in a lateral
decubitus, 6 underwent pure XLIF approach, 1 patient had previous TLIF
surgery, and 3 patients underwent single position lateral surgery (lateral
decubitus fusion and posterior screw fixation). The average estimated blood
loss was 60 cc. The average planning time was 10 min and the average
duration of surgery was 50 min. The average patient age was 54 years and 64%
(22/34) were male. The average BMI was 28.1 kg/m2. There were no
re-interventions due to complications or mal positioned screws.
Conclusion: Minimally invasive spine surgery using
robot-assisted navigation yields an improved level of accuracy, decreased
radiation exposure, minimal muscle disruption, decreased blood loss, shorter
operating theatre time, length of stay, and lower complication rates.
Further follow-up of the patients treated will help compare the clinical
outcomes with other techniques.

## P471: Predicting sustained opioid use after surgery for degenerative

Paul Ogink

1

, Aditya Karhade

Study design: Prediction model study. Objectives:
We aimed to 1) develop and 2) internally validate a machine learning (ML)
prediction model for prolonged opioid use following surgery for degenerative
spondylolisthesis. Methods: We included adult patients who
underwent surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis in two tertiary care
referral spine centers. Our primary outcome measure was prolonged
postoperative opioid use defined as prolonged opioid prescriptions 90-180
days after index surgery. The following variables were selected and
subsequently used for algorithm development: age, body mass index, duration
of symptoms, preoperative laboratory values for hemoglobin and white blood
cell count, and preoperative medication use (opioids, statins and
antihypertensives). Four ML algorithms were developed to predict prolonged
postoperative opioid use and were assessed by discrimination, calibration,

predictive factors were BMI and age. Conclusion: In this study
we developed a ML algorithm with good discrimination and calibration to
predict sustained opioid use after surgery for lumbar degenerative
spondylolisthesis. Utilization of this model could aid clinicians and
healthcare organizations in tailoring their strategies and policies for
reducing sustained opioid use in high-risk patients.
