## P475: Cadaveric laminar torque failure in novel system for stabilizing
the cervical and upper thoracic spine

Manoj Kodigudla

1

, Frank Boehm

2

, Amey Kelkar

1

, Muzammil Mumtaz

1

, Vijay Goel

1

, Sundershan Triparthi

1

, William Lavalle

3

, and Nikunj Patel

4

1

Departments of Bioengineering and Orthopaedic Surgery University of
Toledo, Engineering Center for OrthopaedicResearch Excellence (E-CORE),
Toledo, OH, United States

2

Research and Development, TruSpine Technologies, Plc., New Hartford
NY, United States

3

Department of Orthopedics, SUNY Upstate Medical University,
Syracuse, NY, United States

4

Neurosciences, Institute of Neurosciences, Southmead Hospital,
University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom

Introduction: Novel means of stabilizing the spine are always of
interest to the spinal surgical community as well as the larger health care
delivery ecosystem. A novel strategy being introduced utilizes unique
hook-anchors which are individually fastened to the lamina, these anchors
then being coupled to a rod which stabilizes the construct. A question was
raised regarding the potential for laminar injury by the fastening
mechanism, and to that end, this study was performed at the University of
Toledo. Material and Methods: The hook-anchor which is fastened
to the caudal edge of the lamina is provided with a fixed sublaminar foot
plate and a vertically-adjustable dorsal laminar foot plate, the latter
being actuated by a drive screw. The Manufacturer provided the investigators
at the University of Toledo with a series of “Dummy” clamps, with an
identical actuation mechanism, and which precisely emulated the closing
force of the proposed final anchor design. These included large, medium and
small sizes identical to the design as well. Disarticulated C3-7 vertebrae
from 3 specimens were used in the study, and various sized “clamps,” were
applied to the specimens as deemed size-appropriate. The screws were
actuated with a T8 Driver, and were initially tightened to 6
+ .5 in. lbs. Torque, considering the Company’s
recommendation of 6-8 in. lbs. After inspecting the integrity of the
specimen, the torque was then increased at increments of 4 in.lbs., using a
torque meter, with the end-point being either a) laminar fracture, or b) or
implant failure, or c) a torque of 20 + .5 in. lbs.
was reached, at which point the study was concluded. Maximum torque before
failure was recorded, and a total of 6 data points for each sized anchor was
obtained. Results: At 6 ± .5 in. lbs., all of the clamps were
fastened in a satisfactory fashion and the laminae showed no evidence of
anything disconcerting. In 16 of the specimens, a torque of 18 ± .5 was
achieved without any evidence of laminar damage, and overall, in 13 of the
18 subject laminae, a torque of 20 ± was reached without laminar injury. One
implant had a mechanical failure at 15.7 in. lbs on the left lamina, and was
replaced by another clamp, completing the test on that lamina. One specimen
was excluded because a large anchor was inappropriately utilized therein. In
one specimen, bilateral C6 laminar damage was noted at a torque of 20 ± .5
in. lbs., and in another specimen, left-sided C7 laminar damage was noted,
again at a torque of 20 ± .5. Conclusion: These data offer new
insights into laminar strength, and strongly suggest that this type of
anchor can be secured to the caudal aspect of a cervical lamina at a torque
of 6-8 in. lbs. without concern of laminar damage. This is important when
considering the technique of cervical stabilization being introduced. These
data can, of course, be useful going forward as other strategies and
techniques are introduced.

## P477: Characterization of TumorID technology to differentiate tumor type
in frozen samples

Jacob Sperber

1

, Tanner Zachem

1,2

, Ravi Prakash

1,2

, Gregory Chamberlin

3

, Thomas Cummings

3

, Annee Nguyen

1

, Harrison Hockenberry

1

, Cesar Baeta

4

, Weston Ross

1,2

, Patrick Codd

2,2,5

, Edwin Owolo

1

, Dana Rowe

1

, Tara Dalton

1

, Emily Luo

1

, and C. Rory Goodwin

1,5

1

School of Medicine, Department of Neurosurgery

2

Department of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science

3

Health System, Department of Pathology, Duke University, Durham,
United States

4

Center for Population Health Sciences, Stanford University, United
States

5

Duke Cancer Institute, Durham, United States

Purpose: Neurosurgical tumor resection depends upon
identification of tumorous tissue from non-tumor. The nascent TumorID
technology employs fluorescence spectroscopy to differentiate tumor from
non-tumor. This study investigates the ability of TumorID technology to
classify frozen neurosurgical samples based on tumor type.
Methods: Patients undergoing neurosurgical resection or
biopsy for suspected malignancy with the Department of Neurosurgery at Duke
University School were identified. Frozen sections of samples were prepared
with either hematoxylin and eosin or polychrome. An excitation wavelength of
405nm was used to obtain emission spectra from tissue as previously
validated by the Codd lab. For the most prominent peak at 564 nm, the
maximum intensity value was obtained by averaging 10 independent intensity
measurements centered around the peak. Results: Tissue analyzed
consisted of glioma (n = 242), gonadotroph adenoma (n = 14), prolactinoma (n
= 19), hemangioblastoma (n = 11), squamous cell carcinoma (n = 106),
metastases (n = 5), Rathke cleft cyst (n = 9), inflammation (n = 35), and
radiation necrosis (n = 1). Spectral shape across all tissue types between
550 nm and 650 nm were similar potentially representing eosin emission;
however, signal intensity varied amongst tissue type. Centered around a
wavelength of 564 nm, prolactinoma had a higher mean peak intensity of
0.556, 95% CI [0.507, 0.605], compared to the mean peak intensity for
gonadotroph adenoma of 0.321, 95% CI [0.303, 0.339]. Spectral signature for
radiation necrosis between 450 nm and 565 nm was distinct from all other
tissue types. Conclusion: The TumorID remains a promising tumor
identification tool. This study represents an important step in
characterizing the ability for TumorID technology to discern tumor from
non-tumor in frozen pathology section.
Keywords: Tumor detection; fluorescence spectroscopy

## P478: Telescopic vertebral body replacing implant with improved
functionality: design concept

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

1

Spinal Neurosurgery, Romodanov Neurosurgery Institute, Kyiv,
Ukraine

Introduction: Anterior decompressive corpectomy is frequently
used while surgical care of a number of subaxial cervical spine pathological
states. The most progressive and surgeon easy-to-use way to substitute
vertebral body is telescopic vertebral body implant. The purpose of our
study was to develop a concept of creation improved telescopic vertebral
body implant for anterior subaxial cervical decompression-fusion surgery.
Material and Methods: We’ve searched the database of
National Center for Biotechnology Information using following keywords:
“expandable cage”, “distractable cage”, “expandable vertebral body
replacement”, “distractable vertebral body replacement”, “expandable VBR”,
“distractable VBR”, “distractible cage”, “distractible vertebral body
replacement”, “distractible VBR” and MeSH terms “Spinal Diseases / surgery”,
“Orthopedic Fixation Devices”, “Orthopedic Procedures / instrumentation”,
“Spine / surgery” and selected 24 most frequently used telescopic implants.
The analyzes of results allowed to reveal design features that define
functionality of different implants. Results: Detected
constructive features of implants that influence the surgery results:
• type of implant (integrated or not integrated with anterior
plate);
• design configuration;
• the design of the side walls of the implants and the size of
the perforations;
• number of components;
• universality (interchangeability) of parts;
• type and location of the sliding mechanism;
• type of perception of compression load;
• the way of blocking the implant in the final position;
• the configuration of the endface of the cage contacting with
the end plates of the vertebral bodies;
• the size, location and number of teeth on the end surface of
the implant;
• contact area in the system “implant - vertebral body”;
• the volume of the internal cavity for the composite
material;
• contact area of composite material with the locking plates of
the vertebral bodies;
• type of filling the structure with composite material;
• the possibility of compaction of the composite material in the
“composite material -vertebral body” system after implantation
of implant;
• the number and location of holes to supplement the composite
material after installation;
• implant weight
The search results allowed to develop original vertebral body replacing
implant, that possesses most useful constructive features:
• has the minimum size;
• has a larger cavity compared to that in other devices.;
• has sufficient strength, low metal content, and low weight
• compressive stress is distributed over the entire graft
cross-section, that enables relatively thin wall systems to
withstand sufficiently high compressive load;
• excludes damage to the endplates by teeth of end surfaces
during placement;
• is easy-to-fabricate and easy-to-use.
Conclusion: Big cavity of prototype and proposed installation
method gives a good chance during the operation to compact the composite
material along the entire length of implant. It provides intraoperative
prophylaxis of an undesirable fibrotic fusion of the vertebral motion
segment and maximizes the probability of true bone consolidation.
Preclinical and clinical studies show good results but further research
needed to introduce the final product into clinical practice.

## P479: The role of 3D-printed patient-specific models in the understanding
of complex spine morphologies

Benjamin Hajnal

1,2

, Máté Turbucz

1,2

, Ferenc Bereczki

1,2

, Agoston Jakab Pokorni

1,2

, Zoltan Hoffer

3

, Aron Lazary

1,4

, and Peter E. Eltes

1,4

1

In Silico Biomechanics Laboratory, National Center for Spinal
Disorders, Buda Health Center, Budapest, Hungary

2

School of PhD Studies

3

National Center for Spinal Disorders, Buda Health Center, Budapest,
Hungary

4

Department of Spine Surgery, Department of Orthopaedics, Semmelweis
University, Budapest, Hungary

Introduction: 3D printed models facilitate the understanding of
complex anatomical relationships, aiding preoperative surgical planning.
Their use is beneficial in patient education, but also in reducing the
operative time according to the results of scientific publications from the
last five years. In spine surgery, there is currently no consensus or
recommendation on when 3D printed models should and should not be used. We
aimed to develop a questionnaire-based survey to investigate the usefulness
of 3D printed models in complex spine surgery cases. Material and
Methods: CT scans of patients in 6 complex spine surgery cases
were segmented using Mimics® software. Segmentation accuracy was
quantified using Dice Similarity Index (DSI). The models were fabricated
using fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printing technology. CT images of
the models were taken, segmented and compared with the original virtual
models to assess geometric accuracy. A questionnaire, consisting 6 questions
for each of the cases (36 questions in total that can be answered by a scale
from 1 to 10) was filled out by spine surgeons (n = 41) from multiple
hospitals after reviewing the imaging (RTG, MR, CT) scans and then examining
the 3D printed models in hand. The digital form of the questionnaire was
created using SurveyMonkey® platform. Statistical analysis of the data was
performed using SPSS® 23.0, G*Power software. Results: The
geometric variation of the printed models was < 1 mm in every case. The
responses show that spine surgeons find the models very useful (8.75 ± 0.14,
ɑ = 0.05). Further analysis shows that there is significant difference
between orthopedic and neurosurgeons (p < 0.001), and between groups with
different years of clinical practice (p < 0.05). The additional benefit
of 3D printed models seems to be the greatest in patient education (p <
0.001). Conclusion: For the clinical integration of 3D printed
models, we need to know how surgeons perceive their usefulness. The role of
basic skills is unknown in the acceptance of 3D printed physical models. The
developed questionnaire survey could greatly contribute to the clinical
integration of 3D printed models, providing evidence for different funding
parties.

## P480: Ceramic bone graft substitute (Mg-HA) in spinal fusion: a
prospective pilot study

Giuseppe Tedesco

1

, Cristiana Griffoni

1

, Giovanni Barbanti Bròdano

1

, Angelo Nataloni

2

, and Alessandro Gasbarrini

1

1

Department of Spine Surgery, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli,
Bologna, Italy

2

Finceramica Spa, Faenza, Italy

Introduction: Iliac crest bone graft (ICBG) is considered the
gold standard for spine surgical procedures to achieve a successful fusion
due to its known osteoinductive and osteoconductive properties. However,
complications related to harvesting procedure and donor site morbidity have
been largely reported in literature, favouring the development of a wide
range of alternative products to be used as bone graft extenders or
substitutes for spine fusion. Among all, ceramic-based biomaterials have
been widely studied and employed in the last years as bone graft
substitutes. We report here the results of a prospective pilot study aimed
to evaluating the grade of ossification obtained by the use of an Mg-doped
hydroxyapatite (HA) product to achieve postero-lateral fusion in
degenerative spine diseases. Material and Methods: A
prospective pilot clinical study was conducted at our Centre from February
2017 to March 2020, following the approval of the local Ethics Committee,
with a total number of 20 patients recruited, who were followed up for 18
months. Inclusion criteria were as follows: skeletally mature subjects, at
least 18 years of age at the time of surgery with symptomatic spinal
degenerative disc disease requiring postero-lateral fusion at L1-S1 tract,
signature of the written informed consent for the study. Conventional
posterior approach for lumbar spinal fusion was performed. After the
positioning of pedicle screws, decompression of the cauda and nerve roots
was achieved with hemilaminectomy and foraminotomy. SintLife was apposed on
the hemi-laminae and transvers process on the contralateral side of the
hemilaminectomy, while on the hemilaminectomy side, foramino-arthrectomy was
performed to insert the interbody fusion cage. SintLife is a CE- marked,
implantable, non-active bone graft substitute, available in form of paste,
composed of biomimetic hydroxyapatite (HA) enriched in magnesium ions
(Mg-HA) in a similar amount as in the one found in human bones. Radiographic
and clinical data were collected before surgery and at 3, 6 and 12- 18
months follow-up. Radiographic images were used to determine the degree of
fusion and bone regeneration, determined by an independent radiologist using
the Brantigan classification. Clinical scores (Oswestry Disability Index
(ODI), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and EuroQoL-5L (EQ-5L)) were used to
evaluate the improvement of patients’ health quality following surgery. The
incidence of adverse events, complications, unattended reactions, incidents
was recorded. Results: Results showed a successful degree of
fusion of about 62% at 12 months follow-up and an improvement of quality of
life and health status starting from 6 months FU, as evaluated by clinical
scores (ODI, VAS and EQ-5L). No adverse events related to the biomaterial
were reported. Conclusion: The present pilot study showed a
safety profile of a Mg-doped HA bone graft substitute used to achieve
postero-lateral fusion in the treatment of degenerative spine diseases.
However, the rate of successful fusion was largely inferior to that reported
in the literature for the autologous bone graft, which is the “gold
standard” for spinal fusion.

## P481: Bioactive glass (S53P54) and polyethylene-glycol and glicerol water
soluble synthetic adhesive as a effective fusion promoter in anterior lumbar
interbody fusion surgery

Stipe Corluka

1

, Stjepan Dokuzovic

1

, Jure Pavesic

1

, and Vide Bilic

1

1

Spinal Surgery Division, Department of Traumatology, University
Hospital Centre Sestre Milosrdnice, Zagreb, Croatia

Introduction: Spinal fusion remains the mainstay of treatment
for many different spine conditions and fusion may be achieved in several
different ways, though not all methods are inherently equally effective and
reliable. In principle, the larger the contact area, the shorter the
distance between bony elements, and the presence of living bone (osteogenic,
osteoconductive and osteoinductive properties) all increase the chances of
successful fusion. In certain cases, the gap being fused may be quite wide
and it may be difficult to obtain a sufficient quantity of live autologous
bone graft. Anterior lumbar interbody fusion cages (ALIF, OLIF, LLIF, mesh
and expandable cages) necessarily increase the distance between end plates,
making it difficult to bridge the gap with new bone. In such cases we rely
on synthetic materials which can provide sufficient graft volume, while
reducing donor site morbidity. According to our knowledge there have been no
studies analyzing the fusion capacity of isolated bioactive glass and
polyethylene-glycol and glycerol water soluble synthetic adhesives in
anterior lumbar approaches. We present a retrospective analysis of cases
having undergone single or multilevel anterior lumbar interbody fusion
procedures using interbody cages filled with bioactive glass. Material
and Methods: We analyzed the radiological results of patients
having undergone anterior lumbar interbody fusion procedures using lumbar
interbody cages filled with bioactive glass without additional autologous
bone. Follow-up was performed by standard clinical evaluation, radiographs
at regular intervals, as well as by CT scan at 6 and 12 months to analyze
fusion success/failure through the cage. Results: Patients
having undergone anterior, oblique, or lateral lumbar interbody fusions
through cages displayed successful bony fusion from endplate to endplate
through the cage device at 6 to 12 months follow-up.
Conclusion: Bioactive glass is an effective fusion promoter
with a high rate of successful fusion when used alone in an anterior lumbar
interbody fusion cage.

## P482: Is risk factors of vertebral fractures predictable? BMD, Vit-D,
calcium, and bone turn-over marker measurement

Kwan Ho Park

1

, Jung Hoon Sul

1

, Da Hoon Hong

1

, Ju chul Yang

1

, and Tae Wan Kim

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, VHS Medical Center, Seoul, South
Korea

Introduction: Measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) is the
gold standard for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. However, the BMD
measurement does not provide information on bone quality. We reported the
relationship between BMD, calcium, Vit-D, and Bone turnover markers (BTMs)
in patients with vertebral fracture group. Material and
Methods: This study retrospectively reviewed medical records of
patients who were treated in our institution from 2017 to 2018. A
comparative analysis was carried out between 38 patients with vertebral
fracture (Group A) and 62 patients admitted with no vertebral fracture
(Group B). Sex, age, BMD, calcium, Vit-D, and BTMs were analyzed as
variables affecting vertebral fractures. In this study, BTMs are divided to
formation markers [serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BSAP),
osteocalcin (OC)] and resorption markers [serum C-telopeptide (CTX).
Results: The average age of the subjects was 74.0 ± 6.9
years. The mean BMD were 2.7 ± 1.3 in group A and 1.6 ± 1.0 in group B,
respectively. The mean serum calcium levels were 8.9 ± 0.9 ng/dL and 9.1 ±
0.9 ng/dL, respectively. The mean serum 1,25(OH) vit-D levels were 16.6 ±
10.9 ng/mL and 16.8 ± 7.3 ng/mL, respectively. The mean serum OC levels were
15.8 ± 8.2 ng/mL and 14.7 ± 6.6 ng/mL, respectively. The mean serum CTX
levels were 0.5 ± 0.2 ng/mL and 0.4 ± 0.2 ng/mL, respectively. The mean
serum BSAP levels were 12.0 ± 5.4 mcg/L and 10.2 ± 4.4 mcg/L, respectively.
BMD of group A was lower than that of group B (P &lt; 0.05). The other
variables showed no differences between the 2 groups.
Conclusion: BMD of vertebral fracture patients showed
difference from that of no vertebral fracture group in Korean elderly
population. The occurrence of vertebral fracture is affected by lower BMD
rather than another laboratory findings. The main goal of treatment is to
reduce the prevalence of fractures, maintain stable or increasing BMD.

Introduction: Leptomeningeal Leukaemia in chronic myeloid
leukemia (CML) is a rare phenomenon and represents infiltration of leukemic
blasts in both the subdural and epidural spaces other than bone marrow.
Material and Methods: We report the case of a patient who
was treated for a leptomenengial leukimia in the neurosurgery department, in
the Habib Bourguiba university hospital, Sfax, Tunisia.
Results: We report the findings of a 35-year-old woman who

chemotherapy after the surgery as the baseline treatment for her CML.

of myeloid leukemia. The baseline treatment is chemotherapy after
surgery.

## P485: Iatrogenic vertebral artery injury during anterior cervical spine
surgery: a systematic review

Qing Guan

1

1

Spine Surgery, The First People’s Hospital of Yibin, Yibin,
China

Background: Iatrogenic vertebral artery injury (VAI) during
anterior cervical surgery is rare but potentially catastrophic.
Methods: Causes, presentation, diagnosis, management,
prognosis, and Prevention of VAI were reviewed following Preferred Reporting
Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. English language
studies and case reports published from 1980 to recent were retrieved. Data
on diagnosis, surgical procedures and approach, site and cause of VAI,
management, outcomes, and vertebral artery (VA) status were extracted.
Results: In 25 articles including 54 patients, VAI was
diagnosed during or after surgery commonly indicated for cervical
degenerative diseases (64%), tumors (14%), and trauma (9%). The incidence of
VAI for each side was similar regardless of approach. Common presentations
were unexpected copious surgical bleeding, delayed hemorrhage of
pseudoaneurysm with neck swelling, dyspnea, hypotension, and cervical bruits
caused by arteriovenous fistula. Causes included drilling (61%),
instrumentation (16%), and soft tissue retraction (8%). Direct exposure or
angiography confirmed VAI. Ten patients had VA anomalies; collateral status
was verified in 9 before definitive treatment. Tamponade was adopted for
urgent hemostasis in most cases but with a high incidence of pseudoaneurysm
(48%). Unknown VA status increased occlusion risk and neurologic sequelae
(41%). VA repair and stent placement had excellent Outcomes.
Conclusions: Extensive lateral decompression, loss of
landmarks, and anatomic variations or pathologic status of VA increased VAI
risk. Evaluation of collateral vessels before definitive treatment helped
determine appropriate management and avoid neurologic sequelae. Tamponade
was not recommended as definitive treatment. Meticulous preoperative
evaluation, cautious intraoperative manipulation, and real-time radiographic
guidance reduced VAI risk.

## P486: Postoperative occipital neuralgia in posterior upper cervical spine
surgery: a systematic review

Qing Guan

1

1

Spine Surgery, The First People’s Hospital of Yibin, Yibin,
China

Background: Postoperative occipital neuralgia (PON) after upper
cervical spine surgery can cause significant morbidity and may be
overlooked. Methods: The causes, presentation, diagnosis,
management, prognosis, and prevention of PON were reviewed following the
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)
guidelines. English language studies and case reports published from
inception to recent were retrieved. Data on surgical procedures, incidence,
cause of PON, management, outcomes, and preventive technique were extracted.
Results: Sixteen articles, including 591 patients, were
selected; 93% of the patients with PON underwent C1 lateral mass screw
(C1LMS) fixation, with additional 7% who underwent occipitocervical fusion
without C1 fixation. PON had an incidence that ranged from 1 to 35% and was
transient in 34%, but persistent in 66%. Five articles explained the
possible causes. The primary presentation was constant or paroxysmal burning
pain located mainly in the occipital and upper neck area and partially
extending to the vertical, retroauricular, retromandibular, and forehead
zone. Treatment included medications, nerve block, revision surgery, and
nerve stimulation. Two prospective studies compared the effect of C2 nerve
root transection on PON. Conclusion: Recent PON in upper
cervical spine surgery is a debilitating complication and was most commonly
encountered by patients undergoing C1LMS fixation. The etiology of PON is
partially clear, and the pain could be persistent and hard to cure. Reducing
the incidence of PON can be realized by improving technique. More
high-quality prospective studies are needed to define the effect of C2 nerve
root transection on PON.

## P487: Early mobilization after incidental durotomies, a systematic
review

Elie Najjar

1

, Nasir Quraishi

1

, and Mohamed Hassanin

1

1

The Spine Center of Spinal Studies and Surgery, Nottingham
University Hospital, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: An incidental durotomy is a fearful and not
uncommon complication of spinal surgery. The conventional management
involving a prolonged period of flat bed rest is highly debatable. Indeed,
there are scanty data and no consensus regarding the need or ideal duration
of post-operative bed rest following these dural tears. We systematically
evaluated the relevant literature regarding the outcomes of mobilization
within 24 hours and after 24 hours following an incidental durotomy with
respect to the length of hospital stay, minor complications and reoperation
rates. Methods:A systematic review of the English language
literature dating up until December 2021, was undertaken using search
criteria ((Dural Tear Or Durotomy) and (Mobilization Or Bed rest)) and the
PRISMA guidelines. Isolated case reports were excluded.
Results: Of a total of 243 articles, 11 studies met the
inclusion criteria (1 Level I and 10 level IV evidence) and were analyzed.
Overall, 532 patients (mean age 61.1 years) had an incidental dural tear and
were mobilized within 24 hours. Dural repair was performed in 95.3%
(507/532) of the cases. The average follow-up period was 23.24 months (3 -
80 months). The average length of stay (LOS) for this early mobilized
patients was 3.65 days. Twenty-one out of 532 (3.9 %) patients (11 studies)
required reoperation while the rate of minor complications was 26 out of 230
(11.3%) (9 studies). Additionally, 203 patients of mean age 72 years (7
studies) were mobilized after 24 hours (24 - 144 hours); 96% (194/202)
underwent a primary repair with an average LOS of 6.38 days. Comparing early
to late mobilization, there was a significant reduction in the risk of minor
complications due to early mobilization (13/102 (12.7%) vs 33/106 (31.1%) (p
= 0.006); RR: 0.47, 95CI: 0.27, 0.80), but no significant difference in
major complications and reoperation rates (3 studies) (12/106 (11.3%) vs
11/134 (8.2%) (p = 0.27; RR: 1.55, 95CI: 0.72, 3.35). The overall LOS was
also shorter for early mobilizers (3.65 vs 6.38 days).
Conclusion: Although early mobilization after repaired
incidental dural tears has a similar major complication/ reoperation rates
compared to later mobilization, it significantly decreases the risk of minor
complications and length of hospitalizations.

## P488: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome: analysis of clinical cases,
new diagnostic features, development of diagnostic protocol

Nikita Khusainov

1

, Dmitry Kokushin

1

, Sergey Beljanchikov

1

, Alexandra Filippova

1

, Tatyana Murashko

2

, Sergey Braylov

2

, Maria Pavlova

3

, and Vissarionov Sergey

1

1

Spine Pathology and Neurosurgery

2

Diagnostic Unit, Saint-Petersburg

3

Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, National Medical Research Center
for Pediatric Trauma and Orthopedics, Saint-Petersburg, Russian
Federation

Introduction: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome is a rare but
serious complication in spine deformity surgery. Little is known about
patient predisposition factors except for low weight, same as diagnostic
features in cases of spine deformity due to severe secondary changes of
abdominal content position. CT-angio is used to objectively quantify
aortomesenteric distance and angle which requires use of contrast and
exposes patient to significant amount of radiation. Material and
Methods: We performed retrospective and prospective data
evaluation of 13 patients with severe spinal deformity. CT-angiography was
performed either post-op due to SMA syndrome development or pre-op in cases
where risk factors were present. Aortomesenteric angle and distance were
calculated. Also we evaluated the course direction of SMA and its relation
with deformed vertebral column. In case of decreased distance and angle
endoscopy was performed for evaluation of duodenum. 3 patients underwent
MRI-angiography of the aorta aimed on visualization of SMA as an alternative
to CT-angiography. Results: In 4 patients we observed
left-sided direction of SMA course with decreased aortomesenteric angle and
distance. In 3 out of these 4 patients endoscopic picture of duodenum
compression was present. SMA syndrome occurred in 1 of those patients which
required further Roux duodenojejunostomy. Surprisingly, in 2 patients with
abnormally low aortomesenteric angle and distance we did not observe any
signs of duodenum compression probably due to specific position of the
horizontal part of the duodenum - extremely low and far away from
aortomesenteric triangle. Instead another possible site of duodenum
compression was revealed between SMA and anterior surface of the vertebral
column. For those patients who underwent MRI-angiography of the aorta we
were able to visualize aortomesenteric triangle and measure angle and
distance without using contrast or radiation. Conclusion: We
suggest that one of the predisposing factors for SMA syndrome development is
a left-sided direction of SMA course which might lead to compression of the
horizontal part of the duodenum between SMA and deformed spine. Traditional
measurements of the aortomesenteric angle and distance are not always
acceptable in patients with deformity due to the misalignment of the
duodenum and great vessels. MRI-angiography might be used as an alternative
method of SMA visualization in patients with marked deformity and low weight
without necessity to use contrast and radiation exposure. In cases of
abnormal measurements and SMA direction we would suggest to perform pre-op
endoscopy to evaluate duodenum for possible compression.

for degenerative conditions. The mFI-5 score was calculated based on the
presence of five co-morbidities: congestive heart failure within 30 days
prior to surgery, insulin-dependent or noninsulin-dependent diabetes
mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or pneumonia, partially
dependent or totally dependent functional health status at time of surgery,
and hypertension requiring medication. Multivariate analysis was used to
assess the independent impact of increasing mFI-5 score on the postoperative
morbidity while controlling for baseline clinical characteristics.
Results: 53252 patients were included with the mean age of
64.2 ± 7.2. 7946 suffered medical complications (14.9%), 1565 had surgical
complications (2.9%), and 3385 were readmitted (6.3%), 363 died (0.68%)
within 30 days postoperative (6.3%). The mFI-5 items score was significantly
associated with higher rates of complications, readmission, and mortality in
cervical, thoracic, and lumbar posterior fusion surgery.
Conclusion: The modified 5-item frailty score is a reliable
tool to predict complications, readmission, and mortality in patients
planned for elective posterior spinal fusion surgery.

## P490: Intravenous tranexamic acid reduces blood loss in multilevel spine
surgeries

Raphael Lotan

1

 and Oded Hershkovich

1

1

Edith Wolfson Medical Center, Holon, Israel

Introduction: Complex spine surgeries are associated with
significant blood loss requiring numerous strategies to preserve blood
volume. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is efficacious in reducing blood loss when
used topically during surgery, intravenously with or without postoperative
maintenance treatment. We aimed to evaluate the effect of preoperative
weight independent intravenous administration of 1 gr IV TXA on
perioperative blood loss in lumbar microdiscectomy, single-level lumbar
spinal fusion and multilevel lumbar decompression (two or more levels).
Methods: A retrospective cohort study comparing patients
who underwent microdiscectomy, lumbar single-level fusion and multilevel

## P491: Does marijuana usage affect post-operative care in thoracolumbar
fusions? A retrospective study in a multiethnic population

Henry Hoang

1

, Aaron Hui

1

, Jini Jeon

1

, Dan Berman

1

, Evan Mostafa

1

, Ananth Eleswarapu

1

, and Jonathan Krystal

1

1

Orthopedics, Montefiore Medical Center, Bronx, United
States

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fusions are indicated for the
management of degenerative disc disease, degenerative spondylolisthesis,
spinal stenosis, tumors, fractures and several spinal disorders with more
than 300,000 performed annually. Marijuana usage has become an
often-overlooked risk factor for postoperative complications in
thoracolumbar fusions. Chronic cannabis usage has previously been associated
with increased rates of inpatient neurovascular, thromboembolic, and
pulmonary complications, and less favorable overall discharge disposition. A
comprehensive understanding of the postoperative sequelae within spinal
surgery patients who use cannabis is crucial for the development of
interventions aimed at reducing complications and postoperative
readmissions. The purpose of this study is to therefore compare rates of
readmission, complications, and length of stay between thoracolumbar fusion
patients who do and do not use marijuana. Material and Methods:
A retrospective study of 301 patients who underwent a thoracolumbar fusion
at a single institution in the Bronx from 2016-2018 was performed.
Demographic, surgical, and postoperative variables were collected. Marijuana
usage was confirmed by accessing documentation in the patient’s chart data.
The primary outcome measure was return to the operating room for revision.
Secondary outcomes included return to the emergency department (ED) within
30 days, 90 days, and length of stay (days). Binomial logistic regression
was performed to ascertain the effects of age, BMI, smoking status, and
alcohol use status on the likelihood that participants return to the OR for
revision. The chi-square test of homogeneity was used to determine if there
was a difference in rates of returning to the emergency room within 30 and
90 days. An independent-samples t-test was run to determine if there were
differences in postoperative length of stay between the two groups.
Results: A total of 301 patients were categorized into
marijuana users (N = 75) and non-users (n = 226). Model fit was assessed
using the Hosmer and Lemeshow goodness of fit test, p =.191 indicating that
the model was not a poor fit. The model explained 4.3%% (Nagelkerke R2) of
the variance in heart disease and correctly classified 90.0% of cases. Of
the five predictor variables, only marijuana status was statistically
significant. Marijuana users had 2.5 times higher odds to return to the
operating room for revision compared to non-users, 2.49, (95% CI 1.07 to
5.78), p = .034. 12 (18.7%) marijuana users returned to the emergency
department within 30 days of operation compared to 29 (12.8%) of non-users,
a non-statistically significant difference in proportion of .059, p=.211. 26
(34.7%) marijuana users returned to the emergency department within 90 days
of operation compared to 58 (25.7%), a non-statistically significant
difference in proportion of .09, p = .132 There was a statistically
non-significant difference in length of stay (days) between marijuana users
(9.1 ± 10.5) and non-users (8.1 ± 7.6), with marijuana users staying longer
than non-users, -.96 (95% CI, -3.2 to 1.24),t(301) = -856, p = .393.
Conclusion: Our retrospective analysis identified a
significant association between marijuana usage and return to operative room
for revision follow thoracolumbar surgery. Marijuana usage was not
associated with increased postoperative infections, rates of return to the
emergency department within 30 days of operation, and length of stay.

## P492: Factors associated with increased surgical drain output after

Ashley Duncan

1

, Devender Singh

1

, John Stokes

1

, Matthew Geck

, and Eeric Truumees

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Surgical drains are the source of much scrutiny
and debate in terms of post-operative outcomes, especially those centered
around surgical site infections and overall length of stay. The aim of this
study was to identify factors associated with increased drain output in
adults that have undergone surgical correction for spinal deformity.
Material and Methods: Retrospective analysis was conducted
on 106 adult patients who underwent surgical deformity correction for
degenerative scoliosis or kyphosis over 2.5 years. 26 independent variables
were collected from demographic, clinical, surgical, and post-operative

Results: Overall mean total drain output was 2827.09 ± 1547
mLs. “High Drain Output” (HDO) was defined as greater than the overall upper

decreased the odds of HDO by 17.83%. Conclusion: Surgical time,
number of levels fused, EBL and Cell Saver return were significantly higher
in patients that experienced high drain output postoperatively. Results of
logistic regression identified female sex and lower preoperative Vitamin D
levels as significantly increasing the risk of high drain output. Given the
average complexity of an adult spinal deformity patient, it would be prudent
to conduct another study focusing on three or greater level posterior lumbar
fusions.

## P493: Preventive measures against postoperative nausea and vomiting
(PONV) in spine surgery

Yushi Hoshino

1,2

, Yoshifumi Kudo

2

, Ichiro Okano

2

, Hiroshi Maruyama

2

, Ryousuke Ikeda

1

, Yoshinori Imaizumi

1

, and Tomoaki Toyone

2

1

Department of Orthopedic, Asahi University Hospital, Gifu,
Japan

2

Department of Orthopedic, Showa University Hospital, Tokyo,
Japan

Introduction: PONV (postoperative nausea and vomiting) occurs in
about 30% of patients after spine surgery. Although PONV is uncomfortable
for patients and is a cause of decreased patient satisfaction, there are few
reports on the prevention of PONV in spine surgery. In this study, we
investigated the effect of PONV prevention in spine general anesthesia
surgery. Material and Methods: A total of 188 consecutive spine
surgeries under general anesthesia were performed at our hospital from
January 2020 to August 2021. The mean age of the patients was 67 years. The
sites included 15 cervical, 16 thoracic, and 157 lumbar spine cases. For
these cases, preventive measures were taken with reference to the Apfel
score, which is a PONV risk assessment (female, non-smoker, history of
agitation and PONV, postoperative opioid use). Prophylactic measures
included IV-PCA with Droperidol (Fentanyl), intravenous Dexamethazone at the
time of surgery for women, and intravenous Metoclopramide immediately after
surgery. The incidence of PONV in these patients was evaluated.
Results: PONV occurred in 15 patients (8.0%). The incidence
of PONV was 8.0% in 15 patients, with nausea only in 9 patients (4.9%),
vomiting in 6 patients (3.2%), and the need for additional antiemetic
medication in only 2 patients (1.1%). In our previous report, PONV was
observed in 31.4% of spine surgeries, and the incidence of PONV was clearly
reduced by prophylaxis. In addition, additional antiemetic medication was
required in 62.5% of cases of PONV in our previous report, but was used in
only 13.3% of cases in the present study, and the intensity of PONV was
reduced. Conclusion: The incidence of PONV was significantly
reduced by taking preventive measures focusing on postoperative opioid use
and women, using the Apfel score as a reference. Since the occurrence of
PONV has multiple factors, it is difficult to prevent PONV in patients with
high risk of PONV with a single drug, and multiple preventive measures such
as this one are necessary and effective. In order to achieve this, it is
difficult for orthopedic surgeons alone to prevent PONV, and cooperation
with anesthesiology and other departments is especially important to reduce
the risk of PONV.

## P494: Effect of multimodal analgesia on postoperative acute pain in
posterior lumbar surgery

Yushi Hoshino

1

, Ichiro Okano

2

, Yoshifumi Kudo

2

, Ryousuke Ikeda

1

, Hiroshi Maruyama

2

, Ryo Yamamura

2

, Yoshinori Imaizumi

1

, and Tomoaki Toyone

2

1

Department of Orthopedic, Asahi University Hospital, Gifu,
Japan

2

Department of Orthopedic, Showa University Hospital, Tokyo,
Japan

Introduction: Severe pain in the acute postoperative period is a
risk for persistent pain and decreased patient satisfaction. However, pain
management in the acute postoperative period is often difficult, which may
hinder the early start of rehabilitation and early discharge from the
hospital. In this study, we investigated the effect of multimodal analgesia
using multiple drugs on postoperative analgesia. Material and
Methods: 48 patients underwent lumbar posterior decompression
surgery (Lumbar spinous process splitting laminoplasty) with IV-PCA
(Fentanyl) and postoperative intravenous acetaminophen for postoperative
pain management (Group A, 2018.1-2019.3). In addition to IV-PCA and
postoperative acetaminophen intravenous infusion, 71 patients received
pentazocine intravenous infusion (AP group 2020.1-2021.9) for acute
postoperative pain. Group A: In addition to IV-PCA (fentanyl), acetaminophen
(1000 mg) was administered intravenously twice a day for 4 and 10 hours
after operation. Group AP: In addition to group A, pentazocine (15 mg) plus
normal saline (100 ml) was administered intravenously twice a day, 1 hour
and 7 hours after surgery. For these, postoperative pain was assessed by the
Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), and the intensity of postoperative pain, the
rate of use of additional analgesics, and the rate of complications such as
delirium were compared. Results and Discussions: There were no
significant differences in age, sex, or number of operated vertebrae between
the two groups. The mean NRS was 4.3/4.4 in group A/AP immediately after
surgery, 5.0/3.4 in group A/AP 3 hours after surgery, and 4.3/2.4 in group
A/AP 6 hours after surgery, with the AP group having a significantly lower
NRS at 3 and 6 hours after surgery. There was no significant difference in
NRS after the next day postoperatively between the two groups. There was no
difference in the amount of additional analgesics used or complications such
as delirium between the two groups. The AP group was able to significantly
reduce NRS in the immediate postoperative period and was effective in pain
management in the immediate postoperative period. The AP group also achieved
an NRS of 4 or higher, which is a risk factor for postoperative prolonged
pain, from the early postoperative period, suggesting that the AP group is
effective not only in the acute postoperative period but also for
postoperative prolonged pain. In addition, complications such as delirium do
not increase, and as a result, there is a possibility that early release
from bed and early rehabilitation can be promoted. On the other hand, one of
the goals of multimodal analgesia that uses multiple drugs is to reduce the
amount of opioids used. However, the use of pentazocine increased the amount
of opioids used in this study, and it is necessary to optimize multimodal
analgesia that is suitable for the surgical technique by considering the
drugs used and area block. Conclusion: Multimodal analgesia
with IV-PCA, postoperative acetaminophen, and intravenous pentazocine is
effective in improving postoperative acute pain in lumbar posterior
decompression surgery.

## P495: Anterior migration of a broken scalpel blade during lumbar spine
discectomy : A case report, literature review and management
algorithm

Dejan Čeleš

1

 and Janez Mohar

1

1

Department of Spine Surgery, Orthopaedic Hospital Valdoltra,
Ankaran, Slovenia

Introduction: We report a case of a broken surgical blade
anterior migration during lumbar spine discectomy, review the literature on
similar cases and propose an evidence-based management algorithm for this
type of complication since it has not yet been published. A recent
comparison of different discectomy techniques reported an overall
complication rate of 10.1%. Vascular injuries in lumbar spine surgery are
even rarer (1-5 per 10,000 disc surgeries). Broken surgical blades or other
surgically uncontrolled sharp and pointy objects in the disc space represent
a rare but potentially severe complication during posterior lumbar spine
procedures. Appreciation of vascular, bowel, and urethral anatomy is
crucial. Material and Methods:A 59-year-old female with
previous lumbar decompression and interspinous process device implantation
underwent an instrumented revision of the lumbosacral junction due to
degenerative lateral spinal canal stenosis with worsening leg and
concomitant chronic mechanical back pain. During L5-S1 continuous-motion
oval-shaped incision discectomy, the scalpel blade broke. It moved forward
and partially breached the anterior annulus with every attempt to gain hold
of the blade under fluoroscopic and microscope control. Pedicular screws
were locked to rods, and bed rest was ordered. Prior to vascular surgeon
referral, we performed CT angiography. Results:In a subacute
setting, the patient was laparoscopically revised. The broken scalpel blade
was successfully removed. We found 10 case reports in our literature review
subjected to a full-text review, totaling 13 cases. In total, two vascular
injuries were reported. The most common level of injury was L4-L5,
accounting for 46.2%, followed by L5-S1 at 38.5%. Other levels accounted for
15.4%. Conclusion:Risk factors for encountering a broken blade
are No. 15 blade with narrow junction, calcified posterior longitudinal
ligament and annulus, scalpel blade stabbing-and-turning technique, and
narrowed disc space. Complications arising from anterior sharp object
migration are arteriovenous fistula, pseudoaneurysm, vascular, urethral or
bowel laceration, foreign body granuloma, and intravascular migration of a
foreign body. We advise a stabbing motion-type of the posterior disc annulus
excision during discectomy. In these rare events, posterior removal with
fluoroscopic aid is an option unless the sharp object migrates through disc
space to the anterior annulus. With the anterior breach, vascular or other
retroperitoneal injuries should be actively sought. CT angiography is a
diagnostic method of choice, while US Duplex serves as a follow-up imaging
diagnostics. Sharp object removal from the disc space or retroperitoneum is
always indicated. The gold standard technique for anterior retroperitoneal
revision is a robot-assisted laparoscopy.

## P498: Prediction of rates of revision surgery based on pre-operative

Hania Shahzad

1

, Nazihah Bhatti

1

, Safdar Khan

1

, Frank Phillips

2

, and Elizabeth Yu

1

1

Orthopedics, Wexner Medical Center, The Ohio State University,

2

Orthopedics, Rush University Medical Center, United States

Introduction: Cannabinoid use has been explored in the treatment
of musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain which are both essential components
in the management of spinal disorders. Since the use of medical marijuana
has been linked to a decrease in opioid use postoperatively, it is of
interest to surgeons to recognize the implications of cannabinoid use in the

regression models which were reported as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence
intervals (CI). All data were analyzed in aggregate form using R Statistical
Software version 4.1.0 in the PearlDiver Software. Results: The

be analyzed for TKA and THA as the number of records in the database was too

(OR:1.92 [1.14, 3.25], p-value = 0.02) at 90 days, by 196% (OR:1.96 [1.26,
3.04], p-value = 0.004) at 1 year, by 183% (OR: 1.83 [1.24, 2.72], p-value =
0.003) at 5 years and by 181% (OR: 1.81 [1.22, 2.69], p-value = 0.004) at 10
years. Conclusion: It is theorized that cannabinoids may
adversely affect spinal fusion due to their anti-inflammatory and
immunosuppressive properties. Our results show that cannabinoid use in
opioid naïve patients does not affect revision rates at 10-year intervals
for TKA and PLF. However, the reasons for the association between CUD and
revision rates in the THA group remain unclear. Further research into
exploring the impact of cannabinoid use on peri-operative complications in
various orthopedic procedures needs to be conducted before cannabinoids can
be formally introduced as part of multimodal analgesia.

underwent ACDF from 2010 through quarter 3 of 2020 using the MSpine subset

single-level ACDF group and a multi-level ACDF groups. In addition, each
group was divided into subgroups according to the presence or absence of
HLD. The incidence of surgical and medical complications was queried using
relevant International Classification of Disease and Current Procedural
Terminology codes. Surgical complications included surgical wound
complications, wound infection, and neurological complications. Medical
complications included postoperative sepsis, respiratory failure, pneumonia,
pulmonary embolism/deep vein thrombosis, myocardial infarction,
cerebrovascular accident, renal failure, neurogenic bladder/bowel, and
urinary tract infection/incontinence. Other complications included hardware
removal, revision surgery, and readmission. Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)
was used as a broad measure of comorbidity. Chi-squared analysis, with
populations matched for age, gender, and CCI, was performed to calculate
odds ratios (ORs) of complications among HLD patients relative to non-HLD
patients treated with ACDF. Results: A total of 24,936 patients
who underwent single-level ACDF and 26,921 patients who underwent
multi-level ACDF were included. The mean CCIs for single-level and
multi-level ACDF groups were 2.27 ± 2.14 and 2.36 ± 2.23, respectively. In
terms of surgical complications, in the multi-level ACDF group, wound
complications within 90 days (OR = 1.22, 95% Confidence Index [CI] =
1.03-1.44, p = 0.020) were significantly higher in the patients with HLD.
Among medical complications, myocardial infarction (OR = 1.30, CI =
1.18-1.45, p < 0.001 and OR = 1.26, CI = 1.16-1.38, p < 0.001), renal
failure (OR = 1.08, CI = 1.01-1.16, p = 0.029 and OR = 1.08, CI = 1.02-1.14,
p = 0.009), and UTI/urinary incontinence (OR = 1.16, CI = 1.09-1.22, p <
0.001 and OR = 1.10, CI = 1.04-1.15, p < 0.001) were significantly higher
in the patients with HLD in both groups. Revision surgery (OR = 1.22, CI =
1.10-1.36, p < 0.001) and readmission (OR = 1.13, CI = 1.04-1.23, p =
0.004) after 1 year were significantly higher in the patients with HLD who
underwent multi-level ACDF. Conclusion: In patients who
underwent ACDF, several surgical and medical complications were found to be
higher in patients with HLD than in patients without HLD. Preoperative serum
lipid concentration control and appropriate HLD treatment can prevent
postoperative complications due to HLD in patients who underwent ACDF.

Jiwon Park

Study Design: Retrospective case study. Objectives:

between cage sedimentation following intervertebral fusion and the

Review: There is a claim that the likelihood of the cage

Results: A total of 142 patients were analyzed, and a total

selection during surgery for those patients with low lumbar Hounsefield unit
to avoid cage subsidence.
Keywords: TLIF, BMD, Hounsefield Unit, Cage subsidence

## P501: Acute pancreatitis associated with scoliosis surgery. Could opioids
play a determinant role in its development?

Nahala Aborashed-Amador

1

, Fernando Alvarado Gómez

1

, Andres Motta-Amar

1

, Maria Garcia-Rueda

1

, Helberth González-Rico

1

, Maria Vargas-Osorio

1

, Maria Camila Giraldo Bernal

1

, Carlos Montero-Silva

1

, and Mario Herrera Méndez

1

1

Instituto Roosevelt, Bogota, Colombia

Introduction: Pancreatitis as a complication of scoliosis
correction surgery has been reported, supported by pathophysiological
theories such as hemodynamic imbalance associated with intraoperative
instability and changes in visceral vascular architecture directly related
to tissue distress because of the vascular elongation caused by curve
correction (2-4). In the surgical context, one of the most recent causes
proposed is prolonged postoperative use of opioids at high doses.
Material and Methods: Three pediatric patients who
underwent scoliosis correction surgery, two of them with a diagnosis of
neuromuscular scoliosis secondary to Duchenne (DMD) and cerebral palsy and
one with congenital scoliosis due to hemivertebra. In average, 15 vertebral
segments were instrumented. Two of the patients required two-stage surgery
for definitive correction. Average surgical time was 6.06 hours, with a mean
blood loss of 1.766 ml in the definitive correction. All three patients
required blood product transfusions. Results: Abdominal pain
was the cardinal symptom in the three patients. Progressive pain intensity
and elevation of pancreatic enzyme levels led to the suspicion of
pancreatitis, with a mean of 5 days until diagnosis. Total time of
continuous opioid use during hospitalization was 26 days in average, with
adjustment to the highest dose because of the presence of abdominal pain.
The main opioids used were morphine, tramadol and hydromorphone.
Conservative and surgical management was required in these patients, with
surveillance in the intensive care unit. No major complications were
associated with the pancreatic picture. Conclusion: The
association between prolonged exposure to high-dose opioids and the onset of
pancreatitis in the context of major surgery suggests a potential relation
that warrants further study, given that opioid receptors have been described
in the sphincter of Oddi. This association must be borne in mind in order to
reduce patient morbidity in the context of scoliosis correction surgery.

## P503: Outpatient intermittent percutaneous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
drainage as treatment of CSF leak in spine surgery

Paul Albert Manuel

1

, Gilbert Ranoa

1

, and Michael Louis Gimenez

1

1

Brain and Spine Institute, Cardinal Santos Medical Center, San Juan,
Philippines

Introduction: A dreaded complication of spine surgery is
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Leak. A CSF leak may result in pain, wound healing
complications, infection, increased hospital stay, and/or reoperation. A
gold standard of post operative management of CSF leak is still lacking. The
authors describe a technique of CSF drainage that may improve the current
management of post operative CSF leak without addition hospital stay or
reoperation. Material and Methods: A retrospective case series
review of spine surgery cases performed by 2 attending surgeons from the
Brain and Spine Institute, Cardinal Santos Medical Center, was performed. In
all, 241 charts were reviewed, spanning a 5-year period. There were 18 cases
in which CSF leak was detected. All cases of CSF leak were managed by
outpatient intermittent percutaneous drainage using a gauge 23 butterfly
needle and a 20-cc sterile syringe.Patients were reevaluated at regular
intervals for and underwent repeat drainage every 1-4 days dependent on the
need and persistence of CSF leak. Results: All patients
observed in this study had CSF leak, All patients were treated using
Intermittent percutaneous CSF drainage and none of the patients needed
revision surgery to close the CSF leak. The duration of the leak for the all
patients were at approximately 20 days on average, with a standard deviation
of 15 days. The most common factors noted in the study population were
elderly, greater than 2 operative levels, and corticosteroid use.
Conclusion: The use of Outpatient Intermittent percutaneous
CSF drainage represents a viable alternative in the treatment of CSF leak as
seen in the resolution of signs and symptoms of all 18 patients. On the risk
factors for the occurrence of CSF leak, the most noted factors besides
increased age were the increased number of operative levels, and
corticosteroid use.

## P505: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis safety profile in elective spine
surgery

Mohamed El-Farra

1

, Emily Mills

2

, Christian Jimenez

2

, Samantha Solaru

2

, Hyunwoo Kang

2,3

, Tara Shelby

2

, Andy Ton

2

, Jeffrey C. Wang

2

, Raymond Hah

2

, and Ram Alluri

2

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, Riverside School of
Medicine, Riverside, United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles,
United States

3

Orthopaedic Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical
School, Boston, United States

Introduction: There is currently no consensus regarding
pharmacologic venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in elective spine
surgery. The purpose of this study was to assess the safety profile of VTE
prophylaxis in patients undergoing elective spine surgery. Material
and Methods: Patients who underwent elective spine surgery at a
single institution from January 2019 to October 2019 were included for
analysis. Patients were divided into two cohorts based on whether they
received VTE prophylaxis or not. The patients’ demographics, comorbidities,
surgery performed, and surgical outcomes and complications were recorded via
retrospective chart review. Multivariate regression analysis controlling for
age, gender, body mass index, ethnicity, prior VTE, smoking, procedure type,
levels fused, approach, instrumentation, operative time, estimated blood
loss, and intraoperative complication was conducted to assess for any
significant differences in postoperative hematoma, general postoperative
complications, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE),
outpatient complications readmission, emergency department visits, and
return to the operating room (OR). Results: Of the 318
patients, 247 patients received VTE prophylaxis, and 74 patients did not.
After controlling for confounders with multivariate analysis, there was no
significant difference in postoperative hematoma formation (p = 0.997),
general postoperative complications (p = 0.684), DVT rates (p = 0.860), PE
rates (p = 0.984), outpatient complications (p = 0.196), return to the OR (p
= 0.331), likelihood of emergency department visits (p = 0.061) and
readmission rates (p = 0.071). Conclusion: The present study
found that patients who received VTE prophylaxis after undergoing elective
spine surgery did not have a significant increase in postoperative hematoma,
general complications, return to OR, ER visits, and hospital readmissions.
In addition, VTE prophylaxis did not affect the rate of DVT or PE. Based on
the present study’s results, VTE prophylaxis does not increase the risk of
postoperative complications in patients undergoing elective spine
surgery.

## P506: Evaluating the effect of gastroesophageal reflux disease on
postoperative dysphagia following anterior cervical spine surgery - A
prospective, multicenter study

Aditya Mazmudar

1

, Taylor Paziuk

1

, John Mangan

1

, Khoa Tran

1

, Samuel Oh

1

, Sandy Li

1

, Brandon Sherrod

2

, Erica Bisson

2

, Darrel Brodke

3

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Christopher Kepler

1

, Alexander Vaccaro

1

, Gregory Schroeder

1

, and Jeffrey Rihn

1

1
Rothman Orthopedic Institute at Thomas Jefferson
University, Philadelphia, United States

2
Department of Neurosurgery, Clinical
Neurosciences Center at University of Utah, Salt Lake
City,United States

3
Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University
Orthopaedic Center at University of Utah, Salt Lake
City,United States
Introduction: While there is little doubt that the operative
insult associated with anterior cervical spine surgery imposes a significant
risk for postoperative dysphagia, numerous patient specific risk factors
have yet to be fully explored. The impact of a preoperative diagnosis of
gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) in particular has yet to be evaluated as a
potential risk factor for dysphagia. To our knowledge, no prior prospective
study has reported on the incidence and severity of dysphagia following
anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) based on a patient’s
preoperative diagnosis of GERD. As such, the purpose of this study was to
prospectively evaluate the impact of a preoperative diagnosis of GERD on the
incidence and severity of postoperative dysphagia in a multicenter
population. Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study
was conducted on patients who underwent one- to five-level ACDF After IRB
approval, written informed consent was obtained from all participating
patients. Patients over 18 years of age who underwent an elective ACDF for a
degenerative condition were prospectively enrolled at two academic centers
from the years 2018 to 2020. Patients were asked to complete a preoperative
demographic survey in addition to dysphagia surveys (Bazaz, DSQ, EAT-10)
both preoperatively and at 2, 6, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. Exclusion
criteria included previous cervical fusion at the operative level or surgery
for oncologic, infectious, or traumatic indications. Patients were separated
into two groups: those with and without a preoperative diagnosis of GERD.
Continuous variables were assessed using either an independent t-test or
Mann Whitney U-test for parametric and non-parametric data. All categorical
variables were compared using a chi-square test. Results: A
total of 116 patients met study criteria and were subsequently enrolled.
Overall rates of postoperative dysphagia increased to 47.3% (n = 53) at
2-weeks but eventually decreased towards the preoperative prevalence of
25.0% at the 24-week mark. Patients with preoperative diagnosis of GERD had
lower dysphagia severity scores on a continuous variable analysis in both
the DSQ and EAT-10 surveys at 2-week follow-up in addition to the Bazaz
survey at 24-week follow-up. Our follow up at 24-weeks was 85.7%.
Conclusion: Our study shows that having a preoperative
diagnosis of GERD has no significant effect on the incidence of dysphagia
following ACDF. Nevertheless, having a preoperative diagnosis of GERD does
seem to affect the severity of dysphagia that this patient population
perceives at multiple intervals over a 24-week postoperative period.

## P507: Ipsilateral psoas hematoma development after two adjacent level
endoscopic transforaminal discectomy in prior two level fused
segments

Sukdeb Datta

1

1

Endoscopic Spine Surgery, Datta Endoscopic Back Surgery and Pain
Center, Saddle Brook, United States

Introduction: Transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy
(TFELD) is increasingly gaining popularity as a minimally invasive procedure
to address the disc herniations in the lumbar spine. There is a scarcity of
reports on hemorrhagic complications after endoscopic spine surgeries. We
are reporting a case of psoas hematoma following TFELD. Material and
Methods: We report a case of left sided psoas muscle hematoma in
a 50-year-old male who underwent a transforaminal endoscopic lumbar
discectomy (TFELD) and foraminotomy. He had prior history of fusion at L2-L3
and L4-L5 fusion. The Magnetic resonance (MRI) imaging study showed adjacent
level disease at L3-4 and L5-S1 levels with severe lateral recess and left
foraminal stenosis. TFELD was performed at the adjacent L3-4 and L5-S1
levels. However, on 2nd post-operative day the patient
experienced increasing radicular pain in left lower extremity mainly along
the L5 and S1 distribution. A repeat MRI with and without contrast showed
circumscribed fluid collection within the substance of the left psoas muscle
adjacent to L5-S1 disc level extending along the muscle rostrally and
caudally (4x3x1.5 cm). The collection was non-enhancing on post-contrast T1
images. Infectious pathology was ruled out owing to absent systemic
symptoms, the negative lab results for infection markers and non-enhancement
of the lesion on MRI. The clinic-radiological presentation was suggestive of
psoas hematoma. Due to persistent radicular symptoms which was attributed to
the hematoma, the patient was referred to an interventional radiologist who
performed a computed tomographic (CT) guided aspiration.
Results: Fortunately, we encountered a small
well-circumscribed hematoma without any systemic symptoms and abnormal blood
parameters. Thus, no re-exploration was required. Even the radicular
symptoms resolved over time. The surgeons may consider CT angiographic
embolization and re-operation if the symptoms and abnormal hematologic
parameters warrant. Conclusion: Hemorrhagic complications after
spine surgeries are rare events. Surgeons must rule out the possibility of
psoas hematoma in patients presenting with increasing radicular pain with or
without flank pain following PELD surgeries. Conservative treatment
including wait and watch strategy is usually sufficient. The surgeons should
exercise an immense care while placing the targeting needle.

## P508: Surgical approach and post-operative C5 palsy after decompression
for degenerative cervical myelopathy

Ali Moghaddamjou

1

, Alex Bak

2

, Mohammed Ali Alvi

1

, and Michael Fehlings

1

1

Neurosurgery, University of Toronto, Canada

2

University of Toronto, Canada

Introduction: One of the significant complications following
decompressive surgery to the cervical spine is that of C5 palsy. Despite the
clinical significance of this finding, we do not have strong quality
evidence towards its natural history and strategies to limit the incidence
and duration of this complication. The goal of this project is to leverage
clinical trial data in patients with Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy (DCM)
to enhance our understanding of postoperative C5 palsy. Material and
Methods: Data from the CSM-Protect trial, which was a
multicenter, prospective, randomized clinical trial was used for this
analysis. We identified all adult patients with DCM who received
decompression surgery. We subdivided the data into those patients who had
documented C5 palsy after the surgery and those who did not. The outcome
measure selected was the incidence and duration of C5 palsy post
decompressive surgery. As risk factors for C5 palsy remain unclear, matching
was not performed. One-way ANOVA was used to compare continuous variables
and chi-square tests, or fisher’s exact tests were used for discrete
variables. The level of significance was set to p < 0.05.
Results: In a total of 284 patients that were included, 152
(53.5%) of the patients received surgery via the posterior approach. The
total incidence of C5 palsy was 5.3% (n = 15), which was comparable to
metrics reported in DCM and other degenerative spine diseases. Patients that
received posterior surgery were older (A - 56.4 ± 10.0, P - 60.5 ± 9.9, p =
0.001) and had a greater proportion of males (A - 47%, P - 65.8%, p =
0.002). Both groups had similar proportions of comorbidities in the form of
anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, COPD,
hyperlipidemia, hypercholesteremia, hypertension, thyroid disease,
hepatitis, obesity, and sleep apnea. The anterior approach group had a
greater incidence of fibromyalgia (A - 5.3%, P - 0.7%, p = 0.045). The
incidence of C5 palsy was significantly higher in patients that underwent
posterior decompression compared to those that received anterior
decompression (A - 0.8%, P - 9.2%, p = 0.004). Conclusion: The
incidence of postoperative C5 palsy is significantly higher in patients who
received posterior decompression compared to anterior decompression for
DCM.

Introduction: Spine Surgery is considered a moderate risk for
developing Venous Thromboembolism (VTE). To our knowledge, no study has been
done to determine the incidence of VTE in our local population. We aim to
study this and determine the factors associated with developing VTE post
spine surgery. Material and Methods: A retrospective chart
review was conducted to analyze 892 adult patients who underwent either an

ambulation lowers it. Larger prospective study is needed to identify the
best prophylactic anticoagulation regimen. Prophylactic measures against VTE
are highly recommended, especially amongst high-risk patients.

## P510: Relative benefit of neurophysiologic monitoring during
uncomplicated anterior cervical spine surgery

Torsten Fras

1

 and Christian Fras

1

1

Institute for Spinal Surgery, Broomall, United States

Introduction: Intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring (IOM)
is commonly used in spine surgery; advantages include identification of
intraoperative neurologic decline that may be related to a remediable cause.
Disadvantages include increased time and cost, morbidity associated with the
monitoring procedure, and the potential for false positive alerts prompting
unnecessary action. The study’s goal was to assess whether use of IOM in
routine, uncomplicated cases of anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
(ACDF) surgery was of demonstrable benefit. Material and
Methods: 50 consecutive patients were identified who underwent
one-level ACDF with anterior instrumentation for cervical disc herniation
with radiculopathy without myelopathy. For all cases, a NIMS tube was used
to monitor laryngeal nerve function, and EMG, SSEP, and MEP modalities were
monitored. Hospital and post-operative records were investigated for the
presence of IOM alerts, whether corrective action was taken during surgery,
and the presence of any post-operative neurologic deficits.
Results: In all cases, there were no alerts of laryngeal
nerve dysfunction, or SSEP / MEP abnormality. In 12 cases, transient EMG
irritation activity was documented; in no cases was there any change to the
surgical procedure, such as abandonment of surgery, removal of implant, etc.
There were no instances of new or worsened post-operative neurologic
deficit, and clinical findings of vocal cord dysfunction.
Conclusion: In ACDF with anterior instrumentation for
cervical disc herniation with radiculopathy without myelopathy, IOM use did
not convey any identifiable advantage. Therefore, the data does not support
considering IOM to be required or standard of care for routine,
uncomplicated ACDF surgery.

## 1092

## P511: Lumbar spinous process fixation: peri-operative complication rate
in instrumented posterior fusion

Torsten Fras

1

 and Christian Fras

1

1

Institute for Spinal Surgery, Broomall, United States

Introduction: Spinal fusion surgery is performed to treat many
conditions. Previous studies have demonstrated increased arthrodesis rates
when supplemental instrumentation is utilized: this commonly involves lumbar
pedicle screw fixation. However, traditional surgical techniques for lumbar
pedicle screw insertion can be associated with significant morbidity (up to
54% complication rate). Spinous process fixation (SPF) is an alternate
method of lumbar spine stabilization in fusion procedures, and can be
accomplished with less invasive techniques. This study seeks to assess the
peri-operative complication rate associated with use of SPF in lumbar fusion
operations. Material and Methods: 100 consecutive patients were
identified who had undergone one-level SPF using Aspen MIS Fusion System
(Zimmer Biomet) as part of lumbar fusion surgery with minimum 90 days
post-operative follow-up. All hospital and office records were reviewed. All
complications were recorded. Results: All 100 patients were
followed for minimum 90 days post-operatively. Complications were:
superficial wound dehiscence (2), all responding to local wound care;
superficial wound infection (3), all responding to oral antibiotics;
post-operative urinary retention requiring catheter insertion (1), resolved
spontaneously. There were no reoperations. No other complications were
identified, and no severe complications (eg, deep infection, neurologic
deficit, implant-related complication). Conclusion: The
short-term (within 90 days of surgery) complication rate associated with SPF
in posterior lumbar fusion surgery was 6%. All complications were minor;
there were no major complications, and no cases of re-operation. The
peri-operative complication rate of SPF compares favorably with that of
pedicle screw instrumentation, and in this regard SPF is an alternate option
to use of pedicle screw fixation in selected patients.

## P512: Role of tranexamic acid in reducing peri and post operative blood

Shyamasunder Bhat Neerkaje

, Saktthi Shanmuganathan

, Madhava Pai

, and Ramachandra Theja

which inhibits plasminogen from binding to fibrin and suppresses
fibrinolysis. This way tranexamic acid will help in reducing perioperative
blood loss in major surgeries. The evidence on the efficacy of this agent in
spine surgeries is not sufficient. The purpose of this study was to assess
its efficacy on perioperative blood loss in major spinal surgeries.
Methodology: Pre-operative assessment included
documentation of the patient’s comorbidities, preoperative Hb, PCV, platelet
count, PT/INR and APTT, RFT, serum electrolytes values and ECG. Patients
with age <18 years, blood dyscrasias and renal disorders are excluded
from the study. Based on whether patients have received the drug or not they
will be grouped into patient receiving tranexamic acid (Group A) and patient
not receiving tranexamic acid (Group B). Intra operative data included
levels of decompression, duration of surgery, assessment of blood loss, need
for intraoperative blood transfusion. Post-operative assessment including
repeating the following parameters Hb, PCV, PT/INR, APTT after 24 hours of
surgery, documentation of blood collected in surgical drain and need for any
postoperative blood transfusion. Results: Intraoperative
Transfusion, Hemoglobin (g/dL) (Post-Operative Hb drop), Surgical Drain (mL)
were statistically significant in Group A when compared to Group B.
Conclusion: In spine surgeries, TXA was found to be
effective in reducing the intra-operative and post operative blood loss and
the need for blood transfusion. Keywords: Tranexamic acid (TXA), spine
surgery, blood loss, blood transfusion.
