Department of Neurological Surgery, Montefiore Medical Center/Albert
Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, United States

Introduction: Patients with spinal metastases often require
surgical intervention for cord compression or palliative care. The American
College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program
(ACS-NSQIP) Surgical Risk Calculator was developed to assist surgeons with
estimating 30-day postoperative complications based on patient-specific risk
factors and has been validated within several surgical patient populations.
Since no prior studies have evaluated its performance in patients undergoing
spinal metastasis surgery, we assessed the accuracy of this tool in
predicting postoperative complications. Methods: This was a
single-institution retrospective cohort study. Electronic medical record
(EMR) chart review was performed on consecutive operative patients with
metastatic spine disease from our institution between April 1, 2012 and
April 30, 2022. Preoperative comorbidities and current procedural
terminology (CPT) codes were entered into the ACS-NSQIP calculator
(https://riskcalculator.facs.org/RiskCalculator/) to obtain
predicted complication risk for each patient. Mean predicted risk
percentages were then compared to observed outcomes using receiver operator
characteristic (ROC) curves and two-sided one-sample t-tests. A scatter plot
with regression line was used to compare length of hospital stay.
Results: A total of 153 patients were included in this
study. The overall 30-day postoperative complication rate was 41.2% and
mortality rate was 8.5%. The mean predicted mortality rate was similar to
mean observed mortality (7.9% vs 8.5%, p = 0.352). However, mean predicted
outcomes were significantly lower than mean observed outcomes for all other
measured complications, including any complication, serious complication,
pneumonia, surgical site infection, urinary tract infection, venous
thromboembolism, and return to operating room (p < 0.001). Only mean
postoperative mortality (AUC = 0.749) and sepsis (AUC = 0.709) were found to
be adequately discriminated in ROC analysis, with all other outcomes having
poor predictive value (AUC < 0.700). Finally, the risk calculator was
found to structurally underestimate length of hospital stay in
patient-matched comparison (regression line y = 14.51-0.1x; r2
< 0.001). Conclusion: The ACS-NSQIP risk calculator was
found to be a poor or unreliable predictor for most postoperative
complications in patients undergoing spinal tumor surgery. However, this
tool may be successfully utilized to predict risk of 30-day postoperative
mortality in this patient population. Future work should be done to create
accurate oncology-specific outcome predictors with validation in the spine
population.

## 1156

## P514: The potential role of intraoperative ketamine administration in
reducing postoperative opioid consumption among chronic opioid users in
outpatient spine surgery

Carol Wang

1

, Jennifer Liu

2

, Thomas Sullivan

3

, Kevin Bondar

3

, and Comron Saifi

3

1

Department of Orthopaedics, University of Pennsylvania,
Philadelphia, United States

2

Orthopedics and Sports Medicine

3

Spine Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United
States

Introduction: The rising rate of opioid use disorder in the
United States represents a serious public health crisis. The economic burden
of prescription opioid misuse is extensive. Achieving postoperative pain
control while minimizing opioid overuse and dependence is a continued
challenge in spine surgery. Intraoperative ketamine administration in
patients undergoing spine surgery has been associated with decreased opioid
consumption postoperatively. The present study aimed to determine long-term
postoperative opioid consumption in patients who received intraoperative
ketamine compared to those who did not receive intraoperative ketamine.
Materials and Methods: Patients included in this study
carried a diagnosis of degenerative spinal deformity and had undergone spine
surgery. Patients in the ketamine group received a single bolus of 30, 40,
or 50 mg of ketamine, followed by ketamine infusion at a rate of 1-3
mcg/kg/min until the close of the procedure. Pre- and postoperative opioid
consumption was quantified using cumulative MME. A prescription drug
monitoring program (PDMP) spanning 13 states was used to identify opioid
prescription fills and quantify dosages consumed independent of prescription
source, insurance coverage, or patient self-report. Long-term preoperative
opioid use was defined as filling at least six opioid prescriptions in the
twelve months prior to surgery. Short-term preoperative opioid use was
defined filling an opioid prescription in the 30 days prior to surgery, with
no additional opioid prescription fills in the 180 days prior to surgery.
Study sample characteristics, including demographics, comorbidities,
intraoperative factors, postoperative outcomes, were controlled in the
analyses. Propensity score matching was used. STROBE (Strengthening the
Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology) guidelines were
implemented. Results: A total of 434 participants were
included. Compared to the control group, patient who received intraoperative
ketamine presented with a significantly higher number of readmissions (0.291
± 0.75 vs. 0.475 ± 0.874; p = 0.045), and higher mean opioid usage in the
year prior to surgery (5,089 ± 16,813 vs. 11,801 ± 28,043; p = 0.016). There
was no statistically significant difference noted in postoperative opioid
consumption in opioid-naïve patients and short-term opioid users at 1 month,
3 months, 6 months, or 1 year. There was no difference in incidence of
long-term postoperative opioid use in the opioid-naïve patients in patients
receiving intraoperative ketamine. Among patients with long-term
preoperative opioid use, the patients who received ketamine had consumed 41%
fewer total morphine milligram equivalents (MMEs) (k = 1,209 MMEs; c = 2.062
MMEs; p = 0.008) at one month postoperatively. In subgroup analysis based on
percentile of preoperative opioid use in MMEs, no statistically significant
association was observed between ketamine administration and postoperative
opioid use in any subgroup. Conclusion:There was no significant
change in opioid use at 1, 3, 6, or 12 months postoperatively in the two
groups. There was no difference in the incidence of long-term postoperative
opioid use, VAS at discharge, VAS pain scores, and length of stay. There was
a short-term opioid-sparing benefit to intraoperative ketamine use in
patients with long-term preoperative opioid use. Patients with chronic
preoperative opioid use have a short-term opioid-sparing benefit after
intraoperative ketamine administration.

## 1167

## P515: Anterior spinal fusion surgery associated with lower risk of
stroke, pneumonia, and infection compared to posterior spinal fusion
surgery

Leland McCluskey

1

, Ivan Angelov

2

, Victor Wu

3

, Sachin Gupta

4

, Comron Saifi

2

, and Matthew Cyriac

5

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, St. Francis, Emory Healthcare, Columbus, United
States

2

Spine Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United
States

3

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Texas Health -
Houston, Houston, United States

4

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia,
United States

5

Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Tulane University School of
Medicine, New Orleans, United States

Introduction: The question of approach to lumbar fusion is
debated amongst spine surgeons. While prior studies have shown slight
differences in outcomes, most studies have concluded that both approaches
have similar fusion rates and clinical outcomes. Prior studies have lacked
statistical power. This retrospective cohort study compared the 30 and
90-day postoperative complications between an anterior vs. posterior
approach to lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) in 2010-2018 utilizing the largest
sample to date of direct patient outcomes from a mixed private and public
payer database. Materials and Methods: The MSpine database by
PearlDiver was queried using ICD-9, ICD-10, and CPT codes to identify
patients who had undergone single-level anterior or posterior lumbar
interbody fusion surgery. 30 and 90-day postoperative complications of
single-level ALIF/LLIF and PLIF/TLIF surgery were evaluated in 112,023
patients. Readmission rates, ileus, lower extremity DVT, infection,
pneumonia, and stroke were evaluated for patients with in the anterior
approach group and the posterior approach group. Results: There
were 38,529 (34.4%) patients in the anterior group (ALIF/LLIF) and 73,494
(65.6%) in the posterior group (PLIF/TLIF). At both 30 and 90-days
postoperative, patients undergoing an anterior approach to lumbar interbody
fusion had a higher odds ratio of lower extremity DVT (30-day OR: 1.19,
90-day OR: 1.16; p < 0.05) and ileus complication (30-day OR: 1.87, p
< .05; 90-day OR: 1.81, p < .05). At both 30 and 90-days
postoperative, patients undergoing a posterior approach had a higher odds
ratio of stroke (30-day: OR: 0.79, 90-day OR: 0.87; p < 0.05),
transfusion (30-day OR: 0.66, 90-day OR: 0.69; p < .05), infection
(30-day OR: 0.88, 90-day OR: 0.91; p < .05), and pneumonia complication
(30-day OR: 0.85, 90-day OR: 0.90; p < .05). There was no statistically
significant difference in myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism
between both approaches at 30 and 90-days postoperative.
Conclusion: This study identified differences in
postoperative complications between anterior and posterior approaches at 30
and 90-day postoperative timepoints. The present findings can inform surgeon
treatment decisions for patient profiles. Patients with high risk for
stroke, pneumonia, and infection, or patients with a high likelihood of
requiring postoperative transfusion, may benefit from an anterior approach
for lumbar interbody fusion. Patients with a high risk for developing lower
extremity DVT may benefit from a posterior approach.

## 1211

## P516: Drivers for unplanned readmission following adult spinal
surgery

Comron Saifi

1

, Sarthak Mohanty

2

, and Sachin Gupta

2

1

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital,
Houston, United States

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia,
United States

Introduction: Unplanned readmissions following surgical
intervention are costly to health systems, associated with poor outcomes,
and useful as indicators of healthcare quality and hospital performance.
Discerning independent predictors of hospital readmission is especially
crucial in light of the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, a part of
the Affordable Care Act that allows centers for Medicare and Medicaid
services to penalize hospitals for higher readmission rates. Identifying
independent risk factors for hospital readmission within one-year post-op is
critical to identifying how risk factors change along a longitudinal scale.
The objectives of this study were to assess the incidence of unplanned
readmission after spine surgery at 0-30 days, 31-90 days, 91-180 days, and
180 days, and one year and to identify preoperative and in-hospital risk
factors using a large, single institution database. Materials and
Methods: A retrospective review of 3,079 patients who underwent a
spinal procedure as a principal or secondary procedure was conducted.
Patients with and without unplanned readmission were compared on baseline
characteristics, intraoperative details, and postoperative outcomes.
Baseline characteristics consisted of comorbidities, age, race, sex, smoking
status, pre-operative diagnosis, procedures performed, and post-operative
outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to establish
independent associations with unplanned readmission within one-year post-op.
For adjusted analysis, separate models were constructed using purposeful
selection of covariates, incorporating backward elimination after univariate
testing (p-value = ≤ .10). Separate regression models were constructed for
patients who were readmitted between 0-30 days, 30-90 days, 90-180 days,
between 180 days and 365 days. Statistical significance was defined as
p-value < .05 (two-sided test). Analyses were conducted with SPSS
Statistics 23. Results: 3,079 patients met inclusion criteria.
22.34% were readmitted within one year. 10.49% of patients were readmitted
within 30 days postoperatively, 3.77% between 30 and 90-days
postoperatively, 3.25% within 90 and 180 days postoperatively, and 4.77%
between 180 days and one-year post-operatively. Patients that underwent
procedures of the thoracic spine (p = 0.030) had a higher likelihood of
being readmitted. Smokers (p = 0.034) had a higher likelihood of readmission
compared to non-smokers. Each additional day spent in the hospital during
the postoperative stay resulted in 1.071 higher odds (p < 0.0001) of
readmission. Each additional year of age resulted in 1.021 higher odds (p
< 0.0001) of readmission. Infection was the most common reason for
re-admission. Conclusion: Older patients, patients that
smokers, and patients undergoing thoracic procedures had higher rates for
re-admission after adult spine surgery. Infection was the most common reason
for readmission. Surgeons should consider these factors in management
decisions, clinical follow-up, and in counseling patients regarding the
risks for readmission.

## 1218

## P517: Treatment of a symptomatic CSF fistula after full endoscopic
cervical foraminotomy

Bastian Stemmer

1

, Motov Stefan

1

, Christoph Maurer

2

, and Ehab Shiban

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery

2

Department of Radiology, UK Augsburg, Augsburg, Germany

Introduction: There is limited data on the management and
sequalae of CSF fistulas after endoscopic cervical spine surgery. Case
report: We present a case of a 47-year old female patient with
left-sided C7 radiculopathy, who was advised for a left-sided endoscopic
foraminotomy C7 due to a cervical spondylosis with left-sided paramedian
disc herniation and C7 foraminal stenosis. The patient was discharged on the
first postoperative day after an uneventful course of treatment. However,
she returned 8 days later with tingling dysesthesia in both upper
extremities as well as headache and neck pain, which accentuated and
immobilized her during standing and walking. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
leak was detected on spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A computer
tomography (CT)-guided epidural blood patch was performed but the patients’
symptoms persisted. Therefore a second CT-guided epidural fibrin patch was
executed and the patient improved and was discharged home without
sensorimotor deficits or sequelae. Discussion and Conclusion:
CSF fistulas after endoscopic cervical spine procedures are a rare
complication, which might severely debilitate and immobilize patients.
Thorough analysis of current literature let us conclude that interventional
treatment with epidural fibrin patch appears to be an efficient treatment if
dural tear is not detected and repaired during initial surgery.

## 1235

## P518: Postoperative VTE complications in spinal oncology patients

Ivan Angelov

1

, Takshi Hirase

2

, Thomas Sullivan

2

, and Comron Saifi

1

1

Spine Surgery

2
Department of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine,
Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United States
Introduction: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) is a serious
complication that occurs following spine surgeries. VTE rates are high in
cancer patients especially in those treated with spine tumor excision
procedures. There are no prior studies that investigate the incidence of
postoperative VTE among spinal instrumentation procedures performed on
patients with oncologic spinal pathologies. The authors hypothesized that
spine instrumentation procedures performed on a greater number of levels
will be associated with a higher risk of VTE complications compared to those
involving fewer levels in patients with oncologic spinal pathologies.
Methods and Materials: The 2010 to 2019 National Surgical
Quality Improvement (NSQIP) database was used to identify all patients
undergoing spine instrumentation procedures for spine tumor excision. A
retrospective review of the NSQIP database was performed on all patients
undergoing spinal instrumentation for spine tumor excision between 2010 and
2019. CPT codes of spinal instrumentation procedures were included. Patients
with incomplete records and CPT codes for procedures other than spinal
instrumentation were excluded. Demographics, operative data, hospital length
of stay, 30-day reoperation, 30-day readmission, discharge disposition and
postoperative complications including VTE complications were collected.
Results: A total of 3,155 patients (1752M, 1403F) and 4 CPT
codes were included in the study. The median age was 61 years and median BMI
was 27. There were 637 (20%) transfers from an outside facility and 605
(19%) were smokers. Average operative duration was 284 minutes and median
hospital length of stay was 8 days. There were 2118 (67%) patients treated
with spine instrumentation of 3 to 6 levels (CPT 22842), 631 (20%) patients
with spine instrumentation of 7 to 12 levels (CPT 22843), 379 (12%) patients
with spine instrumentation of two levels (CPT 22840) and 27 (< 1%)
patients with spine instrumentation of at least 12 levels. A total of 173
(5.5%) patients developed at least one VTE complication. Spinal
instrumentation of 12 levels or greater was associated with the highest rate
of VTE (15%) followed by spine instrumentation of 7 to 12 levels (7%), spine
instrumentation of 3 to 6 levels (5%), and spine instrumentation of two
levels (3%). We performed a Pearson's chi-squared test of independence to
verify if the distribution of the presence of VTE complications varies with
the associated CPT code. The chi-squared test resulted in X2 of 13.54, and a
p-value 0.0036. Conclusion: Spine instrumentation on greater
number of vertebral levels is associated with a higher incidence of
postoperative VTE complications compared to instrumentation performed on
fewer levels in patients with oncologic spinal pathologies. There was an
overall VTE rate of 6% in this patient population. This varied based on the
number of levels instrumented with a 3% rate for a 2-level procedure and a
15% rate for a 12-level or greater procedure.

## P519: Preoperative serum albumin predicts length of stay and
perioperative complication following vertebral corpectomy and posterior
stabilization for oncologic spinal pathology

Takshi Hirase

1

, Khaled Taghlabi

2

, Jesus Cruz-Garza

2

, Amir Faraji

2

, Rex Marco

1

, and Comron Saifi

1

1

Department of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine

2

Neurosurgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, United
States

Introduction: Patients undergoing vertebral corpectomy and
posterior stabilization for oncologic spinal pathology have relatively high
rates of perioperative complications. Low preoperative serum albumin levels
have been associated with increased perioperative complications following
elective spine surgeries. The present study aimed to evaluate the hypothesis
that preoperative serum albumin levels are associated with perioperative
outcomes following vertebral corpectomy and posterior stabilization for
oncologic spinal pathology. Methods: The 2010 to 2019 National
Surgical Quality Improvement (NSQIP) database was used to identify all
patients undergoing vertebral corpectomy and posterior stabilization for
spine tumor excision. Multiple logistic regression ordinal models were used
to examine the relationship between preoperative serum albumin levels on
perioperative outcome measures. Receiver operative characteristic (ROC)
curve analysis and Youden index were used to determine preoperative serum
albumin cut-off values for predicting perioperative complications.
Results: A total of 301 patients were included in the
study. Lower serum albumin was associated with longer post-operative LOS (p
< 0.001) and higher incidence of perioperative complications (p <
0.001). ROC curve analysis demonstrated serum albumin < 3.25 g/dL as an
independent predictor for perioperative complications. After multiple
logistic regression modeling, for every unit decrease of serum albumin
(g/dL), there was a 2.3 times higher chance of increase in length of stay by
one week (95% CI: 1.8, 2.7; p < 0.001) and 1.9 times higher chance of
incurring any perioperative complication including surgical site infection,
urinary tract infection, and need for post-operative blood transfusion (95%
CI: 1.3, 2.7; p < 0.001). There were no significant association between
serum albumin and operative time, need for intraoperative transfusion,
30-day reoperation, 30-day readmission, or discharge disposition.
Conclusion: Low serum albumin levels is associated with a
longer postoperative LOS and a higher incidence of perioperative
complications among patients undergoing vertebral corpectomy and posterior
stabilization for tumor resection. Strategies to improve preoperative
nutritional status in patients undergoing this procedure may improve these
outcome measures.

## 1297

## P520: Risk factors for complications and prolonged lenght of stay in a
single institution retrospective cohort of 336 patients

Luigi Falzetti

1

, Cristiana Griffoni

1

, Giovanni Barbanti Bròdano

1

, Carlotta Cavallari

1

, and Alessandro Gasbarrini

1

1

Department of Spine Surgery, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli,
Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Over the last decades the total number of spine
surgery procedures has increased significantly worldwide. Numerous
advancements in surgical techniques, devices and relevant technological
innovations contributed to this increase. Despite these developments, the
incidence of adverse events (AEs) in spinal surgery is still high and
clinically relevant. The goal of this study is to collect the complications
occurring in a referral centre for spinal surgery, using a reliable method
to capture and classify intra-operative and post-operative complications,
namely SAVES v2 system (Spinal Adverse Events Severity system), and to
identify risk factors related to complications and factors influencing
length of stay (LOS). Material and Methods: All AEs of patients
who underwent spinal surgery at our Department between January 2017 and
January 2018 were retrospectively collected. Patients’ characteristics
including sex, age, comorbidities (Charlson Comorbidity Index), ASA score
and prior exposure to spinal surgery, the type and setting (emergency or
elective) of the surgical procedure were collected. The LOS during the index
admission was calculated for each patient. Analyses for potential risk
factors of complication and prolonged LOS were performed using logistic
regression models. Results were reported as odd ratios with 95% confidence
intervals (95% CI). Results: In the 1-year period from January
2017 to January 2018 a total of 336 patients underwent spinal surgery (223
non-oncological and 113 oncological patients). Two-hundred-ten AEs were
recorded retrospectively (30 intraoperative AEs, 138 early postoperative AEs
and 42 late postoperative). Ninety-nine patients (29.5%) had at least one
complication. Intraoperative complications were more frequent in the
oncological group (23 AEs/113 patients) than in the non-oncological group (7
AEs/223 patients). Early post-operative complications were most of the
recorded complications (138/210, 66%) and were more frequent in the
oncological group than in the non-oncological group (46% vs 38%). The rate
of late post-operative complications was similar in the two groups (15% vs
11%). In the non-oncological group, different factors (age > 75 years
old, anatomical region, surgical time > 3 hours, instrumentation,
previous surgeries, type of surgery) were associated with complications but
only surgical time > 3 hours was confirmed as risk factor for
complications at multivariate analysis (OR=5.0 (95%CI:1.8-13.9)). Surgical
time > 3 hours and the presence of a post-operative complication were
associated with increased LOS, however the presence of a post-operative
complication was the only risk factor for increased LOS at multivariate
analysis (OR = 3.3 (95%CI:1.5-7.1)). In the oncological group, surgical time
> 3 hours, instrumentation, previous surgery were factors associated with
complications but only the presence of previous surgeries was confirmed as
risk factor for complications at multivariate analysis (OR = 3.4
(95%CI:1.3-8.6)). Surgical time > 3 hours and post-operative
complications were confirmed as risk factors for prolonged LOS at
multivariate analysis (respectively: OR = 2.7 (95%CI:1.0-7.3), OR = 3.5
(95%CI:1.3-9.3)) while age > 65 and comorbidity index > 2 were not.
Conclusion: Spine surgery has a relatively high incidence
of complications that can lead to increased morbidity and mortality. Better
categorization of complications and recognition of risk factors for
complications and prolonged LOS are fundamental to improve patients’ safety
and clinical outcomes.

## 1302

## P521: White cord syndrome following posterior decompression and fusion
for severe OPLL and an acute cervical traumatic injury - A case report and
review of literature

Sai Gautham Balasubramanian

1

, Prokopis Annis

1

, and Aditya Dahapute

1

1

Spinal Deformity Unit, The Walton Centre NHS Trust, Liverpool,
United Kingdom

Introduction: White cord syndrome (WCS) refers to the
observation of intramedullary hyperintensity due to edema/ischemia and
swelling on postoperative T2-weighted MRI sequences in the setting of
unexplained neurological deficits after cervical spinal cord decompression.
Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury typically occurs after a cervical decompression
surgery, where a chronically compressed spinal cord is injured by
reperfusion following decompression. Patho-physiologically, WCS/Re-Perfusion
Injury occurs due to oxygen derived free radicals as a result of acute
reperfusion to the previously under-perfused cord or direct trauma from
blood flow itself. Intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring (IONM) can
give early warning and detect neurologic deficits which can allow surgeon to
take necessary measurements apart from preventing medico-legal
complications. In this context, we are sharing our experience of a case with
chronic severe OPLL of cervical cord with an acute traumatic cervical spine
injury who underwent decompressive surgery and developed quadriplegia
postoperatively without any perceptible iatrogenic technical cord trauma,
documented by IONM and post-operative MRI with classical signs of RPI/WCS.
Materials & Methods (Case Description): A 63-year-old
male presented with a low velocity fall at home followed by quadriparesis.
X-ray images on presentation showed C6 fracture through upper end plate with
local kyphosis. The CT scan demonstrated C6 fracture with ossification of
the posterior longitudinal ligament from C2-T3, most severe from C2-4 with
C6 fracture which extended posteriorly to bilateral facet joints in addition
to DISH. MRI images showed there is marked spinal canal stenosis from C2
down to C4 due to ossified posterior longitudinal ligament with intrinsic
signal changes in the cord. On decompression, MEP signals were not present
below C4. Immediate post-op MRI was done to rule out any compressive
pathology. MRI showed T2 hyperintensity of the cord at C3 level which
appeared expanded with a central syrinx. Cord oedema was noted at the C3
level. No evidence of epidural haematoma or other compressive lesion at the
operative site and the diagnosis of WCS/RPI was established based on post-op
MRI findings as there were no other discernible cause of Quadriplegia.
Conclusion:White Cord Syndrome is essentially a diagnosis
of exclusion. Very rarely, patients sustain severe/new neurological deficits
post-operatively attributed to WCS. Unless, this is confirmed
post-operatively with classical MRI signs of intramedullary hyperintensity
and other extrinsic causes of cord injury/compression is ruled out, the
diagnosis should not be invoked. IONM can help us detect such an event
occurring intra-operatively and help us take appropriate measures in a
timely manner. IONM should be the standard of care in such cases of
decompressive surgeries where there is a severe chronic compression of
cervical cord and, decompression will trigger a cascade of re-perfusion
injury to the spinal cord leading to disastrous complications. IONM is also
highly beneficial in alerting the surgeons intra-operatively and also
provides a source of permanent record of what exactly happened
intra-operatively to prevent medico-legal complications. Understanding
WCS/RPI is a valid diagnosis in such circumstances would be helpful in
detailed consenting processes and help prevent an additional surgery for the
patient which might further increase the risks of mortality and
morbidity.

## 1358

## P522: The prognostic role of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio,
platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index on
short- and long-term survival following spinal metastasis surgery

Jessica Ryvlin

1

, Seung Kim

1

, Mousa Hamad

1

, Rafael De La Garza Ramos

1

, Saikiran Murthy

1

, Yaroslav Gelfand

1

, and Reza Yassari

1

1

Department of Neurological Surgery, Montefiore Medical Center/Albert
Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, United States

Introduction: The immune system has been shown to play a
significant role in metastatic tumor progression and prognosis, especially
in the setting of surgical intervention. Specific peripheral inflammatory
markers, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR),
platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index
(SII) have similarly shown promise in predicting both short-term and
long-term mortality in a rage of primary tumor types and interventions.
However, these metrics have not been evaluated in patients with metastatic
spine disease. The purpose of this study was to elucidate the predictive
ability of preoperative NLR, PLR, and SII on postoperative 30-day mortality
and overall survival (OS) amongst patients receiving surgery for spinal
metastases. Methods: This was a single-institution
retrospective cohort study. A total of 153 patients who met inclusion
criteria and received surgical intervention for metastatic spine disease
between April 1, 2012 and April 30, 2022 were identified. Electronic medical
records (EMR) were manually reviewed, and collected variables included
patient demographics, medical comorbidities, oncologic history, lab values
within 30 days prior to surgical intervention, and morbidity details. NLR
(n/l), PLR (p/l), and SII (p*n/l) were manually calculated from preoperative
neutrophil (n), platelet (p), and lymphocyte counts (l). Receiver operator
characteristic (ROC) curves with areas under the curve (AUC) were generated
to determine optimal cutoff values based on Youden’s index. Univariate
logistic regression was used to determine significant predictors of 30-day
mortality, after which variables were included in a multivariate logistic
regression model to control for potential confounders in determination of
odds ratios (OR). The Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test and
multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis were used to
determine hazard ratios (HR) in OS analysis. Results: Cutoff
values to define high NLR, PLR, and SII were calculated to be > 10.2,
> 260, and > 2900, respectively. Overall, 36% (55 of 153) of patients
were found to have high NLR, 46% (70 of 153) had high PLR, and 31% (47 of
153) had high SII. The total 30-day mortality rate was 8.5% (13 of 153).
After controlling for potential confounders such as BMI, ECOG performance
status, and primary cancer type, high preoperative NLR (OR = 5.20; 95% CI
1.21-22.28; p = 0.026) and SII (OR=4.92; 95% CI 1.17-20.63; p = 0.029) were
found to be significantly associated with increased odds of 30-day
postoperative mortality. The median OS time in our population was 25.9
months (95% CI 11.8-40.0 months). After controlling for confounding
variables such as ECOG performance status, primary cancer type,
hypoalbuminemia, and smoking history, only high NLR was found to be
significantly associated with overall mortality (HR = 2.31; 95% CI
1.32-4.03; p = 0.003). PLR was found non-significant in adjusted analysis of
both 30-day mortality and OS. Conclusions: In this study,
preoperative high NLR and SII were found to be independently and
significantly associated with 30-day postoperative mortality. High NLR was
also found to be independently associated with increased risk of poor OS.
These metrics may ultimately be used for surgical planning and outcome
prediction in patients with metastatic spinal tumors; however, further
validation is needed in this population.

3

Center for Musculoskeletal Research, Vanderbilt University Medical
Center, Nashville, TN, United States

Introduction: Posterior cervical spine approaches have been
associated with increased rates of wound complications compared to anterior
approaches. While barbed suture wound closure for lumbar spine surgery has
been shown to be safe and efficacious, there is no literature regarding its
use in posterior cervical spine surgery. In a cohort of patients undergoing
elective posterior cervical spine surgery, we sought to compare
postoperative complication rates between barbed and traditional interrupted
suture closure. Material and Methods: A retrospective review of
demographics, past medical history, and operative and postoperative
variables collected from a prospective registry between 07/2016-07/2020 was
undertaken. All patients 18 years+ undergoing elective posterior cervical
fusion were included. The primary outcome of interest was wound
complications, including surgical site infection (SSI), dehiscence, or
hematoma. In addition, numerical rating scale (NRS) neck pain (NP), NRS arm
pain (AP), Neck Disability Index (NDI), and operative time were collected. A
variety of statistical tests were used to compare the two suture groups.
Results: Of 117 patients undergoing posterior cervical
fusion, 89 (76%) were closed with interrupted suture and 28 (24%) with
barbed suture. The interrupted cohort were more likely to have > 1
comorbidity (p < 0.001), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.013), and coronary
artery disease (p = 0.002). No difference in postoperative wound
complications between interrupted/barbed sutures was observed after
univariate (OR 1.07, 95% CI: 0.27-4.25, p = 0.927) and multivariable
logistic regression analysis (OR 0.77, 95% CI: 0.15-4.00, p = 0.756).
Univariate logistic regression revealed no differences in achieving minimal
clinically important difference (MCID) NRS-NP (OR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.28-1.88, p
= 0.508) or NRS-AP (OR 0.68, 95% CI: 0.25-1.90, p = 0.464) at 3 months
between suture groups. The interrupted suture group was less likely to
achieve MCID NDI at 3 months (OR 0.29, 95% CI: 0.11-0.80, p = 0.016).
Conclusion: The use of barbed sutures, compared to
interrupted sutures, was associated with similar postoperative wound
complication rates, including surgical site infection wound, dehiscence, and
hematoma development. However, while both groups experienced improvement in
PROs at 3-month follow-up, more patients closed with interrupted sutures
achieved MCID NDI. The findings of this study should be taken into
consideration by surgeons in selecting suture type in closing posterior
cervical fusion patients.

## P524: Mechanical complications requiring revision surgery in long fusion

Azmi Hamzaoglu

1

, Hamisi Mraja

, and Meric Enercan

1

Scoliosis-Spine Center Istanbul, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Surgical treatment of adult spinal deformity (ASD)

3.9% of the patients due to S1 screw loosening, rod fracture between L2-L5
levels and L5-S1 pseudoarthrosis despite previous interbody fusion. Adult
spinal deformity patients with Multi rod constructs showed less mechanical
complications than Single rod constructs. Obesity (67.6%), PI-LL mismatch
(%66.6) and osteoporosis (52%) were the most common factors related with
mechanical failures. All patients benefit from revision surgery with
improved clinical outcomes.

Introduction: Cortical bone trajectory (CBT) screws have been

minimal access and did not require removal of the original instrumentation.
Material and Methods: 14 patients with single-level
adjacent segment disease at the cephalad end of previous instrumented lumbar
fusion were studied from 2017 till 2022. They were followed up for a minimum
of 24 months. Parameters studied included clinical signs of instability and

of the preexisting instrumentation. Certainly, a meaningful number of cases
need to be curated and studied in order to realise its true
significance.

## P526: Cervical myelopathy surgical outcomes between two neighboring
medical institutions: a comparative analysis

Nyssa Kantorek

1

 and Carlos Bagley

2

1

Medical School, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center,
Dallas, United States

2

Neurological Surgery, University of Texas Southwestern Medical
Center, Dallas, United States

Introduction: Cervical myelopathy consists of degeneration of
the spinal cord involving deficits in neurological function. Previous
studies compared surgical treatment outcomes in different age groups,
however, demographic and socioeconomic influences have not been explored.
This study investigates the differences in outcomes for patients with
cervical myelopathy at a large urban academic medical center and a tertiary
urban safety net facility based on disease severity, demographics, and
socioeconomic information. Due to the safety net hospital status and care
for a patient population that is largely uninsured or lacking in consistent
primary care, we hypothesize that safety hospital patient patients may
present later and experience poorer surgical outcomes than the tertiary
academic facility. Material and Methods: Using data from the
local Spine Registry and ClinDEN databases for patients surgically treated
at UTSW-affiliated hospitals and Parkland Memorial Hospital, it was
essential to establish a proxy for disease severity since there are none
established in the literature. We discovered that pain may be a reliable
method of measuring disease severity since we found that patients who
experienced more pain tended to have worse surgical outcomes and less
satisfaction with surgery. This was measured with the PROMIS pain scale.
Further analysis consisted of correlative studies using R programming
language to see if race/ethnicity, personal medical history, or
socioeconomic status were associated with either worse pain and/or worse
surgical outcomes. After defining these correlations for the two
institutions individually, we then compared the results to find parallels or
differences. Results: Baseline pain served as an adequate proxy
for disease severity for our analysis as determined by measuring the
correlation between the patient reported pain and survey responses regarding
patient satisfaction with their surgical outcome 3 months post-operatively.
Demographic analysis demonstrated Black patients were both more likely to
present with worse pain before and after surgery than their White or other
race counterparts. Only patients with congestive heart failure experienced
worse pain at baseline prior to surgery compared to those with diabetes,
hypertension, and cancer. Peri-operative complications for patients included
constipation, urinary tract infections, kidney failure, myocardial
infarction, and others. The most common complications were constipation and
UTI as expected due to opioid analgesics and prophylactic antibiotics. The
more serious or life-threatening surgical complications all correlated with
worse baseline pain and arguably more severe presentation.
Conclusion: For a public safety net, such as Parkland
Memorial, many of the patients lack insurance and consistent primary care.
For example, many patients utilize the emergency department to fill
medications instead of treating emergent medical concerns. More research is
required on disparities in spinal surgery to determine if potential
solutions, such as screening, are more beneficial than they are harmful for
the patients with limited access to primary, secondary, and tertiary care.
It is also essential to further understand why Black patients and those with
certain personal medical histories are presenting with later disease.
Studies such as these are essential for the understanding of the patients’
perceptions and experiences with cervical myelopathy given the potential
devastating consequences of this condition.

## P527: Grip strength predicts the occurrence of postoperative proximal
junctional kyphosis in patients with degenerative scoliosis

Xueyu Hu

1

1

Spine Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Air Force Military
Medical University, Xi ' an, China

Background: Previous studies have suggested a correlation
between grip strength and paravertebral muscle volume in spine, with greater
grip strength being associated with greater muscle volume. Studies also
reported a significant decrease in paravertebral muscle volume in patients
with proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), in adult spinal deformity patients,
a significant decrease in cross-sectional area of the T10-L2 paravertebral
muscles was observed in patients who developed PJK. Grip strength has been
shown to be a factor in assessing the prognosis of several spinal disorders.
This study hopes to investigate whether grip strength could be used as a
predictor of the occurrence of PJK after surgery in patients with adult
spinal deformity. Methods: This is a prospective case-control
study, patients aged 40-90 years old suffering from degenerative scoliosis
and treated with posterior fusion internal fixation at the First Affiliated
Hospital of Air Force Military Medical University from March 2020 to
December 2021 were selected according to the following criteria. Inclusion
criteria: (1) Suffering from degenerative scoliosis (Cobb angle > 10° in
the coronal plane) and treated with posterior fusion internal fixation; (2)
At least 2 segments fused; (3) At least 2 years of follow-up. Exclusion
criteria: (1) Age < 40 years; (2) Unable to complete clinical and imaging
follow-up; (3) Hand trauma, and other factors might affect the process of
muscle strength measurement; (4) History of congenital scoliosis, vertebral
slippage, spinal trauma, and other spinal surgery. Patients were divided
into high grip strength group and low grip strength group by clustering
based on the grip strength values measured at admission and comparing the
concordance of baseline levels between the two groups. The incidence of PJK,
ODI, EQ-5D scores, early complications such as pulmonary embolism,
intestinal obstruction, urinary tract infection, transient delirium,
epidural hematoma and neurological dysfunction and late complications such
as screw loosening and pseudoarticular formation were compared.
Results: 395 patients were included, there were no
significant differences between the two groups in terms of age, gender,
surgical segment or duration of surgery. However, significant differences
were observed in the number of co-morbidities. The incidence of
postoperative PJK was significantly lower for patients in high grip strength
group compared to those with low grip strength, but there was no significant
difference in postoperative ODI and EQ-5D scores between the two groups. The
incidence of epidural hematoma was significantly lower in the high grip
strength group, but there was no significant difference in the incidence of
other short-term postoperative complications and long-term pseudarthrosis.
Conclusion: In this study, the high grip strength adult
deformity scoliosis patients showed a significant decrease in the incidence
of postoperative PJK, although the high grip strength group had better
performance in ODI and EQ-5D scores, this difference was not statistically
significant.

st

Orthopedic and Traumatology Clinic, IRCCS - Istituto Ortopedico
Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Aim of the present study is to review the
available literature concerning sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain and degeneration
after lumbosacral fixation to identify prevalence and potential risk
factors. Although numerous factors can predispose patients to SIJ
degeneration and pain various clinical studies indicate lumbosacral
arthrodesis as a major cause. Material and Methods: The
PubMed-MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Registry of Controlled Trials and Embase
Biomedical database were searched. Peer-reviewed comparative studies, cohort
studies, case series studies and case control studies, conducted either in a
retrospective or prospective design, that registered data about SIJ pain and
degeneration after lumbosacral fixation were included. Results:
Twenty-one studies including 2678 patients met the inclusion criteria. The
percentage of SIJ pain after lumbosacral fixation diagnosed with injections

underwent spinal fusion, SIJ pain prevalence was higher when arthrodesis was
fixed compared to floating fusions (59% vs 10%, p value > 0.05). The

patients who underwent spinal arthrodesis than in those who did not (75% vs
38.2%, p value = < 0.05). Conclusion: According to current
evidence, patients who received lumbosacral fixation are at risk of SIJ
pain. Number of fused levels, involvement of pelvis or sacrum in the
arthrodesis area, inadequate lumbosacral sagittal alignment and site of bone
graft harvesting could be possible risk factor leading to sacroiliac
degeneration and pain after lumbar spine fixation that should be
investigated by physicians. However, there is a lack of homogeneity of the
studies that address the problem, therefore, further prospective comparative
studies, with a homogeneous architecture and cohorts are needed.

## P531: Orthostatic intorelance during early mobilization after enhance

Weerasak Singhatanadgige

1

, Panapol Varakornpipat

1

, Vit Kotheeranurak

1

, and Worawat Limthongkul

1

1

Orthopedics, Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok,
Thailand

Introduction: Early postoperative mobilization is essential
after spinal surgery. It can reduce pulmonary complication and DVT.
Postoperative orthostatic intolerance (OI) may limit early recovery or lead
to fainting, falls, and fracture. The prevalence of orthostatic intolerance
has not been reported after minimally invasive lumbar interbody fusion. This
study assessed the hemodynamic response to early mobilization after
minimally invasive lumbar interbody fusion with ERAS program. Material
and Methods: Orthostatic intolerance and blood pressure response
to sitting and standing were evaluated by used non-invasive hemodynamic
monitor devices with a two-difference mobilization protocol at preoperative,
6, 12, 24, 48 hours after surgery in 30 patients undergoing single level
Minimally invasive lumbar interbody fusion with an ERAS regimen. Two
protocols were compared: (A) Patients supine, sit and suddenly stand. (B)
Patients supine, sit and rest 30 seconds and stand. Haemoglobin, fluid
balance, and opioid use were recorded. Systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP)
arterial pressure, heart rate (HR), cardiac output (CO), stroke volume (SV)
and oxygen saturation were measured. Results: In standard
protocol (A), no demonstrated OI before surgery, whereas 8 (27%) patients

24, 48 hours. OI was associated with significantly decreased orthostatic

protocol B showed significantly decreased rate of OI at 6 hours compared
protocol A (p < 0.001). Postoperative haemoglobin concentration and
opioid dose was not associated OI. The Clinical outcomes were significantly
improved in all patients. All patients were discharged to home on
postoperative day 3 without complications or readmission.
Conclusion: Twenty-seven percent of patients have OI when
start ambulate at 6 hours after surgery. We suggest that the patients should
rest at sitting position at least 30 seconds before start walking. Start
ambulation after 12 hours is safe without demonstration of OI.

## P532: Paramedian approach versus median approach lumbar puncture: a
systematic review and meta-analysis protocol

Yuan-Dong Zhuang

1

, Fenfen Yao

2

, Xuanjie Chen

2

, Yihang Lin

2

, and Zhengqiong Lai

2

1

Neurosurgery, Fujian Medical University Union Hospital, Fuzhou,
China

2

Basic Medical College, Fujian Medical University, Fuzhou,
China

Introduction: Lumbar puncture is one of the most common
neurosurgical invasive procedures in modern medicine. It is widely and
frequently used by neurosurgery, anesthesiology, pediatrics, and other
departments. However, the application of lumbar puncture in the clinic,
especially the success rate during surgery, has not yet had a clear
technology with the highest success rate. By searching for relevant clinical
trials, we found that lumbar puncture through different approaches has a
significant impact on the experience of doctors and patients during surgery.
This study will review the randomized controlled trial of the lumbar
paramedian approach and compare it with the lumbar median approach.
Material and Methods: A detailed search will be conducted
of Web of Science, Pubmed, Cochrane, and EMBASE without language or
publication type restrictions. The retrieval task is basically completed.
Patients of any age and sexuality will be included in our study. All
analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Results:
We take the number of needle passes as our main results. The secondary
outcomes included the following: the number of attempts, time taken to
identify landmarks, blood tap, periprocedural pain score, and patient's
discomfort during the spinal procedure radicular pain. This study will be
analyzed by calculating the Relative Risk (RR) with a corresponding 95%
Confidence Interval (CI). For continuous outcomes, the weighted mean
difference with 95% CI will be calculated. If a continuous outcome is
reported as a median, we will assume a normal distribution and consider the
median as a mean. If measures of dispersion are reported as a range, 95% CI,
or standard error of the mean, we will calculate the standard deviation (SD)
by using relevant formulae outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic
Reviews of Interventions. Conclusion: Four reviewers will
independently perform a quality assessment. The Cochrane Collaboration’s
tool will be used to assess the risk of selection, performance, detection,
attrition, reporting, and other biases among included randomized trials. If
there is insufficient information provided to make a judgment, we will
categorize the study as having an unclear risk of bias and the original
study authors will be contacted for further information. Trials with one or
more high-risk components will be judged as having an overall high risk of
bias. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale will be used to assess observational
studies on selection, comparability, and exposure. Studies that receive at
least one star in every domain will be categorized as being of high quality.
Any disagreements during the quality assessment will be resolved through
discussion and consensus. If necessary, consult a fifth reviewer. Results
from this study are expected to significantly change clinical practice. By
comprehensively examining the evidence on paramedian approach in comparison
to median approach for lumbar puncture, this review is expected to inform
clinicians on which approach to use for procedures to minimize patient
suffering and improve the success rate.

## P533: Hyperacute postoperative thoracic spine epidural haematoma and it's
uncomplicated spontaneous resolution - a case report

Stjepan Dokuzovic

1

, Jure Pavesic

1

, Stipe Corluka

1

, and Vide Bilic

1

1

Spinal Surgery Division, Traumatology Department, University
Hospital Centre Sestre Milosrdnice, Zagreb, Croatia

Introduction: Spinal epidural haematoma, whether spontaneous or
post-surgical, can be a devastating complication if not promptly recognized
and treated. This condition often requires primary decompression and
drainage (if spontaneous haematoma) or revision surgery (if it is a
postoperative complication). Anterior localization of a thoracic level
postoperative haematoma may require revision surgery, which is significantly
more demanding and more neurologically risky than the initial surgery due to
the possibility of causing further “hits” to the compressed spinal cord.
Material and Methods: We present the case of a young
patient operated on for routine stabilization of a 2 level thoracic vertebra
fractures (Th6 and Th12) who developed total paralysis due to a
postoperative hyperacute epidural haematoma localized anterior to the cord,
however the course was quickly spontaneously reversed prior to revision
surgery. This misfortune was thankfully spontaneously resolved prior to
revision surgery simply by elevating the upper body and having the haematoma
“drain” itself more caudally down the canal where there is more space.
Results: The patient did not have any medical risk factors
for developing such a haematoma postoperatively, though developed a
haematoma regardless, either from the fracture line or from an epidural
venous bleed. Roughly an hour after surgery, complete paralysis was noted.
Upon radiological confirmation by emergency MRI scanning, we elevated the
upper part of the body to prevent cranial migration of the haematoma, and
complete spontaneous resolution ensued over the next 45 minutes.
Conclusion: In cases of epidural haematoma development with
neurological impairment, it is not always necessary to perform emergency
revision surgery. When the bleeding is hyperacute and not coagulated, it may
be possible to let it spontaneously disperse itself along the length of the
canal, thus minimizing its local compressive effect. If prompt neurological
recovery is not witnessed, the option of emergency revision must still be
available.

## P534: Prognostic factors for effective spinal cord stimulation therapy

Kwan Ho Park

1

, Ju chul Yang

, and Tae Wan Kim

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, VHS Medical Center, Seoul, South
Korea

Introduction: Post-surgical spine syndrome (PSSS) is a clinical
entity, defined as persistent or recurrent back and/or leg pain after spine
surgery. Various therapeutic approaches are currently used to treat
refractory chronic pain after spinal surgery. A multidisciplinary approach
is unlikely to benefit from further formal surgical intervention. Surgery
benefits a limited number of conditions, mainly root compression and
instability. It is difficult to predict how and where evidence will lead the
field over the next 5 to 10 years. Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) techniques
via a implanted dorsal column neurostimulator is gaining popularity owing to
its substantial superiority over conventional medical management and/or pain
intervention. These approaches may provide a rescue treatment for patients
who have previously failed surgical and less invasive therapies, offering
relief to a patient population among the most difficult to treat. We assess
and report on which patient groups are effective for SCS. Material and
Methods: Thirty four patients had intractable chronic back and/or
leg pain with a diagnosis of PSSS. All patients who underwent SCS
implantation were retrospectively reviewed. Preoperative mean Visual
Analogue Scale (VAS) score for leg was 7.6. SCS trial was performed to
evaluate patient’s response to SCS procedure. We placed percutaneous or
paddle leads depending on neurological symptoms. SCS system was implanted in
patients with pain reduction more than 50% compared to pre-trial procedure.
The mean follow-up was 56 months. Results: Thirty patients were
men and four were women. The mean age was 58 years. The patients with leg
pain responded favorably to SCS. Back pain of patients did not respond well.
SCS was less effective in patients with surgical indication, neural
compressive lesions or spinal cord lesion. Preoperative mean VAS score for
leg was 7.6 and postoperative VAS score was 4.0. Conclusion:
SCS is an effective treatment option for neuropathic pain of PSSS in the
absence of a viable surgery. It is mainly effective for patients with leg
pain and no neural compressive lesion. Careful patient selection is most
important for the success of SCS therapy.

## P535: Chance fracture pattern presenting in proximal junctional failure:
a case series

Shea Comadoll

, Kenneth Holton

, Jason Haselhuhn

, Paul Soriano

, David Polly

, Michael Schmitz

University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States

Introduction: Chance-type fracture is a kind of proximal
junctional failure (PJF) that may present with instability, neurologic

institution who presented with a specific acute Chance-type proximal
junctional failure of the upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) that occurred

describe the radiographic features of this Chance-fracture variant, its

with a specific fracture pattern of the UIV. All index surgeries were

significant correction of preoperative TL junction kyphosis. The reading
radiologists did not identify the fracture on 73% of radiographs and 46% of
CT scans. Thirteen of the 15 patients were treated with an extension of
fusion. Pedicle screws at the fracture level were salvaged by changing to an
anatomic trajectory. Conclusion: This case series reports a
Chance-type fracture pattern of the UIV that is difficult to detect on plain
films and is a unique cause of PJF. Continued pain at 6-12 weeks, along with
lateral radiographs showing increased proximal junctional angle and
cephalocaudal pedicle widening at the UIV, should raise suspicion about this
unique fracture pattern. Obtaining a CT scan is highly recommended. Low bone
density, LL or LLL overcorrection, and selection of lower thoracic UIV in
the setting of significant TL junction correction may contribute to fracture
risk.

## P536: The use of high-dose tranexamic acid in spine surgery: an analysis

## P537: Does the use of a smoke evacuation device reduce smoke exposure in
the OR? A prospective study

James Hall

1

, Joshua Eisenberg

1

, Alex Coffman

1

, Natalie Glass

1

, Catherine Olinger

1

, Cassim Igram

1

, and Andrew Pugely

1

1

Orthopedics and Rehabilitation, University of Iowa, Iowa City,
United States

Introduction: It is widely accepted that inhalation of smoke,
specifically the particulate matter therein, can cause adverse health
effects. In June 2018, Rhode Island was the first state to enact a law
mandating the use of a smoke evacuation system in the operating room. Nine
more states followed suit in 2020. The presence of dangerous compounds in
surgical smoke is well established in the literature, but few have
investigated the utility of smoke evacuation in spine surgery. With
increased scrutiny on surgical smoke levels, these devices should be further
studied. Therefore, the primary aim of our study was to evaluate the
efficacy of two smoke evacuation systems in reducing surgical smoke levels
in spine surgery. Secondary aims of our study were to determine patient,
facility, or equipment factors that may influence surgical smoke levels.
Material and Methods: Consecutive patients undergoing spine
surgery at a single institution had surgical smoke levels measured utilizing
the PCE instruments particle counter (PCE-PCO 2). Room set-up was
standardized such that the particle counter was positioned on an IV pole
nearest the anesthesiologist. Smoke particle levels were measured during the
first hour of the procedure. The two smoke evacuators used were a smoke
evacuator pencil (SEP) with suction in line with a cautery tip, and a para
incisional vacuum (PIV) that utilizes a large suction tube affixed adjacent
to the wound. The evacuators were compared to one another and to a control
group. We evaluated the relationships between evacuation systems (SEP, PIV,
control) and a) average b) peak levels of 0.3 µm particle size and c)
overall particle count. We then evaluated for relationships with patient,
room and/or surgery factors. Results: In total, 117 patients
were included in the study. SEP was employed in 36 cases, PIV in 43, and no
evacuator in 38. Groups did not vary regarding patient demographics or room
characteristics. There was a significant reduction in average 0.3 µm, peak
0.3 µm, and average overall particle levels when using either the SEP or
PIV. SEP reduced average 0.3 µm, peak 0.3 µm, and average overall particle
levels by 55%, 55%, and 54% respectively. PIV reduced those levels by 68%,
86%, and 72% respectively. Additionally, a significant reduction in peak 0.3
µm particle levels was noted with PIV when compared to SEP. Multivariable
analysis revealed significance in room size and number of operative levels.
Specifically, a smaller operating room and greater number of operative
levels both independently contributed to increased levels of surgical smoke
measured. Significance was defined as p < 0.05. Conclusion:
Our results show that both the SEP and PIV effectively reduce operating room
smoke levels during spine surgery. Furthermore, the PIV shows superiority in
reducing peak smoke levels. This study supports the use of a smoke
evacuation device to reduce surgical smoke levels and thus reduce the
potential associated health risk to operating room personnel.

## P538: Management of lower cervical spine fracture - dislocation
associated with severe traumatic brain injury: case report and surgical
treatment for an uncommon lesion association

Ghassen Gader

1

, Mohamed Amine Gharbi

2

, Mouadh Nefiss

2

, Mohamed Badri

1

, Mohamed Zouaghi

1

, Ramzi Bouzidi

2

, Ihsen Zammel

1

, and Anis Tebourbi

2

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Trauma and Burns Center, Ben Arous,
Tunisia

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Mongi Slim Hospital, La Marsa,
Tunisia

Introduction: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause
for death and severe functional impairment in young adults. Outcome for
severe TBIs is worse when associated to other extracranial traumatisms.
Simultaneous TBI and cervical spine injury (CSI) occurs in 4–8% of TBIs.
CSIs occurring concurrently with severe head injuries deeply worsen the
patient’s condition because of potentialization and occultation of the
traumatic lesions, but also because of some therapeutic situations in which
the management of a lesion may worsen the other. Material and
Methods: We report the case of a patient operated for a TBI
through a decompressive craniectomy, and who needed management for a
fracture-dislocation of the lower cervical spine. Based on this case, we
went through a review of associations between head and cervical spine
trauma, with particular highlights on controversial therapeutic situations
like ours. Case description: We report the case of a 26
years-old male patient, victim of an accidental fall from the roof of his
house, which corresponded to a 6 meters height. He was immediately
transferred to the emergency department. Initial physical exam found a
prostrate patient with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 12/15, with incomplete
tetraplegia. Brain CT scan showed a temporo-parietal fracture associated to
a right hemispheric epidural hematoma with a maximal thickness of 3.2 cm.
Cervical spine CT scan showed comminuted bilateral facet
fracture-dislocation C6 to C7 responsible for an 8 mm antelisthesis. The
patient quickly developed a comatose state with a GCS that decreased to
4/15, associated to a right anisocoria. He was intubated, sedated, and
placed under mechanical ventilation. Regarding the neurologic distress,
surgical management for the intracranial lesion was decided. But viewing the
cervical fracture-dislocation that was prone to worsen on head positioning
prior to the hematoma's evacuation, the patient underwent at first a
reduction and realignment of the cervical spine. This approach was mandatory
as neurosurgical and orthopedic departments were not located at the same
institution, thus the necessity to immobilize the cervical spine before any
transfer. The reduction was processed through closed manual maneuvers by
axial traction and hyperextension. Afterwards, patient was transferred to
the neurosurgical department where the hematoma was evacuated through a
decompressive craniectomy. Three days after, the patient underwent a C6-C7
interbody fusion through an anterior cervical approach using an iliac crest
bone autograft. An anterior cervical screw-plate was used for stabilization.
Reduction was verified peroperatively by fluoroscopy. The outcome was
unfavorable as the patient died three weeks later in the follows of a severe
ventilator-associated pneumonia. Conclusions: TBIs and CSIs are
frequently associated in the course of polytraumas. Head and cervical spine
injuries are systematically assessed in all polytraumas followed by a
comatose state, taking in count that their association may result in
increased mortality and morbidity, an impairment of the quality of life, and
hindering the rehabilitation process.

## P539: Treatment strategy for pedicle fractures of the C2 axis

Jong-Beom Park

1

, Dong-Gune Chang

2

, and Young-Yul Kim

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, The Catholic University of Korea College od
Medicine, Uijeongbu-si, South Korea

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Inje University Sanggye Paik Hospital,
Uijeongbu-si, South Korea

Introduction: C2 pedicle fracture (PF) is not an uncommon
injury1-7 but have been less focused than dens fractures or Hangman’s
fractures. The anatomical structure of the C2 PF differs significantly from
other pedicles of the same cervical spine as well as the lumbar and thoracic
vertebrae. Due to its distinct anatomical features, spine surgeons often do
not understand the exact location of the C2 pedicle and confuse C2 PF with
pars interarticularis fracture. Also, little information is available about
the characteristics and treatment strategy for C2 PFs. We sought to
investigate the characteristics of C2 PF and to propose appropriate
treatment strategy. Material and Methods: A total of 49
patients with C2 PF were included in this study. We divided these patients
into unilateral and bilateral C2 PFs group. The incidence rates and
characteristics of other associated C2 and C2-3 injuries and other cervical
injuries were evaluated. In addition, treatment methods and outcomes were
analyzed. Results: Twenty-two patients had unilateral C2 PFs
and 27 patients had bilateral C2 PFs. Among the cases of unilateral C2 PF,
all patients had one or more other C2 fractures and 20 patients (90.9%) had
one or two C2 body fractures. Meanwhile, among the cases of bilateral C2 PF,
all patients had two or more other C2 fractures and one or two C2 body
fractures. In unilateral C2 PFs, 3 patients with C2-3 anterior slip or
adjacent cervical spine (C1-3) injury underwent surgery and 19 patients
(86.4%) were treated with conservative methods. In bilateral C2 PFs, 3
patients with C2-3 anterior slip or SCI at C2-3 underwent surgery and 24
patients (88.9%) were treated with conservative methods.
Conclusion: Our results showed that C2 PF do not occur
alone and are always accompanied by other associated C2 injuries. C2 PF
should generally be thought of as a more complex fracture type than
Hangman's fracture or dens fracture. In spite of the complex fracture
characteristics, most C2 PF can be managed with conservative treatment.
However, surgical treatments should be considered if the C2 PF are
accompanied by the C2-3 anterior slip and adjacent cervical spine
injury.

## P540: Intraoperative sensory signals predict prognosis for patients with
traumatic cervical spinal cord injury

John Renehan

1

, Ivan Ye

1

, Alexandra Thomson

1

, Daniel Cavanaugh

1

, Eugene Koh

1

, Daniel Gelb

1

, Bryan Ferguson

2

, Bizhan Aarabi

3

, Steven Ludwig

1

, and Vache Hambardzumyan

1

1

Spine Surgery Division, Orthopaedics

2

Anesthesiology

3

Neurosurgery, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore,
United States

Introduction: In patients with traumatic cervical spinal cord
injury (tCSCI), the potential role of intraoperative neuromonitoring as a
prognostic tool has been insufficiently studied. This study aimed to
determine if detectable signals during intraoperative neuromonitoring
portend a greater likelihood of recovery for patients with tCSCI.
Materials and Methods: Patients who underwent decompression
and surgical fixation following tCSCI were retrospectively reviewed through
previously prospectively collected data from the Surgical Timing in Acute
Spinal Cord Injury Study (STASCIS). Improvement in ASIA motor score and AIS
grade conversion rates at final follow-up were compared between patients
with detectable intraoperative neuromonitoring somatosensory evoked
potential (SSEP) signals and those without detectable signals.
Results: A total of 49 patients had intraoperative
neuromonitoring. Patients with incomplete tCSCI had detectable lower
extremity SSEPs more often than patients with complete tCSCI (56.3% vs.
23.5%, p = 0.028). There was no difference in detectable upper extremity
SSEPs between complete and incomplete tCSCI (65.6% vs. 58.8%, p = 0.638). Of

extremity SSEPs had ASIA motor scores similar to the non-detectable cohort
on admission (21.5 vs. 16.2, p = 0.609) but higher ASIA motor scores at
final follow-up (57.5 vs. 27.1, p = 0.041). Of the 32 patients with
incomplete SCI, there was no difference in grade conversion or motor scores
between detectable and non-detectable SSEP cohorts.
Conclusions: The presence of upper extremity SSEP signals
in patients who present with complete tCSCI portends greater improvement in
ASIA motor scores and likelihood of AIS grade conversion at final
follow-up.

## P541: Outcomes in patients with vertebral injury after blunt cervical
spine trauma

Romil Shah

1

, Devender Singh

2

, Ayane Rossano

1

, and Eeric Truumees

2

1

Orthopedics, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, United
States

2

Spine, Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United
States

Introduction: Vertebral artery injury (VAI) occurs in almost 1%
of all blunt trauma hospital admissions. No large study has been conducted
investigating outcomes of VAI in blunt cervical trauma. Aim:
The aim of this study was to evaluate 1-year outcomes in patients with blunt
cervical spine trauma with vertebral artery injuries.
Materials/Methods: Data from the National Trauma Data Bank
(NTDB) of adult patients with cervical vertebral, ligamentous, or
neurological trauma from 2016 and 2017 were analyzed. Patients who died
within 3 days of admission were excluded. Demographic, injury specific
information (mechanism, severity), patient health information, and a
variable indicating the presence of vertebral artery injury were collected
as explanatory variables. Response variables collected included development
of adverse events (DVT/PE, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, hemorrhage,
or neurological deficit) length of stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU)
LOS, and unplanned ICU admission or surgical procedure. Multivariable
regression was used to calculate the risk-adjusted effect of vertebral
artery injury on the presence of adverse events and unplanned events as well
as its relationship with LOS and ICU LOS. Results: 128,908
patients with cervical trauma were reviewed, of which 5,300 had VAI. Of the
patients with VAI, 187 (3.5%) patients had a MI, 156 (2.9%) had a PE/DVT,
196 (3.7%) had a stroke, 1392 (26.3%) had neurologic injury, and 443 (8.4%)
had an unplanned operative procedure or ICU admission. After
risk-adjustment, VAI was associated with a greater than 2-fold increased
risk of increased LOS and ICU LOS (p < 0.001), as well as greater than a
2-fold increased risk of MI, PE/DVT, stroke, and neurologic injury (p <
0.001). Conclusions: Vertebral artery injury in cervical trauma
is associated with increased adverse events and length of stay in the ICU
and in the hospital. Trauma providers should be aware of these increased
risks when treating patients with VAI in cervical trauma.

## P545: Tear drop fractures of the axis: management and treatment of 8

Introduction: Teardrop fractures of C2 are extremely rare. It is

of lower cervical spine. Our objective was to assess the clinical and
radiological result of patients treated for tear drop fracture of the axis.

from 2000 to 2021, including patient who were treated for a tear drop
fracture of C2. We excluded patients who had a multilevel spine injury and

management. Treatment can be conservative if there are no signs of
instability. Surgical management is dedicated to instable fracture or cases
with a big fragment. The outcome is usually satisfying.

## P546: A rare association of two mechanisms in axis fracture

Jlidi Mohamed

1

, Walid Bouaicha

1

, Mohamed Hedi Gharbi

1

, Mouldi Lamouchi

1

, Ayachi Montassar

1

, and Selim Daas

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology Departments, Hospital of Mohamed Taher
Maamouri, Tunisia

Introduction: Upper cervical spine traumas are a serious injury
due to its neurological consequences. They are life-threatening fractures
and have a poor functional outcome, due to its short-, medium- and long-term
complications. C2 fractures are the most frequent. They are the subject of
several descriptive classifications according to the mechanism of injury.
The case that we describe in this work associates two different fracture
entities, either in the location of the fracture line and by the mechanism
of the lesion. These two entities combine to create an unusual fracture.
Material and Methods: A 64-year-old man, with no previous
pathological history, was brought to the emergency department by the civil
protection following a 2-meter fall. The exact mechanism of the trauma was
difficult to precise because the patient had a post-traumatic amnesia. On
admission clinical examination shows forehead dermabrasion, he complained of
both wrists and neck pain. The neurological exam was normal. Peripheral
examination showed a deformity of both wrists without skin or vascular
lesions. A neurosurgery emergency was eliminated. X-rays and CT scan of
cervical spine showed bi-pedicular fracture and "Tear-Drop" fracture, both
on the C2 vertebra with a bifocal fracture of the posterior arch of C1.
X-rays of both wrists showed a bilateral fracture with posterior
displacement of the distal radius. Non-operative treatment was decided and
consisted of immobilization with a five-support neck brace (shoulder,
sternum, back, occiput, lower jaw) for four months until consolidation.
Percutaneous pinning under axillary block was indicated for the fracture of
both wrists. Results: The neurological examination remains
unchanged, and vertical position was allowed on the fourth day
post-traumatic. Dynamic X-rays were requested as soon as the neck brace was
removed and did not show any instability of the cervical spine. Cervical CT
scan at 4 months post-trauma confirmed the consolidation. After 24 months,
the patient did not complain about neck pain and dynamic X-rays of the did
not show any instability. Conclusion: The case we report thus
combined two previously separately described entities with different causal
mechanisms. On one hand, a pedicle fracture of C2, supposedly produced by a
mechanism of sudden hyperextension, and on the other hand, a "Tear-Drop"
fracture of the same vertebra, classically caused by a mechanism of axial
compression. Regarding treatment, we took into account the following
parameters:
- The age of the patient
- The absence of neurological signs
- The absence of concrete clinical data on the long-term evolution of this
type of deformity
- The absence of local kyphosis of C2 on C3
- The fact that the fracture of the antéro-inferior corner of the vertebral
body is secondary to a sudden tensioning of the anterior longitudinal
ligament. In this case, the injury was considered stable and treated
non-surgically.

Luiz Claudio Rodrigues

In the present study we analyzed retrospectively patients who suffered from

vertebral level of lesion, surgically addressed spine levels, year of
occurrence, type of surgery performed, cause of trauma, neurological status
according to the Frankel scale and incidence of immediate complications. The
main cause of cervical spine trauma are motor vehicle accidents, followed by
high falls. Most cases of patients were male (72.7%). O principal fator
causador de fraturas de coluna cervical são os acidentes com veículos
automotores, seguidos de queda de altura. A maioria dos casos ocorreu em
pacientes do gênero masculino (72,7%). It appears that prevention measures
can be taken to diminish the severity of cervical spine trauma and thus,
sequels and rehabilitation time of its victims, specially in big urban
centres on which mobility is mainly by cars, the most related factor to this
type of lesion.

## P549: Delayed tramatic atlantoaxial sponylptosis with type II odontoid

Rakesh Kumar

1

 and John Small

1

1

Adventhealth Carrolwood, United States

Introduction: Traumatic Type 2 odontoid fracture is often
diagnosed early utilizing various criteria after injury. Failure to diagnose
and treat appropriately may prove fatal and the risk is significantly higher
in the elderly. Spondyloptosis in this context is rare. Neurologic deficits
often follow the subluxation. Occipital neuralgia was the presenting symptom
in our patient. This led to the diagnosis. Case Report:
83-year-old woman with ground-level fall hitting the back of the head 6
months earlier was discharged after normal head CT. Progressively increasing

utilization of criteria to exclude cervical spine injury is important.

instability; as is well recognized in rheumatoid arthritis. Open reduction
is often feasible with direct atlantoaxial joint manipulation. As the
posterior arch of Atlas is often intact, this may be used for traction and
reduction avoiding direct force on the lateral mass screws.
