## P550: Surgical treatment of odontoid fractures: surgical strategy and
outcomes of a series of transarticular C1-C2 screw fixation by Magerl's
technique

Sofia Caldeira Dantas

1 2

, André D. Carvalho

1

, Arnaldo Sousa

1

, and Ricardo Rodrigues-Pinto

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Centro Hospitalar Universitário do
Porto, Spinal Unit (UVM), Portugal

2

Department of Orthopaedics, Hospital do Litoral Alentejano,
Portugal

Introduction: Odontoid fractures account for nearly 20% of
cervical spine injuries and, in the elderly, are associated with a high
incidence of nonunion, morbidity and mortality. While these are frail
patients, most studies suggest that elderly surgical treatment should be
offered to those with type II and unstable type III fractures. However, this
approach is still controversial and the ideal surgical technique is not
clearly defined. Material and Methods: This was a retrospective
analysis of a consecutive series of elderly patients with odontoid fractures
submitted to transarticular C1-C2 screw fixation by Magerl’s technique
between 2008 and 2022. Clinical and radiological data were analyzed, as well
as complications and reinterventions during follow-up. Results:
Eighteen cases were included (9 males and 9 females). The last four cases
were performed through a percutaneous approach, while the initial were
performed through an open approach. The average patient age was 75.8 years
old (min. 56; max. 88 years). Most cases were type II fractures that
resulted from a direct trauma (motor vehicle accidents or falls from
height). Seventeen percent presented with some degree of neurological
impairment at admission. The average surgical time was 116.5 ± 40.2 minutes.
No intraoperative complications were reported. The median time of hospital
stay was 9.9 days (min. 2; max. 76 days). From the initial 18 patients 5
were lost to follow-up. The median follow-up time for the remaining patients
was 256 days (min: 64; max: 944). During that time, complications
(infection, neurological impairment, cardiovascular pathologies, respiratory
distress, malpositioning and/or pseudarthrosis) were only reported in 1
patient (7.7%), in which a reintervention was required due to screw
malpositioning. Moreover, 2 patients (15.4%) self‐reported neck pain and
disability. Conclusion: Surgical treatment of odontoid
fractures in the elderly is still controversial. This study demonstrates
that transarticular C1-C2 screw fixation by Magerl’s technique is a viable
technique for the surgical treatment of odontoid fractures in the
elderly.

## P551: Failure factors of orthopedic treatement of a tear-drop C2
fracture: a case report and review of the literature

Safouen Ben Brahim

1

, Mzid Ahmed

1

, Khalil Habboubi

1

, ben mohamed oussama

1

, Hassen Makhlouf

1

, and mondher mestiri

1

1

Adult Orthopedic Departement Pr Mestiri, Mohamed Taib Kassab,
Mannouba, Tunisia

Introduction: Extension teardrop fractures of the axis are
extremely rare cervical spinal fractures. It’s a fracture involving the
triangular fragment at the anteroinferior corner of the vertebral body
following a hyper-extension mechanism. The stability of this lesion and the
choice between orthopedic or surgical treatment remain debated in the
literature. We report a case of a neglected tear-drop fracture of the axis
which was complicated by neurological disorders of both upper limbs.
Case Presentation: Our patient is a 55-year-old woman, with
no medical history, who was the victim of a domestic accident. She had a
3-metre fall, causing polytrauma: cranial, axial and peripheral. The
clinical examination showed complete paraplegia ASIA "A" level T5 associated
with cervico-dorsalgia without neurological deficit of the upper limbs.
Initial investigations showed a complex- fracture of T5 with recoil of the
posterior wall and a C2 tear-drop fracture with posterior signal
abnormalities on the MRI. The course of action was to perform a laminectomy
with posterior synthesis from T3 to T9. For the tear-drop fracture,
orthopedic treatment was initiated. The patient did not recover the
neurological deficit postoperatively (permanent paraplegia). After 3 months,
the patient was referred to us due to the appearance of progressive
neurological disorders of both upper limbs. Investigations showed a vicious
callus of C2 tear-drop fracture with signs of instability and newly spinal
cord signal abnormalities in relation to C2. Results: Given
this neurotoxicity, it was decided to perform a posterior decompression
associated with an occipito-cervical fusion. The postoperative course was
simple. Neurological recovery of the upper limbs was noted.
Conclusion: Although the radiological appearance of a tear
drop fracture of C2 appears simple, it may conceal potentially serious
posterior injuries. most patients with an extension tear drop fracture of
the axis can be treated conservatively but large fragment size, displacement
or angulation, intervertebral disc injury, neurologic deficit, or signs of
instability are reasonable indications for surgical treatment.

Methods: We present the case of a 31-year-old patient with a

at first conservatively. Results: At 6 weeks follow-up we
diagnosed an occipito-cervical subluxation and a displacement of the lateral

## 1427

## P553: Clinical outcomes of surgery for patients with spinal cord injury
aged 75 and older

Takashi Chikawa

1

, Toshihiko Matsumura

1

, and Ayaka Hashimoto

1

1

Orthopedic Surgery, Tokushima Prefecture Naruto Hospital, Naruto,
Japan

Introduction: The population aged 75 and older accounts for
13.3% in our country. The incidence of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI)
will increase as elderly population continue to increase. Although it is
accepted that clinical outcome of surgery for SCI in elderly is lower than
that of younger subject because of greater comorbidity burden, there is a
paucity of evidence in clinical outcome of surgery in elderly SCI patient.
The purpose of this study is to investigate clinical outcome of traumatic
SCI patients underwent surgery and to compare with those of younger patient.
Materials and Methods: From 2019 to 2021, a total of 38
traumatic SCI patient were treated at our hospital. They were divided into
two groups. Group A consisted of 21 patients aged 75 years and older and
group B consisted of 17 patients younger than 75 years. In group A, there
were 10 male and 11 female and their mean age was 83 years. Ten patients had
cervical SCI, 9 patients had thoracic SCI and 2 patients had lumbar spinal
and cauda equina injury. In group B, there were 14 male and 3 female and
their mean age was 58 years. Six patients had cervical SCI, 6 patients had
thoracic SCI, and 5 patients had lumbar spinal and cauda equina injury. All
patients in group A had comorbidities such as dementia, Parkinson’s
diseases, diabetes, malignant tumor, cardiovascular diseases and chronic
renal failure. On the other hand, Six patients of 17 patients had no
comorbidities in group B. Decompression was performed in 2 patients and
decompression and fusion were performed in 19 patients in group A.
Decompression was performed in 3 patients and decompression and fusion were
performed in 14 patients in group B. In the current study, time from injury
to surgery, time from hospitalization to surgery and Frankel grade before
and after surgery were extracted from the electric medical record.
Results: In group A and B, time from injury to surgery was
8.7 days and 8.1, time from hospitalization to surgery was 4.8 days and 5.1
days, respectively. There was no statistically significant difference
between both groups. Of 21 patients in group A, the Frankel grade before
surgery was B in 3, C in 12 and E in 3. At follow-up, C in 1, D in 13 and E
in 7, all showed improvement by one grade or more. Of 17 patients in group
B, the Frankel grade before surgery was C in 9, D in 1 and E in 7. At
follow-up, D in 3 and E in 14. Improvement in Frankel grade of group B
significantly superior than that of group A. Conclusion:
Improvements of Frankel grade in elderly SCI patients was inferior than
younger patient. Factors including preoperative comorbidity burden, lack of
physiologic reverse by aging and feeling capacity of the spinal cord might
affect the clinical outcome.

## P554: Post-traumatic cervical epidural hematoma in children

Ghorbel Mohamed

1

, Ines Cherif

1

, Daoud Ahmed

1

, Kolsi Fatma

1

, Bel Mabrouk Yassin

1

, and Boudouara Zaher

1

1

Neurosurgery, Habib Bourguiba Hospital, Sfax, Tunisia

Introduction: Cervical epidural hematoma is a rare phenomenon in
children. It was first described in 1963 and most of cases are spontaneous.
However, trivial injury of the cervical spine without any lesions on bone
structures can sometimes cause a serious damage of the neurovascular
elements leading to an hematoma. This pathology requires a quick diagnosis
and emergent treatment consisting on the evacuation of the hematoma which
provide a good prognosis. Material and Methods: We present a
case of a patient who was treated for cervical epidural hematoma in the
department of neurosurgery in the Habib Bourguiba hospital, in Sfax,
Tunisia. Results: We present a case of a 12 years-old girl who
was admitted in our service for torticollis, cervico brachial neuralgia and
brachial weakness. Three weeks before admission she suffered a neck injury
while falling from the bed. On admission, the neurologic exam showed a
neurologic deficit with left brachial paresis. X-ray of the cervical spine
was done with no signs of traumatic lesion. MRI of the cervical spine
revealed the presence of compressive epidural hematoma spanning C3 to C7
which was evacuated urgently after a large Laminoplasty within « open door
technique ». There was a large collection of old blood which was
liquefied making its evacuation easy. Postoperatively, the patient presented
an excellent recovery and the general motor strength of the arm was
regained. Conclusion: Cervical epidural hematoma is quite rare
in children with incidence of 0.1 per 100. Adequate neurological
examination, diagnostics and urgent surgical intervention are of paramount
importance for accomplishing good results. Early and persistent
rehabilitation are the condition for achieving maximal recovery.

## P555: Optimal segmental sagittal alignment for anterior

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

, Ievgenii Slynko

Introduction: Vertical cylindrical mesh implant and anterior
rigid plate is the most common combination for performing subaxial cervical
spine anterior decompression and fusion surgery. Despite the considerable
clinical experience, there is currently no consensus on optimal correction
of the height of the operated spinal motion segment and the formation of a
certain segmental profile in the surgical intervention zone. The purpose of
our study was to improve the state of sagittal kyphosis of the operated
segment in the long-term postoperative period in patients who underwent
anterior subaxial cervical fusion. Material and Methods: We

physiological curvature of the operated segment in the long-term
postoperative period. The obtained data have both clinical and experimental-
biomechanical confirmation.

## P556: Number of screws changes the stress-stain state when using
vertebral body replacing implants for anterior subaxial cervical
reconstruction

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Michael Karpinsky

3

, and Oleksandr Yaresko

3

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

3

Biomechanical Laboratory, Sytenko Institute of Spine and Joint
Pathology, Kharkiv, Ukraine

Introduction: Anterior decompression and fusion is the most
widely spread surgery for subaxial cervical spine traumatic injuries.
Implantation of a vertebral body prosthesis is important step when reaching
the tasks facing the surgeon. Along with the undeniable advantages of the
use of fusion systems of various modifications there is a risk of migration
due to the imperfection of the methods of fixing prosthesis to the vertebral
bodies. The aim of the work was to analyze the stress-strain state model of
cervical spine with a substituted C5 vertebra with telescopic prosthesis.
Material and Methods: Two variants of the prosthesis: with
one or two monocortical screws for fixation to a vertebral body were
examined. We obtained the critical values of the stress system with "fixing
element - the vertebral body" in various physiological states of the
cervical spine: axial load, flexion, extension, rotation. The influence of
the fixation method on the load distribution within the main supporting
elements of the vertebral-motion segment was analyzed. Results:
The application of “classical” implant fixation to the adjoining vertebrae
using the paired screws does not have essential advantages over the
mono-screw fixation. The evaluation of von Mises equivalent stresses
demonstrates essentially higher loading on the implant fixing elements using
two screws which definitely increases the amount of risk factors, causing
the local imbalance between the processes of bone regeneration and
desorption with the domination of latter. Such tendency, undoubtedly, may to
some degree facilitate the reduction of the fixing element capacities. At
the same time, the mono-screw fixation due to the reduction of loading on
the construction fixing elements determines some increase of tensions on the
support structures of vertebrae adjoining the resected one, however, no
essential peaks of the increase of loading on separate elements are
observed. Conclusion: The presence of the second fixing screw
leads to the tension increase in the system “cortical screw-vertebral body”.
The usage of one screw facilitates more equal distribution of tensions in
the system “implant-vertebra” and may be advantageous as to the reduction of
the stabilizing constructions migration frequency.

significant frequency of functional disorders in the long-term period. The
surgical treatment of subaxial cervical spine traumatic injuries can be
performed using various types of fusion systems. The purpose of our study
was to assess the stabilizing ability of various types of systems for
anterior subaxial cervical fusion based on the segmental kyphosis index of
the operated segment in patients with traumatic cervical spine lesion.
Material and Methods: We have analyzed X-ray patterns of
the cervical spine in 70 patients who underwent anterior subaxial cervical

## 1934

## P560: Is surgical therapy is equally emphatic as conservative treatment
in acute traumatic cord syndrome

Gyan Ranjan

1

 and Kumar Anand

2

1

Orthopaedics, Curesta Hospital, India

2

Orthopaedics, Anand Hospital, India

Introduction: Acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS) is a
clinical entity characterized by motor deficit causing a predominant
weakness of the upper limbs bladder dysfunction and varying degrees of
sensory loss below the level of the lesion. Most common incomplete traumatic
cervical cord injury pattern. Accounts for 20% of all cervical spinal cord
injuries. ATCCS has a heterogenous etiology. Hyperextension injury acute
disc herniations .fractures or dislocations of the upper cervical spine.
There are only few studies which have compared conservative with surgical
treatment. Their studies are flawed by the poor study design in which they
have included unstable injuries in surgical group and stable injuries in
conservative group. So we see that there is paucity in the literature
regarding ideal modality of treatment of stable variety of TCCS. Aims
and Objectives: The purpose of this retrospective study is to
compare the motor score improvement and functional status in surgically and
conservatively treated patients with stable ATCCS. Materials and
Methods: 106 consecutive patients with ATCCS admitted to our
spinal unit at CHARAK PALIKA HOSPITAL, NEWDELHI and MGM medical college
Kishanganj over a period of 10 years. Patients divided into three groups
based on their etiology. Only stable injuries taken, i.e. only patients with
PIVD and spinal stenosis group taken in our study.44 patients excluded and
62 recruited in the study. 32 opted for surgical management and 30 for
conservative treatment. Pre , intra and post operative data were collected
and analysed. Observation and Results: Our study proves that
there has been statistically significant improvement in UL,LL motor score,
spasticity grade and SCIM score in both surgical and conservative groups (p
value < 0.05). However there has been longer hospital (p value 0.68) and
ICU (0.74) stay in conservative group, and neurological recovery time (0.62)
and bowel, bladder recovery time (0.43) was more in this group, however
which is not statistically significant. Thus we see that results of
conservative management are equally good to surgical in TCCS.
Conclusion: With this available evidence, these patients
with ATCCS secondary to an extension injury in a stenotic canal without
fracture/dislocation/instability/disc herniation can be given an option to
undergo initial conservative management followed by surgery at a later date
if there is a neurological deterioration or there is a plateau of
neurological recovery. There is a need for high quality prospective
randomized control trials to resolve this controversy.

in a Mayfield carbon headholder. The navigation frame was placed on the head

cm skin incision on both sides and the optimal placement of C1 screws. A
transverse rod was then placed connecting the two screws under the fascia.
The patients were prospectively evaluated in terms of their clinical,
functional, and radiological outcomes with a follow-up of 6 months.
Results: A total of 4 screws were placed in two patients by
this technique with a mean follow up of 6 months. The mean duration of
surgery was 123 minutes and the average blood loss was 20 mL. The patients
were discharged from the hospital within two days after the surgery. The
intraoperative O-arm scan and follow-up CT showed correct placement of
screws and wound healing. There were no complication regarding the
atlanto-axial stability. Patients returned to their occupation within 2
months. Conclusion: Percutaneous isolated C1 ring
osteosynthesis allows a motion-preserving option in unstable C1 fractures.
This percutaneous navigated technique can safely compete most commonly used
surgical procedures. This mini-invasive method reduce the blood loss during
the surgery, hospital stay and preserve the functional status.

## P563: Predictors of neurological recovery after subaxial cervical spine
and spinal cord injury

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Ievgen Cheshuk

2

, and Milan Vorodi

2

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: Cervical spine injury is one of the most severe
musculoskeletal system lesion, due to high disability and neurological
disorders. Despite great number of studies, the influence of various factors
on neurological disorders regression in patients with traumatic subaxial
cervical spine injury at the level is insufficiently studied. The idea of
our study was to investigate the nature and influence value of various
factors on neurological disorders regression. Material and
Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of surgical
treatment results of 98 patients aged 18 to 65 years (43.25; 95% CI: 39.77 ÷
46.73) with subaxial cervical spine trauma and neurological disorders
qualified ASIA A-D. The control term of the examination was 1 year after
surgery. We used the following factors: Gender, Age, Circumstances of
injury, The nature and The degree of spine damage, The size of the
compression factor, Segmental kyphosis, General cervical lordosis, Baseline
neurological disorders, Value of spinal cord injury, Type of spine fusion
system. We defined the dynamics of recovery as the difference between the
final on the primary sum of points when evaluated by the International
Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury. In order to
identify significant factors, the method of step-by-step adaptation of the
multiple regression model was used. Results: The processing of
the data revealed the factors most critical for neurological recovery: the
initial level of impairment, the victim's age, the time from injury to
surgery, the spinal cord compression value, the type of fusion system (R2 =
0.6; F = 11.7 [20; 97], p < 0.0001). For ASIA B and ASIA C patients
kyphosis in fused segments is associated with neurological recovery slowdown
(R2 = 0.51; F = 17.15 [1; 56], p = 0.0001). For ASIA A neurological
recovery, the most significant factors were the value of spinal cord damage
and surgery performed within 8-24 hours after injury (R2 = 0.51; F = 150.5
[2, 21], p < 0.0001). Conclusion: We found that a
significant number of dissimilar factors influence the neurological
disorders recovery. These predictors of outcome may be used to guide
treatment decisions and prognosis.

## P564: Severity and type of traumatic subaxial cervical injury in
prediction of neurological deficit

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Milan Vorodi

2

, and Ievgen Cheshuk

2

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: Neurological dysfunction is the most severe
complication of traumatic subaxial cervical spine injury. A comprehensive
approach and assessment of the injured spine as a single structure,
including the contents of the vertebral canal as well, allow achieving the
maximum possible therapy results. The purpose of study was to evaluate the
dependence of neurological disorders value on type and severity of traumatic
subaxial cervical injury. Material and Methods: We performed
retrospective analysis of 140 patient’s cases that were hospitalized at the
Institute of Neurosurgery with subaxial cervical traumatic injury. All
patients were assessed for the type of the damage using the AO Subaxial
Cervical Spine Classification (AO SCSC), the severity of injury using the
Cervical Spine Injury Severity Score (CSISS). Neurological status was
defined as the sum of points according to the International Standards for
Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI). Estimation of
dependences was performed using regression analysis. Results:
The most severe neurological symptoms are determined in groups A4 and C.
Values on ISNCSCI scale are 97 (40 ÷ 144) points and 83 (42 ÷ 178) points,
respectively. Slightly higher rates are registered for A3 type of injury:
196 (131.5 ÷ 288.5) points. Within other groups, the median values are in
the range from 251 to 289 points with a fairly wide interquartile range. The
Kruskal-Wallis test showed the significance of the differences (χ2 = 31.58,
df = 7, p < 0.001). The linear regression model of neurological
dysfunction dependence on the severity of damage is characterized by a high
level of reliability (F = 19.6 [1; 138], p < 0.0001), but also a fairly
low coefficient of determination: 0.215. On average, an increase in CSISS by
one point leads to a decrease in ISNCSCI by 30 points within the analyzed
range of values. When analyzing the linear multifactor dependence of
neurological disorders value on type and severity of traumatic subaxial
cervical injury, the prognostic efficiency of the model was determined as
42.5% (F = 7.577 [15; 124], p < 0.0001). Conclusion: The
obtained data show that not only the absolute values of the instability and
the type of the injury, but also the relationship of these factors plays a
significant role in determining the value of neurological disorders in
patients.

## P565: AOSpine subaxial classification in determining optimal treatment
strategy

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Ievgenii Slynko

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, and Yurii Derkach

1

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The AOSpine Subaxial Cervical Spine Injury
Classification System was introduced to improve clinical management of
patients with different types of traumatic lesion. At the same time, this
classification does not have clear recommendations regarding treatment
strategy. The purpose of our study was to determine the optimal treatment
tactics for patients with various types of injuries based on AOSpine
subaxial classification system. Material and Methods: A
retrospective review was made of 164 patients with cervical spine trauma who
were admitted to Institute of Neurosurgery between 2008 and 2018. Surgical
management for each patient was determined with the main goal of spinal cord
decompression, fixation, and alignment, considering instability level
(Cervical Spine Injury Severity Score). Retrospectively, all patients were
classified by 3 neurosurgeons independently, using the AOSpine Subaxial
Cervical Spine Injury Classification System morphological types (A1-C).
Results: The analysis identified 4 types of surgical
interventions: Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion (ACDF - 4.9%),
Anterior Cervical Corpectomy and Fusion (ACCF - 65.9%), laminectomy without
or with stabilization (7.3) and combined anterior-posterior fusion (21.9%).
Isolated ACDF was used only for type A fractures: A1 - 50% of cases, A2 -
9.5% and A3 - 2.4%. In two cases A3 type and 5 cases A4 type, combined
fusion was used, due to damage of facet joints with compression of the nerve
roots. In the absolute majority of cases - 83.8% of all A type lesions, ACCF
was used. For type B1 fractures, ACCF was registered in all cases, while
surgical treatment of types B2 and B3 was characterized by an almost uniform
distribution of ACCF, posterior decompression and combined methods: 34.8%,
30.4% and 34.8% for B2 and, respectively and 31.3%, 25% and 43.8% for B3.
With type C lesions, in 56% of cases - 14 - patients we used combined
surgery while in 40% cases - 10 patients - ACCF. Were used no other
decompression and fusion methods with this type of injury.
Conclusion: AOSpine Subaxial Cervical Spine Injury
Classification System is an effective tool for describing the nature of
subaxial cervical spine damage. Further research is required to unify
surgical tactics based on the classification types of lesions. ACCF is the
most prevalent method of surgical correction of traumatic lesions at the
subaxial level of the spine.

Introduction: Anterior odontoid screw fixation is a safe
technique used for fixation of type 2 and rostral type 3 odontoid fractures.

achieved union rate of 80-100%. Requires a reduced odontoid to allow for

## P567: Stentoplasty versus spine jack in traumatic vertebral body
fractures, a systematic review

Elie Najjar

1

, Mohamed Hassanin

1

, Ali Mardashti

1

, and Nasir Quraishi

1

1

The Center of Spine Studies and Surgery, Nottingham University
Hospital, Nottingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: The treatment of traumatic vertebral fractures
(Types A and B1) has always been controversial, with no existing consensus.
With recent advances in the field of sagittal balance, minimally invasive
techniques that reduce and maintain vertebral and regional kyphotic
deformities such as Stentoplasty and Spine Jack are becoming popular.
Methods: A systematic review of the English language
literature dating up to March 2022 was undertaken using the key words:
“expandable intravertebral implant”, “armed kyphoplasty”, “Vertebral Body
Stenting” or “Stentoplasty” and “SpineJack”. PRISMA guidelines were
followed. Results: Of a total of 158 articles, 7 studies met
the inclusion criteria (1 level III and 6 level IV) and were analyzed.
Overall, 159 patients of mean age 51.2 years (range 31 – 75) with 189
traumatic vertebral fractures AO type A (97%) and B1 (3%) were treated using
Spine Jack. 81% of the fractures were in the thoracolumbar area. The
preoperative average Visual Analog Score (VAS) of 6.5 (4-9.2) kyphotic
deformity was 13.9 degrees (6.4 -22.6). The average follow up was 15 months
(6-37 months). Post-operatively, VAS improved to 2.2 (0.1-3.5), a difference
of 5 [p value < 0.0001, 95CI: 5.01, 5.64] and the kyphotic angle from
Spine Jack reduced to7.9 (1.9 – 15) with a difference of 6.14 [p value <
0.0001, 95CI: 4.69, 7.58]. The rate of cement leak was 51/141 (36%), 1 case
had a Dural tear, 1 case required revision due to further collapse and 4
cases had adjacent level fractures. Additionally, 122 patients of mean age
49 years (range 15-90) underwent Stentoplasty for traumatic 120 AO type A
vertebral fractures and were followed up to 14 months (3-34). 85% of the
fractures were in the thoracolumbar area. The average preoperative VAS was
8.9 (8-9.7) which improved to 5 (4-6) post operatively. There was not enough
data to conduct a meta-analysis for stentoplasty post-operative kyphothic
angle changes, but three separate studies show a significant reduction in
the Kyphotic Angle from an average of 10.9 (5.5-22) to 6 (0.5-17) degrees (a
difference of 4.9 degrees). 16% (9/57) of the cases had cement leak. No
other complications were documented. Conclusion: The use of
Spine jack in traumatic vertebral fractures had similar clinical outcomes(
VAS difference 4.3 vs 3.9) and kyphotic angle reduction ( 6.14 vs 4.9)
compared to Stentoplasty, but with a higher rate of cement leak (36% vs 16%)
and complications (4.2% vs 0%).

## P568: Double balloon kyphoplasty results in better radiographic outcomes

fractures

Oded Hershkovich

1

 and Raphael Lotan

1

1

Edith Wolfson Medical Center, Holon, Israel

Introduction: Studies found unilateral and bilateral kyphoplasty
to have comparable clinical outcomes. Only a few studies compared
radiographic results using unilateral vs. simultaneous bilateral approaches.
We aimed to examine and compare the radiographic results of unilateral (UKP)
vs. bilateral simultaneous double-balloon kyphoplasty (DKP) for treating
symptomatic vertebral compression fractures (VCF). Methods: A
retrospective cohort of all patients treated for VCF by DKP and UKP over
five years in a single medical center. From 2009 to 2012, we performed UKP
routinely; since 2012, DKP was the routine due to potential benefits in
vertebral realignment. We evaluated pre and post-surgical fracture
characteristics: vertebral height, sagittal and coronal Cobb angle, and
fracture reduction. Statistical analysis Included a t-test for independent
variables and Pearson Correlation. Results: The study cohort
consists of 81 patients (75.8 years ± 10.86) with 119 vertebras who
underwent surgery. We performed 89 UKP on fractured vertebras and 30 DKP on
30 vertebrae. UKP average fluoroscopy radiation exposure was 15.8 mGy
(±11.5) per level compared to 11.2mGy (±8.7) for DKP, p = 0.03. DKP showed
significant fracture reduction, 2.8 degrees of Cobb angle, equaling patient
positioning effect on fracture reduction. Conclusion: DKP
allows better fracture reduction than UKP, equaling the effect of patient
positioning without increased radiation exposure or adverse events.
Key Words: Osteoporotic fractures, Vertebral Compression fractures, Balloon
Kyphoplasty
Abbreviations: Osteoporotic Vertebral Compression Fractures = VCF; Balloon
Kyphoplasty = BKP; Unilateral Balloon Kyphoplasty (UKP); Bilateral
Simultaneous Double-Balloon Kyphoplasty (DKP).

Highlights

• We aimed to examine the immediate radiographic effects of UKP vs. DKP for
treating symptomatic VCF.
• We found that DKP results in better fracture reduction than UKP, equaling
the effect of patient positioning without increased radiation exposure or
adverse events.

Objective: To analyse therapeutical strategies applied to

## P572: Mono-axial versus poly-axial pedicle screw fixation for
thoraco-lumbar fractures: a randomised controlled trial

Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

1,2

, Islam Abd El-Hameed

2

, Mahmoud Ibrahim

2

, Ahmed Hassan

2

, and Mohamed El-Meshwawy

2

1

Spine Center, Helios Klinikum Erfurt, Erfurt, Germany

2

Orthopaedics and Trauma, Assiut University Hospitals, Assiut,
Egypt

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures are the most common spine
fractures. Posterior transpedicular screw fixation is commonly used in
surgical treatment of these fractures. To date, there is no consensus as to
whether a mono-axial or poly-axial pedicle screw should be used in fixation
of thoracolumbar fractures. This study aims to compare short segment
mono-axial to poly-axial pedicle screw fixation in thoracolumbar fractures
regarding radiological and clinical outcomes. Material and
Methods: This is a randomized controlled trial done in a
university hospital on 50 consecutive patients with thoracolumbar fractures
who met the inclusion criteria divided in two equal groups, group (I)
mono-axial pedicle screw fixation and group (II) poly-axial screw fixation.
Included were patients with type A3 and A4 (according to AOSpine
classification) thoracolumbar fractures between D9 – L3 without neurological
deficits. Excluded were pathological or osteoporotic fractures,
multi-segmental fractures, polytraumatized patients, fractures older than 14
days and fractures with load-sharing score 7 or more. All patients received
open posterior short-segment fixation with instrumentation of the fractured
vertebra. The primary outcome was the sagittal index, and the secondary
outcomes were local kyphotic angle, regional kyphotic angle, anterior
vertebral height, middle vertebral height, posterior vertebral height and
interpedicular distance. Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Visual Analogue
Scale (VAS) were used as Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs). All
patients were followed up at 3,6, and 12 months postoperatively.
Results: There were no statistically significant
differences regarding the demographic data (age, sex, co-morbidities, type,
and level of fracture) between both groups. Regarding the sagittal index,
local and regional kyphotic angles, anterior, middle, posterior vertebral
height and the interpedicular distance among the studied group, the mean
post-operative values were significantly improved in both groups. The mean
values for correction of sagittal index, local and regional kyphosis were
higher in the mono-axial group however, this difference was statistically
insignificant (p > 0.05). Also, the mean correction loss was higher in
the poly-axial group however, this difference was statistically
insignificant (p > 0.05). There were no statistically significant
differences in the mean ODI (16.92 ± 4.35 mono-axial group vs. 16.36 ± 4.56
poly-axial group; p = 0.87) and VAS (4.16 ± 1.62 mono-axial group vs. 3.78 ±
1.66 poly-axial group; p = 0.39) after one year. Conclusion:
There is no statistically significant difference between mono-axial and
poly-axial pedicle screws as regards reduction, correction of deformity and
maintenance of correction in management of acute thoracolumbar fractures.
Also, the patient reported outcomes (ODI and VAS) were not statistically
significant between both groups.

## 542

## P573: Spine injuries after ejection seat evacuatio in fighter aircraft of
the German Armed Forces from 1975 to 2021

Fabian Sommer

1

, Pravesh Gadjradj

1

, and Torsten Peppig

1

1

Neurological Surgery, Weill Cornell, Flushing, United
States

Introduction: The ejection seat is one of the most important
rescue tools for military aircrews. However, the high ejection speeds place
high loads on the pilots, which is mainly absorbed by the pilot's spine. The
differentiated evaluation of spinal injuries is of particular importance, as
this has a decisive influence on the further personal life and career of the
affected aircrews. Factors influencing the occurrence of a fracture as well
as the impact of a spinal injury on military flight certification have not
been addressed sufficiently to date. Material and Methods: We
conducted a retrospective evaluation of ejection seat evacuations in German
Armed Forces combat aircraft accidents between 1975 and 2021. The total
number of aviation accidents with ejection seat initiations and the survived
ejections were collected. Accident-specific data and pilot-specific data
were collected. In addition, it was evaluated whether aircrews were military
flight recertified after the accident. The type of spinal injury and the
location of the injury were evaluated. In addition to the descriptive
statistics, two logistics regression models were developed to assess
prediction values of accident and pilot-specific factors for spine injuries.
Results: A total of 103 aircrews were included in this
retrospective analysis. The overall prevalence of spine injuries was 63.7%
and the overall prevalence of major injuries was 33.0%. In the first
regression model analysis, there was no association with pilot flight
experience, age, height, weight, and BMI and being diagnosed with a spine
fracture. Similarly, aircraft type, altitude, and airspeed were not
associated with the occurrence of spine fractures. In the regression model
of analysis for predictors of rejection in military flight recertification
after ejection seat evacuation, lumbar spine fractures were associated with
higher odds of being rejected for recertification. Conclusion:
Military aircraft crews have a high risk of suffering from a spine injury
after emergency evacuation using an ejection seat. In the subsequent medical
workup, special attention should be paid to the spine and ideally a
consultation with a spine surgeon should be performed. Lumbar spine
fractures may have big consequences for military flight certification,
therefore special attention should be paid to successful rehabilitation.

Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

radiographs, CT (computed tomography) and MRI. Radiographic parameters
including vertebral body compression (Anterior Vertebral Height AVH, Middle
Vertebral Height MVH, Posterior Vertebral Height PVH), canal compromise,
sagittal alignment measured by Cobb angle and type of fracture according to
AO classification (morphological component) were digitally measured. Two
blinded investigators measured all the above mentioned parameters
independently. Results: 160 patients were included. The ASIA
score had significant correlation with sagittal alignment measured by Cobb’s
angle (r = -0.22, p < 0.001), vertebral height compression percentage
measured by AVH (r = -0.26, p < 0.001), and MVH (r = -0.28, p <
0.001), type of the fracture according to AO classification (morphological
part) (p < 0.001) and canal comprise if it was > 50% of the total
canal space (r = -0.34, p =< 0.001) but it has insignificant correlation
with percentage of compression of canal comprise if it was < 50% of the
total canal space (r = -0.12, p = 0.56) and also has insignificant
correlation with PVH (r =- 0.17, p = 0.12). Conclusion: Our
study concluded that there is a positive correlation between neurological
damage and sagittal alignment, vertebral compression, type of the fracture
according to AO classification and high grades of canal compromise (>
50%). But, there is no positive correlation with low grades of canal
compromise (< 50%) in thoracic and lumbar spine fractures patients.

## 731

## P575: Interventional management of single-segment osteoporotic vertebral
compression fractures in the elderly: our experience from 157 cases

Nikolaos Gkantsinikoudis

1

, Christos Siopis

1

, and Stylianos Kapetanakis

1,2

1

Spine Department and Deformities, Interbalkan European Medical
Center, Thessaloniki, Greece

2

Department of Minimally Invasive and Endoscopic Spine Surgery,
Athens Medical Center, Greece

Introduction: Osteoporotic Vertebral Compression Fractures
(OVCFs) constitute a frequent clinical condition with substantial associated
morbidity and mortality, principally encountered in elderly individuals.
Clinical management of these lesions is crucially determined by a plethora
of factors as patient’s general health status, fracture’s anatomical and
biomechanical features and potential neurologic compromise. We hereby
present our clinical outcomes of interventional management of OVCFs with
Minimally Invasive Augmentation (MIVA) procedures [Vertebroplasty (VP) and
Kyphoplasty (KP)] and open Posterolateral Instrumented Fusion (PLF) surgery
in elderly individuals. Material and Methods: One-hundred and
fifty-seven (157) elderly patients with single-segment OVCF were enrolled in
this prospective investigation. Major determinants for selection of
respective therapeutic strategy were the potential related
clinical/radiological segmental instability and the underlying neurologic
status. Seventy-seven (77) patients underwent MIVA procedures (VP or KP,
depending on vertebral height diminution) and eighty (80) open PLF surgery.
Evaluation of enrolled individuals was performed via clinical examination
and performance of determined patient-reported outcome measures as Visual
Analogue Scale (VAS) and Short-Form 36 (SF-36) Medical Health Survey
Questionnaire, for pain and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL)
assessment, respectively. All patients were evaluated preoperatively and at
sequential chronic intervals during a 2-year follow-up period.
Results: All patients were successfully operated, featuring
no major perioperative complications. Analysis of recorded outcome measures
showed that all indices of SF-36 questionnaire exhibited a statistically
significant improvement at all follow-up checkpoints, demonstrating albeit
the maximal amelioration at 3 months with subsequent stabilization with
minimal amelioration until the end of follow-up. On the contrary, VAS score
values were stabilized at 6 months postoperatively, featuring no further
significant quantitative alteration. Conclusion: Interventional
management of OVCFs in elderly patients with MIVA (VP, KP) procedures or
open PLF surgery, depending on determined patient- and condition-related
characteristics, represents a safe and effective strategy with favorable
outcomes in HRQoL.

## 801

## P576: Single Spinejack is each fractured vertebra is feasible to achieve
a significant fracture reduction and corresponding satisfactory outcome by
proper strategy of placing Spinejacks

Chien-Jen Hsu

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics, Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital,
Kaohsiung, Taiwan

Introduction: Spinejack was one of the most commonly used
augment devices for kyphoplasty. Bilateral placement of Spinejacks into a
vertebra for kyphoplasty was suggested by the manufacture company.
Considering medical expense controlled by insurance, we therefore intended
to investigate the surgical complications and clinical outcomes for patients
undergoing kyphoplasty with one single Spinejack in each fractured vertebra.
Material and Methods: We conducted kyphoplasty by applying
single Spinejack into fractured vertebra for 45 patients from January 2018
to December 2020. By examining the MR images preoperatively, we chose the
more collapsed side for placing the Spinejack unless the pedicle fractured.
Considering high risk for cement leakage through fractured pedicle, the
placement of Spinejack was therefore shifted to the other pedicle. The
Spinejacks were placed across the midline or at least touching the midline
of vertebra for effective expansion bilaterally. A vending trocar was
routinely inserted at the other side for decompression while injecting the
cement. The fluidity of cement was attenuated by extend the setting of
cement if we decided to inject cement through the side of Spinejack first.
Otherwise, we started to inject cement initially through the trocar to fill
the less comminuted side for preventing early leakage outside the vertebra.
The following supplement of cement depended on the distribution of cement
filling through alternative injection of cement bilaterally under the guide
of c-arm image intensifier. We usually stopped cement injection if the
filling of cement realized or approached the pre-opertaive plan.
Results: Excluding 4 patients without complete follow-up
for at least 12 months, 41 patients with 46 fractured vertebrae were
investigated. They were 12 male and 29 female patients with average age of
70.5 years. The mean BMD was -2.87. The fractured levels were T7 in 1
patient, T11 in 3 patients, T12 in 18 patients, L1 in 15 patients, L2 in 4
patients, L3 in 2 patients, and L5 in 1 patient. Except radiographic
assessment, the clinical symptoms were assessed by the SF-36 questionnaire.
The average clinical score of SF-36 improved from 52 to 81 in the final
follow-up at the OPD or by the telephone inquiry. However, the average SF-36
score reached 87 in case of excluding three patients with unsatisfactory
outcomes. These three patients reported poor outcomes that were re-operated
because of new vertebral fracture. The radiographic assessment demonstrated
an average 40% restoration of supposed height of fractured vertebra. The
average reduction of kyphotic angle is 11 degrees. Three patients developed
loss of vertebral height reduction more than 25% but only one was
re-operated by mini-invasive instrumentation. Conclusion:
Although the original recommendation from the manufacture company was
placing Spinejacks through bilateral pedicle into a fractured vertebra,
kyphoplasty by applying only one single Spinejack for each fractured
vertebra achieved a satisfactory reduction of vertebral collapse in this
study. The clinical outcomes assessed by SF-36 questionnaire demonstrated a
significant improvement in addition to evident reduction of vertebral height
and kyphotic angle. Considering cost-effectiveness of Spinejack-augmented
kyphoplasty, one single Spinejack was feasible to achieve satisfactory
outcomes clinically and radiologically.

## 830

## P577: The use of the AO Spine PROST (Patient Reported Outcome Spine
Trauma) among SCI patients - Healthcare professionals' perspective and
development of version 2.0

Aline J. Hakbijl

1

, Marcel Post

1

, Cumhur Oner

2

, and Said Sadiqi

2

1
Department of Spinal Cord Injury Rehabilitation,
De Hoogstraat Rehabilitation, Utrecht, The
Netherlands

2

Department of Orthopaedics,
University Medical Center, Utrecht, The Netherlands

Introduction: The provision of appropriate surgery, medical care
and rehabilitation can have significant effect on disability in people with
spinal cord injury (SCI). To learn what surgical and rehabilitation
treatments are most effective and to compare them in a reliable and valid
fashion, it is important to standardize classification and outcome
measurements. To meet these requirements, the AO Spine Knowledge Forum
Trauma developed the Patient Reported Outcome Spine Trauma (AO Spine PROST).
This tool was developed for people with spine trauma and minor or no
neurological impairment. To the best of authors’ knowledge, it is adopted
worldwide with currently being translated into 17 languages. In the current
study, the applicability of the AO Spine PROST for people with
motor-complete SCI was examined from the perspective of the healthcare
professionals. Also, recommendations were made for adjustments of the tool.
Material and Methods: A discussion meeting with SCI
rehabilitation physicians in the Netherlands was performed, followed by an
international online survey among healthcare professionals involved in the
care of people with SCI. Participants rated the comprehensibility,
relevance, acceptability, feasibility and completeness of the AO Spine PROST
on a 1-5 point scale (5 most positive). Comments could be provided per
question. The discussion meeting was audio taped, meaningful phrases
transcribed, and analyzed thematically. The results of the international
survey was compared with the results of the discussion meeting using
descriptive statistics. The comprehensibility, relevance, acceptability,
feasibility, and completeness of the tool were analyzed by calculating
frequency tables using SPSS. Results: A total of 13 physicians
attended the discussion meeting. The survey was completed by 196
participants worldwide. Comparable results were obtained from the discussion
meeting and the international survey. Comprehensibility (mean 4.1 ± 0.8),
acceptability (4.0 ± 0.8), relevance (3.9 ± 0.8), completeness (3.9 ± 0.8),
and feasibility (4.1 ± 0.7) were rated positively for use in people with
motor-complete traumatic or non-traumatic SCI. A few participants questioned
the relevance of items about the lower extremities (e.g. Walking) or
indicated the lack of questions about respiration/breathing and
complications. Conclusion: The AO Spine PROST was found to be
applicable for people with motor-complete traumatic or non-traumatic SCI.
This study formed the basis for recommendations in adapting the tool
(version 2.0) in order to make it applicable to the entire spine trauma
patient population, including patients with (severe) SCI. With this modified
version, the AO Spine PROST is expected to be even more useful both in the
clinics and for research purposes, contributing to the comparison of spine
trauma outcomes in a valid and reliable fashion with the potential to reduce
the ongoing controversies in spine trauma care.

## 846

## P578: AOSpine Thoracolumbar Injury Classification System (AO TLICS): a
study on its validation in junior surgeons

Zion Hwang

1

, Jason Bernard

2

, Timothy Bishop

2

, Jan Herzog

2

, Shahnawaz Haleem

2

, Tesfaladet Kurban

2

, Bisola Ajayi

2

, Emily Tsang

1

, Priyanshu Saha

1

, and Darren Lui

2

1

St. George's University of London, London, United Kingdom

2

Trauma and Orthopaedics, St. George's University Hospital, London,
United Kingdom

Introduction: Classification systems exist to safely guide
inexperienced surgeons’ management to result in optimal patient outcomes,
but the spine community is yet to agree upon a single thoracolumbar injury
classification system. Several studies have investigated the reliability of
the newest addition, AO TLICS, drawing inconclusive results for some
subtypes. Their analyses focus on AO TLICS’ reliability from the point of
view of each subtype rather than the injury and its management algorithm,
which has greater clinical importance. The binary (yes/no) questionnaire
format used in previous studies fails to assess surgeons’ abilities to
recognise and label an injury and, equally importantly, what classification
an injury does not fall under. In addition, many
assume all assessor responses have equal weighting regardless of their level
of experience. Therefore, this study aims to mitigate these issues by asking
participants to rate each injury by its full classification and by assessing
whether juniors surgeons’ assessment of injuries using AO TLICS agree with
their senior counterparts, thus contributing further data on the topic to
validate the reliability of AO TLICS. Material and Methods: In
2019-2020, two surveys were sent two months apart to the same group of
assessors, consisting of eight junior surgeons and one orthopaedic spine
consultant surgeon. There was a 100% response and participation rate. Spine
MRI scans of the same 11 patients were assessed on the number and full
classification of injuries. Data analysis was performed using Microsoft
excel with the consultant surgeon's answers used as the comparison standard.
Results: The average agreement was 81.3% for wedge
injuries, 81.8% for burst injuries and 86.6% for tension band injuries.
There was only one case of hyperextension injury at 87.5% and one Type C
injury at 100% agreement. On average junior surgeons showed 86.7% agreement
with surgical management but only 45.8% agreement with conservative
management. Further assessment showed 90.8% agreement on the vertebral level
injured, 85.4% agreement of Type C injuries, 67.0% of Type B injuries and
82.1% of Type A injuries. When classifying by subtypes, junior doctors
showed only 33.9% agreement for B subtypes and 50.9% for A subtypes.
Conclusion: AO TLICS is comprehensive and accurate in
junior surgeons overall, but poorer agreement is seen when classifying into
subtypes, especially for Type B injuries. AO TLICS accurately facilitates
junior surgeons’ recognition of which injuries require surgical management
but generally errs on the side of surgical management, which results in the
potential for unnecessary surgeries.

## 883

## P579: Surgical treatment of traumatic fractures of the thoracic and
lumbar spine: a systematic review

Said Sadiqi

1

, Timon Vercoulen

1,2

, Menco Niemeyer

3

, Felix Peuker

3

, Jorrit-Jan Verlaan

1

, and Cumhur Oner

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery

2
Orthopaedic Surgery, Diakonessenhuis,
Utrecht, The Netherlands

3

Trauma Surgery, UMC Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands

Introduction: Controversies remain on the optimal treatment of
thoracic- and lumbar spine fractures. These fractures are treated either
surgical or non-surgical. Surgical treatment aims to reduce the fracture,
prevent further post-traumatic spinal deformity, maintain spinal alignment
and perform a neural decompression if needed. However, there is no consensus
on the choice of surgical approach and technique. No comprehensive
up-to-date overview is available that facilitates the comparison of the
different surgical methods for these fractures. The goal of this study is to
reproduce and update an earlier systematic review from 2004 by this research
group. All published articles in the past two decades were reviewed, and the
outcomes of different surgical techniques were quantified and analyzed.
Materials and Methods: A systematic literature search was
performed in PubMed and EMBASE® using the search term ‘Spinal
fractures’ for articles published between 2001-2020. Inclusion criteria
were: > 18 years of age; including more than 10 cases; a minimum of 12
months follow-up; adequate description of the surgical procedure; using
generally accepted outcome instruments; surgery performed within three weeks
after trauma. Article screening was performed by four researchers. Studies
were categorized per surgical technique groups: Posterior open (PO),
Posterior percutaneous (PP), Stand-alone vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty (SA),
Anterior endoscopic (AS), Anterior open (AO), Posterior percutaneous and
anterior open (POAO), Posterior percutaneous and anterior endoscopic (PPAS),
Posterior open and anterior open (POAO), Posterior open and anterior
endoscopic (POAS). The PO group was used as a reference group for comparison
and statistical analysis. Results: 103 articles could be
included. Of these studies we could extract 138 cohorts using PO (n = 75),
PP (n = 39), SA (n = 13), AO (n = 5), PPAO (n = 1), PPAS (n = 1), POAO (n =
2) or POAS (n = 2). Pre-operatively, there were more type A fractures in the
SA and PP group compared to the other groups. Moreover, there were more
subjects with neurological impairment (ASIA grade C or D) in the AO group
compared to the other groups. Often, concomitant surgical interventions such
as an additional vertebra- or kyphoplasty, transpedicular spongioplasty,
fusion or a graft was applied. Surgical duration and blood showed no major
differences between groups. Post-operative complications were scarcely
reported. Pre-operative mean Cobb values were lowest in the SA group. The
overall correction obtained at follow-up was lowest in the SA group (1.06
degrees) and most in the AO group (7.65 degrees). Conclusion:
This comprehensive systematic review describes quantitative data to provide
the best possible comparison between different surgical techniques for the
treatment of thoracic and lumbar spine fractures. For type A fractures,
without severe neurological deficit, PP is most researched and can be
combined with vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty (SA) when a kyphosis correction
is needed. Furthermore, PO is feasible in almost all types of fractures and
there seems to be particular use for this technique when additional
posterior decompression or fusion is required which cannot be achieved by
more minimal invasive methods. Overall, all surgical techniques led to
neurological stabilization or improvement. Also, future randomized
controlled trials are imperative for a true comparison of surgical
methods.

## 902

## P580: Vertebral augmentation with cranio-caudal expandable devices in
acute versus subacute/chronic vertebral fractures of thoracolumbar junction.
Complications, clinical and radiological results

Andrea Zanirato

1,2

, Emanuele Quarto

1,2

, and Matteo Formica

1,2

1

IRCCS Ospedale Policlinico San Martino, Genoa, Italy

2

University of Genoa, DISC, Genoa, Italy

Introduction: The use of cranio-caudal expandable devices in
acute (< 8 weeks) and subacute/chronic (> 8 weeks) thoracolumbar
fractures has been proposed for pain control and kyphotic deformity
correction. The aim of this study was to compare the complication rate,
clinical and radiological results of vertebral augmentation with
cranio-caudal expandable devices in relation to timing of thoracolumbar
junction fracture (T10-L2). Material and Methods: The patients
who underwent one-level vertebral augmentation with a cranio-caudal
expandable device for a traumatic and osteoporotic vertebral fracture of the
thoracolumbar junction were enrolled. A minimum follow-up (FU) of 2 years
was established. Vertebral fractures were classified in acute (< 8 weeks)
and subacute/chronic (> 8 weeks). Complications were assessed as
intraoperative or postoperative. Clinical results were evaluated
preoperatively according to a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Oswestry
Disability Index (ODI). Radiological parameters included vertebral wedge
angle (VWA) and segmental kyphosis (SK). Results: Forty-seven
patients were included: 26 acute (Group-A) and 21 subacute fractures
(Group-B). The mean FU was 28.6 ± 2.6 months. The subgroups were
statistically homogeneous for preoperative clinical and radiological
parameters. No intraoperative complications were reported. In the
postoperative FU, 4 adjacent fractures were recorded in Group-B (p =
0.03).  Both groups exhibited a significant improvement in pain and
functional status after surgery, which was maintained up to the final
follow-up. The mean initial VWA was 15.4 ± 7.1° for Group-A and 17.1 ± 6.1°
for Group-B. Post-operative values were 7.4 ± 5.2° for Group-A (p < 0.05)
and 8.4 ± 5.1° for Group-B (p < 0.05). A similar loss of reduction (p
> 0.05) at 3 months was noted in both group: 0.6 ± 2.1° in Group-A and
0.8 ± 0.7° in Group-B. There was no further loss of reduction after 3
months. The mean initial SK was 12.0 ± 8.1° for Group-A and 13.7 ± 7.2° for
Group-B. Post-operative values were 7.1 ± 6.1° for Group-A (p < 0.05) and
7.5 ± 4.9° for Group-B (p < 0.05). A significant loss of segmental
kyphosis correction was noted during the FU in Group-B (SK at the last FU
12.1 ± 5.2°). Conclusion: Vertebral augmentation with
cranio-caudal expandable devices demonstrated promising clinical results in
both groups. In subacute and chronic vertebral fractures, a higher rate of
adjacent fractures was recorded. Furthermore, during the FU, the progressive
degeneration of the discs adjacent to fractured vertebral led to an increase
of segmental kyphosis. The opportunity of a stand-alone vertebral
augmentation with craniocaudal devices in subacute and chronic vertebral
fractures of the thoraco-lumbar junction should be carefully evaluated.

## 909

## P581: Cauda equina syndrome after gunshot injury at the lumbar spine: a
case report and narrative review

Pedro Torres

1

, Andre Castilho

1

, David Israel

1

, and Daniel Araujo

1

1

Spine Surgery, Hospital Unimed, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

Introduction: Gunshot wounds (GSW) is an important cause of
injuries of the spine, especially in the younger population and have high
mortality and morbidity impact. Beside been common in military population,
gunshot injury is becoming more prevalent in civilian population, especially
in developing countries, causing a great impact on health system costs. It
is the second most common cause of all spinal lesions (13-17%) and in some
countries the incidence is even higher than traffic accidents. GSW have a
wide spectrum of clinical presentation, with different associated injuries,
hemodynamic status, vertebral fractures, and neurological deficits. Spinal
Cord and Cauda Equina lesions can occur from different, yet concomitant
factors, such as the direct impact of the bullet, thermic lesion, the
concussive effect of the bullet, the tissue cavitations and the impairment
of blood supply (disrupted or thrombosed vessels). In this study, we present
a case of a male patient with cauda equina syndrome due to a gunshot injury
and a narrative review of the topic. Material and Methods: We
report a case of a 25-year-old patient who suffered a gunshot injury in the
lumbar spine. He was transferred to a spine trauma center after 5 days of
his injury. He presented pain in lower limbs, saddle paresthesia and urinary
retention. The patient had no motor or sensory compromise in lower limbs. A
computed tomography scan revealed the presence of the projectile in the
vertebral canal, at the L1’s right lateral recess. Research was made on
PubMed database for review studies and case reports about gunshot injuries
and gunshot wounds to the spine, spinal cord, and cauda equina. Were used
the terms “Gunshot Wound AND SPINE”. We also made a manual search, and the
most recent and relevant articles were selected for our analysis.
Results: Patient underwent surgery five days after the
trauma, having an open decompression through partial laminectomy and
projectile removal. No macroscopic lesion of the dura mater was observed
during surgery. Patient had a complete resolution of the lower limbs pain in
the first day after surgery and recovered urinary control and sensibility
after one month of surgery. Conclusion: Gunshot injuries to the
spine remains a very important subject to address. After admitted at the
trauma center, patient must undergo for clinical stabilization,
investigation of associated injuries, complete neurologic evaluation, and
imaging studies. The conservative treatment consists of wound care,
antibiotics, tetanus vaccination, stabilization, and rehabilitation.
Surgical treatment is controversial and depends of location in the spine,
neurological impairment, clinical condition and usually consists of open
laminectomy with or without stabilization. The only absolute indications are
cutaneous or pleural liquor fistula and documented progression of the
neurological deficit associated with compression of the neural elements. The
main prognostic factor is the initial neurological status, followed by the
affected segment and spinal cord preservation or transection. Studies report
a rate of recovery 53-65.3% for patients with partial deficits.

## 937

## P582: Transpedicular fixation of thoracic spine fracture in patient with
von Willebrand disease - a case report

Jovana Grupkovic

1

, Slavisa Zagorac

1

, Milos Vasic

1

, Uros Novakovic

1

, Milos Mladenovic

1

, Uros Dabetic

1

, Radmila Klacar

2

, Dragana Vracevic

2

, and Goran Tulic

2

1

Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology

2

Anaesthesiology and Reanimatology, University Clinical Center of
Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia

Introduction: Von Willebrand disease is a coagulation disorder
that is caused by a quantitative and qualitative defect of the von
Willebrand factor (vWF), which increases the risk of perioperative bleeding
and associated complications. This can be successfully prevented with
substitution therapy by von Willebrand factor (vWF) or factor VIII (FVIII).
The aim of our article is to present a patient with Th4 fracture that was
treated with transpedicular fixation with minimal perioperative bleeding and
complications. Case Report: We present a case of a 30-year-old
male injured by falling down the stairs and on admission diagnosed with
isolated injury - fracture of Th4 vertebrae. Previously he was diagnosed
with von Willebrand disease by laboratory analysis of aPTT before routine
tonsillectomy 3 years prior to admission. The patient was examined by a
hematologist, he denied spontaneous bleeding prior to admission, and he
stated he had right radiocarpal joint surgery without complications. He
suffered a fracture to Th4 - AO Spine Thoracolumbar Injury Classification
System type A2 - split fracture. Neurovascular status was intact.
Preoperative laboratory findings: Hgb 131 g/l, WBC 5.8 x 10⁹/l, PLT 240 ×
109, aPTT 36.1s, Ddimer 0.17 (0.5 cutoff), FVIII 61%, vWFAc
49%, vWFAg 40%, factor IX 71%, factor XI 93%, factor XII 127%. The HAEMATE P
(the morning of surgery 1000 IU IV) was administrated. The surgery
(transpedicular fixation Th3-Th5) was performed without any complication and
without significant bleeding, it lasted two hours and one dose of red blood
cells concentrate was administrated. Postoperative neurovascular status was
intact. The first 2 postoperative days the patient was treated with 1000
IU\12h of HAEMATE P, and the next three days with one dose daily. On the
third postoperative day the drain was extracted and the volume of the
drained serohemorrhagic content was 400 ml. The patient was treated with
Fraxiparine (0,3 ml SC/24h) pre- and postoperative. Discussion:
Spine injuries are most often caused by a fall from height. VWF disease
prevalence is up to 1% worldwide, with around 0.01% of patients having
significant symptoms. The most common clinical symptoms are mucocutaneous
bleeding and bleeding after trauma and surgery. There are three types of von
Willebrand disease: type I which is partial quantitative deficiency and the
most common (70-80% of cases). The appearance of spine injuries has a
relatively wide range – from mild strains to fractures and dislocations of
the vertebral body with/without spinal cord injury. The accepted
classification of the spine fractures is AO thoracolumbar classification
system, which divides fractures into three types – A, B, and C. Management
of spine fractures can be conservative and surgical. If surgical treatment
is necessary it is paramount to choose an appropriate approach. The
treatment plan for patients with von Willebrand disease requires a
multidisciplinary approach. Conclusion: In patients with von
Willebrand disease and spinal traumatic injuries that require surgical
treatment, preoperative preparation has to be multidisciplinary. This means
good cooperation of orthopedic surgeons, anesthesiologists and hematologists
in order to perform a successful surgery without preventable complications,
and increase patients quality of life.

## 943

## P583: Posterior thoracolumbar instrumented fusion for compression
fractures: long or mixed assembly?

Mouldi Lamouchi

1

, Jlidi Mohamed

1

, Ayachi Montassar

1

, Walid Bouaicha

1

, Mohamed Hedi Gharbi

1

, and Selim Daas

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Hospital of Mohamed Taher
Maamouri, Nabeul, Tunisia

Introduction: The Magerl classification defines compressions
fractures as compression fractures type A. This injury is most likely to
occur as a result of trauma, and is mainly located at the thoracolumbar
junction. Traditionally, the preferred method for stabilization of an
unstable burst fracture is the long fixation with instrumentation of at
least 2 levels above and below the fractured vertebrae. It was thought that
this would provide the necessary stability for fracture healing while
minimizing the risk of post traumatic kyphosis or hardware failure at the
expense of relative vertebral motion. Mixed fixation with instrumentation of
2 levels above and 1 level below the fractured vertebrae has gained
popularity as this decreases surgical time, but most importantly preserves
vertebral motion segments. The objective of our study is to compare these
two different posterior spine fixation methods for burst fracture fixation
of the thoracolumbar junction. Material and Methods: This is a
descriptive and analytic single center retrospective study with a 10 year
follow up. We included thoracolumbar compression fractures treated by
posterior fusion with a long assembly or a mixed assembly. Two groups have
been identified: Group A includes 53 patients treated with a long assembly
(2 levels above the fracture and 2 levels below). Group B includes 28
patients treated with a mixed assembly (2 levels above the fracture and one
level below). The evaluation of results was done by calculating the
variation of radiological parameters between pre-operative radiographs,
postoperative radiographs and last follow-up radiographs. The gain is the
preoperative value minus the postoperative value. The loss of correction is
the value at the last follow-up minus the postoperative value.
Results: The average follow-up of the study was 57 months
(15 months - 144 months). The gain in regional kyphosis was 9.75° for group
A and 9.04° for group B. The gain in vertebral kyphosis was 8.15° and 8.85°
for group A and B respectively. At the last follow-up of group A, the loss
in regional kyphosis (RK) was 0.63°, the loss in vertebral kyphosis (VK) was
0.67 and the loss of traumatic regional angulation (TRA) was 0.653. At the
last follow-up of group B, the loss in RK was 1°, the loss in VK was 0.78°
and the TRA loss was 0.963. At this stage, there was no significant
difference between the two groups. Osteoarthritic degeneration of the upper
and/or lower level was observed in 24 patients in group A and 16 patients in
group B. Conclusion: A mixed fixation method with
instrumentation of 2 levels above and 1 below for the thoracolumbar burst
fractures showed the highest correction of kyphosis angle both at immediate
and final follow-up and also the lowest implant failure at final
follow-up.

## P584: A pure conus medullaris syndrome with thoracolumbar burst fracture
is not so rare

Tokumitsu Mihara

Division of Orthopedic Surgery, Department of Sensory and Motor

Objective: To research the features of pure conus medullaris
syndrome (PCMS) with thoracolumbar burst fracture. Methods: The

fracture from 2008 to 2020. The patients were divided into three groups:
Group N: no neurological deficits, Group L: lower limb paralysis, and Group
P: PCMS. Age, gender, body mass index (BMI), mechanism of injury, the spinal
canal encroachment and effective spinal canal area ratio, and local kyphotic
angle of the patients were investigated. Results: Twenty-four
patients were included in this study and were divided into three groups. The
number of patients in Groups N, L, and P were 8, 10, and 6, respectively.
Age, gender, BMI, mechanism of injury, level of burst fracture, and local
kyphotic angle were found to be similar. The spinal canal encroachment ratio
in Group N, Group L, and Group P were 29% (16%-53%), 61% (36%-87%), and 39%
(29%-48%), respectively. The ratios in Groups N and P were significantly
lower than that in Group L. The effective spinal canal area ratios in Groups
N, L, and P were 63.2% (51%-79%), 38.2% (18%-64%), and 61.3% (57%-65%),
respectively. The ratios in Groups N and P were significantly higher than
that in Group L. All patients in Group P relatively smooth improve in
dysuria after surgery, even if a patient underwent surgery long time after
injury. Conclusions: PCMS with thoracolumbar burst fracture was
not rare. The bladder dysfunction in PCMS was considered as an early symptom
of the neurological disorder and the cause of it was persistent pressure
from the bone fragment.

## P585: Initial experience with augmented reality-assisted pedicle screws
in spinal trauma surgery

Samuel Brehm

1

, Abby Carey-Ewend

1

, Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Matthew De la Paz

1

, Karma Barot

1

, Ahmed Hanafy

1

, Michael Kann

1

, Raj Lavadi

1

, Ahmedh Hussein

1

, Alexander Yahanda

1

, Alexander Perdomo-Pantoja

1

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, Julio Jauregui

2

, and Camilo Molina

1

Neurosurgery

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University, St. Louis, United
States

Introduction: The field of trauma medicine has long been a stage
for novel technology to demonstrate its advances in healthcare. In these
instances, assessing injuries and formulating a plan requires a rapid
response and integration of equipment and machines capable of providing that
insight quickly and accurately. Technology that demonstrates such an
advantage in trauma cases can imply a similar edge in non-emergent cases,
while the inverse is not necessarily true. The importance of operative
outcomes in spinal surgery is paramount given the significant neurologic
sequelae possible if spinal decompression, stabilization, and correction of
deformity, when necessary, are not achieved. Augmented reality
head-mounted-display (AR-HMD) is a novel technology that is designed to
provide surgeons with a CT-guided 3-dimensional recapitulation of an
individual patient’s spinal anatomy in real time and space. In this case
series, the use AR-HMD in trauma cases is explored to determine whether the
use of AR in spinal surgeries affects multiple outcomes, including surgery
time, blood loss, length of stay, and complications. Materials and
Methods: We recruited a retrospective cohort of patients who
underwent navigated pedicle screw placement guided by AR-HMD at the Barnes
Jewish Hospital from January 1, 2021, to January 30, 2022. From this, a
cohort of 7 traumatic cases were found where AR-HMD was utilized during the
surgery. Clinical patient information was collected, and metrics were
calculated using Microsoft Excel. Results: The cohort had a
mean age of 67 years, included 4 female and 3 male patients, and had an
average body mass index of 29.6. Four of the patients had a one-level
fracture, two patients had a two-level fracture, and one patient had a
three-level fracture. The mechanism of injury included falls (3), neoplasms
(2), 1ankylosing spondylosis (1), and hardware failure (1). They had an
average surgical invasiveness index (SII) of 8.3. Intra-operatively, there
was a mean blood loss of 400mL, mean 1.1 transfusion units used, and mean OR
time of 3 hours and 27 minutes. The average length of stay in the hospital
was 24.9 days, with two patients discharging home, one discharging to an
intermediate care facility, two discharging to skilled nursing facilities,
and two patients discharging to other rehabilitation facilities.
Conclusion: This case series illustrates the utility of
AR-HMD for instrumentation of the spine under various scenarios of spinal
trauma. The urgency to treat a spinal pathology constitutes a major hurdle
for the adoption of novel technologies in spine surgery. The average blood
loss, length of hospital stay, transfused units are comparable to the
outcomes observed in robotic-assisted surgery. This study is an early
attempt to demonstrate that AR-HMD can provide equitable outcomes compared
to the traditional surgical practices and can be quickly adopted in Level 1
trauma centers withoutextensive adaptations
