## P586: Thoracolumbar fractures open versus minimally invasive
approach

Oscar González

1,2

, Jorge Garcés Gallardo

2

, Luis Benavides

2

, Cristian Flores Ferrada

1

, Luis Medina

1

, Gustavo Canessa

1,2

, Ramón Segovia

1,2

, Tatiana Saavedra

1

, Patricio Campos Carrasco

1

, Marco Guevara

1

, Jorge Medina

1

, and Natalia Rolack

1

1

Neurosurgery, Complejo Asistencial Víctor Ríos Ruíz, Los Angeles,
Chile

2

Neurology, Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción,
Concepción, Chile

Introduction: Vertebral Fractures accounting for 17% of hospital
discharges from the Neurosurgical Unit of our Hospital. Of these, 40%
correspond to injuries of the thoracic and lumbar segments and about half
require surgical treatment. From 2016 surgeries with MIS techniques have
been performed regularly in our Center, either through mini-open approaches
or with percutaneous procedures. This is an extension of our previous
experience about treatment of thoracolumbar spine fractures adding most
cases with posterior MIS techniques. Material and Methods:
Retrospective Study. Case series of adult patients who suffered fractures of
the thoracic and/or lumbar segments, who received some type of surgical
treatment via a posterior approach, either traditional open, mini-open, or
percutaneous surgery. All patients were treated in "Complejo Asistencial
Víctor Ríos Ruíz" Los Angeles Chile, between January 2016 and December 2019.
Osteoporotic fractures or pathological bone fractures were not included.
Data collection from electronic clinical records, neuroimaging records. All
CT scans were categorized using the current Aospine thoracolumbar fracture
classification. Statistical analysis with Stata v12. For continuous
variables, the unpaired Student's t test was used and for dichotomous
variables, the Chi square test was used, with 95% confidence intervals.
Results: 95 cases were selected for analysis, of which 63%
were male and 37% female. The average age was 50,2 years (SD 17-81). The
most frequent Mechanisms of injury were falls (46.3%) followed by traffic
accidents (38%). The most frequent injuries were type A4, A3 and C. The most
frequently affected segment was the thoraco-lumbar hinge (65%), followed by
thoracic injuries (30%). 85% of the patients were admitted ASIA E, 4% ASIA D
and 12% ASIA A. 47.4% patients were treated with open technique, 52.6% with
less invasive techniques (mini-open or MIS) and one hybrid case. The mean
time from injury to surgery was 4.0 days (SD: 0 - 16), there were no
differences between groups. Hospital stay and postoperative days were
greater in the open technique group. In this group, the average number of
levels operated and the average number of screws used per surgery were also
greater. The average surgical time was longer in the open surgery group, as
was intraoperative blood loss. In relation to post-surgical complications
and the need for reoperation, these were only observed in the open surgery
group. There were no significant differences between the two groups in terms
of post-surgery angulation and decreased height of the vertebral body.
Conclusion: Minimally invasive techniques for the treatment
of thoracolumbar fractures are an alternative that is at least as safe and
effective as the open technique. It has the advantage of shortening
hospitalization times, intraoperative blood loss and postoperative pain,
allowing early rehabilitation. In addition, it is very useful in the context
of polytraumatized patients and in damage control surgery. It is an option
for an important variety of traumatic spinal injuries.

## 1118

## P587: Percutaneous fixation in thoracolumbar fractures: a remote island
reality

João Cruz

1

, Joana Rodrigues

1

, Tiago Canas

1

, Emanuel Homem

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

, and Luís Soares

1

1

Hospital do Divino Espírito Santo, Ponta Delgada, Portugal

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures are the most common spinal
injuries, are more common in men (male-to-female ratio 2:1). About 50–70% of
these fractures occur in the thoracolumbar segment (T11-L2). Posterior
short-segment fixation remains the most commonly used surgical technique for
these fractures and contrary to classical open surgery, the minimally
invasive percutaneous pedicle screw placement needs smaller incision, less
blood loss, less dissection of paraspinal muscles, less postoperative pain,
and faster recovery. This retrospective study analyzed the clinical and
imaging information of patients who underwent percutaneous transpedicular
fixation for thoracolumbar fractures at our hospital. Material and
Methods: From April 2019 to March 2022 all consecutive
trauma-related spine surgeries at a single institution were revised and
percutaneous transpedicular fixation cases were selected (n = 39).
Demographical, clinical and radiological data was collected retrospectively,
including Cobb angle, percentage of anterior vertebral height (AVH%), AO
classification and surgical time. Visual analogue scale (VAS) was evaluated
pre, post and 6 months after surgery, and Oswestry disability index (ODI)
was evaluated at 6 months post-op. Results: Surgical technique:
under general anesthesia, patients were placed prone on a Maquet surgical
bed. A C-arm system was used to determine skin incision, control pedicle
screws insertion and confirm final positioning. Neuromonitoring was not
consistently used. After surgery: all patients began rehabilitation on the
day of surgery and no bracing was used. The patients were followed for at
least 6 months (follow-up). 39 patients underwent percutaneous pedicle screw
fixation (72.73% with screwing of the fractured vertebra): 27 males and 12
females, and the mean age was 46.7 years. The main trauma cause was fall
from height, most common fractured level was L1, and most frequent type of
fracture AO A4. The mean surgical time was 79.785 min. There were no
intraoperative complications. During the follow-up period, there were one
infection and 1 patient with one screw pullout, but no neurological
impairment was found. The mean pre-operative VAS score was 6.2,
postoperative 2.4 and at the last follow-up 1.4. The mean pre-operative ODI
at 6 months was 5.4. Radiographic outcomes: The Cobb angle improved from
11.84º prior to surgery to 6.98 post surgery, and 7.84 at the last
follow-up. The AVH% increased from a mean of 64.1% pre-surgery to 75.9 post
surgery, and 72.3% at the last follow-up. Conclusion: In our
experience, the percutaneous short-segment pedicle screw fixation with or
without screwing of the fractured vertebra are both safe and effective in
the treatment of thoracolumbar fractures.

## 1124

## P588: The importance of intraoperative neuromonitoring in thoracolumbar
fractures

João Cruz

1

, Joana Rodrigues

1

, Tiago Canas

1

, Emanuel Homem

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

, and Luís Soares

1

1

Hospital do Divino Espírito Santo, Ponta Delgada, Portugal

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures are the most common spinal
injuries. Posterior short-segment fixation remains the most commonly used
surgical technique for these fractures. We report a rare case of
intraoperative loss of potentials during instrumentation of a non-fractured
pedicle with an intermediate screw and brief review of current literature
for evidence to support or limit the use of intermediate screws for
thoracolumbar fractures and intraoperative neuromonitoring. (IOM).
Material and Methods: A 28-year male patient admitted to
the emergency department after air transportation from a secondary hospital
due to fall from height (4 meters) with head and spine trauma. The patient
had past medical history of drug abuse. Hemodynamically stable and excluded
life-threatening conditions the patient underwent secondary assessment.
Whole body CT and Spine MRI documented a T5 bony Chance fracture, AO spine
B2, TLICS 7, ASIA E. Results: The patient was submitted to
percutaneous pedicle screw fixation with screwing of the fractured vertebra
with C arm system to determine skin incision, control pedicle screws
insertion and confirm final positioning. IOM was used throughout the entire
procedure. While instrumenting T6 right pedicle (deemed intact on the
preoperative CT) the patient had a sudden loss of potentials in right side,
corresponding to a spinal cord compression, despite apparent well-placed
screw on fluoroscopic images. After screw removal full neurological
potential was recovered and final construct revised. Postoperative
in-hospital stay went uneventful and the patient was discharged without
neurological deficits (ASIA E). He began rehabilitation 2 days after surgery
and was provided thoracolumbar rigid braces for 3 months. The patient’s
current follow-up is 6 months: the pain has resolved and there are no
neurological nor hardware complications. Review of current available
literature on percutaneous instrumentation of the fractured-vertebra
supports its use, because it reduces implant failure rate and postoperative
VAS and has the best effect on postoperative anterior vertebral height ratio
(AVHR) and sagittal Cobb angle (SCA). Conclusion: The authors
reckon that despite the available literature supporting the use of
intermediate screws in intact pedicle fractured vertebrae body caution would
be advised, especially in centers without IOM and/or 3D imaging devices.

## 1128

## P589: Vascular complications in percutaneous spine surgery: the uninvited
unwelcomed guest

Emanuel Homem

1

, Joana Rodrigues

1

, Tiago Canas

1

, João Cruz

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

, and Luís Soares

1

1

Hospital do Divino Espírito Santo, Ponta Delgada, Portugal

Introduction: Vascular injury rarely occurs during spine
surgery. During pedicular screw insertion, the perforation of the anterior
ligament may lead to vessel injury, with associated arteriovenous fistula
(AVF) and pseudoaneurysm formation. Historically, early surgical
intervention has been the treatment of choice for traumatic AVFs.
Disadvantages of open repair include technically demand procedures,
increased comorbidity, and significant blood loss. Endovascular techniques
that allow for a less invasive repair and prevent permanent hemodynamic
sequelae are a quite attractive alternative in this setting. These are
especially advantageous when there is an extensive hematoma surrounding the
vascular lesion, making anatomical differentiation difficult for open
repair. We describe a rare case of lumbar artery pseudoaneurysm secondary to
percutaneous posterior lumbar spine fixation. Material and
Methods: A 63-year male patient admitted to the emergency
department due to a motorcycle accident with spine trauma. The patient had
past medical history of alcohol abuse. Due to acute respiratory distress
syndrome the patient was admitted to ICU. When hemodynamically stable and
excluded life-threatening conditions, the patient underwent secondary
assessment. Whole body CT and Spine MRI documented a retroperitoneal
haematoma associated with a L1 bony Chance fracture, AO spine B2, TLICS 7,
ASIA E. Results: At the 10th day after admission the
patient underwent percutaneous short-segment transpedicular fixation with
intermediate screws (6S) of T12 to L2 vertebrae. The procedure was
uneventful and the patient was transferred to Intermediate Care Unit.
Post-surgery contrast abdominopelvic CT was performed to access
retroperitoneal hemorrhage evolution, which documented a 31x22mm right
lumbar artery pseudoaneurysm at L1 level, absent in the pre-operative
imaging exams. A vascular surgical consultation was placed following which
an angiogram was performed from a femoral approach. Due to pseudoaneurysm
progression (40x27mm) CT-guided thrombin injection was performed 2 days
later. CT angiography, 5 days after the procedure, showed lesion relapse and
another CT-guided embolization with ethylene-co-vinyl alcohol was performed
the following day. Endovascular embolization achieved resolution of the
pseudoaneurysm, regression of the hematoma and recovery of the patient
during the 6-month follow-up. Conclusion: The authors report
this rare case of iatrogenic vascular injury following posterior fixation of
thoracolumbar fracture to highlight the importance of correct placement of
pedicular screws and support endovascular techniques as a safe and efficient
alternative for surgical repair, especially in patients with multiple
comorbidities and anatomically challenging locations.

## 1178

## P590: Is there still a place for short fixation in the treatment of
thoracolumbar junction fractures?

Jlidi Mohamed

1

, mouldi lamouchi

1

, Ayachi Montassar

1

, Walid Bouaicha

1

, Mohamed Hedi Gharbi

1

, and Selim Daas

1

1

Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Hospital of Mohamed Taher
Maamouri, Nabeul, Tunisia

Introduction: Injuries of the thoracolumbar junction are the
most frequent and result from the transition between the rigid and fixed
thoracic spine and the mobile and dynamic lumbar spine. This biomechanical
feature makes it particularly vulnerable and constitutes a therapeutic
challenge. The aim of our work is to describe the functional, clinical and
anatomical results of short fixation (one vertebra above and one vertebra
below the fractured vertebra). Material and Methods: This is a
retrospective study over a period of 10 years between January 2010 and
January 2020. We included patients operated on for dorsolumbar junction
fractures by short fixation (one vertebra above the fracture and one
vertebra below). The fractures were classified according to Magerl. The
evaluation of the results is done on postoperative X-rays and at the last
follow-up by calculating the different radiological parameters. Functional
evaluation is done using the Oswestry score and the Dallas
self-questionnaire. Results: Our series includes 22 patients
with an average of age of 44.2 years. None of our patients had an initial
neurological deficit. All fractures were compression fractures. Type A3 is
the most frequent (11 cases). The average of operating time was 67.68
minutes. The average of blood loss is 350.91 ml. The postoperative vertebral
kyphosis was 14.27°, and at last follow-up was 16.73°. The postoperative
regional kyphosis was 13.77° and at last follow-up was 16.86°. The
postoperative regional traumatic angulation was 10.82 and at last follow-up
was 13.86. At last follow-up, the loss in regional kyphosis was 3.09. The
loss in vertebral kyphosis was 2.50. The loss in regional traumatic
angulation was 3.13. 86.36% of patients have adjacent segment disease. At
last follow-up, Oswerty's score was 31.50. Dallas score was 25. The average
time off work was 136.67 days. 27.27% of patients returned to work without
reclassification. Four patients developed sepsis, two of them early. There
were 4 cases of pseudoarthrosis, and one case of screw fracture.
Conclusion: Traditionally, the preferred method for
stabilization of thoracolumbar junction fracture required the
instrumentation of atleast 2 levels above and below the fractured vertebrae.
It was thought that this would provide the necessary stability for fracture
healing while minimizing the risk of posttraumatic kyphosis or hardware
failure at the expense of relative vertebral motion. Currently, mixed
fixation (2 levels above and 1 level bellow the fracture) are taking their
place and they remain a subject of debate. The short fixation (1 level above
and 1 level below the fracture) are losing their indications because of the
more frequent complications and especially the loss of reduction and
adjacent segment disease

## P591: Fracture dislocation of the thoracic spine in 91-years old patient

percutaneously

Hamdan Abdelrahman

1,2

, Seyed Emadaldin Sadat

, Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad

, and Ali Ezzati

Spine Surgery, Helios-Hospitals Erfurt, Erfurt, Germany

2

Orthopedics and Trauma, Asiut Universty Hospital, Asiut,
Egypt

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures are the most common injury
of the spine accounting for more than half of all spinal trauma cases.
Thoracolumbar fracture-dislocations are, however, uncommon and represent
less than 3% of these injuries. We report a case of fracture-dislocation of
the thoracolumbar spine without neurological deficit in an elderly patient
operated upon minimally invasive with cement augmented percutaneous
transpedicular posterior fixation. We also review similar cases described in
the literature. Materials and Methods: A 91-year-old female
with post-traumatic fracture dislocation at the T6-T7 level without
neurological deficit, after falling downstairs, was managed as emergency

intraoperative or postoperative complications were detected. The patient
could be mobilized on the first postoperative day. His Visual Analogue Scale

months follow-up. The patient died 6 months later because of cardiac causes.

fracture-dislocations need to be managed carefully to achieve a good
outcome. Minimally invasive reduction and stabilization could be achieved
even in elderly osteoporotic patients. This minimizes surgical trauma,
postoperative analgesics, and shortens hospital stay.

## P592: Bone scan as a diagnostic tool for diagnosing vertebral compression
fractures

Saeda Haj

1

, Alon Rod

1

, Daniel Weiner-Kalish

2

, Elite Arnon-Sheleg

2,3

, and Nimrod Rahamimov

1,2

1

Department of Orthopedics B and Spine Surgery

2

Azrieli Faculty of Medicine, Bar Ilan University, Safed,
Israel

3

Nuclear Medicine and Diagnostic Radiology, Galilee Medical Center,
Nahariya, Israel

Introduction: The diagnosis of vertebral compression fractures
(VCF) is usually based on spine radiographs and Computed Tomography (CT) but
they may not be able to differentiate between acute and old fractures, a
crucial treatment decision parameter. Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI) is the method of choice for determining the
fracture's age but is not used routinely because of its higher costs and
lower availability. Bone scan is a relatively available and low-cost method.
It has a higher sensitivity for VCF than conventional radiographs and can
demonstrate the amount of osteogenic activity in the fracture, which will
change according to the fracture's age. Our study hypothesis was that bone
scan will provide us with information regarding the fracture age,
eliminating the need for magnetic resonance imaging. Material and
Methods: A retrospective study was conducted using data from our
hospital electronic health records. Included were 180 consecutive patients
admitted to the Galilee Medical Center with a suspected acute VCF who
underwent thoraco-lumbar spine CT scanning and triple phase bone scan with
Single Photon Computed Tomography (SPECT) of the whole spine during the
hospitalization period. Results: Overall, 120 women and 60 men
were included (mean age 74.2 years). 13 were excluded because of missing
data. 2,417 (94.0%) vertebrae had no evidence of fresh fracture on bone scan
and CT. 161 (6.3%) fresh VCFs were diagnosed in both CT and bone scan. 27
(16.2%) patients had fresh VCFs on the bone scan while CT was normal. 37
(22.1%) patients had fresh VCFs on the CT while the bone scan was negative
or with low uptake. Conclusion: The combination of CT and bone
scanning is an effective tool for evaluating vertebral fractures to
determine: 1. If a fracture found on CT is fresh or not 2. To find occult
fresh compression fractures not found on CT. This is information is crucial
for proper treatment choice.

## 1201

## P593: Outcome of early surgical intervention in spinal trauma patients,
an overview of 245 spinal trauma patients

Ammar Dogar

1

, Haseeb Hussain

1

, Ahsan Atta

1

, and Omar Aziz

1

1

Department of Orthopaedics And Spine, Ghurki Trust Teaching
Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: The prognosis for spinal cord injuries varies
depending on the severity of the injury. There is always hope of recovering
some function with spinal cord injuries. The completeness and location of
the injury will determine the prognosis., The sooner treatments are
implemented to strengthen muscles below the level of the spinal cord injury,
the better the prognosis. The first year of recovery is the hardest as the
patient is just beginning to adjust to his or her condition. The use of
physical and occupational therapy during this time is the key to recovery.
The extent of the function fully returning is typically seen in the first
two years after the initial injury. Objective: To determine the
neurological outcome of patients who presented early with those whose
presented late. Materials and Methods: It was a descriptive
case series done in the Department of Orthopaedics and Spine between Jan
2016 to Dec 2019. 245 patients who presented to ER or OPD with spinal trauma
were included. Those patients who were operated elsewhere or having trauma
of more than 10 days or those who were managed conservatively were excluded.
After admission, history, examination and investigations surgical
intervention were done on same day. Every patient were followed regularly
for 2 years to assess the neurology. The data was analyzed using SPSS 17.00
Version. Results: There were 109 total patients that presented
with spine trauma. 183 (74%) were male and 62 (26%) were females. Male to
female ratio was 2.11:1. Of the 245 total patients that presented 173 (71%)
were below 40 years of age and 72 (28.5) patients were above 40. 38 (15.6%)
had trauma to the cervical spine, 76 (31.2%) to the thoracic spine, 7 (2.8%)
to the thoracolumbar spine and 122 (50.5%) to the lumbar spine. 177 (72.5%)
patients had a fall from height. 58 (23.9%) were involved in road traffic
accidents. 1 (.9%) had assault and 3 (2.8%) had sports injuries. At the time
of presentation out of 245 patients, 218 (89%) had their neurology involved
while 26 (11%) had intact neurology. 41 (16.5%) presented within the first
24 hrs while 203 (83.5%) presented after 24 hrs. All the patients were
operated on the same day of admission. Among the 41 patient who presented
with in 24 hours, 27 patients having full recovery with in 12.66 ± 1.2
months. While the late presenters only 45 patients get fully recovered after
2 year follow up while 42 patients having partial neurology recovery and 24
having just sensory improvement and 92 having no improvement after two year
follow up. Conclusion: Spinal trauma is an emergency and having
high morbidity and mortality rate. Early presentation and surgical
intervention in spinal trauma patients having good neurological outcome as
compared to delayed presentation and surgery.

## P594: Giant thoracolumbar pseudomeningocele: unusual evolution of

Mohamed Amine Gharbi

Orthopedic and Trauma Surgery, Mongi Slim Marsa University Hospital

Introduction: Spinal pseudomeningoceles are a common
complication of large iatrogenic tears in the dural-arachnoid layer.
Materials and Methods: We hereby report a case of an
unusual giant dorsolumbar pseudomeningocele arising after a traumatic dural
tiny tear. Results: We report a case of a 32-year-old patient,
a victim of a road traffic accident which caused severe polytrauma including
a C2 Magerl type fracture of T11, with a partial neurological deficit

## P595: MIS short-segment fixation & Unipedicular screw manipulation
technique; a novel method with surgical technique

Brian Chin

1

, Joshua Wong

1

, Jiong Hao Tan

1

, and Naresh Kumar

1

1

Orthopaedic Surgery, National University Health Systems, Singapore,
Singapore

Introduction: MIS spine surgery has revolutionized fixation of
thoracolumbar fractures with burst elements. Recent studies have proven that
percutaneous pedicle screw instrumentation is as effective as open
instrumentation, with reduction in intraoperative blood loss and operative
duration. Techniques such as short-segment pedicle screw fixation including
the fractured vertebra has shown satisfactory radiological correction and
functional outcomes, avoiding the need for extensile posterior constructs.
In the present study, we describe our technique utilizing unipedicular index
vertebra fixation and manipulation in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) for
thoracolumbar fractures with burst elements. To the author’s knowledge, this
technique is not well described in literature as open approaches are often
adopted for the above. We aim to highlight the two-year radiological &
functional outcomes of 20 consecutive patients who underwent this technique.
Material and Methods: A retrospective review of
prospectively collected data was conducted on 20 patients with thoracolumbar
fractures with burst elements who underwent fixation using our technique.
Patient data collected included demographic characteristics, mechanism of
injury, associated injuries, neurological deficit at time of admission with
pre- & post-operative neurological evaluation and length of hospital
stay. Radiological investigations included plain radiographs, CT-spine with
reconstruction and MRI-spine which provided data for radiological fracture
classifications such as AO Spine and derivation of TLICS score, as well as
preoperative planning. Radiological investigations in the postoperative
period were carried out by standing radiographs or EOS whole spine at each
postoperative follow-up up to two years. Radiological parameters - vertebral
wedge angle, regional kyphosis angle, coronal cobb angle, anterior and
posterior vertebral body heights were recorded at preoperative,
intraoperative, postoperative, and up to 2-year follow-up. Clinical outcome
scores of VAS and ODI were also recorded at similar time-points.
Results: Radiological outcomes reflect significant lordotic
corrections of the vertebral wedge angles up to 2-year follow-up when
compared to preoperative values (intraoperative: p = 0.06; postoperative: p
= 0.001; 3-month: p = 0.002; 6-month: p = 0.004; 1-year: p = 0.011; 2-year:
p = 0.016). Additionally, significant lordotic corrections of regional
kyphosis angles (intraoperative: p = 0.00; postoperative: p = 0.00; 3-month:
p = 0.031; 6-month: p = 0.039) and increases in anterior vertebral body
heights (postoperative: p = 0.001; 3-month: p = 0.010; 6-month: p = 0.020)
up to 6-month follow-up was found. Preoperatively, median VAS of 85 (range
30 to 100) and ODI of 90 (range 40 - 98) were recorded. Statistically
significant improvements in VAS and ODI were found across all timepoints
when compared to preoperative values, with a mean VAS of 11.5 (S.D 4.8) and
ODI of 9.9 (S.D 4.5) at 2-year follow-up. Conclusion: Surgical
management of thoracolumbar fractures with or without neurological deficit
has a role in reducing nursing requirements and postoperative morbidity in
patients with polytrauma and other associated injuries. Our approach in
treating thoracolumbar fractures with burst elements using MIS short-segment
fixation and unipedicular screw manipulation technique shows satisfactory
radiological correction & high rates of fracture union, whilst reducing
approach-related morbidity & improving functional outcomes.

## 1386

## P596: Thoracolumbar vertebral burst fractures treated by short segment
fixation with index screw and transpedicular transcorporeal bone grafting: A
clinico radiological analysis pre-post radiological study.

Prabhat Agrawal

1

1

Orthopaedics, AIIMS Patna, Patna, India

Introduction: The treatment of thoracolumbar fractures is
controversial. Short segment pedicle screw fixation has been used as a
treatment of choice for many years yet it is associated with loss of
reduction and undesirable implant failure. In 1994, Dick et al introduced an
additional screw in the fractured vertebra leading to the 6 screw construct
to treat the thoracolumbar fractures but screws at the fractured site has
led to inconsistent effect including collapse of the fractured vertebra
leading to reduction in the vertebra height and non-union. While long
segment fixation incorporates multiple normal mobile spinal segments leading
to spinal stiffness. Transpedicular intracorporeal bone grafting proposed by
Liao et al, has a comparative advantage of union of the fractured vertebra
but the incidence of vertebral collapse still persists due to non-support of
the graft under axial loading. Considering both the additional screw at the
fractured site and transpedicular bone grafting have disadvantages as
non-union and collapse respectively, combining both the procedures should
not only fill the void of the fractured vertebra leading to better union but
should also impart mechanically more stable construct due to presence of an
additional screw in the fractured vertebra. Methodology: The
pre-operative clinical examination was done and scoring was done using the
ASIA score, Denis work score and Denis pain score. The pre-operative
radiograph of the thoracolumbar spine was evaluated to identify the
fractured vertebra level and to calculate the radiological parameters like
sagittal index, vertebral wedge angle, anterior body compression, Gardner’s
kyphosis angle, regional kyphosis, posterior wall angles, Cobbs angle. CT of
the thoracolumbar spine was done and the canal clearance at fractured site
was measured in mid sagittal sections, location of void in the vertebral
body in axial cuts and status of the pedicles of the fractured vertebra were
assessed. Results: There were 50 patients on whom we did
transpedicular intracorporeal bone grafting with index screw short segment
screw fixation. The average preoperative kyphosis angle was 22.3_ ± 6.6_,
which was corrected to 5.6_ ± 4.8 immediately after surgery (p < 0.001).
At final follow-up, the mean local kyphosis angle was 10.3_ ± 5.2_; loss of
correction was 4.7_ ± 2.7_ (p < 0.001). The average preoperative anterior
body height was 46.6% ± 12.5%, which improved to 85.7% ± 9.4% immediately
after surgery (p < 0.001). Anterior body height restored by surgery was
39.2% ± 13.3%. Anterior body height at 6-month follow-up was 74.9% ± 12.0%,
and the average loss of body height correction was 10.8% ± 7.0% (p <
0.001). Conclusion: The outcomes of this study confirmed that
the use of two additional augmenting screws in the fractured body with
short-segment pedicle screws and intracorporeal bone grafting is sufficient
for most thoracolumbar burst fractures, to attain fracture reduction,
maintain alignment achieve union and prevent vertebral collapse.

## 1445

## P597: Surgical outcome following delayed short segment posterior fixation
of unstable thoracolumbar junction injury

Dewan Shamsul Asif

1

, Safwat binte Salam

1

, and Sk Sader Hossain

2

1

Neurosurgery, Anwer Khan Modern Medical College, Dhaka,
Bangladesh

2

Neurosurgery, Al Manar Hospital, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Introduction: Spinal cord injury due to traumatic accidents of
the thoracolumbar spine is a major cause of disability throughout the world.
Due to unavailability of operation theatre schedule most of the spine
injured patients are managed conservatively or there is inadvertent delay in
surgery. This prospective study was designed to evaluate neurological
recovery and functional outcome following delayed short segment posterior
fixation of thoracolumbar junction injuries classified according to TLICS
system. Material and Methods: 38 TLJ injured patient followed
up after surgery for 84 months. The purpose of this study is to report the
surgical outcome of thoracolumbar junction fractures treated with
short-segment pedicle instrumentation. All patients had neurologic deficit
at the time of presentation. The unstable spine was fixed based on
Thoracolumbar Injury Classification Score system (TLICS), between 7-82 days
after trauma, by posterior short segment instrumentation. Neurological
recovery and functional status assessed in the follow-up period at one,
three, six- and eighty-four-month’s interval by ASIA impairment scale and
Oswestry Disability Index respectively. Results: There were 36
male and 2 female patients with average age 29.42 ± 8.11 years (range 17-50
years). Fall from a height was the most common (79%). Most of the patients
were farmer or day labour. Most frequent level fractures were at D12 and L1
comprising 76.3%. 10 (26.3%) patients had type A compression fracture and 28
(73.7%) patients had type B distraction type fracture. There were
preoperatively 2 (5.3%) patients with ASIA grade A, 3 (7.9%) patients with
ASIA grade B, 27 (71.1%) patients with ASIA grade C and 6 (15.8%) patients
with ASIA grade D. There was no neurological deterioration after surgery. At
final follow up of 22 patients, 96.87% exhibited neurological improvement
for at least one ASIA grade. There was a statistically significant relation
between pre-operative MRI interpretation and operative findings of posterior
ligamentous complex injury. There were no per-operative complications and
only 15.8% had different kinds of complications post-operatively. On
admission most of the patients were bed bound. But at six follow up ODI mean
score was 19.06 ± 6.67 (range 8-35) i.e. most of patients were in minimal
disability state. We could finally follow up 22 patients at 84 months
interval over telephone. Among 38 patients 2 patient died due to bed sore
complications. Rest of 20 patients are doing their daily job with minimal
disability at 84 months. Conclusion: It became clear that
careful diagnostic imaging examination, especially MRI, should be conducted
in order to eliminate the existence of posterior ligamentous or osseous
pathologies. Where early surgery is a distant dream delayed operative
outcome showed very promising results. Especially in our society where a
dependent person is more than a diseased itself and if these patients were
not treated properly, they would not only lose their employment but could be
a permanent burden and nuisance for their family. Although long term
follow-up evaluation needs to be verified radiologically, the long-term
functional follow-up results suggest a favorable outcome for delayed
short-segment posterior instrumentation of traumatic thoracolumbar junction
injuries.

## P599: Pedicle screws length and crosslinks as factors of stabilization
reliability of thoracolumbar junction traumatic injuries: finite element
study in lateroflection

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Ievgen Cheshuk

2

, Milan Vorodi

2

, Michael Karpinsky

3

, and Oleksandr Yaresko

3

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department

3

Biomechanical Laboratory, Sytenko Institute of Spine and Joint
Pathology, Kharkiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The zone of the thoracolumbar junction is the most
susceptible to traumatic injuries due to anatomical and physiological
features. Accordingly, the stabilization of this spine requires high
reliability. Extensive clinical experience of transpedicular stabilization
usage has revealed a number of factors hypothetically or actually
determining the reliability of fixation. The main are the depth of screw
insertion and the use of crosslinks. The effect of lateroflexion on the
operated spine as one of the most unfavorable types of loading is
considered. Material and Methods: Mathematical finite element
model of a fragment of the human thoracolumbar spine (Тh9-L5) was developed
in biomechanics laboratory of Sytenko Institute of Spine and Joint
Pathology. We modeled the result of decompression-stabilizing surgery with
total removal of the anterior and posterior support complexes of the
vertebral bodies Th12‒L1 including installation of vertebral body replacing
implant and fixation with a transpedicular system using 4 pairs of screws
(into the vertebral bodies Th10, Th11, L2 and L3). Lateroflexion was modeled
by applying a load of 350 N acting from right to left on the body and facet
processes of the Th9 vertebra. Results: When evaluating the
model without crosslinks and using monocortical pedicle screws, it was found
that the maximum loading values in the Th10, Th11, L2, and L3 vertebral
bodies were 3.4, 2.0, 3.5, and 8.6 MPa, respectively; and in the screws in
these vertebrae - 48.4, 48.3, 23.3 and 43.5 MPa. When using bicortical
screws without crosslinks - respectively 3.1, 2.5, 3.8, 9.6 MPa and 49.9,
51.9, 25.8, 44.8 MPa for bodies and screws; when using a combination of
short screws and crosslinks - 3.2, 2.0, 2.6, 7.5 MPa and 47.6, 47.5, 22.6,
41.2 MPa; when using crosslinks and bicortical screws - 3.0, 2.2, 2.7, 8.8
MPa and 48.3, 49.6, 24.3, 42.5 MPa. Conclusion: In
lateroflexion monocortical pedicle screws cause lower critical loading rates
compared to long screws at all control points of the model. Crosslinks in
combination with both short and long screws help to reduce stress levels.
The use of monocortical pedicle screws in combination with transverse ties
seems to be the most biomechanically effective in lateroflexion.

## 1619

## P600: Comparison between surgical outcome of short segment versus long
segment transpedicular stabilization for treatment of thorocolumbar
fracture

Md Yousuf Ali

1

 and Samrat Parajuli

2

1

Spine Surgery, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Bangabandhu Sheikh
Mujib Medical University, Dhaka, Bangladesh

2

Orthopedic Surgery, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University,
Dhaka, Bangladesh

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fracture is one of the most common
spinal traumas. It was still indeterminate whether short-segment (SS)
fixation was more effective and preferable than long-segment (LS) fixation.
We therefore conducted this meta-analysis to assess the comparative safety
and efficacy of SS and LS fixation for the treatment of thoracolumbar
fracture. The indications for operative treatment and type of stabilization
procedures for the treatment of thoracolumbar fracture remain controversial.
Material and Methods: The study was conducted at Department
of Orthopedic Surgery, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University (BSMMU)
and different private clinics at Dhaka, from July 2006 to June 2020. Surgery
was performed in multiple centers by the same spine surgeon to evaluate the
efficacy of short-segment fixation compared with that of long-segment
fixation in terms of the radiological and clinical outcomes in thoracolumbar
burst fractures. Total of 422 thoracolumbar fracture patients who underwent
the treatment with SS fixation (n = 217) and LS fixation (n = 205) were
included. Results: The outcomes of this study indicated that
outcome regarding implant failure, anterior body height loss (ABHL), cobb
angle (CA) and restoration ratio of compromised canal is better in the LS
fixation group than those of SS fixation group. However, SS group
significantly reduced surgical time when compared with LS group. There was
no significant difference regarding blood loss, complication rate, Sagittal
Index (SI) and kyphotic angle (KA). Radiological assessment of the kyphotic
angle was performed using the Cobb method immediately after the operation
and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively. The clinical outcomes were
evaluated using the Frankel score and ASIA grade criteria at the last
follow-up in Short segment and long segment respectively. The sex ratio,
mean age of patients, and composition of the fractured vertebral body were
similar in both groups. In the long-segment and short-segment group, 195
(95.1%) and 198 (91.2%) cases showed excellent or good outcomes,
respectively. In long segment the mean preoperative angle of injured
vertebra was 18.5°, the mean postoperative angle was 8.8°, the mean angle at
6 month’s follow-up was 10.5°, the mean initial correction was 9.9°, and the
mean loss of correction was 1.9°. So, the mean overall correction was found
8.0°. Whereas in Short segment the mean preoperative angle of injured
vertebra was 19.7°, the mean postoperative angle was 8.6°, the mean angle at
6 month’s follow-up was 11.9°, the mean initial correction was 11.1°, the
mean loss of correction was 3.3°. So, the mean overall correction was found
7.8°. There was no statistically significant difference in the average loss
of kyphosis correction between the two groups (p > 0.05).
Conclusion: In conclusion, short-segment pedicle screw
fixation including the fractured vertebral body might be as effective as
long-segment pedicle screw fixation for the treatment of unstable
thoracolumbar spinal fracture.

## 1630

## P601: New AO spine thoracolumbar injury classification system can predict
subsequent adjacent osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture after
balloon kyphoplasty

Takayuki Ogawa

1

, Chikako Shinozaki

1

, Takashi Chikawa

2

, and Akihiro Nagamachi

3

1

Orthopedics, Kaisei General Hospital, Kagawa, Japan

2

Orthopedics,Tokushima Prefecture Naruto Hospital, Tokushima,
Japan

3

Orthopedics, Yoshinogawa Medical Center, Tokushima, Japan

Introduction: Balloon kyphoplasty (BKP) is a minimal invasive
technique to treat symptomatic osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture
(OVCF). BKP is a relatively effective surgical procedure, however, we
sometimes encountered complications such as subsequent adjacent OVCF or
cement leakages. Subsequent OVCF causes sever back pain and kyphosis,
reducing patient quality of life. Preoperative estimation of subsequent
adjacent OVCF occurrence may help selecting other optional surgery or
planning rehabilitation program after BKP. New AO spine thoracolumbar injury
classification system (AO system) showed substantial reliability and
reproducibility among the surgeons. In this current study, we used AO system
to classify OVCF preoperatively and investigated incidence of subsequent
OVCF after BKP in each type of AO system. Material and Methods:
Between March, 2016 and March, 2022, 72 thoracolumbar OVCF were treated with
BKP. Patients with hemodialysis, Parkinson’s disease, malignant disease and
former BKP were excluded from this study. A total of 52 patients
participated in this study. There were 18 male and 34 female and their mean
age was 80 years. All patients underwent standing plain X-ray, CT and MRI
before surgery, 1 week, 2 months and 4 months after the surgery. All
fracture type were classified according to AO system before surgery.
Occurrence of subsequent adjacent OVCF in each type of AO system was
observed in follow-up period. Results: Thirty-seven patients
had no subsequent OVCF during the observation period, their mean age was 81
years. Fifteen patients had subsequent adjacent OVCF, their mean age was 79
years. Mean T-score of bone mineral density (BMD) of patients with
subsequent OVCF and without subsequent OVCF were -1.33 and -2.24,
respectively. There was no statistically significant difference of patient’s
demographics between two groups. Seventeen patients classified into A1, and
no subsequent OVCF was observed. Twenty-one patients classified into A3, and
subsequent OVCF observed in 2 patients. Eight patients classified into A4,
and subsequent OVCF observed in all patients. Six patients classified into
B2, and subsequent OVCF observed in 5 patients. Incidence of subsequent OVCF
of each type was 0% in A1, 9.3% in A3, 100% in A4 and 83.3% in B2.
Statistically significant difference of incidence was observed among 4 types
of OVCF (chi-square test p < 0.001). Conclusion: This study
demonstrated that AO system can estimate occurrence of subsequent adjacent
OVCF after BKP. Type A4 and B2 were found to be more prone to subsequent
adjacent OVCF.

## 1706

## P602: Posterior approach in surgical management of traumatic
spondyloptosis of thoracolumbar junction

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Ievgen Cheshuk

2

, and Milan Vorodi

2

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The thoracolumbar junction is the most common
location of traumatic spinal injuries and contains 50-60% of all fractures
of the thoracic and lumbar spine. Spondyloptosis is not very frequent, but
one of the most severe types of traumatic injury, that is characterized by a
gross violation of spine axis in one or more planes. Traumatic
spondyloptosis is divided into reducible and irreducible, depending on the
possibility of intraoperative restoration of the spinal axis without
resection of the damaged vertebra. Material and Methods: We
performed a retrospective analysis of the patients’ database admitted in
Romodanov Neurosurgery Institute of National Academy of Medical Sciences of
Ukraine over the past 4 years (2017 to 2020) to identify all cases with
traumatic irreducible spondyloptosis of the thoracolumbar junction.
Results: Five patients aged from 18 to 52 years (mean 31.2
years) were revealed. The minimum period from injury to surgery was 14 days,
maximum 3 months and 2 days (average 42.2 days). All patients had a
neurological deficit of ASIA A at the time of admission. The score by TLICS
scale was 8 points. All the patients had the injury of
laterospondyloroptosis type: in three cases as an isolated displacement only
in the coronary plane, in two combined - in the coronary and sagittal. We
performed surgery by isolated posterior approach in all cases. As a body
replacement system in 2 patients, we used a vertical cylindrical implant
(Mesh), in 3 patients - a telescopic body replacing implant. The method of
bicortical implantation of transpedicular screws was applied. The
transpedicular system was strengthened by two cross links of the rod-to-rod
type. We managed to achieve the restoration of spine axis in both the
coronary and sagittal planes. Subsequent terms of control examinations were
2; 6 and 12-18 months of the postoperative period. We observed regression of
neurological disorders in two patients, in one case to ASIA B, in another to
ASIA C. Conclusion: Isolated posterior approach has
demonstrated high efficacy in the surgical management of traumatic
irreducible spondyloptosis of the thoracolumbar junction, allowed both to
restore the axis of the spine and to provide the stability of fusion.

## 1712

## P603: What is the best decision-making classification of traumatic
thoracolumbar junction injuries?

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Ievgen Cheshuk

2

, and Milan Vorodi

2

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The thoracolumbar junction is one of the most
"typical" areas of traumatic changes when exposed to a mechanical load on
the human body. Currently, a specific classification for injuries of the
thoracolumbar junction has not been developed, therefore, when describing
injuries in this zone, grading schemas characterizing the whole thoracic and
lumbar spine are used. Material and Methods: A retrospective
analysis of the treatment tactics was carried out in 96 patients with
traumatic injuries of the thoracolumbar junction, who attended the
outpatient department of the A.P. Romodanov Institute in the period from
2019 to 2021. The average age of patients is 41.3 years. The ratio of men
and women is 3.6:1.0. We analyzed the patients’ data who underwent both
surgical treatment and conservative therapy. All injuries were ranked using
F. Magerl et al. and AOSpine classifications. Neurological status was
assessed using the ASIA scale (American Spinal Injury Association), the
nature of the lesion was specified using the McCormack criteria. Statistical
data processing was performed using the Random Forest machine learning
algorithm. Results: The most frequent injuries according to the
classification of F. Magerl et al. were A3.1 (14.58%), A3.2 and B2.3 (8.33%
each), according to the AOSpine classification - type C (26.04%), subtypes
B2 (17.71%) and A4 (16.67%). When assessing the relationship between the
nature of damage and the level of neurological disorders, the overall error
rate for F. Magerl et al. and AOSpine classifications were 69.79% and 66.67%
respectively. The greatest relationship between the nature of
osteoligamentous lesions and neurological disorders is typical for patients
with ASIA B and E. In the treatment of patients, open posterior
decompression of the spinal canal in combination with transpedicular
stabilization (40.62%), isolated posterior stabilization without
decompression (25.0%), a combination of decompressive laminectomy,
posterolateral corpectomy with interbody fusion using a body-replacing
system supplemented with transpedicular fixation (14.58%), less often
conservative therapy (9.38%) and percutaneous cementoplasty (7.29%). The
nature of the injury makes it possible to unambiguously determine the
optimal method of therapy using the classification of F. Magerl et al. with
a probability of 58.33%, when applying the AOSpine classification - with a
probability of 55.21%. When building models taking into account the nature
of damage, the level of neurological disorders and McCormack criteria, it
was found that the error in unambiguously determining the most effective
method of treatment when using the classification of F. Magerl et al. is
26.04%, when using the AOSpine classification - 21.88%.
Conclusion: The type of the injury, ranked using the
classifications of AOSpine and F. Magerl et al., does not allow choosing the
optimal method for the treatment of traumatic lesion of the thoracolumbar
junction. The use of additional predictors significantly improves the
accuracy of the forecast. When applying the AOSpine classification, the best
results were recorded. The use of the AOSpine classification is more
promising for the development of a multifactorial algorithm for the
treatment of traumatic injuries of the thoracolumbar junction.

## P604: Some biomechanical considerations regarding pedicle screw insertion
depth and role of crosslinks in thoracolumbar junction fracture: a study
under compressive loads

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Iaroslav Tsymbaliuk

2

, Michael Karpinsky

3

, and Oleksandr Yaresko

3

1

Spinal Neurosurgery

2

Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Romodanov Neurosurgery
Institute, Kyiv, Ukraine

3

Biomechanical Laboratory, Sytenko Institute of Spine and Joint
Pathology, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: The thoracolumbar junction is one of the most
frequently damaged parts of the human spine when exposed to a traumatic
factor. Corpectomy in combination with posterior decompression and
restoration of the spinal support function is often performed using an
interbody implant and posterior transpedicular stabilization to achieve
adequate decompression and stabilization in severe traumatic injuries of
this level. The surgery of a type is characterized by significant
instability of the operated segment and determines increased requirements
for the rigidity and reliability of posterior fixation. We have modeled the
situation of a two-level corpectomy with subsequent replacement of bodies
with a mesh implant and posterior transpedicular stabilization with 8
screws. Material and Methods: We developed a mathematical
finite element model of the human thoracolumbar spine, the components of
which are the vertebrae Th9 ‒ Th11 and L2-L5 (vertebrae Th12-L1 are
removed), as well as elements of metal structures vertebral replacing
implant and transpedicular system. We modeled four variants of
transpedicular fixation: system with short screws and screws passing through
the cortical layer of anterior wall of vertebral body, as well as with two
cross links and without them. The stress-strain state of the models was
studied under the influence of a vertical compressive distributed load,
which was applied to the body of the Th9 vertebra and its articular
surfaces. The load value was 350 N, which corresponds to the weight of the
upper body. Results: We determined that transpedicular fixation
of the thoracolumbar vertebrae with the use of long screws reduces the level
of tension in the bone elements of the models. In the area of screw entry
into the pedicle of the T10, T11, L2 and L3 vertebral arch, the load when
using short screws was 3.1, 1.7, 3.9 and 12.1 MPa, respectively, when using
bicortically installed screws - 2.9, 1 8, 3.8 and 10.6 MPa. The addition of
two cross-links also reduces the maximum load values in critical areas of
the model to a certain extent. In the case of a combination of short screws
and two cross-links, the load in these areas was 2.8, 1.7, 3.6 and 11.5 MPa,
when using bicortical screws and cross-links - 2.8, 1.6, 3.3 and 9.3 MPa.
The study of the stress-strain state of other parts of the model revealed a
similar trend. Conclusion: The use of long screws with fixation
in the cortical bone of anterior part of the vertebral bodies reduces the
level of tension in the bone elements of the models. The use of cross links
gives greater rigidity to the transpedicular system, that also reduces the
tension in the bone tissue.

## 1746

## P605: Spinal subdural hematoma in ankylosing spondylitis patients without
coagulation therapy: case study of two patients

Inka Berglar

1

, Laura Snyder

2

, and Gabriella Paisan

2

1

Neuroradiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United
States

2

Neurosurgery, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, United
States

Introduction: Patients with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are at
high risk of significant spinal trauma after relatively low impact events
such as ground level falls. Due to the osteopenic nature of the disease
process, complex spinal fractures are common in these patients.
Additionally, patients may sustain rare traumatic complications from these
fractures, such as spinal subdural or epidural hematomas. Traumatic spinal
subdural hematoma (SSDH) is extremely rare with only a few cases described
in the literature and is typically associated with antiplatelet or
anticoagulant use. In this case series, we describe two cases of traumatic
SSDH in patients with ankylosing spondylitis without anticoagulation or
antiplatelet therapy, which has not previously been reported in the
literature. Material and Methods: Case study.
Results: Ankylosing spondylitis is an important subtype of
an interrelated group of rheumatic diseases and AS patients are particularly
vulnerable to severe spinal injuries following relatively minor traumas due
to the ankylosing process of the spine. Most traumatic spinal hematomas are
epidural and SSDHs account for only a fracture of cases of spinal hematomas.
Treatment options vary between conservative and surgical management and
indications for surgical evacuation are dependent on the clinical context of
the patient and their injury. Conclusion: This is the first
detailed report of two posttraumatic AS patients with SSDHs without prior
anticoagulation therapy. Although the etiology is not yet fully understood,
these cases demonstrate that the appearance of SSDHs can be highly variable
and can occur after only minor trauma in AS patients. While epidural and
especially subdural spinal hematomas are extremely rare in general, AS
patients are more likely to develop these hemorrhages and they should be
considered as a possible cause of spinal cord injury in this population and
may also require surgical evacuation.

## P606: Thoracic fracture dislocation with bilateral locked facet joints -
a modified reduction technique

Jure Pavesic

1

, Stjepan Dokuzovic

1

, Stipe Corluka

1

, and Vide Bilic

1

1

Spinal Surgery Division, Traumatology Department, University
Hospital Centre Sestre Milosrdnice, Zagreb, Croatia

Introduction: Thoracic spine fracture dislocations with
bilateral locked facets pose a challenge for safe and effective
intraoperative reduction. Several techniques have been described, though
they may in some contexts prove hazardous or ineffective. Material and
Methods: We present a modification to previously described
reduction techniques where the force required to perform the reduction is
dispersed over several elements of the reduction process as to minimize
further trauma from the reduction process itself. Results: When
other techniques fail due to extreme rigidity, increasing reduction force is
not always an option due to the possibility of screw pull-out, lamina
fracture, or sudden forceful reduction which may potentially cause a second
hit to the spinal cord. Force dispersion by technique modification is our
preferred method to reduce required forces and make the reduction safer for
the cord and remaining healthy bone. Conclusion: Our
modification may be a reliable and safe method for highly rigid locked
fracture-dislocations of the thoracic spine, though further validation is
required.

## P607: Results of the placement of thoracolumbar transpedicular screws in

Saul Solorio Pineda

spine. This technique consists of placing screws through the pedicle and
directed towards the vertebral body through a posterior approach and placing
a system of titanium bars. Objective: To analyze the results of
precision and malposition of thoracolumbar transpedicular screws guided by

A retrospective, observational and descriptive analysis of 124 patients over
14 years of age who presented spinal cord injury with data of vertebral
instability and/or fractures in the thoracolumbar region who underwent
transpedicular fixation with titanium screws by open posterior guided
approach was performed. by fluoroscopy in the period from January 1, 2016 to
December 31, 2019. Results: The most frequently performed
approach was the thoraco-lumbar in 52.62% of the cases, 910 screws were
placed, 75.8% of the cases 8 screws were placed per patient and the
percentage of good placement in our cases was 91.21% (n = 830).
Conclusion: The surgical technique described is safe with
precision percentages comparable to that described in the literature and
with a low percentage of complications.
Keywords: Pedicle screw, fluoroscopy, computed tomography

## P608: Multicenter validation of a CT criteria for thoracolumbar posterior
ligamentous complex injury: study protocol and preliminary results

Mohamed Ali

1

1

Neurosurgery, Prince Mohamed Bin Abdelaziz Hospital, Riyadh, Saudi
Arabia

Introduction: Two recent single-institution studies have
proposed criteria for posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) status in Computed
Tomography (CT) based on the number of positive CT findings. PLC should be
considered injured if ≥ 2 positive CT findings based on a high positive
predictive value (PPV, 91%) for PLC injury in MRI, indeterminate PLC (M1
modifier) if there is a single positive CT finding (PPV 31%), and intact if
there are no positive CT findings (PPV 9%). This retrospective multicenter
study aims to validate those CT criteria for PLC injury in a large,
independent population from diffident settings. Materials &
Methods: Three hundred fifty-seven consecutive patients with at
least one vertebral body fracture (T1-L5) who underwent CT and MRI within
ten days of injury will be enrolled in participating centers. Patients with
translation injury, osteoporotic or pathological fractures or incomplete
imaging were excluded. At least two reviewers from each center will assess
CT for the following findings according to proposed definitions: facet joint
malalignment, facet joint widening, horizontal laminar fracture, spinous
process fracture, and interspinous widening. The reference standard is PLC
injury defined by black stripe discontinuity due to supraspinous or
ligamentum flavum rupture. Each reviewer will interpret all de-identified
CT/ MRI images independently, blinded to clinical data and other readings,
within a 4-week interval. When the two reviewers disagreed about the MRI's
PLC status or the Number of CT findings, the case was resolved by a third
reviewer. Prior consensus training will be done for all reviewers to
standardize the imaging interpretation protocol. Multivariate association
between CT findings and PLC injury will be examined. Results:
the preliminary results from multiple centers will be presented. The
diagnostic accuracy of combinations of those CT findings with independent
association with PLC injury will be examined (0, 1, ≥2 findings). The
following measures will be reported: sensitivity, specificity, accuracy,
positive and negative predictive values, and positive and negative
likelihood ratio. Inter-intraobserver reliability in identifying each CT
finding or combinations of CT findings will be assessed using Cohen’s kappa
(k) and Fleiss kappa statistics. Conclusion: We provided a
comprehensive methodology for a multicenter validation of a CT criteria for
PLC injury. A multicenter design is needed to improve generalizability of
the findings. A retrospective study with well balanced study population is
more feasible thana prospective design.
Keywords: Posterior ligamentous complex, thoracolumbar fractures, imaging
algorithm, Computed tomography, Magnetic resonance imaging

Introduction: The variability of S2 alar iliac (S2AI) screw

as 66% depending on the type of imaging used for assessment. No studies have
compared the type of screw used in S2AI fixation and the impact on hardware

incidence of hardware failure and revision rates between cannulated vs

## P610: The postoperative pedicle screw position after dorsal

Felix Zimmermann

, Kohl Katharina

, Eric Mandelka

1

, Paul Alfred Grützner

1

, Jochen Franke

1

, and Vetter Sven

1

1

BG Klinik Ludwigshafen, Ludwigshafen, Germany

Background: Intraoperative cone beam CT (CBCT) imaging in dorsal
instrumentation facilitates pedicle screw positioning. However, this effect
may be reduced due to artifacts that affect image quality in patients with
obesity. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether intraoperative
CBCT leads to an improved postoperative screw position independent of body
weight. Materials and Methods: A total of 71 patients (18
patients with a BMI > 30 kg/m2, 53 patients with a BMI < 30
kg/m2) who underwent dorsal instrumentation with
intraoperative CBCT imaging were included in study groups one (SG1) and two
(SG2). In SG1, 128 pedicle screws were implanted, compared with 361 in SG2.
Patient BMI was defined according to the WHO recommendations. The pedicle
screw position in postoperative computed tomography was assessed using the
Gertzbein-Robbins classification. Results: In SG1 (BMI > 30
kg/m2), a total of 107 (83.6%) pedicle screws showed no
relevant perforation (type A + B), and 21 (16.4%) pedicle screws showed
relevant perforation (type C – E) in the postoperative computed tomography.
In SG2 (BMI < 30 kg/m2), 328 (90.9%) screws were classified as
type A + B, and 33 (9.1%) screws were classified as type C – E in the
postoperative computed tomography. There were significant differences
between the values of SG1 and SG2 (p = 0.03). Conclusion: The
included patients with obesity showed significantly worse pedicle screw
positions postoperatively after dorsal instrumentation with intraoperative
CBCT imaging than the included normal-weight patients. Consequently, obesity
seems to have a negative effect on the postoperative pedicle screw position
after dorsal instrumentation despite intraoperative CBCT imaging.
Keywords: spine, dorsal instrumentation, pedicle screw, cone-beam CT,
patients with obesity, BMI.

## P611: Fragile lumbar chance fracture in patients with ankylosing
spondylitis- Right or wrong for surgical indication

Takahiro Iizuka

1

, Tetsuro Takai

1

, Tokuji Kashiro

1

, and Hiroshige Debata

1

1

Orthopedic Spine Surgery, Kouseikai Takai Hospital, Nara,
Japan

Introduction: Chance Fracture is Classified as Type B1-3 (AO
spine Classification System). This fracture is considered to be a failure of
the whole vertebral column caused by high-energy flexion or extension force.
We experienced 4 patients with Fragile Chance Fracture with ankylosing
spondylitis and also osteoporosis. Osteoporotic vertebral compression
fractures are common fractures as fragile fractures in elderlies. Chance
Fractures with Ankylosing Spine are challenging against conservative
therapies which frequently resulted in non-union. This type of fracture
requires surgical fixation in the early stage of its onset.
Aims: We reported unwonted Fragile Chance Fracture in
patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis and Osteoporosis in extremely elder
patients. We would like to discuss the indications and significance of
Fragile Chance Fractures in extremely elder patients from these patients.
Results and Cases Reports: We experienced Four patients
from 2016-2022 with this TypeB1 fractures. Average age 83 (81-87). All of
them were male and also caused by a fragile fall on the floor, not by
high-energy trauma i.e. traffic accident. All patients were treated with
vertebral plasty using HA sticks, posterior local bone plantations, and
posterior instrumentations 2 above and 2 below of fractured site. Operation
time was 1.5-2 hours and Blood loss was less than 200 ml. All patients were
relieved from intractable pain and discharged within 2-3 weeks. EVENITY
(romosozumab aqqg from AMGEN) was applied to all patients.
Discussions: First of all, we should discuss the surgical
indications for extremely elder patients in aging societies. Unwonted trauma
in the elderly should be treated quickly (data from hip fractures) and also
less invasive in terms of surgical time and blood loss. Fragile Chance
fracture in ankylosing spine is one of the most intractable vertebral
fractures which resulted in prolonged pain and delayed neural damage.
Especially in elderlies, surgical timing loss would sometimes result in loss
of life expectancy. We suggest a quick decision for surgical treatment if
they would be tolerable for surgical stress of 1.5-2 hours and 200ml blood
loss. The delayed surgical indication would spoil all the results in Fragile
Chance Fractures in elderlies.

## P612: Acute management of spinal cord injury: a retrospective analysis
from a Portuguese referral centre

Rita Faria

1

, Sara Diniz

2

, Carolina Luísa Lemos

1

, and Ricardo Rodrigues-Pinto

2

1

Instituto de Ciências Biomédicas Abel Salazar, Portugal

2

Orthopaedic Department, Centro Hospitalar Universitário do Porto,
Portugal

Introduction: Acute spinal cord injury entails significant
impairment in patients’ quality of life and elevated financial costs to the
healthcare system and society. Early access to specialized care and surgical
decompression within 24 hours post-injury have been associated with improved
outcomes and are, therefore, currently recommended. Centro Hospitalar
Universitário do Porto holds a dedicated Spinal Unit which has a rota
through the year that designates an on-call spine surgeon to treat spine and
spinal cord injury patients. Nevertheless, data regarding the timing of
treatment of these patients is not documented. The aim was to characterize
patients with spinal cord injury that underwent surgery at Centro Hospitalar
Universitário do Porto and their pathway to definitive care post-injury.
Material and Methods: A single-centre retrospective study
was performed. Adult patients with pre-operative diagnosis of traumatic
spinal injuries that underwent surgery at Centro Hospitalar Universitário do
Porto over the course of 4 years were identified and classified with
baseline American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale grades, which
were reassessed after a year. The times of first hospital admission, arrival
at the site of definitive care and surgery were collected. Patients were
classified by injury mechanism, anatomical level of injury, neurological
injury, admissions at intermediate hospitals and timings of surgery. The
relationship between severity of neurological injury and time to surgery was
evaluated. Results: 208 patients were included, most of whom
were males. Falls were responsible for the majority of injuries. 33.7% of
the patients had neurological deficits, 37.1% of which had the worst pattern
level (ASIA A). 40 (57.1%) patients with neurological injuries were first
admitted at an intermediate hospital. 44 (63.8%) were submitted to surgery
in the first 12 hours, 10 (14.5%) between 12-24 hours and 15 (21.7%) after
24 hours. Patients with more severe neurological injuries were operated
significantly faster (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Admissions at
intermediate hospitals represent a potentially modifiable system-related
cause for delays. Based on these results perhaps an effort should be made in
order to create a streamlined path to definitive care for patients with
acute spinal cord injury.

## P613: Hitting the target: bullseye trauma in motor vehicle
accidents

Aisha Jeffers

1

, Georgina Crate

1

, Simon Weil

1

, Dimitrios Teslios

1

, Mohamed Abdalla

1

, Bisola Ajayi

1

, Jason Bernard

1

, Timothy Bishop

1

, and Darren Lui

1

1

Neurosciences, St. Georges Hospital, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: A ‘bullseye injury’ is a colloquial term in the UK
for a head injury involving impact to a structure, typically a windscreen,
with the shatter pattern similar to that of a target. The patient can be
either internal or external to the vehicle that has been hit. It is a
colloquial term with a heterogenous variety of mechanism of injury often
insinuating a significant injury severity score (ISS). To the authors
knowledge there are no studies characterising the Orthopaedic injuries and
identifying the prevalence of head and spinal injuries associated with
bullseye trauma. Methods: A retrospective study reviewed a
major trauma centre prospectively collected database between 31/10/2017 and
16/03/2020 searching for the term ‘bullseye’. Identification of head and
spinal injuries were examined. Velocity of injury, type of fractures
sustained and accompanying injuries were assessed. The injury severity score
(ISS) was also calculated for all patients. Results: 129
patients were identified with 102 patients having complete records for
review. The categories were Pedestrians (n = 60), cyclists (n = 14),
motorcyclists (n = 15) and car (n = 13). All patients underwent Full body
Trauma CT scans. The mean ISS was 9.2 and for motorbike injuries 13.5.
Severe injury is denoted ISS > 15 with external bullseye traumas occurred
in pedestrians (20%), cyclists (21%), motorbikes (21%) whereas patients with
internal bullseye injuries within the car was only 7%. Mortality occurrences
were 5% in pedestrians and 7% in cyclists. 4.6% of patients presenting with
a bullseye injury sustained spinal injuries. These patients were all male,
mean age 52.6 (range 57y – 74y). As a whole, the majority of patients were
pedestrians struck by cars (58%) followed by motorcyclists (16%). Therefore
the predominant mechanism in this group of patients was noted to be an
external bullseye injury (83%). Of those patients, all sustained concomitant
axial skeleton fractures with 50% being adjacent spinal segment fractures.
33% of spinal fractures were isolated fractures, with multiple fractures
being seen in 66% of cases. The majority of the fractures sustained were
noted to be stable (83%), with 0% requiring surgical fixation. C spine
injuries occurred in: Pedestrians (1%), Cyclists (14%), Motorcyclists (0%)
and Cars (15%). Head Injuries occurred in: Pedestrians (23%), Cyclists
(21%), Motorcyclists (6%) and Cars (7%). Conclusions:
‘Bullseye’ injuries have a variety of mechanisms where patients are internal
or external to the motor vehicle when they strike the windscreen. Severe
Injuries ISS > 15 occur 1 in 5 of all external mechanisms. Head and
cervical spine injuries constitute 15% pedestrians, 35% cyclists, 6%
motorcyclists and 22% motor vehicles. The spinal injuries reported were most
commonly stable. With 0% requiring surgical fixation. Of the patients with
concomitant head injuries, 60% were reported to have intracranial
haemorrhage. Decompression was not required in any of these cases. 5-7% of
pedestrian or cyclists having this injury will be fatal.

## P615: Floating spine and other types of associated multiple simultaneuos
unstable vertebral fractures. Descriptive study

Guillermo Ricciardi

1,2

, Lyanne Romero Valverde

2

, Santiago Formaggin

1,2

, Ignacio Gabriel Garfinkel

1,2

, Gabriel Genaro Carrioli

, and Daniel Oscar Ricciardi

Spine Team - Traumatology and Orhopaedics, Centro Médico Fitz Roy,
Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Argentina

2

Spine Team - Traumatology and Orthopaedics, Sanatorio Güemes, Ciudad
de Buenos Aires, Argentina

Introduction: The association of two non-contiguous unstable
vertebral fractures is rare with only a few previous publications, limited
to case reports or brief case series. The association of two non-contiguous
vertebral fracture dislocations has received different names in the
literature including “in bloc” dislocation and “floating spine”. We aim to
present a series of patients with associated multiple and simultaneous
unstable vertebral fractures (Type B or C). Material and
Methods: Descriptive study of patients with high-energy spinal
cord trauma and associated multiple unstable and simultaneous vertebral

B (ligament injury) and/or type C (subluxation/dislocation) multiple
vertebral fractures were included. Patients with incomplete medical records,

were excluded. Demographic and clinical data was registered considering
trauma mechanism, spine region, classification, floating spine injury type,
pre- and postoperative neurological status according to ASIA disability
scale, associated injuries and comorbidities, surgical approach,
instrumentation levels involved, complications, radiographic and clinical
evolution. Results: We registered 5 patients (1 woman and 4
men) with two simultaneous unstable vertebral fractures, including 4 cases
(80%) of non-contiguous fractures and 3 (60%) with 2 simultaneous

(type B or C) due to high-energy trauma. A rare injury association, with

addition to the well-known association of simultaneous type C fractures
(floating spine), we describe the association of type B (B2 or B3) with type
C fractures as a variant of non-contiguous and simultaneous unstable
vertebral injuries.

## P616: Invasive intrathecal devices for monitoring of the spinal cord cord
perfussion pressure: systematic review

Som Singh

1

, Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Julio Jauregui

2

, Samuel Brehm

1

, Karma Barot

1

, Abby Carey-Ewend

1

, Ahmed Hanafy

1

, Michael Kann

1

, Matthew De la Paz

1

, Michael Olufawo

1

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, and Camilo Molina

1

1

Neurosurgery

2

Orthopaedic Surgery, Washington University, St. Louis, United
States

Introduction: It is well-known that systemic hypotension after
spinal cord injury (SCI) contributes to cord ischemia, but also aggressive
mean arterial pressure (MAP) management can favor secondary injury to the
spinal cord. Let alone, this requirement requires clinical consideration of
complications related to vasopressor usage in the attempt to maintain target
MAP which could make the consideration that direct MAP augmentation could be
cumbersome compared to alternative hemodynamic mechanisms. In lieu of the
problems of using MAP to guide the acute perfusion needs of the spinal cord,
methods for monitoring the spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) to guide
hemodynamic management of SCI in the setting of SCI. The objective of this
study was to identify the health effects of using different invasive
intrathecal device. Material and Methods: An electronic
database search was conducted for studies that evaluated intrathecal devices
to monitor the spinal cord perfusion, their health effects properties and
adverse events. Data extracted included study design, patient population,
characteristics of the intrathecal device, health effects details, as well
as rates of adverse events. The ROB2 and the ROBINS-I rating scales were
used to assess the risk of bias of the reported health effects.
Results: Out search yielded 3,919 unique citations, 23 of
which met the eligibility criteria and were summarized in this study. 8
studies (7 observational and 1 randomized clinical trial) evaluated the
effects of lumbar drain catheter. These studies found that episodes of SCPP
< 50 mmHg were associated with failure to achieve neurological
improvement by at least one AIS grade after 6 months at follow up (OR 0.9, p
0.031). In addition, clinical adherence to the target perfusion range of 65
mm Hg was positively related to neurological improvement by at least one
ASIA grade. These studies did not reported any major adverse events. 15
studies assessed the effect of a Codman pressure probe inserted at the site
of injury. These group of studies informed that the SCPP values at
90-100mmHg are associated with the best ASIA recovery at 9-12 months (OR
1.039, p 0.002). These studies reported a 7% incidence of persistent CSF
leakage requiring revision after device insertion. The risk of bias among
all included studies ranged from low-to-serious risk of bias across all
domains. Conclusion: We found two approaches to measure the
spinal cord perfusion pressure: via lumbar catheter drains and Codman
pressure probes inserted at the site of injury. The included studies overall
showed positive correlation between SCPP measurement and neurological
improvement post-injury, however due to the moderate to high risk of bias of
the studies it is difficult to ascertain the true health effects of these
interventions. Monitoring SCPP with a Codman probe has value to monitor
physiological changes close to the site of injury, however requires a
duroplasty procedure; lumbar drains can be easily inserted but have the
disadvantage of not being close to the site of injury. Further investigation
is needed to clarify the true effects of these interventions, optimal
set-up, required infrastructure, clarify the risk, benefits and
alternatives.

## P617: Multi-state modeling for prediction of neurological recovery in
ASIA A spinal cord injury

Ali Moghaddamjou

1

, Alex Bak

2

, Jefferson Wilson

1

, and Michael Fehlings

1

1

Neurosurgery, University of Toronto, Canada

2

University of Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Predicting prognosis after a complete traumatic
Spinal Cord Injury (tSCI) has been challenging given varying disease
courses, clinical histories, and patient populations. To improve our
understanding of tSCI and enhance the clinical prediction of outcomes we
propose to model disease progression, transition probabilities, and patient
characteristics. Material and Methods: Patients with ASIA A
injury were identified from 3 prospective, multi-center datasets. A-priori
we identified age, injury region, and early surgery as covariates in our

transition of AIS grades of AIS A patients. These results support early
aggressive treatment for ASIA A patients and consideration of patient
trajectories and injury region in decision making.
