## P658: Spinal solitary fibrous tumor: a case report

Sliti Firas

1

, Nessrine Nessib

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, nadhir karmani

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Alaa Belhadj

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Solitary fibrous tumors of the spine are extremely
rare tumors. Most solitary fibrous tumors originate in the thoracic spine,
then in the cervical spine and finally in the lumbar spine with only 6 cases
reported in the literature. Involvement of the vertebral body is an even
rarer entity with 4 cases found. Material and Methods: We
report the cas of a 29-year olf female treated in the neurosurgery
department at the Mongi Ben Hamida National Institute of Neurology in
Tunisia. Results: Our patient was initially treated for a
right-sided cauda equina hemisyndrome, with an expansive process on imaging
that destroyed the 4th lumbar vertebra. The patient underwent surgery with
incomplete removal of the tumor process by a posterior approach. The
anatomopathological study concluded to a solitary fibrous tumor of the
hemangiopericyte type (Grade III WHO). The patient reconsulted for
recurrence of the symptomatology 2 years later, with a tumor recurrence on
imaging. She underwent embolization followed by subtotal excision by
posterior approach. Subsequently, she was reoperated for additional L4
corporectomy and anterolateral excision. The patient received 22 sessions of
radiotherapy postoperatively. Currently, at 4 years post-op, imaging shows
no recurrence. Conclusion: Solitary fibrous tumors of the
spine, especially of the lumbar spine, are extremely rare. The diagnosis of
certainty remains histological. The management of these tumors is poorly
codified and there is currently no recognized adjuvant treatment. Only
complete removal of the tumor can control its evolution. Prolonged follow-up
is in all cases essential to detect early local or general recurrences.

## 1458

## P659: Tumour masquerading as sciatica

Sushant Srivastava

1

, Virendra Agrawal

1

, Kaustubh Sawant

1

, Tushar Patil

1

, and Harish Pawar

1

1

Orthopaedics, Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya Shatabdi Hospital, Mumbai,
India

Introduction: Nerve sheath tumors can be found in different
regions of the spinal cord, with the cervical cord region being the most
common site, followed by the thoracic and lumbosacral regions .Spinal
schwannomas, along with the meningiomas, are the most common spinal nerve
sheath tumors. A Schwannoma is defined as a benign tumor of the nerve sheath
which arises from Schwann cells. Schwannomas most frequently involve the
head and neck area, and also the major nerve trunks. They usually also
appear on the flexor aspects of the limbs, especially near the elbow, wrist
and knee. Also, the spinal roots and the cervical plexus, the vagus,
peroneal and ulnar nerves are the most commonly affected. Materials
and Methods: Presenting a case of 29 yr old male complaining of
severe pain radiating from lower back region to the right lower limb. The
neurological examination showed MRC Grade 5 power and normal reflexes for
bilateral lower limbs. Local examination showed a hard mass near the
sacro-iliac joint. Radiological investigations showed the mass to be a
multilobulated 3.2 x 3.6 x 3.4 cm sized hyperintense mass on T2/STIR along
the right gluteus maximus muscle. The patient was explained of this
condition. An oval , multilobulated and well encapsulated tumour was found
near the gluteus maximus muscle. Its origin was unclear and attempts were
made to trace it. Later the lesion was excised en bloc surgically. After the
surgery, presenting symptoms disappeared immediately. Histopathologic
examination showed schwannoma. One year following excision of the lesion,
the patient remained asymptomatic, with no evidence of local recurrence or
any complication. Results: Surgical excision of the tumour
causing symptoms is curative and provides the patient immediate and
permanent relief of symptoms. However, in literature there have been several
reports of a incidences of neurological complications like new or worsening
pain and motor weakness after excision of the schwannoma. In our patient, en
bloc surgical excision was performed and he was symptom free and displayed
no clinical or any radiographic evidence of recurrence of the tumour after
12 months of postoperative follow-up. Conclusion: To treat a
case of sciatica the most important tools with a clinician are the detailed
and complete clinical history, thorough physical examination and
radiological investigation like magnetic resonance imaging to reach the
pertinent solution. Careful and complete surgical excision of the tumour
lesion is curative, which provides immediate and permanent remission of
symptoms without any complication.

Background: Inadequate sleep has been reported to affect mood
and function. Psychiatric comorbidity is seldom reported in primary
intradural-extramedullary spinal cord tumors (IDEM-SCT) patients. Generally,
minimal perioperative improvement outcomes have been evidently reported in
degenerative spine patients with underlying depressive comorbid status but
this information highly lacking in the primary spinal cord tumor population.
Methods: Following Institutional Review Board (IRB) of

Significance was set at (p < 0.05). Results: Overall, 92
patients with IDEM-SCTs were matched in this study, [NDP_IDEM-SCT]; n = 46

< 0.05). At baseline, the incidence of disability assessed by NDI or ODI
was significantly higher in the [NDP_IDEM-SCT] patient group, (p < 0.05)
but no significant difference between W.H.O. gradings was observed. At
2-year postoperative, the incidence of neck or back pain was significantly
higher in the [DP_IDEM-SCT] patient group concomitant with decreased patient
satisfaction rate, (p < 0.05). Conclusions: This study
indicated that IDEM-SCT patients with baseline depressive status were also
vulnerable to metabolic aberrations, particularly, in those with ApoEε2
(rs7412) variant genotype who showed less adequate average sleep time
(average of ≤ 6.5 hours per day). The ApoEε2 (rs7412) variant genotype
expression dysfunction in these DP patients suggests the potential negative
effects of psychiatric comorbidity on modulating the physiological
cardio-metabolic function of ApoEε2 (rs7412) as this gene variant is known
to robustly control serum lipid profile. A baseline DP status was also
associated with increased 2-year postoperative pain, and patient
dissatisfaction rates. Future studies are encouraged to explore the
relationship between ApoEε2 (rs7412) variant and DP status and how these
facets overlap in spine patients. The anticipated findings would help
uncover the clinical impacts of these entities in spine patient
population.

## 1510

## P662: Spinal localization of brown tumors: a case report and a review of
literature

Sliti Firas

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Alaa Belhadj

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Nadhir Karmani

1

, Khansa Abderrahmane

1

, Imed Ben Said

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: The brown tumor is a benign bone lesion that is
the consequence of a hyperparathyroid state. It is less frequent in cases
with secondary hyperparathyroidism but is common in patients with chronic
renal failure at the hemodialysis stage. The spinal location remains,
nevertheless, exceptional and requires a particular management especially in
case of nerve compression. Material and Methods: We present the
case of a 40-year-old patient with a 20-year history of hepatitis C on
interferon and chronic renal failure at the hemodialysis stage for 10 years,
with renal osteodystrophy. She has been on calcium and vitamin D
supplementation for 2 years. For the past 6 weeks, this patient has had a
progressive intermittent medullary claudication without sphincter disorders.
A few months earlier, she complained of back pain resistant to
anti-inflammatory drugs. Spinal radiography had shown indirect signs of
renal osteodystrophy. Examination on admission found spastic paraparesis,
posterior cord syndrome and a T10 sensory level. Spinal CT and spinal MRI
showed a lytic expansive lesion of the posterior arch of T11 compressing the
spinal cord posteriorly. We performed a laminectomy of T10 and T11 with
total resection of the lesion. The tumor was red-gray, friable and mildly
hemorrhagic. The postoperative follow-up showed a progressive regression of
the motor deficit and total disappearance of his back pain. Histological
examination showed a bone tumor with two cellular contingents:
multi-nucleated giant cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and
mononuclear spindle cells, associated with a brown deposit of hemosiderin.
This appearance is strongly consistent with a brown bone tumor.
Results: Although brown tumors are benign in nature, they
are a reflection of failed treatment of renal osteodystrophy in chronic
renal failure patients on hemodialysis. Bone remodeling in these patients is
related to a disorder in the regulation of phosphocalcium metabolism. This
results in a state of permanent hypocalcemia responsible for a so-called
secondary hyperparathyroidism. These brown tumors are uncommon, observed in
1.5 to 13% of chronic renal failure patients.The spinal location is
exceptional. Brown tumors of the spine are usually asymptomatic but may
present with a picture of slow or sometimes acute spinal cord compression
secondary to a pathologic vertebral fracture. It is a pathologic
proliferation of osteoclasts into multinucleated giant cells with brown
hemosiderin deposition in the stroma. Rigorous reinforcement of calcium and
vitamin supplementation treatment can break the vicious circle of bone
hyper-remodeling. Surgery is usually not indicated except in the case of
spinal localization where urgent spinal decompression is required in case of
functional threat. Para thyroidectomy is only indicated in secondary
hyperparathyroidism when the pararthormone level cannot be controlled.
Conclusion: Spinal localization of brown tumors is rare but
it is a diagnosis that should be considered in the presence of suggestive
radiographic findings in patients with chronic renal failure. Treatment is
based on calcium supplementation and surgery is usually performed in case of
neurological emergency.

## P665: Giant aneurysmal bone cyst of the spine: an illustrative case of

course, our patient presented a severe exacerbation of her clinical
symptoms. Surgical approach was then validated. It consisted in tumor
debulking paravertebral soft tissue dissection, posterior decompression and
D11 D12 L4 L5 pedicle screw fixation. Clinical amelioration was rapidly
gained. The patient gained good neurological recovery without any adverse
effect in the final follow-up. Pathology exam confirmed the diagnosis. She
is programmed for a lateral approaches along with urology surgeons to
complete the retroperitoneal extension. Conclusion: ABC of the
spine is a benign tumor that can present with a wide variety of non-specific
symptoms. Local extension to the epidural space can jeopardize the
neurological outcome. For some aggressive types in the lumbar spine,
anterior extension to the retroperitoneal space (urinary tract) can have
malignant consequences. Pain management, careful preparing for surgery,
prompt resection of the lesion as well as spinal stability reconstruction
can promote good recovery and minimal adverse effect.

Neurosurgery, Fattouma Bourguiba Hospital, Sfax, Tunisia

Introduction: Malignant lymphoma can involve the central nervous
system either primarily or by secondary spread, which tends to occur late in
the disease as part of widespread dissemination. Lymphoma presenting as
primary tumors of the spinal cord are extremely uncommon. Materials
and Methods: We report tow cases of primary malignant lymphoma in
a spinal cord. Results: The first case was about a

function, if the patient had a neurologic deficit. The combined modality
treatment after surgical decompression resulted in improvement of the
neurologic symptoms and remission of the lymphoma.

Introduction: Terminal filum ependymoma is a rare tumor of the
cauda equina that accounts for 30-40% of all spinal ependymomas. It affects
adults between 30 and 40 years old. In this work we report the clinical,
radiological and therapeutic characteristics and the postoperative evolution
of these tumors. Material and Methods: We report the case of
two patients who was treated for an ependymomas of the terminal filum in the

microsurgical excision is the best way to limit recurrence and to have a

## P672: Paraganglioma of the cauda equina

Ghorbel Mohamed

Neurosurgery, Habib Bourguiba Hospital, Sfax, Tunisia

Introduction: Paragangliomas of the cauda equina are rare
tumors. The revealing symptomatology is usually radiculalgia with low back
pain, which may be associated with sphincter disorders. The reference
treatment is surgical resection. Material and Methods: We
report the case of a patient operated for a paraganglioma of the cauda
equina in our department of neurosurgery in the Habib Bourguiba university
hospital, in Sfax, Tunisia. Results: This is a 64-year-old
patient with no particular pathological history who consulted for bilateral

found a predominantly right paraplegia with abolition of the patellar and

complete surgical removal of the tumor. The histological examination
concluded to a paraganglioma. Conclusions: Paragangliomas of
the cauda equina are rare tumors whose histological appearance is close to
neurinomas. The treatment of these tumors remains complete surgical
excision, most often requiring the sacrifice of the supporting nerve root.
The absence of tumor residue after excision makes recurrence exceptional. No
additional treatment is recommended.

## P673: Survival and surgical outcomes of breast cancer spinal metastases
in a National Tertiary Centre

Sandra O'Malley

1

, Jake McDonnell

1

, Gráinne Cunniffe

1

, and Seamus Morris

1

1

Trauma and Orthopaedics, Mater Misericordiae University Hospital,
Dublin, Ireland

Introduction: Breast cancer is one of the most common cancer
types in women and due to advances in various therapies the frequency of
long-term sequelae has increased; 10 to 30% of patients with primary
malignancies are expected to develop spinal epidural metastases, and since
Patchell’s landmark study in 2005 there is increased demand for aggressive
therapies including surgery to optimize patient outcomes. However, there is
limited evidence for managing individual histopathological types of cancers.
This study was restricted to patients with spinal metastases from breast
cancer to limit differences as a result of various different tumour types.
Material and Methods: A retrospective review was carried
out on all patients that underwent spinal surgery for breast cancer spinal
metastases causing instability, cord compression or irretractable pain from
2005 to 2020. Patients were followed up for 2 years after surgery. Hospital
records were assessed for demographic, clinical, operative and radiological
parameters. Univariate and multivariate analyses were used to assess the
data. Results: 90 patients underwent surgery over a 15-year
period in a National Tertiary referral centre for spinal injuries. Median
patient age at time of breast cancer diagnosis was 53.3 years (range 32-78
years), median patient age at time of spinal surgery for metastases was 57.8
years (range 35-82 years). 44 deaths occurred during the follow-up period,
median age at death was 60.4 years (range 35-82). There were 20 deaths in
the first 6 months post-surgery and an additional 24 deaths within the first
2 years post-surgery. Conclusion: The volume of surgery
increased throughout the study period, suggesting an increase in
presentation of spinal metastases as predicted from long-term sequelae or a
combination of treatment shift to more aggressive decompressive surgery. The
most important predictor of survival was no neurological deficit
pre-operatively, followed by time from diagnosis of breast cancer to surgery
for spinal metastases.

## P674: Cryptogenic spinal epidural hemangioma: case report

Andrea Veroni

1,2

, Roberto Spnelli

1,2

, Mattia Seida

1,2

, Simone Zironi

1,2

, Giulia Ghisellini

1,2

, Villiam Dallolio

1,2

, Vitaliano Nizzoli

1,2

, and Marco Ruini

1,2

1

Neurosurgery, Ospedale di Suzzara, Suzzara, Italy

2

Neurosurgery, GVM Care & Research - Salus Hospital, Reggio
Emilia, Italy

Introduction: Epidural hemangioma is extremely rare, accounting
for only 4% of all extradural spinal tumors, and only 171 epidural
hemangiomas are reported since 1929. The most common symptoms include
myelopathy or radicular pain with or without deficit. Our case report is
about a patient treated for a herniated disc by microsurgical technique,
which reveals an epidural spinal hemangioma during surgery, without any
suspicion at preoperative radiological exams. Materials and
Methods: Introduction to the case report. We describe a case
report who find no equals in literature. The patient went our observation
for a typical radicular pain with L5/S1 herniated disc. The patient
underwent all common conservative treatments without any benefit. We
therefore proceeded performing herniectomy with microsurgical technique.
Results: The surgical operation. The patient underwent a
standard approach for herniectomy. During the normal manipulation of the
nerve root, the L5 root appeared to progressively swollen itself. The roots
was both L5 and also S1 free, and the swollen of the L5 root was not clear
if it was due to vascular, neoplastic or everything else. In addition, we
have informed the patient about the herniectomy and its specific risks and
benefits, and so we weren’t having a patient’s valid consensus to facing the
unknown lesion. Consequently, we decided to conclude the surgical operation,
referring any attempt to biopsy or remove the lesion after adequate
radiological study and a share planning. Then we informed the patient and
followed up him, who presented a good recovery, with complete resolution of
neurological deficits and pain. However, the MRI revealed a minimal trend in
enlargement of the lesion. We explain the risk and benefits and the patient
decided to approve the surgical removal of the lesion. So, we performed an
emi-laminecthomy. We identified the lesion and we noted that the L5 root was
upper and well separately from the lesion. We isolated the lesion and
removed it, and the histhopathological examination revealed an epidural
hemangioma, not visible in the preoperative MRI. The patient returned early
to his normal life, without deficits or pain. Discussion: Our
interpretation of this case report is that originally there was a vascular
nidus compressed by the herniated disc. The high pressure of the herniated
disc reduced the caliber of the vessel nidus of the hemangioma to a virtual
size. Consequently to the removal of the herniated fragment, the reduction
of the pressure on the vessels nidus enabled instantly the hemangioma to
swollen the caliber of its anomalous vessels growing its global volume.
Conclusions: Our case is characterized by a clinical
presentation like no other in the literature reports, because the patient
haven't specific symptoms due to the hemangioma, before the diagnosis. Also
if the spinal hemangioma is a very rare pathology, we experienced that it
can happened and exceptionally it can develop during surgery. So it is huge
important to know this eventuality, in order to manage it with properly
timing and surgical planning.

## P675: The inflammatory pseudotumor, the great imitator in an unusual
location

Sliti Firas

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Sinda Laafif

1

, Khalil Ghedira

1

, Imed Ben Said

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Inflammatory pseudotumor is an uncommon tumor,
initially described in the lung. It can affect different organs. It is a
controversial entity. In the nervous system, this pathology is difficult to
diagnose because its clinical and radiological presentation is not specific.
Material and Methods: We present the case of a 40-year-old
patient with no previous pathological history who was admitted to the
hospital with left S1 low back pain of progressive onset for two months. The
neurological examination did not reveal any deficit or Irritative phenomena.
MRI showed an infiltrative epiduritis extending from T10 to L2 without
obvious disc and vertebral body involvement. This epidural lesion totally
engages the spinal cord, which is narrowed and compressed anteriorly, and is
attached to the posterior ligament. It also causes bilateral foraminal
entrapment with bilateral medial L5-S1 disc herniation with intramedullary
right L5 and S1 radicular impingement. A laminectomy from T10 to L2 was
performed, uncovering a localized fibrous, whitish, non-hemorrhagic dural
thickening organized in an onion bulb. A macroscopically total resection was
performed. Histological examination of the resection specimens showed the
existence of a characterized inflammatory process compatible with the
diagnosis of an inflammatory pseudotumor. Results: The
inflammatory pseudotumor corresponds to an aspect of inflammatory mass whose
symptomatology depends on its location. Relatively ubiquitous, it is rarely
described in the central nervous system. This unusual lesion represents a
wide spectrum of clinical presentation posing diagnostic problems for both
pathologists and clinicians. The main differential diagnosis of extradural
inflammatory pseudotumors is lymphoma and also metastases, myeloma and
meningioma. Without biopsy, the differential diagnosis is difficult.
Conclusion: Inflammatory pseudotumors (IPT) are benign
lesions of unknown etiology, probably an immunological response to traumatic
or infectious aggression. Sometimes considered an IgG4-related autoimmune
disorder. They may present as an isolated or multicentric lesion. Central
nervous system involvement is rare. Only nine cases of epidural IPT have
been reported to date. It is clinically and radiologically a diagnosis of
exclusion.

## P676: Spinal schwannomas: a review and institutional experience

Sliti Firas

1

, Skander Guediche

1

, Abdelhafidh Slimane

1

, Nadhir Karmani

1

, and Jalel Kallel

1

1

Neurosurgery, National Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Spinal schwannomas are benign tumors that develop
from Schwann cells of the spinal roots. They account for 35% of
extramedullary intradural tumors, 80% of them along the spinal cord and 20%
in the cauda equina. The carrier root is often a sensitive root, which
explains the frequency of the revealing radicular pain. Neuromas are most
often sporadic, but can be part of a neurofibromatosis type II.
Material and Methods: This is a retrospective study spread
over 8 years (2010-2017) concerning 36 cases of spinal schwannomas, treated
and followed up at the neurosurgery department of the National Institute of
Neurology, Tunisia. Results: The average age of our patients is
52 years (10-76 years). There was a male predominance of 61% with a sex
ratio of 1.5. The circumstances of discovery were dominated by radicular
syndrome in 62% of cases. 53% of the patients presented spinal pain. 73% of
the patients presented sensory disorders such as paresthesia. Sphincter
disorders were present in 22% of cases. The clinical picture is silent for a
long time, and the diagnostic delay is variable according to the location
and volume of the neuromas. They are responsible for a spinal cord
compression syndrome in 73% of cases, a spinal syndrome (45%) and a lesion
syndrome (56%). Magnetic resonance imaging was performed in all our
patients. The most frequent localization was cervical in 36% of cases,
dorsal in 30% and lumbar in 34% of cases. Multiple neuromas were found in
11% of cases. All patients underwent posterior surgery, allowing
macroscopically complete removal of the tumor in all cases. 60% of the
patients underwent postoperative MRI at a distance, confirming complete
removal of the tumor. The immediate postoperative course was simple in all
our patients. 7 patients (20%) presented a postoperative motor and sensory
deficit, 5 of whom recovered after rehabilitation. Conclusion:
This study also allowed us to study the evolution of patients treated for
spinal schwannoma. Their detection at an early stage of evolution, a
primordial parameter to improve the prognosis, has been greatly facilitated
by the development and better accessibility of neuro-diagnostic techniques.
The prognosis also depends on the quality of the resection, which can be
complete in some cases only at the expense of nerve sacrifice. This balance
is sometimes difficult to weigh, with on the one hand a non-negligible risk
of tumor recurrence, and on the other hand the fear of producing
neurological sequelae in patients who did not have them before surgery.

## P677: Management of metastatic epiduritis : a review of 50 cases

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Khalil Ghedira

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,

Introduction: The spine may be the site of metastasis in 40% of
patients with neoplastic pathology. The aim of our work is to describe the
epidemiological, clinical and paraclinical characteristics of metastatic
epiduritis, to review the therapeutic modalities and to evaluate the
clinical evolution of the patients. Materials and Methods: This
is a retrospective study of 50 patients admitted for metastatic epiduritis
to the neurosurgery department at the Mongi Ben Hamida National Institute of
Neurology in Tunisia between 2011 and 2018. Results: The mean
age was 54.11 years. Motor deficit was the most frequent reason for

neurosurgical emergency. Their diagnosis must not be delayed and this as
soon as the first symptoms appear. MRI is the best examination to confirm
the diagnosis. Urgent surgical management allows for a chance of recovery.
Radiotherapy and physical rehabilitation are necessary in the subsequent
management.

## P678: The importance of inpatient and outpatient palliative care
utilization at the end of life for patients with spine metastases

Edwin Owolo

1

, Dana Rowe

1

, Meghan Price

1

, Jacob Sperber

1

, Tara Dalton

1

, Harrison Hockenberry

1

, Isabel Prado

1

, Arif Kamal

1

, Margaret Johnson

1

, Brandon Bishop

1

, Antoinette Charles

1

, and C. Rory Goodwin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Duke University School of Medicine,
Durham, United States

Introduction: Given the significant symptom burden associated
with spine metastases (SM), specialty Palliative Care(PC) can be
instrumental in improving patient quality of life(QoL). Therefore, it is
important to identify/address disparities in access to this intervention to
ensure comprehensive and equitable care. Objective: The purpose
of this study is to assess the impact of sociodemographic and treatment
factors on inpatient PC (IPPC) and outpatient PC (OPPC) utilization in
patients with SM. Methods: We evaluated IPPC and OPPC
utilization in a cohort of 270 patients seen by our institution’s Brain and
Spine Metastases Tumor Board from February 2018- February 2020. Patient
demographics, oncologic history, interventions received, OPPC and IPPC
consultations/encounters, and clinical outcomes were collected via
retrospective chart review. Statistical analyses compared characteristics
and outcomes between patients who did or did not utilize IPPC and/or OPPC.
Results: 47 (17.4%) and 73 (27.0%) patients received at
least one IPPC consult or OPPC visit, respectively. We observed that Black
patients received IPPC consults at a higher rate than non-Black patients
(25.9% vs 15.1%, p = 0.077), while White patients received OPPC consults at
higher rates than non-White patients (27.7% vs 20.0%, p = 0.13). Patients
who received surgical intervention or radiation therapy had higher rates of
OPPC utilization than those who did not (36.9% vs 21.7%,p = 0.011; 31.6% vs
19.2%,p = 0.033, respectively). Patients who received an IPPC consult had
worse median overall survival (OS) than patients who did not (6.5 months vs.
24.2 months) while OPPC consultation was associated with a survival
advantage (11.2 months vs 19.2 months for those seen by OPPC and not).
Conclusion: We present several race and intervention-based
differences in OPPC and IPPC utilization for patients with SM. Further work
is needed to better appreciate PC utilization trends and identify
interventions that may improve the equity and accessibility of PC for this
patient population.

## P679: Lumbar spine osteosarcoma with large retroperitoneal extension and
vascular attachment: a case report and literature review

Pablo Sanchez Quinones

1,2,3

, Andres Felipe Pineda-Martínez

1,2

, Juan Felipe Abaunza-Camacho

1,2,3

, Javier M Saavedra

1,2,3

, William M Riveros

1,2,3

, Jorge Torres-Mancera

1,2,3

, and Camilo Benavides-Burbano

1,2,3

1

Neurosurgery Department, Center for Research and Training in
Neurosurgery CIEN, Bogotá, Colombia

2

Neurosurgery Department, Hospital Universitario de La Samaritana,
Bogotá, Colombia

3

Neurosurgery Department, Hospital Universitario Mayor Méderi,
Bogotá, Colombia

Introduction: Osteosarcoma of the spine (OS) is a rare, highly
malignant tumor representing 3-5% of all osteosarcomas. It is a tumor with
potential local invasive destruction and metastatic spread. OS has the worst
5‐year survival of all spinal sarcomas (39%). Its independent prognosis
factors include age (> 60 years old) and advanced stage that produces
poor outcomes. Surgical management in OS positively affects prognosis and
produces favorable survival. Its goal is curative resection with negative
margins. However, it depends on location, adjacent structures,
aggressiveness, and size. Surgical technique is controversial over the
superiority of intralesional versus en-bloc resection. Larger size and
adjacent neurovascular structures imply challenging surgical management.
Material and Methods: We report a case of a 41-year-old
female with L4 spinal osteosarcoma with large retroperitoneal extension
treated with a first posterior elements en-bloc resection with lumbar
arthrodesis and second stage anterior en-bloc resection with L4
vertebrectomy. Results: A 41-year-old female complained of
chronic lumbar pain exacerbated one month prior to admission. She had a
history of pathologic L4 fracture three years previously, with reported
osteoblastic osteosarcoma Ki67 10% in a percutaneous biopsy without
complementary management. Physical examination showed vertebral pain in the
lumbar spine. The neurological exam was intact. Lumbar MRI and abdominal
angio-CT showed a 120 x 87 x 97 mm calcified lesion of the L4 vertebral body
with facet, epidural and abdominal extension without central canal
compromise. Additionally, right displacement of aortic bifurcation and both
common iliac arteries without occlusion was identified. Bone scintigraphy
discarded other lesions, and lower-limbs electromyography was normal.
Surgical management was indicated with a first stage posterior and second
stage anterior en-bloc tumoral resection. At first, a posterior approach was
completed with L4 partial vertebrectomy and L3-L4 and L4-L5 discectomy. A
viaflex bag was positioned anterior to the thecal sac to protect neuronal
structures during second stage approach. Finally, L2-L3 and L5-S1 polyaxial
screws were placed and fixated, achieving lumbar arthrodesis. One week
later, an anterior approach was made. A retroperitoneal approach, lymph node
drainage, and vascular release from feeding vessels of the aorta and the
posterior wall of the vena cava was performed with an oncologic surgeon.
En-bloc mass resection was performed, and anterior L3-L4 and L4-L5
discectomy with L4 total vertebrectomy was completed. Epidural Viaflex bag
was identified and removed. Then, vertebral body reconstruction using an
expandable cage was completed. Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring
remained normal during both approaches. Postoperative bleeding was present,
with a requirement of 10 units of red-blood-cell transfusion. Secondary
mesenteric ischemia was encountered, and the patient required colostomy plus
antibiotic management for peritonitis. Finally, the patient responded well
and was discharged without neurological deficit. Conclusion:
Osteosarcoma of the lumbar spine is an uncommon and challenging disease. The
surgical approach depends on tumoral size, localization, and involvement of
adjacent vascular structures. When an abdominal extension is present, a
multidisciplinary surgical treatment with aggressive posterior and anterior
approaches could be an excellent option since it provides an impact on
survival and reduces postoperative complications.

## P680: Atlantoaxial Langerhans cell histiocytosis manifesting as painful
torticolis

Nessrine Nessib

1

, Mohamed Zairi

2

, Kais Bouzouita

1

, Sofiene Bouali

1

, Mohsni Ahmed Amine

2

, Ahmed Msakni

2

, Rim Boussetta

2

, and Nessib Mohamed Nabil

2

1

Neurosurgery, Mongi ben Hamida Institute of Neurology, Tunis,
Tunisia

2

Orthopedics, Bechir Hamza Children's Hospital, Tunis,
Tunisia

Introduction: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare
disorder of clonal proliferation of dendritic cell mostly seen in children.
It consists in various clinical manifestations from a single lytic bone
lesion to multisystemic lesions with organ dysfunction. Atlantoaxial
involvement by LCH is very rare, especially in a young child. The aim of
this work was to describe the management challenges of treatment of a rare
localization of Langerhans cell histiocytosis in the craniocervical junction
complicated by spinal instability and deformity. Materials and
Methods:A 6-year-old child consulted for painful torticollis
evolving for two weeks without fever. Patient has no medical and surgical
history or cervical spine trauma. The clinical examination objectified a
torticollis without neurosensory deficit. Cervical spine x-ray showed spinal
deviation without bone lesions. Specialized examinations have been
requested. Results: Cervical spine CT scan concluded in an
atlantoaxial rotational dislocation with bone involvement of C1 and C2. The
MRI objectified the presence of spinal cord compression at the CCJ and a
soft-tissue mass between C1-C2. Bone scintigraphy showed two fixation
locations. One at the cranio-cervical junction, the other at the level of
the left iliac crest. Bone biopsy at the lesion of the iliac crest concluded
in Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The biological explorations objectified a
pancytopenia. The child had medical treatment such as corticosteroids and
vinblastine. For bone lesions and instability of the cranio-cervical
junction, two-stage surgery was performed. Stabilization of the skull by
halo-vest. Then enlargement of foramen magnum, C1 laminectomy and
non-instrumented occipito-C2 arthrodesis. At 3-years of follow-up, the
cervical spine was stable without torticollis and the child has
healed. Conclusion: Damage to the craniocervical junction
during Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a source of spinal instability and
deformity. Surgical stabilization must be urgent before the appearance of a
sensory-motor deficit. The two-stage approach non-instrumented vertebral
arthrodesis was desirable in growing children.

## 1885

## P681: Primary bone tumors of the spine: assessment of 20 years single
center experience

Zohra Souei

1

, Mohamed Boukhit

1

, Nessrine Nessib

1

, Souhaiel Khalfaoui

1

, Maher Hadhri

1

, and Mehdi Darmoul

1

1

Neurosurgery, Fattouma Bourguiba University Hospital, Monastir,
Tunisia

Introduction: Primary bone tumors of the spine are relatively
rare, and make up a heterogeneous group of neoplasms that can pose
diagnostic and treatment challenges. Material and Methods: We
retrospectively studied 19 cases of primary bone tumors of the spine that
were diagnosed and managed at the Neurosurgery department of Monastir
University Hospital in Tunisia. We aim to review through this study,
epidemiologic, clinical, imaging and management features in these tumors in
order to provide an appropriate treatment strategy. Results:
Sixteen males and four women aged between 5 and 78 years were included in
the study. The mean age of our population was 46.8 years with a male
predominance. The mean diagnostic delay was up to 18 months. Back pain and
progressive limbs weakness were. The lesions were located in the cervical
spine in 3 patients, thoracic spine in 4 patients, and lumbar spine in 4,
and sacral region in 7 patients. Total spondylectomy was realized in six
patients. Histological types included osteoid osteoma (2), Brown tumor (2),
osteoblastoma (4), chordoma (4), lymphoma (2), Ewing sarcoma (2) and primary
plasmocytoma (4). Adjuvant treatment with radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy
was performed in 13 cases. Three cases of chordoma recurred within 11 months
and tumor control was obtained in 15 cases after a median follow up period
of 2.5 years (range 1-11 years). Conclusion: Primary malignant
tumors are markedly more frequent than benign tumors of the spine. Early
intervention is necessary to restore the spinal stability, decompress the
spinal cord and realize the maximum tumor resection allowing a better tumor
control.

## 1886

## P682: Spinal cord compression secondary to voluminous thoracic primary
extraosseous Ewing's sarcoma: presentation of an anecdotic and catastrophic
disease

Andres Vargas

1

, Borja Ferrandez Pujante

1

, and Marc Valera Mele

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Hospital Clinico San Carlos, Madrid,
Spain

Introduction: Ewing’s Sarcoma (ES) is a rare osseous tumor, with
an annual incidence of 3 cases per 1.000.000 people, mainly affecting large
bones. Spinal Affection (SA) is anecdotic (less than 5% of all ES cases),
including primary extra-osseous tumors with SA being no more than 13 cases
reported in literature between 1969 and 2015. Tipically, SA tumors present a
highly aggressive histology compatible with Primitive Neuroectodermic Tumor
(PNET). Spinal Surgery role in the disease is fundamental due to its
multiple benefits derived from decompression of neural structures,
restoration of spinal stability and from the reduction of tumor volume,
this, also contributing to improve the response to adjuvant therapy. We
present the case of a young patient presenting with a severe Spinal Cord
Compression (SCC) syndrome secondary to a voluminous cervical primary
extra-osseous tumor with histologic diagnosis of ES. Material and
Methods: A previously healthy 32-year-old male patient presented
to the Emergency Room (ER) with 48 hours progressive paraparesis associating
bladder dysfunction. During his ER admittance muscle power of 2/5 according
to mMRC and C7-T1 sensitive level was evidenced. Urgent magnetic resonance
imaging revealed a thoracic-soft-tissue mass with C6-C7-T1-T2 spinal canal
invasion and severe SCC and displacement. The patient underwent C7-T1
laminectomy, tumor debulking and resection for decompression and C6
bilateral lateral-mass arthrodesis, C7 left unilateral pedicular screw due
to right pedicular tumoral involvement and T1-T2 bilateral pedicular screw
under fluoroscopic control. No complications related with arthrodesis or
wound healing were present. Pathology analysis revealed a highly cellular
tumor compatible with ES. During his admittance the patient had a stable
evolution, with partial motor recovery (distal predominance), requiring
in-patient rehabilitation program. Results: The patient was
discharged to a National highly specialized rehabilitation center for
treatment of spinal cord injury and is receiving high-dose chemotherapy
including Vincristine, Etoposide, Ifosfamide and Actinomicin-D, with a
complete tumoral response according to the last PET-Scan. Anterior approach
by a cervico-sternotomy and C7-T1 corpectomy to complement posterior
arthrodesis is pending due to recent chemotherapy and request of a fourth
chemotherapy cycle. Conclusion: SA of ES is a poor prognostic
tumor due to its highly aggressive histology and the possibility of debuting
with a severe neurological deficit. Surgery for decompression and spinal
stabilization represents an important tool when addressing urgent treatment
of this disease, in addition with aggressive adjuvant therapy. Close
follow-up is recommended in order to evaluate tumor response to adjuvant
therapy, residual tumor behavior and spinal stability.

## 1899

## P683: Rare case of epidural metastasis of thymoma

Joao Oliveira

1

, Mário Vale Campos

1

, and Pedro Ribeiro da Cunha

1

1

Neurocirurgia, Centro Hospitalar Lisboa Ocidental, Lisboa,
Portugal

Introduction: Malignant thymoma is a rare, slow growing,
anterior mediastinal tumor, that is often associated with extrathoracic
metastasis (up to 15%, mostly liver, kidney and bone). Local invasion and
intrathoracic spread are relatively common. Despite the highly aggressive
behaviour of malignant thymoma, spinal metastasis is exceptionally rare,
with less than 50 cases reported in the literature. Material and
Methods: A 48 year old-man, with medical background of an
operated thymoma in 2013, initially presented with discrete hemiparesis in
2017, then on May 2018 presented with intense axial pain in the
cervico-dorsal transition that irradiates to the right superior limb.
Physical examination revealed intense cervico-dorsal pain in axial
transition with irradiation to the right superior limb. Neurological
examination revealed paresis of both distal superior limbs (hands), worst on
the right. Right hypoesthesia on C6-C8. Without evident deficit on inferior
limbs. TC guided biopsy confirmed metastasis in D1 of thymoma. Cervical MRI
revealed infiltration of all vertebral body of D1, predominantly lytic
areas, with anterior and posterior epidural component towards C7-D2 with
dural contact, without deformity and no medular hypersignal. PET revealed
captation only in D1 level. The patient was submitted to 5 radiotherapy
sessions, with pain relieve but unfortunately without neurological
remission. Due to weak response to radiotherapy and lack response to
chemotherapy, the patient was submitted to surgery, with circumferential
decompression of C7-D2 through a posterior approach, with cervico-dorsal
fixation and vertebroplasty. Results: Pathology confirmed an
epidural infiltration of neoplasia with thymic differentiation, compatible
with epidural metastasis of Thymoma. Postoperative course was uneventfully,
with progressive neurological improvement. Conclusion: Spinal
epidural metastasis should be suspected in all cancer patients with back
pain. Because metastasis to the spine from thymoma are very rare, there are
no treatment guidelines. Nevertheless, surgical management of the metastatic
lesion is the most appropriate, for the preservation of the patient quality
of life.

## 1960

## P684: Association between urbanicity and outcomes among patients with
spinal cord ependymomas in the United States

Jacob Sperber

1

, Edwin Owolo

1

, Nancy Abu-Bonsrah

1

, Corey Neff

1

, Cesar Baeta

2

, Chuxuan Sun

1

, Tara Dalton

1

, David Sykes

1

, Harrison Hockenberry

1

, Brandon Bishop

1

, Antoinette Charles

1

, Jill Barnholtz-Sloan

3

, Carol Kruchko

3

, Kyle Walsh

1

, Sheng-fu L. Lo

4

, Daniel Sciubba

1,4

, Quinn Ostrom

1

 and C. Rory Goodwin

1

1

Department of Neurosurgery, Duke University School of Medicine,
Durham, United States

2

Center for Population Health Sciences, Stanford University, Durham,
United States

3

Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States

4

Long Island Jewish Medical Center and North Shore University
Hospital, Northwell Health, United States

Purpose: Spinal Cord Ependymomas (SCE) represent the most common
intramedullary spinal cord tumors among adults. Access to neurosurgical care
can be greatly influenced by patient location. This study investigates the
association between the outcomes of SCE patients in metropolitan and
non-metropolitan areas. Methods: Patients with diagnosis of SCE
between 2004 and 2019 were identified within the Central Brain Tumor
Registry of the United States. Multivariable logistic regression models were
constructed to evaluate the association between urbanicity and SCE
treatment. Cox proportional hazard models were used to understand the effect
of surgical treatment, county urbanicity, age at diagnosis and the
interaction effect between age at diagnosis and surgery, on the survival
time of patients. Results: 7,577 patients were identified, with
6,454 (85%) residing in metropolitan and 1223 (15%) in non-metropolitan
counties. Demographics were not associated with differences in the type of
surgery received when stratified by urbanicity. Regardless of metropolitan
status, American Indian/Alaska Native and Hispanic ethnicities were
associated with reduced odds of receiving surgery alone. Black Non-Hispanic
and Hispanic ethnicities were associated with increased odds of receiving
comprehensive treatment (radiation and surgery). Diagnosis of SCE at later
ages was linked with elevated mortality (HR = 4.83, p < 0.001). Gross
total resection was associated with reduced risk of death (HR = 0.47, p =
0.018). However, among older patients, gross total resection resulted in
increased risk of death (HR = 1.02, p < 0.008). Conclusion:
The relationship between patient residential location and access to
neurosurgical care is critical to ensuring equitable distribution of care.
This study represents an important step in delineating areas of existing
disparities.
